(Surat al-An'am)

Meccan, except for verses 20, 23, 91, 93, 114, 141, 151, 152 and 153, which are Medinan. It has 165 verses. It was revealed after Surat al-Hijr.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It is Meccan, and it was revealed all at once. The valley was filled with it, and seventy thousand angels accompanied it. The angels descended and filled the space between the two mountains. The Messenger (ﷺ) summoned the scribes, and they wrote it down that same night, except for six verses, which are Medinan: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [al-An'am: 151] to the end of the three verses, His saying ﴿They have not measured Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and His saying ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 21].

It is also reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No surah of the Qur'an was revealed to me all at once except Surat al-An'am. The devils never gathered for any surah of the Qur'an as they gathered against it. It was sent to me with Jibril, accompanied by fifty angels (or: fifty thousand angels), who escorted it and surrounded it until they settled it in my breast as water settles in a basin. Allah has honored me and you through it with an honor that will never humble us after it. In it is the refutation of the arguments of the polytheists, and it contains a promise from Allah that He will not break."

It is also reported from Ibn al-Munkadir: "When Surat al-An'am was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) glorified Allah and said: 'The angels who escorted this surah filled the horizon.'"

The scholars of the foundations (al-Usuliyyun) said: This surah is distinguished by two kinds of excellence. The first is that it was revealed in one single descent. The second is that seventy thousand angels escorted it. The reason for this is that it contains proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), justice, prophethood, the return (to God), and the refutation of the doctrines of the false and the atheists. This shows that the science of the foundations ('ilm al-usul, the science of the fundamental principles of belief) is of the utmost grandeur and eminence. Furthermore, the revelation of what pertains to the legal rulings is subject to what is beneficial, so Allah sends it down according to their need and in accordance with events and occurrences. As for what pertains to the science of the foundations, Allah sent it down all at once. This shows that learning the science of the foundations is obligatory immediately (ʿala al-fawr), not deferred (ʿala al-tarakhi).

﴿Praise belongs to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darkness and the light. Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾.

Know that the thorough discussion of His saying ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾ has already appeared in the commentary on Surat al-Fatihah, and there is no harm in repeating some of those benefits. Here there are issues (masa'il, i.e., points of discussion):

The first issue: on the difference between madh (praise), hamd (commendation) and shukr (gratitude).

Know that madh is more general than hamd, and hamd is more general than shukr.

As for the proof that madh is more general than hamd: madh is due to the rational being and to the non-rational. Do you not see that just as it is fitting to praise a rational man for the various kinds of his virtues, so too a pearl may be praised for its beautiful shape and the delicacy of its form, and a ruby may be praised for the utmost clarity and polish of its surface, so one says: "How beautiful it is! How pure it is!" As for hamd, it is due only to the chooser who acts, for the bounty and kindness that proceed from him. Thus it is established that madh is more general than hamd.

As for the proof that hamd is more general than shukr: hamd is an expression of glorifying the agent because of the bounty that proceeds from him, whether that bounty reaches you or reaches someone else. Shukr, however, is an expression of glorifying him because of a bounty that has reached you and come into your possession. Thus, from what we have mentioned, it is established that madh is more general than hamd, and hamd is more general than shukr.

Having understood this, we say: The reason He did not say "Madh (praise) belongs to Allah" is that we have shown that madh may be due to the chooser who acts, and it may also be due to others. As for hamd, it is due only to the chooser who acts. So His saying ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾ is an explicit statement that the originator of the existence of this world is a chooser who acted by His power and will. He created it by power and volition, and He is not a cause that necessitates its effect in the way a cause necessitates its effect. There is no doubt that this point is very great in religion. As for why He did not say "Shukr (gratitude) belongs to Allah": we have shown that shukr is an expression of glorifying Him because of a bounty that proceeded from Him and reached you. This suggests that if the servant mentions His glorification because of a blessing that has reached him, then the primary goal for him is the arrival of the blessing to him, and this is a lowly level. But when he says "Praise belongs to Allah," this shows that the servant praises Him because He deserves praise, not merely because He delivered the blessing to him. Thus sincerity is more perfect, the heart's absorption in witnessing the light of the Truth is more complete, and its severance from everything other than the Truth is stronger and more firm.

The second issue: hamd is a singular noun prefixed with the definite article (al-), so it signifies the essence of the reality (asl al-mahiyyah).

[Page 119]

Having established this, we say: His saying ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾ indicates that this reality belongs to Allah. This prevents the attribution of hamd to anyone other than Allah. This therefore requires that all forms of hamd, praise and glorification belong only to Allah, glorified is He.

If it is objected: Gratitude to a benefactor is obligatory, like the gratitude of a student to his teacher, the gratitude of subjects to a just ruler, and the gratitude of a person to one who has done him good, as he (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah."

We reply: The one who is truly praised and thanked is none other than Allah. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: the proceeding of a good deed from a servant depends on the arising of the motive for doing good in the servant's heart. The arising of that motive in the heart is not from the servant himself; otherwise he would need another motive to bring it about, and this would lead to an infinite regress. Rather, its arising is from none other than Allah, glorified is He. So when that motive arises, the act becomes obligatory, and when it departs, the act becomes impossible. Thus the true doer of good is none other than Allah. Therefore, the one truly deserving every praise is Allah, exalted is He.

The second: every created being who does good to another does so either to bring about a benefit or to avert a harm. As for bringing about a benefit, he hopes through that good deed for something that becomes a cause of joy in his heart, or for some recompense, whether small or great, in this world, or for finding reward in the Hereafter. As for averting harm, when a person sees an animal in distress or affliction, his heart softens toward it, and that softness is a particular pain that arises in the heart at the sight of that animal falling into that harm. When he tries to rescue that animal from that harm, the softness leaves his heart, and he becomes free of heart and at ease. So that good deed is as if it were a means that freed the heart from the pain of sensory tenderness. Thus it is established that everyone other than the Truth benefits from doing good either by bringing about a benefit or by averting a harm. As for the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, He does good and gains from it neither the bringing about of a benefit nor the averting of a harm. Therefore the true doer of good is none other than Allah, exalted is He. For this reason, the one deserving all forms of hamd is Allah, and so He said: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾.

The third: every good deed that any creature undertakes is not fully beneficial except through the goodness of Allah. Do you not see that if Allah had not created the various kinds of bounty, a person would not be able to deliver that wheat and those fruits to others? Likewise, if He, glorified is He, had not given man the five senses by which he can benefit from those bounties, he would be incapable of benefiting from them. And if He, glorified is He, had not given him a sound temperament and a healthy constitution, he would not be able to benefit from them. Thus it is established that every good deed that proceeds from a benefactor other than Allah, exalted is He, is not fully beneficial except through the goodness of Allah, exalted is He. At this point it becomes clear that there is no true benefactor except Allah, and no one truly deserving of praise except Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾.

The fourth: the benefit from all bounties is not possible except after the existence of the one who benefits, after he has come to be living, capable and knowing. The bounty of existence, life, power and knowledge is none other than from Allah, glorified is He. The basic nurturing and the various provisions are obtained only from Allah, glorified is He, from the beginning of childhood until the end of life. Then, when a person reflects on the signs of the wisdom of the Most Merciful in the creation of man, and reaches what Allah, exalted is He, has deposited in his organs of various benefits and interests, he knows that these are an ocean without shore, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you were to count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. So even if we grant that a servant can bestow favor upon others, the favors of a servant are like a drop, while the favors of Allah have no end, first or last, outward or inward. For this reason, the one deserving absolute praise and absolute commendation is none other than Allah, glorified is He. Therefore He said: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾.

* * *

The third issue: He said ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾ and did not say "I praise Allah," for several reasons.

The first: hamd is an attribute of the heart.

[Page 120]

A person may sometimes need to utter this expression while his heart is heedless of the meaning of hamd and praise. If, at that moment, he said "I praise Allah," he would be lying and would deserve blame and punishment, since he would be reporting a claim about something that did not exist at that time. But when he says "Praise belongs to Allah," its meaning is that the reality and essence of hamd belongs to Allah, exalted is He. This statement is true and correct whether the meaning of praise and commendation is present in his heart or not. His speaking these words is a noble act of worship and an exalted obedience. Thus the difference between these two expressions becomes clear.

The second: It is reported that Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him), commanding him to give thanks. Dawud said: "O my Lord, how can I thank You, when my thanks cannot come about except that You enable me to thank You? And that enabling is an additional bounty, which itself requires thanks from me as well, and that leads to an endless chain. How can I have the capacity to perform what has no end?" Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Dawud: "Since you have recognized your inability to thank Me, you have indeed thanked Me."

Having understood this, we say: If the servant said "I praise Allah," it would be a claim that he has brought hamd and gratitude, and so that question would be directed at him. But if he says "Praise belongs to Allah," there is no claim in it that the servant has brought praise and commendation. Rather, it contains only that He, glorified is He, deserves praise and commendation, whether or not the servant is able to bring that praise. Thus the difference between these two expressions becomes apparent from this aspect.

The third: If he said "I praise Allah," this would indicate that he mentioned his own praise and did not mention the praise of others. But when he says "Praise belongs to Allah," it includes His praise and the praise of others, from the beginning of the creation of the world until the end, when those accountable settle in the degrees of Paradise and the depths of the Fire. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their call therein will be, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be, "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. So this statement is more excellent and more complete.

* * *

The fourth issue: Know that this expression is mentioned at the beginning of five surahs. The first of them is al-Fatihah, where He said: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2].

Second part of Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 1:

Secondly: at the beginning of this surah, He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The first [praise in al-Fatihah] is more general, because "the worlds" (al-'alam) is an expression for every existent other than Allah the Exalted. So His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ includes every existent other than Allah the Exalted. As for His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾, it includes only the creation of the heavens, the earth, the darknesses and the light, and does not include the rest of the beings and the originated things. Thus the praise mentioned at the beginning of this surah is, as it were, a part of the divisions that fall under the praise mentioned in the surah of al-Fatihah, and a detailing of that sentence.

Thirdly: Surah al-Kahf, where He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down upon His servant the Book﴾ [al-Kahf: 1]. This too is a praise specific to a particular kind of blessing, which is the blessing of knowledge, guidance and the Qur'an; and in summary, the blessings that come through the sending of the Messengers.

Fourthly: Surah Saba', which is His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Saba': 1]. This too is one of the divisions that fall under His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Fifthly: Surah Fatir, where He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1]. It is also evident that this is one of the divisions that fall under His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Thus it becomes clear that the complete universal statement is the praise mentioned at the beginning of al-Fatihah, namely His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. This is because every existent is either necessarily existent in itself (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi) or possibly existent in itself (mumkin al-wujud li-dhatihi). The necessarily existent in itself is one, namely Allah the Exalted, and whatever else is other than Him is possible, and every possible thing cannot enter existence except by the bringing-into-being and the bringing-about of Allah the Exalted. Existence is a blessing, so bringing into being is a bestowal and a nurturing. For this reason He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and that He the Exalted is the Nurturer of everything other than Him and the Benefactor to everything other than Him. Thus that statement is the comprehensive universal statement that fulfils the purpose.

Page 121

As for the praises mentioned at the openings of these surahs, each of them is as if it were a division of that praise and a kind of its types.

If it is said: What is the difference between the Creator (al-Khaliq), the Originator (al-Fatir) and the Lord (al-Rabb)? Also, why did He say here: ﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾ in the form of the past tense verb, while in the surah of Fatir He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ in the form of the active participle?

We answer the first question: creation (al-khalq) is an expression for determination (al-taqdir), and with regard to the Real, glory be to Him, it is an expression for His knowledge that penetrates all universals and particulars, reaching the essences of all beings and possibilities. As for His being Originator (fatir), it is an expression for bringing into being and innovation. So His being Creator is an indication of the attribute of knowledge, and His being Originator is an indication of the attribute of power, and His being Lord and Nurturer includes both matters, so that is more complete.

As for the answer to the second: creation is an expression for determination, and with regard to Allah the Exalted it is an expression for His knowledge of the known things. Knowledge of a thing may precede the existence of the known, for do you not see that we can know a thing before it enters existence? As for bringing a thing into being, it occurs only at the time the effect exists, according to our school's view that power affects the existence of the object of power only at the time the object exists. For this reason He said: ﴿created the heavens﴾, meaning that He was knowing of them before their existence; and He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], meaning that He is Originator of them and Brings them into being only when they exist.

Fifth issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: What is meant by it is "Praise Allah the Exalted", and it came in the form of a report for several benefits:

One: that His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ conveys the teaching of both the wording and the meaning; had He said "Praise", the combination of these two benefits would not have been achieved.

Second: that it indicates that He, the Exalted, deserves praise whether or not any praiser praises Him.

Third: that the purpose of it is to mention the proof, so mentioning it in the form of a report is more fitting.

The second opinion, which is the view of most exegetes, means: "Say: All praise is due to Allah." They said: The evidence that what is meant is teaching the servants is that He, the Exalted, said in the course of the surah: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4], and this statement is only fitting to be spoken by servants. The point is that when He, glory be to Him, commanded praise, and it has been established in minds that praise is only good for a blessing, this command then becomes a driving force for the responsible person to reflect on the kinds of Allah the Exalted's blessings upon him. Then those blessings are used as evidence for two noble aims:

The first: these blessings came into being after they were non-existent, so there must be a originator and a producer, and that is not the servant himself, because everyone wishes to obtain all kinds of blessings for himself. Had the obtaining of blessings for the servant been through the servant's own power and choice, then each one would have reached all kinds of blessings, since no one exists who does not want to obtain every blessing for himself. Since it is established that the coming into being of these blessings requires an originator, and it is established that this originator is not the servant, it is necessary to affirm an originator who is Irresistible and Powerful, namely Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

The second aim of this statement: hearts are naturally inclined to love one who does good to them and to hate one who does evil to them. When Allah the Exalted commands the servant to praise, and the command to praise is something that drives him to remember the various kinds of Allah's blessings, that obligation drives the servant to remember the various kinds of Allah's blessings upon him. Since those blessings are numerous, beyond limit and counting, remembering them becomes a cause for the firm establishment of love of Allah the Exalted in the servant's heart. Thus it is established that reminding of blessings yields

Page 122

these two noble benefits:

One: inferring from their coming into being the affirmation of the existence of Allah the Exalted.

Second: that the awareness that they are blessings causes the manifestation of love of Allah in the heart. The purpose of all acts of worship is only these two matters. For this reason this noble Book begins with this statement, when He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Know that this statement is a sea without shore, because "the world" ('alam) is the name for everything other than Allah the Exalted, and everything other than Allah is either a body, or inhering in a body, or neither a body nor inhering in one, which are the spirits. Then bodies are either celestial or elemental. As for the celestial ones, the first of them is the Glorious Throne, then the Lofty Footstool. It is obligatory for the intelligent person to know what the Throne is, what the Footstool is, and to know their attributes and conditions; then to reflect on what the Preserved Tablet, the Pen, the Rafraf, the Frequented House and the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary are, and to know their realities; then to contemplate the layers of the heavens and the manner of their extension, their bodies and their distances; then to reflect on the fixed and wandering stars; then to reflect on the world of the four elements and the three generated kinds, which are minerals, plants and animals; then to reflect on the wisdom of Allah the Exalted in creating small and weak things such as bedbugs and mosquitoes; then to move from these to knowing the genera of accidents and their near and distant species, and the manner of benefits obtained from each of their kinds; then to move from these to recognizing the ranks of the lower, higher, Throne-bearing and celestial spirits, and the ranks of the holy spirits, free from the bonds of bodies, which are indicated by His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. When he gathers all these things together to the extent of his capacity and power, then an atom of knowledge of the world, which is everything other than Allah the Exalted, has come into his intellect. Then at this point he knows that everything that has acquired existence and the perfections of existence in its essence, in its attributes, its conditions and its relations, is from the bringing-into-being of the Real, from His bounty and from His existence. At this point he understands from the meaning of His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ an atom. This is a sea without shore and a speech without end. And Allah knows best.

Sixth issue: Although we have mentioned that His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is treated as if it were the saying "Say: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds", we mentioned it because His saying within the surah ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4] is only fitting for the servant, so for this reason we needed that implied supposition there. As for this surah, which is His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾, it is not far-fetched that what is meant by it is Allah the Exalted's praise of Himself.

Once this is established, we say: this indicates in some respect that He, the Exalted, is far removed from any likeness in His essence, attributes and acts. That is because His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ runs in the manner of self-praise, which is ugly among creatures in ordinary experience. When He commanded us to do this, this shows that the Real cannot be measured by analogy to creation. Just as this is ugly from creatures while it is not ugly from the Real, so not everything that is ugly from creatures must be ugly from the Real. By this method it becomes necessary to refute the statements of the Mu'tazilah that what is ugly from us must be ugly from Allah.

When you know by this method that His acts do not resemble the acts of creatures, likewise His attributes do not resemble the attributes of creatures, and His essence does not resemble the essences of creatures. At this point absolute transcendence and complete sanctification arise, free from His being similar to anything else in essence, attributes and acts. He, Allah, is One in His essence, without partner in His attributes, without equal; One in His acts, without likeness. Exalted and sanctified is He. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first: concerning the questions directed at this verse, which are three:

First question: His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ runs in the manner of saying: "The learned man came to me", for this indicates the existence of another man who is not learned, otherwise there would be no need to mention this attribute. Similarly here: "All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth" seems to imply that there is another god who did not create the heavens and the earth; otherwise what is the benefit of this attribute?

The answer: We have explained that His saying "Allah" runs in the manner of a proper name. When an attribute is mentioned for a proper name, the purpose of mentioning the attribute is not distinction, but rather to inform that the named entity is described by that attribute. An example: when we say "the man, the learned one", "the man" is a common noun, and the common noun applies to many individuals, so the purpose here of mentioning the attribute is to distinguish this man by this description from the rest of men. But when we say "Zayd the learned", "Zayd" is a proper name, which indicates only this specific essence, because proper names stand in place of pointing; so when we describe it with the attribute, it is impossible that the purpose be distinguishing that person from others; rather the purpose is to inform that the named entity is described by this attribute. Since the word "Allah" belongs to the category of proper names, the matter is necessarily as we have stated. And Allah knows best.

Second question: Why did He mention the heavens before the earth, while the apparent sense of the revelation indicates that the creation of the earth preceded the creation of the heaven?

**Translation:**

The answer: the heavens are like the circle, and the earth is like the center. The existence of the circle necessitates the determination of the center, but not conversely, for the existence of the center does not necessitate the determination of the circle, since infinitely many circles may surround one center. Thus, since the heavens are prior to the earth in this respect, it is necessary to mention the heavens before the earth.

**The third question:** Why did He mention the heavens in the plural form and the earth in the singular, even though the earths are also many, as is evident from His saying: ﴿and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]?

The answer: The heavens serve as the agent (fa'il) and the earth serves as the recipient (qabil). If the heavens were one, the effect would be uniform, and this would disrupt the interests of this world. But if they are many, the planetary connections (al-ittisalat al-kawkabiyya) differ, and by means of them the four seasons and all the other varying conditions arise, and through these differences the interests of this world are realized. As for the earth, it is a recipient of the effect, and a single recipient suffices for receiving. As for the indication of the aforementioned verse that the earths are many, we have explained the manner of that in the commentary on that verse. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** Know that the purpose of this verse is to mention the proof of the existence of the Creator. Its argument is that the bodies of the heavens and the earth were determined in specific matters, with specific measures, and this could not occur except through the specification of a free-choosing agent (al-fa'il al-mukhtar).

As for the explanation of the first premise, it is from several aspects:

The first: every specific sphere (falak) has been assigned a specific magnitude, while it was permissible for it to be larger or smaller than that.

The second: every sphere has a magnitude composed of parts, and the part that is included could have been located outside, and vice versa. Therefore, the placement of each of them in its particular position is a permissible matter.

The third: motion and rest are both permissible for all bodies, on the evidence that the corporeal nature is one, and the necessary attributes of one thing are one. So when rest and motion are valid for some bodies, they must be valid for all of them. Thus the specification of the celestial body with motion rather than rest is a specification with a permissible matter.

The fourth: every motion can occur faster than it does and slower than it does, so the specification of that particular motion with that specific degree of speed or slowness is a specification with a permissible matter.

The fifth: every motion that occurs directed toward a direction could occur directed toward all other directions, so its specification with occurring in that particular manner is a specification with a permissible matter.

The sixth: every sphere is such that there exists another body either above it or below it, and it was permissible for its placement to be contrary to that order. On the evidence that since bodies are equal in corporeal nature, whatever is valid for some of them is valid for all of them, so its specification with that place and order was a permissible matter.

The seventh, which is that the motion of every sphere has a beginning. For a motion without a beginning is impossible, because the reality of motion is transition from one state to another, and this transition requires that it be preceded by something else, while the "first" (having no predecessor) contradicts being preceded by something else, and the combination of the two is impossible. Thus it is established that every motion has a beginning, and the specification of the onset of its occurrence at that time, rather than before or after it, is a specification with a permissible matter.

The eighth: since bodies are equal in complete quiddity (al-mahiyya al-tamma), the attribution of some of them with celestial nature and some with elemental nature, rather than the reverse, is a specification with a permissible matter.

The ninth: their motions are an act of a free-choosing agent, and whenever it is so, it has a beginning. The explanation of the first premise is that if the influencing cause of them were an essentially necessitating cause ('illa mujibah bi'l-dhat), then the permanence of that cause would necessitate the permanence of its effects, and thus the permanence of that cause would necessitate the permanence of each of the parts constituting this motion. Since that is impossible, it is established that the influencing cause of them is not an essentially necessitating cause, but a free-choosing agent. And when it is so, it is necessary that this agent be prior to these motions, and this necessitates that they have a beginning.

The tenth: it has been established by proof that there exists outside the world a void without end. This is evident from our knowing by necessity that if we supposed ourselves standing at the edge of the highest sphere, we would distinguish between the direction that is in front of us and the direction that is behind us, and the establishment of this distinction is known by necessity. Given that, it is established that there exists outside the world a void without end. And given that, the existence of this world in this space in which it exists rather than the other spaces is a permissible matter.

Thus, by these ten aspects, it is established that the bodies of the heavens and the earths differ in attributes and conditions, and so it is permissible in reason for their opposites and contraries to occur. Therefore this particular specification must occur only through a determinant (murajjih) and a measurer (muqaddir). Otherwise, one of the two sides of the possible would be preferred over the other without a determinant, and that is impossible.

Once this is established, we say: there is no meaning to creation (al-khalq) except determination (al-taqdir). Since reason has shown the occurrence of determination through these ten aspects, the occurrence of creation through these ten aspects is necessary. For this reason He said: ﴿Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. And God knows best. Some people have said: the purpose of mentioning the heavens and the earth, and the darknesses and the light, is to draw attention to the benefits contained in them.

Know that the benefits of the heavens are too numerous for volumes to encompass even a part of them. This is because the heavens, in relation to the offspring of this world, act as the father, and the earth in relation to them acts as the mother. So the active causes are celestial, and the receptive causes are terrestrial, and through them the affair of the three kinds of offspring is completed. A thorough explanation of this is not possible.

As for His saying: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The verb (ja'ala) transitively takes one object when it means "brought into being and originated," as in His saying: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, and it takes two objects when it means "rendered," as in His saying: ﴿and they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. The difference between creation (khalq) and making (ja'l) is that creation carries the meaning of determination, while making carries the meaning of conferring and rendering, such as bringing something into being from something, or rendering one thing into another. Among its uses is His saying: ﴿and made from it its mate﴾ [al-A'raf: 189], His saying: ﴿and We created you in pairs﴾ [al-Naba': 8], and His saying: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ [Sad: 5]. The word "making" is appropriate here because light and darkness, as they alternate, it is as if each of them is generated from the other.

**The second issue:** Regarding the words ﴿the darknesses and the light﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: that what is meant by them are the two sensible matters perceived by the sense of sight. What strengthens this is that the word is literal (haqiqa) for them, and also that when these two are joined with the mention of the heavens and the earth, nothing is understood from them except these two sensible conditions.

The second: al-Wahidi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ means the darkness of polytheism, hypocrisy and disbelief, and the light means the light of Islam, faith, prophethood and certainty. And it is reported from al-Hasan that he said: it means disbelief and faith. There is no discrepancy between these two statements, so al-Hasan's statement is like a summary of Ibn 'Abbas's statement.

One may say: interpreting the word according to the first aspect is preferable, for the reason we mentioned, that the principle is to interpret the word according to its literal meaning, and because when the mention of the darknesses and the light is joined with the heavens and the earth, nothing is understood from it except what we have mentioned.

Al-Wahidi said: the preferable course is to interpret the word as referring to both together. I say this is problematic, for it is interpreting the word in its figurative sense (majaz), and a single word in a single respect cannot be interpreted as both literal and figurative at once.

**The third issue:** He mentioned the darknesses before the light only because darkness is an expression of the absence of light from a body that is capable of receiving light, and it is not an expression of an existential quality opposed to light. The proof of this is that when one person sits near a lamp and another sits far from it, the distant one sees the near one and sees that air as clear and luminous, whereas the near one does not see the distant one and sees that air as dark. Had darkness been an existential quality, it would have been present in relation to these two persons, and since the matter is not so, we know that darkness is not an existential quality.

Given that this is established, we say: the non-existence of created things precedes their existence, so darkness precedes light in determination and in actual realization, and therefore it is necessary to place it first in wording. What strengthens this is what is related in divine reports (al-akhbar al-ilahiyya), that He, exalted is He, created the creation in darkness, then sprinkled upon them of His light.

**The fourth issue:** One may ask: why did He mention the darknesses in the plural form and the light in the singular form? We say: as for one who interprets the darknesses as disbelief and the light as faith, his statement here is clear, for truth is one and falsehood is many. As for one who interprets them as the sensible quality, the answer is that light is an expression of that complete and strong quality, and then it admits of gradual diminishment, and those degrees are many. For this reason He expressed the darknesses in the plural form.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾.

Know that 'adl (equalizing) is taswiya (making equal). It is said: "He equalized the thing with the thing" when he made it equal to it. The meaning of ﴿ya'diluna﴾ is that they associate others with Him.

If it is asked: upon what is the statement ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ conjoined?

We say: it may be conjoined with His saying ﴿Praise be to God﴾, in the sense that God is worthy of praise for all that He created, since He created it only as a blessing; ﴿then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾, so they disbelieve in His blessing. It may also be conjoined with His saying ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾, in the sense that He created these great things that none other than Him can create, and then they ascribe equals to Him, a lifeless thing that has no power over anything at all.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of "then" (thumma)?

We say: its benefit is to express amazement that they would ascribe equals to Him after the clarity of the signs of His power. And God knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who created you from clay, then decreed a term; and there is a named term with Him; yet you still doubt﴾.

Know that this statement may be intended to mention another of the proofs for the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, and it may be intended to mention the proof for the truth of the Return (ma'ad) and the truth of the Resurrection (hashr).

As for the first possibility, its explanation is that when God, exalted is He, argued from His creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of darkness and light to the existence of the Wise Creator, He followed this with an argument from His creation of man to establish this claim. So He said: ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾. The well-known view is that it means He created them from Adam, and Adam was created from clay; for this reason He said: ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾. But I have another view on this, which is that man is created from semen (maniy) and from the blood of menstruation (damm al-tamth), and these two are generated from blood, and blood is only generated from food, and food is either animal or plant. If it is animal, then the situation regarding how that animal is generated is like the situation regarding how man is generated. So it remains that it is plant, and it is established that man is created from plant foods, and there is no doubt that these are generated from clay. Thus it is established that every human being is generated from clay. This view, in my opinion, is closer to the truth.

Having known this, we say: here, clay has generated the drop (nutfah) through this described process. Then from the drop there were generated the various kinds of organs, differing in attribute, form, color and shape, such as the heart, the brain and the liver, and the kinds of simple organs such as the bones, the cartilage, the ligaments, the tendons and others. The generation of different attributes from a homogeneous substance is not possible except by the determination of a wise Determiner and a merciful Governor, and that is what is sought.

[p. 127]

As for the second possibility, namely that the purpose of this statement is to establish the matter of the Return: we say that since it has been established that the fashioning of the human body came about because the Wise Agent and the Merciful Determiner arranged the creation of these organs upon these differing attributes by His wisdom and power, and that power and wisdom remain after the death of the living being, He will be capable of restoring them and restoring life into them, and this indicates the soundness of the doctrine of the Return.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then decreed a term﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: the word qada' (decree) may come in the sense of judgment and command, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra: 23]; and in the sense of report and informing, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture﴾ [al-Isra: 4]; and in the sense of completing an act when it is accomplished, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. From this is the saying of people: "So-and-so fulfilled so-and-so's need." As for ajal (term), in the language it is an expression for the appointed time for the end of a period. The ajal of a person is the appointed time for the end of his life, and the ajal of a debt is its due time for the end of the deferral in it. Its root is from deferment; it is said: ajila al-shay' ya'jal ujulan, and he is ajil when it is delayed, and al-ajil is the opposite of al-'ajil.

Having known this, His saying ﴿then decreed a term﴾ means that He, exalted is He, specified the death of each one by a determined time, and that specification is an expression for the connection of His will to bringing about that death at that time. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 15].

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and there is a named term with Him﴾.

Know that the explicit wording of this verse indicates that each human being has two terms. The exegetes differed in explaining them in several ways:

The first: Abu Muslim said: His saying ﴿then decreed a term﴾ means the terms of those who have passed away from among the creation, and His saying ﴿and there is a named term with Him﴾ means the terms of those who remain from among the creation. He specified this second term by being "named with Him," because when those who passed away died, their terms became known; but as for those who remain, they have not yet died, so their terms have not become known. For this meaning He said: ﴿and there is a named term with Him﴾.

The second: the first term is the term of death, and the named term with God is the term of the Resurrection, because the duration of their life in the Hereafter has no end and no termination, and no one knows the state of this term except God, glorified and exalted is He.

The third: the first term is what lies between a person's creation and his death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection, which is the barzakh.

The fourth: the first is sleep, and the second is death.

The fifth: the first term is the measure of what has passed of each person's life, and the second term is the measure of what remains of each person's life.

The sixth, which is the view of the philosophers of Islam (hukama' al-Islam): every human being has two terms:

One of them: the natural terms (al-ajal al-tab'iyyah).

The second: the terms of forcible termination (al-ajal al-ikhtiramiyyah). As for the natural terms, they are those which, if that temperament remained preserved from external accidents, its duration would end at such-and-such a time. As for the terms of forcible termination, they are those which occur through some external cause, such as drowning, burning, the sting of insects, and other troublesome matters. His saying ﴿named with Him﴾ means known to Him, or its name is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The meaning of "with Him" is similar to what a man says in a matter: "In my view (indi) the matter is such-and-such," meaning this is my belief and my opinion.

If it is said: an indefinite subject (al-mubtada' al-nakirah), when its predicate is an adverbial phrase, must be postponed; so why was it permissible to front it in His saying ﴿and there is a named term with Him﴾?

We say: because it has been specified by a qualifier, so it came close to a definite noun, like His saying: ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221].

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿yet you still doubt﴾, we say: al-miryah and al-imtira' mean doubt.

Know that if we say the purpose of mentioning this statement is to argue for the existence of the Creator, then its meaning is: after the manifestation of such a compelling proof, you still doubt concerning the soundness of monotheism (tawhid). And if the purpose is to affirm the doctrine of the Return, then likewise, and God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 3:**

**Allah's saying, the Exalted: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾**

Know that if we say that the purpose of the preceding verse is to establish the proof for the existence of the Creator (al-sani') who is All-Powerful and Choosing (al-qadir al-mukhtar),

we say: the purpose of this verse is to demonstrate that He, the Exalted, knows all that is known. The two preceding verses prove perfect power, and this verse proves perfect knowledge. Then the attributes that are required for divinity (al-uluhiyyah) are complete. If we say that the purpose of the preceding verse is to establish the proof for the validity of the Return (al-ma'ad), then the purpose of this verse is to complete that demonstration. This is because the deniers of the Return denied it for two reasons:

The first: they believe that the cause of the coming into being of the human body is the mixture of the natures (imtizaj al-tabai'), and they deny that the cause of it is an All-Powerful, Choosing agent.

The second: they accept that, but they say: "He is not knowing of particulars (al-juz'iyyat), so He cannot distinguish the obedient from the disobedient, nor distinguish the parts of Zayd's body from the parts of 'Amr's body." Then He, the Exalted, established by the two preceding verses that He is All-Powerful and Choosing, not a necessitating cause ('illah mujibah), and He established by this verse that He, the Exalted, knows all that is known. Then all the doubts on which the saying of denying the Return and the validity of the Gathering and Dispersal (al-hashr wa-al-nashr) rest are nullified. This is the discussion concerning the arrangement (nazm) of the verse. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Those who hold that Allah, the Exalted, is restricted to a place (bi-al-makan) have held fast to this verse, namely His saying: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens﴾, and that indicates that God is settled in the heaven. They said: this is also reinforced by His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you?﴾ [al-Mulk: 16]. They said: "It does not necessarily follow that He would be in the earth, because of His saying in this verse: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth.﴾ That requires His existence in both places together, and that is impossible." We say: We are agreed that He is not present on the earth, and abandoning one of the two apparent meanings does not necessarily entail abandoning the other apparent meaning without evidence. So the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens﴾ must remain as that apparent meaning. Also, some readers stop at His saying: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens﴾, then begin: ﴿and on the earth He knows your secret﴾, and the meaning is that He, glorified is He, knows your secrets that exist on the earth, so His saying "on the earth" is attached to His saying "your secret." This is the complete statement.

Know that we first establish the proof that it is not possible to take this statement in its apparent meaning, and that is from several aspects:

**The first:** He, the Exalted, said in this surah: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 12]. So by this verse He made clear that everything in the heavens and the earth is possessed by Allah, the Exalted, and is owned by Him. So if Allah were one of the existing things in the heavens, it would follow that He would be owned by Himself, and that is impossible. A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 6]. If they say: "His saying: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ requires that everything in the heavens belongs to Allah, except that the word 'ma' is specific to that which does not reason, so the Essence of Allah, the Exalted, does not enter into it." We say: We do not accept that, and the proof for it is His saying: ﴿By the heaven and He who built it, and by the earth and He who spread it out, and by a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 5-7]. A parallel to it is ﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 3]. And there is no doubt that the intended meaning of the word "ma" here is Allah, glorified is He.

**The second:** His saying: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens﴾ either means that He exists in all the heavens, or it means that He exists in one heaven. The second is an abandonment of the apparent meaning. The first is of two kinds, because either the presence of Him, the Exalted, in one of the heavens is the same as His presence in the rest of the heavens, or it is different. The first requires that one single spatial entity (al-mutahayyiz al-wahid) be present in two places, and that is false by the self-evident judgment of reason.

The second requires that He, the Exalted, be composed of parts and portions, and that is impossible.

**The third:** If He were existing in the heavens, He would be limited and finite, and everything that is like that is capable of accepting increase and decrease, and everything that is like that has its restriction to a specific measure by the specification of one who specifies and the determination of one who determines, and everything that is like that is originated (muhdath).

**The fourth:** If He were in the heavens, then either He would be able to create another world above the heavens or He would not be able. The second entails His being incapacitated, and the first requires that if He did that, He would be located beneath this world, and the people deny that He is beneath the world.

**The fifth:** He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], and He said: ﴿And We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], and He said: ﴿And He is the one who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], and He said: ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. All of that nullifies the saying that Allah, the Exalted, has a place and a direction (al-makan wa-al-jihah). Thus it is established by these proofs that it is not possible to take this statement in its apparent meaning, so interpretation (ta'wil) is obligatory, and it is of several aspects:

**The first:** His saying: ﴿He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾ means: He is Allah in the management (tadbir) of the heavens and the earth, just as one says: "So-and-so is in such-and-such a matter," meaning in its management and the arrangement of its affairs. A parallel to it is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And He is the one who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84].

**The second:** His saying "He is Allah" is a complete statement, then He began and said: ﴿in the heavens and on the earth He knows your secret and your open﴾. The meaning is that He, glorified and exalted is He, knows in the heavens the secrets of the angels, and on the earth He knows the secrets of mankind and the jinn.

**The third:** The statement is in the form of inversion (al-taqdim wa-al-ta'khir), and the intended meaning is: He is Allah, who knows in the heavens and on the earth your secret and your open. Among the things that strengthen these interpretations is that our saying "He is Allah" is like our saying "He is the excellent, the knowing." The word "huwa" (He) is mentioned here to convey restriction (al-hasr). This benefit is only achieved if we make the word "Allah" a derived noun (ism mushtaqq). But if we make it the proper name of a specific individual serving as a definite designation, it is not correct to attach this word to it. And if we make our saying "Allah" a meaningful word, its meaning becomes "the One worshipped in the heaven and on the earth," and on this assumption the question is dissolved. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** The intended meaning of "the secret" is the attributes of the hearts, which are the motives (al-dawa'i) and the deterrents (al-sawarif). The intended meaning of "the open" is the actions of the limbs (a'mal al-jawarih). He placed the mention of the secret before the mention of the open because the agent in an act is the totality of power together with motive. So the motive, which belongs to the category of the secret, is the one that is effective in the actions of the limbs called the open. It is established that knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect, and the cause is prior to the effect, and what is prior in essence must be mentioned first in wording.

* * *

**[Page 130]**

**The third issue:** His saying: ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾ raises a question: actions are either actions of the hearts, which are called the secret, or actions of the limbs, which are called the open. So actions do not go outside the secret and the open. Therefore His saying: ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾ would entail the conjunction of a thing with itself, and that is invalid.

The answer: It is necessary to interpret His saying "what you earn" as what a person deserves for his act of reward and punishment. The conclusion is that it is interpreted as "what is acquired" (al-muktasab), just as one says: "This wealth is the earnings (kasb) of so-and-so," meaning what he acquired. It is not permissible to interpret it as the earning itself, for otherwise it would entail the conjunction of a thing with itself, as you have stated in the question.

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates that a human being is an acquirer (muktasib) of the act. And "kasb" is the act that leads to obtaining a benefit or averting a harm. For this reason, the act of Allah is not described as "kasb," because He, the Exalted, is exalted above bringing benefit and averting harm. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 4–5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.ﴩ 

Know that when He first spoke about monotheism (tawhid), secondly about the Return (ma'ad), and thirdly about that which establishes these two matters, He then mentioned what relates to establishing prophethood (nubuwwah), and He began with it by making clear that these disbelievers turn away from reflecting upon the proofs (dala'il), not paying attention to them. This verse indicates that blind imitation (taqlid) is invalid and that reflection upon the proofs is obligatory; for were it not so, God would not have censured those who turn away from the proofs.

Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The "min" in His saying ﴿min ayah﴾ (any sign) is for the total inclusion of the genus which occurs in negation, like your saying: "No one came to me (ma atani min ahad)."

The second, which is His saying ﴿min ayati rabbihim﴾ (from the signs of their Lord), is for partition (tab'id), and the meaning is: No proof whatsoever appears to them from among the proofs upon which contemplation and consideration are obligatory, except that they turn away from it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them; so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, arranged the states of these disbelievers into three levels. The first level is their turning away from reflecting upon the proofs and contemplating the clear signs.

The second level is their denying them. This level is greater than what preceded it, because one who turns away from something may not deny it, but rather be heedless of it and not engage with it; when he becomes one who denies it, he has gone beyond mere turning away.

The third level is their mocking them, because one who denies something may not carry his denial to the point of mockery; when he reaches this limit, he has reached the furthest extreme of rejection. So God made clear that those disbelievers reached these three levels in this order.

They differed regarding what is meant by "the truth" (al-haqq). It was said: it is the miracles (mu'jizat). Ibn Mas'ud said: The moon split in Mecca and was cleft into two halves; one half departed and one half remained. It was also said: it is the Qur'an. It was said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: it is the law (shar') that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, and the rulings that Muhammad (ﷺ) came with. It was said: it is the promise and the threat, with which He sometimes encourages them and sometimes warns them by means of it. The most appropriate view is that all of these are included in it.

Page 131

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾, what is meant by it is the threat and the deterrence from that mockery. Therefore the "news" (anba') must be understood not as the mere news itself, but as the punishment which God announced. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a while﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. When a wise person threatens, he may say: "You will know the news of this matter when that which you fear befalls you." This is so because the purpose of the report, which is the threat, is the attainment of knowledge of the punishment that will descend. So the punishment itself, when it descends, confirms that report until doubt is removed from it. Then, this punishment may be understood as the punishment of this world, which appeared on the day of Badr, and it may be understood as the punishment of the Hereafter.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, generations We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent down abundant rain upon them and made rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins and produced after them other generations.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, forbade them from that aversion, denial and mockery through threat and warning, He followed it with what serves as admonition and counsel on this subject. So He admonished them with the previous generations, such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the people of Shuʿayb, Pharaoh and others.

If it is asked: What is the *qarn* (generation)? We say: al-Wāḥidī said: the *qarn* is the people who are contemporaries in a period of time. So the period in which a people gather and then separate by death is a *qarn*, because those who come after them are other people who are contemporaries, so they are another *qarn*. The evidence for this is his saying, peace be upon him: "The best of generations is my generation." Its derivation is from *al-aqrān* (equals/contemporaries). Since people's lifespans are for the most part sixty, seventy or eighty, some said: the *qarn* is sixty, others said: it is seventy, and a group said: it is eighty. The closer view is that it is not determined by a specific fixed span of time that admits no increase or decrease; rather, what is meant is the people of each age, so when most of them have passed, it is said: the *qarn* has passed.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, described the previous generations with three kinds of attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿We had established them on the earth as We have not established you.﴾ The author of al-Kashshāf said: *makkana lahu fī al-arḍ* means He made for him a place, and the like of it, on his land. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the land﴾ (Al-Kahf: 84), and ﴿Did We not establish them?﴾ (Al-Qaṣaṣ: 57). As for *makkantuhu fī al-arḍ*, its meaning is *athbattuhu fīhā* (I established him in it), and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We had established them in that wherein We have not established you﴾ (Al-Aḥqāf: 26). Because the two meanings are close, Allah combined them in His saying: ﴿We had established them on the earth as We have not established you.﴾ The meaning is: We did not give the people of Makkah the like of what We gave ʿĀd, Thamūd and others of expansiveness in bodies, abundance in wealth and reliance on the means of this world.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿And We sent down the sky upon them abundantly﴾ means rain and downpour. So *al-samāʾ* here means the rain, and *al-midrār* means the one of abundant milk; its origin is from their saying: *darra al-labanu* when a large quantity comes to the one milking it. So *al-midrār* may be an attribute of the clouds, and it may be an attribute of the rain. It is said: *saḥābun midrārun* when its rains are continuous. The pattern *mif'āl* comes in an attribute when intensification is intended. Muqātil said: *(midrāran)* means successive, time after time. In *al-midrār* the masculine and feminine are equal.

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿And We made the rivers flow beneath them﴾, and what is meant by it is the abundance of gardens.

Know that the purpose of these attributes is that they found from the benefits of this world more than what the people of Makkah found. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that, despite their greater might in this world through these aspects, and despite their great numbers and their expansiveness in wealth and body, there befell them when they disbelieved what you have heard. This meaning necessitates reflection and awakening from the sleep of heedlessness and the slumber of ignorance. There remain here some questions:

The first question: In this statement there is nothing but that they perished, yet this perishing is not specific to them; rather the prophets and all the believers also perished. How then is it appropriate to bring this statement in the context of warning against disbelief, when it is shared between the disbeliever and others?

The answer: The purpose of it is not warning merely by death and perishing; rather the purpose is that they sold the religion for the world, so they lost it and remained in severe punishment because of deprivation from religion. This meaning is not shared between the disbeliever and the believer.

The second question: How did He say (*a-lam yarawū*, "Have they not seen?") when the people did not affirm the truthfulness of Muḥammad, peace be upon him, regarding what he reports of them, and they also did not witness the events of the earlier nations?

The answer: The narratives of the earlier ones are well known among creation, so it is remote to say that they did not hear these accounts; and merely hearing them suffices for taking lesson.

The third question: What is the benefit in mentioning the creation of other generations after them?

The answer: The benefit is to alert to the fact that He, exalted is He, is not burdened by destroying them and emptying their lands of them, for He is able to bring into being in their place other people who will repopulate their lands with them, as in His saying: ﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾ (Ash-Shams: 15). And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 7:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but evident magic."﴾

Know that those who rebel against accepting the call of the prophets are many groups.

The first group are those who went to excess in loving this world and seeking its pleasures and appetites, until they became absorbed in them and seized their possession. This became an obstacle preventing them from accepting the call of the prophets. These are the ones whom God, exalted is He, mentioned in the preceding verse, and He explained that the pleasures of this world are passing, while the punishment of disbelief is lasting. It is not rational to bear everlasting punishment for the sake of fleeting, base pleasures. The second group are those who regard the miracles of the prophets, upon them be peace, as being of the category of magic and not of the category of miracles. These are the ones God, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse. Here there are some issues.

The first issue: God, exalted is He, explains in this verse that these disbelievers, if they had witnessed a book descending from heaven upon you, O Muhammad, all at once, would not have believed in it, but would have taken it to be magic and trickery. What is meant by His saying ﴿on paper﴾ is that if the book had descended as a single whole, on a single sheet, and they had seen it, touched it, and witnessed it directly, they would have criticized it and said that it is magic.

If it is said: Is the appearance of a book and its descent from heaven one of the category of miracles or not? If it is not of the category of miracles, then their denial of its indicating prophethood would not be objectionable. And it cannot be said that it is of the category of miracles, because the angel is able to bring it down from heaven, and before one believes in the truthfulness of the prophets and messengers, the infallibility of the angels is not known. And before believing in the messengers, there is no doubt that we permit that the descent of that book from heaven might be by some of the jinn and devils, or by some of the angels whose infallibility has not been established. And if this possibility stands, then the descent of the book from heaven has ceased to be a proof of truthfulness.

We say: The intended meaning is not what you have mentioned. Rather, the intended meaning is that if they saw it, they would remain in doubt about it and say, "Only our eyes have been dazzled." But if they touched it with their hands, the visual perception would be strengthened by the tactile perception, and it would reach the utmost degree of clarity and strength. Then these people would remain in doubt as to whether that which they saw and touched exists or not. This indicates that they had reached in ignorance the limit of sophistry. This is the intended meaning of the verse, not what you have mentioned. And God knows best.

The second issue: The al-Qadi said: This verse indicates that it is not permissible for God, exalted is He, to withhold from the servant a favor (lutf) which He knows, if He were to grant it, he would believe upon it. For He explained that He does not send down this book for the reason that, if He sent it down, they would say this statement. And it is not permissible for Him to inform of this except that it is known that if they had accepted it and believed in it, He would certainly have sent it down. Thus by this the obligation of favor (lutf) is established. Someone may say: His saying, "If God had sent down to them this book, they would have said this statement," does not indicate that He would send it down to them if they had not said this statement, except by way of the argument from implication (dalil al-khitab), and that, according to him, is not a valid proof. Moreover, not everything God does is obligatory upon Him, and this verse, if it indicates anything, indicates the occurrence of the act, not the obligation of its occurrence. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be reprieved.﴾ ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have covered over them what they cover over.﴾

Know that this is the third type of the doubts of those who deny prophethood. They say: If God sent a messenger to creation, that messenger would necessarily be one of the angels, for when they are of the company of the angels, their knowledge is greater, their power is stronger, their awe is more magnificent, their distinction from creation is more perfect, and doubts and suspicions about their prophethood and their mission are fewer.

Page 134

When a wise one wishes to achieve an important matter, whatever leads more strongly to the attainment of that aim is preferable. Since doubts about the prophethood of angels are fewer, it follows that if God sent a messenger to creation, that messenger should be one of the angels. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾

Know that God, exalted is He, answered this doubt in two ways.

As for the first: His saying: ﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾. The meaning of "qada'" (decision) is completion and obligation, and we have mentioned the meanings of qada' in Surat al-Baqarah. Here there are several aspects:

The first: the sending down of an angel to humans is a manifest sign, so if an angel were sent down to these disbelievers, perhaps they would not believe, as He said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them and We gathered against them everything before them, they would not have believed unless God willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. And if they do not believe, it becomes obligatory to destroy them with the punishment of annihilation, for the custom of God is that when a manifest sign appears, if they do not believe, the punishment of annihilation comes upon them. So here God did not send the angel down to them, lest they deserve this punishment.

The second aspect: when they witness the angel, their souls would depart from the terror of what they see. Its explanation: when a son of Adam sees an angel, he either sees him in his original form or in the form of a human. If it is the first, the son of Adam would not remain alive. Do you not see that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw Gabriel (peace be upon him) in his original form, he fainted? And if it is the second, then the one seen is a person in the form of a human, and the state in that case does not differ whether he himself is an angel or a human. Do you not see that all the messengers saw the angels in human form, like the guests of Abraham, the guests of Lot, those who scaled the sanctuary, and like Gabriel when he appeared to Mary as a well-formed man?

The third aspect: the sending down of an angel is a manifest sign functioning as compulsion and the removal of choice, and that undermines the validity of the obligation.

The fourth aspect: although the sending down of an angel would dispel the aforementioned doubts, it strengthens the doubts from another angle. For whatever miracle appeared at his hand, they would say: "This is your act; you did it by your own choice and power, and if we had obtained the same power, strength and knowledge as you, we would have done the same as you did." So we know that although the sending down of an angel dispels the doubt from the aforementioned aspects, it strengthens the doubt from these aspects.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾, the benefit of the word "thumma" (then) is to alert that the non-granting of respite is more severe than the decision of the matter, because the sudden arrival of severity is more severe than severity itself.

As for the second: His saying: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, that is, We would have made him in the form of a human. The wisdom in this has several matters:

One: that kind is more inclined toward its own kind.

Second: that humans cannot bear to see an angel.

Third: that the obedience of angels is strong, so they would despise the obedience of humans, and perhaps would not excuse them for undertaking sins.

Fourth: that prophethood is a bounty from God, so He singles out whomever He wills of His servants for it, whether he is an angel or a human.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And We would have covered over them what they cover over.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: One says "labastu al-amr 'ala al-qawm, albisuhu labsan," meaning: when you make a matter resemble something to them and render it obscure. Its root is covering with a garment, and from it comes "labisa al-thawb" (he wore the garment), because it serves to conceal the self. The meaning is that if We made the angel in the form of a human, they would think that angel was a human, and their question would return: "We do not accept the mission of this person." The realization of the matter is that if God did that, God's act would become similar to their act of confusion. It would be confusion because people would think he is a human when he is not so; and their act would be confusion because they tell their people, "He is a human like you, and a human cannot be a messenger from God, exalted is He."
