The heart of the Messenger would constrict upon hearing it, so He mentioned that (matter) so that it would become a cause for lightening the burden on the heart, because one of the things that lightens the burden on the heart is sharing in the cause of the trial and grief. So it was as if it were said to him: these many kinds of ill manners with which they treat you have existed among all previous generations with their prophets, so you are not unique in this path.

As for His saying: ﴿So there befell those who mocked them that which they used to mock at﴾, and its parallel is His saying: ﴿And the evil plan does not befall except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. In its interpretation there are many views from the people of linguistics, and they are all close in meaning:

Al-Nadr said: it became obligatory upon them (wajaba 'alayhim).

Al-Layth said: "al-hayq" is what befalls a person of deception or evil that he does, so that it descends upon him. It is said: "Allah made their deception befall them (ahaqa Allahu bihim makrahum)," and "their deception befell them (haqa bihim makruhum)."

Al-Farra' said: "haqa bihim" refers back to them.

It was also said: "haqa bihim" means that this befell them.

Al-Zajjaj said: "haqa" means "ahata" (encompassed).

Al-Azhari said: Al-Zajjaj interpreted "haqa" in the sense of "ahata," and its derivation is from "al-hawq," which is that which surrounds the head of the penis (al-kamarah).

Another discussion concerning the verse is that the word "ma" in His saying: ﴿what they used to﴾ has two views:

The first: that what is meant by it is the Qur'an and the Shari'ah, which is what Muhammad (peace be upon him) brought. According to this interpretation, this verse falls under the category of omission of the modifier (hadhf al-mudaf), and the meaning would be: "So there befell them the punishment of that which they used to mock."

The second view: that what is meant by it is that they used to mock the punishment with which the Messenger threatened them of its descent. According to this interpretation, there is no need for this supposition (idmar).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth, then look how was the end of those who denied.﴾

Know that just as He, exalted is He, consoled His Messenger with the previous verse, so likewise He warned the people with this verse, and said to His Messenger: Say to them: Do not be deceived by what you have found of the world and its good things, and what you have attained of its pleasures and desires. Rather, travel through the earth so that you may know the truth of what the Messenger has told you about the descent of punishment upon those who denied the messengers in past ages. For when you journey through the earth and travel through the lands, you will certainly witness those traces, and thus reflection will be complete and insight will be strengthened.

If it is asked: What is the difference between His saying (fa-unzuru, "then look") and His saying (thumma unzuru, "then look")?

We say: His saying (fa-unzuru) indicates that He, exalted is He, made looking a consequence of travelling, as if it were said: Travel for the sake of looking, and do not travel the way of the heedless.

Page 136

As for His saying: ﴿Travel through the earth, then look﴾, its meaning is the permission to travel through the earth for trade and other benefits, and the obligation to look at the traces of those who perished. Then God, exalted is He, drew attention to this difference by the word "then" (thumma), because of the great distance between what is obligatory and what is permitted. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 6, verse 12:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah." He has prescribed for Himself mercy. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the purpose of establishing this verse is to establish the existence of the Creator (al-Sani', the Maker), to establish the return (al-ma'ad, the life after death), and to establish prophethood (al-nubuwwah). Its explanation is that the conditions of the higher and lower worlds indicate that all these bodies are described by attributes which they could have had in their opposites and contraries. When this is so, the specification of each part of the bodily parts with its particular attribute must be because the Wise, Capable, Choosing Creator specified it with that particular attribute. This indicates that the world, together with all that is in it, belongs to Allah, may He be exalted.

Once this is established, His being capable of restoration, gathering and resurrection is established, because the first composition occurred only because He, may He be exalted, is capable of all possibilities and knowing of all knowable things, and this power and knowledge cannot cease. Therefore the validity of restoration a second time is necessary. Also, it is established that He, may He be exalted, is a King who is obeyed, and the King who is obeyed is the one who has command and prohibition over his servants, and there must be a messenger. This indicates that sending prophets and messengers from Allah, may He be exalted, to creation is not impossible. Thus it is established that this verse is sufficient to establish these three matters. And since the mention of these three issues preceded, Allah mentioned this verse after them to confirm the totality of those matters in the way we have explained. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?"﴾ is a question, and His saying "Say: To Allah" is the answer. Allah commanded him to ask first and then to answer second. This is fitting only in a place where the answer has become so evident that no denier can deny it and no repeller can repel it. And since we have shown that the signs of createdness and contingency are manifest in the essences of all bodies and in all their attributes, it is inevitable that acknowledging that they are all entirely owned by Allah, may He be exalted, and are under His ownership, His disposal and His power, is the case. Therefore He commanded him to ask first and then to answer second, so that this would indicate that acknowledging this meaning is something for which there is absolutely no way to repel. Also, the people were acknowledging that the whole world belongs to Allah, and that it is under His ownership, disposal, dominance and power in this sense, as He said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25]. Then, when He had shown by this means the perfection of His divinity and power and the full effect of His disposal over the world of creatures, He followed it with the perfection of His mercy and beneficence towards creation, and said: ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾. It is as if He, may He be exalted, said: He has not been content for Himself not to bestow favour, and He must promise favour; rather, He always bestows favour and always promises favour in the future, and despite this He has prescribed that for Himself and made it obligatory by way of grace and generosity.

They differed about what is meant by this mercy. Some said: that mercy is that He, may He be exalted, gives them respite for the duration of their lives, lifts from them the punishment of uprooting, and does not hasten the punishment for them in this world. It was also said: the meaning is that He prescribed for Himself mercy for whoever abandons denial of the messengers, repents, turns back in devotion, believes them, and accepts their law.

Know that many reports have come concerning the vastness of Allah's mercy. From the Prophet (ﷺ) he said: "When Allah finished creating, He wrote a book: 'My mercy has preceded My wrath.'"

If it is said: mercy is the will for good, and wrath is the will for retribution, and the apparent meaning of this report requires that one of the two wills precedes the other, and what is preceded by something else is created, then this requires that the will of Allah, may He be exalted, be created.

We say: the intended meaning of this precedence is precedence in quantity, not precedence in time. It is reported from Salman that when Allah, may He be exalted, created the heavens and the earth, He created one hundred mercies, each mercy filling the space between the heavens and the earth. So with Him are ninety-nine mercies, and He distributed one mercy among the creatures, and by it they show compassion and mercy to one another. When the end comes, He will restrict it to the righteous.

As for His saying: ﴿He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾, there are several discussions:

**The first:** The lam in His saying "layajma'annakum" (He will surely gather you) is the lam of an implied oath, and the estimate is: "By Allah, He will surely gather you."

**The second discussion:** They differed as to whether this statement is a new independent sentence (mubtada', a beginning) or connected to what precedes it. Some said it is an independent sentence, because He, may He be exalted, showed the perfection of His divinity by His saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah"﴾. Then He showed, may He be exalted, that He shows mercy to them in this world by granting respite and repelling the punishment of uprooting, and showed that He will gather them until the Day of Resurrection. So His saying "He has prescribed for Himself mercy" means that He grants them respite, and His saying "He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection" means that He does not grant them respite, but rather resurrects them and calls them to account for everything they did.

The second view is that it is connected to what precedes it, and the estimate is: "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," and "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself that He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection."

It was also said: when He said "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," it is as if it were said: "And what is that mercy?" So it was said: it is that He ﴿will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾. This is because, were it not for the fear of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, there would be chaos and disorder, order would be lost, and confusion would be widespread. So the threat of the Day of Resurrection becomes one of the greatest causes of mercy in this world. Therefore His saying "He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection" serves as an explanation of His saying "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy."

**The third discussion:** His saying "Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah" is a statement given in the third-person form (lafz al-ghaybah), while His saying "He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection" is a statement given in the form of direct address (al-mukhatabah). The purpose of it is emphasis in the threat, as if it were said: Since you know that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is His dominion, and you know that the Wise King does not neglect the affairs of His subjects, and it is not permissible in His wisdom that He should equate the obedient with the disobedient, or the one occupied with service with the one who turns away from it, then do you not know that He will establish the Resurrection, bring together all creatures, and call them to account for everything?

**The fourth discussion:** Concerning the phrase "ila yawm al-qiyamah" (to the Day of Resurrection), there are several views:

The first: that "ila" is a supplementary particle, and the estimate is: "He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection." It was also said: "ila" here means "fi" (in), that is: "He will surely gather you in the Day of Resurrection."

It was also said: there is an ellipsis, meaning: "He will surely gather you to the place of gathering on the Day of Resurrection," because gathering is to a place, not to a time. It was also said: "He will surely gather you in this world by creating you generation after generation, until the Day of Resurrection."

As for His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe﴾, there are several discussions:

**The first:** In this verse there are two views.

The first: that His saying "alladhina" (those who) is in the accusative case as an apposition (badal) for the pronoun in His saying "layajma'annakum" (He will surely gather you), and the meaning is: He will surely gather these polytheists who have lost their souls. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The second, which is the view of al-Zajjaj: that His saying ﴿those who have lost their souls﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and His saying ﴿they will not believe﴾ is its predicate (khabar), because His saying "layajma'annakum" encompasses everyone: those who have lost their souls and others. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day; and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, while He feeds and is not fed? Regarding the verse there are several issues:

He said: In the first verse He mentioned the heavens and the earth, since there is no place other than them; and in this verse He mentioned the night and the day, since there is no time other than them. And I say: Here is another subtle point, namely that the beginning occurred with the mention of place and what is in place, then He mentioned after it time and what is in time. That is because place and what is in place are closer to minds and thoughts than time and what is in time, due to subtleties mentioned in pure rational sciences; and complete instruction is that which begins with the most evident and ascends to the more hidden and then the more hidden. This is what relates to the aspect of the arrangement.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾ conveys restriction (hasr), and the implied meaning is: these things belong to Him and not to other than Him. This is the truth, because every existent is either necessary in its own essence (wajib li-dhatihi) or possible in its own essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). The necessary in its essence is none other than the One, and whatever is other than that One is possible. The possible does not come into existence except by the bringing into existence of the Necessary in its essence, and whatever comes into being through His bringing into existence and origination belongs to Him. Thus it is established that whatever is other than that existent necessary in its essence is His possession and under His ownership. For this reason He said, ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day.﴾

The third issue: Regarding the interpretation of this resting (sukun) there are two opinions:

The first: that what is meant by it is the thing that came to rest after it had moved. Accordingly, what is meant is everything that settles in the night and the day, from beasts and the whole of living creatures on land and sea. On this view, they said there is an elision in the verse, and the implied meaning is: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests and moves in the night and the day,﴾ like His saying: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning heat and cold, and He suffices with mentioning one of them over the other, because that is known from the mentioned indication. The second opinion: that what is meant by this resting is not its opposite, motion; rather, what is meant is resting in the sense of dwelling (hulul), as one says: so-and-so rests in such-and-such a land when his place is in it, and from it is His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 45]. On this interpretation, what is meant is: to Him belongs everything that occurs in the night and the day. The implied meaning is: everything that is in the time and the period, whether moving or still; and this interpretation is preferable and more complete. So everything that time passes over and that falls under time is originated (muhdath), and every originated thing necessarily has an originator, and the agent of that act must be prior to it, and what is prior to time must be prior to the moment and the time; so the moments do not pass over Him, the hours do not pass through Him, and it is not true of Him that He was and will be.

The purpose of this is to refute those who say that God, exalted is He, acts by necessity of His essence; so He drew attention to the fact that, although He owns all originated things, He is a free and choosing agent who hears, sees, and knows the secret and what is more hidden. Having established these meanings, He said: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?⟩

Know that there is a difference between saying: ﴿Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?⟩ and saying: "Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?" [with the object placed differently]. This is because the denial applies to taking other than Allah as a protector, not to taking a protector as such; and you have known that they put first what is most important and what they are concerned with, namely. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Do you then command me to worship other than Allah?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64] and His saying: ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ [Yunus: 59].

* * *

Page 140
Then He said: ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth.﴾ It was read as "Fatiri al-samawati" in the genitive as a description of Allah, and in the nominative by supposing a hu (He), and in the accusative as a praise. Al-Zuhri read "fatara al-samawat." It is reported from Ibn Abbas: I did not know the meaning of "Fatir al-samawat" until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: "Ana fatartuha," meaning: I began it. Ibn al-Anbari said: The root of fatr is splitting a thing at its beginning; so His saying: ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ means their Creator and Originator by the composition whose way is that splitting and joining occur in it when things are combined with one another. Since splitting may occur in a state of splitting for repair, and in another state for corruption, the Originator of the heavens is of repair only. And His saying: ﴿Do you see any rifts?⟩ [al-Mulk: 3] and ﴿When the sky is split asunder⟩ [al-Infitar: 1] are of corruption, though their root is one.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿while He feeds and is not fed,⟩ meaning: He is the Provider to others, and no one provides for Him.

If it is said: How did you interpret feeding as provision, when He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they feed Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 57], and conjunction requires difference?

We say: There is no doubt that there is a difference between them; however, it may be good to make one of them a metonym for the other because of the great closeness between them. The purpose of the verse is that all benefits come from Him, and benefit cannot be attributed to Him. It was read as "wa la yutʿamu" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ; and Ibn al-Ma'mun reported from Yaʿqub: "wa huwa yuṭʿamu wa la yuṭʿimu," with the first verb passive and the second active; and on this reading the pronoun refers to the one mentioned in His saying: "Other than Allah." Al-Ashhab read "wa huwa yuṭʿimu wa la yuṭʿimu" with both verbs active, and it was interpreted to mean: He feeds and does not ask to be fed. Al-Azhari related: aṭʿamtu in the sense of istaṭʿamtu. It is also permissible that the meaning is: He feeds at times and does not feed at other times, according to what the interests require, like His saying: "He gives and withholds, extends and restricts, enriches and impoverishes."

Know that what is mentioned at the start of the verse is the prohibition of taking other than Allah, exalted is He, as a protector. He argued for it by saying that He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and that He feeds and is not fed. Where this is the case, taking another as a protector is impermissible. As for the demonstration that He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth: we have shown that whatever is other than the One is possible in its essence, and what is possible in its essence does not come to exist except by the bringing into existence of another; so it follows that whatever is other than Allah is obtained through His bringing it into existence and origination. Thus it is established that He, glory be to Him, is the Originator of every existent other than Himself. As for the demonstration that He feeds and is not fed, it is evident, because feeding is an expression for conveying benefits, and not seeking food is an expression for not benefiting. And since He is necessary in His essence, He is inevitably self-sufficient and exalted above benefiting from anything else. Thus it is proven by demonstration that He, exalted is He, is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and that He feeds and is not fed; and when this is established, it is rationally impossible to take another as a protector, because what is other than Him is in need in its essence, in all its attributes, and in all that is under its hand. The Truth, glory be to Him, is Self-Sufficient in His essence, Generous in His essence. Abandoning the Self-Sufficient, Generous One and going to the poor, needy one is forbidden by clear reason.

Having understood this, we say: It has been stated earlier in this book that the original meaning of walī in the language is: the one who is near. We have mentioned the aspects of its derivations. So His saying: ﴿Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?⟩ forbids nearness to other than Allah, exalted is He. This requires purifying the heart from turning toward other than Allah, exalted is He, and cutting off attachments to everything other than Allah, exalted is He.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to be the first to submit,⟩ and the reason is that the Prophet ﷺ is the foremost of his community in Islam

Page 141
because of His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to that, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am: 163], and Moses' saying: ﴿Glory be to You, I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾ [al-A'raf: 143].
* * *
Then He said: ﴿and do not be among the polytheists.⟩ Its meaning: I have been commanded to submit and forbidden from association. Then, when He, exalted is He, made clear that His Messenger was commanded to submit, then followed it with his being forbidden from polytheism, He said after it: ﴿Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.⟩ The purpose is that if I oppose Him in this command and prohibition, I become deserving of the great punishment.

If it is said: His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day﴾ indicates that he, peace be upon him, feared for himself from disbelief and disobedience; and if that were not permissible for him, he would not have been fearful.

The answer: The verse does not indicate that he feared for himself; rather the verse indicates that if disbelief and disobedience were to proceed from him, he would fear. This extent does not indicate the occurrence of fear. Its example is our saying: If five is even, it is divisible into two equal parts; this indicates that five is even, but not that it is divisible into two equal parts. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I fear﴾: Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read "innī" with a fatḥa on the yā'. Abu 'Amr and the rest read it with the yā' silent (sukun).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is spared it that Day, He has truly had mercy on him. That is the manifest triumph.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

First issue: Know that Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (yaṣrif) with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ra'. The subject of the verb (ṣarf) in this reading is the pronoun referring to "my Lord" in His saying: ﴿Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾. The implied sense is: whoever He turns away from him that Day, namely the punishment.

The proof for this reading is His saying: (faqad raḥimahu, "then He has truly had mercy on him"). Since this is a verb attributed to the pronoun of the Name of God Exalted, it is necessary that the matter in the other word be in this form too, so that the two verbs agree. On this reading, the turning away of the punishment is attributed to God Exalted, and the mercy after it is likewise attributed to God Exalted. As for the others, they read: ﴿man yuṣrafʿanhu﴾ with the passive form of the verb (fiʿl mā lam yusamma fāʿiluh, the verb whose subject is not named), and the implied sense is: whoever has the punishment of that Day turned away from him. This is acceptable because He Exalted attributed the punishment to the Day in His saying: ﴿the punishment of a tremendous Day﴾. Therefore He attributed the turning away to it. The implied sense is: whoever has the punishment of that Day turned away from him.

Second issue: The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the Day itself be what is turned away, and that is impossible. Rather, what is meant is the punishment of that Day, and this omission is acceptable because it is known.

* * *

Third issue: The verse indicates that obedience does not necessitate reward, and disobedience does not necessitate punishment, because He Exalted said: ﴿Whoever is spared it that Day, He has truly had mercy on him﴾, meaning: everyone from whom God turns away the punishment on that Day has truly been shown mercy by Him. This is only fitting if that turning away occurs by way of grace (tafaddul). But if it were obligatory and due, it would not be proper to say of it that He had mercy on him. Do you not see that if it is ugly for a master to strike his servant, then when he does not strike him, it is not said that he has shown him mercy? But when it is good for him to strike him and he does not strike him, then it is said that he has shown him mercy. So this verse indicates that every punishment that is averted and every reward that is attained is, in its origin, a grace and a bounty from God Exalted. This agrees with what is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one among people will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His mercy." And he placed his hand above his head, and prolonged his voice with it.

* * *

Fourth issue: The judge (al-Qadi, ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: The verse indicates that whoever is not punished in the Hereafter among those from whom punishment is turned away must necessarily be rewarded. This refutes the saying of those who claim that among the responsible persons from whom punishment is turned away there are some who are not rewarded, but He graces them.

If it is objected: Is it not the case that whoever God does not punish and graces is one to whom the manifest triumph has come, and this would refute the indication of the verse for your view?

We say: What you have mentioned is rebutted in several respects:

The first: that grace (tafaddul) is like a beginning from God Exalted, and this is not something sought from the act, while triumph (fawz) is attaining what is sought, so it must yield something sought.

The second: that the manifest triumph cannot be interpreted as grace, but must be interpreted as what implies an emphasis on the greatness of the blessing, and that is only reward.

The third: that the verse is coordinated with His saying: ﴿Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day﴾, and the counterpart of punishment is reward, so this mercy must be interpreted as reward.

Know that this argument is very weak, and its weakness is evident, so there is no need to go into it at length. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is another proof demonstrating that it is not permissible for a rational person to take other than Allah as a protector (waliyy). Its explanation is that harm (ḍarr) is a name for pain, grief and fear, and whatever leads to them or to one of them. Benefit (naf') is a name for pleasure, delight, and whatever leads to them or to one of them. Good (khayr) is a name for the common quality between repelling harm and attaining benefit. When this is the case, the restriction is established: a person is either in harm or in good, because the removal of harm is good, whether or not pleasure is attained in it. Once this restriction is established, Allah the Exalted has made clear that minor and major harms are not repelled except by Allah, and that minor and major goods are not attained except by Allah. The proof that this is so is that what exists is either necessary in its own essence (wajib li-dhatihi) or possible in its own essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). As for what is necessary in its own essence, it is one; therefore everything other than it is possible in its own essence, and what is possible in its own essence does not exist except through the bringing-into-being of the necessary in its own essence. Everything other than the Truth has come into being only through the bringing-into-being and creation of the Truth. Thus it is established that the repelling of all harms is not achieved except by Him, and the attaining of all goods and benefits is not except by Him. Through this clear rational proof, the correctness of what the verse indicates is established.

If it is said: We see that a person repels harms from himself by his wealth and by his helpers and supporters, and good comes to him through his own earning and through the help of others, and that undermines the generality of the verse. Also, the head of harms is disbelief, so it must be said that it is not repelled except by the help of Allah the Exalted. And the head of goods is faith, so it must be said that it is not attained except by the bringing-into-being of Allah the Exalted. If the matter were so, a person should not deserve punishment for committing disbelief, nor reward for committing faith. Also, we see that a person benefits by taking medicine and is harmed by consuming poisons, and all of this undermines the apparent meaning of the verse.

The answer to the first: every act that proceeds from a person proceeds from him only when a motive (dā'ī) calls him to it, because an act without a motive is impossible, and the existence of that motive is nothing but from Allah the Exalted. On this basis, the whole is from Allah the Exalted, and the same applies to every one of the questions you have raised.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, mentioned the touching of harm and the touching of good, but He distinguished the first from the second in two respects:

The first: He, exalted is He, placed the mention of the touching of harm before the mention of the touching of good, and this is an alert that all harms must be followed by good and safety.

The second: He said regarding the touching of harm ﴿there is none to remove it except Him﴾, and regarding the touching of good He mentioned ﴿then He is over all things competent﴾. So for good He mentioned His being capable of all things, and this indicates that Allah's will to bring about goods prevails over His will to bring about harms. All these doubts together indicate that the side of Allah's mercy prevails in His will, as He said: "My mercy has preceded My wrath."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the attributes of perfection are confined to power and knowledge. If they say: "How then did you omit necessary existence (wujub al-wujud)?"

We say: That is identical with the essence, not an attribute subsisting in the essence. For an attribute subsisting in the essence depends on the essence, and what depends on the essence depends on something other than it; so it would be possible in its own essence and necessary through something else. This would entail that a necessity arises before necessity, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that it is identical with the essence. It is also established that the attributes which are perfections are in reality power and knowledge. So His saying, ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾, indicates the perfection of power, and His saying, ﴿and He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾, indicates the perfection of knowledge. His saying, ﴿And He is the Subduer﴾, implies restriction (qasr), meaning that no one is described with the perfection of power and the perfection of knowledge except the Real, glorified is He. At this point it becomes evident that there is no one perfect except Him, and everyone other than Him is deficient.

Having understood this, we say: As for the indication of His being Subduer regarding power, it is because we have shown that everything other than the Real, glorified is He, is possible in existence in its own essence, and what is possible in its own essence does not have its existence preponderate over its non-existence, nor its non-existence over its existence, except through His preponderance, determination, bringing into existence and origination. So in reality He is the One who subdues the possibilities, at times on the side of preponderance of existence over non-existence, and at times on the side of preponderance of non-existence over existence. Within this category falls His subduing them by death, poverty and humiliation, and within it falls

page 144
all that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26] to the end of the verse. As for His being Wise, it is not possible to interpret it here as knowledge, because "the All-Aware" indicates knowledge, so repetition would follow, and that is not permissible. Therefore it must be interpreted as His being ordering (muhkam) in His acts, meaning that His acts are firmly ordered, perfected, safe from all forms of defect and corruption. And the Khabir (All-Aware) is the one who knows a thing that is reported. Al-Wahidi said: Its interpretation is that He is the one who knows what may be reported. He said: Khabar is your knowledge of a thing; you say: "I have khabar of it," meaning knowledge, and its origin is from khabar, because it is one of the paths of knowledge.

* * *

The second issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) used this verse to argue that He, exalted is He, exists in the direction which is above the world, and this is rejected. Several points prove this:

The first: If He were existing above the world, He would either be so small that no part of Him is distinguished from another part, or He would be extended, spreading in the directions and dimensions.

The first entails that He would be in smallness and insignificance like an indivisible atom. If that were permissible, why would it not be permissible that the God of the world be some of the particles mixed with the dust motes lying in the window of a house? No intelligent person would say that. And if the second, then He would be divisible and partible, and that is impossible for God.

The second: He is either infinite from all directions, and then increase and decrease would be applicable to Him. Whatever is like that, its being specified with its determined quantity is by the specification of a specifier, so it is originated. Or He is finite from some sides and not others, so the side described as finite is other than the side described as infinite, and that entails division and partition.

The third: Place is either explained as the enclosing surface or as extension and void. If it is the first, we say: The bodies of the world are finite, so outside the world there is no void, no plenum, no place, no "where," and no direction, and therefore the presence of the essence of Allah, the Exalted, there is impossible. If it is the second, we say: The void is equal in its parts in its reality, and if that is so, then if it were valid for Allah to be present in one part of that void, it would be valid for Him to be present in all the other parts. And if that were so, then His presence in it would be by the specification of a specifier, and whatever is done by a choosing agent is originated, so the presence of His essence in the part is originated. His essence does not separate from that presence, and what does not separate from the originated is itself originated, so it would follow that His essence is originated, and that is impossible.

The fourth: Extension and void are things capable of division and partition, and whatever is like that is possible in its essence and needs an originator, and its originator would be prior to it, so the essence of Allah, the Exalted, would have existed before the existence of the void, the direction, the "where," and the space.

Once this is established: after space, direction and void, the essence of Allah, the Exalted, must remain as it was; otherwise change would have occurred in the essence of Allah, the Exalted, and that is impossible.

Once this is established, it is necessary to affirm that He is exalted above spaces and directions at all times.

The fifth: It has been established that the world is a sphere, and once this is established, whatever is above the heads of the people of Rayy is beneath the feet of other people.

Once this is established: either it is said that He, exalted is He, is above specific peoples, or it is said that He, exalted is He, is above all. The first is invalid, because His being above some entails His being beneath others, and that is invalid. The second entails that He, exalted is He, encompasses the sphere of the heavens, and so the outcome becomes that the God of the world is a heavenly sphere encompassing all the spheres, and no Muslim says that.

The sixth: The word "above" (fawqiyyah) in this verse is preceded by one word and followed by another. As for being preceded, it is preceded by the word "the Subduer," and "the Subduer" indicates perfection of power and completeness of capacity. As for being followed by a word, it is followed by His saying: "His servants," and this word indicates being owned and being subject to power, so that "above" must be taken to mean the "aboveness" of power, not the "aboveness" of direction.

page 145
If it is said: What you have mentioned is the opposite of your own statement, that His saying, ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾, indicates the perfection of power. So if we take the word "above" to mean aboveness of power, it would entail repetition, and therefore it must be taken to mean aboveness of place and direction.

We say: The matter is not as you have said, because the essence may be described as subduing some and not others, and His saying, ﴿over His servants﴾, indicates that this subduing and power is general with respect to all.

The seventh: When He mentioned this verse as a rebuttal to those who take other than Allah as a protector, the implication is as if He said: He, exalted is He, is above all His servants, and when the matter is so, it is impossible to take other than Allah as a protector. This conclusion can only properly be built upon those aboveness-statements if the intended aboveness is aboveness by power and might. As for if the intended aboveness were aboveness of direction, that would not serve this purpose, because merely being located in a direction above does not necessarily entail that reliance upon Him in all matters is beneficial, or that return to Him in all demands is required. But when we take it to mean aboveness of power, this conclusion is rightly built upon it. Thus it becomes evident from the totality of what we have mentioned that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned, not what the anthropomorphists mentioned. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "Allah is Witness between me and you. This Qur'an was revealed to me that I may warn you by it, and whomever it reaches." Do you indeed bear witness that there are other gods with Allah?" Say: "I do not bear witness." Say: "He is only one God, and I am free of what you associate."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the verse indicates that the greatest and most mighty of testimonies is the testimony of Allah, exalted is He. Then He explained that the testimony of Allah is established, but the verse does not indicate in which of the matters that testimony was established. So we say: it is possible that what is meant is the establishment of Allah's testimony to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and it is possible that what is meant is the establishment of this testimony to the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

As for the first possibility: Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the leaders of the people of Mecca said: "O Muhammad, Allah did not find anyone other than you as a messenger! We do not see anyone who believes you. We asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that there is no mention of you among them concerning prophethood. So show us someone who will testify for you to prophethood." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse and said: Say, O Muhammad: "What thing is greater as testimony than Allah, so that they acknowledge prophethood?" For the greatest of things as testimony is Allah, glorified and exalted is He. So when they acknowledge that, say: "Allah is witness for me to prophethood, for He revealed this Qur'an to me, and this Qur'an is a miracle, because you are the eloquent and the masters of rhetoric, and you have been unable to produce its like. So if it is a miracle, then Allah's manifesting it in accordance with my claim is a testimony from Allah that I am truthful in my claim." The summary: they asked for an acceptable witness who would testify to his prophethood, so He, exalted is He, made clear that the greatest of things as testimony is Allah, then made clear that He testified to his prophethood, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "Allah is Witness"﴾. This is a clear explanation.

As for the second possibility: that what is meant is the establishment of this testimony to the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

Know that this discussion must be preceded by a premise, which is: we say that matters are of three categories. Among them are those whose establishment is impossible by transmitted (scriptural) proofs, for everything upon whose soundness the soundness of transmission depends cannot be established by transmission, otherwise circularity would follow. Among them are those whose establishment is impossible by reason, which is everything whose existence and non-existence are both rationally possible, so there is no impossibility in either side at all; therefore, certainty about one of the two sides specifically is not possible except by transmitted proof. And among them are those whose establishment is possible both by reason and by transmission together, which is every rational matter whose knowledge does not depend on something else, so it is therefore possible to establish it by transmitted proofs.

Having known this, we say: His saying, ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "Allah is Witness between me and you"﴾ is about establishing the oneness, and the disavowal of partners, rivals, equals, likes and similars.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "Allah is Witness"﴾, meaning: the affirmation of tawhid is the true and obligatory position, and the affirmation of shirk is false and rejected.

The second issue: It is reported from Jahm that he denied that Allah, exalted is He, is a "thing" (shay').

Know that he did not dispute that Allah, exalted is He, is an existing essence and reality, but he denied naming Him, exalted is He, as a "thing," so this is a dispute only over wording. The majority argued for naming Allah as "a thing" from this verse, and its argument is that He said: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Then in answering this question He mentioned His saying: "Allah," and this necessitates that He, exalted is He, is a thing, just as if one said: "Which of people is most truthful?" and it was said: "Gabriel," this answer would be wrong, because Gabriel is not among people; so likewise here.

If it is said: His saying, ﴿Allah is Witness between me and you﴾ is a complete, independent sentence that has no connection to what precedes it, because His saying "Allah" is a subject, and His saying "is Witness between me and you" is its predicate, and it is a complete sentence independent in itself, with no connection to what comes before it.

We say: the answer is in two ways:

The first: We say that His saying, ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?"﴾ is without doubt a question, and it must have an answer, either stated or omitted.

If we say the answer is omitted, we say: this is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, even if the answer is omitted, that omitted part must be something indicated by what is stated and suitable to that place.

The answer suitable to His saying, ﴿What thing is greatest as testimony?﴾ is that it is said: "It is Allah," and then it is said after it: ﴿Allah is Witness between me and you﴾. On this reading, it is also valid to use this verse as evidence that He, exalted is He, is named by the name "thing." This completes the explanation of this proof.

Page 147
There is another proof on this issue, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The meaning of "His Face" is His essence. This indicates that He, exalted is He, excepted His own self from His saying "everything," and the excepted item must be included within what it is excepted from, so this indicates that He, exalted is He, is named by the name "thing."

Jahm argued against the validity of this name with several arguments:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. The meaning would be: there is nothing like His like, and the essence of each thing is like the like of its own self. So this is an explicit statement that Allah, exalted is He, is not named by the name "thing." And one cannot say that the kaf is superfluous, with the sense: "nothing like Him," because making a word of the words of the Qur'an meaningless and void is not befitting for people of religion to resort to, except in extreme necessity.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Creator of everything﴾ [al-Zumar: 62].

If He were named "thing," it would follow that He is the creator of Himself, which is impossible and cannot be said. It is said: this is a general expression that has been subject to specification. We reply: specification is permissible only in a rare, anomalous case that is not regarded or paid attention to, so its existence is treated as its non-existence, and the word "all" is applied to the majority as an indication that the remainder is treated as nonexistent. And it is known that if the Creator, exalted is He, were named by the name "thing," He would be the greatest and most noble of things, and applying the word "all" while this category is excluded from it would be pure falsehood, not a case of specification.

The third: the use of His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. A name is only beautiful because its named referent is beautiful, namely that it indicates an attribute of perfection and a description of majesty. The word "thing" is the most general of all things, so its referent is found in the best and the most vile of things, and whenever that is so, the thing named by this word is not an attribute of perfection nor a description of majesty. Therefore it is necessary that it is not permissible to call upon Allah, exalted is He, by this name; since this name is not among the most beautiful names, and Allah, exalted is He, commanded that He be called upon by the most beautiful names, it is necessary that it is not permissible to call upon Allah, exalted is He, by this name. And everyone who forbade calling upon Allah by this name said: this word is not at all one of the names of Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth: that the name "thing" encompasses the non-existent, so it is necessary that it is not permissible to apply it to Allah, exalted is He.

The explanation of the first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23]. He called what he would do tomorrow by the name "thing" in the present, and what he will do tomorrow is non-existent at present, so this shows that the name "thing" applies to the non-existent.

And if this is established, then our saying that He is a thing does not convey the distinction of His essence from all other essences by a known attribute or a distinguishing particularity, nor does it convey that He exists; so this would be a word conveying no benefit at all with respect to Allah, exalted is He, and so it would be pure futility, and therefore it is necessary, or not permissible, to apply it to Allah, exalted is He.

The answer to these arguments is to say: since the proofs conflict, we say: the word "thing" is the most general of words, and whenever the specific is true, the general is true. So whenever it is true of Him that He is an essence and reality, it must be true of Him that He is a thing, and that is what was to be proven. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿This Qur'an was revealed to me that I may warn you by it, and whomever it reaches﴾, the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, revealed this Qur'an to me so that I may warn you by it, and this is addressed to the people of Mecca. His saying "and whomever it reaches" is a conjunction with those addressed from the people of Mecca, i.e., that I may warn you by it, and that I may warn everyone whom the Qur'an reaches from the Arabs and non-Arabs. It has been said: from both humans and jinn; and it has been said: whoever it reaches until the Day of Resurrection. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he saw Muhammad ﷺ. On this interpretation there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the implied wording is: "and I was revealed this Qur'an that I may warn you by it, and whomever this Qur'an reaches." However, this returning pronoun is omitted, being indicated by the context,

Page 148
as one says: "The one whom I saw is Zayd," and "The one whom I struck is 'Amr." There is another interpretation of His saying "and whomever it reaches," namely that His saying "and whomever it reaches" means "and whoever has reached puberty (ihtalama) and reached the age of legal responsibility (taklif)." According to this, there is no need to posit an omitted returning pronoun. However, the majority holds the first view.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿Do you indeed bear witness that there are other gods with Allah?" Say: "I do not bear witness." Say: "He is only one God, and I am free of what you associate"﴾, we say: there are two points of discussion in it:

The first point of discussion: Ibn Kathir read "a'innakum" with a hamza, then a light kasra after it resembling a silent ya', without a madd; Abu 'Amr and Qalun from Nafi' read the same, except that he elongates (madd); and the rest read with two hamzas, without madd.

The second point of discussion: This is an interrogative whose meaning is denial and rejection. Al-Farra' said: "Another" was not said, because "gods" (alihah) is a plural, and the plural may take the feminine, as He said: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180], and He said: ﴿Then what of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51], and did not say "the first" nor "the first ones." All of that is correct.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "I do not bear witness." Say: "He is only one God, and I am free of what you associate"﴾

Know that this statement indicates the obligation of tawhid and disavowal of shirk in three ways:

The first: His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not bear witness"﴾, meaning: I do not bear witness to what you mention of establishing partners.

The second: His saying: ﴿Say: "He is only one God"﴾. The particle "innama" (only) conveys restriction, and the word "one" is explicit in tawhid and the negation of partners.

The third: His saying: ﴿and I am free of what you associate﴾, which is an explicit declaration of disavowal of establishing partners. Thus the indication of this verse on the obligation of tawhid is established by the greatest methods of explanation and the most eloquent forms of emphasis. The scholars said: it is recommended for one who embraces Islam at the outset to utter the two testimonies and to disavow every religion other than the religion of Islam. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, stated explicitly that it is recommended to add disavowal (tabarri) to the testimony, based on His saying: ﴿and I am free of what you associate﴾ immediately after the explicit declaration of tawhid.

He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾.

Know that in the previous verse we have related that the disbelievers asked the Jews and the Christians about the description of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and they denied that the Torah and the Gospel indicate his prophethood. So God, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse that God's testimony to the truth of his prophethood is sufficient for its establishment and confirmation. Then in this verse He explained that they lied in their claim that "we do not know Muhammad, peace be upon him," because they recognize him through prophethood and messengership just as they recognize their sons. This is according to what is narrated: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, Umar said to Abdullah ibn Salam: "God has sent down to His Prophet this verse, so what is this recognition?" He said: "O Umar, I recognized him among you when I saw him just as I recognize my son, and I am more certain of Muhammad than of my son, because I do not know what women have done, and I testify that he is truth from God, exalted is He."

[Page 149]

Know that the apparent meaning of this verse requires that their knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, be like their knowledge of their sons. There is an objection to this, which is to say: What is written in the Torah and the Gospel is either merely that a prophet will appear at the end of time calling people to the true religion, or what is written in it is this meaning together with the specification of the time, the place, the lineage, the attribute, the physical description and the form. If it is the first, then that degree alone does not indicate that this person is Muhammad, peace be upon him, so how can it be correct to say: their knowledge of his prophethood is like their knowledge of the sonship of their sons? If it is the second, then it must be that all the Jews and Christians know necessarily from the Torah and the Gospel that Muhammad, peace be upon him, is a prophet from God, exalted is He, and lying against a great multitude is not permissible, because we know necessarily that the Torah and the Gospel did not contain these complete and perfect details. For this detail either is said to have remained in the Torah and the Gospel at the time of the Messenger's appearance, peace be upon him, or it is said that these details did not remain in the Torah and the Gospel at the time of his appearance because distortion (tahrif) had reached them before that. The first is false, because concealing such complete details in a book that reached the people of the East and the West is impossible. The second is also false, because on this assumption the Jews and Christians of that time were not knowing of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) as they know the sonship of their sons, and then this statement falls.

The answer to the first: it is said that what is meant by ﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾ is the Jews and the Christians, and they were capable of reflection and inference (nazar wa istidlal), and they had witnessed the manifestation of miracles (mu'jizat, signs that confirm prophethood) upon the Messenger, peace be upon him. So through those miracles they knew that he was a messenger from God. The purpose of comparing one of the two kinds of knowledge with the second kind is only this degree that we have mentioned.

As for His saying: ﴿those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

The first: that His saying "those" (alladhina) is a qualifier of the first "those," so their governing element is one, and the intended meaning is the threat against the obstinate who recognize and yet deny.

The second: that His saying "those who have lost their souls" is a subject (mubtada'), and His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ is its predicate (khabar). Regarding His saying ﴿those who have lost﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: that they lost their souls in the sense of the everlasting destruction that befell them because of disbelief.

The second: it has come in the exegesis that there is no disbeliever or believer except that he has a station in Paradise. So whoever disbelieves, his station passes to whoever embraces Islam, and so he has lost himself and his family, in that his station is inherited by another.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾ ﴿And the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, passed judgment on those deniers with loss in the first verse, He explained in this verse the cause of that loss, which is two matters:

The first of them is that one fabricates a lie against Allah, and this fabrication has several aspects:

The first: the disbelievers of Makkah used to say: "These idols are partners of Allah, and Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded us to worship them and draw near to them." They also used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Then they attributed to Allah the prohibition of the baheerah and the saa'ibah.

The second: the Jews and the Christians used to say that it is established in the Torah and the Gospel that these two laws are not subject to abrogation (naskh) or alteration, and that no prophet will come after them.

The third: what Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us with it."﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

The fourth: the Jews used to say: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and they used to say: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80].

The fifth: some of their ignorant ones used to say: "Allah is poor and we are rich," and similar falsehoods that they attributed to Allah are many, and all of them are fabrications from them against Allah.

The second type of the causes of their loss is their denial of the signs of Allah. What is meant by it is their disparagement of the miracles of Muhammad (ﷺ), their slander concerning them, and their denial that the Qur'an is a overpowering, manifest miracle. Then, when He, may He be exalted, related these two matters about them, He said: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾, meaning they will not attain their aims in this world or in the Hereafter, but will remain in deprivation and abandonment.

As for His saying: ﴿And the Day We gather them all﴾, regarding the governing element of His saying "and the Day" (wa-yawma), there are several opinions:

The first: it is omitted, and its estimate is "and the Day We gather them was such-and-such," and it was left out so that it would remain in vagueness, which is more effective in instilling fear.

The second: the estimate is "remember the Day We gather them."

The third: that it is conjoined to an omitted element, as if it were said: "The wrongdoers will never succeed, and the Day We gather them."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾, the intent of it is rebuke and reproach, not inquiry. It is possible that its meaning is "Where are the partners themselves?" and it is possible that the intended meaning is "Where is their intercession for you and your benefit from them?" On both aspects, the speech is nothing but reproach, censure, and affirmation in their souls that what they used to presume has been despaired of, and this becomes a warning for them in the abode of this world about the corruption of this way. The relative pronoun's returning element in His saying ﴿whom you used to claim﴾ is omitted, and the estimate is: "whom you used to claim that they are intercessors," so the object of "claim" has been omitted because the question indicates it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Every claim in the Book of Allah is a lie."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 23–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then their temptation will be only that they will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ ﴿See how they lie against themselves, and what they used to invent has strayed away from them.﴾

Know that there are several issues here:

The first issue: Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read ﴿thumma lam takun fitnatuhum﴾ with a taʾ marked from above (tāʾ munqaṭah min fawq) and fitnatuhum in the nominative (marfūʿ). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read thumma lam yakun with a yāʾ and fitnatahum in the accusative (manṣūb). As for the reading with the taʾ marked from above and the accusative of fitnah, here the phrase "an qālū" (that they said) is in the nominative position, being the subject (ism) of takun. It is feminine because the predicate is feminine, as in the saying "man kānat ummuka" (who your mother was). Or because what they said is, in meaning, a temptation (fitnah). It is also permissible to interpret "illā an qālū" as "illā maqālatuhum" (except their statement). As for the reading with the yāʾ marked from below and the accusative of fitnatahum, here the phrase "an qālū" is in the nominative position, being the subject of yakun, and fitnatahum is the predicate. Al-Wāḥidī said: the preferred reading is that of the one who makes "an qālū" the subject rather than the predicate, because when "an" is joined to a verb it cannot be described, and so it resembles a pronoun in being impossible to qualify. Just as when a noun and a pronoun come together, making the pronoun the subject is preferable to making it the predicate, so too here. You say, "kunta al-qāʾima" (I was the standing one), making the pronoun the subject and the noun the predicate; so also here. We say that the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, "wallāhi rabbanā," with the accusative of rabbanā, is for two reasons:
The first: by an implied verb, "aʿnī" (I mean) and "adhkuru" (I mention).
The second: as a vocative, that is, "wallāhi yā rabbanā" (by Allah, O our Lord). The rest read it with a kasrah on the bāʾ, making it an attribute (ṣifah) of Allah, exalted is He.

The second issue: al-Zajjāj said: the interpretation of this verse is good in the language, and none knows it except one who knows the meanings of speech and the varied usages of the Arabs in this. That is because Allah, exalted is He, had shown that the polytheists were tempted by their shirk and were consumed with love of it. So in this verse He informs that their temptation with their shirk, and their persistence in it, was only that they disavowed it and distanced themselves from it, and so they swore that they had not been polytheists. An example: you see a person who loves a disreputable man of bad character, and when he falls into trouble because of him he disowns him, and it is said to him, "Your love for so-and-so was not but that you dissociated yourself from him." So the meaning of temptation here is their being tempted by the idols. This interpretation is reinforced by what ʿAṭāʾ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he said: ﴿thumma lam takun fitnatuhum﴾ means "their shirk in the world." This statement reverts to an elision of a modifier, because the meaning is: "Then the outcome of their temptation will not be but disavowal." A similar example is your saying, "Your love for so-and-so was not but that you fled from him and abandoned him."

* * *

The third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse implies that they swore on the Day of Resurrection that they had not been polytheists, and this implies that they dared to lie on the Day of Resurrection. Scholars differ on this in two positions:

The first: this is the view of Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and al-Qāḍī: that the people of the Resurrection cannot dare to lie. They argued for this with several arguments:

The first: the people of the Resurrection know Allah by necessity (bi'l-iḍṭirār), for if they knew Him by reasoning, the place of standing on the Resurrection would become a place of obligation, and that is false. And if they know Allah by necessity, it must be that they are compelled to not commit ugly acts, in the sense that if they sought to commit an ugly act, Allah would prevent them from it; for with the removal of obligation, if this meaning did not obtain, that would be letting them loose to commit ugly acts, and that is not permissible. It is thus established that the people of the Resurrection know Allah by necessity, and it is established that whenever this is so, they are compelled to abandon ugly acts, and that implies that none of the people of the Resurrection dares to commit an ugly act.

If it is said: why is it not permissible to say that it is not permissible for them to commit ugly acts, given that they are rational? We say: why is it not permissible to say that this lie did occur from them, because when they witnessed the terrors of the Resurrection their intellects were disturbed, so they uttered this false statement while their intellects were impaired? Or it may be said that they forgot that they were polytheists in the world.

The answer to the first: it is not permissible for Him, exalted is He, to gather them and direct the rebuke at them with His saying, "Where are your partners?" and then relate of them what amounts to an excuse while they are non-rational, because this does not befit the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He. Moreover, those who are obligated must be rational on the Day of Resurrection, so that they may know that in what Allah deals with them they are not wronged.

The answer to the second: forgetting what they were upon in the abode of the world while in full possession of reason is remote, because a rational person cannot forget such states, however long the time has been. A person can forget only trivial matters. Were it not so, we would allow that a rational person had held great offices for a long time and yet forgot them, and it is known that permitting this leads to sophistry.

The second argument: the people who dared that lie either were not rational or were rational. If we say they were not rational, that is false, because it does not befit the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, to relate the speech of madmen in the context of pleading an excuse. And if we say they were rational, then they know that Allah, exalted is He, is Knowing of their states and Aware of their deeds, and they know that permitting a lie about Allah is impossible, and that they gain from that lie nothing but increased hatred and wrath. When this is the case, their daring in such a state to lie is ruled out.

The third argument: if they lied on the standing of the Resurrection and then swore to that lie, they would have committed these two kinds of ugliness and sin, and that entails punishment, and so the Hereafter would become a place of obligation; and they have agreed that the matter is not so. As for saying that they do not deserve punishment or blame for that lie and that false oath, this implies that Allah, exalted is He, has granted permission to commit ugly acts and sins, and that is false. Thus by these arguments it is established that the people of the Resurrection are not permitted to dare ugly acts and lies.

Once this is established, they say that His saying, ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists,﴾ is to be understood as: "we were not polytheists in our belief and our assumptions," because the people used to believe of themselves that they were monotheists, distant from shirk.

If it is said: on this interpretation they would be truthful in what they reported, since they reported that they were not polytheists in their own estimation; so why did Allah, exalted is He, say, ﴿See how they lie against themselves﴾? Our answer: what is contained in His saying, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ does not include that they lied in what was mentioned earlier, His saying, ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists,﴾ so that this question would bind us. Rather, it is permissible that the meaning is: "See how they lied against themselves in the abode of the world, in matters they used to report about, such as their claim that they were upon correctness and that what they were upon was not shirk." Lying is possible of them in the abode of the world, and it is only negated of them in the Hereafter. The summary is that the purpose of His saying, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ is the difference between the two states: that in the abode of the world they used to lie and not guard against it, while in the Hereafter they guard against lying, but at a time when truthfulness no longer benefits them. Since one of the two matters is connected to the other, Allah, exalted is He, showed this to the Messenger, and made clear how the state of these people, because of their shirk, will be in the Hereafter when they make excuses, while in the abode of the world they used to lie against themselves and claim that they were upon correctness. This is the substance of al-Qāḍī's speech in establishing the view chosen by Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī.

The second view, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes, is that the disbelievers do lie in this statement. They said: the evidence that disbelievers may lie on the Day of Resurrection consists of several points:

The first: He, exalted is He, related of them that they say, ﴿Our Lord, take us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers,﴾ while He, exalted is He, informed of them by His saying, ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden,﴾ [al-Anʿām: 28].

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they have something. Unquestionably, they are the liars,﴾ [al-Mujādilah: 18], after His saying, ﴿and they swear upon falsehood﴾ [al-Mujādilah: 14]. So He compared their lying in the Hereafter with their lying in the world.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, relating of them, ﴿One of them will say, "How long did you remain?" They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 113]. All of this indicates that at some times they dared to lie.

The fourth: His saying, relating of them, ﴿And they will call, "O Mālik, let your Lord decree upon us [our end]."﴾ while they knew that He, exalted is He, would not decree their release.

The fifth: that He, exalted is He, in this verse related of them that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists." To take this to mean that what is meant is "we were not polytheists in our assumptions and beliefs" contradicts the apparent sense. Then to take His saying after that, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ to mean that they lied in the world entails dismantling the arrangement of the verse, directing the beginning of the verse to the states of the Resurrection and its end to the states of the world, and this is extremely remote.

As for his saying, "either they lied in a state of full reason or in a state of diminished reason," we say: it is not far-fetched to say that when they witnessed the terrors of the Resurrection and beheld the causes of intense fear, their intellects were disturbed, so they uttered this speech at that time. As for his saying, "how does it befit the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, to relate what they said in a state of disturbed reason," this would produce intense fear upon hearing this speech while they were in the world, and the purpose of revealing these verses is nothing other than that.

As for his second point, that the obligated must be rational on the Day of Resurrection, we say: the disturbance of their reason for one hour, at the time they speak this speech, does not prevent their reason from being whole at all other times. This is the complete discussion of this issue, and Allah knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ what is meant is their denial that they were polytheists. And His saying, ﴿and what they used to invent has strayed away from them,﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon His saying, "they lied." Its estimated sense is: "and how what they used to invent, by worshipping the idols, has strayed away from them, so that it did not avail them anything at all." That is because they used to hope for the intercession of those idols and their support on their behalf.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then their temptation will be only that they will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ ﴿See how they lie against themselves, and what they used to invent has strayed away from them.﴾
