Just as when a noun and a pronoun come together, making the pronoun the subject is preferable to making it the predicate, so too here. You say, "kunta al-qāʾima" (I was the standing one), making the pronoun the subject and the noun the predicate; so also here. We say that the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, "wallāhi rabbanā," with the accusative of rabbanā, is for two reasons:
The first: by an implied verb, "aʿnī" (I mean) and "adhkuru" (I mention).
The second: as a vocative, that is, "wallāhi yā rabbanā" (by Allah, O our Lord). The rest read it with a kasrah on the bāʾ, making it an attribute (ṣifah) of Allah, exalted is He.

The second issue: al-Zajjāj said: the interpretation of this verse is good in the language, and none knows it except one who knows the meanings of speech and the varied usages of the Arabs in this. That is because Allah, exalted is He, had shown that the polytheists were tempted by their shirk and were consumed with love of it. So in this verse He informs that their temptation with their shirk, and their persistence in it, was only that they disavowed it and distanced themselves from it, and so they swore that they had not been polytheists. An example: you see a person who loves a disreputable man of bad character, and when he falls into trouble because of him he disowns him, and it is said to him, "Your love for so-and-so was not but that you dissociated yourself from him." So the meaning of temptation here is their being tempted by the idols. This interpretation is reinforced by what ʿAṭāʾ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he said: ﴿thumma lam takun fitnatuhum﴾ means "their shirk in the world." This statement reverts to an elision of a modifier, because the meaning is: "Then the outcome of their temptation will not be but disavowal." A similar example is your saying, "Your love for so-and-so was not but that you fled from him and abandoned him."

* * *

The third issue: The apparent meaning of the verse implies that they swore on the Day of Resurrection that they had not been polytheists, and this implies that they dared to lie on the Day of Resurrection. Scholars differ on this in two positions:

The first: this is the view of Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and al-Qāḍī: that the people of the Resurrection cannot dare to lie. They argued for this with several arguments:

The first: the people of the Resurrection know Allah by necessity (bi'l-iḍṭirār), for if they knew Him by reasoning, the place of standing on the Resurrection would become a place of obligation, and that is false. And if they know Allah by necessity, it must be that they are compelled to not commit ugly acts, in the sense that if they sought to commit an ugly act, Allah would prevent them from it; for with the removal of obligation, if this meaning did not obtain, that would be letting them loose to commit ugly acts, and that is not permissible. It is thus established that the people of the Resurrection know Allah by necessity, and it is established that whenever this is so, they are compelled to abandon ugly acts, and that implies that none of the people of the Resurrection dares to commit an ugly act.

If it is said: why is it not permissible to say that it is not permissible for them to commit ugly acts, given that they are rational? We say: why is it not permissible to say that this lie did occur from them, because when they witnessed the terrors of the Resurrection their intellects were disturbed, so they uttered this false statement while their intellects were impaired? Or it may be said that they forgot that they were polytheists in the world.

The answer to the first: it is not permissible for Him, exalted is He, to gather them and direct the rebuke at them with His saying, "Where are your partners?" and then relate of them what amounts to an excuse while they are non-rational, because this does not befit the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He. Moreover, those who are obligated must be rational on the Day of Resurrection, so that they may know that in what Allah deals with them they are not wronged.

The answer to the second: forgetting what they were upon in the abode of the world while in full possession of reason is remote, because a rational person cannot forget such states, however long the time has been. A person can forget only trivial matters. Were it not so, we would allow that a rational person had held great offices for a long time and yet forgot them, and it is known that permitting this leads to sophistry.

The second argument: the people who dared that lie either were not rational or were rational. If we say they were not rational, that is false, because it does not befit the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, to relate the speech of madmen in the context of pleading an excuse. And if we say they were rational, then they know that Allah, exalted is He, is Knowing of their states and Aware of their deeds, and they know that permitting a lie about Allah is impossible, and that they gain from that lie nothing but increased hatred and wrath. When this is the case, their daring in such a state to lie is ruled out.

The third argument: if they lied on the standing of the Resurrection and then swore to that lie, they would have committed these two kinds of ugliness and sin, and that entails punishment, and so the Hereafter would become a place of obligation; and they have agreed that the matter is not so. As for saying that they do not deserve punishment or blame for that lie and that false oath, this implies that Allah, exalted is He, has granted permission to commit ugly acts and sins, and that is false. Thus by these arguments it is established that the people of the Resurrection are not permitted to dare ugly acts and lies.

Once this is established, they say that His saying, ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists,﴾ is to be understood as: "we were not polytheists in our belief and our assumptions," because the people used to believe of themselves that they were monotheists, distant from shirk.

If it is said: on this interpretation they would be truthful in what they reported, since they reported that they were not polytheists in their own estimation; so why did Allah, exalted is He, say, ﴿See how they lie against themselves﴾? Our answer: what is contained in His saying, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ does not include that they lied in what was mentioned earlier, His saying, ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists,﴾ so that this question would bind us. Rather, it is permissible that the meaning is: "See how they lied against themselves in the abode of the world, in matters they used to report about, such as their claim that they were upon correctness and that what they were upon was not shirk." Lying is possible of them in the abode of the world, and it is only negated of them in the Hereafter. The summary is that the purpose of His saying, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ is the difference between the two states: that in the abode of the world they used to lie and not guard against it, while in the Hereafter they guard against lying, but at a time when truthfulness no longer benefits them. Since one of the two matters is connected to the other, Allah, exalted is He, showed this to the Messenger, and made clear how the state of these people, because of their shirk, will be in the Hereafter when they make excuses, while in the abode of the world they used to lie against themselves and claim that they were upon correctness. This is the substance of al-Qāḍī's speech in establishing the view chosen by Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī.

The second view, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes, is that the disbelievers do lie in this statement. They said: the evidence that disbelievers may lie on the Day of Resurrection consists of several points:

The first: He, exalted is He, related of them that they say, ﴿Our Lord, take us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers,﴾ while He, exalted is He, informed of them by His saying, ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden,﴾ [al-Anʿām: 28].

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they have something. Unquestionably, they are the liars,﴾ [al-Mujādilah: 18], after His saying, ﴿and they swear upon falsehood﴾ [al-Mujādilah: 14]. So He compared their lying in the Hereafter with their lying in the world.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, relating of them, ﴿One of them will say, "How long did you remain?" They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 113]. All of this indicates that at some times they dared to lie.

The fourth: His saying, relating of them, ﴿And they will call, "O Mālik, let your Lord decree upon us [our end]."﴾ while they knew that He, exalted is He, would not decree their release.

The fifth: that He, exalted is He, in this verse related of them that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists." To take this to mean that what is meant is "we were not polytheists in our assumptions and beliefs" contradicts the apparent sense. Then to take His saying after that, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ to mean that they lied in the world entails dismantling the arrangement of the verse, directing the beginning of the verse to the states of the Resurrection and its end to the states of the world, and this is extremely remote.

As for his saying, "either they lied in a state of full reason or in a state of diminished reason," we say: it is not far-fetched to say that when they witnessed the terrors of the Resurrection and beheld the causes of intense fear, their intellects were disturbed, so they uttered this speech at that time. As for his saying, "how does it befit the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, to relate what they said in a state of disturbed reason," this would produce intense fear upon hearing this speech while they were in the world, and the purpose of revealing these verses is nothing other than that.

As for his second point, that the obligated must be rational on the Day of Resurrection, we say: the disturbance of their reason for one hour, at the time they speak this speech, does not prevent their reason from being whole at all other times. This is the complete discussion of this issue, and Allah knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿See how they lie against themselves,﴾ what is meant is their denial that they were polytheists. And His saying, ﴿and what they used to invent has strayed away from them,﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon His saying, "they lied." Its estimated sense is: "and how what they used to invent, by worshipping the idols, has strayed away from them, so that it did not avail them anything at all." That is because they used to hope for the intercession of those idols and their support on their behalf.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed veils over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had explained the condition of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, He followed it with that which necessitates despair of the faith of some of them, so He said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: Abu Sufyan, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, Umayya and Ubayy, the two sons of Khalaf, al-Harith ibn 'Amir, and Abu Jahl were present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they listened to the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ). They said to al-Nadr: "What is Muhammad saying?" He said: "I do not know what he is saying, but I see him moving his lips and speaking the fables of the ancients, like what I used to tell you about the reports of the earlier generations." Abu Sufyan said: "Indeed, I see some of what he says as true." Abu Jahl said: "Never!" So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed veils over their hearts, lest they understand it﴾. And al-Akinna is the plural of kinan, which is that which shields a thing and covers it, like inan and a'inna; its verb is kananta and aknantu. As for His saying: (lest they understand it), al-Zajjaj said: the position of "an" is in the accusative as an object of purpose, and the meaning is: "We have placed veils over their hearts out of dislike that they should understand it." When the "lam" was omitted, the dislike was put in the accusative, and when the dislike was omitted, its accusative case passed to "an." As for His saying: ﴿and in their ears a deafness﴾, Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-Waqr is heaviness in the ear.

صفحة ١٥٤

The second issue: Our companions argued with this verse that He, may He be exalted, may turn a person away from faith, prevent him from it, and come between a man and it, because this verse indicates that He placed the heart within the covering that prevents it from faith, and that is what is sought. The Mu'tazila said: It is not possible to apply this verse to its apparent meaning, and the following points show this:

The first: He, may He be exalted, sent down the Qur'an only to be a proof for the Messenger against the disbelievers, not to be a proof for the disbelievers against the Messenger. If the intent of this verse were that He prevented the disbelievers from faith, they would be able to say to the Messenger: "Since Allah has decreed that He has prevented us from faith, why does He blame us for abandoning faith, and why does He call us to perform faith?"

The second: If He prevented them from faith and then called them to it, that would be imposing on the incapable, which is negated by clear reason and by His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqara: 286].

The third: He, may He be exalted, related the explicit statement of these words from the disbelievers in the context of blame, so He said: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are in coverings against that to which you call us, and in our ears is deafness"﴾, and He said in another verse: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised." Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqara: 88]. If Allah, may He be exalted, has related this doctrine from them in the context of blaming them, it is impossible for Him to mention it here in the context of rebuke and reproach, otherwise contradiction would follow.

The fourth: There is no dispute that the people were understanding, hearing and reasoning.

The fifth: This verse came in the context of blaming them for abandoning faith, and if this hindrance and prevention were from Allah, may He be exalted, they would not be blamed, but rather would be excused.

The sixth: His saying: ﴿until, when they come to you disputing﴾ indicates that they were understanding and distinguishing truth from falsehood. At this point they said that an interpretation is necessary, and it is of several kinds:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The people used to listen to the recitation of the Messenger (ﷺ) so that by hearing his recitation they might reach knowledge of his place at night, and then aim to kill him and harm him. At that time Allah, glory be to Him, would cast sleep upon their hearts, and this is what is meant by the veils, and He would make their hearing heavy so they could not hear that recitation because of that sleep, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and in our ears is deafness﴾.

The second: The person whom Allah knows will not believe and will die in disbelief, Allah marks his heart with a particular sign by which the angels deduce, on seeing it, that he will not believe, so that sign became an indication that they do not believe.

Once this is established, we say: it is not far-fetched to call that sign a covering and a preventing veil, although that sign in itself does not prevent faith.

The third interpretation: When they persisted in disbelief, obstinately insisted upon it and resolved upon it, their turning away from faith in such a state became like a covering preventing faith, so Allah mentioned the covering as a metaphor for this meaning.

The fourth interpretation: When He prevented them from the favours (lutf) which are only suitable to be bestowed upon one who has been guided, and He left them devoid of these because of their evil conduct, and entrusted their affair to themselves, it is not far-fetched that He attributes that to Himself, saying: ﴿and We have placed veils over their hearts﴾.

The fifth interpretation: That this statement came as a report of what they used to say: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are in coverings against that to which you call us, and in our ears is deafness"﴾.

The answer to the arguments they relied upon, to show that it is not possible to take the coverings and the deafness as meaning that Allah prevented them from faith, is that we say: rather, the clear rational proof establishes the correctness of this meaning. That is because the servant who committed disbelief, if he was not able to bring about faith, then our statement is correct that He is the One who compelled him to disbelief and prevented him from faith. As for if we say: the one capable of disbelief was capable of faith, then we say: it is impossible for that capacity to become the source of disbelief rather than faith, except when that motive is joined to it, and you have learned in this book that the combination of capacity with the motive necessitates the act. So disbelief, on this supposition, is from Allah, may He be exalted, and that motive that drives to disbelief is a covering of the heart against faith, and a deafness of the hearing against hearing the proofs of faith. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that the rational proof agrees with what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates.

And when the correctness of what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates has been established by rational evidence, it is obligatory to interpret this verse accordingly, acting upon both the proof and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾, mentioning it in the singular form, then He said: (upon their hearts), mentioning it in the plural form. This is fine because the form "man" is singular in wording and plural in meaning.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: and if they see every proof and argument, they will not believe in it, because Allah has placed veils over their hearts. This verse indicates the invalidity of the first interpretation that we related from al-Jubba'i. Also, if the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We have placed veils over their hearts﴾ were the casting of sleep upon the hearts of the disbelievers so that they could not reach his place by hearing his voice, then His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, and We have placed over their hearts﴾ would not fit this discourse. Furthermore, if the meaning were what al-Jubba'i mentioned, it would have been necessary to say: "And We have placed veils over their hearts, lest they hear it," because the purpose al-Jubba'i mentioned is only achieved by preventing them from hearing the voice of the Messenger, peace be upon him. As for preventing them from his speech itself and from understanding his intent, it has no connection to what al-Jubba'i mentioned. Thus the falsity of his statement is evident. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until, when they come to you disputing with you﴾, know that this statement is another sentence, arranged upon what precedes it, and "until" in this position is the one after which sentences occur. The sentence is His saying: ﴿when they come to you disputing with you﴾; "those who disbelieve say" and "disputing with you" are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). His saying: ﴿those who disbelieve say﴾ is an explanation of His saying: (disputing with you). The meaning is that their denial of the signs reached the point that they dispute with you and oppose you, and their disputing is explained by their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The root of asatir is from satr, which is to make a thing extended and composed, and from it comes satr of a book and satr of planted trees. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said satr and satar; whoever says satr, its plural for the few is asțur and for the many is sutur, and whoever says satar, its plural is asfar. Al-asatir is the plural of the plural. Al-Jubba'i said: the singular of asatir is usturah, usturat, siyr and siyra. Al-Zajjaj said: the singular of asatir is usturah, like ahadith and uhdutha. Abu Zayd said: asatir is among the plurals that have no singular, like 'abadid. Then the majority said: asatir al-awwalin is what the ancients wrote. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is the narratives of the ancients which they used to write down, that is, they used to inscribe them. As for the saying of one who explains asatir as trivialities, that is a meaning but not an explanation. And since the fables of the ancients, such as the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar, are speech with no benefit in it, asatir al-awwalin was therefore explained as trivialities.

* * *

The fourth issue: Know that the aim of the people in saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ was to disparage the Qur'an's being miraculous, as if they said: this speech is of the same kind as all other written tales and recounted stories of the ancients, and if it is of the kind of those books containing narratives of the ancients and accounts of the earlier people, it is not a miracle breaking the norm. Al-Qadi answered this by saying: this objection is refuted, because it would follow that if it were within your power to produce its equal, you would have to bring that counterpart, and since you were unable to do so, it is evident that it is miraculous. One may say: the people could have said: "Although we are masters of this Arabic tongue, we do not know how books are composed and authored, and we are not fit for that." And our inability to compose does not imply that the Qur'an is miraculous, because we have shown that it is of the same kind as all other books containing the narratives of the ancients and the stories of the earlier people.

Know that the answer to this objection will come in the verse mentioned after this.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 26:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it, and they destroy none but themselves, though they perceive not.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they had criticised the Qur'an's being miraculous by saying that it is among "the fables of the ancients" and "the tales of the former peoples," He explained in this verse that they forbid it and keep away from it. The Qur'an has already been mentioned, and so has Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore the pronoun in His saying "from it" may refer either to the Qur'an or to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. For this reason the exegetes differed. Some said: ﴿they forbid it and keep away from it﴾ means: from the Qur'an, from reflecting upon it and from listening to it. Others said: rather, the meaning is that they forbid [people] from the Messenger.

Know that forbidding [people] from the Messenger, peace be upon him, is not what is meant in the literal sense; rather, it must mean forbidding an action connected with him, peace and blessings be upon him, which is not mentioned. Hence there are two opinions. Some said: the meaning is that they forbid [people] from believing in his prophethood and from acknowledging his mission. 'Ata' and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, who used to forbid the Quraysh from harming the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and then would keep away from him and would not follow him in his religion.

The first opinion is more fitting, for two reasons:

The first: all the verses preceding this verse imply censure of their way, so likewise His saying ﴿and they forbid it﴾ should be understood as referring to a blameworthy matter. If we took it to mean that Abu Talib forbade harming him, this wording would not fit.

The second: He said after that: ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾, meaning by it what has already been mentioned. It is not appropriate that the intended meaning of ﴿they forbid it﴾ be forbidding harm to him, because that is good and does not entail destruction.

If it is said: His saying ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾ relates to His saying ﴿and keep away from it﴾, not to His saying ﴿they forbid it﴾, because the meaning is that they keep far from him by abandoning his religion and refusing to agree with him, and that is blameworthy; so what you have cited to prefer this view is not sound.

Page 157
We say: the apparent sense of His saying ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾ relates to everything mentioned before, since it is like saying: so-and-so keeps far from such-and-such a thing and shuns it, and harms by that none but himself. Thus this harm is not tied to one of the two matters to the exclusion of the other.

The second issue: Know that those disbelievers treated the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with two kinds of ugliness:

The first: they forbade people from accepting his religion and from acknowledging his prophethood.

The second: they kept away from him. Al-na'y means distance; it is said: naʾā yanʾā (نأى ينأى) when he went far away. Then He said: ﴿and they destroy none but themselves, though they perceive not.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, they destroy none but themselves through their persistence in disbelief and their excess in it, and they do not perceive that they are destroying themselves and sending themselves to the Fire by what they commit of disbelief and disobedience. And Allah knows best.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the description of those who forbid following the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and who keep away from obeying him, saying that they destroy themselves, He explained the manner of that destruction with this verse, and in it there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, "If only you could see" (wa-law tara), requires an answer, but it has been omitted to magnify the matter and to exalt its importance. Its omission is permissible because the addressee knows it, and similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an and in poetry. If you estimate the answer, the estimate would be: "you would see the evil of their final state," or "you would see the evil of their condition." Omitting the answer in such cases is more eloquent in meaning than stating it. Do you not see that if you said to your servant, "By God, if I come to you!" and then fell silent about the answer, his thoughts would go to all kinds of hateful things: beating, killing, breaking, and his fear would grow greatly, and he would not know which of these possibilities you intend. But if you said, "By God, if I come to you, I will surely beat you," and then gave the answer, he would know that you had not gone beyond beating, and no kind of hateful thing other than beating would occur to his mind. Thus it is established that omitting the answer is stronger in producing fear. Some have said: the answer of "law" is mentioned in some respects, and the estimate is: "If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire, wailing and saying: 'Would that we were returned and did not deny the signs of our Lord, and would be among the believers.'"

The second issue: His saying, "when they are made to stand" (wuqifu). It is said: "I made him stand" (waqaftuhu waqfan), and "I made him stand" (waqqaftuhu wuqufan), just as one says "I made him return" (raja'tuhu ruju'an). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "they were made to stand over the Fire" (wuqifu 'ala al-nar) may bear three aspects:

First: it may be that they were made to stand near it while seeing it, so they are standing, awaiting entry into the Fire.

Second: it may be that they were made to stand over it while it was beneath them, meaning that they were made to stand above the Fire upon the Sirat, which is a bridge over Hell.

Third: its meaning is that they came to know its reality, from your saying "I made so-and-so stand over the speech of so-and-so," i.e., I taught him its meaning and made it known to him.

There is also a fourth aspect: that they are inside the Fire, with the Fire encompassing them, and they are immersed in it. On this interpretation, "upon" ('ala) has been placed in the position of "in" (fi). It is correct on this interpretation to say "they were made to stand upon the Fire," because the Fire has levels and tiers, some above others, so the sense of elevation is valid there.

If it is asked: why did He say "If only you could see," which indicates the future, and then said after it "when they were made to stand," where "when" (idh) is for the past, and then said after it "they said," which also indicates the past?

We say: the word "idh" is used in place of "idha" when the speaker wishes to emphasize repetition and confirmation and to remove doubt, because the past has occurred and become established. Thus, expressing the future with a word laid down for the past conveys emphasis from this consideration.

The third issue: Al-Zajjaj said: the inclination (imala) in "al-nar" is good and excellent, because what follows the alif is kasra, which is the letter ra', as if it were repeated in the tongue, so the kasra in it becomes like two kasras.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: "So they will say: 'Would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers'," there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, "Would that we" (ya layta-na), indicates that they wished to be returned to the world. As for His saying, "and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers," there are two views:

One of them: that it falls within the wish, and the estimate is that they wished to be returned to the world and not to be deniers, and to be believers.

If they say: this is false, because He, exalted is He, judged them to be liars by His saying at the end of the verse, "And indeed they are liars," and one who wishes is not described as a liar.

We say: we do not concede that one who wishes is not described as a liar, because whoever expresses a wish has implicitly informed that he desires that thing, so it is not far-fetched that he be called a liar regarding it. An example: a man says, "Would that God would grant me wealth, so that I might be good to you." This is a wish that has the force of a promise. If he were granted wealth and did not treat his companion well, it would be said that he lied in his promise.

The second view: that the wish is complete at His saying, "Would that we were returned." As for His saying, "and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers," this is a fresh statement, and His saying at the end of the verse, "And indeed they are liars," refers back to it. The estimate of the speech is: "Would that we were returned; then they said: 'If we were returned, we would not deny the religion, and we would be among the believers.' Then He, exalted is He, called them liars and made clear that if they were returned they would deny and turn away from faith."

The second issue: Ibn 'Amir read "nuradd" and "nukadhdhibu" with the nominative (raf') in both, and "nakuna" with the accusative (nasb). Hamzah and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read "nuradd" with the nominative, and "nukadhdhiba" and "nakuna" with the accusative in both, and the rest read with the nominative in all three. From this it results that they agreed on the nominative in His saying "nuradd," because it is undoubtedly within the wish. As for those who read "wa-la nukadhdhibu, wa-nakunu" with the nominative, there are two aspects:

The first: that it is coordinated with His saying "nuradd," so that all three fall within the wish. On this, they wished to be returned, not to deny, and to be believers.

The second aspect: that "wa-la nukadhdhibu" and what follows it are cut off from the first, so the estimate is: "Would that we were returned, while we do not deny the signs of our Lord and we are among the believers." They thus guarantee that they will not deny, on the assumption that the return occurs. The meaning is: "Would that we were returned, while we do not deny the signs of our Lord, whether we are returned or not," i.e., we have already witnessed and seen that with which we will never deny again. Sibawayh said: this is like your saying "leave me, and I will not return," where what is sought by the request is that it be left; as for not returning, it is not included in the request. Likewise here: what is included in this wish is the return, while abandoning denial and performing faith are not included in the wish, but rather they are attained whether the return occurs or not. Al-Zajjaj and the grammarians mentioned these two aspects, and they said: the second aspect is stronger, namely that the return is included in the wish and what follows it is a pure statement. They argued for it by saying that God called them liars in the second verse, saying "And indeed they are liars," and one who wishes cannot be called a liar. This is the choice of Abu 'Amr. This argument has been cited to support its soundness, but we have answered this argument and mentioned that it is not strong.

As for those who read "wa-la nukadhdhiba, wa-nakuna" with the accusative, there are several aspects:

The first: by implying "an" (that) as a response to the wish, the estimate being: "Would that we were returned and that we not deny."

The second: that the waw is replaced from the fa', the estimate being: "Would that we were returned, so we would not deny," so the waw here has the position of the fa' in His saying, "Had I but a return, I would be among the good-doers" [Az-Zumar: 58]. This aspect is strengthened by what is reported: that Ibn Mas'ud used to read "fa-la nukadhdhiba" with the fa' in the accusative.

The third: that its meaning is the state (hal), the estimate being: "Would that we were returned while not being deniers," as the Arabs say: "Do not eat fish and drink milk," i.e., do not eat fish while drinking milk.

Know that on this reading, all three matters fall within the wish. As for how the one who wishes can be called a liar, its explanation has already preceded. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, which is that he read "wa-la nukadhdhibu" with the nominative and "wa-nakuna" with the accusative, the estimate is that he makes His saying "wa-la nukadhdhiba" fall within the wish, in the sense that: if we are returned as non-deniers, we will be among the believers. And God knows best.

The third issue: His saying, "So they will say: 'Would that we were returned, and we would not deny'," there is no doubt that what is meant is the wish for their return to the state of obligation, because the word "return" (radd), when used for the future from one state to another, what is understood from it is the return to the first state. It is evident that one who committed a shortcoming and then witnessed hardships and conditions because of that shortcoming wishes to be returned to the first state, in order to strive to remove all aspects of shortcoming. It is known that the disbelievers fell short in the abode of the world, so they wish to return to the world to make up for those shortcomings, and that making up is not achieved by returning to the world alone, nor by abandoning denial alone, nor by performing faith alone, but rather the making up is achieved only by all these three matters together. Therefore it is necessary to include these three within the wish.

If it is said: how is it proper for them to wish for return, when they know that return will never occur at all?

The answer has several aspects:

First: perhaps they did not know that return would not occur.

Second: even if they knew that this would not occur, this knowledge does not prevent the arising of the desire for return, like His saying, exalted is He: "They desire to come out of the Fire" [Al-Ma'idah: 37], and like His saying: "Pour upon us some water, or some of what God has provided you" [Al-A'raf: 50]. Since it is valid for them to desire these things while knowing they will not occur, then wishing for them is closer, because the domain of wishing is broader, since it is valid to wish for what it is not valid to desire among the three past matters.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: The meaning of "bal" (but, rather) here is a rejection of their statement. The implication is: they did not wish to return to the world, and to abandon denial and attain faith, out of a desire for belief, but rather out of fear of the punishment which they had witnessed and seen with their own eyes. This indicates that desire for faith and obedience benefits only when that desire is a desire for it, because it is faith and obedience; as for desire for it in order to seek reward and out of fear of punishment, it is not beneficial.

The second issue: The intended meaning of the verse is that there appeared to them in the Hereafter what they had concealed in the world. Scholars have differed about what it was that they concealed, in several respects:

The first: Abu Rawq said: Among the polytheists, at some of the stations of the Resurrection, they deny polytheism, saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. Then Allah makes their limbs speak, and they testify against them to their disbelief. That is when there appeared to them what they used to conceal before. Al-Wahidi said: The people of tafsir hold this view.

The second: Al-Mubarrad said: There appeared to them the calamity of their beliefs and deeds and the evil of their outcome. That is because their disbelief was not manifest to them, since the harms of their disbelief were hidden; so when they became apparent on the Day of Resurrection, Allah, exalted is He, said without doubt: ﴿But there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾.

The third: Al-Zajjaj said: There appeared to the followers what their leaders had concealed from them concerning the matter of resurrection and rising again. He said: The proof of the soundness of this view is that He, exalted is He, mentioned right after it: ﴿And they said: There is only our life of this world, and we shall not be resurrected﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fourth: Some said: This verse concerns the hypocrites, who used to conceal disbelief and show Islam, and on the Day of Resurrection what they concealed appeared, and it became evident to others that they had previously been hypocrites.

The fifth: It has been said: There appeared to them what their scholars used to conceal of denying the prophethood of the Messenger, his description and attributes in the books, and the good tidings of him, and what they used to distort from the Torah of what indicates this.

Know that the wording admits of many meanings, and the intent of all of them together is that their disgrace appeared in the Hereafter and their veils were torn away. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9].

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾. The meaning is that if He, exalted is He, were to return them, there would not come from them abandonment of denial and performance of faith; rather, they would continue upon their former way of disbelief and denial.

If it is said: The people of the Resurrection have known Allah by necessity and have witnessed the various kinds of punishment and torment. So if Allah, exalted is He, were to return them to the world, how is it possible, in these circumstances, to say that they would return to disbelief in Allah and to disobedience of Allah?

We say: al-Qadi said: The interpretation of the verse: ﴿And if they were returned﴾ to the state of moral obligation (taklif). The return to this state happens only if there did not occur in the Resurrection knowledge of Allah by necessity and there did not occur there the witnessing of the terrors and the torment of Hell. So this condition must necessarily be implied in the verse. However, we say this answer is weak, because the purpose of the verse is to show their extreme obstinacy in disbelief and their lack of desire for faith. If we assume the absence of knowledge of Allah in the Resurrection and the absence of witnessing the terrors of the Resurrection, there would be no particular wonder in the people's persistence in their former disbelief, because their persistence in disbelief would be like the persistence of all other disbelievers in disbelief in the world. Thus we know that the condition mentioned by al-Qadi cannot be considered at all.

Having understood this, we say: al-Wahidi said: This verse is among the clear proofs against the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. This is because Allah, exalted is He, informed about a people upon whom His decree had passed in eternity regarding polytheism, and that prior decree concerning them; otherwise a sensible person would not doubt what he has witnessed. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾. And there is an objection to this, namely that it may be said: no report has preceded so that this denial should be directed toward it.

The answer: We have explained that among them is one who said: the element entering into the wish is merely His saying: ﴿Would that we were returned﴾; as for the rest, it is information. And among them is one who said: rather, the whole thing enters into the wish, because the inclusion of denial within the wish is also permissible, since wishing indicates information implicitly and by consequence, like the saying of one who says: "If only Zayd had come to us, so we would eat, drink and converse." Thus it is here. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "There is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be raised."﴾

Know that there are two opinions regarding the verse.

The first: He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse that what they used to conceal had become apparent to them. So in this verse He clarifies that what they used to conceal is the matter of the Return (ma'ad, the afterlife), the gathering (hashr) and the raising (nashr). This is because they used to deny it and conceal its truth, and they would say: "There is nothing for us but this worldly life," and there is, after this life, neither reward nor punishment.

The second: the implied meaning of the verse is: "Even if they were returned, they would go back to what they had been forbidden, and they would deny the gathering and the raising, and say: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be raised.﴾"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 30:

Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when Allah, exalted is He, related their denial of the gathering (al-hashr), the scattering (al-nashr), the resurrection (al-ba'th) and the Final Hour (al-qiyamah) in the first verse, He explained in this verse the manner of their condition on the Day of Resurrection, and He said: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. Know that a group of the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) clung to this verse and said: The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the people of the Resurrection stand before Allah and close to Him, and that this indicates He, exalted is He, is in a state whereby He is present in one place at times and absent from it at other times.

Know that this is an error, because the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that they stand over Allah, exalted is He, as one of us stands over the ground, and that indicates His being elevated over the very essence of Allah, exalted is He, which is by consensus false. Therefore it is necessary to resort to interpretation (ta'wil), and it is of several aspects:

The first interpretation: that the intended meaning is ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over﴾ what their Lord promised them of the punishment of the disbelievers and the reward of the believers, and over what He informed them of concerning the matter of the Hereafter.

The second interpretation: that the intended meaning of this standing is knowledge (al-ma'rifah), as a man says to another, "I stood over your speech," meaning, "I came to know it."

The third interpretation: that the intended meaning is that they are made to stand for the sake of questioning, and the speech has come out in the manner of what is customary from the standing of a servant before his master, and the purpose of it is to express the intended meaning in eloquent and articulate words.

The second issue: The purpose of this verse is that Allah, exalted is He, related about them in the first verse that they deny the Resurrection and the resurrection in this world, then He explained that in the Hereafter they will acknowledge it. So the meaning is that their state in this denial will turn into acknowledgment, because they witnessed the Resurrection, the reward and the punishment. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾

If it is said: This statement indicates that Allah, exalted is He, says to them, "Is this not the truth?" and this is seemingly contradictory to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174]. The answer is that His saying ﴿and will not speak to them﴾ is to be understood as: He will not speak to them with good, beneficial speech. On this interpretation the contradiction disappears. Then He, exalted is He, explained that when He says to them, "Is this not the truth?" they say: "Yes, by our Lord." The purpose is that they acknowledge its being the truth together with swearing and oath. Then He, exalted is He, says to them: ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾. He chose the word "taste" because in every state they find it with the perception of one who tastes, in the intensity of sensation. His saying ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾ means: because of your disbelief. Know that He, exalted is He, did not mention this statement as an argument for the validity of the doctrine of the gathering and the scattering, because that proof has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah in His saying: ﴿He it is who created you from clay, then decreed a term﴾ [al-An'am: 2], as we established and explained it. Rather, the purpose of this verse is deterrence and rebuke against this position and this saying.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 31:

﴿Those who denied the meeting with God have indeed lost, until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they say, "O our grief over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾

In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: know that the purpose of this verse is to explain another state of those who deny the resurrection and the Last Day, and it has two aspects:

The first: the occurrence of loss.

The second: the bearing of great burdens.

As for the first type, which is the occurrence of loss, its explanation is that God, exalted is He, created the material substance of the luminous, holy soul, and gave it these bodily instruments and physical tools, and gave it intellect and reflection so that by using these instruments and tools it may attain true knowledge and virtuous character, whose benefits are great after death. When a person uses these instruments, tools, intellectual power and reflective power to acquire these transient pleasures and cut-off happinesses, and then reaches the end of his life, he has suffered a manifest loss, because the capital has perished, and the profit which he thought was the goal has also perished and ended. Thus nothing remains in his hand, neither any trace of the capital nor anything of the profit. This is the manifest loss. This loss occurs only for one who denies the resurrection and the Last Day and believes that the ultimate of happiness and the end of perfections is these hasty, perishing happinesses. As for one who believes in the resurrection and the Last Day, he is not deceived by these bodily happinesses, nor is he content with these hasty goods, but strives to prepare provision for the Day of Return, so loss does not befall him. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that those who denied the meeting with God and rejected the resurrection and the Last Day have suffered manifest loss, and that when they arrive at the station of the Resurrection they will grieve over their neglect in obtaining provision for the Day of Return.

The second aspect of their loss: they carry their burdens upon their backs. The explanation of this is that the perfection of happiness lies in turning toward God, exalted is He, occupying oneself with His worship, striving in His love and service, and likewise in detachment from the world, abandoning love of it, and severing the bond between the heart and it. Whoever denies the resurrection and the Last Day does not strive to prepare provision for the station of the Resurrection, nor strive to sever the bond between his heart and the world. So when he dies, he remains like a stranger in the world of spiritual realities, and like one cut off from his loved ones and relatives who were in the world of physical things. So he suffers great regrets because of the lack of provision and his failure to find a way to associate with the people of that world, and he suffers great pains because of being cut off from the pleasures of this world and being barred from enjoying the goods of this world.

So the first is what is meant by His saying: ﴿They say, "O our grief over what we neglected concerning it!"﴾

And the second is what is meant by His saying: ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾. This is the explanation of the purpose of this verse.

The second issue: what is meant by loss is the missing of a great reward and the incurring of a great punishment. And ﴿those who denied the meeting with God﴾ means those who rejected the resurrection and the Last Day. We have elaborated on the explanation of this expression at His saying: ﴿those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. This metonymy is apt because the station of the Resurrection is a station in which no one has any command except God, exalted is He, and no one has any power to benefit or harm, to raise or to lower, except God. As for His saying: ﴿until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾, know that the word "until" (ḥattā) is a limit for His saying "they denied" and not for His saying "has lost," because their loss has no limit. The meaning of "until" here is that the ultimate of their denial is the regret on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that they kept denying until the Hour appeared suddenly.

If it is said: they only regret at the time of their death.

We say: since death is an occurrence among the conditions of the Hereafter and its preliminaries, it has been placed in the category of the Hour and named by its name. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has already come." The meaning of "the Hour" is the Resurrection. There are several reasons for naming the Day of Resurrection by this name:

The first: the Day of Resurrection is called the Hour because of the speed of the reckoning in it, as if it were said: it is only the hour of reckoning.

The second: the Hour is the time at which the Resurrection occurs. It is called an hour because it comes upon people in an hour that no one knows except God, exalted is He. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, said: "suddenly" (baghtatan)? "Baghta" and "baghtah" mean the sudden coming. The meaning is that the Hour comes only all at once, because no one knows when its coming will be or at what time its occurrence will be. As for His saying "suddenly" (baghtatan), it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "surprising," or as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as if it were said: "the Hour surprised them with a surprise."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say, "O our grief!"﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of calling out to grief is to alert the people to the grief that will befall them. The Arabs express the magnification of such matters by this expression, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O grief upon the servants!﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30], and ﴿O our grief over what I neglected in God's side!﴾ [al-Zumar: 56], and ﴿She said, "O woe to me! Shall I give birth?"﴾ [Hud: 72]. This is more emphatic than saying: "Grief is upon us for our neglect." Similar to this is ﴿When they entered upon Joseph﴾ [Yusuf: 84]; its interpretation is: "O people, take heed of the sorrow that has befallen me," so the address falls upon one other than the one actually addressed. Sibawayh said: when you say "O wonder!" (yā ʿajabāh), it is as if you said: "O wonder, come forth and be present, for this is your time."

Having understood this, we say: there are two interpretations of the calling out here:

The first: the calling is directed to the grief, and its purpose is to alert the addressees; this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The second: the one called is the grief itself, meaning: this is your time, so appear; this is the view of Sibawayh.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿over what we neglected concerning it﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: Abu ʿUbayda said: one says "I neglected the matter" (farraṭtu fī al-shay'), meaning I wasted it. So His saying "farraṭnā" means we abandoned and wasted. Al-Zajjaj said: "farraṭnā" means we preceded in weakness; he took it from the expression "farata fulān" when someone went ahead and preceded, and "farrata al-shay'" when he put it forward. Al-Wahidi said: so tafrīṭ, in his view, is the advancing of shortcoming.

The second discussion: as for the pronoun in His saying "concerning it" (fīhā), to what does it refer? There are several views:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "concerning the world." The objection to this is that the world has not been mentioned, so how can this pronoun refer to it? The answer is that reason shows that the place of shortcoming is none other than the world, so it is apt for the pronoun to refer to it for this meaning.

The second: al-Hasan said: the meaning is "O our grief over what we neglected concerning the Hour," meaning: over what we neglected in preparing provision for the Hour and acquiring readiness for it.

The third: the pronoun refers to the sense of "what" in His saying "we neglected" (farraṭnā), meaning: our grief over the deeds and acts of obedience that we neglected.

The fourth: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the pronoun refers to the transaction, because when He, exalted is He, mentioned loss, this indicated the occurrence of a deal and a sale.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾. Know that what is meant by their saying "O our grief over what we neglected concerning it" is an indication that they did not secure for themselves what would make them deserving of reward. And His saying ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾ is an indication that they did secure for themselves what made them deserving of the great punishment, and there is no doubt that this is the extreme of loss. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "burdens" (awzār) are sins and transgressions. The lexicographers said: "wizr" is weight, and its origin is from carrying; one says "wazartu al-shay'," meaning I carried the thing, I carry it as a burden (wizr). Then sins were called "awzār," because they weigh down the back of the one who commits them. His saying ﴿and no bearer shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Anʿam: 164] means: no soul shall carry a burden. Abu ʿUbayda said: one says to a man, when he spreads out his garment and places goods in it, "Carry your load." "Awzār al-ḥarb" are the heavy weights of weapons. The vizier (wazīr) of a ruler is the one who bears the weight of what is entrusted to him of administering the rule, that is, he carries it. Al-Zajjaj said: "while they carry their burdens" means they carry the weight of their sins.

They differed about the manner in which they carry the burdens. The exegetes said: when the believer comes out of his grave, something meets him which is the most beautiful of things in form and the most fragrant in scent, and it says: "I am your righteous deed. You used to ride me in the world, so ride me today." That is His saying: ﴿On the Day when We gather the God-fearing to the Merciful as a delegation﴾ [Maryam: 85]; they said: "as riders." And when the disbeliever comes out of his grave, something meets him which is the ugliest of things in form and the most foul in scent, and it says: "I am your corrupt deed. You used to ride me in the world, so I shall ride you today." That is His saying: ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: heaviness is understood in the literal sense, and it is also understood in the figurative and attributive sense; one says "the address of so-and-so was heavy upon me," meaning I disliked it. So the meaning is that they suffer the punishment for their sins as the heaviness of that is felt by them. Others said: the meaning of His saying ﴿while they carry their burdens﴾ is that their burdens do not leave them, just as you say "your person is before my eyes," meaning your remembrance is constant with me.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾ The meaning is: wretched is the thing that they bear, that is, carry. The thorough explanation of this expression is mentioned in surah al-Nisa' at His saying: ﴿and evil as a way﴾ [al-Nisa': 22].
