**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 6, verse 32**

[Quranic text] ﴿The life of this world is nothing but play and amusement. But the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God. Will you not then use your reason?﴾

Regarding this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that those who deny the resurrection and the Last Day have a great desire for this world and for attaining its pleasures. God, exalted is He, therefore mentioned this verse to alert them to its baseness and worthlessness.

Know also that this life itself cannot be condemned, because the righteous joys of the Hereafter can only be earned in this present life. For this reason, two opinions have arisen concerning the interpretation of this verse:

The first opinion: What is meant is the life of the disbeliever. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He means the life of the people of polytheism and hypocrisy. The reason this life is described in this way is that the life of the believer contains righteous deeds, so it is not mere play and amusement."

The second opinion: This applies generally to the life of both the believer and the disbeliever, and what is meant is the pleasures attained in this life and the good things sought in it. It is called play and amusement because a person, while occupied with play and amusement, takes delight in it, but when it passes and ends, nothing remains of it except regret. Likewise, this life, when it passes, leaves nothing behind except grief and remorse.

Know that there are several reasons for calling this life play and amusement:

First: The duration of amusement and play is brief and quickly ends and vanishes, and the duration of this life is likewise.

Second: Play and amusement inevitably lead, for the most part, to some kind of unpleasantness, and the pleasures of this world are likewise.

Third: Play and amusement occur only when one is deceived by the outward appearances of things. But when one reflects thoroughly and uncovers the realities of matters, play and amusement do not remain at all. Likewise, play and amusement are fit only for children and the ignorant and heedless. As for the intelligent and the wise, they rarely engage in play and amusement. Thus, taking delight in the good things of this world and benefiting from its goods arises only among the heedless who are ignorant of the realities of things. As for the wise who verify matters, they know that all these goods are deception and have no genuine reality in truth.

Fourth: Play and amusement have no praiseworthy outcome.

Thus, by the combination of these aspects, it is established that worldly pleasures and conditions are play and amusement, and have no genuine reality. When God, exalted is He, had made this clear, He said after it: ﴿But the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God.﴾ He described the Hereafter as being better. What indicates that the matter is so is the existence of differences between the conditions of this world and the conditions of the Hereafter in several respects:

One of them: The good things of this world are base, and the good things of the Hereafter are noble.

The proof that the matter is so consists of several aspects:

The first: The good things of this world are nothing but the satisfaction of the two appetites (the appetite for food and the appetite for sex), and this is at the utmost baseness. The evidence is that base animals share with humans in this, and indeed the condition of those animals in it is sometimes more complete than the condition of humans. For the camel eats more, the rooster and the sparrow copulate more, the wolf is more capable of corruption and tearing, and the scorpion is more capable of inflicting pain. Among the things that indicate their baseness is that if they were noble, then increasing them would increase nobility. Thus it would necessarily follow that the person who devoted his whole life to eating and copulating would be the noblest of people and the highest in rank. But it is self-evident that the matter is not so; rather, such a person is hated, loathed, and despised, and is described as a beast, a dog, or something even lower. Among the things that indicate this is that people do not take pride in these conditions but conceal them. For this reason, intelligent people, when engaged in intercourse, hide themselves and do not perform these acts in the presence of people. This indicates that these acts do not bring nobility but deficiency. Among the things that also indicate this is that when people revile one another, they mention in the insult nothing but words that refer to intercourse. Had that pleasure not been of the kind of deficiencies, the matter would not be so. Among the things that indicate it is also that these pleasures, in their reality, come down to the removal of pains. For this reason, whoever is hungrier and has a greater need, his delight in these things is more complete and stronger. And when the matter is so, it becomes clear that these pleasures have no reality in truth. Another thing that indicates it is that these pleasures quickly change, quickly vanish, and quickly end.

Thus, through these many aspects, the baseness of these pleasures is established. As for the spiritual felicities, they are noble, lofty, lasting, and sacred. For this reason, if all creatures imagine in a person great knowledge and intense withdrawal from bodily pleasures, they naturally magnify him, serve him, and consider themselves slaves to that person and wretched in comparison to him. This indicates the testimony of the original nature (fitrah) to the baseness of bodily pleasures and the perfection of the rank of spiritual pleasures.

The second aspect: concerning the proof that the good things of the Hereafter are superior to the good things of this world. We say: Suppose these two kinds were equal in excellence and virtue, still the attainment of the good things promised on the Day of Resurrection is certain. But the attainment of the good things promised on the morrow of this world is not known, nor even presumed. For how many a mighty ruler in the morning of a day has become beneath the dust by the end of that same day! And how many a great commander has risen to kingship and rule, then by evening has become a humiliated captive! This difference also necessitates the disparity between the two kinds.

The third aspect: Suppose a person finds after this day another day in this world, yet he does not know whether he will be able to benefit from the wealth, good things, and pleasures he has gathered or not. But as for everything he has gathered of the causes of felicity, he knows with certainty that he will benefit from it in the abode of the Hereafter.

The fourth aspect: Suppose he will benefit from them, yet his benefit from the good things of this world will not be free of the admixture of disliked things and the mingling of forbidden and fearful matters. For this reason it has been said: "Whoever seeks what has not been created for him exhausts himself and is not granted it." It was asked: "And what is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The joy of a whole day."

The fifth aspect: Suppose he benefits from those wealths and good things on the morrow, yet those benefits are transient, passing, and false. And the more those benefits are strong, delightful, complete, and excellent, the greater and more complete are the sorrows that arise at their passing and ending, as the poet al-Mutanabbi said:

"The greatest grief to me is joy whose possessor is certain that it will depart."

Thus, by what we have mentioned, it is established that the felicities and good things of this world are described by these great defects and complete deficiencies, while the felicities of the Hereafter are free of them. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the Hereafter is more complete, more excellent, more lasting, more pious, more deserving, and more fitting.

**The second issue:** Ibn ʿAmir recited (ولَدارُ الآخِرَةِ) with the noun "dar" (abode) in the genitive construct with "al-akhirah" (the Hereafter). The rest read ﴿ولَلدّارُ الآخِرَةُ﴾, making "al-akhirah" an adjective (naʿt) of "al-dar". As for the reading of Ibn ʿAmir, its justification is that the adjective, in reality, is distinct from the noun it qualifies, so the construct is valid from this standpoint. A parallel to this is their saying "bariḥat al-ūlā" (last night) and "yawm al-khamīs" (Thursday) and "ḥaqq al-yaqīn" (certain truth). But according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun), this construct is not permitted. They said: because the adjective is the same as the thing described, and it is impossible to add a thing to itself.

Know that this is based on the premise that the adjective is the same as the thing described, and that is problematic, because it is conceivable to imagine the thing described separated from the adjective, and if the thing described were identical with the adjective, that would be impossible. The position of those (who permit the construct) has a subtle basis which can be argued, but it is not appropriate for this place. Then the Basrans mentioned another justification for the validity of Ibn ʿAmir's reading. They said: He did not make "al-akhirah" an adjective of "al-dar", but made it an adjective of "al-sa‘ah" (the Hour), so it is as if he said: "wa-dar al-sā‘ah al-ākhirah" (and the abode of the final Hour).

If it is said: According to this assumed construction that you have mentioned, the word "al-akhirah", which is the adjective, has been placed in the position of the thing described, which is "al-sa‘ah", and that is unacceptable. We reply: It is not unacceptable if the adjective has come to be used as a noun, and the word "al-akhirah" has been used as a noun. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first (life)﴾ [al-Duha 93:4]. As for the reading of the majority, it is clear, because it requires making "al-akhirah" an adjective of "al-dar", and that is the literal meaning, and whenever it is possible to keep speech on its literal meaning, there is no need to depart from it. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** They differed concerning the intended meaning of "al-dar al-akhirah" (the Abode of the Hereafter), in several views:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It is Paradise, and it is better for those who guard against disbelief and disobedience.

Al-Hasan said: What is meant is that the Hereafter itself is good.

Al-Asamm said: Adhering to the deeds of the Hereafter is good.

Others said: The bliss of the Hereafter is better than the bliss of this world, in that it is lasting, everlasting, protected from impurities, and safe from ending and passing away.

\* \* \*

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿For those who are mindful of God﴾. Thus He clarified that this superiority is attained only by one who is among those who guard against disobedience and major sins. As for the disbeliever and the wicked, it is not so! For the world, in relation to him, is better than the Hereafter, as he (peace be upon him) said: "The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever."

Then He said: (أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ) "Will you not then use your reason?" Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir read (أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ) with the letter ta' (second person, "you") here, and in Surat al-Aʿraf, Yusuf, and Ya-Sin. Ḥafs, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read in "Ya-Sin" with the letter ya' (third person), and the rest with ta'. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Yaḥyā, read in Yusuf with ta', and the rest with ya'. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of al-Aʿsha and al-Burjumi, read all of these with ya'. Al-Wahidi said: Whoever reads with ya' means: "Will not those who are mindful of God understand that the Abode of the Hereafter is better for them than this abode? So that they act for what will attain them the lofty rank and everlasting bliss, and do not slacken in seeking what leads to that." Whoever reads with ta', the meaning is: "Say to them: 'Will you not understand, O you who are addressed, that this is better?'" And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you; but it is not you whom they deny, but it is the signs of God that the wrongdoers repudiate﴾.

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the groups of the disbelievers were many sects:

Among them were those who denied his prophethood, because they rejected the idea that a human being could be a messenger, and they said: the Messenger of God must be of the kind of the angels. God Exalted has mentioned the doubt of these people in this surah and answered it.

Among them were those who said: Muhammad informs us of the gathering and resurrection after death, and that is impossible. They used the impossibility of resurrection as a basis for attacking his mission. God Exalted has mentioned this and answered it with the many arguments that have already been mentioned.

Among them were those who would abuse him to his face with foolishness and with speech that is not fitting; this is what God Exalted mentioned in this verse.

They differed about what that grieving thing was.

It was said: they used to say that he was a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer and a madman; this is the view of al-Hasan.

It was said: they used to declare openly that they did not believe in him and did not accept his religion and law.

It was said: they used to attribute to him lying and fabrication.

The second issue: Nafi' read "yuhzinuka" (لَيُحْزِنُكَ) with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, while the rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the zāy. Both are dialectal forms: one says ḥazanani kadha and aḥzanani kadha (it grieved me and it grieved me).

The third issue: Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "fa-innahum la yukdhibunaka" (فَإنَّهم لا يُكْذِبُونَكَ) with a light pronunciation, while the rest read yukadhdhibunaka (يُكَذِّبُونَكَ) with a doubled dhāl. Regarding these two readings there are two views:

The first: that there is a clear difference between them. They then mentioned two aspects in explaining the difference:

One of them: al-Kisa'i read with the light form and argued that the Arabs say kadhabta al-rajul (كَذَبْتَ الرَّجُلَ) when you attribute lying to him and to his producing false speech, and akdhabtuhu (أكْذَبْتَهُ) when you inform that what he relates is a lie, even if he did not fabricate it himself.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of kadhabtuhu is "I said to him: you have lied"; and the meaning of akdhabtuhu is that what he brought is a lie in itself, without claiming that the speaker deliberately invented that lie and brought it by way of fabrication and intent. It is as if the people believed that Muhammad, peace be upon him, did not mention that by way of fabrication and deception, but rather imagined the validity of that prophethood and that mission, except that what he imagined is in itself false.

The second aspect: Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that the meaning of "la yukadhdhibunaka" (لا يُكَذِّبُونَكَ) is that they do not find you lying, because they know you for truthfulness and trustworthiness, just as one says ahmadtu al-rajul (أحْمَدْتُ الرَّجُلَ) when you find him praiseworthy and therefore love him, and ahsantu mahmadatahu (أحْسَنْتُ مَحْمَدَتَهُ) when you encounter him in these states.

The second view: that there is no difference between these two readings. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that the meaning of both readings is one, because the sense of the form taf'il is attribution to lying, by saying to him "you have lied", just as you say dhannabtuhu (ذَنَّبْتُهُ), fassaqtuhu (فَسَّقْتُهُ) and khaṭṭa'tuhu (خَطَّأْتُهُ), meaning "I said to him: you did these things". And saqqaytuhu (سَقَّيْتُهُ) and ra''aytuhu (رَعَّيْتُهُ), meaning "I said to him: may God water you and protect you". This meaning also came in af'altu: they said asqaytuhu (أسْقَيْتُهُ), meaning "I said to him: may God water you". Dhu al-Rummah said:

Page 169

And I made him drink, until, because of what I express, his stones and his playgrounds almost speak to me.
That is, I attribute him to watering by saying: may God water you. According to this estimation the meaning of both readings is one, except that fa''altu is used when they want to attribute to him a matter more than af'altu does.

The fourth issue: The apparent meaning of this verse requires that they do not deny Muhammad, peace be upon him, but that they repudiate the signs of God. Scholars differed on how these two matters are reconciled, in several ways:

The first way: the people did not deny him in private, but they denied him openly and repudiated the Qur'an and prophethood. Then, to validate this way, they cited reports:

One of them: that al-Harith ibn 'Amir from Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, by God you have never lied to us, but if we follow you we will be snatched from our land; so we do not believe in you for this reason."

The second: it is related that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq said to Abu Jahl: "O Abu al-Hakam, tell me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar? For there is no one here except us." He said to him: "By God, Muhammad is truthful and has never lied; but if the Banu Qusayy take the banner, the watering, the custody of the Ka'bah and the prophethood, what then will remain for the rest of Quraysh?" Then this verse was revealed.

Having known this, we say: the meaning of the verse on this estimation is that the people do not deny you in their hearts, but they repudiate your prophethood with their tongues and their outward speech. This is not unlikely, and its parallel is His saying, in the story of Moses: ﴿And they repudiated them, though their souls acknowledged them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

The second way of interpreting the verse: they did not say that you are a liar, because they had tested you for a long time and an extended period and found in you no lie at all, and they called you "the Trustworthy"; so they did not say about you that you are a liar, but they repudiated the validity of your prophethood and your mission. Either because they believed that Muhammad had some kind of derangement and deficiency, and on account of it he imagined himself to be a messenger from God—and by this estimation they do not attribute lying to him—or because they said that he did not lie in other matters, but is trustworthy in all of them except this one single matter.

The third way of interpretation: when the overpowering miracles appeared in accordance with his claim, yet the people persisted in denial, God Exalted said to him: "These people have not denied you, but they have denied Me." Its parallel is that if a man insults the slave of another man, and that other man says: "O slave, he has not insulted you, but he has insulted me." The purpose is not to negate the insult from the slave, but rather to magnify the matter and glorify its importance. Its explanation: the insult to that slave takes the place of insulting him. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you are only pledging allegiance to God﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

The fourth way of interpretation, which is a statement that came to mind: it is said that the intended meaning of His saying "fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka" is that they do not single you out with this denial, but rather they deny the indication of the miracle as proof of truthfulness absolutely. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿but it is the signs of God that the wrongdoers repudiate﴾. The meaning is that they say of every miracle that it is sorcery, and they deny the indication of the miracle as proof of truthfulness altogether. So the estimation is: they do not deny you specifically, but rather the people deny all the prophets and messengers. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and were harmed until Our victory came to them. And none can alter the words of Allah. And there has already come to you some of the news of the messengers.﴾

In the verse there are two issues:

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, removed grief from the heart of His Messenger in the previous verse by explaining that denying him is like denying Allah, exalted is He. In this verse He mentions another way of removing grief from his heart, namely by explaining that all the (other) nations treated their prophets in this same manner, and that those prophets were patient over their denial and harm until victory, conquest and triumph came to them. So you are more deserving of adopting this way, because you have been sent to all the worlds. So be patient as they were patient, and you will triumph as they triumphed. Then Allah, exalted is He, confirmed and strengthened this promise by His saying: ﴿And none can alter the words of Allah﴾, meaning that His promise to you of victory is true and sincere, and it is impossible for failure or alteration to reach it. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Our word has already preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ [As-Saffat: 171], and His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed, "Surely I will prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 21]. In sum, failure in the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is impossible. His saying: ﴿And there has already come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ means: their report in the Qur'an, how We saved them and destroyed their people.

Al-Akhfash said: "min" (مِن) here is extra (ṣilah), as you say "aṣābanā min maṭar" (rain reached us). Others said: this is not permissible, because it is not added in an affirmative sentence; it is only added with negation, as you say: "mā atānī min aḥad" (no one came to me). Here it is for partitive (tab'īḍ), for what reached the Messenger, peace be upon him, is the narrative of some of the prophets, not the narrative of all of them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Of them are those We have related to you and of them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir: 78]. The subject of "jā'a" (came) is an implied pronoun, implied because of what is mentioned indicating it, and its estimated form is: "And there has certainly come to you a report from the reports of the messengers."

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And none can alter the words of Allah﴾ indicates our position concerning the creation of acts (khalq al-af'āl). This is because everything that Allah informs us will occur, that report is impossible to change, and when that report is impossible to change, the change of what it reports about is also impossible. So when Allah informs about some of them that they will die upon disbelief, it is impossible for them to abandon disbelief. Thus, obligating him to faith would be obligating him with what cannot be borne. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if their turning away is grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign, [then do so]. And had Allah willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant.﴾

Page 171
There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that "al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manaf came to the Prophet ﷺ along with a group of Quraysh, and they said: 'O Muhammad, bring us a sign from Allah, as the prophets used to do, and then we will believe in you.' Allah refused to bring them one, so they turned away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this grieved him, so this verse was revealed." The meaning is: And if their turning away from faith in you and the soundness of the Qur'an is grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky, then do it.

The answer (jawab) is omitted, and this omission is fine because it is known to minds. The nafaq (tunnel) is a passage in the earth that has an exit to another place, and from it comes nafaqa' al-yarbuʿ (the escape hole of the jerboa), because the jerboa pierces the earth down to its burrow, then climbs from that burrow to the surface of the earth from another side, so it is as if it has tunneled the earth, that is, made an exit for itself from another side. From this also the hypocrite (munafiq) is so named, because he conceals other than what he shows, like the nafiqa' that the jerboa makes. As for the sullam (ladder), it is derived from salama (safety), and it is that which conveys you to your ascent. The purpose of this statement is that the Messenger should cut off his hope regarding their faith, and that he should not be distressed because of their turning away from faith and their inclination toward disbelief.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾. Its implied sense: And had Allah willed their guidance, He would have gathered them upon guidance. And whenever He did not gather them upon guidance, it must be said that He did not will their guidance, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, does not will faith from the disbeliever, but rather wills his remaining upon disbelief. What brings this apparent meaning closer is that the disbeliever's capacity for disbelief is either suitable for faith or not suitable for it. If it is not suitable for it, then the capacity for disbelief entails disbelief and is not suitable for faith, so the Creator of this capacity must necessarily have willed this disbelief from him. But if this capacity, just as it is suitable for disbelief, is also suitable for faith, then, since the relation of capacity to both sides is equal, the preponderance of one side over the other is impossible except by a preponderant motive (daʿiyah murajjihah). The obtaining of that motive is not from the servant, otherwise an infinite regress (tasalsul) would occur. Thus it is established that the Creator of that motive is Allah, exalted is He. And it is established that the combination of the capacity with the motive obtained necessitates the act. Thus it is established that the Creator of the combination of that capacity together with that motive, which entails that disbelief, wills that disbelief and does not will that faith. This certain proof is strong and manifest through this verse, and there is no clearer explanation than that the proof agrees with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

The Mu'tazilah said: The intended meaning is: had Allah willed to compel them to faith, He would have gathered them upon it. The qadi said: Compulsion (ilja') is that He makes them know that if they attempted other than faith He would prevent them from it, and then they would refrain from doing anything other than faith. An example of this: if one of us were in the presence of the sultan, and a great number of his attendants were present there, and this man knew that if he intended to kill the sultan they would kill him immediately, then this knowledge becomes a barrier preventing him from intending to kill that sultan, and that becomes a cause for his being compelled to abandon that act. So it is likewise here.

When you know compulsion, we say: He, exalted is He, only abandoned this compulsion because it would remove their obligation (taklif), so that what proceeds from them would be as if it had not proceeded; and He only willed that they benefit by what they choose of their own selves, in terms of the path to reward, and that is not possible except by choice.

The answer: He, exalted is He, willed from them the undertaking of faith in a state in which the summoner to faith and to disbelief is on an equal footing, or in a state in which that preponderance obtains. The first is the imposition of what cannot be borne, because the command to bring about preponderance in the state of equality is an imposition of the combining of two contradictories, which is impossible. And if it is the second, then the preponderant side becomes necessary to occur, and the non-preponderant side becomes impossible to occur, and all these divisions contradict what they mentioned of capability and choice, so their statement falls entirely. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, at the end of the verse: ﴿so do not be among the ignorant﴾. It is a prohibition addressed to him concerning this state, and this prohibition does not entail his engaging in such a state, just as His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48] does not indicate that he ﷺ obeyed them and accepted their religion. The intended meaning is that your grief over their denial should not be intense, and it is not permissible for you to be distressed by their turning away from you, for if you did that your state would approach the state of the ignorant. The purpose of the harshness of this address is distancing and warning him against such a state. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Only those who listen respond, while the dead—Allah will raise them, then to Him they will be returned.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, explained the cause of their being in a state where they neither accept faith nor abandon disbelief, and so He said: ﴿Only those who listen respond.﴾ That is, those whom you are eager to have believe you are in the position of the dead who do not hear, and only one who hears responds. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80]. Ali ibn Isa said: the difference between yastajību (to respond, to accept) and yujību (to answer) is that yastajību refers to accepting what one has been called to, whereas yujību does not necessarily carry that sense, because one may answer with opposition, like the speaker who asks, "Do you agree with this school of thought or oppose it?" and the answerer says, "I oppose it."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿while the dead—Allah will raise them﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

The first: it is a parable for His power to compel them to respond. The meaning is: He, exalted is He, is the one who is able to raise the dead from their graves on the Day of Resurrection, then to Him they will be returned for recompense. Likewise here, He, exalted is He, is the one able to give life to the hearts of these disbelievers with the life of faith, and you are not able to do so.

The second opinion: the meaning is: and these dead, meaning the disbelievers, Allah will raise them, then to Him they will be returned; then they will hear. Before that, there is no way for them to hear. It was also read as ﴿yarjiʿūn﴾ with a fatḥa on the yāʾ.

I say: There is no doubt that a body devoid of the soul manifests stench, pus, discharge, and all kinds of decay, and the best condition for it is to be buried under the earth. Also, a soul devoid of reason is a madman who deserves chains and imprisonment. Reason in relation to the soul is like the soul in relation to the body. Also, reason without knowledge of God, His attributes, and obedience to Him is like something lost and void. So the relation of tawḥīd (affirmation of God's oneness) and ma'rifa (knowledge) to reason is like the relation of reason to the soul, and the relation of the soul to the body. Thus the knowledge of God and love for Him is the spirit of the spirit. The soul devoid of this knowledge is in the state of the dead. For this reason God described those obstinate disbelievers as "the dead." And God knows best.

[Page 173]

The Exalted said: ﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾

Know that this is the fourth type of the doubts raised by those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). They said: "If he were a messenger from Allah, why did He not send down to him an overpowering sign and a dazzling miracle?"

It is related that some of the heretics (al-mulhida) criticized [the claim that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought a miracle] and said: "If Muhammad (ﷺ) had brought a miraculous sign, it would not be correct for those unbelievers to say, ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him?﴾ and He would not have said, ﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾"

The answer to this is that the Qur'an is an overpowering miracle and a dazzling proof, as evidenced by the fact that he (ﷺ) challenged them with it, and they were unable to produce its equal, and this indicates that it is a miracle.

It remains to be said: if the matter is as such, then how did they say, ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾

We say: the answer to this is in several respects.

The first respect: perhaps the people criticized the Qur'an's being a miracle out of stubbornness and obstinacy, and said: it belongs to the genre of books, and a book cannot be of the genre of miracles, as in the case of the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel. And because of this doubt they demanded a miracle.

The second respect: they demanded overpowering miracles of the same kind as the miracles of the other prophets, such as splitting the sea, raising the mountain over them, and reviving the dead.

The third respect: they demanded additional signs and miracles out of capriciousness and obstinacy, such as sending down angels, or making the sky fall in pieces, and the rest of what He related about the unbelievers.

The fourth respect: the intended meaning is what the Exalted related of some of them in His saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Anfal: 32] All these aspects are possible meanings of the wording of the verse.

Then the Exalted answered their question with His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign,"﴾ meaning: He, the Exalted, is able to bring into being what you asked for and to accomplish what you proposed. ﴿but most of them do not know.﴾ Scholars differed in interpreting this phrase in several ways:

The first way: the intended meaning is that when He had sent down a dazzling sign and an overpowering miracle, namely the Qur'an, then demanding more was a matter of arbitrary and baseless domination and obstinacy. Allah, glorified is He, has the judgment and the command: if He wills He does, and if He wills He does not. His acting is only in accordance with pure will according to the view of Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni school), or in accordance with what is beneficial according to the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). On either assessment, His acts do not conform to people's proposals and demands; if He wills, He answers them, and if He wills, He does not answer them.

The second way: when the overpowering miracle and the dazzling proof that suffices had appeared, they had no excuse or pretext left. After that, if Allah the Exalted were to grant them that proposal, they might propose a second, a third, a fourth, and so on without end, and that would lead to the proof never being settled and the argument never being completed. Therefore, at the outset, it was necessary to close this door and to be content with the overpowering miracle and the dazzling proof that had already come.

The third way: if the Exalted had given them the overpowering miracles they demanded, then, had they not believed upon their appearance, they would have deserved the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal). The mercy of Allah required protecting them from this trial, so He did not give them this demanded thing, as a mercy from Him, the Exalted, toward them, even though they do not know the manner of this mercy. For this reason He said: ﴿but most of them do not know.﴾

The fourth way: the Exalted knew of them that they sought these miracles not for the sake of benefit but out of spite and fanaticism, and He knew that if He gave them what they asked for they would not believe. For this reason He did not give them what they demanded, since He, the Exalted, knew there was no benefit in that. Thus the meaning of His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ is that the people do not know that, since they demanded that out of obstinacy and fanaticism, Allah the Exalted would not give them what they demanded; and if they had been knowing and rational, they would have demanded it for the sake of seeking benefit, and then Allah the Exalted would have given them that demanded thing in the most perfect manner. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 38 (part 1 of 3)**

[p. 175]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird that flies on its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.﴾

Concerning the verse, there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the establishment of the coherence (nazm) of the verse, we say there are two aspects to it.

The first: In the previous verse, He, may He be exalted, showed that if sending all the miracles were in their interest, He would have done so and would have displayed them. But since displaying them was not in the interest of those under obligation (mukallafun), He did not display them. This answer is only complete if it is established that He, may He be exalted, attends to the interests of those under obligation and bestows favour upon them in this way. So He made clear that the matter is so, and He established it by saying: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird that flies on its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾, in the reaching of God's bounty, care, mercy and kindness to them. This is like a matter that is witnessed and perceived by the senses. If the effects of His care reach all the animals, then if displaying these overpowering miracles were in the interest of those under obligation, He would have done so and displayed them, and it would be impossible for Him to withhold them, since it is evident that He has not withheld from any of the animals their interests and benefits. This indicates that He, may He be exalted, did not display those miracles because displaying them would harm the interests of those under obligation. This is the aspect of the coherence and the connection between this verse and what precedes it, and God knows best.

The second aspect concerning the manner of the coherence: Al-Qadi said: When He, may He be exalted, mentioned the disbelievers first, and showed that they will return to God and be gathered, He then also showed, by His saying ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird that flies on its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾, that [they too will be gathered]. The purpose is to show that just as the gathering and resurrection occur for humans, they also occur for the beasts.

The second issue: An animal is either of the kind that crawls or of the kind that flies. Every animal God has created does not escape these two attributes: either it crawls or it flies. There are questions concerning the verse:

The first question: Among animals are some that do not fall under these two categories, such as the fish of the sea and all that swims in water and lives in it.

The answer: It is not far-fetched to describe them as a "creature" (dabbah) insofar as they move (tadibb) in the water, or they are like birds, since they swim in water just as birds swim in the air. However, describing them with crawling is closer to the language than describing them with flying.

The second question: What is the benefit of restricting the creature to being "on the earth"?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: He singled out what is on the earth for mention, rather than what is in the heavens, on the basis of what is more evident, because what is in the heavens, although it is created like us, is not apparent.

The second: The purpose of mentioning this statement is that since God's care is present in these animals, if displaying the overpowering miracles were in the interest [of humans], God would not have prevented their display. This purpose is only fulfilled by mentioning what is of lower rank than humans, not by mentioning what is of higher status than them. For this reason He restricted the creature to being on the earth.

The third question: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿that flies on its two wings﴾, given that every bird flies only on its two wings?

The answer to this has several aspects:

The first: This attribute is mentioned only for emphasis, like His saying "a female she-goat" (na'jatun unthā), and like one says: "I spoke to him with my mouth," and "I walked to him on my two feet."

The second: A man may say to his servant, "Fly on my errand," meaning "hurry." In this sense, flying may occur without wings. The poet al-Hamasi said:

*They flew to it in groups and singly.*

So He mentioned the wing to make this expression clear regarding birds.

The third: He, may He be exalted, said in describing the angels: ﴿Who made the angels messengers having wings, two, three and four﴾ [Fatir: 1]. So here He mentioned His saying ﴿nor any bird that flies on its two wings﴾ in order to exclude the angels from it. We have already shown that the purpose of this statement is only fulfilled by mentioning what is of lower status than humans, not by mentioning what is of higher status than them.

The fourth question: How did He say ﴿communities﴾ (umam) when the words "creature" and "bird" are singular?

The answer: Since His saying ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird﴾ indicates the sense of comprehensiveness (istighraq) and dispenses with saying "there are no creatures nor birds," His saying ﴿communities﴾ was therefore taken according to the meaning.

The fifth question: His saying ﴿communities like you﴾. Al-Farra' said: It is said that every kind of beast is a community (ummah), and there is a hadith: "Were it not that dogs are a community among the communities, I would have ordered their killing," so he made dogs a community.

Given this, we say: The verse indicates that these creatures and birds are like us, but there is nothing in it indicating in which respects this likeness occurs. It cannot be said that the intended meaning is the likeness in every respect, for otherwise it would be necessary that they be like us in form and creation, and that is false. Thus it is clear that there is no indication that this likeness occurs in every condition and matter. Therefore, they explained that.

The answer: People have differed in specifying the matter in which God, may He be exalted, judged there to be likeness between humans and the creatures and birds, and they mentioned several views:

The first view: Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "It means they recognize Me, declare Me one, glorify Me and praise Me." To this view a great group of exegetes went, and they said: These animals know God, praise Him, declare Him one and glorify Him. They based this on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 44], and on His saying about the animals: ﴿Each has indeed known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur: 41], and on the fact that He, may He be exalted, addressed the ant and addressed the hoopoe. We have thoroughly examined the establishment and verification of this view in these verses.

It is reported from Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The minds of beasts have been kept from everything except four things: knowledge of God, seeking provision, knowledge of male and female, and the readiness of each of them for its partner."

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever kills a sparrow in vain will come on the Day of Resurrection crying out to God, saying: 'O Lord, this one killed me in vain, it did not benefit from me, and it did not let me eat of the insects of the earth.'"

The second view: The meaning is "communities like you" in being communities and groups, and in being created such that some of them resemble others, some are at ease with others, and some breed from others, like humans. However, a questioner may say: Interpreting the verse in this way does not give a meaningful benefit, because it is a matter known to everyone that animals have these characteristics, so there is no benefit in reporting about them.

The third view: The meaning is that they are like us in that God arranged them, created them, and undertook their provision. This is close to the second view, in that it is like reporting something whose occurrence is known by necessity.

The fourth view: The meaning is that just as He has counted in the Book everything related to the conditions of humans, such as their lifespan, provision, term, happiness and misery, so likewise He has counted in the Book all these conditions for all animals. They said: The evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾, and there is no benefit in mentioning this statement immediately after His saying ﴿but they are communities like you﴾ except what we have mentioned.

The fifth view: He, may He be exalted, intended that they are like us in that they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection and their rights will be delivered to them, as it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Retribution will be taken for the hornless (jamma') from the horned (qarna')."

The sixth view: What we have chosen in the coherence of the verse, namely that the disbelievers asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to bring overpowering, manifest miracles. So God, may He be exalted, made clear that His care has reached all the animals just as it has reached humans. Whoever has had His mercy and bounty reach the point that He does not withhold it from the animals, He is more worthy of not withholding it from humans. Thus God's preventing the display of those overpowering miracles indicates that there is no interest for those questioners in displaying them, and that displaying them according to their demand and their proposal would bring great harm back upon them.

[p. 177]

The seventh view: What Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi transmitted from Sufyan ibn Uyayna, that when he recited this verse he said: "There is no human on earth except that there is in him a resemblance to some of the beasts. Some of them advance like the lion, some run like the wolf, some bark like the dog, some strut like the peacock, and some resemble the pig, for if good food is placed before him he leaves it, and if a man gets up from his excrement, he laps at it. Likewise we find among the sons of Adam one who, if he hears fifty wise sayings, does not memorize one of them; but if he errs once, he memorizes that, and he does not sit in a gathering without relating it from it."

Then he said: "Know, my brother, that you are only keeping company with beasts and predators, so be extremely cautious and wary. This is the sum of what has been said on this point."

The third issue: Those who believe in metempsychosis (tanasukh, the transmigration of souls) hold that if human souls are happy, obedient to God, and characterized by true knowledge and pure morals, then after death they are transferred into the bodies of kings, and perhaps they say that they are transferred into association with the world of angels. But if they are wretched, ignorant and disobedient, they are transferred into the bodies of animals, and the more wretched and deserving of punishment those souls are, the more they are transferred into the body of a baser animal with more misery and toil. They argued for the correctness of their view with this verse, saying: The plain meaning of this verse indicates that there is no creature or bird except that it is like us. The word "likeness" requires equality in all essential attributes, while in accidental, separable attributes, equality is not required for the establishment of likeness. Then those who hold this view added to it, saying: It has been established by this that the souls of all animals know their Lord and know what happiness and misery will befall them, and that God has sent to each kind among them a messenger from their own kind. They argued for this by saying that this verse establishes that the creatures and birds are communities, and then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And there is no community but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24], which is an explicit statement that each group of these animals has a messenger whom God sent to it. Then they reinforced this with the story of the hoopoe, the story of the ant, and the other stories mentioned in the Qur'an.

Know that the doctrine of metempsychosis has been refuted by sound proofs in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (ʿilm al-uṣūl, the principles of legal theory). As for this verse, we have mentioned what suffices regarding the truth of the likeness in some of the matters mentioned, so there is no need to establish what the people of metempsychosis have stated. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾, and concerning what is meant by "the Book" there are two views:

The first view: It means the Book preserved in the Throne and in the world of the heavens, which contains all the conditions of created beings in complete detail, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The pen has dried with what is to exist until the Day of Resurrection."

The second view: It means the Qur'an, and this is more apparent, because when the definite article (al-) is attached to a singular noun, it refers to the previously known referent, and the previously known referent of "the Book" among Muslims is the Qur'an. Therefore "the Book" in this verse must mean the Qur'an.

Given this, one may ask: How did He, may He be exalted, say ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾, when it does not contain the detailed content of the science of medicine, the detailed content of the science of calculation, nor the detailed content of many topics and sciences, nor does it contain the detailed positions of people and their proofs in the sciences of the foundations and the branches (of jurisprudence)?

The answer is: the statement "We have not neglected anything in the Book" (ma faratna fi al-kitab min shay') must be understood as restricted to the explanation of the things that must be known and fully grasped. Its clarification is in two respects.

The first: the word tafrit (neglect) is never used, whether in negation or affirmation, except regarding what must be made clear, because no one is blamed for neglect or shortcoming in failing to do what is not needed. This term is only mentioned when one falls short in what is needed.

The second: all or most of the verses of the Qur'an indicate, by direct correspondence, by inclusion, or by necessary implication, that the purpose of sending down this Book is the explanation of the religion, the knowledge of God, and the knowledge of God's rulings. And when this restriction is known from the whole Qur'an, the unrestricted statement here is to be carried over to that restricted meaning.

As for his claim that this Book does not comprise all the sciences of the principles (usul) and the branches (furu'):

We say: as for the science of the principles (usul al-din), it is wholly present in it, because the foundational proofs are mentioned in it in the most eloquent manner. As for the narrations of the schools of law and the detailed opinions, there is no need for them. As for the details of the science of the branches (furu' al-fiqh), we say: the scholars have two opinions here:

The first: they said that the Qur'an indicates that consensus (ijma'), the report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid), and analogical reasoning (qiyas) are valid proofs in the Sharia. So whatever is indicated by one of these three sources is, in reality, present in the Qur'an. Al-Wahidi (may God have mercy on him) gave three examples for this meaning:

The first example: it is reported that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: "Why should I not curse those whom God has cursed in His Book?" — meaning the tattooer (al-washima) and the one who has herself tattooed (al-mustawshima), the one who joins hair (al-wasila) and the one who has it joined (al-musta wsila). And it is reported that a woman read the entire Qur'an, then came to him and said: "O son of Umm 'Abd, I recited last night what is between the two covers, and I did not find in it the cursing of the tattooer and the one who has herself tattooed." He said: "If you had recited it, you would have found it. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and among what the Messenger of God brought to us is that he said: 'God has cursed the tattooer and the one who has herself tattooed.'" I say: this meaning can be found in the Book of God in a clearer way than that, for He, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿They invoke none but a rebellious devil﴾ ﴿God cursed him﴾ [al-Nisa': 117, 118], so He passed a judgment of cursing upon him, then enumerated after that his evil deeds, and among them His saying: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will change the creation of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 119]. The apparent meaning of this verse requires that changing the creation incurs the curse.

The second example: it is mentioned that al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) was sitting in the Masjid al-Haram and said: "Do not ask me about anything except that I will answer you from the Book of God, the Exalted." A man said: "What do you say about the muhrim (one in ihram) who kills a wasp?" He said: "There is nothing upon him." The man said: "Where is this in the Book of God?" He said: "God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾." Then he mentioned a chain of transmission to the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Hold fast to my sunna and the sunna of the rightly guided caliphs after me." Then he mentioned a chain of transmission to 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) that he said: "For the muhrim, killing a wasp is permissible." Al-Wahidi said: so he answered him from the Book of God by deriving with three levels. I say: here there is another path closer than this, namely that the basic principle regarding the property of Muslims is inviolability. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He said: ﴿He does not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36], and He said: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. So He forbade consuming people's property except through trade. When there is no trade, it must remain upon the original principle of prohibition. These general texts require that the muhrim who killed the wasp has nothing due upon him, because holding to these general texts yields a ruling at a single level.

As for the path mentioned by al-Shafi'i: it is an appeal to generality through four levels. The first: holding to the generality of His saying
صفحة ١٧٩
﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7].
One of the matters included under this is the Prophet's command, peace be upon him, to follow the rightly guided caliphs.

The second: holding to the generality of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Hold fast to my sunna and the sunna of the rightly guided caliphs after me."

The third: showing that 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, was among the rightly guided caliphs.

The fourth: the report from 'Umar that he did not require anything in this matter; thus it is established that the path we mentioned is closer.

The third example: al-Wahidi said: "It is reported in the hadith of the hired laborer who committed zina that his father said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Judge between us by the Book of God.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will judge between you both by the Book of God,' then he ruled for flogging and exile for the laborer, and stoning for the woman if she confessed." Al-Wahidi said: there is no mention of flogging and exile in the text of the Book, and this shows that everything the Prophet ﷺ ruled upon is itself the Book of God.

I say: this example is correct, because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44], and everything the Messenger, peace be upon him, explained falls under this verse. Thus it is established by these examples that when the Qur'an indicates that consensus is a proof, that the report of a single transmitter is a proof, and that analogy is a proof, then every ruling established through one of these three methods is, in reality, established by the Qur'an. At this point the saying of God, the Exalted, ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ is correct. This is the articulation of this view, which the majority of jurists have undertaken to support.

One may object: the substance of this view is that since the Qur'an indicates that the report of a single transmitter and analogy are valid, every ruling established by either of these two principles is in reality established by the Qur'an. However, we say: reading His saying ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ in this sense is not permissible, because ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ is mentioned in the context of magnifying this Book, extolling it and praising it. If we interpret this verse in this meaning, nothing producing magnification would result from it. For if we supposed that God, the Exalted, had said: "Act upon consensus, the report of a single transmitter, and analogy," the meaning they mention would be obtained from this statement; yet a meaning that can be obtained from this brief wording cannot be made the basis for praising the Qur'an and extolling it on account of its containing it. For this would produce great praise and complete commendation only if it could not be obtained by another method more concise than it. But since we have shown that this intended category can be derived and obtained by the concise wording we mentioned, we know that it cannot be cited in glorifying the Qur'an. Thus it is established that this verse is mentioned in the context of magnifying the Qur'an, and it is established that the meaning they mention does not convey the magnification of the Qur'an. Therefore it must be said that this verse may not be interpreted in that meaning. This is the utmost that can be said in articulating this view.

The second view on the interpretation of this verse is the view of those who say: the Qur'an is sufficient in explaining all the rulings. Its articulation: the default is the discharge of obligation (bara'at al-dhimma) regarding all obligations, and the burdening of the obligation requires a separate proof. And to specify the categories in which no obligation has been imposed is impossible, because the categories in which no obligation has been imposed are infinite, and specifying what has no end is impossible; rather, specification is possible only for the finite. For example, God, the Exalted, has a thousand obligations upon His servants, and He mentioned them in the Qur'an and commanded Muhammad, peace be upon him, to convey those thousand to the servants. Then He said after that: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾, so its meaning is that there is no further obligation from God upon creation beyond that thousand. Then He confirmed this verse with His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and with His saying: ﴿Nothing wet or dry but is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. This is the articulation of the position of these people, and the detailed examination of it belongs to the science of usul al-fiqh. And God knows best.

صفحة ١٨٠

Let us now return to the exegesis. We say: His saying ﴿of any thing﴾ (min shay'). Al-Wahidi said: "min" is redundant, like the saying: "No one came to me." Its articulation: "We have not left in the Book anything that we did not explain." I say: the word "min" is partitive, so the meaning is: "We have not neglected in the Book some part of a thing the responsible person needs," and this is the utmost emphasis that He, the Exalted, left nothing out, of what the responsible person needs to know, in this Book.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾, the meaning is that God, the Exalted, gathers the beasts and birds on the Day of Resurrection. This is reinforced by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [al-Takwir: 5], and by what is reported, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Retribution will be taken for the hornless (sheep) from the horned." Scholars have two views on this:

The first view: God gathers the animals and birds not to deliver compensation to them, and this is the view of the Mu'tazilah. This is because inflicting pain on them as a consequence of a prior wrong is only good if there is compensation (iwad), and since delivering compensation to them is obligatory, God gathers them in order to deliver those compensations to them.

The second view: the view of our companions (the Ash'arites) that it is impossible for anything to be obligatory upon God; rather God gathers them merely by will and volition and by the requirement of divinity. They argued that the view that compensation is obligatory upon God is impossible and false, on several grounds:

The first argument: obligation is defined as that whose omission entails blame, and for God to be liable to blame is impossible, because God is perfect in His essence, and one who is perfect in his essence cannot be conceived as being liable to blame through an external cause, since what belongs to the essence does not cease upon the occurrence of something external.

The second argument: God is the owner of all created things, and an owner may justly dispose of what he owns without any need for compensation.

The third argument: if it were good to inflict harm upon another for the sake of compensation, it would follow that it would be good for us to inflict harms on others for the sake of taking on compensation without their consent, and that is false. Thus it is established that the view of compensation is false. And God knows best.

Having understood this, let us mention some of the branch issues that the Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) mentioned in this chapter.

The first branch: the Qadi said: every living creature that deserves compensation from God for the pains that befell it, and that compensation has not reached it in this world, then God must gather it in the Hereafter by reason in order to fully provide that compensation to it. As for the one that is not like this, its gathering is not obligatory by reason; however, God has informed that He gathers all, so by way of revelation this is affirmed. We said that among animals there are some that never deserve compensation at all, because they may remain throughout their lives protected from pains, and then God causes them to die without any pain whatsoever. For it has not been established by proof that death must necessarily be accompanied by some pain, and on this assumption such an animal does not deserve compensation at all.

The second branch: every animal whose slaughter God has permitted is owed compensation from God. These are of several kinds: among them are those permitted to be slaughtered for eating; among them are those permitted to be slaughtered because they are harmful, such as ravaging predators and harmful insects; among them are those God afflicted with diseases; and among them are those for which God permitted heavy loads to be placed upon them and their use in arduous tasks. As for when people wrong them, that compensation is owed by that wrongdoer; and when some of them wrong others, that compensation is owed by that wrongdoer.

صفحة ١٨١

If it is said: when something whose meat is not eaten is slaughtered in the proper manner of dhakat, upon whom is the compensation?

He answered: that is an injustice, and the compensation is owed by the slaughterer. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ "forbade slaughtering an animal except for food (ma'kalah)."

Section 3: The third point: what is meant by the compensation ('iwad) is great benefits, reaching such a degree of majesty and elevation that, were this animal rational and aware that it had no way to obtain that benefit except through bearing that slaughter, it would accept it. This is the compensation for the sake of which infliction of pain and harm is good.

Section 4: The position of al-Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) and most of the Mu'tazilah of Basra is that the compensation is cut off (i.e., it is not perpetual). Al-Qadi said: this is the view of most of the commentators, for they said that after He (Exalted is He) has furnished the compensation to it, He will turn it into dust, and at this point the disbelieving one will say: "Would that I were dust." Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi said: the compensation must be perpetual. Al-Qadi argued for his view by saying that it is good for one of us to undertake a difficult task while the wage is cut off, so we know that causing pain to another is not conditioned on the wage's permanence. Al-Balkhi argued for his view by saying: it is not possible to cut off that compensation except by causing that animal to die, and causing it to die entails pain, and that pain entails another compensation, and so on without end.

The answer to this: it has not been established by proof that causing death cannot be achieved except together with infliction of pain. And God knows best.

Section 5: If an animal has a right to compensation from another animal, then if the wronging animal has a right to compensation from God (Exalted is He), He transfers that compensation to the one wronged. If the matter is not so, God (Exalted is He) completes that compensation. This is a summary of the rulings on compensation according to the view of the Mu'tazilah. And God knows best.

**[Commentary of al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on Surah 6, verse 39]**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darknesses. Whomever Allah wills, He lets go astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path.﴾

Concerning it are issues:

**The first issue: regarding the connection of the verse (wajh al-nazm), there are two opinions.**

The first: He, exalted is He, explained the state of the disbelievers, that they had reached such a degree of disbelief that it was as if their hearts had become dead to accepting faith, by His saying: ﴿Only those who hear will respond, and the dead, Allah will raise them﴾. So He mentioned this verse as a confirmation of that meaning.

The second: when He, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾, that they indicate that they are under the management of an eternal Manager and under the decree of a wise Decreer, and that Allah's care encompasses them and His mercy reaches them, He said after it: "And those who deny these proofs and reject these wonders are deaf who hear no speech at all, dumb who do not speak the truth, plunged in the darknesses of disbelief, heedless of reflecting upon these proofs."

[p. 182]

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued by this verse that guidance and misguidance are only from Allah, exalted is He. Its explanation: He, exalted is He, described them as being deaf and dumb, and as being in darknesses, and this is an indication of their being blind. So it is precisely like His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills, He lets go astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path﴾, and this is explicit that guidance and misguidance are only from Allah, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah said: the answer to this is in several aspects.

**The first aspect:** al-Jubba'i (d. 303 AH) said: its meaning is that He, exalted is He, makes them deaf and dumb on the Day of Resurrection at the gathering. And they will be like that in reality, in that He will make them in the Hereafter deaf and dumb in the darknesses, and He will lead them astray by that from Paradise and from its path, and send them to the Fire. Al-Qadi (Abd al-Jabbar) affirmed this statement, saying that He, exalted is He, explained in other verses that He will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf, their abode being Hell.

**The second aspect:** al-Jubba'i also said: it is possible that they are like that in this world, so it is a figurative extension, in that by their denial of the signs of Allah, exalted is He, they are in darknesses, not guided to the benefits of religion, like the deaf and dumb who are not guided to the benefits of this world. So He likened them in this respect to them, and applied to them the like of their attributes by way of comparison.

**The third aspect:** al-Ka'bi said: His saying ﴿deaf and dumb﴾ is to be taken as insult and humiliation, not that they were literally like that. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah wills, He lets go astray﴾, al-Ka'bi said: this is not in the form of a metaphor, because He, exalted is He, though He stated the matter briefly here, has explained it in other verses, which is His saying: ﴿And Allah lets the wrongdoers go astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 27], and His saying: ﴿And He does not lead astray by it except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and His saying: ﴿And those who were guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17], and His saying: ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16], and His saying: ﴿Allah makes firm those who believe with the firm word﴾ [Ibrahim: 27], and His saying: ﴿And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69]. Thus it is established by these verses that the will concerning guidance and misguidance, although it is stated in general terms in this verse, is specified and detailed in other verses, so this general statement must be interpreted in light of those detailed ones.

Then the Mu'tazilah mentioned interpretations of this verse in detail, in several aspects:

**The first:** that what is meant by His saying ﴿in darknesses, whomever Allah wills, He lets go astray﴾ is to be understood as the withholding of divine favors (al-alṭaf, sing. lutf), so they become, in that case, like the deaf and dumb.

**The second:** ﴿whomever Allah wills, He lets go astray﴾ on the Day of Resurrection from the path to Paradise and from finding the reward, and whomever He wills to guide to Paradise, He places him on a straight path, which is the path that the believers travel to Paradise.

It has been established by proof that He, exalted is He, does not will this misguidance except for one who deserves punishment, just as He does not will guidance except for the believers.

Know that these aspects which those people have strained to are only acceptable to resort to if it is established by reason that this speech cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning. But since it has been established by a decisive rational proof that this speech can only be taken according to its apparent meaning, resorting to these strained aspects is extremely far-fetched. We have shown that the act does not occur except upon the occurrence of the motive (al-da'i), and we have shown that the creator of that motive is Allah, and we have shown that when it occurs, the act becomes necessary. These three premises necessitate the certainty that disbelief and faith are from Allah, and by His creating, decreeing and bringing them into being. And when the correctness of this apparent meaning has been established by this decisive demonstration, resorting to these strained interpretations is certainly invalid. Also, we have traced these aspects with refutation and rebuttal in the

[p. 183]

explanation of His saying: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], and in the rest of the verses, so there is no need to repeat them. The closest of them is that this misguidance and guidance are dependent upon the will; and according to what they have said, it is an obligation upon Allah, exalted is He, that He must do it, whether He wills or refuses. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs﴾. They differed concerning what is meant by those signs. Some said: the Qur'an and Muhammad (ﷺ). Others said: it encompasses all the proofs and evidences, and this is the most correct opinion. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 40–41:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?﴾ ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills, and you forget what you associate with Him.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the extent of the ignorance of those disbelievers, He also explained from their condition that when a calamity or a trial befalls them, they turn in fear to Allah, exalted is He, and seek refuge in Him, and do not rebel against His obedience. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Farra' said that the Arabs have two usages of "ara'ayta" (أرَأيْتَ):

The first: the sight of the eye. When you say to a man, "ara'aytaka" (أرَأيْتَكَ), the meaning is: "Have you seen yourself?" Then it is made dual and plural, so we say "ara'aytakuma" (أرَأيْتَكُما) and "ara'aytakum" (أرَأيْتَكم).

The second meaning: that you say "ara'aytaka" and mean "inform me." When you intend this meaning, you keep the ta' open in every case: you say "ara'aytaka," "ara'aytakuma," "ara'aytakum," "ara'aytakunna."

Having understood this, we say: the position of the Basrans is that the second pronoun, which is the kaf in your saying "ara'aytaka," has no place in i'rab (grammatical case-marking, the grammatical function of a word), and the proof is His saying: ﴿He said: Have you seen this one whom you have honored above me?﴾ [al-Isra': 62]. It is also said: "ara'aytaka Zaydan ma sha'nuhu" (Have you seen Zayd, what is his affair?). If you made the kaf a place in i'rab, it would be as if you were saying: "Have you seen yourself, Zayd, what is his affair?" and that is corrupt speech. Thus it is established that the kaf has no place in i'rab; rather it is a particle for the purpose of address. Al-Farra' said: If the kaf were for emphasis, the dual and plural would fall upon the ta', as they fall upon it when the kaf is absent. But when the ta' is opened in addressing a plural, and the sign of the plural falls upon the kaf, this shows that the kaf is not mentioned for emphasis. Do you not see that if the kaf were dropped, it would not be proper to say to a group "ara'ayta"? Thus it is established by this that the verb is directed at the kaf, and that it is obligatory, necessary, and required.

Al-Wahidi answered this: This argument is refuted by the kaf of "dhalika" and "ulaika," for the sign of the plural falls upon them even though they are particles of address, stripped of nominality. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Nafi' recited "ara'aytakum," "ara'ayta," "afara'ayta," "ara'aytaka," "afara'aytaka," and similar forms throughout the Qur'an with the hamza lightened, and al-Kisa'i omitted the hamza throughout the Qur'an, while the rest read with the hamza. As for the lightening of the hamza, what is meant is making it between the hamza and the alif, by the regular (qiyasi) lightening. As for al-Kisa'i's position, it is good, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited with it, and it is frequent in poetry. The Arabs have spoken in similar cases by dropping the hamza for lightening, as they said "wa-slhu" (and ask him), and as Ahmad ibn Yahya recited:

"And if I do not fight, then dress me in a veil"

by dropping the hamza. He intended "fa-albisuni" with the hamza retained. As for those who read with the lightening of the hamza, the reason is that the hamza is the 'ayn (middle radical) of the verb. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: The meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, said to Muhammad, peace be upon him: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers: If the punishment of Allah comes upon you in this world, and the punishment comes upon you at the establishment of the Hour, will you turn to other than Allah to repel that affliction and harm, or will you turn in it to Allah, exalted is He? And since it is known by necessity that they turn only to Allah, exalted is He, in repelling affliction and trial, and not to the idols and images, therefore He said: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾, meaning: you do not turn in seeking the removal of affliction and trial except to Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and He removes that for which you call upon Him﴾, i.e., He removes the harm for which you called upon Him, ﴿and you forget what you associate with Him﴾. In this there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is that you abandon the idols and do not call upon them, because you know that they neither harm nor benefit.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is that in your abandoning their invocation you are in the position of one who has forgotten them, and this is the saying of al-Hasan, for he said: They turn away with the turning away of one who forgets. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them with a good wind and they rejoice in it, a violent wind comes upon them and the waves come upon them from every place, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah﴾ [Yunus: 22], and they do not mention the idols.

The fourth issue: This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, may answer supplication if He wills, and may not answer it, for He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾. One may say: His saying ﴿Call upon Me, I will answer you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] conveys certainty of the answer. How then is the way to reconcile the two verses?

The answer: We say: at times He, exalted is He, decides on the answer, and at times He does not decide, either according to pure will, as is the saying of our companions, or according to the consideration of what is beneficial, as is the saying of the Mu'tazila. And since both matters are present, the two verses came in accordance with these two aspects.

The fifth issue: The sum of this discourse is as if He, exalted is He, is saying to the worshippers of idols: If you turn to Allah, exalted is He, at the descent of hardships, and not to the idols and images, then why do you proceed to worship idols, from which you derive no benefit whatsoever? This discourse is only beneficial if the citing of proof and evidence is accepted. But if that is rejected and the obligatory duty is pure imitation, this discourse would be void. Thus it is established that this verse is the strongest proof that the foundation of religion is argument and evidence. And Allah knows best.
