﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you, and We seized them with misfortune and hardship, that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they had been doing.﴾

Know that in the first verse He, exalted is He, explained that the disbelievers, when severe hardships descend upon them, return to Allah, exalted is He. Then in this verse He explained that they do not return to Allah at every kind of hardship. Rather, they may remain persistent in disbelief, stubbornly fixed upon it, not returning to Allah, exalted is He. This indicates our doctrine that if Allah does not guide a person, that person will not be guided, whether or not he witnesses the awesome signs. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: there is an omission in the verse, and the implied meaning is: "And We certainly sent to communities before you messengers, and they opposed them, so We seized them with misfortune and hardship." The omission is good because it is understood from the mentioned context. Al-Hasan said: "al-ba'sa' (misfortune)" is the severity of poverty, from *al-bu's* (distress), and "al-darra' (hardship)" is illnesses and pains.

Then He said: ﴿that perhaps they might humble themselves﴾. The meaning is: We only sent the messengers to them and only imposed misfortune and hardship upon them in order that they might humble themselves. *Al-tadarru'* (humbling oneself) means submissiveness and abandoning rebelliousness. Its root is from *al-du'ara'* (humility/lowliness), which is lowliness. It is said: *ḍara'a al-rajulu yaḍra'u ḍarā'atan*, so he is *ḍari'* (humble, weak). The meaning is that He, exalted is He, informed His Prophet that He had sent before him to peoples who had reached such hardness that they were seized with severity in their persons and their wealth, yet they did not submit and did not humble themselves. The purpose of this is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ).

If it is said: Does not His saying ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾ indicate that they did humble themselves? And here He says: "their hearts became hard and they did not humble themselves."

We say: Those are one group of people, and these are other people. Or we say: Those humbled themselves to seek the removal of the affliction, but they did not humble themselves sincerely for Allah, exalted is He. Because of this distinction, the negation and affirmation are appropriate.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ Its meaning is the negation of humbling. The implied sense is: "they did not humble themselves when Our might came upon them." The mention of the word *lawlā* (why not / if only... not) indicates that they had no excuse for abandoning humbling except their obstinacy, their hardness, and their self-admiration in their deeds, which Satan made attractive to them. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: al-Jubba'i argued with His saying: ﴿that perhaps they might humble themselves﴾, and said: This indicates that He, exalted is He, only sent the messengers to them, and only imposed misfortune and hardship upon them, with the intention that they humble themselves and believe, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, willed faith and obedience from all.

The answer: The word *la'alla* (perhaps) indicates hope and wishing, and that is impossible with respect to Allah, exalted is He. You have interpreted it as indicating the will for this sought outcome, whereas we interpret it as meaning that He, exalted is He, dealt with them in a manner which, if it came from other than Allah, the intended meaning of it would be this sense. As for explaining the ruling and will of Allah, exalted is He, that is impossible according to what has been established by proof. Then we say: If this verse indicates your view from this aspect, it indicates the opposite of your view from another aspect, because it indicates that they did not humble themselves due to the hardness of their hearts and because Satan made their deeds attractive to them.

We say: If that hardness came about through their own act, they would need another cause for its existence, and it would entail infinite regress (*tasalsul*). If it came about through the act of Allah, then our position is correct. Also, suppose the disbelievers only undertook this ugly act due to Satan's beautification. Then we ask: Why did Satan remain persistent in this ugly act? If that was due to another devil, it would regress infinitely. If these assessments are invalidated, they ultimately conclude that everyone sometimes proceeds to good and other times to evil, because of the motives that arise in his heart. Then it is established that those motives do not arise except by the creation of Allah, exalted is He. At that point our statement is correct and their statement is entirely invalidated. And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 44–45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the last remnant of the people who had wronged was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

Know that this statement completes the first story. Allah, the Exalted, has explained that He first seized them with misfortune and adversity so that they would humble themselves. Then, in this verse, He explained that when they forgot what they had been reminded of, namely the misfortune and adversity, We opened for them the gates of everything, and We moved them from misfortune and adversity to ease and comfort, and to all kinds of blessings and bounties. The point is that the Exalted dealt with them by subjecting them to hardships and calamities at one time, and they did not benefit from it. So He moved them from that state to its opposite, which is opening the gates of good things for them and facilitating the causes of joy and happiness for them. They did not benefit from this either. This is like a compassionate father who is harsh with his child at times and gentle with him at other times, seeking his improvement. ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given﴾ of good and blessings, they did nothing more than rejoice and become insolent, without being moved to gratitude or hastening to repentance and apology. Therefore, ﴿We seized them suddenly﴾.

Know that His saying, ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾, means: We opened for them the gates of every good thing that had been closed to them. ﴿Until, when they rejoiced﴾, that is, until, when they thought that the misfortune which had befallen them was not a form of retribution from Allah, and when Allah opened for them the gates of good things, they thought that this was because they deserved it. At that point it became clear that their hearts had become hardened and dead, and that there was no hope of them being awakened by any means. Therefore Allah surprised them with punishment from where they did not perceive. Al-Hasan said: "In this verse there is a scheme against the people, by the Lord of the Ka'bah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you see Allah giving to a person who persists in sins, that is istidraj (a gradual leading-on) from Allah, the Exalted," and then he recited this verse. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: They were seized in a state of ease and comfort so that their regret over what they had lost of the state of safety and well-being would be greater. His saying, ﴿then they were in despair﴾, means: despairing of every good.

Al-Farra' said: al-mublis is the one whose hope has been cut off, and for this reason it is said of one who falls silent when his argument fails: "qad ablasa" (he has been struck dumb). Al-Zajjaj said: al-mublis is one who is intensely grieved and sorrowful. In the language, al-iblas can mean despair of salvation when destruction arrives, it can mean the cutting off of an argument, and it can mean bewilderment at the calamity that falls upon the soul. These meanings are close to one another.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who had wronged was cut off.﴾ Al-dabir is that which follows a thing from behind, like a child to a parent. It is said: "Fulan dabara al-qawm, yadburuhum, duburan and dabaran," when he was their last. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"They were uprooted by a punishment that cut off their last remnant, and they could not avert it nor were they helped."

Abu Ubayda said: the dabir of a people is their last member, the one who comes after them. Al-Asma'i said: al-dabir is the origin, and it is said: "Allah cut off his dabir," meaning Allah removed his origin.

As for His saying, ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: its meaning is that He, the Exalted, praised Himself for cutting off their last remnant and uprooting their root, because that was counted as a great blessing upon those messengers in removing their evil from those prophets.

The second: since the Exalted knew the hardness of their hearts, it necessarily follows that the longer their lives lasted, the more kinds of their disbelief and sins would increase, and by that they would deserve greater punishment and torment. So their annihilation and death in that state required that they would become deserving of those additional punishments. Thus it was counted as a favour upon them.

The third: this praise and commendation came about because of Allah's favour upon them in that He imposed obligations upon them, removed from them every excuse and pretext, and managed their affairs in every possible good way. This was done by first seizing them with misfortune and adversity, then moving them to bounties and blessings, and granting them respite, and sending prophets and messengers to them. When they only increased in persistence in error and disbelief, Allah annihilated them and purified the face of the earth from their evil. Thus His saying, ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, is for those numerous blessings that came before.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 44–45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾ ﴿So the last remnant of the people who had wronged was cut off. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 46:**

﴿Say: "Have you considered: if God were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal over your hearts, what god other than God could bring them back to you? Behold how We vary the signs, yet still they turn away."﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the purpose of this statement is to mention what indicates the existence of the Wise, Chooser Creator (al-Sani' al-Hakim al-Mukhtar). Its explanation is that the noblest of the human organs are the hearing, the sight, and the heart. The ear is the place of the faculty of hearing, the eye is the place of the faculty of sight, and the heart is the place of life, intellect, and knowledge. If these attributes were removed from these organs, the human condition would be disrupted and his interests in this world and in religion would be nullified. It is known by necessity that the one able to bring about these powers in them and to protect them from calamities and dangers is none other than God. Since this is so, the Bestower of these lofty blessings and exalted bounties is God, glory be to Him, and so it must be said that the one deserving of veneration, praise, and worship is none other than God Most High. This indicates that the worship of idols is a false and corrupt path.

**The second issue:** They mentioned regarding His words, ﴿and seal over your hearts﴾, several meanings:

First: Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is "and sets a seal upon their hearts, so they do not understand guidance."

Second: its meaning is "and removes your intellects until you become like madmen."

Third: the intended meaning of this sealing is causing death, i.e., He causes your hearts to die.

**The third issue:** His words, ﴿who is a god other than God﴾: "man" (مَن, who) is in the nominative case by being the subject (mubtada', inchoative), its predicate (khabar) is "a god" (إلَهٌ), and "other than" (غَيْرُ) is a qualifier (sifah) of it. His words, ﴿bring them back to you﴾: this pronoun (هاء, "him/it") refers to the meaning of the verb. The implied sense is: "who is a god other than God who could bring you back that which was taken from you?"

**The fourth issue:** It is narrated from Nafi': "بِهُ انْظُرْ" (with a ḍammah on the hā'), and this is according to the dialect of one who recites, ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ (al-Qasas: 81), where he dropped the waw to avoid the meeting of two sukun (unvocalized letters), so it became "بِهُ انْظُرْ". The rest read it with a kasrah on the hā'. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "يَصْدِفُونَ" (yaṣdifūn) with ishmam of the zay (a faint hint of the zay). The rest read it with the ṣād, meaning they turn away from it. One says ṣadafa 'anhu, meaning a'rada 'anhu (he turned away from it). The intended meaning of "variation of the signs" (taṣrīf al-āyāt) is presenting them in various and numerous forms, such that each one strengthens what precedes it in reaching the desired goal. Thus He, Most High, mentions that despite this exaggeration in making things understood, in establishing and clarifying and disclosing, behold, O Muhammad, how they turn away and refuse.

**The fifth issue:** Al-Ka'bi said: this verse indicates that He, Most High, enabled them to understand and did not create in them aversion and turning away. Had God been the Creator of their disbelief, this statement would have no meaning. Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued from this very verse and said: He, Most High, has made clear that He exaggerated in manifesting this proof, in establishing and refining it, and in removing the aspects of doubt from it. Then, despite this exaggeration that cuts off every excuse, they only increased in disbelief, misguidance, and obstinacy. This indicates that guidance and misguidance are attained only by God's guidance and only by His leading astray. Thus it is established that the indication of this verse for our position is stronger than its indication for theirs. And God knows best.

Know that the preceding proof was specific to the seizing of hearing, sight and heart. This, however, is general to all kinds of punishment. The meaning is: no one repels any kind of punishment except God, glorified is He, and no one brings about any good among the goods except God, glorified is He. Therefore He must be the one worshipped with all kinds of worship, not other than Him.

If it is said: what is meant by His words, ﴿suddenly or openly﴾? We say: the punishment that comes to them either comes to them without a preceding sign indicating its coming, or comes with such a sign preceding it. The first is "suddenness" (al-baghtah), and the second is "openly" (al-jahrah). God Most High named the first "suddenness" because it overtakes them unexpectedly, and He named the second "openly" because the punishment itself has fallen upon them while they recognised it, such that if they had been able to guard against it, they would have guarded against it.

It is related from al-Hasan that he said: ﴿suddenly or openly﴾ means by night or by day. Al-Qadi said: this statement must be understood in terms of what was mentioned earlier, because if that punishment came to them by night while they had witnessed its precursor, it would not be "suddenly," and if it came by day while they were not aware of its precursor, it would not be "openly." But when we understand it in the sense mentioned earlier, the statement is coherent.

If it is said: then what is meant by His words, ﴿Will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾ given that, as you know, when punishment descends it does not distinguish (between people).

We say: although destruction in appearance includes the righteous and the wicked, in reality destruction is specific to the wrongdoing, wicked people, because the righteous, by the descent of those harms upon them, merit great kinds of reward and lofty ranks with God Most High. That, although it is a trial in appearance, entails great felicities.

As for the wrongdoers, when the trial descends upon them, they have lost both this world and the Hereafter together. Therefore God Most High described them as "destroyed," and this is an indication that the believing, pious, pure person is the happy one, whether he is in trial or in ease and blessings, and that the corrupt, disbelieving person is the wretched one, however his affair turns and his circumstances vary. And God knows best.

He, exalted is He, has previously related about the disbelievers that they said: "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" [Yunus: 20]. God, exalted is He, mentioned in His answer to them the many aspects that have already been discussed. Then He mentioned this verse. Its purpose is that the prophets and messengers were sent only as bearers of good news and warners, and they have no power to produce signs or to bring down miracles. Rather, that is entrusted to the will of God, exalted is He, His word, and His wisdom. So He said: ﴿We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners﴾, bearing good news of reward for acts of obedience and warning of punishment for acts of disobedience. ﴿Whoever believes and does righteous deeds, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾, meaning whoever accepts their message and comes with faith, which is the work of the heart, and with righteous conduct, which is the work of the body. ﴿But those who deny Our signs, the punishment will touch them﴾. The meaning of "touch" (masss) in the language is the meeting of two things without any separation.

Al-Qadi said: He, exalted is He, attributed the punishment of the disbelievers to their being defiant (fasiqun, i.e., those who transgress and depart from obedience). This implies that every defiant person is in the same position. It is answered: this is contradicted by the fact that He singled out those who denied the signs of God for this threat. This indicates that whoever does not deny the signs of God is not subject to the threat at all. Moreover, this implies that the threat is grounded in their defiance. So why do you say that the defiance of one who knows God and affirms the oneness of God (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwah), and the return (ma'ad) is equal to the defiance of one who rejects these matters? And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me. Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Will you not then reflect?﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is part of the discourse on His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-An'am: 37]. Allah the Exalted said: Say to these peoples, "I was only sent as a bringer of good news and a warner, and it is not for me to dictate to Allah the Exalted." Allah the Exalted commanded him to negate three matters from himself:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah.﴾ Know that the people used to say to him: "If you are a messenger from Allah, then ask Allah to widen for us the benefits of this world and its goods, and to open for us the doors of its happiness." So Allah the Exalted said: Say to them, "I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah. He gives sovereignty to whom He wills, exalts whom He wills, and abases whom He wills; the good is in His hand, not in mine." The word khaza'in (treasuries) is the plural of khizana (a store), which is the name for the place in which a thing is stored; and khazn (storing) of a thing is safeguarding it in such a way that hands cannot reach it.

The second of them is His saying: ﴿Nor do I know the unseen.﴾ Its meaning is that the people used to say to him: "If you are a messenger from Allah, then you must inform us of what will happen in the future of benefits and harms, so that we may prepare to obtain those benefits and to ward off those harms." So Allah the Exalted said: Say, "I do not know the unseen, so how do you ask of me these demands?"

The summary is that in the first stage they asked of him great wealth and abundant goods, and in the second stage they asked him to inform them of the hidden things, so that by knowing those hidden things they might attain benefits and avoid harms and corruptions. The third of them is His saying: ﴿Nor do I tell you that I am an angel.﴾ Its meaning is that the people used to say: ﴿What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and marries and mixes with people. So Allah the Exalted said: Say to them, "I am not one of the angels."

Know that people differed regarding what the benefit is in mentioning the negation of these three states.

The first view: What is meant by it is that the Messenger should show from himself humility before Allah, submission to Him, and acknowledgment of His servanthood, so that he is not believed in with a belief like the belief of the Christians in al-Masih, peace be upon him.

The second view: The people used to propose to him that he display compelling and powerful miracles, such as their saying: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra': 90], to the end of the verse. Allah the Exalted said at the end of that verse: ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Was I anything but a human messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 93], meaning: I claim nothing but messengerhood and prophethood. As for these matters that you have requested, their attainment is not possible except by the power of Allah. So the purpose of this speech was to show helplessness and weakness, and that he does not independently bring about these miracles that they requested of him.

The third view: What is meant by His saying: ﴿I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah﴾ is: I do not claim that I am described with the power that befits God the Exalted. And His saying: ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾ means: nor do I claim that I am described with the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. By the combination of these two statements it results that he does not claim divinity.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Nor do I tell you that I am an angel,﴾ because after divinity there is no rank higher in status than the angels. So the summary of the speech is as if he were saying: I do not claim divinity, nor do I claim angelhood, but I claim messengerhood, and this is a station that it is not impossible for a human to attain. So how do you unite in denying my words and rejecting my claim?

The second issue: al-Jubba'i said: the verse indicates that the angel is superior to the prophets, because the meaning of the speech is: I do not claim a station above my station, and had the angel not been superior, this would not be valid. al-Qadi said: if the purpose of what he negated is the way of humility, then the closer view is that this indicates the angel is superior; but if what is meant is negating his power over acts that only the angels are capable of, then it does not indicate that they are superior.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ apparently indicates that he acts only by revelation, and it indicates two rulings.

The first ruling: This text indicates that the Prophet ﷺ did not judge on his own accord in any of the rulings, and that he did not exercise ijtihad; rather all his rulings proceed from revelation. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is nothing but revelation that is revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 3, 4].

The second ruling: The deniers of qiyas (analogical reasoning) said: it is established by this text that he, peace be upon him, did not act except by the revelation that descended upon him, so it is obligatory that none of his community may act except by the revelation that descended upon him, due to His saying: (So follow him) [al-An'am: 153]. This negates the permissibility of acting by qiyas. Then He reinforced this statement with His saying: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike?﴾ Because acting without revelation runs in the manner of the blind man's action, and acting in accordance with the descent of revelation runs in the manner of the seeing man's action.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ Its purpose is to alert that it is obligatory upon the intelligent person to know the difference between these two categories and not to be heedless of recognizing it. And Allah knows best.

[Page 192]

Know that when God, exalted is He, described the Messengers as bringers of good news and warners, He commanded the Messenger in this verse to warn, saying: ﴿Warn with it those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾. The verse raises several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-Indhar* (warning, meaning informing someone of the place of danger). As for His words "with it," Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj said it refers to the Qur'an. The evidence for this is God's words just before this verse: ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾. Al-Dahhak said that "with it" means "with God." The first view is preferable, because warning and frightening happen through speech and words, not through the Essence of God, exalted is He.

* * *

As for His words ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾, there are several views:

The first: They are the disbelievers already mentioned. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to frighten them about the punishment of the Hereafter, and some of them were affected by this frightening. It would occur to their hearts that what Muhammad says might indeed be true. Thus it is established that this speech is fitting for these people, and it is not permissible to apply it to the believers, because the believers know that they will be gathered to their Lord, and knowledge is the opposite of fear and doubt. It may be objected that the believers may also be included in it, because although they are certain of the gathering, they are not certain of the punishment that is feared, since they consider it possible that one of them might die in faith and righteous deeds, and also possible that they might not die in this state. For this reason, they were fearful of the gathering, because they regarded the occurrence of punishment as possible and were afraid of it.

The second view: It refers to the believers, because they are the ones who affirm the truth of the gathering, the resurrection, the raising up, and the Last Day, so they are the ones who fear the punishment of that Day.

The third view: It encompasses everyone, because there is no sane person who does not fear the gathering, whether he is certain it will occur or is doubtful about it. This is because it is by consensus not known to be false by necessity. Therefore this fear exists with respect to everyone. Also, because he (peace be upon him) was sent to all people and was commanded to convey the message to all of them, but in this verse those who fear the gathering are singled out, because their benefit from this warning is more complete, since their fear moves them to prepare provisions for the Day of Return.

**The second issue:** The Mujassima (literalist anthropomorphists) held onto God's words ﴿that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾. This requires that God be specific to a place and direction, because the word "to" (*ila*) indicates the endpoint of a movement.

The answer: What is meant is the place that their Lord has appointed for their assembly and for judgment over them.

**The third issue:** His words ﴿for them there is no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "there is not" (*laysa*) is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if it were said: "free from any protector or intercessor," and the governing element in it is "those who fear." Then there is a discussion here: If what is meant by ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ is the disbelievers, then the statement is clear, because they have no intercessors with God. This is because the Jews and Christians used to say: ﴿We are the sons of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and God refuted them in this, and He also said in another verse: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir: 18], and He also said: ﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48]. If what is meant is the Muslims, then we say: His words ﴿for them there is no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾ do not contradict our doctrine of affirming intercession for the believers, because the intercession of the angels and the Messengers for the believers occurs only by God's permission, as He says: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. Since that intercession is by God's permission, it is in reality from God, exalted is He.

[Page 193]

**The fourth issue:** His words ﴿so that they may become God-conscious﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: "Warn them so that they may fear in this world and refrain from disbelief and sins." The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: This indicates that God wanted piety and obedience from the disbelievers. The discussion of this type of argument has already preceded many times.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 52:**

Concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance. Nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them, that you would drive them away and thereby be among the wrongdoers.﴾

On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** It is related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The chiefs of Quraysh passed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while with him were Suhayb, Khabbab, Bilal, Ammar and others of the weak among the Muslims. They said: 'O Muhammad, are you content with these people over your people? Shall we be followers of these? Drive them away from yourself, perhaps if you drive them away we will follow you.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I am not one to drive away the believers.' They said: 'Then set them apart from us when we come, and when we have sat, seat them with you if you wish.' He said: 'Yes,' hoping for their faith." And it is related that Umar said to him: "If only you would do it, so that we might see what they become." Then they insisted and said to the Messenger, peace be upon him: "Write for us a document to that effect." He called for the parchment and for Ali to write it, and then this verse was revealed. He threw down the parchment, and Umar apologized for his statement. Salman and Khabbab said: "It was revealed concerning us." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would sit with us, and we would draw so near to him that our knees touched his knee, and when he wished to rise he would rise away from us. Then there was revealed His saying: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], so he stopped rising from us until we rose from him, and he said: "Praise be to Allah who did not take me until He commanded me to keep myself patient with a people from my community: with you is my life and with you is my death."

**The second issue:** Those who object to the infallibility (ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from this verse in several ways:

The first: He, peace be upon him, drove them away, and Allah forbade him from that driving away, so that driving away was a sin.

The second: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿that you would drive them away and thereby be among the wrongdoers﴾, and it is established that he drove them away, so it must be said that he was among the wrongdoers.

The third: He, the Exalted, related of Noah, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿I am not one to drive away those who believe﴾ [Hud: 29]. Then Allah commanded Muhammad, peace be upon him, to follow the prophets, peace be upon them, in all good deeds, when He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. By this route it was obligatory upon Muhammad, peace be upon him, not to drive them away, so when he drove them away that was a sin.

The fourth: He, the Exalted, mentioned this verse in surah al-Kahf, and added to it, saying: ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. Then He forbade him in another verse from turning towards the adornment of the worldly life, saying: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward that which We have bestowed upon categories of them, the splendor of the worldly life﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131]. Since he was forbidden from turning towards the adornment of the world, and then in that verse it was mentioned that he desires the adornment of the worldly life, that was a sin.

The fifth: It is related that those poor men, whenever they entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after this incident, he, peace be upon him, would say: "Welcome to one whom my Lord rebuked me concerning," or words to this meaning, and this too indicates a sin.

As for the answer to the first: he, peace be upon him, did not drive them away for the sake of belittling them or disdaining their poverty. Rather, he appointed a specific time for their sitting, other than the time when the chiefs of Quraysh attended. His aim in this was gentleness in bringing them into Islam. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, was reasoning that these poor Muslims would not miss, through this treatment, any matter of importance in this world or in religion, whereas these unbelievers would miss religion and Islam; so preferring this side was the better course. At most it may be said that this ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) was an error, but error in ijtihad is forgiven.

As for his second argument, that driving them away makes him among the wrongdoers:

Its answer is that wrongdoing (zulm) is the placing of a thing in other than its proper place. The meaning is that those weak poor people deserved honor from the Messenger, peace be upon him, so if he drove them away from that gathering this would be wrongdoing, but it falls under abandoning what is preferable and most excellent, not under abandoning obligations. The same answer applies to all the other arguments: we interpret all these points as abandoning what is more excellent, more perfect, more preferable and more fitting. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Ibn Amir recited ﴿bil-ghudwati wal-ʿashiyy﴾ with a waw and with a damma on the ghayn, and likewise in surah al-Kahf, while the rest recited with an alif and a fatha on the ghayn (al-ghadāt). Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "The preferred reading is the common one, al-ghadāt, because it is used indefinitely, so it was possible to make it definite by prefixing the article al-. As for ghudwa, it is definite, being a proper noun coined for it; and if that is so, then the prefixing of the article must be prohibited for it, just as it is prohibited for all other definite nouns. The writing of this word with a waw in the mushaf does not indicate their view. Do you not see that they wrote al-salawa with a waw though it is an alif? So likewise here." Sibawayh said: "Ghudwa and bukra (morning) are each made a name for a category, just as they made Umm Hubayn a name for a known animal." He said: "Yunus related from Abu Amr that if you say, 'I met him one day of the days, at ghudwa or bukra,' and you intend the definite, you do not apply tanwin." These matters strengthen the common reading. As for the reading of Ibn Amir, the reasoning is that Sibawayh said: "al-Khalil maintained that it is permissible to say, 'I came to you today at ghudwa and bukra,' so he made them like ḍaḥwa (forenoon)." And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: that by "calling upon" is meant prayer, i.e., they worship their Lord through the prescribed prayers, which are the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid.

It was also said: by "the morning and the evening" are meant the two ends of the day, and mention of these two parts is a reminder of their constancy in the five prayers.

The second opinion: that by "calling upon" is meant remembrance (dhikr). Ibrahim said: "The calling here is remembrance, and the meaning is that they remember their Lord at the two ends of the day."

**The fifth issue:** The anthropomorphists (mujassima) have relied, in establishing body parts for Allah, the Exalted, on His saying ﴿seeking His countenance (wajhahu)﴾, and on the other similar verses, such as His saying ﴿and the countenance of your Lord remains﴾ [al-Rahman: 27].

The answer: His saying ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1] requires complete oneness, and that contradicts being composed of organs and parts. Thus it is established that interpretation (ta'wil) is necessary, and it is of two kinds:

The first: His saying ﴿seeking His countenance﴾ means seeking Him; but they mention the word "countenance" for glorification, just as one says, "This is the face of the opinion" and "This is the face of the proof."

The second: whoever loves an essence loves to see its face, so seeing the face is a consequence of love. For this reason the "face" is used as a metaphor for love and the seeking of pleasure. The complete discussion of this has already passed in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115].

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them.﴾ They differed over what the pronoun in His saying "their account" (ḥisābihim) and "upon them" (ʿalayhim) refers to.

The first opinion: that it refers to the polytheists. The meaning is: nothing of the account of the polytheists is upon you, nor is your account upon the polytheists; rather Allah is the One who manages His servants as He wills and intends. The purpose of this statement is that the Prophet ﷺ bears this proposal from these unbelievers, for perhaps they will enter Islam and be freed from the punishment of disbelief. So Allah said: do not be constrained by whether they guard against disbelief or not, for Allah, the Exalted, is the Guide and the Manager.

The second opinion: that the pronoun refers to those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, namely the poor, and this is closer to the apparent meaning. The evidence for it is that the pronoun in His saying ﴿that you would drive them away and thereby be among the wrongdoers﴾ necessarily refers to these poor men, so all the other pronouns must also refer to them. On this reading, the commentators mentioned two views concerning His saying ﴿Nothing of their account is upon you﴾:

One of them: the unbelievers criticized the faith of those poor men, and said: "O Muhammad, they only gathered with you and accepted your religion because they find food and clothing with you by this means; otherwise they are empty of your religion." So Allah, the Exalted, said: if the matter is as they say, then you are only required to judge by the outward; and if they have an inward that is not pleasing to Allah, then their account is binding upon them and does not extend to you, just as your account upon you does not extend to them. Compare His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

If it is said: Was not His saying ﴿Nothing of their account is upon you﴾ sufficient, so that He added to it His saying ﴿nor is your account upon them﴾?

We say: the two sentences are made as one sentence, aimed at one meaning, which is the meaning in His saying ﴿and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾; and this meaning is not complete except by both sentences together, as if it were said: neither you nor they will be held to account for the reckoning of the other.

The second opinion: "Nothing of the reckoning of their provision is upon you, so that you would become weary of them and drive them away, nor is the reckoning of your provision upon them; rather the Provider of them and of you is Allah, the Exalted. So leave them to be with you and do not drive them away."

Know that this story resembles the story of Noah, peace be upon him, when his people said to him: ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 111]. Noah, peace be upon him, answered them, and ﴿said: "And what is my knowledge of what they used to do? Their account is only upon my Lord, if you were aware."﴾ By "the lowest" they meant the weavers and those who practised base trades; so likewise here.

His saying ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾ is the answer to the negation and its meaning: nothing of their account is upon you so that you would drive them away, in the sense that their account was not upon you such that because of that account you would drive them away. His saying ﴿and thereby be among the wrongdoers﴾ may be taken as coordinated with His saying ﴿that you would drive them away﴾ in the sense of causation, since being a wrongdoer is the effect of driving them away and is caused by it.

As for His saying ﴿and thereby be among the wrongdoers﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

The first: ﴿and thereby be among the wrongdoers﴾ against yourself, by this driving away.

The second: that you would be among the wrongdoers against them, because since they deserved greater nearness and welcome, driving them away would be wrongdoing towards them. And Allah knows best.

**Q. 6:53**: ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others, that they might say, "Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" Is Allah not most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾

Issues:

**First issue:** Know that in this verse God explains that each person is tested through his counterpart. Those disbelieving leaders, the wealthy, used to envy the poor Companions for being foremost in Islam and quick to accept it. They said: "If we entered Islam, we would be obliged to submit to these poor, destitute people and acknowledge their precedence." That would be hard for them. A parallel is God's words: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ (al-Qamar 54:25) and ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ (al-Ahqaf 46:11). As for the poor Companions, they saw those disbelievers in comfort, pleasure, good things, abundance, and ease, and they would say: "How have these conditions come to these people while we remain in this hardship, constraint, and scarcity?" God said: ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others.﴾ So each of the two groups sees the other as ahead of it in religious ranks, while the other group sees the first as ahead of it in worldly ranks. They would say: "Is this the one whom God has preferred over us?!" As for the true verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), they are those who know that whatever God does is true, right, wise, and correct, and that there is no objection to it, either by the sovereign right of ownership (al-malikiyya), as our companions (the Ash'aris) say, or according to what is beneficial, as the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist school) say. They were patient in times of trial and grateful in times of blessings and favours. These are the ones about whom God said: ﴿Is Allah not most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾

**Second issue:** Our companions used this verse as evidence in the question of the creation of acts, in two respects:

The first: His words ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others﴾ state explicitly that the sending of that trial is from God. The purpose of that trial is none other than their objection against God for making those poor men leaders in religion. Objecting against God is disbelief, and this indicates that He is the Creator of disbelief.

The second: God related of them that they said: ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ The meaning of ﴿on whom Allah has bestowed favour﴾ is that He bestowed on them faith in God and following the Messenger. This indicates that these qualities come about only from God, Exalted. For if the originator of faith were the servant, then God would not have bestowed this faith on him; rather, the servant would have bestowed favour upon himself with this faith. So this verse becomes evidence for our view on this question from these two respects. [p. 197]

al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili scholar) answered this, saying: trial in obligation is that which requires hardship. We did that so that they would say, "Are these...?" meaning that some of them would say to others, as a question and not as a denial, ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ by faith?

al-Ka'bi (another Mu'tazili scholar) answered it by saying: ﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others﴾ so that they would be patient or grateful. Then the outcome of their affair was that they said: ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ following the pattern of His words: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8).

The answer to both respects: this is a departure from the apparent meaning without any evidence, especially since rational proof stands in support of this apparent meaning. For when witnessing these conditions necessarily produces arrogance, and arrogance necessarily produces disobedience and persistence in disbelief, and what necessitates a necessity is itself a necessity, then the objection stands. And God knows best.

**Third issue:** Concerning the manner in which some are tried by others, there are several aspects:

The first: wealth and poverty were both causes for this trial, as we mentioned in the story of Noah (peace be upon him), and as He said in the story of the people of Salih: ﴿The arrogant ones among his people said, "We certainly disbelieve in that which you have believed"﴾ (al-A'raf 7:76).

The second: the trial of the noble by the lowly.

The third: the trial of the intelligent by the foolish.

In summary: the attributes of perfection are varied and differing, and they never all combine in one human being whatsoever; rather they are distributed among creatures. Attributes of perfection are loved for their own sake, so each person envies his companion for the attributes of perfection God has given him.

As for the one who knows God's secret in destiny and decree, he is content with his own share, refrains from encroaching upon creatures, and lives a good life in this world and the Hereafter. And God knows best.

**Fourth issue:** Hisham ibn al-Hakam said: God does not know particulars except at the time they occur. He used this verse as evidence, since trial means testing and examination, and that is valid only for seeking knowledge. His answer has already been given more than once.

The Quranic verse: "And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: 'Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.'" (6:54)

Regarding this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: people differed concerning His words: "And when those who believe in Our signs come to you." Some said: it is general in its application to everyone who has this description.

Others said: rather, it was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah (ahl al-suffah, the companions who lived in the shaded area of the Prophet's Mosque), whom the polytheists asked the Messenger, peace be upon him, to drive away and distance. So Allah honoured them with this honour. This is because He, exalted is He, first forbade the Messenger, peace be upon him, from driving them away, and then commanded him to honour them with this kind of honour.

'Ikrimah said: "When the Prophet ﷺ saw them, he would begin with the greeting of peace and say: 'Praise be to Allah who has placed in my community one whom I have been commanded to begin with the greeting of peace.'"

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: that 'Umar, when he apologised for his statement and sought Allah's forgiveness for it, and said to the Messenger, peace be upon him: "I only intended good by it," this verse was revealed.

Others said: rather, it was revealed concerning a people who committed sins, then came to him ﷺ displaying remorse and regret, and this verse was revealed concerning them. The closest of these opinions is that this verse be taken in its general sense, so everyone who believes in Allah enters under this honour.

Here there is a difficulty for me: people agreed that this surah was revealed all at once. If that is so, how is it possible to say of each of its verses that the cause of its revelation was this particular event?

The second issue: His words, "And when those who believe in Our signs come to you," contain lofty secrets. This is because everything other than Allah, exalted is He, is a sign of the existence of Allah, exalted is He, and signs of His attributes of majesty, generosity and greatness, and signs of His oneness. What is other than Allah has no limit, and what has no limit cannot be fully comprehended by the intellect in detail. However, it is possible for a person to come to know some of the signs and use knowledge of them as a means to knowing Allah, exalted is He, then believe in the rest in summary. Then throughout his life he is like a wanderer in those deserts and a swimmer in those seas. Since they have no end, the servant's ascent through the stations of those signs likewise has no end, and this is a general principle whose details have no end. Then when the servant becomes described by this attribute:

At this point Allah commanded Muhammad ﷺ to say to them: "Peace be upon you," and this greeting is glad tidings of the attainment of safety. His words, "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," are glad tidings of the attainment of mercy after that safety. As for safety, it is by deliverance from the sea of the world of darkness, the seat of corporeal things, the source of calamities and transgressions, and the place of change and alteration. As for honours, they are by reaching the enduring righteous things and the pure immaterial beings, and by reaching the spaciousness of the world of lights and ascending through the stations of the pavilions of majesty.

The third issue: al-Zajjaj reported from al-Mubarrad that safety (salamah) in the language has four meanings. Among them: "I greeted him with salam (salaman)," which means supplication. Among them: it is one of the names of Allah, exalted is He. Among them: Islam. And among them: the name of a great tree, which I think is so named because of its safety from calamities; and it is also the name of hard stones, which is likewise because of their safety from softness.

Then al-Zajjaj said: As for His words, "Peace be upon you," the word salam here may bear two interpretations:

One: that it is the verbal noun of sallamtu (I greeted), tasliman and salaman, like al-sarah from al-tasrih. The meaning of "sallamtu 'alayhi salaman" is: I prayed for him that he be safe from calamities in his religion and his self. So salam means greeting (taslim).

The second: that salam is the plural of salamah, so the meaning of your saying "al-salamu 'alaykum" is "al-salamah 'alaykum" (safety upon you).

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: Some people said: al-Salam is Allah, exalted is He, so the meaning of "al-salamu 'alaykum" is: Allah is upon you, that is, upon your protection. But this is far-fetched in this verse because salam is indefinite in His words, "say: Peace be upon you," and if it were definite this interpretation would be valid.

I say: I have written full and complete discourses on our saying "salamun 'alaykum," and I wrote them in the surah of al-Tawbah. They are off the subject of this place, so when I transfer them to this place the discussion is complete, and Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His words, "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," there are issues:

The first issue: the phrase "kutiba kadha 'ala fulan" indicates obligation, and the word "'ala" also indicates obligation, and the combination of the two is an intensification of obligation. This necessitates that He, subhanahu, is merciful to His servants and compassionate towards them as an obligation. The rational scholars differed about the cause of this obligation. Our companions (the Ash'ari school) said: He, subhanahu, has the right to dispose of His servants as He wills and desires, except that He made mercy obligatory upon Himself as a matter of bounty and generosity.

The Mu'tazilah said: His knowledge of the ugliness of ugly deeds and His knowledge that He is free from needing them prevents Him from undertaking ugly deeds, and if He did them it would be injustice, and injustice is ugly, and the ugly is impossible for Him. This issue is among the clear issues in the science of usul (principles of jurisprudence and theology).

The second issue: this verse indicates that it is not impermissible to name the essence of Allah, exalted is He, "nafs" (self). Also His words, "You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Yours" (5:116), indicate this, and "nafs" here means essence and reality. As for the meaning of body and blood, Allah, exalted and glorified is He, is sanctified from that. For if He were a body, He would be composite, and the composite is contingent. Also, He is One, and the One cannot be composite, and what is not composite is not a body. Also, He is Self-Sufficient as He said: "And Allah is the Self-Sufficient" (47:38), and the Self-Sufficient cannot be composite, and what is not composite is not a body. Also, bodies are alike in their complete quiddity, so if He were a body He would have a like, and that is false, because of His words: "There is nothing like Him" (42:11). As for rational proofs, they are numerous, manifest, dazzling, strong and clear, and praise be to Allah for that.

The third issue: the Mu'tazilah said that His words, "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," contradict saying that He creates disbelief in the disbeliever and then punishes him for it forever, and contradict saying that He prevents him from faith and then commands him, while that prevention is in effect, to believe, and then punishes him for not believing.

Our response: He is the Harmer, the Benefiter, the Giver of life and the Causer of death. So He, exalted is He, has done that far-reaching mercy and has done this far-reaching subjugation, and there is no contradiction between the two matters.

The fourth issue: some people said: when He commanded the Messenger to say to them, "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," this was from the words of Allah, exalted is He, and from His speech. This indicates that He, subhanahu wa ta'ala, said to them in this world: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy." The realisation of this statement is that He, exalted is He, promised some people that He would say to them after death: "Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful" (36:58). Then some people spent their lives in worship until in their worldly life they became as if they had transferred to the world of the Resurrection. Inevitably, the greeting promised after death became, for these people, while they are in this world, a reality. Others said: No, rather this is the speech of the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. And his saying: "Whether on either of the two interpretations, it is a lofty rank."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "That whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends," and there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: know that this does not include repentance from disbelief, because this statement is addressed to those whom He described with His words: "And when those who believe in Our signs come to you." So it is established that what is meant by it is the repentance of a Muslim from disobedience. What is meant by His words "in ignorance" is not error and mistake, because that has no need of repentance. Rather, what is meant is that one commits disobedience because of desire. So the purpose is to explain that if a Muslim commits a sin while knowing it is a sin and then repents from it with genuine repentance, Allah, exalted is He, accepts his repentance.

The second issue: Nafi' read "annahu man 'amila minkum" with fath on the alif and "fa-innahu ghafur" with kasr on the alif. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read with fath on both. The rest read with kasr on both. As for the fath of the first, it is as an explanation of mercy, as if it were said: "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself that whoever of you does evil..." As for the fath of the second, it is taken as a substitute for the first, like His words: "Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones you will be brought forth?" (23:35), and His words: "It is prescribed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray" (22:4), and His words: "Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell?" (9:63).

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Whoever reads the first with fath has made it a substitute for mercy. As for the one after the fa', it is on the basis that he supplied a predicate for it, its estimate being: "then for him is that He is Forgiving and Merciful," that is, for him is His forgiveness; or he supplied a subject of which "anna" is the predicate, as if it were said: "then His command is that He is Forgiving and Merciful."

As for whoever reads both with kasr, because when He said: "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," this statement was complete, then He began and said: "Indeed, whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, then indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful." So the fa' entered as the answer to the conditional, and inna is kasra because it entered upon a subject and predicate, as if you said: "then He is Forgiving and Merciful." However, the discourse with "anna" as emphasis is the view of al-Zajjaj. Nafi' read the first with fath and the second with kasr, because he made the first a substitute for mercy and began a new sentence after the fa'. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His words, "whoever of you does evil in ignorance." al-Hasan said: Everyone who commits disobedience is ignorant. Then they differed: it was said that he is ignorant of the measure of the reward he has missed and the punishment he has deserved. It was also said that although he knows that the outcome of that act is blameworthy, he preferred fleeting pleasure over abundant lasting good, and whoever prefers little over much is called ignorant in common usage.

The summary of the discussion is that although he is not ignorant, since he did what befits the ignorant, the word "ignorant" was applied to him. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Umar when he advised accepting what the disbelievers had proposed, and he did not know that it was corrupting. A parallel to this verse is His words: "Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance" (4:17).

The fourth issue: His words, exalted is He, "then repents after it and makes amends." His words "repents" (tāba) indicate regret for the past, and His words "makes amends" (aslaha) indicate that he is bringing righteous deeds in the future. Then He said: "then indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful." So He is Forgiving by means of removing punishment, and Merciful by means of bestowing reward, which is the ultimate in mercy. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, and that the way of the guilty may become clear﴾.

The meaning is: just as We have detailed for you in this surah Our proofs for the soundness of tawhid (Divine oneness), prophethood, qada' (divine decree) and qadar (divine measure), so likewise do We distinguish and detail for you Our proofs and arguments in establishing every truth that the people of falsehood deny. His saying, ﴿and that the way of the guilty may become clear﴾, is a conjunction upon the meaning, as if it were said: "so that the truth may appear and so that it may become clear." This omission is good because it is known. The reciters differed regarding His saying, "li-tastabin" (that it may become clear). Nafi' recited "litastabin" with the ta', and "sabilu" in the accusative (sabila), and the meaning is: that you, O Muhammad, may make clear the way of these guilty ones. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "liyastabin" with the ya', and "sabilu" in the nominative (sabilu). The rest recited with the ta', and "sabilu" in the nominative, on the basis of the feminine gender of sabil. The people of the Hijaz treat sabil as feminine, while the Banu Tamim treat it as masculine. The Qur'an has come with both, for He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And if they see the way of rectitude, they will not take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146], and He says: ﴿and they turn others away from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked﴾ [Ibrahim: 3].

If it is said: Why did He say, ﴿and that the way of the guilty may become clear﴾ and not mention the way of the believers?

We say: The mention of one of the two categories indicates the second. Like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], where He did not mention the cold. Also, when two opposites are such that no intermediate state exists between them, then when the distinctive feature of one of the two categories becomes clear, the distinctive feature of the other category becomes clear as well. Truth and falsehood have no intermediary between them, so when the path of the guilty becomes clear, the path of those who are upon the truth also becomes clear without doubt.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 56–58:
