**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 59:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "If I had with me what you are seeking to hasten, the matter would have been decided between me and you. And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers."﴾

Know that the meaning of ﴿If I had with me﴾ is: within my power and capacity, ﴿what you are seeking to hasten﴾ of the punishment, ﴿the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾: I would have destroyed you quickly, out of anger for my Lord and as retribution for your denial of Him, and I would have been quickly relieved. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ and of what wisdom requires regarding the time and the measure of their punishment. The meaning is: I do not know the time of the punishment of the wrongdoers. Allah, exalted is He, knows it, so He delays it until its time. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. And not a leaf falls but that He knows it. And there is not a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but that it is in a clear register.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, said in the first verse: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning that He, glorified is He, is the Knower of everything, so He hastens what it is best to hasten and delays what it is best to delay. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-mafatih* (the keys) is the plural of *miftah* and *maftah*. *Al-miftah* with a kasra is the key with which one opens, and *al-maftah* with a fatha on the mim is the treasury; every treasury for a category of things is a *maftah*. Al-Farra' said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, its keys would burden a band of men﴾ [al-Qasas: 76] that it means its treasuries. So the word *al-mafatih* may mean the keys, and it may mean the treasuries. On the first reading, He has made keys for the unseen in the manner of metaphor, because keys are the means by which one reaches what is in the treasuries secured with locks and bolts. The one who knows those keys and how to use them to open those locks and bolts can reach what is in those treasuries through them. Likewise here, since the Real, glorified is He, knows all knowables, He expressed this meaning by the phrase mentioned, and it has been read as *mafatih* (keys). On the second reading, the meaning is: with Him are the treasuries of the unseen. On the first reading, what is meant is knowledge of the unseen; on the second, what is meant is power over all possibilities, as in His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. The philosophers have a remarkable discourse on the interpretation of this verse, built upon their principles, for they said: It is established that knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect, and that knowledge of the effect is not a cause of knowledge of the cause.

*Page 9*

They said: Once this is established, we say: What exists is either necessary in its essence or possible in its essence. The necessary in its essence is none but Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Everything other than Him is possible in its essence, and the possible in its essence does not come into existence except by the influence of the necessary in its essence. Everything other than the Real, glorified is He, exists by His bringing into being, comes to be by His creating, and occurs by His causing it to occur, either without intermediary, or through one intermediary, or through many intermediaries, in the order descending from Him lengthwise and breadthwise. Once this is established, we say: His knowledge of His essence necessitates His knowledge of the first effect issuing from Him; then His knowledge of that first effect necessitates His knowledge of the second effect, because the first effect is a proximate cause of the second effect. We have mentioned that knowledge of the cause necessitates knowledge of the effect. Thus, knowledge of the unseen is nothing but the Real's knowledge of His own particular essence; then from His knowledge of His essence there results for Him His knowledge of the effects issuing from Him in their considered order. And since His knowledge of His essence has not come about except for His essence, it is correct to say, without doubt: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He.﴾ This is the method of this group who interpreted this verse on the basis of this method.

Then know that there is another subtle point here, namely that purely rational propositions are difficult to know completely and perfectly, except for complete intellects who have become accustomed to turning away from propositions of sense and imagination and have grown used to calling forth abstract intelligibles; such a person is almost rare. His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ is a purely rational, abstract proposition, so the person whose intellect is strong enough to encompass the meaning of this proposition is exceedingly rare. The Qur'an was revealed so that all creation might benefit from it. So here there is another way: whoever states a purely rational, abstract proposition, when he wishes to convey it to the intellect of everyone, mentions for it an example from sensible matters that falls under the universal rational proposition, so that this intelligible, with the help of this sensible example, becomes understood by everyone. The matter in this verse came according to this rule, for He said first: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾, then He reinforced this universal, abstract intelligible with a sensible particular, saying: ﴿And He knows what is on the land and in the sea﴾, because one of the categories of Allah's knowables is all the creatures of the land and the sea. Sense and imagination have come to know the greatness of the conditions of the land and the sea, so mentioning this sensible thing reveals the reality of the greatness of that intelligible.

There is another subtle point in this: He, exalted is He, mentioned the land first, because man has witnessed the conditions of the land and the abundance in it of cities, villages, deserts, mountains and hills, and the abundance in them of animals, plants and minerals. As for the sea, the intellect's grasp of its conditions is less, yet the senses indicate that the wonders of the seas are in general more numerous, their length and breadth greater, and what is in them of animals and kinds of creatures more marvellous. When imagination calls forth the image of the sea and the land in these aspects, then recognizes that their whole is a base part of the categories falling under His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾, this sensible example becomes strengthening and completing of the greatness contained under His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He.﴾ Then, just as He revealed the greatness of His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ by mentioning the land and the sea, He revealed the greatness of the land and the sea by His saying: ﴿And not a leaf falls but that He knows it﴾. This is because the intellect calls forth everything on the face of the earth of cities, villages, deserts, mountains and hills, then calls forth how many stars and trees are in them, then calls forth that the condition of no leaf changes except that the Real, glorified is He, knows it. Then it passes from this example to another example more striking in form, which is His saying: ﴿nor a grain within the darknesses of the earth﴾. This is because the grain is at the utmost of smallness, while the darknesses of the earth are a place in which the greatest and largest bodies remain hidden. So when one hears that this small grain cast into the darknesses of the earth, despite their vastness and greatness, does not escape the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, at all, these examples become a reminder of a great magnitude and lofty majesty of the meaning indicated by His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾, such that intellects are bewildered by it and thoughts and minds fall short of reaching its beginnings. Then, when He, exalted is He, had strengthened the matter of this purely abstract intelligible by mentioning these sensible particulars, after mentioning them He returned to mentioning that rational, purely abstract proposition in another expression, saying: ﴿nor anything moist or dry but that it is in a clear register﴾, and this is the very same as what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He.﴾ This is what we have understood in interpreting this noble, exalted verse. And from Allah is success.

* * *

**The second issue:** The theologians (*mutakallimun*) said: He, exalted is He, is the Creator of the world with its substances and accidents in a manner of perfect firmness and precision, and whoever is thus is knowing of them; so it is necessary that He, exalted is He, be knowing of them. The philosophers said: He, exalted is He, is the origin of all possibles, and knowledge of the origin necessitates knowledge of the effect; so it is necessary that He, exalted is He, be knowing of all of them.

Know that this argument is among the strongest proofs that He, exalted is He, knows all the temporal particulars. For since it has been established that He, exalted is He, is the origin of everything other than Himself, it is necessary that He be the origin of these particulars through their effect. Thus it is necessary that He, exalted is He, know these changes and temporal things insofar as they are changing and temporal, and that is what was sought.

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, is far above any counterpart or equal. Its explanation: His saying ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ conveys restriction, that is, with Him and not with other than Him. If another existent necessary in existence were to exist, the keys of the unseen would also be present with that other, and then the restriction would be void. Also, just as the wording of the verse indicates this oneness, so the rational proof supports it. Its explanation: the basis for knowing effects, results and products is knowledge of the agent, and the first agent of all possibles is the Real, glorified is He. So the first key to knowledge of all knowables is knowledge of Him, glorified is He; but knowledge of Him belongs to none but Him, because what is other than Him is an effect, and knowledge of the effect does not give knowledge of the agent. Thus it became clear by this proof that the keys of the unseen are with none but the Real, glorified is He. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** It has been read as ﴿nor a grain, nor anything moist, nor anything dry﴾ with the nominative (*raf'*), and there are two possibilities for it:

The first: that it be a conjunction upon the position (*mahall*) of *min waraqatin* (of a leaf).

The second: that it be nominative as a beginning (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being ﴿except in a clear register﴾, like your saying: "No man among them and no woman but is in the house."

**The fifth issue:** His saying: ﴿except in a clear register﴾ has two opinions:

The first: that this clear register is none other than the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. And this is the correct view.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that Allah, may His praise be great, recorded the manner of the knowables in a register before He created creation, as He, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿No disaster strikes in the earth or among yourselves but that it is in a register before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid: 22].

The benefits of this register are several:

One of them: that He, exalted is He, only recorded these conditions in the Preserved Tablet so that the angels might stand upon the penetration of Allah's knowledge into the knowables, and that nothing of what is in the heavens and the earth is hidden from Him. Thus there is in this a complete and perfect lesson for the angels entrusted with the Preserved Tablet, for they compare with it what occurs in the page of this world and find it in agreement with it.

Second: it may be said that He, exalted is He, mentioned what He mentioned of the leaf and the grain as an admonition to the responsible persons regarding the matter of reckoning, and as an information that nothing of all that they do in this world escapes Him; for if He does not neglect conditions in which there is no reward, no punishment and no obligation, then that He would not neglect conditions that involve reward and punishment is more fitting.

Third: He, exalted is He, knows the conditions of all existents, so it is impossible for them to change contrary to that knowledge, otherwise ignorance would follow. When He recorded the conditions of all existents in that register in complete detail, it was also impossible for them to change, otherwise falsehood would follow; so the recording of the totality of conditions in that register becomes a complete determinant and a full cause that it is impossible for what is late to precede or for what is early to be delayed, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The pen has dried over what is to be until the Day of Resurrection." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 60:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who takes your souls by night, and knows what you have committed by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a term appointed may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return. Then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained His perfect knowledge in the previous verse, He explained His perfect power in this verse, which is His being able to transfer essences from death to life and from sleep to wakefulness, and His sustaining them in all states, and His managing them in the best manner during sleep and wakefulness.

As for His saying, ﴿It is He who takes your souls﴾, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, puts you to sleep, so He takes your souls, by which you are able to perceive and discern, just as He, majestic is His majesty, said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that die not during their sleep. Then He retains those for which He has decreed death, and sends the others until an appointed term﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. So God, majestic is His majesty, withdraws the spirits from activity through sleep just as He withdraws them through death.

Here there is a discussion: there is no doubt that the sleeper is alive, and whenever he is alive, his spirit is not entirely seized. If that is so, it is not correct to say that God has caused him to die (tawaffahu). So there must be an interpretation here, namely that in the state of sleep the sensitive spirits recede from the outer to the inner, so the outer senses become inactive in their functions. Thus during sleep the outer body becomes inactive in some functions, and at death the whole body becomes inactive in all functions. Thus a resemblance arises between sleep and death from this consideration, and so the use of the words tawaffa (taking in full) and death for sleep is correct from this aspect.

Then He said: ﴿and knows what you have committed by day﴾, meaning the deeds you have earned by day. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and what you have taught of the hunting beasts﴾, and what is meant by them is the hunting creatures among birds and beasts of prey; their singular is jāriḥah. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿those who have committed evil deeds﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21], i.e., those who earned. In sum, what is meant by it is the deeds of the bodily members.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾, i.e., He returns your spirits to you during the day, and resurrection (al-ba'th) here means wakefulness. Then He said: ﴿that a term appointed may be fulfilled﴾, i.e., your written lifespans, and this is His saying: ﴿and a term appointed with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 2]. The meaning is: He raises you from your sleep until you reach your appointed terms. The meaning of qada' (fulfilment) is the decisive completion of a matter, and the meaning of the fulfilment of the term is the separation of the period of life from other periods by death.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He puts them to sleep first and then wakes them a second time, this was running in the manner of giving life after causing death. Therefore He used this as evidence for the correctness of resurrection and the Last Day, saying: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, in your nights and your days and in all your states and deeds.

Know that this is another kind of proof indicating the perfection of God's power and the perfection of His wisdom. Its establishment is that we have already explained earlier that it is not permissible for the intended meaning of this verse's "above" (al-fawqiyya) to be spatial, in place and direction. Rather, it is necessary that the intended meaning be "above" in terms of dominance and power, as one says: "The command of so-and-so is above the command of so-and-so," meaning he is higher and more effective. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The hand of God is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. Among what confirms that this is the intended meaning is that His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ indicates that this subjugation came about through this aboveness, and the aboveness that yields the attribute of subjugation is the aboveness of power, not the aboveness of direction, since it is known that one who is elevated in place may still be subjugated. The establishment of this subjugation is from several aspects:

The first: He is the Subduer of non-existence through origination and bringing into being.

The second: He is the Subduer of existence through annihilation and corruption, for He, exalted is He, is the One who moves the contingent (mumkin) from non-existence to existence at one time and from existence to non-existence at another. There is no existence except by His bringing it into being, and no non-existence except by His causing it to cease, among contingent things.

The third: He is the Subduer of every opposite by its opposite, so He subdues light with darkness and darkness with light, and day with night and night with day. The full establishment of this is in His saying: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty from whom You will, and You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26].

Once you have understood the method of this discourse, know that it is a sea without shore, for every created thing has an opposite: the above has its opposite, the below; the past has its opposite, the future; light has its opposite, darkness; life has its opposite, death; power has its opposite, impotence. Reflect on the remaining states and attributes so that you know that the occurrence of opposition between them necessitates for them subjugation, impotence and deficiency, and the presence of these attributes in contingent things indicates that they have a governing Lord who is powerful, subduing, exalted above opposite and equal, sanctified above likeness and form, as He said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾.

The fourth: This body is composed of the four temperaments, which are mutually repellent, hateful, and distant by nature and property, so their union must be by the compulsion of a compeller. Whoever said that this compeller is the human soul erred, and this is what Ibn Sina mentioned in al-Isharat, because the attachment of the soul to the body occurs only after the temperament is established and the constituents are balanced. The one who subdues these temperaments in their union is prior to this union, and what is prior to the occurrence of the union is different from what comes after the occurrence of the union. Thus it is established that the one who subdues these temperaments in union is none other than God, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Also, the body is dense, lower, dark, corrupt, putrid, while the spirit is subtle, higher, luminous, shining, enduring, pure, clean, so between them is the utmost repellence and distance. Then He, glorified is He, joined them together by way of compulsion and power, and made each of them completed by its companion, benefiting from the other. The spirit preserves the body from putrefaction, corruption and dispersal, and the body becomes an instrument for the spirit in attaining eternal felicities and divine knowledge. This union and this benefit are none other than by God's subjugation of these temperaments, as He said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Also, when the spirit enters the body, He gave the spirit power to do both opposites and capacity for both extremes, except that the preponderance of doing over not doing at one time and not doing over doing at another is impossible except when there arises the decisive motive free of any obstacle. When that motive does not arise, doing and not doing are both impossible, so the agent's undertaking of an act at one time and abstaining at another, due to the arising of that motive in his heart from God, operates in the manner of compulsion, and thus He is Subduer over His servants from this aspect. When you reflect on these chapters, you will know that the contingent things, the originated things, the upper things, the lower things, the essences and the attributes are all subdued under God's subjugation, subjected under God's disposal, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾, the meaning is that among the totality of His subjugation of His servants is His sending guardians over them. These guardians are those referred to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For him are successive angels before and behind him, guarding him by the command of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], and His saying: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers﴾ [al-Infitar: 10-11]. They agreed that the purpose of the presence of these guardians is the recording of deeds. Then they differed: some of them say that they record obedience, disobedience and permissible acts, all of them, by the evidence of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What sort of book is this that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that with every person there are two angels: one on his right and the other on his left. When the person speaks a good deed, the one on the right records it, and when he speaks an evil deed, the one on the right says to the one on the left: "Wait for him, perhaps he will repent of it. If he does not repent, record it against him." The first view is stronger, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ indicates guardians of all, without specification.

The second investigation: the apparent meaning of these verses indicates that the awareness of these guardians concerns sayings and actions. As for the states of the hearts, namely knowledge and ignorance, there is nothing in these verses that indicates their awareness of them. As for sayings, it is due to His saying: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready﴾ [Qaf: 18]; and as for actions, it is due to His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 10-12]. As for faith, disbelief, sincerity and associating partners, the evidence does not indicate the angels' awareness of them.

The third investigation: they mentioned, regarding the benefit of appointing angels over the children of Adam, several aspects:

The first: when the responsible person knows that angels are assigned to him, counting his deeds for him and recording them in scrolls that will be displayed before the heads of witnesses at the standing places of the Resurrection, this is more restraining for him from vile acts.

The second: it is possible that the benefit in the recording is that those scrolls will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, since weighing deeds is not possible, but weighing scrolls is possible.

The third: God does what He wills and decrees what He desires. It is obligatory upon us to believe in everything the Law has brought, whether we comprehend its wisdom or not. This is the summary of what the people of the Sharia have said. As for the people of wisdom (philosophers), their statements on this topic have differed in several ways:

The first aspect: the later among them said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾, and among that subjugation is that He mixed the opposing temperaments and blended the repellent elements. When a mixture resulted between them, that mixture became prepared, by virtue of that mixing,
صفحة ١٤
to receive the governing soul and the sensory, motive and articulate faculties. They said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ is those souls and faculties, for it is they that guard those subdued temperaments in their mixtures.

The second aspect: the view of some of the ancients, that these human souls and human spirits differ in their substances and vary in their quiddities; some of them are good and some are wicked, and likewise concerning intelligence and dullness, freedom and baseness, nobility and lowness, and other attributes. For each group of these lower spirits there is a celestial spirit which is to them like a compassionate father and a merciful master, assisting them in their affairs in their waking and their sleeping, sometimes by way of visions and at other times by way of inspirations. The wicked spirits have principles from the world of the spheres, and so do the good spirits, and those principles are called in their terminology the "complete temperament," meaning that those celestial spirits are complete and perfect in those temperaments and characters, while these lower spirits generated from them are weaker than them, because the effect is in every respect weaker than its cause. And the practitioners of talismans and spiritual charms have much discourse on this subject.

The third aspect: the soul attached to this body. There is no doubt that the souls separated from bodies, since they are equal to these in nature and quiddity, incline towards this soul because of the resemblance and agreement between them, and they too are attached in some way to this body and become helpers to this soul in the requirements of its nature. Thus it is established by these three aspects that what the true Sharia has brought is not something the philosophers may refuse, for all of them have acknowledged what is close to it. Since the matter is so, the insistence of the ignorant among them upon denial is false. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in death﴾, here there are two investigations:

The first investigation: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], and He said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. These two texts indicate that the taking of souls is only by God, exalted is He. Then He said: ﴿Say: The angel of death who is charged with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and this requires that taking only occurs from the angel of death. Then He said in this verse: ﴿Our messengers take him﴾. These three texts appear as though contradictory.

The answer: the taking in reality occurs by God's power, exalted is He, while in the outward knowledge it is entrusted to the angel of death, who is the absolute chief in this matter, and has helpers, attendants and supporters. So the attribution of taking to these three is fitting according to the three considerations. And God knows best.

The second investigation: some people said: these messengers by whom the taking occurs are the very same guardians, so during the period of life they guard them by the command of God, and at the coming of death they take them. Most of them, however, hold that those who undertake guarding are other than those who undertake the matter of taking. There is no indication in the wording of the verse showing the difference, but what most of them inclined to is the second view. Also, it has been established by rational analogies that the angels who are the sources of mercy, goodness and comfort are different from those who are the origins of sorrow and grief. A group of angels are those called the "spiritual ones" (Ruhaniyyun), for they bestow spirit, comfort and fragrance, and some of them are called the "Karubiyyun" (Cherubim), for they are the sources of distress, grief and sorrows.

The third investigation: the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: The angel of death who is charged with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11] is that he is one angel, the chief of the angels charged with seizing souls. And what is meant by the guardians mentioned in this verse are his followers and partisans. From Mujahid: He made the earth like a basin before the angel of death, so that he takes whomever he takes; and there is no household but that he circles over them twice each day. And there have come in the reports wondrous states concerning the attributes of the angel of death and the manner of his death at the passing away and ending of the world.

The fourth investigation: Hamza recited "tawaffahu" with an alif, with imala, while the rest recited with a ta'. The first is due to the verb being placed before its subject and because the plural may be masculine, and the second is according to the feminine form of the plural.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 61–62 (part 2 of 2):

[Page 16]

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they do not fail (in their duty)﴾, meaning they do not fall short in what Allah has commanded them. This indicates that the angels entrusted with seizing souls do not fall short in what they have been commanded. His words about the angels of the Fire, ﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6], indicate that the angels of punishment do not fall short in those duties. Whoever affirms the infallibility (ʿisma) of the angels in these circumstances affirms their infallibility absolutely. Thus this verse proves the absolute infallibility of the angels.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾, there are several discussions concerning it.

The first: It has been said that those who are returned are the angels, meaning that just as the children of Adam die, those angels also die. It has also been said: rather, those who are returned are human beings, meaning that after their death they are returned to Allah. Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs that the human being is not merely this bodily structure. The plain sense of this verse indicates that death occurs to the servant, and it indicates that after death he is returned to Allah. The dead person, while dead, cannot be returned to Allah, because that return is not by place or direction, since He, exalted is He, is transcendent above place and direction. Rather, that return must be interpreted as being submissive to the judgment of Allah and obedient to the decree of Allah. And if he were not living, this meaning would not apply to him. So it is established that here there is both death and life. As for death, it is the portion of the body. What remains is that life is the portion of the self (nafs) and the spirit (rūḥ). Since He, exalted is He, said ﴿then you are returned to Allah﴾, and it is established that what is returned is the self and the spirit, it is established that the human being is nothing but the self and the spirit, and that is what was sought.

Know that His words ﴿then you are returned to Allah﴾ imply that the spirit existed before the body, because the return from this world to the presence of majesty only occurs if it existed before attaching to the body. A parallel to this is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and His words ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾ [Yunus: 4]. It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah created the spirits two thousand years before the bodies." The argument of the philosophers that human souls did not exist before the existence of the body is a weak argument, the weakness of which we have explained in the rational books.

The second discussion: The word "ilā" (إلى, "to") indicates the end of a goal. So His words "ilā Allāh" ("to Allah") imply affirming place and direction for Allah, exalted is He, and that is false. Therefore it is obligatory to interpret it as meaning that they are returned to a place where there is no owner and no judge other than Him.

The third discussion: In this verse He, exalted is He, named Himself with two names:

The first: al-Mawlā (the Master). You already know that the word al-mawlā and the word al-walī are both derived from al-waly, meaning nearness. He, glory be to Him, is the Near and the Far, the Manifest and the Hidden, as in His words ﴿We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], and His words ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7]. Also, the one who frees a slave is called a mawlā, and this is like an indication that He freed them from punishment. This is what is meant by His words, "My mercy precedes My wrath." Also, He attributed Himself to the servants, saying ﴿their true Master﴾, and He did not attribute them to Himself, and that is the utmost of mercy.

[Page 17]

Also, He said "their true Master", and the meaning is that in this world they were under the false dominations of masters, namely the self (nafs), desire (shahwa), and anger (ghaḍab), as He said: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. When a person dies, he is freed from the false dominations of these masters and passes under the dominion of the true Master.

The second name: al-Ḥaqq (the True). They differed over whether it is one of the names of Allah, exalted is He. It has been said: al-ḥaqq is a verbal noun (maṣdar), the opposite of al-bāṭil (the false), and verbal nouns do not apply to agents except metaphorically, as when we say "so-and-so is justice (ʿadl)," "hope (rajāʾ)," "help (ghiyāth)," "generosity (karam)," or "bounty (faḍl)." It is possible to say that al-ḥaqq is that which exists, and the thing most worthy of existence is Allah, glory be to Him, because He is necessary in His own essence. So the thing most worthy of being true is He Himself. Know that it has been read as "al-ḥaqqa" in the accusative, as praise, like your saying "al-ḥamdu lillāhi al-ḥaqqa" (praise belongs to Allah, the True).

* * *

As for His words, ﴿Judgment belongs to Him alone, and He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: His words ﴿Judgment belongs to Him alone﴾ mean that there is no judgment except for Allah. This is reinforced by His words ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 57]. This necessitates that no one has judgment over anything except Allah, and this necessitates that all good and evil are by the judgment and decree of Allah. Had Allah not decreed happiness for the fortunate and wretchedness for the wretched, that would not have come about.

The second issue: Our companions (Ash'aris) said that this verse indicates that obedience does not necessitate reward, nor disobedience necessitate punishment. For if that were established, then the obedient person would have a right upon Allah, namely receiving reward, and that contradicts what the verse indicates, that judgment belongs to Allah alone.

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i (Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i, the Mu'tazili theologian) used this verse as proof that the speech (kalām) of Allah is created (ḥādith). He said: If His speech were eternal, He would have to be speaking the reckoning now and before His creation, and that is impossible, because reckoning requires recounting a deed that has already occurred. Our companions opposed him with knowledge: He, exalted is He, was knowing before creation that it would come into existence, and after its existence He became knowing that it had come into existence before that. Thus no change in knowledge follows from this. So why would it not be permissible for speech to be the same? And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: They differed about the manner of this reckoning. Some said: He, exalted is He, reckons the creation Himself in a single instant, His speech not occupying Him from speech. Others said: rather, He commands the angels, so that each angel reckons one of the servants; for if He reckoned the disbelievers Himself, He would speak with them, and that is false, because of His words about the disbelievers, ﴿nor will He speak to them﴾. As for the philosophers, they have discussion in explaining this reckoning, namely that it is completed only by presenting two premises.

The first premise: The multiplication and repetition of actions produces firmly rooted, strong, and stable dispositions (malakāt), and complete induction (istiqrāʾ tām) reveals the soundness of what we have mentioned. Do you not see that whoever is more persistent in some action, the firm and complete disposition in that action becomes stronger in him?

The second premise: Since repetition of an action produces the firmly rooted disposition, it must be that each of those actions has an effect in producing that disposition. Rather, it must be that every part of a single action has some effect in producing that disposition. The wise have given examples for this principle:

[Page 17 continues in the text as follows]

The first example: Suppose we have a great ship such that if a hundred thousand mann (a unit of weight) were loaded into it, it would sink in the water by only one span (shibr). Then if only one grain of wheat were loaded into it, this small amount of a heavy body placed in that ship causes it to sink in the water by a small amount, however small it becomes, to the point that the senses cannot perceive it and the imagination cannot grasp it.

The second example: It has been established among the philosophers that the simple bodies have natural shapes that are spheres. The surface of water must therefore be a sphere, and the arcs resembling one another from circles surrounding a single center differ. The curvature of an arc taken from the great circle is less than the curvature of an arc resembling the first taken from a smaller circle. If this is the case, then when a cup is filled with water and placed beneath a mountain, the convexity of the surface of that water is greater than its convexity when the cup is placed above the mountain. And whenever the convexity is greater and larger, the cup's capacity for water is greater. This implies that the cup's capacity for water while beneath the mountain is greater than its capacity for water while above the mountain. However, this degree of difference is such that the senses and imagination cannot perceive it, because it is extremely small.

The third example: Two people, one standing near the other. Their feet are closer to the center of the world than their heads, because heavy bodies descend from the expanse of the encompassing sphere toward the narrowness of the center. However, that degree of difference is not perceptible to the senses and imagination.

Now that you know these examples, and know that the multiplication of actions produces dispositions, we say: No action of good or evil, whether small or great, fails to produce an effect in the self, either toward happiness or toward wretchedness. At this point, by this decisive proof, the soundness of His words, exalted is He, is revealed: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ and ﴿whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7–8]. Since it is established that actions produce dispositions, and the actions issuing from the hand are what affect the acquisition of a specific disposition, and likewise the actions issuing from the foot, there is no doubt that the hands and feet will be witnesses on the Day of Resurrection against the human being, meaning that those psychic effects came about in the substances of the souls through these actions issuing from these limbs. So the issuing of those actions from that particular limb functions as testimony to the coming about of those specific effects in the essence of the self.

As for the reckoning: its purpose is to know what remains of income and expenditure. Since we have shown that every atom of good and evil deeds has an effect in producing one of these states in the essence of the self, whether one of the pure and virtuous states or one of the blameworthy and base states, and there is no doubt that these deeds were varied, some of them necessarily came into conflict with others. After these conflicts occur, a specific measure of good character remains in the self, and another measure of blameworthy character. When the body dies, the measure of that good character and the measure of that blameworthy character become manifest. That manifestation occurs in the indivisible instant, which is the instant in which the self's attachment to the body is severed. This state is therefore expressed by the swiftness of reckoning. These are the statements made in applying the prophetic wisdom to philosophical wisdom. And Allah is the One who knows the realities of matters.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾, the meaning is that among the totality of His subjugation of His servants is His sending guardians over them. These guardians are those referred to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For him are successive angels before and behind him, guarding him by the command of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], and His saying: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers﴾ [al-Infitar: 10-11]. They agreed that the purpose of the presence of these guardians is the recording of deeds. Then they differed: some of them say that they record obedience, disobedience and permissible acts, all of them, by the evidence of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What sort of book is this that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that with every person there are two angels: one on his right and the other on his left. When the person speaks a good deed, the one on the right records it, and when he speaks an evil deed, the one on the right says to the one on the left: "Wait for him, perhaps he will repent of it. If he does not repent, record it against him." The first view is stronger, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ indicates guardians of all, without specification.

The second investigation: the apparent meaning of these verses indicates that the awareness of these guardians concerns sayings and actions. As for the states of the hearts, namely knowledge and ignorance, there is nothing in these verses that indicates their awareness of them. As for sayings, it is due to His saying: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer ready﴾ [Qaf: 18]; and as for actions, it is due to His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 10-12]. As for faith, disbelief, sincerity and associating partners, the evidence does not indicate the angels' awareness of them.

The third investigation: they mentioned, regarding the benefit of appointing angels over the children of Adam, several aspects:

The first: when the responsible person knows that angels are assigned to him, counting his deeds for him and recording them in scrolls that will be displayed before the heads of witnesses at the standing places of the Resurrection, this is more restraining for him from vile acts.

The second: it is possible that the benefit in the recording is that those scrolls will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, since weighing deeds is not possible, but weighing scrolls is possible.

The third: God does what He wills and decrees what He desires. It is obligatory upon us to believe in everything the Law has brought, whether we comprehend its wisdom or not. This is the summary of what the people of the Sharia have said. As for the people of wisdom (philosophers), their statements on this topic have differed in several ways:

The first aspect: the later among them said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾, and among that subjugation is that He mixed the opposing temperaments and blended the repellent elements. When a mixture resulted between them, that mixture became prepared, by virtue of that mixing,
صفحة ١٤
to receive the governing soul and the sensory, motive and articulate faculties. They said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ is those souls and faculties, for it is they that guard those subdued temperaments in their mixtures.

The second aspect: the view of some of the ancients, that these human souls and human spirits differ in their substances and vary in their quiddities; some of them are good and some are wicked, and likewise concerning intelligence and dullness, freedom and baseness, nobility and lowness, and other attributes. For each group of these lower spirits there is a celestial spirit which is to them like a compassionate father and a merciful master, assisting them in their affairs in their waking and their sleeping, sometimes by way of visions and at other times by way of inspirations. The wicked spirits have principles from the world of the spheres, and so do the good spirits, and those principles are called in their terminology the "complete temperament," meaning that those celestial spirits are complete and perfect in those temperaments and characters, while these lower spirits generated from them are weaker than them, because the effect is in every respect weaker than its cause. And the practitioners of talismans and spiritual charms have much discourse on this subject.

The third aspect: the soul attached to this body. There is no doubt that the souls separated from bodies, since they are equal to these in nature and quiddity, incline towards this soul because of the resemblance and agreement between them, and they too are attached in some way to this body and become helpers to this soul in the requirements of its nature. Thus it is established by these three aspects that what the true Sharia has brought is not something the philosophers may refuse, for all of them have acknowledged what is close to it. Since the matter is so, the insistence of the ignorant among them upon denial is false. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in death﴾, here there are two investigations:

The first investigation: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], and He said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. These two texts indicate that the taking of souls is only by God, exalted is He. Then He said: ﴿Say: The angel of death who is charged with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and this requires that taking only occurs from the angel of death. Then He said in this verse: ﴿Our messengers take him﴾. These three texts appear as though contradictory.

The answer: the taking in reality occurs by God's power, exalted is He, while in the outward knowledge it is entrusted to the angel of death, who is the absolute chief in this matter, and has helpers, attendants and supporters. So the attribution of taking to these three is fitting according to the three considerations. And God knows best.

The second investigation: some people said: these messengers by whom the taking occurs are the very same guardians, so during the period of life they guard them by the command of God, and at the coming of death they take them. Most of them, however, hold that those who undertake guarding are other than those who undertake the matter of taking. There is no indication in the wording of the verse showing the difference, but what most of them inclined to is the second view. Also, it has been established by rational analogies that the angels who are the sources of mercy, goodness and comfort are different from those who are the origins of sorrow and grief. A group of angels are those called the "spiritual ones" (Ruhaniyyun), for they bestow spirit, comfort and fragrance, and some of them are called the "Karubiyyun" (Cherubim), for they are the sources of distress, grief and sorrows.

The third investigation: the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: The angel of death who is charged with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11] is that he is one angel, the chief of the angels charged with seizing souls. And what is meant by the guardians mentioned in this verse are his followers and partisans. From Mujahid: He made the earth like a basin before the angel of death, so that he takes whomever he takes; and there is no household but that he circles over them twice each day. And there have come in the reports wondrous states concerning the attributes of the angel of death and the manner of his death at the passing away and ending of the world.

The fourth investigation: Hamza recited "tawaffahu" with an alif, with imala, while the rest recited with a ta'. The first is due to the verb being placed before its subject and because the plural may be masculine, and the second is according to the feminine form of the plural.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 61–62 (part 2 of 2):

[Page 16]

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they do not fail (in their duty)﴾, meaning they do not fall short in what Allah has commanded them. This indicates that the angels entrusted with seizing souls do not fall short in what they have been commanded. His words about the angels of the Fire, ﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6], indicate that the angels of punishment do not fall short in those duties. Whoever affirms the infallibility (ʿisma) of the angels in these circumstances affirms their infallibility absolutely. Thus this verse proves the absolute infallibility of the angels.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾, there are several discussions concerning it.

The first: It has been said that those who are returned are the angels, meaning that just as the children of Adam die, those angels also die. It has also been said: rather, those who are returned are human beings, meaning that after their death they are returned to Allah. Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs that the human being is not merely this bodily structure. The plain sense of this verse indicates that death occurs to the servant, and it indicates that after death he is returned to Allah. The dead person, while dead, cannot be returned to Allah, because that return is not by place or direction, since He, exalted is He, is transcendent above place and direction. Rather, that return must be interpreted as being submissive to the judgment of Allah and obedient to the decree of Allah. And if he were not living, this meaning would not apply to him. So it is established that here there is both death and life. As for death, it is the portion of the body. What remains is that life is the portion of the self (nafs) and the spirit (rūḥ). Since He, exalted is He, said ﴿then you are returned to Allah﴾, and it is established that what is returned is the self and the spirit, it is established that the human being is nothing but the self and the spirit, and that is what was sought.

Know that His words ﴿then you are returned to Allah﴾ imply that the spirit existed before the body, because the return from this world to the presence of majesty only occurs if it existed before attaching to the body. A parallel to this is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and His words ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾ [Yunus: 4]. It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah created the spirits two thousand years before the bodies." The argument of the philosophers that human souls did not exist before the existence of the body is a weak argument, the weakness of which we have explained in the rational books.

The second discussion: The word "ilā" (إلى, "to") indicates the end of a goal. So His words "ilā Allāh" ("to Allah") imply affirming place and direction for Allah, exalted is He, and that is false. Therefore it is obligatory to interpret it as meaning that they are returned to a place where there is no owner and no judge other than Him.

The third discussion: In this verse He, exalted is He, named Himself with two names:

The first: al-Mawlā (the Master). You already know that the word al-mawlā and the word al-walī are both derived from al-waly, meaning nearness. He, glory be to Him, is the Near and the Far, the Manifest and the Hidden, as in His words ﴿We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], and His words ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7]. Also, the one who frees a slave is called a mawlā, and this is like an indication that He freed them from punishment. This is what is meant by His words, "My mercy precedes My wrath." Also, He attributed Himself to the servants, saying ﴿their true Master﴾, and He did not attribute them to Himself, and that is the utmost of mercy.

[Page 17]

Also, He said "their true Master", and the meaning is that in this world they were under the false dominations of masters, namely the self (nafs), desire (shahwa), and anger (ghaḍab), as He said: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. When a person dies, he is freed from the false dominations of these masters and passes under the dominion of the true Master.

The second name: al-Ḥaqq (the True). They differed over whether it is one of the names of Allah, exalted is He. It has been said: al-ḥaqq is a verbal noun (maṣdar), the opposite of al-bāṭil (the false), and verbal nouns do not apply to agents except metaphorically, as when we say "so-and-so is justice (ʿadl)," "hope (rajāʾ)," "help (ghiyāth)," "generosity (karam)," or "bounty (faḍl)." It is possible to say that al-ḥaqq is that which exists, and the thing most worthy of existence is Allah, glory be to Him, because He is necessary in His own essence. So the thing most worthy of being true is He Himself. Know that it has been read as "al-ḥaqqa" in the accusative, as praise, like your saying "al-ḥamdu lillāhi al-ḥaqqa" (praise belongs to Allah, the True).

* * *

As for His words, ﴿Judgment belongs to Him alone, and He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: His words ﴿Judgment belongs to Him alone﴾ mean that there is no judgment except for Allah. This is reinforced by His words ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 57]. This necessitates that no one has judgment over anything except Allah, and this necessitates that all good and evil are by the judgment and decree of Allah. Had Allah not decreed happiness for the fortunate and wretchedness for the wretched, that would not have come about.

The second issue: Our companions (Ash'aris) said that this verse indicates that obedience does not necessitate reward, nor disobedience necessitate punishment. For if that were established, then the obedient person would have a right upon Allah, namely receiving reward, and that contradicts what the verse indicates, that judgment belongs to Allah alone.

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i (Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i, the Mu'tazili theologian) used this verse as proof that the speech (kalām) of Allah is created (ḥādith). He said: If His speech were eternal, He would have to be speaking the reckoning now and before His creation, and that is impossible, because reckoning requires recounting a deed that has already occurred. Our companions opposed him with knowledge: He, exalted is He, was knowing before creation that it would come into existence, and after its existence He became knowing that it had come into existence before that. Thus no change in knowledge follows from this. So why would it not be permissible for speech to be the same? And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: They differed about the manner of this reckoning. Some said: He, exalted is He, reckons the creation Himself in a single instant, His speech not occupying Him from speech. Others said: rather, He commands the angels, so that each angel reckons one of the servants; for if He reckoned the disbelievers Himself, He would speak with them, and that is false, because of His words about the disbelievers, ﴿nor will He speak to them﴾. As for the philosophers, they have discussion in explaining this reckoning, namely that it is completed only by presenting two premises.

The first premise: The multiplication and repetition of actions produces firmly rooted, strong, and stable dispositions (malakāt), and complete induction (istiqrāʾ tām) reveals the soundness of what we have mentioned. Do you not see that whoever is more persistent in some action, the firm and complete disposition in that action becomes stronger in him?

The second premise: Since repetition of an action produces the firmly rooted disposition, it must be that each of those actions has an effect in producing that disposition. Rather, it must be that every part of a single action has some effect in producing that disposition. The wise have given examples for this principle:

[Page 17 continues in the text as follows]

The first example: Suppose we have a great ship such that if a hundred thousand mann (a unit of weight) were loaded into it, it would sink in the water by only one span (shibr). Then if only one grain of wheat were loaded into it, this small amount of a heavy body placed in that ship causes it to sink in the water by a small amount, however small it becomes, to the point that the senses cannot perceive it and the imagination cannot grasp it.

The second example: It has been established among the philosophers that the simple bodies have natural shapes that are spheres. The surface of water must therefore be a sphere, and the arcs resembling one another from circles surrounding a single center differ. The curvature of an arc taken from the great circle is less than the curvature of an arc resembling the first taken from a smaller circle. If this is the case, then when a cup is filled with water and placed beneath a mountain, the convexity of the surface of that water is greater than its convexity when the cup is placed above the mountain. And whenever the convexity is greater and larger, the cup's capacity for water is greater. This implies that the cup's capacity for water while beneath the mountain is greater than its capacity for water while above the mountain. However, this degree of difference is such that the senses and imagination cannot perceive it, because it is extremely small.

The third example: Two people, one standing near the other. Their feet are closer to the center of the world than their heads, because heavy bodies descend from the expanse of the encompassing sphere toward the narrowness of the center. However, that degree of difference is not perceptible to the senses and imagination.

Now that you know these examples, and know that the multiplication of actions produces dispositions, we say: No action of good or evil, whether small or great, fails to produce an effect in the self, either toward happiness or toward wretchedness. At this point, by this decisive proof, the soundness of His words, exalted is He, is revealed: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ and ﴿whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7–8]. Since it is established that actions produce dispositions, and the actions issuing from the hand are what affect the acquisition of a specific disposition, and likewise the actions issuing from the foot, there is no doubt that the hands and feet will be witnesses on the Day of Resurrection against the human being, meaning that those psychic effects came about in the substances of the souls through these actions issuing from these limbs. So the issuing of those actions from that particular limb functions as testimony to the coming about of those specific effects in the essence of the self.

As for the reckoning: its purpose is to know what remains of income and expenditure. Since we have shown that every atom of good and evil deeds has an effect in producing one of these states in the essence of the self, whether one of the pure and virtuous states or one of the blameworthy and base states, and there is no doubt that these deeds were varied, some of them necessarily came into conflict with others. After these conflicts occur, a specific measure of good character remains in the self, and another measure of blameworthy character. When the body dies, the measure of that good character and the measure of that blameworthy character become manifest. That manifestation occurs in the indivisible instant, which is the instant in which the self's attachment to the body is severed. This state is therefore expressed by the swiftness of reckoning. These are the statements made in applying the prophetic wisdom to philosophical wisdom. And Allah is the One who knows the realities of matters.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 6, verses 63–64:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Who delivers you from the darknesses of land and sea, when you call upon Him humbly and in secret: "If He delivers us from this, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ ﴿Say: "Allah delivers you from it and from every distress, yet you associate others with Him."﴾

Know that this is another kind of proof that indicates the perfection of divine power and the perfection of divine mercy, grace and beneficence. In it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿Who delivers you﴾ (*yunajjikum*) with the doubled letter (*tashdid*) in both words, while the rest read it without doubling (*takhfif*). Al-Wahidi said: "The doubled and the undoubled forms are two dialectal forms (*lughatan*) derived from *najā* (to deliver). If you wish, you may form it with a hamza (*anjā*), and if you wish, you may form it by doubling the middle radical (*najjā*), like *afraḥtuhu* and *farraḥtuhu*, and *aghramtuhu* and *gharramtuhu*. In the Qur'an: ﴿So We delivered him and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 72], and in another verse: ﴿And We delivered those who believed﴾ [Fussilat: 18]. Since the revelation came in both forms, the two readings are shown to be equal in excellence, but the preferred reading is the doubled form, because this deliverance from God happened on more than one occasion." Also, Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read *khifyatan* (secretly) with a kasra on the *kha'*, while the rest read it with a damma; both are dialectal forms. On this same divergence occurs in Surat al-A'raf. Al-Akhfash also reported regarding *khufyatan* and *khifyatan* that both are dialectal forms. Also, *al-khufyah* (with a damma) derives from *al-ikhfa'* (concealment), while *al-khīfah* (with a kasra) derives from *al-rahab* (awe).

Also, ﴿If You deliver us﴾ (*la'in anjaytanā*) from this. Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *la'in anjānā* in the third person (*al-mughāyabah*), while the rest read *la'in anjaytanā* in the second person (*al-khiṭāb*). As for the first group, those who read in the third person, they differed: Asim read with *tafkhīm* (emphatic, full pronunciation of the vowel), while the rest read with *imālah* (inclination of the vowel). The argument of those who read in the third person is that what precedes this word and what follows it is expressed in the third person. What precedes it is His saying ﴿you call upon Him (*tad'ūnahu*)﴾, and what follows it is His saying ﴿Say: "Allah delivers you from it"﴾. Also, reading in the second person requires an implied subject (*iḍmār*), the sense being: "They say: If You deliver us," and an implied subject is contrary to the original form. The argument of those who read in the second person is His saying in another verse: ﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾ [Yunus: 22].

**The second issue:** ﴿the darknesses of land and sea﴾ is a metaphor for their terrors and horrors. It is said of a severe day: "a dark day" (*yawm muẓlim*), and "a day with stars" (*yawm dhū kawākib*), meaning that its darkness has intensified until it has become like night. The real meaning of the statement is that the matter becomes severe for him, the manner of escape becomes confused for him, and the path to salvation becomes dark for him. Some have taken it in its literal sense, saying: As for the darknesses of the sea, they are the gathering together of the darkness of night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of clouds, to which are added fierce winds and terrifying waves, so they do not know how to escape, and the fear is immense. As for the darknesses of land, they are the darkness of night, the darkness of clouds, and intense fear from not being guided to the right path. The point is that when these causes that necessitate intense fear come together, a person does not turn back except to Allah, may He be exalted. This turning back occurs outwardly and inwardly, because in this state a person greatly sincerely devotes himself in the presence of Allah, may He be exalted, and his hope is severed from everything other than Allah, may He be exalted. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿humbly and in secret﴾. Thus Allah, may He be exalted, explained that when the sound disposition (*al-fiṭrah al-salīmah*) and original creation bear witness in this state that there is no refuge except Allah, and no reliance except on the grace of Allah, this sincerity must remain in all states and times. But it is not so. A person, after attaining safety and deliverance, attributes that safety to physical causes and commits shirk.

Among the exegetes is one who says: the purpose of this verse is to criticize the divinity of idols and images. I say: attachment to anything other than Allah in the path of worship comes close to being attachment to an idol, and the people of realization (*ahl al-taḥqīq*) call it hidden shirk (*al-shirk al-khafī*).

The wording of the verse indicates that when these hardships occur, a person does several things:

First: supplication (*al-du'ā'*).

Second: humility (*al-taḍarruʿ*).

Third: sincerity of the heart (*al-ikhlāṣ bi-l-qalb*), which is what is meant by His saying ﴿and in secret﴾.

Fourth: the commitment to occupy oneself with gratitude (*al-shukr*), which is what is meant by His saying ﴿If He delivers us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, explained that He delivers them from those terrors and from all other causes of fear and distress. Then that person commits shirk. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Lost is whoever you call upon besides Him, except Him﴾ [al-Isra': 67], and His saying: ﴿And they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Yunus: 22]. In sum, the practice of most of creation is that when they witness a terrifying matter, they become sincere, and when they move to security and ease, they commit shirk.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, explained that He delivers them from those terrors and from all other causes of fear and distress. Then that person commits shirk. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Lost is whoever you call upon besides Him, except Him﴾ [al-Isra': 67], and His saying: ﴿And they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Yunus: 22]. In sum, the practice of most of creation is that when they witness a terrifying matter, they become sincere, and when they move to security and ease, they commit shirk.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confuse you into sects and make you taste the violence of one another. Look how We vary the signs, that they may understand.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is another kind of evidence for tawhid (the oneness of God), mixed with a type of warning. He, exalted is He, made clear that He is able to deliver punishment to them by these various means. As for sending punishment upon them at times from above them and at times from beneath their feet, there are two opinions:

The first: to take the wording in its literal sense. We say: the punishment that descends upon them from above is like the rain that descends upon them from above, as in the story of Noah, and the thunderbolt that descends upon them from above, and likewise the shout that descends upon them from above, as the people of Lot were pelted, and as the companions of the elephant were struck. As for the punishment that emerges from beneath their feet, it is like the earthquake (al-rajfah) and like the sinking of Qarun. It has also been said that it is the withholding of rain and plants. In sum, this verse encompasses all kinds of punishment that can descend from above and emerge from below.

The second opinion: that this wording be taken in its figurative sense. Ibn Abbas, in a report from Ikrimah, said: "a punishment from above you" means from the rulers, and "from beneath your feet" means from the slaves and the lowly. As for His saying, ﴿or to confuse you into sects﴾, know that shiya' (sects) is the plural of shi'ah, and every people who gather upon a matter are a shi'ah, and its plural is shiya' and ashya'. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿as was done with their like before﴾ [Saba: 54]. Its root is from al-shiya', which is following (al-tabaʿ), and the meaning of shi'ah is those who follow one another. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿yalbisakum﴾

[Page 20]

﴿shiya'an﴾ means: He will mix your affair with a mixing of agitation, not a mixing of agreement, so that He makes you factions, and you are not one group. When you are in disagreement, some of you fight others, and this is the meaning of His saying ﴿and make you taste the violence of one another﴾. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "When Gabriel, peace be upon him, brought down this verse, it grieved the Messenger, peace be upon him, and he said: What will remain of my community if they are dealt with in this way? Gabriel said to him: I am only a servant like you, so ask your Lord for your community. So he asked his Lord that He not do this to them. Gabriel said: Indeed Allah has secured them from two things: that He not send upon them a punishment from above them as He sent it upon the people of Noah and Lot, nor from beneath their feet as He caused the earth to swallow Qarun. And He did not protect them from being confused into sects by divergent desires, and from making some of them taste the violence of others with the sword." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "My community will split into seventy-two sects, and one sect will be saved." In another report: "All of them are in Paradise except the zanadiqah (heretics)."

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿or to confuse you into sects﴾ is that He, exalted is He, drives them toward divergent desires and conflicting doctrines. It is evident that the truth among them is only one, and whatever is other than it is false. This implies that He, exalted is He, may drive the responsible person toward false belief. And His saying ﴿and make you taste the violence of one another﴾: there is no doubt that most of it is injustice and disobedience. This indicates that He, exalted is He, is the creator of good and evil. The opponent answered this by saying that the verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is able to do it, and in our view Allah is able to do the ugly. The dispute is only over whether He, exalted is He, actually does that or not.

The answer: the way of holding to the verse is something else, for He said: ﴿He is the One able﴾ to do that, and this conveys restriction (hasr). Therefore it must be that other than Allah is not able to do that. This divergence among people exists, and it has been established by the implication of the stated restriction that this is not issued from other than Allah, so it must be issued from Allah, and that conveys the required conclusion.

The third issue: The imitators (al-muqallidah) and the literalists (al-hashwiyyah) said: this verse is among the strongest proofs for prohibiting reflection and argumentation, because opening those doors results in disagreement and dispute in religions, and the dispersal of creation into sects and religions, and that is blameworthy by the ruling of this verse, and what leads to the blameworthy is blameworthy. Therefore opening the door of reflection and argumentation in religion must be blameworthy. Its answer is easy, and Allah knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿Look how We vary the signs, that they may understand.﴾ Al-Qadi said: This indicates that He, exalted is He, intended by varying these signs and establishing these clear proofs that everyone should understand those evidences and that everyone should comprehend those clear proofs. Our answer: rather, the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, did not vary these signs except for those who comprehend and understand; as for one who turns away and rebels, He, exalted is He, did not vary these signs for them. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 66–67:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿But your people have denied it, though it is the truth. Say: "I am not a guardian over you."﴾ ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know.﴾

Concerning what the pronoun in His words ﴿But your people have denied it, though it is the truth. Say: "I am not a guardian over you."﴾ ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know.﴾ refers to, there are several opinions:

The first: it refers to the punishment mentioned in the previous verse, ﴿and it is the truth﴾, meaning that it must certainly descend upon them.

The second: the pronoun in "bihi" (by it) refers to the Qur'an, and it is the truth, meaning in its being a Book sent down from Allah.

The third: it refers to the variation of the signs (taṣrif al-āyāt), and it is the truth; because they denied that these things are indications. Then He said: ﴿Say: "I am not a guardian over you"﴾, meaning: I am not a keeper over you so as to requite you for your denial and your turning away from accepting the proofs; I am only a warner, and Allah is the One who will requite you for your deeds. Ibn ʿAbbas and the exegetes said: it was abrogated by the verse of fighting; but this is far-fetched. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾. The word "mustaqarr" may be the place of settling, and it may be the settling itself; because what exceeds the triliteral form has its verbal noun in the form of the passive participle, such as "madkhal" and "makhraj", meaning "idkhal" and "ikhraj" (entry and exit). The meaning: for every report that Allah, exalted is He, gives, there is a time or a place in which it occurs without deviation or delay. And if you take "mustaqirr" to mean "istiqrar" (settling), the meaning is that for every promise and every threat from Allah, exalted is He, there is a settling, and they must come to know that the matter is as Allah, exalted is He, has reported it, at its manifestation and its descent. And as for that with which He warned the disbelievers, it may be that what is meant by it is the punishment of the Hereafter, and it may be that what is meant by it is the domination of the Muslims over the disbelievers by war, killing and subjugation in this world.
