﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a different talk. And if Satan makes you forget, do not sit, after the remembrance, with the wrongdoing people.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, said in the first verse: ﴿Your people denied it, though it is the truth. Say: I am not a guardian over you.﴾ Thereby He made clear that those who deny this religion, the Messenger is not obligated to keep company with them or to be a watcher over them. Then He made clear in this verse that if those deniers add to their disbelief and denial mockery of the religion and slander against the Messenger, then one must be careful to avoid their company and abandon sitting with them. The verse contains several issues:

**The first issue:** His words ﴿And when you see﴾. It has been said that this is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ while the intended meaning is someone else. It has also been said that the address is to someone other than him, meaning: "And when you see, O listener, those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses." Al-Wahidi transmitted that the polytheists, whenever they sat with the believers, would fall upon the Messenger of God ﷺ and the Qur'an, so they would revile and mock, and so He commanded that they not sit with them until they engage in a different talk. The word *khawd* (vain, idle engagement) in the language means discussion carried out in a manner of frivolity and play. He, exalted is He, said, relating the words of the disbelievers: ﴿We used to engage in vain talk with those who engaged in it﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:45]. And when a man is asked about a people and he says, "I left them engaging in *khawd*," this indicates that they had begun uttering words that should not be mentioned. Among the Hashawiyya (a label for a group of literalist traditionalists) is one who relies on this verse to forbid reasoning and debate concerning the essence of God, exalted is He, and His attributes. He said: because that is engaging in vain talk concerning the verses of God, and engaging in vain talk concerning the verses of God is forbidden by this verse. The answer to this is: we have transmitted from the exegetes that the meaning of "*khawd*" is beginning to speak of the verses of God, exalted is He, in the manner of slander and mockery. We have also shown that the word "*khawd*" was established in the original language for this meaning, so this argument falls. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** Ibn 'Amir read ﴿yunsiyannaka﴾ with the doubled consonant (shadda). *Fa'ala* and *af'ala* operate in one and the same manner, as we have explained in several places. In the revelation is the verse ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq 86:17]. The preferred reading is the reading of the majority, because of His words: ﴿None made me forget it except Satan﴾ [al-Kahf 18:63]. The meaning of the verse is: if you forget and sit, then do not sit after the remembrance; and stand up when you remember. *Al-dhikra* is a noun for reminder, as said by al-Layth. al-Farra' said: *al-dhikra* can carry the meaning of *al-dhikr* (remembrance). His words ﴿with the wrongdoing people﴾ mean with the polytheists.

**The third issue:** His words ﴿turn away from them﴾. This turning away may occur by standing up from them, and it may occur by other means. When He said afterward ﴿then do not sit after the remembrance﴾, this became evidence that the intended meaning is turning away from them by rising from their presence. Here there are questions:

**First question:** Is it permissible for this turning away to be by a means other than rising from them? The answer: those who cling to the apparent wording of the expressions and claim that they must be applied according to their apparent sense do not permit that. Those who say that the meaning is what is to be considered permitted it. They said: because the aim is to make disapproval manifest, so any means that achieves this aim is permissible to adopt.

**Second question:** If the Messenger feared from rising from them, is he still obligated to rise?

The answer: every act that was made obligatory upon the Messenger is obligatory upon him, whether the effect of fear appears or not. For if we permitted him to abandon an obligation because of fear, then confidence in the obligations he conveyed to us would collapse. As for other than the Messenger, at extreme fear the obligation may drop from him, because his abandoning it does not lead to the aforementioned harm.

**The fourth issue:** His words ﴿And if Satan makes you forget, do not sit after the remembrance﴾ indicate that the obligation is dropped from the one who forgets. Al-Jubba'i said: if lack of knowledge of a thing causes the obligation to fall, then lack of ability to do a thing is more deserving of causing the obligation to fall. This indicates that the charge of what is beyond one's capacity does not occur. It also indicates that capability exists before the act, for if it were not present except together with the act, it would not have existed before the act, and so the disbeliever would not be able to believe, and so the command to believe would not be directed at him. Know that these statements have been mentioned often in this book together with their answers, so we will not lengthen the discussion by mentioning the answers. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 69–70:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nothing of their reckoning falls upon those who fear God, but it is a reminder, so that perhaps they may fear God.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: The Muslims said, "If we, whenever the polytheists mock the Qur'an and engage in discussion about it, were to withdraw from them, we would not be able to sit in the Sacred Mosque and circumambulate the House." So this verse was revealed, and a concession was granted to the believers to sit with them, remind them, and make them understand.

He said: The meaning of the verse, ﴿Nothing of their reckoning falls upon those who fear God﴾, refers to those who fear [avoid] polytheism, major sins and grave immoralities. ﴿Of their reckoning﴾ means of their sins. ﴿Nothing, but it is a reminder﴾. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian) said: The word *dhikra* (reminder) may be in the nominative position (raf') or in the accusative position (nasb). As for its being in the nominative position, it is on two grounds:

The first: *wa-lakin 'alaykum dhikra*, meaning, "but upon you is a reminder," that is, that you remind them. It is also permissible that it means *wa-lakinna alladhi ta'murunahum bihi dhikra*, "but what you enjoin upon them is a reminder." According to the first interpretation, *dhikra* means "reminding"; according to the second, *dhikra* means "remembrance/admonition." As for its being in the accusative position, the implied meaning is: *dhakkiruhum dhikra* ("remind them a reminder"), *la'allahum yattaqun* ("so that perhaps they may fear God"). The meaning is: perhaps that reminder will prevent them from engaging in those vanities.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement, and whom the life of this world has deceived, and remind by it, lest a soul be delivered to ruin for what it has earned; it will have, besides Allah, no protector and no intercessor; and if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it. Those are the ones delivered to ruin for what they earned; for them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

Know that these are the ones mentioned in His words: ﴿those who engage in discussion about Our signs﴾. The meaning of *dhirhum* ("leave them") is: turn away from them. It does not mean that one should abandon warning them, because He said after it: ﴿and remind by it﴾. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63]. What is intended is abandoning keeping their company and being gentle with them, not abandoning warning and frightening them.

Know that He, the Exalted, commanded the Messenger to abandon those who are characterized by two attributes:

The first attribute: that among their traits is that they have taken their religion as play and amusement. There are several interpretations of this:

First: What is meant is that they took their religion, which they were obligated to and called to, namely the religion of Islam, as play and amusement, insofar as they mocked it and ridiculed it.

Second: They took what is play and amusement, namely the worship of idols and other things, as their religion.

Third: The disbelievers used to make judgments about the religion of Allah merely by whim and wishful thinking, such as prohibiting the *sawa'ib* and *bahair* (certain animals), and they did not exercise any caution at all regarding matters of religion, but were content merely with imitation (*taqlid*). So Allah the Exalted described them as having taken their religion as play and amusement.

Fourth: Ibn Abbas said: Allah made for every people a festival which they honor, pray in, and enliven with the remembrance of Allah the Exalted. Then most people became polytheists, and the People of the Book took their festival as amusement and play, other than the Muslims, for they took their festival as Allah the Exalted had prescribed it.

Fifth, which is the closest [to the truth]: the one who is genuinely committed to the religion is the one who supports the religion because proof has been established that it is true, sound and correct. As for those who support it in order to use it as a means to acquire positions and leadership, to prevail over an opponent, or to amass wealth, they have supported the religion for the sake of the world. Allah has judged the world in all the other verses to be play and amusement. Thus what is meant by His words, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾, is an indication of those who use their religion as a means to their worldly gain. If you reflect on the condition of most of creation, you will find them characterized by this attribute and included in this state. And Allah knows best.

The second attribute: His words, ﴿and whom the life of this world has deceived﴾. This confirms the fifth interpretation we mentioned, as if He, the Exalted, were saying: they took their religion as play and amusement only because the life of this world deceived them. Because the love of the world took hold of their hearts, they turned away from the reality of religion and confined themselves to adorning outward appearances, in order to use them as a means to the trinkets of this world.

Having understood this, His words, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾, mean: turn away from them, do not care about their denial and mockery, and do not give them any weight in your sight. ﴿And remind by it﴾. They differed over what the pronoun in His words *bihi* ("by it") refers back to. It was said: "remind by the Qur'an." It was also said: He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾, and what is meant is the religion which they are obligated to adopt and believe in its validity. So His words, ﴿And remind by it﴾, mean: by that religion, because the pronoun must refer back to the nearest antecedent, and the religion is the nearest antecedent, so the pronoun must refer to it.

As for His words, ﴿lest a soul be delivered to ruin for what it has earned﴾, the author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: The root meaning of *ibsal* is prevention, and from it comes the expression *hadha 'alayka basl*, meaning "this is forbidden to you, prohibited." The *basil* (brave man) is so called because he refrains (*imtina'*) from his opponent, or because he is intensely stern-faced; one says *basara al-rajul* when a man's frowning intensifies, and when it increases they say *basala*. The *'abis* is one whose face is contracted.

Having understood this, we say: Ibn Abbas said: ﴿delivered to ruin for what it has earned﴾ means: it will be held as a pledge in Hell for what it earned in the world. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it will be handed over to destruction, that is, it will be prevented from its aims and forsaken. Qatada said: it will be imprisoned in Hell. And it is reported from Ibn Abbas that *tubsal* means "disgraced," and *ubsilu* means "they were disgraced." The meaning of the verse is: remind them with the Qur'an and with the requirements of the religion, out of fear that they will be confined in the fire of Hell because of their crimes, so that perhaps they will fear and thus guard themselves.

Then He, the Exalted, said: (*laysa laha*), that is, the soul has ﴿no protector and no intercessor besides Allah, and if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it.﴾ That is, even if it offers every ransom (*fida'*), and *'adl* means ransom, that ransom and that compensation will not be accepted from it. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The subject of *yu'khadh* ("be accepted") is not *'adl* ("ransom"), because *'adl* here is a verbal noun (masdar), so the act of taking cannot be attributed to it. As for His words, ﴿nor will any ransom be accepted from it﴾, it means "that by which ransom is paid," so it is correct to attribute the action to it. We say: the meaning of "taking" as "accepting" is attested, for He said: ﴿and takes the charities﴾ [al-Tawba: 104], that is, accepts them. When this is established, the "taking" here is understood as "accepting," and the question is resolved. And Allah knows best.

The purpose of this verse is to show that the ways of escape for that soul are closed off: there is no protector to ward off that feared harm, no intercessor who will intercede for it, and no ransom that will be accepted so that deliverance might be achieved through its acceptance. Even if the entire world were made as a ransom from the punishment of Allah, it would not benefit. When these three means of escape in this world are established, and it is established that they are of no use at all in the Hereafter, and it becomes clear that there is nothing there except *ibsal*, which is being held as a pledge, confined, and surrendered, then there is absolutely no repeller for it from the punishment of Allah the Exalted. And when a person conceives of the manner of this punishment, he almost trembles whenever he commits the disobedience of Allah the Exalted. Then He, the Exalted, explained what caused them to become held as pledges and confined, saying: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ This is the extreme in describing pain. And Allah knows best.

Having understood this, His words, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾, mean: turn away from them, do not care about their denial and mockery, and do not give them any weight in your sight. ﴿And remind by it﴾. They differed over what the pronoun in His words *bihi* ("by it") refers back to. It was said: "remind by the Qur'an." It was also said: He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾, and what is meant is the religion which they are obligated to adopt and believe in its validity. So His words, ﴿And remind by it﴾, mean: by that religion, because the pronoun must refer back to the nearest antecedent, and the religion is the nearest antecedent, so the pronoun must refer to it.

As for His words, ﴿lest a soul be delivered to ruin for what it has earned﴾, the author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: The root meaning of *ibsal* is prevention, and from it comes the expression *hadha 'alayka basl*, meaning "this is forbidden to you, prohibited." The *basil* (brave man) is so called because he refrains (*imtina'*) from his opponent, or because he is intensely stern-faced; one says *basara al-rajul* when a man's frowning intensifies, and when it increases they say *basala*. The *'abis* is one whose face is contracted.

Having understood this, we say: Ibn Abbas said: ﴿delivered to ruin for what it has earned﴾ means: it will be held as a pledge in Hell for what it earned in the world. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it will be handed over to destruction, that is, it will be prevented from its aims and forsaken. Qatada said: it will be imprisoned in Hell. And it is reported from Ibn Abbas that *tubsal* means "disgraced," and *ubsilu* means "they were disgraced." The meaning of the verse is: remind them with the Qur'an and with the requirements of the religion, out of fear that they will be confined in the fire of Hell because of their crimes, so that perhaps they will fear and thus guard themselves.

Then He, the Exalted, said: (*laysa laha*), that is, the soul has ﴿no protector and no intercessor besides Allah, and if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it.﴾ That is, even if it offers every ransom (*fida'*), and *'adl* means ransom, that ransom and that compensation will not be accepted from it. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The subject of *yu'khadh* ("be accepted") is not *'adl* ("ransom"), because *'adl* here is a verbal noun (masdar), so the act of taking cannot be attributed to it. As for His words, ﴿nor will any ransom be accepted from it﴾, it means "that by which ransom is paid," so it is correct to attribute the action to it. We say: the meaning of "taking" as "accepting" is attested, for He said: ﴿and takes the charities﴾ [al-Tawba: 104], that is, accepts them. When this is established, the "taking" here is understood as "accepting," and the question is resolved. And Allah knows best.

The purpose of this verse is to show that the ways of escape for that soul are closed off: there is no protector to ward off that feared harm, no intercessor who will intercede for it, and no ransom that will be accepted so that deliverance might be achieved through its acceptance. Even if the entire world were made as a ransom from the punishment of Allah, it would not benefit. When these three means of escape in this world are established, and it is established that they are of no use at all in the Hereafter, and it becomes clear that there is nothing there except *ibsal*, which is being held as a pledge, confined, and surrendered, then there is absolutely no repeller for it from the punishment of Allah the Exalted. And when a person conceives of the manner of this punishment, he almost trembles whenever he commits the disobedience of Allah the Exalted. Then He, the Exalted, explained what caused them to become held as pledges and confined, saying: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ This is the extreme in describing pain. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Shall we call upon other than Allah that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered, who has companions calling him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us.'" Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And that you establish prayer and fear Him, and He it is to whom you will be gathered.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is the refutation of the idol-worshippers, and it reinforces His statement before it: ﴿Say: "I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides Allah."﴾ [al-An'am: 56]. So He said: ﴿Say: "Shall we call upon other than Allah?"﴾, meaning: shall we worship, besides Allah, the One who benefits and harms, that which has no power to benefit us or to harm us, and be turned back on our heels, returning to polytheism after Allah has rescued us from it and guided us to Islam? It is said of everyone who turns away from the truth to falsehood that he has gone backward, and that he returned on his heels, and returned backward (al-qahqara). The reason for this is that the original state of a human being is ignorance, and then when he progresses and matures, knowledge is attained by him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾ [al-Nahl: 78]. So when one returns from knowledge to ignorance once again, it is as though he has returned to the first state. For this reason it is said: "So-and-so was turned back on his heels."

* * *

As for His statement: ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth﴾, know that He, the Exalted, described this person with three types of attributes:

The first attribute: His statement: ﴿whom the devils have enticed﴾. Concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: Hamzah recited ﴿istahwahu﴾ with an inclined alif and in the masculine form, while the rest recited it with the feminine ta'; because the plural may be treated as masculine in terms of the meaning of plurality, and may be treated as feminine in terms of the meaning of a group.

The second issue: They differed concerning the derivation of ﴿istahwathu﴾, on two views:

The first view: that it is derived from hawiy (falling) in the earth, which is descending from a high place into a low, deep depression at the bottom of the earth. Allah the Exalted therefore likened the state of this one who has strayed to it, in His statement: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 31]. And there is no doubt that the state of this person, when he falls from a high place into a dark, deep depression, is one of extreme agitation, weakness and bewilderment.

The second view: that it is derived from following desire and inclination, for whoever is like this may well reach the extreme of confusion. The first view is preferable, because it is more complete in indicating bewilderment and weakness.

The second attribute: His statement: ﴿bewildered (hayran)﴾. Al-Asma'i said: one says hara yahiru hayratan and hayaran, and al-Farra' added hayaranan and hayrurah. The meaning of hayrah is hesitation in a matter such that one cannot find its way out. From this one says: "The water is bewildered in the cloud," meaning it wanders about, and "the garden became bewildered with water" when it became full, so the water wandered within it. Know that this parable is of the utmost beauty, because the one who falls from a high place into a deep depression falls while spinning around himself, since a stone, as it descends from above to below, descends in a spiral; and this necessitates complete wandering and bewilderment. Also, at the time of his descent he does not know whether he will fall upon a place where his affliction will increase because of his falling upon it or decrease. So when you consider the totality of these states, you will know that you will not find a better or more complete example of the bewildered, wandering, fearful one than this example.

The third attribute: His statement: ﴿He has companions calling him to guidance: "Come to us."﴾ They said: this verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, for he used to call his father to disbelief, while his father used to call him to faith and command him to return from the path of ignorance to guidance, and from the darkness of disbelief to the light of faith. It was also said: the meaning is that this misguided disbeliever has companions who call him to that misguidance and name it guidance; but this is far-fetched. The correct view is the first.

Page 26

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance"﴾, meaning: it is the complete, beneficial, noble guidance, just as when you say: "Zayd's knowledge is (true) knowledge, and 'Amr's kingdom is (true) kingdom," its meaning is what we have mentioned of establishing the matter of perfection and nobility.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾. Know that His statement: ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the (true) guidance﴾ encompasses all categories of commanded acts and the avoidance of all prohibited acts. The explanation of this statement is that whatever Allah's command relates to is either an act or an abstention.

As for the first category: it is either of the domain of deeds of the heart, or of the domain of deeds of the limbs. The chief of the deeds of the heart is faith in Allah and submission to Him, and the chief of the deeds of the limbs is prayer. As for what belongs to the domain of abstentions, it is taqwa, which is an expression for guarding oneself against everything that is not fitting. When Allah, glorified is He, first clarified that the beneficial guidance is the guidance of Allah, He followed that general statement with mention of its noblest categories in order: namely Islam, which is the chief of the spiritual acts of obedience; prayer, which is the chief of the bodily acts of obedience; and taqwa, which is the head of the domain of abstentions and of guarding against everything unseemly. Then He explained the benefits of these deeds, saying: ﴿and He it is to whom you will be gathered﴾, meaning that the benefits of these deeds appear only on the Day of Gathering, Resurrection and the Hereafter.

If it is asked: how is the conjunction of His statement ﴿and that establish prayer﴾ to His statement ﴿and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ appropriate?

We say: al-Zajjaj mentioned two possibilities concerning it:

The first: that the implied meaning is: "We have been commanded, so it was said to us: submit to the Lord of the worlds, and establish prayer."

If it is asked: granted that what you have mentioned is the meaning, what is the wisdom in turning away from this apparent expression and the structure agreeable to reason, to that expression whose meaning reason cannot arrive at except through interpretation?

We say: this is because the disbeliever, so long as he persists in his disbelief, is like an absent stranger, so he is addressed with the address of absent persons, and it is said to him: ﴿and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾. When he submits, believes and enters into faith, he becomes like a near and present one, so he is addressed with the address of those present, and it is said to him: ﴿and that you establish prayer and fear Him, and He it is to whom you will be gathered﴾. The purpose of mentioning these two kinds of address is to draw attention to the difference between the states of disbelief and faith; and its explanation is that the disbeliever is distant and absent, while the believer is near and present. And Allah knows best.

[Page 27]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth with truth, and the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. And His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained in the preceding verses the corruption of the way of those who worship idols, He mentioned here what indicates that there is no deity except God alone. This is this verse, and in it He mentioned many kinds of proofs.

The first of them is His saying: ﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth with truth.﴾ As for His being the Creator of the heavens and the earth, we have explained that in His saying: ﴿Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Anʿam: 1]. As for His having created them with truth, it is similar to His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat Al ʿImran: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Al ʿImran: 191], and His saying: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Anbiya': 16], and ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39]. And concerning it there are two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the opinion of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni scholars), is that He, may He be exalted, is the owner of all created things, the owner of all beings, and the owner's disposal of his property is good and correct absolutely. Therefore that disposal is good absolutely and true absolutely.

The second opinion, which is the opinion of the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites), is that the meaning of His being true is that He acts in accordance with the interests of the legally responsible persons (mukallafin) and corresponds to their benefits. The Qadi said: "This verse includes that He created the legally responsible person first, so that he can benefit from the creation of the heavens and the earth. The philosophers of Islam (Hukama' al-Islam) have another method in this regard, which is to say: He deposited in these great bodies powers and properties, by means of which effects and movements proceed from them that correspond to the interests and benefits of this world."

The second of them is His saying: ﴿and the day He says, "Be," and it is.﴾ Regarding the interpretation of this verse there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is "the estimation" (al-taqdir): "He is the One who created the heavens and the earth and created the day He says, 'Be,' and it is." What is meant by this day is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that He, may He be exalted, is the Creator of this world and of everything in it, of the spheres, the natures and the elements, and the Creator of the Day of Resurrection and of the resurrection, and of returning the spirits to the bodies in the manner of "Be, and it is."

The second interpretation: we say that His saying "the truth" (al-haqq) is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿and the day He says, "Be," and it is﴾ is an adverbial phrase (zarf) indicating the predicate. The estimation is: "His saying 'the truth' is occurring, ﴿and the day He says, 'Be,' and it is,﴾" like your saying: "Fighting is on Friday," meaning: "fighting occurs on Friday." What is meant by His saying being true on that day is that He, glory be to Him, does not decree except with truth and sincerity, because His decrees are free from injustice and futility.

The third of them is His saying: ﴿And His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown.﴾ His saying ﴿And His is the dominion﴾ indicates restriction (al-hasr), and the meaning is that there is no sovereign on the day the Trumpet is blown except the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted. Thus what is meant by the second statement is the affirmation of the true command, free from futility and falsehood, and what is meant by this statement is the affirmation of complete and perfect power, which has no repeller and no opponent.

If someone says: "God's word is true at every time, and His power is complete at every time. So what is the benefit of specifying this day with these two attributes?"

We say: Because this day is the day on which no one benefits or harms, and so the matter is as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And the matter on that day belongs to God﴾ [al-Infitar: 19]. For this reason this specification is fitting.

The fourth of them is His saying: ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed,﴾ its estimation being: "and He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed."

Know that we have mentioned in this complete book that He, glory be to Him, did not mention the conditions of resurrection on the Day of Judgment except that He affirmed in it two principles:

One of them: that He is able over all possibilities.

The second: that He is knowing of all known things. For if He were not able over all possibilities, He would not be able to resurrect, gather, or return the spirits to the bodies. And if He were not knowing of all particulars, that would also not be valid from Him, because the obedient might be confused with the disobedient, the believer with the disbeliever, and the truthful (siddiq) with the heretic (zindiq), so the original purpose of resurrection and the Day of Judgment would not be achieved. But when the existence of these two attributes is established by proof, the purpose and the aim are complete. So His saying ﴿And His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ indicates perfect power, and His saying ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ indicates perfect knowledge. Therefore it necessarily follows from the combination of the two that His word is true, that His judgment is truthful, and that His rulings are free from injustice, futility and falsehood.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ What is meant by His being Wise is that He is correct in His actions, and by His being All-Aware is that He knows their realities without confusion and without ambiguity. And God knows best.

The second issue: We have mentioned in many parts of this book that what is meant by His saying ﴿Be, and it is﴾ is not an address or a command, because if that command were to something non-existent, it would be impossible, and if it were to something existent, it would be a command that the existent become existent, which is impossible. Rather, what is meant by it is alerting to the effectiveness of His power and will in bringing beings into existence and originating existing things.

The third issue: His saying ﴿the day the Trumpet is blown.﴾ There is no doubt that what is meant by it is the Day of Gathering, and there is no doubt among the people of Islam that God, glory be to Him, created a horn into which an angel from among the angels blows, and that horn is called the Trumpet (al-Sur), as God, may He be exalted, mentioned this meaning in several places in the Noble Book. However, they differed about what is meant by "the Trumpet" in this verse, in two opinions:

The first opinion: that what is meant is that horn into which one blows, and its description is mentioned in the rest of the surahs.

The second opinion: that al-Sur is the plural of ṣūrah (form), and blowing into the forms (al-nafkh fi al-ṣuwar) is an expression for blowing into the forms of the dead. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-Ṣuwar is the plural of ṣūrah, like ṣawf and ṣawfah (wool and a piece of wool). Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: Abu al-Fadl al-ʿArudi informed me, from al-Azhari, from al-Mundhiri, from Abu al-Haytham, who said: "A group claimed that al-Ṣuwar is the plural of al-ṣūrah, just as al-ṣawf is the plural of al-ṣawfah and al-thum is the plural of al-thumah (garlic). This was narrated from Abu ʿUbayda." Abu al-Haytham said: "This is a gross error, because God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and He formed you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir: 64], and He said: ﴿and the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99]. So whoever reads (wa-nufikha fi al-suwar) and reads (faʾahsana suwarakum) has invented a lie and altered the Book of God. Abu ʿUbayda was a man of reports and rarities, and he had no knowledge of grammar." Al-Farra' said: "Every plural in the form of the masculine singular whose plural preceded its singular takes the feminine singular marker (ha') added to it. Examples of this category are ṣawf, wabar, shaʿr, quṭn and ʿushb: each of these nouns is a name for its whole genus, and when its single unit is singled out, a ha' is added to it, because the plural of this category preceded its singular. If ṣawfah had preceded ṣawf, they would have said ṣawfah and ṣawaf, and busrah and busar, just as they said ghurfah and ghuraf, and zulfah and zulaf. As for al-ṣūr, meaning the horn, it is singular, and it is not permissible to say its singular is ṣūrah. Rather, the form of a human is pluralized as ṣuwar, because its singular preceded its plural." Al-Azhari said: "Abu al-Haytham has spoken well in this statement, and in my view nothing other than what he held is permissible." I say: What strengthens this view is that if the meaning were the breathing of the spirit into those forms, God would have attributed that blowing to Himself, because God attributes the breathing of spirits into forms to Himself, as He said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29], and He said: ﴿So We breathed into it of Our spirit﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], and He said: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. As for blowing the Trumpet in the sense of blowing into the horn, He, may He be exalted, does not attribute it to Himself, as He said: ﴿When the horn is sounded﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 8], and He said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom God wills. Then it is blown again, and at once they are standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. This is the complete statement on this discussion, and God knows best what is correct.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 74 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error."﴾

There are several issues in this verse.

The First Issue: Know that He, glorified is He, often argues against the polytheists of the Arabs by citing the circumstances of Abraham, peace be upon him. This is because all the sects and religions acknowledge his virtue. The polytheists acknowledged his virtue and affirmed that they were among his descendants. The Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims all venerate him and recognize the greatness of his rank. Therefore, God mentioned the account of his condition in the context of arguing against the polytheists.

Know that this great station, namely the acknowledgment by most people of knowledge of his virtue and the loftiness of his rank, has not been granted to anyone as it has been granted to the Friend (Khalil) [of God], peace be upon him. The reason is that a covenant (mu'ahada) took place between the Lord and the servant, as He said: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:40]. Abraham fulfilled the covenant of servanthood, and God bore witness to this, sometimes in summary and sometimes in detail.

As for the summary, it is in two verses:
The first is His saying: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:124]. This is God's testimony that he completed the covenant of servanthood.
The second is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:131].

As for the detail: he, peace be upon him, disputed in establishing monotheism and refuting the notion of partners and rivals in many situations.

The first situation in this regard is his debate with his father, when he said to him: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and cannot avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam 19:42].

The second situation is his debate with his people, which is His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ [Al-An'am 6:76].

The third situation is his debate with the king of his time, when he said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:258].

The fourth situation is his debate with the disbelievers through action, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:58]. Then the people said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:68]. Then, after this incident, he, peace be upon him, offered his son [for sacrifice], saying: ﴿Indeed, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾ [Al-Saffat 37:102]. At this point it became established that Abraham, peace be upon him, was among the young men (fityan), because he surrendered his heart to knowledge, his tongue to proof, his body to the fire, his son to the sacrifice, and his wealth to the guests.

Then he, peace be upon him, asked his Lord, saying: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [Al-Shu'ara' 26:84]. Thus, by the generosity of God, exalted is He, it was necessary that He answer his supplication and fulfil his request in this matter. Therefore, He answered his supplication and accepted his call, and made him acceptable to all the sects and communities until the Day of Resurrection. Since the Arabs acknowledged his virtue, God made his debate with his people a proof against the polytheists of the Arabs.

The Second Issue: Know that there is no one in the world who affirms for God a partner equal to Him in necessary existence, power, knowledge, and wisdom. However, the Dualists (Thanawiyya) affirm two gods: one of them is wise and does good, and the other is foolish and does evil. As for occupying oneself with the worship of other than God, the adherents of this are many. Among them are the worshippers of the stars, who are of two groups. Among them are those who say: He, glorified is He, created these stars and delegated the management of this lower world to them. So these stars are the governors of this world. They said: It is therefore incumbent upon us to worship these stars. Moreover, these spheres and stars worship God and obey Him. Among them are extremist people who deny the Creator and say: These spheres and stars are bodies whose existence is necessary in themselves, and non-existence and annihilation are impossible for them, and they are the ones who govern the affairs of this lower world. These are the pure Dahriyya (materialists who attribute everything to time). Among those who worship other than God are the Christians, who worship the Messiah. Among them also are the worshippers of idols.

Know that there is a discussion here that cannot be avoided, namely that there is no religion older than the religion of the idol-worshippers. The evidence for this is that the oldest prophets whose histories have reached us in detail is Noah, peace be upon him, and he came only to refute the idol-worshippers, as God said, relating about his people that they said: ﴿Do not leave your gods, nor leave Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr﴾ [Nuh 71:23]. This indicates that the religion of the idol-worshippers already existed before Noah, peace be upon him. That religion has persisted until this time, for most of the inhabitants of the far regions of the earth still continue upon this religion. A doctrine of this kind cannot be self-evidently false to the intellect. But the knowledge that this stone carved at this moment is not the one that created me and created the heavens and the earth is a necessary knowledge, and a necessary knowledge cannot be denied by a large multitude in agreement. Thus it becomes clear that the religion of the idol-worshippers is not that the idol is the creator of the heavens and the earth. Rather, they must have an interpretation of it, and the scholars have mentioned many aspects of it. We have discussed this topic at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, and there is no harm in repeating it here to increase the benefits.

The first interpretation, which is the strongest, is that people observed that the changes in the conditions of this lower world are linked to the changes in the conditions of the stars. For according to the nearness and distance of the sun from the zenith, the four seasons occur, and because of the occurrence of the four seasons, the various conditions in this world arise. Then people observed the conditions of the rest of the stars and believed that good fortunes and misfortunes are connected with the manner in which they occur in the ascendants (tawali') of people under various conditions. When they believed this, it prevailed upon the assumptions of most creatures that the origin of the occurrence of events in this world is the celestial connections and the astral correspondences. When they believed this, they exaggerated in venerating them. Then among them, some believed that they are necessary in their own essence, and among them, some believed that they are created by the Supreme God, but they said: Although they are created by the Supreme God, they are the ones who govern the conditions of this world. These are the ones who affirmed intermediaries between the Supreme God and the conditions of this world. Under both assumptions, these people occupied themselves with worshipping and venerating them. Then, when they saw that these stars often disappear from sight for most of the time, they made for each star an idol from the substance attributed to it. They made the idol of the sun from gold and adorned it with the stones attributed to the sun, which are the ruby and the diamond. They made the idol of the moon from silver, and so on by analogy. Then they devoted themselves to the worship of these idols, and their purpose in worshipping these idols was the worship of those stars and seeking nearness to them. At this point of the discussion it becomes clear that the primary intention in worshipping these idols is the worship of the stars.

As for the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them, they have here two stations:
One of them is establishing proofs that these stars have absolutely no influence on the conditions of this world, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:54], after having shown that the stars are subjugated.
The second is that even if it is assumed that they do something and effects proceed from them upon this world, the signs of origination (huduth) are present in them, and therefore it is necessary that they are created. And occupying oneself with the worship of the origin is more fitting than occupying oneself with the worship of the branch.

The evidence that the essence of the religion of the idol-worshippers is what we have mentioned is that when He related about the Friend (Khalil), may the blessings of God be upon him, that he said to his father Azar: "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error," he thereby issued a ruling that the worship of idols is ignorance. Then, when he proceeded to mention the proof, he established proof that the stars, the moon, and the sun are not fit for any of them to be divine. This indicates that the religion of the idol-worshippers essentially reverts to the claim that these stars are divine, otherwise this verse would become contradictory and incoherent. When you know this, it becomes clear that there is no way to refute the doctrine of worshipping idols except by refuting that the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars are gods governing this world.

The Second Aspect: Concerning the explanation of the true doctrine of the idol-worshippers, what Abu Ma'shar Ja'far ibn Muhammad, the astrologer of Balkh, may God have mercy on him, mentioned in some of his books: he said that many people of China and India affirmed God and the angels, but they believed that He, exalted is He, is a body and has a form, like the most beautiful of forms, and that the angels also have beautiful forms, except that they are all concealed from us by the heavens. Therefore, they made images and statues of pleasing appearance, beautiful to look at and in form. They would make one image of extreme beauty and say: it is the temple (haykal) of God. And another image below the first, and they would make it in the likeness of the angels. Then they would persist in worshipping them, intending by that worship to seek nearness to God and to the angels. If what Abu Ma'shar mentioned is correct, then the cause of worshipping idols is the belief that God is a body and in a place.

The Third Aspect on this topic: These people believe that God, exalted is He, delegated the management of each of the regions to a specific angel. He also delegated the management of each part of the divisions of the world's kingdom to a specific celestial spirit. So they say: the governor of the seas is one angel, the governor of the mountains is another angel, the governor of the clouds and rains is an angel, the governor of provisions is an angel, and the governor of wars and battles is another angel. When they believed this, they made for each of those angels a specific idol and a specific temple, and they asked from each idol what befits that celestial spirit of effects and management. The people have other interpretations besides these three, which we mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, but we shall suffice here with this amount of explanation. And God knows best.

* * *

The Third Issue: The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the name of Abraham's father is Azar. Some said: his name is Tarah. Al-Zajjaj said: there is no disagreement among the genealogists that his name is Tarah. Some of the heretics (mulhida) took this as a criticism of the Qur'an and said: this genealogy is an error and is not correct. The scholars have two positions here:

The first position: The name of Abraham's father, peace be upon him, is Azar. As for their statement that the genealogists agreed that his name was Tarah, we say this is weak, because that consensus arose only because some of them follow others in taking it on authority (taqlid), and ultimately that consensus returns to the statement of one or two, such as Wahb, Ka'b, and others. Perhaps they relied on what they found from the reports of the Jews and Christians, and there is no weight given to that in the face of the explicit statement of the Qur'an.

The second position: Suppose that his name was Tarah. Then we have here several aspects:

The first aspect: Perhaps Abraham's father was called by both names. It may be said that his original name was Azar and Tarah was made his epithet (laqab), so this epithet became famous and the name became obscure. God mentioned him by the name. It is also possible that the opposite is true, namely that Tarah was his original name and Azar was a dominant epithet. God therefore mentioned him by this dominant epithet.

The second aspect: The word Azar may be a particular descriptive term in their language. It was said that Azar is a term of blame in their language, meaning "the one who errs," as if it were said: "when Abraham said to his erring father," as if he reproached him for his deviation, his disbelief, and his departure from the truth. It was also said that Azar means "the old, decrepit man" in Khwarazmian, and this is also an original Persian word.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 74 (part 2 of 2):

Know that these two opinions may be adopted only by someone who holds that the Qur'an may contain a few words that are not from the language of the Arabs.

The third opinion: Azar was the name of an idol that Abraham's father worshipped. God named him with this name for two reasons:

The first: he (the father) made himself devoted exclusively to its worship. Whoever is extremely devoted to someone may give the name of the beloved to the lover. God the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day We shall summon every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra': 71].

The second: the intended meaning is "the worshipper of Azar," so the first term (the idol's name) was omitted and the second term (the genitive complement) was put in its place.

The fourth opinion: Abraham's father, peace be upon him, was Tarah, and Azar was his paternal uncle. The word "father" (ab) may be applied to an uncle, as God the Exalted related about the sons of Jacob that they said: ﴿We shall worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. It is known that Ishmael was the paternal uncle of Jacob, yet they applied the word "father" to him. So it is the same here.

Know that these far-fetched interpretations would be necessary only if there were a clear proof that Abraham's father was not named Azar. No such proof exists at all. So what need compels us to these interpretations? The strong evidence that the matter is as the apparent meaning of this verse indicates is that the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists were most eager to deny the Messenger (peace be upon him) and to show their hatred toward him. Had this lineage been false, it would have been customary for them to remain silent about refuting him. Since they did not refute him, we know that this lineage is correct. And God knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: The Shi'ah said that none of the Messenger's fathers and forefathers (peace be upon him) was a disbeliever. They rejected the claim that Abraham's father was a disbeliever, and they mentioned that Azar was Abraham's paternal uncle and not his father. They argued for their view with several arguments:

The first argument: The fathers of the prophets were not disbelievers. Several points indicate this:

Among them is God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Who sees you when you stand up, and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 218-219].

It has been said that its meaning is that he was transferring his spirit from one prostrating person to another. With this interpretation, the verse indicates that all of Muhammad's (peace be upon him) fathers were Muslims. In that case it is necessary to be certain that Abraham's father (peace be upon him) was a Muslim.

If it is said: God's saying ﴿and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 219] may have other meanings:

The first: when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated, the Messenger (ﷺ) went around the houses of the Companions that night to see what they were doing, because of his great eagerness for the acts of obedience that appeared from them. He found their houses like beehives, because of the many voices he heard of their recitation, glorification and declaration of God's oneness. So what is meant by God's saying ﴿and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 219] is his (ﷺ) going around among those who prostrate that night.

The second: The intended meaning is that he (peace be upon him) used to lead the congregation in prayer, so his "movement among those who prostrate" means his being among them and mixing with them during standing, bowing and prostration.

The third: The intended meaning is that your condition is not hidden from God, whenever you stand and move about with those who prostrate, occupied with the affairs of religion.

The fourth: The intended meaning is the movement of his gaze over those who pray behind him. The evidence for this is his (peace be upon him) saying: "Complete the bowing and the prostration, for I see you from behind my back." So these four meanings are among what the apparent wording of the verse may bear, and so your objection falls.

The reply: The wording of the verse is open to all of them, so there is no reason to interpret the verse as one of them rather than the rest. Therefore we must interpret it as including all of them, and in that case the purpose is achieved. Also among what indicates that none of Muhammad's (peace be upon him) fathers was an idolater is his (peace be upon him) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of the pure men to the wombs of the pure women." And God the Exalted said: ﴿The polytheists are only impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. This requires that it be said that none of his forefathers was an idolater.

Given this, we say: it has been established by what we mentioned that Abraham's father (peace be upon him) was not a polytheist, and it has been established that Azar was a polytheist. Therefore it is necessary to be certain that Abraham's father was a person other than Azar.

The second argument, that Azar was not Abraham's father (peace be upon him): This verse indicates that Abraham (peace be upon him) addressed Azar with harshness and roughness. Addressing one's father with roughness is not permissible, and this indicates that Azar was not Abraham's father. We say that Abraham addressed Azar with harshness and roughness in this verse for two reasons:

The first: It has been read (wa-idh qala Ibrahimu li-abihi Azaru) with the ending of "Azaru" in the nominative (ḍamma), and this is to be understood as a vocative address. Calling one's father by his proper name is among the greatest kinds of rudeness.

The second: He said to Azar: ﴿Indeed I see you and your people in clear error﴾ [al-An'am: 74]. This is among the greatest kinds of rudeness and insult. So it is established that he (peace be upon him) addressed Azar with rudeness. We say that addressing one's father with rudeness is not permissible for several reasons:

The first: God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. This is general with regard to both a disbelieving father and a believing father. He also said: ﴿Do not say to them "Uff," nor scold them﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. This too is general.

The second: When God the Exalted sent Moses (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh, He commanded him to be gentle with him, saying: ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. The reason for this is that such conduct would be a way of safeguarding the right of Pharaoh's upbringing. Here, then, the father is more deserving of gentleness.

The third: Calling with gentleness has greater effect on the heart, whereas harshness produces aversion and distance from acceptance. For this reason God the Exalted said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. So how could such roughness befit Abraham (peace be upon him) in calling his father?

The fourth: God the Exalted related about Abraham (peace be upon him) his forbearance, saying: ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, penitent﴾ [Hud: 75]. How could such rudeness befit a forbearing man toward his father?

By these arguments it is established that Azar was not Abraham's father (peace be upon him), but rather his paternal uncle. As for his father, he was Tarah. The word "father" may be applied to an uncle, as we mentioned, that the sons of Jacob called Ishmael "father" because he was Jacob's father, although he was actually his paternal uncle. And he (peace be upon him) said: "Return my father to me," meaning the uncle al-Abbas.

Also, it is possible that Azar was the father of Abraham's mother (peace be upon him), and this too may be called "father." The evidence for this is God's saying: ﴿And of his descendants, David and Solomon﴾ [al-An'am: 84], down to His saying "and Jesus," where Jesus is counted among Abraham's descendants, even though Abraham (peace be upon him) was Jesus's grandfather through the mother.

As for our companions (the Sunni scholars), they claim that the father of the Messenger of God was a disbeliever, and they mention that the explicit text of the Book in this verse indicates that Azar was a disbeliever and was Abraham's father (peace be upon him). Also, God the Exalted's saying: ﴿The plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disowned him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114] indicates our view. As for God's saying ﴿and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 219], we said that this verse can bear all the other meanings. As for the claim that the verse is to be interpreted as including all of them, we say: this is impossible, because it is not permissible to apply a homonymous (mushtarak) word to all of its meanings, and it is also not permissible to apply a word to both its literal and its figurative meaning at once. As for his (peace be upon him) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of the pure men to the wombs of the pure women," this is to be understood as meaning that nothing illegitimate (siffah) ever occurred in his lineage. As for the claim that harshness toward a father does not befit Abraham (peace be upon him), we say: perhaps he persisted in his disbelief, and because of his persistence he deserved that harshness. And God knows best.

The fifth issue: "Azar" has been read in the accusative (naṣb), in which case it is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "li-abihi" ("to his father"), and in the nominative (ḍamm), as a vocative. Someone asked me: "Azar has been read with these two readings. But as for God's saying ﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron﴾ [al-A'raf: 142], "Aaron" has been read in the accusative, and it has never been read in the nominative at all. So what is the difference?" I said: The reading with the nominative is to be understood as a vocative, and calling by the name is a form of belittling the one addressed. That is suitable to the story of Abraham (peace be upon him), because he was persistent in his disbelief, so it was fitting to address him with harshness to deter him from that ugly act. As for the story of Moses (peace be upon him), Moses (peace be upon him) was appointing Aaron as his deputy over his people, so belittling him was not fitting in that situation. Therefore, it is indeed the case that the reading with the nominative was not permissible there.

The sixth issue: Scholars differ over the interpretation of the word "ilah" (god). The most correct view is that it means "the one worshipped." This verse supports this view, because they (the idolaters) attributed to the idols only that they were worshipped. For this reason Abraham said to his father: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am: 74], and this indicates that the interpretation of the word "ilah" is "the one worshipped."

The seventh issue: Abraham's speech (peace be upon him) in this verse contains a mention of the rational proof against the corruption of the view of the idol-worshippers, in two ways:

The first: His saying ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ indicates that they used to hold that there are many gods. But the view that there are many gods is false by the rational proof understood from God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods besides God, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22].

The second: If these idols had the power to bring about benefit and harm, one idol would have been sufficient. Since one was not sufficient, this indicates that, even if they are many, there is no benefit at all in them.

The eighth issue: Some scholars have used this verse to argue that the obligation to know God the Exalted and the obligation to occupy oneself with thanking Him are known by reason and not by revelation. They said: Because Abraham (peace be upon him) judged them to be in error, and had there not been a rational obligation, he would not have judged them to be in error, since that doctrine was prior to the call of Abraham. But one may reply: it was error by the ruling of the revealed law of the prophets who came before Abraham (peace be upon him).

[Page 35]

**His words, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among those with certainty.﴾**

There are several issues here.

**First issue:** The *kaf* in *kadhalika* ("thus") is for comparison (tashbih). *Dhalika* is a demonstrative referring to something absent that has already been mentioned. What was mentioned earlier is that he (peace be upon him) denounced the worship of idols, in his words: ﴿Indeed, I see you and your people in clear error.﴾ The meaning is: Just as We showed him the ugliness of idol-worship, so We show him the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Here there is a subtle rational point. The light of God's majesty, exalted is He, shines constantly, never ceasing or disappearing at all. Human spirits are deprived of those lights only because of a veil, and that veil is nothing but preoccupation with other than God, exalted is He. When this is so, the manifestation (tajalli) occurs in proportion to the removal of that veil. Therefore Abraham's words, peace be upon him: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ are a sign of condemning preoccupation with the worship of other than God, exalted is He, because everything other than God is a veil from God, exalted is He. When that veil was removed, the dominion of the heavens was fully manifested to him. So His words, ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens﴾ mean: after the removal of preoccupation with other than God, there came to him the light of the manifestation of God's majesty, exalted is He. Thus the word "thus" (*kadhalika*) was the source of this noble, spiritual benefit.

**Second issue:** One may say: this showing had already taken place in the earlier time, so it would have been better to say, "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth." Why did it deviate from this wording to His words, ﴿And thus do We show﴾?

We say: The answer to this has several aspects.

The first: The sense of the verse is, "And thus We were showing Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," so this is in the manner of narrating about the past. The meaning is that when He, exalted is He, related about him that he spoke harshly to his father in zeal for the true religion, it was as if it were said: How did Abraham reach this great level in the strength of his religion? It was answered that We had been showing him the dominion of the heavens and the earth from the time of his childhood, so that he would become among those with certainty at the time of his maturity.

The second aspect of the answer, which is higher and more noble than what came before, is this: We say that the purpose of God's showing Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth is not merely that Abraham should see this dominion. Rather, the purpose is that he should see it and thereby be led (*yatawassal*) to knowledge of God's majesty, His holiness, His exaltation, and His greatness. It is known that God's creatures, although finite in their essences and attributes, the aspects of their indications (*dalalat*) upon the essences and attributes are infinite. I heard our teacher, the Imam, the father, Umar Diya' al-Din, may God have mercy on him, say: I heard the Shaykh Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari say: I heard Imam al-Haramayn say: The known things of God, exalted is He, are infinite, and His knowledge of each one of those known things is also infinite. This is because the indivisible substance (*al-jawhar al-fard*) can be located in spaces without end, one after another, and can be described by attributes without end, one after another. All those hypothetical states indicate the wisdom and power of God, exalted is He, as well. If the indivisible substance and the part that cannot be divided are like this, how then is it with the whole dominion of God, exalted is He? Thus it is established that the indication of God's sovereignty and dominion upon the qualities of His majesty and the marks of His greatness and might is infinite. And the acquisition in the minds of creatures of infinite known things all at once is impossible. Therefore there is no way to attain those knowledges except that some of them occur after others, without end and without a final limit in the future. For this reason, God knows best, He did not say, "And thus We showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth," but rather said: ﴿And thus do We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ This is what is meant by the saying of the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqun*): The journey *to* God has an end, but the journey *in* God has no end. And God knows best.

* * *

**Third issue:** *Malakut* means *mulk* (dominion, sovereignty), and the *ta'* is for intensification, like *rahabut* from *rahba* (dread) and *raghabut* from *raghba* (desire).

Know that concerning the explanation of this showing there are two opinions.

The first: God showed him the dominion with the eye. They said: God split the heavens for him until he saw the Throne and the Footstool, and up to where the upper limit of the physical world ends. He split the earth for him until it reached the other surface of the physical world. He saw what is in the heavens of wonders and marvels, and he saw what is in the depths of the earth of wonders and marvels. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: When Abraham was taken by night (*usriya*) to the heaven, and he saw what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, he saw a servant committing an abomination, so he invoked destruction upon him and upon another. God, exalted is He, said to him: "Desist from My servants. They are in one of two states: either I will make from among them a good offspring, or they will repent and I will forgive them, or the Fire is behind them."

The Qadi (al-Qadi) criticized this report on several grounds.

The first: The people of the heaven are the near angels (*al-malaikat al-muqarrabun*), and they do not disobey God. So it is not fitting to say that when he was raised to the heaven he saw a servant committing an abomination.

The second: The prophets do not invoke the destruction of a sinner except by the command of God, exalted is He. And if God permits it, it is not possible that He would prevent the granting of his supplication.

The third: That supplication is either correct or mistaken. If it was correct, why did He reject it the second time? And if it was mistaken, why did He accept it the first time? Then he said: When solitary reports (*akhbar al-ahad*) come in contradiction to the proofs of reason, it is obligatory to suspend judgment about them.

The second opinion: This showing was by the eye of insight (*basira*) and reason, not by the outward sight and the outward sense. Those who held this view argued with several proofs.

The first proof: The dominion of the heavens is an expression for the sovereignty of the heaven, and sovereignty is an expression for power, and God's power is not seen; it is known only by reason. This is a decisive statement, unless it is said that what is meant by the dominion of the heavens and the earth is the very heavens and earth themselves. But on this assumption, the word *malakut* is wasted and no benefit is derived from it.

The second proof: He, exalted is He, mentioned this showing at the beginning of the verse in summary form, namely His words, ﴿And thus do We show Abraham﴾ [al-Anʿam: 75], then explained it afterward by His words, ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star﴾ [al-Anʿam: 76]. So the mention of this argument came as an explanation and elaboration of that showing. Therefore it is necessary to say that this showing was an expression for this argument.

The third proof: He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾ [al-Anʿam: 83]. A sight with the eye does not become an argument against his people, because they were absent from it and they used to deny Abraham concerning it. They could not have accepted Abraham's claim in that matter except by a separate proof and a manifest miracle. The argument which Abraham presented against his people was the reasoning from the stars, in the way the Qur'an articulated. For those proofs were manifest to them just as they were manifest to Abraham.

The fourth proof: The showing of the whole world yields necessary knowledge (*al-ʿilm al-darury*) that the world has a god, powerful over all possible things. Such a state does not, by its occurrence in a person, bring about deserving praise and honor. Do you not see that the disbelievers in the Hereafter know God by necessity, and in that knowledge they have no praise and no reward? But reasoning from the attributes of creatures to the existence of the Creator, His power and His wisdom, that is what yields praise and honor.

The fifth proof: Just as He, exalted is He, said concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And thus do We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, so He said concerning this community: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. Just as that showing was by the inner insight and not by the outward eye, so likewise concerning Abraham it is not far-fetched that the matter is the same.

The sixth proof: When he, peace be upon him, completed his reasoning with the star, the moon, and the sun, he said after that: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Anʿam: 79]. So a judgment was made about the heavens and the earth, that they are created, on account of the proof he mentioned concerning the star, the moon, and the sun. If that proof were not general over all the heavens and the earth, the general judgment would be based on a specific proof, and that is an error. Thus it is established that the proof was general, and so the mention of the star, the moon, and the sun was like an example of the showing of the dominion. Therefore it is necessary that what is meant by the showing of the dominion is the clarification of the manner in which they indicate, by their change, their possibility, and their origination, the existence of a God who is knowing, powerful, and wise. So this showing is by the heart, not by the eye.

The seventh proof: Certainty (*al-yaqin*) is an expression for knowledge derived by reflection when it is preceded by doubt. And His words, exalted is He, ﴿that he might be among those with certainty﴾ are like the purpose of that showing, so the sense of the verse becomes: We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth in order that he may become among those with certainty. Since certainty is knowledge derived from proof, it is necessary that this showing be an expression for reasoning.

The eighth proof: All of God's creatures indicate the existence of the Creator and His power by one aspect, namely that they are originated and possible (*muhdatha mumkina*), and everything originated and possible is in need of a Creator. When a person knows this one aspect, it suffices for him in reasoning to the Creator. It is as if, by knowing these two premises, he has surveyed the whole dominion with the eye of his intellect and heard with the ear of his intellect their testimony of need and dependence. And this vision is a lasting vision that never disappears at all. Moreover, it does not preoccupy one away from God; rather it occupies the heart and spirit with God. As for the sight of the eye, a person cannot see many things with the eye all at once in a complete manner. Do you not see that whoever looks at a written page does not see from that page a complete and perfect vision except one letter? If he fixes his gaze on another letter and occupies his sight with it, he becomes deprived of perceiving the first letter, or of seeing it. Thus it is established that seeing many things at once is not possible. And even if it were possible, it would not be lasting, and even if it were lasting, it would preoccupy one from God, exalted is He. Do you not see that He praised Muhammad, peace be upon him, for abstaining from this sight, when He said: ﴿The gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. Thus it is established by the totality of these proofs that this showing was a showing according to the insight of the intellect, not according to the outward sight.

If it is said: On this interpretation, the vision of the heart is attained by all monotheists, so what virtue is attained for Abraham by means of it?

We say: Although all monotheists know the principle of this proof, the comprehension of the traces of God's wisdom in each one of the creatures of this world, according to their kinds, species, categories, individuals, and states, is something that is attained only by the greatest of the prophets, peace be upon them. For this reason, "our Messenger, peace be upon him, used to say in his supplication: 'O God, show us things as they really are.'" Thus this difficulty is removed. And God knows best.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** They differed concerning the *waw* in His words, ﴿and that he might be among those with certainty﴾, and they mentioned several aspects concerning it.

The first: The *waw* is superfluous (*za'ida*), and the sense is: We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth so that he may reason by them, so that he may be among those with certainty.

The second possibility: that this is a new, independent statement explaining the purpose of the showing. The meaning would be: "And so that he might be among those who have certainty, We showed him the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth."

The third: the showing may itself result in increased misguidance, as in the case of Pharaoh, about whom Allah says: ﴿And We showed him all Our signs, but he denied and refused﴾ [Ta-Ha: 56]. Yet it may also result in increased guidance and certainty. Since the showing could bear these two possibilities, Allah said concerning Ibrahim (peace be upon him): We showed him these signs so that he would see them, and so that he would be among the certain, not among the deniers. And Allah knows best.

Fifth issue: Certainty (yaqin) is knowledge that arises after the removal of doubt through reflection (ta'ammul). For this reason, the knowledge of Allah Most High is not described as "certainty," because His knowledge is not preceded by doubt and is not derived from thought and reflection. Know that a person, at the beginning of his reasoning, does not have his heart free of doubt and suspicion in some respects. When the proofs multiply, agree, and correspond, they become a cause for the attainment of certainty, and this is for several reasons:

The first: each of those proofs produces a kind of impression and strength, so the strength continues to increase until we reach firm conviction.

The second: the frequency of acts produces a settled disposition (malakah). Thus, repeated reasoning from various proofs toward a single conclusion works like repeated study of a single lesson. Just as much repetition yields firm memorization that does not leave the heart, so too here.

The third: when the heart reasons, it is very dark. When the belief derived from the first proof arises in it, the light of that reasoning mingles with the darkness of the other qualities present in the heart, so a state arises in it resembling a state mixed of light and darkness. When the second reasoning occurs, its light mingles with that first state, so radiance and brightness become more complete. Just as when the sun approaches the rising point, its light first appears, which is dawn, so the first reasoning is like dawn. Then, just as dawn keeps increasing as the sun draws nearer to the zenith, and when the sun reaches the zenith full light is attained, so too the servant: whenever his contemplation of the levels of Allah's created beings is greater, the dawning of the light of knowledge and monotheism becomes more manifest. However, the difference between the sun of knowledge and the sun of the world is that the physical sun has a specific limit in its rising and ascent beyond which it cannot ascend further, whereas the sun of knowledge, reason, and monotheism has no end to its ascent and no limit to its increase.

Thus His saying: ﴿And thus We showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ indicates the levels of proofs and clear evidences, and His saying: ﴿so that he might be among those who have certainty﴾ indicates the degrees of the lights of manifestation and the dawning of the sun of knowledge and monotheism. And Allah knows best.

The commentary on the verses 76 to 79:

God the Exalted said: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾ ﴿When he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ ﴿When he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater."
