But when it set, he said, "O my people, I am free of what you associate with God."﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth, as a upright monotheist, and I am not of those who associate others with God.﴾

Page 39 (continued)

In this verse there are several issues.

First issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿When the night covered him﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying ﴿Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾, and His saying ﴿And thus We showed﴾ is a clause placed as a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

Second issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: It is said "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" and "ajannahu al-layl" (both meaning the night covered him). It is said of everything you conceal: "janna" and "ajanna." It is also said: "jannahu al-layl," but the preferred form is "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" and "ajannahu al-layl." This is the statement of all the lexicographers. The meaning of "janna" is "to conceal," and from it come al-jannah (the garden), al-jinn (the jinn), al-junun (madness), al-jann (the hidden), al-janin (the fetus), al-mijann (shield), al-janan (cover), al-mujann (the shield) and al-majannah (the grave), all of which return in origin to concealment and hiding. Some grammarians said: "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" means that the night became dark upon him; for this reason "ʿalā" enters after it, just as you say "aẓlama." As for "jannahu," it means he concealed it, without implying the meaning of "aẓlama."

Third issue: Know that most of the exegetes mentioned that the king of that time saw a dream, and the interpreters of dreams interpreted it as meaning that a boy would be born who would contend with him for his kingdom. So that king ordered the slaughter of every boy who was born. Ibrahim's mother conceived him and did not reveal her pregnancy to the people. When her labor came, she went to a cave in a mountain, gave birth to Ibrahim, and sealed the entrance with a stone. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came and put his finger in the infant's mouth, and he sucked it, and his provision came out of it. Gabriel, peace be upon him, took care of him, and his mother would come to him occasionally and nurse him. He remained in this state until he grew up, understood, and realized that he had a Lord. He asked his mother and said to her: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "And who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said to the father: "And who is your lord?" He said: "The king of the land." Ibrahim, peace be upon him, recognized their ignorance of their Lord, so he looked out from the door of that cave, seeking to see something by which he could infer the existence of the Lord, glorified is He, and he saw the star that was the brightest of the stars in the sky. He said: "This is my lord," and so on to the end of the story.

Then those who hold this view disagreed. Some said that this happened after he reached puberty and the pen of accountability had been applied to him. Others said that this happened before puberty. Most of the verifying scholars agreed on the invalidity of the first view and argued against it with several proofs:

The first proof: The claim that the star is a lord is disbelief (kufr) by consensus, and disbelief is not permissible for prophets by consensus.

The second proof: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had already known his Lord before this event through evidence. The evidence for the correctness of what we have mentioned is that God informed us that he said before this event to his father Azar: ﴿Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error.﴾

The third proof: God related that he invited his father to monotheism and to abandoning the worship of idols gently, when he said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees and does not benefit you at all?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2]. In this place He related that he invited his father to monotheism and to abandoning idol-worship with harsh words and forbidding speech. It is known that whoever invites others to God the Exalted gives precedence to gentleness over harshness and softness over severity, and does not engage in rebuke and severity except after a long period and complete despair. This indicates that this event occurred after he had invited his father to monotheism many times and in various ways. There is no doubt that he only occupied himself with inviting his father after finishing with the important matter of his own soul. Thus it is established that this event occurred some time after he had come to know God.

The fourth proof: This event occurred after God showed him the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, until he saw what is above the Throne and the Footstool and what is beneath them, down to what is beneath the moist earth. How could it be fitting for one whose station in religion is such, and whose knowledge of God is such, to believe in the divinity of the stars?

Page 40

The fifth proof: The signs of the createdness of the celestial spheres are manifest in fifteen aspects or more. With these manifest aspects, how could it be fitting for the least intelligent of intellects, in his share of reason and understanding, to claim the lordship of the stars, let alone the most intelligent of the intelligent and the most knowledgeable of the scholars?

The sixth proof: God said describing Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84]. The least degree of a sound heart is that it be free from disbelief. He also praised him, saying: ﴿And We had given Ibrahim his guidance before, and We were knowing of him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 51], meaning: We gave him his guidance earlier, from the first time of reflection. His saying ﴿and We were knowing of him﴾ means: knowing of his purity and perfection. A parallel to this is God's saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

The seventh proof: His saying: ﴿Thus We showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be of the certain ones﴾, meaning: so that he might, by means of that showing, be among the certain ones.

Then He said after it: ﴿When the night covered him﴾, and the "fa'" (then) requires sequence. Thus it is established that this event occurred after Ibrahim had become one of the certain, knowing ones of his Lord.

The eighth proof: This event occurred due to Ibrahim's debate with his people. The evidence for this is that when God mentioned this story He said: ﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Ibrahim against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83], and He did not say "against himself." So it is known that this discussion took place with his people in order to guide them to faith and monotheism, and not because Ibrahim was seeking religion and knowledge for himself.

The ninth proof: The people say that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, only began contemplating the stars, the moon and the sun while he was in the cave. This is false, because if the matter were as they say, how could he say: ﴿O my people, I am free of what you associate﴾, while he was in the cave, with no people and no idol?

The tenth proof: God said: ﴿His people argued with him. He said, "Do you argue with me about God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 80]. How could they argue with him when they had already seen him and he had not seen them? This indicates that he, peace be upon him, only occupied himself with contemplating the stars, the moon and the sun after he had mingled with his people and seen them worshipping idols, and they had invited him to worship them. So his saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ was a rebuttal of them and an alert to them about the corruption of their view.

The eleventh proof: God related that he said to the people: ﴿And how should I fear what you associate, when you do not fear that you have associated with God﴾ [al-An'am: 81]. This indicates that the people had frightened him with the idols, as God related about the people of Hud, peace be upon him, that they said to him: ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54]. It is known that such speech does not fit the cave.

The twelfth proof: That night was preceded by a day, and there is no doubt that the sun had risen on the previous day and then set. So he should have used its previous setting as evidence that it is not fit for divinity, and if the sun's fitness for divinity is invalidated by this argument, then it is invalidated for the moon and the star all the more so. This is if we say that the purpose of this event was to attain knowledge of God for himself. As for if we say that its purpose was to press the argument upon the people and overwhelm them, then this question does not arise, because it is possible to say that his conversation with the people happened to coincide with the rising of that star, then the debate continued until the moon rose and the sun rose after it. On this assumption the question does not arise.

Thus it is established by these manifest proofs that it is not permissible to say that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said with certainty: "This is my lord." If this is invalid, there remain two possibilities:

The first: It may be said that this statement of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, came after puberty, but its purpose was not to affirm the lordship of the star. Rather, its purpose was one of seven matters:

The first: It may be said that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not say "This is my lord" as an report, but its purpose was that he was debating the worshippers of the star, and their doctrine was that the star is their lord and their god. So Ibrahim, peace be upon him, mentioned that statement in their own words and expression, so that it would return to them and he would refute it. An example of this: when one of us debates someone who holds that the body is eternal and says: "Is the body eternal? If so, why do we see it composed and changing?" He only said "The body is eternal" as a repetition of the opponent's words, in order to force the impossibility upon him. Similarly here, he said "This is my lord," and the purpose was to relate the opponent's statement. Then he mentioned right after it what shows its falsehood, which is his saying: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ This is the view relied upon in the answer. The evidence for it is that God indicated at the beginning of the verse this debate by His saying: ﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Ibrahim against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83].

The second interpretation: We say that his saying "This is my lord" means "This is my lord in your assumption and belief." An example: one who opposes an anthropomorphist says mockingly, "His god is a bounded body," meaning in his assumption and belief. God the Exalted said: ﴿And look at your god, to which you remained devoted﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97], and He said: ﴿On the day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 62]. Moses, may the blessings of God be upon him, used to say: "O God of gods." The meaning is that He is the god of the gods in their assumption. And He said: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], meaning in your own estimation.

The third answer: The intended meaning is a question in the form of denial, but the interrogative particle was dropped as being unnecessary, because the context indicates it.

The fourth: The statement may contain an implied verb of saying. The estimate is: "He said: they say, 'This is my lord.'" Omitting a verb of saying is common, as in His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations of the House, and Ismail, [they said], "Our Lord"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], meaning they say "Our Lord." And His saying: ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him, [saying], "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God in position"﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], meaning they say "We do not worship them except..." Similarly here the estimate is: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to his people: "They say, 'This is my lord,'" meaning: "This is the one who manages me and raises me."

The fifth: Ibrahim mentioned this statement mockingly, as one says of a humble man who has become master of a people: "This is your master," in mockery.

**[Page 42]**

The sixth aspect: he (ﷺ) wished to refute their claim that the stars are lords, but he knew, from their adherence to their ancestors' ways and the remoteness of their dispositions from accepting proofs, that if he openly called them to God Most High, they would not accept it and would not heed him. So he took a path by which he could lead them to listen to the argument. This was by saying words that suggest he was supporting them in their doctrine that the stars are lords, while his heart, may the blessings of God be upon him, was at peace in faith. His aim in this was to be able to present the proof that refutes and invalidates their doctrine, and to have them accept his words. The full explanation is this: since he found no way to call them other than this one, and he was commanded to call to God, he was in the position of one compelled to utter a word of disbelief. It is known that under compulsion it is permissible to utter a word of disbelief with the tongue. God Most High said: ﴿Except one who is compelled while his heart is firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. If it is permissible to utter a word of disbelief for the sake of preserving one person's life, then it is all the more permissible to utter a word of disbelief to rescue a whole world of rational beings from disbelief and everlasting punishment, and that would be more fitting. Also, one who is compelled to abandon prayer, if he prays until he is killed, deserves a great reward. Then, when the time of fighting against the unbelievers comes, and he knows that if he occupied himself with prayer the army of Islam would be defeated, then at that point it is obligatory for him to abandon prayer and occupy himself with fighting. Indeed, if he prayed and abandoned fighting, he would be sinful, whereas if he abandoned prayer and fought, he would deserve reward. Moreover, we say: whoever is in prayer and sees a child or a blind person about to drown or be burned is obligated to cut off his prayer to rescue that child or that blind person from that calamity. So likewise here: Abraham (peace be upon him) spoke this word in order to show agreement with his people, so that when he presented to them the proof that refutes their doctrine, their acceptance of that proof would be more complete and their benefit from hearing it would be more perfect.

Something that strengthens this aspect is that God Most High related a similar method from him in another place, namely His saying: ﴿So he glanced a glance at the stars﴾ ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am sick"﴾ ﴿so they turned their backs and departed﴾ [al-Saffat: 88–90]. This is because they used to draw inferences from knowledge of the stars about the occurrence of future events, so Abraham agreed with them outwardly in this method, although he was innocent of it inwardly. His purpose was to use this method as a means to smash the idols. If agreement in outward appearance is permissible here, although he was innocent of it inwardly, then why should it not be permissible in our matter to be so? Also, the theologians (mutakallimun) have said: it is possible for God Most High to manifest extraordinary events (kharq al-‘adah) at the hands of one who claims divinity, because the form and shape of such a claimant indicates his lie, so no deception arises from the manifestation of those extraordinary events at his hand. But it is not permissible for them to be manifested at the hand of one who claims prophethood, because that would entail deception. So likewise here. His saying, "This is my lord," does not entail misguidance, because the proofs of its falsity are clear, and in uttering this statement there is a great benefit, namely drawing them on to accept the proof. Therefore it was permissible. And God knows best.

The seventh aspect: when the people called him to worship the stars, they were in that debate until the brilliant star (al-najm al-durri) rose. Then Abraham (peace be upon him) said, "This is my lord," meaning: this is the lord to whom you are calling me. Then he fell silent for a time until it set, and then he said: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾. This is the full explanation of these answers on the first possibility, namely that he (may the blessings of God be upon him) uttered this statement after reaching maturity.

As for the second possibility, namely that he said it before reaching maturity and while close to it, its explanation is that God Most High had endowed Abraham with complete intellect and pure disposition, so the affirmation of the Creator, glorified be He, occurred to his mind before his maturity. He reflected and saw the star, and said, "This is my lord." Then, when he observed its movement, he said: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾. Then God Most High perfected his maturity in the course of this inquiry, and he said at once: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you associate﴾. This possibility is unobjectionable, although the first possibility is more worthy of acceptance because of the many proofs we have mentioned. Moreover, this debate took place with Abraham (peace be upon him) at the time he was occupied with calling his people to monotheism. And God knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: Abu ‘Amr and Warsh, from Nafi‘, read ﴿ru’iya﴾ (رُئِيَ) with a fatha on the rā’ and a kasra on the hamza wherever it occurs. Ibn ‘Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa’i read both with a kasra. When a kaf or a hā’ follows the alif, as in ra’aka (رَآكَ) and ra’aha (رَآها), then Hamzah and al-Kisa’i read it with a kasra, while Ibn ‘Amir reads it with a fatha. Yahya, from Abu Bakr, from ‘Asim, related the same as Hamzah and al-Kisa’i. When an alif of wasl follows it, as in ra’a al-shamsa (رَأى الشَّمْسَ) and ra’a al-qamar (رَأى القَمَرَ), then Hamzah, Yahya from Abu Bakr, and Nasr from al-Kisa’i read the rā’ with a kasra and the hamza with a fatha. The rest read all of that with a fatha on both the rā’ and the hamza. They agreed that in ra’ukam (رَأوْكَ) and ra’uhu (رَأوْهُ) it is with a fatha.

Al-Wahidi said: As for the one who reads both the rā’ and the hamza with a fatha, his reasoning is clear, namely leaving the alif in its original form, as in ra‘a (رَعى) and rama (رَمى). As for the one who reads the rā’ with a fatha and the hamza with a kasra, he inclined the hamza toward a kasra so that the alif in ra’a would incline toward the yā’, while leaving the rā’ with a fatha in its original form. As for the one who reads both with a kasra, it is so that the vowel of the rā’ becomes similar to the vowel of the hamza. Al-Wahidi discussed this subject at length in his Kitab al-Basit, so let the reader refer to it. And God knows best.

The fifth issue: the story we have mentioned, that Abraham (peace be upon him) was born in a cave, that his mother left him, and that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was raising him, is all in general terms. Al-Qadi said: Everything that resembles miracles is not permissible, because bringing a miracle before the time of the claim to prophethood is not permissible according to them. This is what is called irhas (preparatory signs before prophethood), unless a messenger from God is present at that time, in which case those extraordinary events are considered miracles of that prophet. But according to our companions, irhas is permissible, and so the doubt is removed. And God knows best.

* * *

The sixth issue: Abraham (peace be upon him) used the setting of the star as evidence that it cannot be his lord and creator. It is incumbent upon us here to examine two matters:

One: what is ufool (setting, أُفُول)?

Two: how does setting indicate that the star is not lord?

We say: ufool is an expression for the hiding of a thing after its appearance.

Having understood this, an objector may ask: setting indicates createdness only insofar as it is a motion. On this assumption, rising would also be an indication of createdness. So why did Abraham (peace be upon him) abandon proving their createdness by rising, and rely in establishing this claim on setting?

The answer: there is no doubt that rising and setting share in indicating createdness. But the proof that prophets employ when calling all creation to God must be apparent and manifest, such that both the intelligent and the dull, and the rational, share in understanding it. The indication of createdness by motion, though certain, is subtle, and only the superior among creatures know it. As for the indication of setting, it is an apparent indication that everyone knows, for a star loses its authority at the time of setting. So the indication of setting for this purpose is more complete. Also, some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: Being-in-possibility (al-hawa fi khatrat al-imkan) is a setting, and the best speech is that which contains a portion for the elite, a portion for the middling, and a portion for the common people. The elite understand from setting possibility (imkan), and everything possible is needy, and the needy is not free of need, so one must arrive at One who is exempt from possibility, so that needs are cut off by His existence, as He said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. As for the middling, they understand from setting general motion, so every moving thing is created, and every created thing is in need of the Eternal Powerful. Hence the setting one cannot be a god; rather, God is the One whom that setting one needs. As for the common people, they understand from setting the going down, and they observe that every star that approaches setting and going down loses its light, its brightness diminishes, its power departs, and it becomes like one deposed. Whoever is like this is not fit for divinity. Thus this single expression, namely His saying: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾, is a statement comprising the portion of the near ones, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left, so it was the most complete proof and the most excellent demonstration.

There is another subtle point here: he (peace be upon him) was debating with them while they were astrologers (munajjimun). The doctrine of the astrologers is that when a star is in the eastern quarter and rising toward the middle of the sky, it is strong and of great influence. But when it is in the western part and near setting, it is weak in influence and small in power. By this subtle point he signaled that God is the One whose power does not change into inability and whose perfection does not change into deficiency. Your doctrine is that a star, while in the western quarter, is weak in power, deficient in influence, and incapable of governing, and that indicates a defect in its divinity. Thus it becomes clear, according to the astrologers' own view, that setting has a special property in making it necessary to impugn its divinity. And God knows best.

As for the second stage, namely the explanation that a star's being setting prevents its lordship: someone may also say: at most, its setting indicates its createdness, but its createdness does not prevent it from being a lord to Abraham and an object of worship for him. Do you not see that the astrologers and the proponents of intermediaries say that the Supreme God created the stars, originated them and brought them into existence, and then these stars create plants and animals in this lower world? So it is established that although the setting of the stars indicates their createdness, it does not prevent them from being lords for humans and gods for this world.

Our answer: here we have two stages.

The first stage: let the meaning of "lord" and "god" be the existent being in whom needs are cut off. Once it is established by the setting of the stars that they are created, and it is established in the immediate judgment of minds that everything created is in its existence needy of something else, it becomes necessary to affirm that these stars in their existence need something other than themselves. And once this meaning is established, it is impossible for them to be lords and gods in the sense that needs are cut off at their existence. Thus it is established that their being setting necessitates impugning their being lords and gods in this interpretation.

The second stage: let the meaning of "lord" and "god" be the one who is the creator of us and the originator of our essences and attributes. We say: the setting of the stars indicates that they are incapable of creating and originating, and that it is not permissible to worship them. Its explanation is in several ways:

The first: their setting indicates their createdness. Their createdness indicates their need for an eternal, powerful agent. And the powerfulness of that powerful one must be eternal; otherwise his powerfulness would need another powerful one, and this would lead to an infinite regress, which is impossible. Thus it is established that his powerfulness is eternal.

Having established this, we say: a thing that is capable for Him is capable for Him only by virtue of its possibility, and possibility is one in all possibles. Thus it is established that what is the basis for some possibles being capable for God Most High is present in all possibles, so it is necessary that all possibles be capable for God Most High.

[Page 45]

Once this is established, it follows that none of the contingent things can come into existence through other than Him, as we have shown, by definitive proofs in the science of the foundations (*'ilm al-usul*), the validity of these positions.

The conclusion is that it has been established by proof that the setting of the stars indicates that they are originated (*muhdathah*). Although this meaning is established only through many premises. Also, their being originated in themselves necessitates the judgment that they cannot be capable of creating and originating. Although this meaning is established only through many premises. The proofs of the Qur'an mention only the basic premises. As for elaboration and detail, that belongs to the science of dialectic (*'ilm al-jadal*). When God Most High mentioned these two premises in a allusive manner (*'ala sabil al-ramz*), He was content to mention them alone in explaining that the stars have no power to create and originate. For this reason, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) argued from their setting to the impossibility of their being lords and gods over the events of this world.

The second aspect: the setting of the stars indicates their origination, and their origination indicates that in their existence they need a Creator who is powerful and chooses. That agent is the one who created the spheres and the stars. Whoever is capable of creating the stars and spheres without any intermediary whatsoever is all the more capable of creating man, since the one who can create the greater thing must necessarily be able to create the lesser thing. This is alluded to in His saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir 40:57], and in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, and He is the All-Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:81]. Thus it has been established by this method that the Supreme God must be capable of creating mankind and of governing the lower world without the mediation of the celestial bodies. Since this is the case, devotion to the Supreme God is more fitting than devotion to the sun, the stars, and the moon.

The third aspect: if it were valid that some of the stars were originators and creators, this possibility would remain for all of them. In that case, a person would not know whether his Creator is this star, that other one, or the totality of the stars, and he would remain doubtful about knowing his Creator. But if we know the totality and attribute creation, origination, and governance to the Creator of the totality, then we can know the Creator and Originator, and we can devote ourselves to worshipping Him and thanking Him. Thus it has been established by these aspects that just as the setting of the stars indicates the impossibility of their being eternal, it likewise indicates the impossibility of their being gods of this world and lords of animals and humans. And God knows best. This is the full account of the establishment of this proof.

If it is said: There is no doubt that that night was preceded by a day and a night, and the setting of the stars, the moon, and the sun occurred during the previous night and the previous day. By this explanation, the setting that occurred on that night has no additional benefit.

The answer: We have explained that he (may the blessings and peace of God be upon him) presented this proof only to the people whom he was calling away from worshipping the stars toward monotheism. It is not unlikely to say that he (peace be upon him) was sitting with those people one night and was rebuking them for worshipping the stars. While he was in the midst of establishing that discourse, his gaze fell upon a shining star. When it set, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: "If this star were a god, it would not have moved from ascending to setting, and from strength to weakness." Then, in the course of that discourse, the moon rose and set. So he repeated that discourse to them, and the same applies to the sun. This is the sum of what comes to mind regarding the establishment of Ibrahim's proof, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him.

Sixth issue: Al-Ghazali philosophized in some of his books and interpreted the star as the animal rational soul that belongs to each star, the moon as the rational soul that belongs to each sphere, and the sun as the immaterial intellect (*'aql mujarrad*) that belongs to all of these. Abu 'Ali ibn Sina used to interpret setting as possibility (*imkan*). Al-Ghazali claimed that what is meant by their setting is their possibility in themselves, and he claimed that what is meant by His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ is that all these things are contingent in their existence by their essences (*mumkin al-wujud li-dhatiha*), and every contingent thing must have an effector, and it must ultimately lead to the Necessary Existent (*wajib al-wujud*).

Know that this discourse is not objectionable. However, it is far-fetched to apply the wording of the verse to it. Some people interpreted the star as the sense perception, the moon as the imagination and the estimative faculty, and the sun as the intellect. What is meant is that these three perceptive faculties are deficient and finite, and that the Governor of the world has dominion over them and subdues them. And God knows best.

* * *

Seventh issue: His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ indicates several rulings:

[Page 46]

First ruling: This verse indicates that God Most High is not a body, for if He were a body, He would be absent from us forever, and thus would be setting forever. Also, it is impossible that God Most High descend from the Throne to the heaven at one time and ascend from the heaven to the Throne at another, for otherwise the meaning of setting would be realized.

Second ruling: This verse indicates that God Most High is not a locus for originated attributes, as the Karramiyyah claim, for otherwise He would be changing, and then the meaning of setting would be realized, and that is impossible.

Third ruling: This verse indicates that religion must be based on proof and not on blind imitation (*taqlid*), for otherwise this argument would have no benefit whatsoever.

Fourth ruling: This verse indicates that the prophets' knowledge of their Lord is acquired through reasoning (*istidlaliyyah*) and not necessary (*darurriyyah*), for otherwise Ibrahim would not have needed to argue.

Fifth ruling: This verse indicates that there is no way to attain knowledge of God Most High except through reflection and reasoning about the conditions of His creatures, for if knowledge of Him could be attained by another way, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) would not have turned to this method. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my Lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾

Concerning it there are two issues:

First issue: It is said: "The moon rose (*bazagha*)" when it began to rise, and "the sun rose" when the beginning of its rising appeared, and "rising stars" (*nujum bawazigh*). Al-Azhari said: It seems to be derived from *al-bazgh*, which is splitting, as if with its light it splits the darkness. The meaning of the verse is that he considered the moon in the same manner as he considered the star.

Second issue: His saying ﴿Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾ indicates that guidance is only from God Most High. The word "guidance" cannot be taken to mean enablement (*al-tamakkun*), removal of excuses, or setting up proofs, because all of that was already present. Thus the guidance he was seeking after those things had been realized must necessarily be something additional to them.

Know that the view that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) held our position is too clear to be confused by any intelligent person, for in this verse he attributed guidance to God Most High, and likewise in His saying: ﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:78], and likewise in His saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim 14:35].

* * *

[Page 47]

As for His saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord; this is greater."﴾ there are several issues:

First issue: He said "this" about the sun even though it is feminine, and he did not say "this one" (*hadhihi*), for several reasons:

One: The sun (*al-shams*) is in meaning light and radiance, so the word was taken in its interpreted sense and was made masculine.

Two: The sun has no feminine marker in it, so when its wording resembled the masculine wording and its interpretation was the interpretation of light, the masculine was permissible for these two reasons.

Three: He meant "this rising one" or "this that I see."

Four: The purpose of it is observing courtesy, which is avoiding the feminine when mentioning a word that indicates lordship.

Second issue: His saying ﴿This is greater﴾: what is meant is the greatest of the stars in body and the strongest in power, so it was more deserving of divinity.

If it is said: Since setting occurs in the sun, and setting prevents the attribute of lordship, once it is established that the attribute of lordship is impossible for the sun, its being impossible for the moon and the rest of the stars is even more so. By this method it becomes clear that mentioning this statement about the sun suffices instead of mentioning it about the moon and the stars. So why did he not limit himself to mentioning the sun, for the sake of brevity and conciseness?

We say: Proceeding from the lesser to the lesser, ascending to the higher and the highest, has a kind of effect in explanation, clarification, and emphasis that cannot be obtained otherwise, so mentioning it in this way is preferable.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, I am free from what you associate."﴾ the meaning is that, since it has been established by proof that these stars are not fit for lordship and divinity, he therefore disassociated himself from polytheism.

One may say: Grant that it has been established by proof that the stars, the sun, and the moon are not fit for lordship and divinity; yet this does not necessarily entail the negation of partners in an absolute sense and the affirmation of absolute monotheism. So why did he, on the basis of the establishment of the proof that these stars are not fit for lordship, proceed to firmly affirm monotheism absolutely?

The answer: The people were in agreement on the negation of all other partners, and they only disputed this specific form. When it was established by proof that these things are neither lords nor gods, and by consensus the negation of others was established, the firm negation of partners in absolute terms was therefore realized.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾ there are two issues:

First issue: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim pronounced the *ya'* in "wajhiya" with a fatha, and the rest did not pronounce this fatha.

Second issue: This statement cannot be taken in its apparent sense; rather, what is meant is "I have directed my worship and my obedience." The reason for the permissibility of this figurative usage is that whoever obeys another and submits to his command turns his face toward him, so turning the face toward him is made a metaphor for obedience.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿to Him who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ there is a subtle point: He did not say "I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth," but rather left out this wording and said "I have turned my face to Him who..." The meaning is that the turning of the face of the heart is not toward Him, for He is exalted above place and direction; rather, the turning of the face of the heart is toward serving and obeying Him for the sake of His servanthood. Therefore, the omission of the word "toward" (*ila*) here and the sufficiency of the preposition *li* ("to/for") is clear evidence that the object of worship is exalted above place and direction. The meaning of *fatara* is that He brought the two into existence, and its root is from splitting; it is said: "the tree split open (*tafattara*) with leaves and flowers" when it brings them forth. As for *hanif*, it means one who inclines. Abu al-'Aliyah said: The *hanif* is one who faces the House (the Ka'bah) in his prayer. It was also said: it is one who turns away from every object of worship other than God Most High.

Page 39

The commentary on the verses 76 to 79:

God the Exalted said: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾ ﴿When he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ ﴿When he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, I am free of what you associate with God."﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth, as a upright monotheist, and I am not of those who associate others with God.﴾

Page 39 (continued)

In this verse there are several issues.

First issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿When the night covered him﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying ﴿Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾, and His saying ﴿And thus We showed﴾ is a clause placed as a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

Second issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: It is said "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" and "ajannahu al-layl" (both meaning the night covered him). It is said of everything you conceal: "janna" and "ajanna." It is also said: "jannahu al-layl," but the preferred form is "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" and "ajannahu al-layl." This is the statement of all the lexicographers. The meaning of "janna" is "to conceal," and from it come al-jannah (the garden), al-jinn (the jinn), al-junun (madness), al-jann (the hidden), al-janin (the fetus), al-mijann (shield), al-janan (cover), al-mujann (the shield) and al-majannah (the grave), all of which return in origin to concealment and hiding. Some grammarians said: "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" means that the night became dark upon him; for this reason "ʿalā" enters after it, just as you say "aẓlama." As for "jannahu," it means he concealed it, without implying the meaning of "aẓlama."

Third issue: Know that most of the exegetes mentioned that the king of that time saw a dream, and the interpreters of dreams interpreted it as meaning that a boy would be born who would contend with him for his kingdom. So that king ordered the slaughter of every boy who was born. Ibrahim's mother conceived him and did not reveal her pregnancy to the people. When her labor came, she went to a cave in a mountain, gave birth to Ibrahim, and sealed the entrance with a stone. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came and put his finger in the infant's mouth, and he sucked it, and his provision came out of it. Gabriel, peace be upon him, took care of him, and his mother would come to him occasionally and nurse him. He remained in this state until he grew up, understood, and realized that he had a Lord. He asked his mother and said to her: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "And who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said to the father: "And who is your lord?" He said: "The king of the land." Ibrahim, peace be upon him, recognized their ignorance of their Lord, so he looked out from the door of that cave, seeking to see something by which he could infer the existence of the Lord, glorified is He, and he saw the star that was the brightest of the stars in the sky. He said: "This is my lord," and so on to the end of the story.

Then those who hold this view disagreed. Some said that this happened after he reached puberty and the pen of accountability had been applied to him. Others said that this happened before puberty. Most of the verifying scholars agreed on the invalidity of the first view and argued against it with several proofs:

The first proof: The claim that the star is a lord is disbelief (kufr) by consensus, and disbelief is not permissible for prophets by consensus.

The second proof: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had already known his Lord before this event through evidence. The evidence for the correctness of what we have mentioned is that God informed us that he said before this event to his father Azar: ﴿Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error.﴾

The third proof: God related that he invited his father to monotheism and to abandoning the worship of idols gently, when he said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees and does not benefit you at all?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2]. In this place He related that he invited his father to monotheism and to abandoning idol-worship with harsh words and forbidding speech. It is known that whoever invites others to God the Exalted gives precedence to gentleness over harshness and softness over severity, and does not engage in rebuke and severity except after a long period and complete despair. This indicates that this event occurred after he had invited his father to monotheism many times and in various ways. There is no doubt that he only occupied himself with inviting his father after finishing with the important matter of his own soul. Thus it is established that this event occurred some time after he had come to know God.

The fourth proof: This event occurred after God showed him the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, until he saw what is above the Throne and the Footstool and what is beneath them, down to what is beneath the moist earth. How could it be fitting for one whose station in religion is such, and whose knowledge of God is such, to believe in the divinity of the stars?

Page 40

The fifth proof: The signs of the createdness of the celestial spheres are manifest in fifteen aspects or more. With these manifest aspects, how could it be fitting for the least intelligent of intellects, in his share of reason and understanding, to claim the lordship of the stars, let alone the most intelligent of the intelligent and the most knowledgeable of the scholars?

The sixth proof: God said describing Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84]. The least degree of a sound heart is that it be free from disbelief. He also praised him, saying: ﴿And We had given Ibrahim his guidance before, and We were knowing of him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 51], meaning: We gave him his guidance earlier, from the first time of reflection. His saying ﴿and We were knowing of him﴾ means: knowing of his purity and perfection. A parallel to this is God's saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

The seventh proof: His saying: ﴿Thus We showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be of the certain ones﴾, meaning: so that he might, by means of that showing, be among the certain ones.

Then He said after it: ﴿When the night covered him﴾, and the "fa'" (then) requires sequence. Thus it is established that this event occurred after Ibrahim had become one of the certain, knowing ones of his Lord.

The eighth proof: This event occurred due to Ibrahim's debate with his people. The evidence for this is that when God mentioned this story He said: ﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Ibrahim against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83], and He did not say "against himself." So it is known that this discussion took place with his people in order to guide them to faith and monotheism, and not because Ibrahim was seeking religion and knowledge for himself.

The ninth proof: The people say that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, only began contemplating the stars, the moon and the sun while he was in the cave. This is false, because if the matter were as they say, how could he say: ﴿O my people, I am free of what you associate﴾, while he was in the cave, with no people and no idol?

The tenth proof: God said: ﴿His people argued with him. He said, "Do you argue with me about God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 80]. How could they argue with him when they had already seen him and he had not seen them? This indicates that he, peace be upon him, only occupied himself with contemplating the stars, the moon and the sun after he had mingled with his people and seen them worshipping idols, and they had invited him to worship them. So his saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ was a rebuttal of them and an alert to them about the corruption of their view.

The eleventh proof: God related that he said to the people: ﴿And how should I fear what you associate, when you do not fear that you have associated with God﴾ [al-An'am: 81]. This indicates that the people had frightened him with the idols, as God related about the people of Hud, peace be upon him, that they said to him: ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54]. It is known that such speech does not fit the cave.

The twelfth proof: That night was preceded by a day, and there is no doubt that the sun had risen on the previous day and then set. So he should have used its previous setting as evidence that it is not fit for divinity, and if the sun's fitness for divinity is invalidated by this argument, then it is invalidated for the moon and the star all the more so. This is if we say that the purpose of this event was to attain knowledge of God for himself. As for if we say that its purpose was to press the argument upon the people and overwhelm them, then this question does not arise, because it is possible to say that his conversation with the people happened to coincide with the rising of that star, then the debate continued until the moon rose and the sun rose after it. On this assumption the question does not arise.

Thus it is established by these manifest proofs that it is not permissible to say that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said with certainty: "This is my lord." If this is invalid, there remain two possibilities:

The first: It may be said that this statement of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, came after puberty, but its purpose was not to affirm the lordship of the star. Rather, its purpose was one of seven matters:

The first: It may be said that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not say "This is my lord" as an report, but its purpose was that he was debating the worshippers of the star, and their doctrine was that the star is their lord and their god. So Ibrahim, peace be upon him, mentioned that statement in their own words and expression, so that it would return to them and he would refute it. An example of this: when one of us debates someone who holds that the body is eternal and says: "Is the body eternal? If so, why do we see it composed and changing?" He only said "The body is eternal" as a repetition of the opponent's words, in order to force the impossibility upon him. Similarly here, he said "This is my lord," and the purpose was to relate the opponent's statement. Then he mentioned right after it what shows its falsehood, which is his saying: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ This is the view relied upon in the answer. The evidence for it is that God indicated at the beginning of the verse this debate by His saying: ﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Ibrahim against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83].

The second interpretation: We say that his saying "This is my lord" means "This is my lord in your assumption and belief." An example: one who opposes an anthropomorphist says mockingly, "His god is a bounded body," meaning in his assumption and belief. God the Exalted said: ﴿And look at your god, to which you remained devoted﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97], and He said: ﴿On the day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 62]. Moses, may the blessings of God be upon him, used to say: "O God of gods." The meaning is that He is the god of the gods in their assumption. And He said: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], meaning in your own estimation.

The third answer: The intended meaning is a question in the form of denial, but the interrogative particle was dropped as being unnecessary, because the context indicates it.

The fourth: The statement may contain an implied verb of saying. The estimate is: "He said: they say, 'This is my lord.'" Omitting a verb of saying is common, as in His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations of the House, and Ismail, [they said], "Our Lord"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], meaning they say "Our Lord." And His saying: ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him, [saying], "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God in position"﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], meaning they say "We do not worship them except..." Similarly here the estimate is: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to his people: "They say, 'This is my lord,'" meaning: "This is the one who manages me and raises me."

The fifth: Ibrahim mentioned this statement mockingly, as one says of a humble man who has become master of a people: "This is your master," in mockery.

**[Page 42]**

The sixth aspect: he (ﷺ) wished to refute their claim that the stars are lords, but he knew, from their adherence to their ancestors' ways and the remoteness of their dispositions from accepting proofs, that if he openly called them to God Most High, they would not accept it and would not heed him. So he took a path by which he could lead them to listen to the argument. This was by saying words that suggest he was supporting them in their doctrine that the stars are lords, while his heart, may the blessings of God be upon him, was at peace in faith. His aim in this was to be able to present the proof that refutes and invalidates their doctrine, and to have them accept his words. The full explanation is this: since he found no way to call them other than this one, and he was commanded to call to God, he was in the position of one compelled to utter a word of disbelief. It is known that under compulsion it is permissible to utter a word of disbelief with the tongue. God Most High said: ﴿Except one who is compelled while his heart is firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. If it is permissible to utter a word of disbelief for the sake of preserving one person's life, then it is all the more permissible to utter a word of disbelief to rescue a whole world of rational beings from disbelief and everlasting punishment, and that would be more fitting. Also, one who is compelled to abandon prayer, if he prays until he is killed, deserves a great reward. Then, when the time of fighting against the unbelievers comes, and he knows that if he occupied himself with prayer the army of Islam would be defeated, then at that point it is obligatory for him to abandon prayer and occupy himself with fighting. Indeed, if he prayed and abandoned fighting, he would be sinful, whereas if he abandoned prayer and fought, he would deserve reward. Moreover, we say: whoever is in prayer and sees a child or a blind person about to drown or be burned is obligated to cut off his prayer to rescue that child or that blind person from that calamity. So likewise here: Abraham (peace be upon him) spoke this word in order to show agreement with his people, so that when he presented to them the proof that refutes their doctrine, their acceptance of that proof would be more complete and their benefit from hearing it would be more perfect.

Something that strengthens this aspect is that God Most High related a similar method from him in another place, namely His saying: ﴿So he glanced a glance at the stars﴾ ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am sick"﴾ ﴿so they turned their backs and departed﴾ [al-Saffat: 88–90]. This is because they used to draw inferences from knowledge of the stars about the occurrence of future events, so Abraham agreed with them outwardly in this method, although he was innocent of it inwardly. His purpose was to use this method as a means to smash the idols. If agreement in outward appearance is permissible here, although he was innocent of it inwardly, then why should it not be permissible in our matter to be so? Also, the theologians (mutakallimun) have said: it is possible for God Most High to manifest extraordinary events (kharq al-‘adah) at the hands of one who claims divinity, because the form and shape of such a claimant indicates his lie, so no deception arises from the manifestation of those extraordinary events at his hand. But it is not permissible for them to be manifested at the hand of one who claims prophethood, because that would entail deception. So likewise here. His saying, "This is my lord," does not entail misguidance, because the proofs of its falsity are clear, and in uttering this statement there is a great benefit, namely drawing them on to accept the proof. Therefore it was permissible. And God knows best.

The seventh aspect: when the people called him to worship the stars, they were in that debate until the brilliant star (al-najm al-durri) rose. Then Abraham (peace be upon him) said, "This is my lord," meaning: this is the lord to whom you are calling me. Then he fell silent for a time until it set, and then he said: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾. This is the full explanation of these answers on the first possibility, namely that he (may the blessings of God be upon him) uttered this statement after reaching maturity.

As for the second possibility, namely that he said it before reaching maturity and while close to it, its explanation is that God Most High had endowed Abraham with complete intellect and pure disposition, so the affirmation of the Creator, glorified be He, occurred to his mind before his maturity. He reflected and saw the star, and said, "This is my lord." Then, when he observed its movement, he said: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾. Then God Most High perfected his maturity in the course of this inquiry, and he said at once: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you associate﴾. This possibility is unobjectionable, although the first possibility is more worthy of acceptance because of the many proofs we have mentioned. Moreover, this debate took place with Abraham (peace be upon him) at the time he was occupied with calling his people to monotheism. And God knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: Abu ‘Amr and Warsh, from Nafi‘, read ﴿ru’iya﴾ (رُئِيَ) with a fatha on the rā’ and a kasra on the hamza wherever it occurs. Ibn ‘Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa’i read both with a kasra. When a kaf or a hā’ follows the alif, as in ra’aka (رَآكَ) and ra’aha (رَآها), then Hamzah and al-Kisa’i read it with a kasra, while Ibn ‘Amir reads it with a fatha. Yahya, from Abu Bakr, from ‘Asim, related the same as Hamzah and al-Kisa’i. When an alif of wasl follows it, as in ra’a al-shamsa (رَأى الشَّمْسَ) and ra’a al-qamar (رَأى القَمَرَ), then Hamzah, Yahya from Abu Bakr, and Nasr from al-Kisa’i read the rā’ with a kasra and the hamza with a fatha. The rest read all of that with a fatha on both the rā’ and the hamza. They agreed that in ra’ukam (رَأوْكَ) and ra’uhu (رَأوْهُ) it is with a fatha.

Al-Wahidi said: As for the one who reads both the rā’ and the hamza with a fatha, his reasoning is clear, namely leaving the alif in its original form, as in ra‘a (رَعى) and rama (رَمى). As for the one who reads the rā’ with a fatha and the hamza with a kasra, he inclined the hamza toward a kasra so that the alif in ra’a would incline toward the yā’, while leaving the rā’ with a fatha in its original form. As for the one who reads both with a kasra, it is so that the vowel of the rā’ becomes similar to the vowel of the hamza. Al-Wahidi discussed this subject at length in his Kitab al-Basit, so let the reader refer to it. And God knows best.

The fifth issue: the story we have mentioned, that Abraham (peace be upon him) was born in a cave, that his mother left him, and that Gabriel (peace be upon him) was raising him, is all in general terms. Al-Qadi said: Everything that resembles miracles is not permissible, because bringing a miracle before the time of the claim to prophethood is not permissible according to them. This is what is called irhas (preparatory signs before prophethood), unless a messenger from God is present at that time, in which case those extraordinary events are considered miracles of that prophet. But according to our companions, irhas is permissible, and so the doubt is removed. And God knows best.

* * *

The sixth issue: Abraham (peace be upon him) used the setting of the star as evidence that it cannot be his lord and creator. It is incumbent upon us here to examine two matters:

One: what is ufool (setting, أُفُول)?

Two: how does setting indicate that the star is not lord?

We say: ufool is an expression for the hiding of a thing after its appearance.

Having understood this, an objector may ask: setting indicates createdness only insofar as it is a motion. On this assumption, rising would also be an indication of createdness. So why did Abraham (peace be upon him) abandon proving their createdness by rising, and rely in establishing this claim on setting?

The answer: there is no doubt that rising and setting share in indicating createdness. But the proof that prophets employ when calling all creation to God must be apparent and manifest, such that both the intelligent and the dull, and the rational, share in understanding it. The indication of createdness by motion, though certain, is subtle, and only the superior among creatures know it. As for the indication of setting, it is an apparent indication that everyone knows, for a star loses its authority at the time of setting. So the indication of setting for this purpose is more complete. Also, some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: Being-in-possibility (al-hawa fi khatrat al-imkan) is a setting, and the best speech is that which contains a portion for the elite, a portion for the middling, and a portion for the common people. The elite understand from setting possibility (imkan), and everything possible is needy, and the needy is not free of need, so one must arrive at One who is exempt from possibility, so that needs are cut off by His existence, as He said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. As for the middling, they understand from setting general motion, so every moving thing is created, and every created thing is in need of the Eternal Powerful. Hence the setting one cannot be a god; rather, God is the One whom that setting one needs. As for the common people, they understand from setting the going down, and they observe that every star that approaches setting and going down loses its light, its brightness diminishes, its power departs, and it becomes like one deposed. Whoever is like this is not fit for divinity. Thus this single expression, namely His saying: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾, is a statement comprising the portion of the near ones, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left, so it was the most complete proof and the most excellent demonstration.

There is another subtle point here: he (peace be upon him) was debating with them while they were astrologers (munajjimun). The doctrine of the astrologers is that when a star is in the eastern quarter and rising toward the middle of the sky, it is strong and of great influence. But when it is in the western part and near setting, it is weak in influence and small in power. By this subtle point he signaled that God is the One whose power does not change into inability and whose perfection does not change into deficiency. Your doctrine is that a star, while in the western quarter, is weak in power, deficient in influence, and incapable of governing, and that indicates a defect in its divinity. Thus it becomes clear, according to the astrologers' own view, that setting has a special property in making it necessary to impugn its divinity. And God knows best.

As for the second stage, namely the explanation that a star's being setting prevents its lordship: someone may also say: at most, its setting indicates its createdness, but its createdness does not prevent it from being a lord to Abraham and an object of worship for him. Do you not see that the astrologers and the proponents of intermediaries say that the Supreme God created the stars, originated them and brought them into existence, and then these stars create plants and animals in this lower world? So it is established that although the setting of the stars indicates their createdness, it does not prevent them from being lords for humans and gods for this world.

Our answer: here we have two stages.

The first stage: let the meaning of "lord" and "god" be the existent being in whom needs are cut off. Once it is established by the setting of the stars that they are created, and it is established in the immediate judgment of minds that everything created is in its existence needy of something else, it becomes necessary to affirm that these stars in their existence need something other than themselves. And once this meaning is established, it is impossible for them to be lords and gods in the sense that needs are cut off at their existence. Thus it is established that their being setting necessitates impugning their being lords and gods in this interpretation.

The second stage: let the meaning of "lord" and "god" be the one who is the creator of us and the originator of our essences and attributes. We say: the setting of the stars indicates that they are incapable of creating and originating, and that it is not permissible to worship them. Its explanation is in several ways:

The first: their setting indicates their createdness. Their createdness indicates their need for an eternal, powerful agent. And the powerfulness of that powerful one must be eternal; otherwise his powerfulness would need another powerful one, and this would lead to an infinite regress, which is impossible. Thus it is established that his powerfulness is eternal.

Having established this, we say: a thing that is capable for Him is capable for Him only by virtue of its possibility, and possibility is one in all possibles. Thus it is established that what is the basis for some possibles being capable for God Most High is present in all possibles, so it is necessary that all possibles be capable for God Most High.

[Page 45]

Once this is established, it follows that none of the contingent things can come into existence through other than Him, as we have shown, by definitive proofs in the science of the foundations (*'ilm al-usul*), the validity of these positions.

The conclusion is that it has been established by proof that the setting of the stars indicates that they are originated (*muhdathah*). Although this meaning is established only through many premises. Also, their being originated in themselves necessitates the judgment that they cannot be capable of creating and originating. Although this meaning is established only through many premises. The proofs of the Qur'an mention only the basic premises. As for elaboration and detail, that belongs to the science of dialectic (*'ilm al-jadal*). When God Most High mentioned these two premises in a allusive manner (*'ala sabil al-ramz*), He was content to mention them alone in explaining that the stars have no power to create and originate. For this reason, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) argued from their setting to the impossibility of their being lords and gods over the events of this world.

The second aspect: the setting of the stars indicates their origination, and their origination indicates that in their existence they need a Creator who is powerful and chooses. That agent is the one who created the spheres and the stars. Whoever is capable of creating the stars and spheres without any intermediary whatsoever is all the more capable of creating man, since the one who can create the greater thing must necessarily be able to create the lesser thing. This is alluded to in His saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir 40:57], and in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, and He is the All-Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:81]. Thus it has been established by this method that the Supreme God must be capable of creating mankind and of governing the lower world without the mediation of the celestial bodies. Since this is the case, devotion to the Supreme God is more fitting than devotion to the sun, the stars, and the moon.

The third aspect: if it were valid that some of the stars were originators and creators, this possibility would remain for all of them. In that case, a person would not know whether his Creator is this star, that other one, or the totality of the stars, and he would remain doubtful about knowing his Creator. But if we know the totality and attribute creation, origination, and governance to the Creator of the totality, then we can know the Creator and Originator, and we can devote ourselves to worshipping Him and thanking Him. Thus it has been established by these aspects that just as the setting of the stars indicates the impossibility of their being eternal, it likewise indicates the impossibility of their being gods of this world and lords of animals and humans. And God knows best. This is the full account of the establishment of this proof.

If it is said: There is no doubt that that night was preceded by a day and a night, and the setting of the stars, the moon, and the sun occurred during the previous night and the previous day. By this explanation, the setting that occurred on that night has no additional benefit.

The answer: We have explained that he (may the blessings and peace of God be upon him) presented this proof only to the people whom he was calling away from worshipping the stars toward monotheism. It is not unlikely to say that he (peace be upon him) was sitting with those people one night and was rebuking them for worshipping the stars. While he was in the midst of establishing that discourse, his gaze fell upon a shining star. When it set, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: "If this star were a god, it would not have moved from ascending to setting, and from strength to weakness." Then, in the course of that discourse, the moon rose and set. So he repeated that discourse to them, and the same applies to the sun. This is the sum of what comes to mind regarding the establishment of Ibrahim's proof, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him.

Sixth issue: Al-Ghazali philosophized in some of his books and interpreted the star as the animal rational soul that belongs to each star, the moon as the rational soul that belongs to each sphere, and the sun as the immaterial intellect (*'aql mujarrad*) that belongs to all of these. Abu 'Ali ibn Sina used to interpret setting as possibility (*imkan*). Al-Ghazali claimed that what is meant by their setting is their possibility in themselves, and he claimed that what is meant by His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ is that all these things are contingent in their existence by their essences (*mumkin al-wujud li-dhatiha*), and every contingent thing must have an effector, and it must ultimately lead to the Necessary Existent (*wajib al-wujud*).

Know that this discourse is not objectionable. However, it is far-fetched to apply the wording of the verse to it. Some people interpreted the star as the sense perception, the moon as the imagination and the estimative faculty, and the sun as the intellect. What is meant is that these three perceptive faculties are deficient and finite, and that the Governor of the world has dominion over them and subdues them. And God knows best.

* * *

Seventh issue: His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ indicates several rulings:

[Page 46]

First ruling: This verse indicates that God Most High is not a body, for if He were a body, He would be absent from us forever, and thus would be setting forever. Also, it is impossible that God Most High descend from the Throne to the heaven at one time and ascend from the heaven to the Throne at another, for otherwise the meaning of setting would be realized.

Second ruling: This verse indicates that God Most High is not a locus for originated attributes, as the Karramiyyah claim, for otherwise He would be changing, and then the meaning of setting would be realized, and that is impossible.

Third ruling: This verse indicates that religion must be based on proof and not on blind imitation (*taqlid*), for otherwise this argument would have no benefit whatsoever.

Fourth ruling: This verse indicates that the prophets' knowledge of their Lord is acquired through reasoning (*istidlaliyyah*) and not necessary (*darurriyyah*), for otherwise Ibrahim would not have needed to argue.

Fifth ruling: This verse indicates that there is no way to attain knowledge of God Most High except through reflection and reasoning about the conditions of His creatures, for if knowledge of Him could be attained by another way, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) would not have turned to this method. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my Lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾

Concerning it there are two issues:

First issue: It is said: "The moon rose (*bazagha*)" when it began to rise, and "the sun rose" when the beginning of its rising appeared, and "rising stars" (*nujum bawazigh*). Al-Azhari said: It seems to be derived from *al-bazgh*, which is splitting, as if with its light it splits the darkness. The meaning of the verse is that he considered the moon in the same manner as he considered the star.

Second issue: His saying ﴿Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾ indicates that guidance is only from God Most High. The word "guidance" cannot be taken to mean enablement (*al-tamakkun*), removal of excuses, or setting up proofs, because all of that was already present. Thus the guidance he was seeking after those things had been realized must necessarily be something additional to them.

Know that the view that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) held our position is too clear to be confused by any intelligent person, for in this verse he attributed guidance to God Most High, and likewise in His saying: ﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:78], and likewise in His saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim 14:35].

* * *

[Page 47]

As for His saying: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my Lord; this is greater."﴾ there are several issues:

First issue: He said "this" about the sun even though it is feminine, and he did not say "this one" (*hadhihi*), for several reasons:

One: The sun (*al-shams*) is in meaning light and radiance, so the word was taken in its interpreted sense and was made masculine.

Two: The sun has no feminine marker in it, so when its wording resembled the masculine wording and its interpretation was the interpretation of light, the masculine was permissible for these two reasons.

Three: He meant "this rising one" or "this that I see."

Four: The purpose of it is observing courtesy, which is avoiding the feminine when mentioning a word that indicates lordship.

Second issue: His saying ﴿This is greater﴾: what is meant is the greatest of the stars in body and the strongest in power, so it was more deserving of divinity.

If it is said: Since setting occurs in the sun, and setting prevents the attribute of lordship, once it is established that the attribute of lordship is impossible for the sun, its being impossible for the moon and the rest of the stars is even more so. By this method it becomes clear that mentioning this statement about the sun suffices instead of mentioning it about the moon and the stars. So why did he not limit himself to mentioning the sun, for the sake of brevity and conciseness?

We say: Proceeding from the lesser to the lesser, ascending to the higher and the highest, has a kind of effect in explanation, clarification, and emphasis that cannot be obtained otherwise, so mentioning it in this way is preferable.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, I am free from what you associate."﴾ the meaning is that, since it has been established by proof that these stars are not fit for lordship and divinity, he therefore disassociated himself from polytheism.

One may say: Grant that it has been established by proof that the stars, the sun, and the moon are not fit for lordship and divinity; yet this does not necessarily entail the negation of partners in an absolute sense and the affirmation of absolute monotheism. So why did he, on the basis of the establishment of the proof that these stars are not fit for lordship, proceed to firmly affirm monotheism absolutely?

The answer: The people were in agreement on the negation of all other partners, and they only disputed this specific form. When it was established by proof that these things are neither lords nor gods, and by consensus the negation of others was established, the firm negation of partners in absolute terms was therefore realized.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾ there are two issues:

First issue: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim pronounced the *ya'* in "wajhiya" with a fatha, and the rest did not pronounce this fatha.

Second issue: This statement cannot be taken in its apparent sense; rather, what is meant is "I have directed my worship and my obedience." The reason for the permissibility of this figurative usage is that whoever obeys another and submits to his command turns his face toward him, so turning the face toward him is made a metaphor for obedience.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿to Him who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ there is a subtle point: He did not say "I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth," but rather left out this wording and said "I have turned my face to Him who..." The meaning is that the turning of the face of the heart is not toward Him, for He is exalted above place and direction; rather, the turning of the face of the heart is toward serving and obeying Him for the sake of His servanthood. Therefore, the omission of the word "toward" (*ila*) here and the sufficiency of the preposition *li* ("to/for") is clear evidence that the object of worship is exalted above place and direction. The meaning of *fatara* is that He brought the two into existence, and its root is from splitting; it is said: "the tree split open (*tafattara*) with leaves and flowers" when it brings them forth. As for *hanif*, it means one who inclines. Abu al-'Aliyah said: The *hanif* is one who faces the House (the Ka'bah) in his prayer. It was also said: it is one who turns away from every object of worship other than God Most High.

Page 39

The commentary on the verses 76 to 79:

God the Exalted said: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾ ﴿When he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ ﴿When he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, I am free of what you associate with God."﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth, as a upright monotheist, and I am not of those who associate others with God.﴾

Page 39 (continued)

In this verse there are several issues.

First issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿When the night covered him﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying ﴿Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾, and His saying ﴿And thus We showed﴾ is a clause placed as a parenthetical interjection between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

Second issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: It is said "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" and "ajannahu al-layl" (both meaning the night covered him). It is said of everything you conceal: "janna" and "ajanna." It is also said: "jannahu al-layl," but the preferred form is "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" and "ajannahu al-layl." This is the statement of all the lexicographers. The meaning of "janna" is "to conceal," and from it come al-jannah (the garden), al-jinn (the jinn), al-junun (madness), al-jann (the hidden), al-janin (the fetus), al-mijann (shield), al-janan (cover), al-mujann (the shield) and al-majannah (the grave), all of which return in origin to concealment and hiding. Some grammarians said: "janna ʿalayhi al-layl" means that the night became dark upon him; for this reason "ʿalā" enters after it, just as you say "aẓlama." As for "jannahu," it means he concealed it, without implying the meaning of "aẓlama."

Third issue: Know that most of the exegetes mentioned that the king of that time saw a dream, and the interpreters of dreams interpreted it as meaning that a boy would be born who would contend with him for his kingdom. So that king ordered the slaughter of every boy who was born. Ibrahim's mother conceived him and did not reveal her pregnancy to the people. When her labor came, she went to a cave in a mountain, gave birth to Ibrahim, and sealed the entrance with a stone. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came and put his finger in the infant's mouth, and he sucked it, and his provision came out of it. Gabriel, peace be upon him, took care of him, and his mother would come to him occasionally and nurse him. He remained in this state until he grew up, understood, and realized that he had a Lord. He asked his mother and said to her: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "And who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said to the father: "And who is your lord?" He said: "The king of the land."
