His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How should I fear what you have associated [with Allah], while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has not sent down to you any authority? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you should know?﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing – for them there is security, and they are [rightly] guided.﴾

Know that this is part of the continuation of the answer to the earlier speech. The implied meaning is: how should I fear the idols, which have no power to benefit or harm, while you do not fear [the consequences of] shirk, which is the greatest of sins?

As for His saying ﴿for which He has not sent down to you any authority﴾, there are two interpretations:

First: His saying ﴿for which He has not sent down to you any authority﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for the impossibility of any proof or authority existing for such a matter. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 117], meaning that there cannot be any proof for it.

Second: It is not rationally impossible that one be commanded to take those images and figures as a qibla for supplication and prayer. So His saying ﴿for which He has not sent down to you any authority﴾ means: the absence of any command concerning it. The summary of this speech is: "Why do you deny me security in a place of security, and do you not deny yourselves security in a place of fear?" He did not say, "So which of us has more right to security, I or you?", to avoid praising himself; so he turned away from that to His saying ﴿which of the two parties﴾, meaning the two parties of polytheists and monotheists. Then he resumed the answer to the question with His saying ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾. This is part of the completion of Abraham's speech in the argument, and the meaning is: those who attain absolute security are those who combine these two attributes:

The first of them: belief (iman), which is the perfection of the theoretical faculty.

The second of them: ﴿and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, which is the perfection of the practical faculty.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They are the ones for whom there is security, and they are [rightly] guided.﴾ Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) hold to this verse in one respect, and the Mu'tazilah hold to it in another respect.

As for the way our companions hold to it: we say that He, may He be exalted, made the absence of wrongdoing a condition for the belief that entails security. If abstaining from wrongdoing were one of the constituent parts of the name "belief", this restriction would be pointless. Thus it is established that the grave sinner (fasiq) is a believer, and by this the saying of the Mu'tazilah is refuted. As for the way the Mu'tazilah hold to it: He, may He be exalted, made the attainment of security conditional upon two things together, belief and the absence of wrongdoing; therefore security must not be attained by the grave sinner, and that entails that he incurs the threat (wa'id).

Our companions answered this in two ways:

The first answer: by ﴿and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ is meant wrongdoing as shirk, based on His saying, may He be exalted, quoting Luqman when he said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13]. So what is meant here is those who believe in Allah and do not ascribe to Allah a partner in worship.

The proof that this is what is meant is that this story, from its beginning to its end, was revealed only to negate partners, rivals and equals, and it contains no mention of acts of obedience or worship; therefore the wrongdoing here must be understood as that.

The second answer: the threat against the grave sinner among the people of prayer is such that Allah may punish him, and it is possible that He may pardon him. In either case, security is removed and fear is present; so from the absence of security it does not follow with certainty that punishment will occur. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 83:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His words "And that" (wa-tilka) refer to a statement that preceded, and there are several views on it:

The first: it refers to his words, ﴿I do not like those that set.﴾

Page 51

The second: it refers to the fact that the people said to him: "Are you not afraid that our gods will afflict you with madness because you have insulted them?" He said to them: "Are you not afraid, you who have committed shirk against God and equated in worship between the Creator and Manager of the world and the carved wood and the made idol?"

The third: that the intended meaning is all of these.

Having understood this, we say: His words "And that" (wa-tilka) is a subject (mubtada'), His words ﴿Our argument﴾ are its predicate (khabar), and His words ﴿which We gave to Abraham﴾ are a qualifier (sifah) of that predicate.

The second issue: His words ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham﴾ indicate that this argument came to be in the intellect of Abraham, peace be upon him, through God's giving it and His manifesting that argument in his intellect. This indicates that faith and disbelief only come about by the creation of God, exalted is He. This is further confirmed by His words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, for the meaning is that God, exalted is He, raised the degrees of Abraham because God gave him that argument. Had the attainment of knowledge of that argument come from Abraham and not from God, exalted is He, then Abraham, peace be upon him, would have been the one who raised the degrees of his own self, and then His words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ would have been false. Thus it is established that this is the clear statement of our position on the question of guidance and misguidance.

The third issue: this verse is among the strongest proofs against the corrupt view of the Hashwiyya (literalists) in criticizing reflection (nazar), establishing the argument, and mentioning evidence. This is because God established for Abraham, peace be upon him, the attainment of elevation and success in high degrees, because he mentioned the argument concerning monotheism, established it, and defended it. That indicates that there is no rank after prophethood and messengership higher or more noble than this rank.

The fourth issue: Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "darajat" (degrees) with tanwin, without an annexation (idafah), while the rest read it with idafah. The meaning of the first reading is: We raise whom We will to many degrees, so "man" is in the accusative position. Ibn Muqsim said: this reading is more indicative of some being preferred over others in rank and elevation. Abu 'Amr said: the idafah indicates a single degree and many degrees, while the tanwin indicates only many degrees.

The fifth issue: They differed regarding these degrees. It was said: they are the degrees of his deeds in the Hereafter. It was said: those arguments are lofty degrees, because they necessitate great reward. It was said: We raise whom We will in this world through prophethood and wisdom, and in the Hereafter through Paradise and reward. It was said: We raise by degrees whom We will through knowledge. Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs that perfect happiness lies in spiritual attributes and in distance from corporeal attributes.

The proof for this is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people.﴾

Then He said after it: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾ This indicates that the cause for the attainment of this elevation is the giving of that argument. This requires that the soul's standing upon the reality of that argument and its being informed of its radiance necessitated the rising of the spirit from the depths of the corporeal world to the heights of the spiritual world. This indicates that there is no elevation and no happiness except in spiritual matters. And God knows best.

As for the meaning of ﴿Wise, Knowing﴾, the meaning is that He raises by degrees only whom He wills in accordance with wisdom and knowledge, not by the dictates of desire or recklessness, for the acts of God are free from futility, corruption and falsehood.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 84–88 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided, and Noah We guided before, and from his descendants David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿And Zachariah and John and Jesus and Elias; each was of the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot; and each We preferred above the worlds.﴾ ﴿And from their fathers and their descendants and their brothers; We chose them and guided them to a straight path.﴾ ﴿That is the guidance of God; He guides therewith whom He wills of His servants. And had they associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been lost from them.﴾

There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, related about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he manifested God's proof concerning monotheism, supported it, and defended it, He enumerated the aspects of His blessings and favour upon him.

The first of them is His saying: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham.﴾ The meaning is: "It is We who gave him that argument, guided him to it, and made his intellect comprehend its reality." He mentioned Himself with the expression that indicates majesty, which is the plural of grandeur, in accordance with what great kings say: "We did, We said, We mentioned." When He mentioned Himself here with the expression that indicates majesty, that majesty must be complete, lofty and noble, and this indicates that God's giving Abraham, peace be upon him, that argument is among the noblest blessings and the most excellent grades of gifts and bestowals.

The second: He, exalted is He, singled him out with elevation and with reaching the lofty and high ranks. This is His saying: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾

The third: He made him honoured in this world, because He made the noblest of people, namely the prophets and messengers, from his progeny and descendants, and He perpetuated this honour in his offspring until the Day of Resurrection, for one of the greatest kinds of joy is a person's knowledge that prophets and kings will come from his lineage. The purpose of these verses is to enumerate the kinds of God's blessings upon Abraham, peace be upon him, as a reward for his standing in defence of the proofs of monotheism. So He said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac⁠﻿﻿﻿ ⁠﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿ ⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ ⁠

Then God Most High said: ﴿That is the guidance of God; He guides with it whom He wills of His servants﴾. Know that this guidance must be understood as the knowledge of monotheism (tawhid) and the declaring of God Most High free of association (shirk), because He said after it: ﴿And if they had associated, what they used to do would have been nullified for them﴾. This indicates that the meaning of that guidance is what functions as the opposite of association.

Since it has been established that the meaning of this guidance is the knowledge of God's oneness, and since He Most High has stated explicitly that this guidance is from God Most High, it follows that faith (iman) is not attained except by the creation (khalq) of God Most High. Then He Most High concluded this verse by negating association, saying: ﴿And if they had associated﴾. The meaning is that these prophets, if they had associated, their acts of obedience and their worship would have been nullified for them. The purpose of this is to establish monotheism and to invalidate the path of association. As for the discussion of the reality of nullification (ihbat), we have treated it exhaustively in Surat al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 89:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment, and the prophethood. If these disbelieve in them, We have already entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them.﴾

Page 56
Know that His saying, "Those" (ulā'ika), is a reference to those whose mention preceded it, namely the eighteen prophets whom God Exalted mentioned before this, and then God Exalted mentioned that He gave them the Book, the judgment, and the prophethood.

Know that conjunction (al-ʿatf) necessitates difference, so these three terms must indicate three distinct matters.

Know that the judges over creation are of three groups:

The first: those who judge the inner states of people and their souls, and they are the scholars (ʿulamāʾ).

The second: those who judge the outward aspects of creation, and they are the sultans, who govern people by force and dominion.

The third: the prophets, who are those to whom God Exalted gave knowledge and insights by which they are able to exercise control over the inner states of creation and their souls. Also, He gave them power and capacity by which they are able to exercise control over the outward aspects of creation. Since they combined these two attributes, they were without doubt the judges in the absolute sense.

Once you have understood this introduction, His saying, ﴿We gave them the Book﴾, is a reference to His giving them abundant knowledge. His saying, "the judgment" (al-ḥukm), is a reference to His making them judges over people, whose judgment was binding upon them according to the outward appearance. His saying, "and the prophethood," is a reference to the third rank, which is the lofty, elevated, noble degree upon the attainment of which the attainment of the two preceding ranks is based. People have many interpretations of these three terms, and what we have mentioned is what we prefer.

Know that His saying, ﴿We gave them the Book﴾, may mean by this giving the initial bestowal of revelation and the sending down of it upon him, as in the scrolls of Abraham, the Torah of Moses, the Gospel of Jesus, and the Qur'an of Muhammad (ﷺ). It may also mean that God gives him a complete understanding of what is in the Book and comprehensive knowledge of its realities and secrets. This is the preferable view, because God did not send down to each of the eighteen mentioned prophets a divine book specifically and individually.

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾, and what is meant is: if the disbelievers of Quraysh disbelieve in this monotheism and in the denunciation of polytheism, ﴿We have already entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. On this there are issues:

First issue: they differed about who that people are, in several views.

It was said: they are the people of Medina, namely the Helpers (Anṣār).

It was said: the Emigrants and the Helpers.

Al-Hasan said: they are the eighteen prophets mentioned earlier, and this is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Zajjaj said: the evidence for this is His saying, Exalted, after this verse: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾.

Abu Rajaʾ said: it means the angels, and this is far-fetched, because the word "people" (qawm) rarely applies to other than the children of Adam.

Mujahid said: they are the Persians.

Ibn Zayd said: whoever does not disbelieve is among them, whether he is a king, a prophet, one of the Companions, or one of the Successors.

Second issue: His saying, Exalted, ﴿We have already entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾, indicates that He created them only for faith. As for others, God did not create them for faith; for if God had created all for faith, then the clarification and the empowering and the performance of the favours would have been shared between the believer and the non-believer, and then His saying ﴿We have already entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾ would have no meaning.

Al-Kaʿbi answered this from two aspects:

The first: that God, at their faith and after it, increased the believers in His favours, benefits, and noble rulings in what none but God can count. And in the answer he mentioned a second aspect, saying: Even supposing that He equalized (them), some of them would, if they fell short and did not benefit, be such that it is valid to say, according to the outward appearance, that the blessings of God did not reach him, like a father who equalizes between two children in giving, yet it is valid to say that he gave one of them and not the other when that other has wasted and corrupted it.

Know that the first answer is weak, because the favours inviting to faith are shared between the disbeliever and the believer; and specification is not permissible according to the Mu'tazila. The second is also invalid, because when the father equalized between the two children in giving, and then one of them squandered his share, what sensible person would be permitted to say that the father did not bestow favour upon him and did not give him anything?

Third issue: this verse indicates that God Exalted will support His Prophet, strengthen his religion, and make him dominant over everyone who opposes him, victorious over everyone who disputes with him. What God Exalted reported in this place has occurred, so this is in the manner of reporting the unseen, and therefore it is a miracle. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance. Say: I do not ask you any reward for it; it is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: There is no doubt that His saying ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided﴾ refers to the prophets mentioned earlier, and there is no doubt that His saying ﴿so follow their guidance﴾ is a command to Muhammad, peace be upon him. The discussion concerns determining the matter in which God commanded Muhammad to follow them. Some people said: The intended meaning is that he follows them in the matter upon which they all agreed, namely the affirmation of tawhid (the oneness of God) and His transcendence above everything unfitting to Him in His essence, attributes, actions and all rational matters. Others said: The intended meaning is following them in all noble characteristics and sublime, perfect qualities, such as patience over the harm of the foolish and pardoning them. Others said: The intended meaning is following them in their laws (shara'i'), except what the evidence specifies; and on this interpretation this verse is evidence that the law of those before us binds us. Others said: He, exalted is He, only mentioned the prophets in the preceding verse to show that they were guarded against shirk (associating partners with God), striving to nullify it, as evidenced by His concluding that verse with His saying: ﴿And had they associated partners with God, what they used to do would have been nullified for them﴾. Then He affirmed their persistence in monotheism and their rejection of shirk with His saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, We have already entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾.

Then He said in this verse: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided﴾, i.e., guided them to nullifying shirk and affirming tawhid, ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, i.e., follow them in negating shirk, affirming tawhid, and bearing the foolishness of the ignorant in this matter. Others said: The wording is absolute, so it is to be understood in its entirety, except what a separate (munfasil) evidence specifies. The judge (al-Qadi) said: It is far-fetched to take this verse as a command to the Messenger to follow the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, in their laws, for several reasons:

The first: their laws are different and contradictory, so it is not valid, given their contradiction, that he be commanded to follow them in those contradictory rulings.

The second: guidance refers to the proof (dalil), not to the act itself.

Page 58

And if this is established, we say: the proof for the continuation of their law was specific to those times and not to other times, so following them in that guidance would mean knowing the obligation of those acts only at those times. How could one derive from this the following of their laws at all times?

The third: that he, peace be upon him, following them in their laws would require that his station be lower than theirs, and that is invalid by consensus. Thus it has been established by these considerations that this verse cannot be taken to mean the obligation to follow them in their laws.

As for the answer to the first: His saying ﴿so follow their guidance﴾ encompasses everything. As for what you mentioned about some rulings being contradictory according to their laws, we say: that general statement must be restricted in this instance, and it remains a proof regarding the rest.

As for the answer to the second: if he were commanded to reason with the same proof that the earlier prophets used, that would not be following; for when the Muslims reasoned from the createdness of the world to the existence of the Creator, it is not said that they are following the Jews and Christians in this matter. This is because the one who reasons with a proof is original in that ruling and has no connection whatsoever with those before him, and following and imitation only occur when the act of the first is a cause for the obligation of the act upon the second. By this explanation the objection falls away.

As for the answer to the third: God, exalted is He, commanded the Messenger to follow all of them in all noble qualities and honorable characteristics, and that does not entail that he is of lower rank than them; rather it entails that he is of higher rank than all of them, as will be explained later, God willing. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that this verse indicates that the law of those before us binds us.

The second issue: Scholars have used this verse as evidence that our Messenger, peace be upon him, is more excellent than all the prophets, peace be upon them. The argument is this: we have shown that the qualities of perfection and attributes of nobility were distributed among all of them. David and Solomon were among those who were thankful for blessings; Job was among those who were patient in trial; Joseph combined both of these states; Moses, peace be upon him, was the possessor of a strong, dominant law and manifest miracles; Zechariah, John, Jesus and Elijah were people of asceticism; Ishmael was the possessor of truthfulness; Jonah was the one who humbly supplicated. Thus it is established that God mentioned each of these prophets because the predominant trait in each was a specific one of the praiseworthy and noble qualities. Then, when He mentioned them all, He commanded Muhammad, peace be upon him, to follow all of them together. So the implication is as if God had commanded Muhammad ﷺ to gather from the qualities of servanthood and obedience all the attributes that were distributed among all of them. When God commanded him with this, it is impossible to say that he fell short in attaining them; thus it is established that he attained them. And when this is the case, it is established that he combined in himself the qualities of goodness that were scattered among all of them. And when this is the case, it must be said that he is more excellent than all of them collectively. And God knows best.

The third issue: Al-Wahidi said: His saying (guided by God) is evidence that they were specially favored with guidance, for if He had guided all the obligated people, His saying ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided﴾ would have no point of specification.

The fourth issue: Al-Wahidi said: Linguistically, iqtida' (following an example) means the second person performing the same act as the first because the first performed it. Al-Lihyani related from al-Kisa'i that he said: one says, "li bika qudwah" and "qidwah" (I have an example in you).

Page 59

The fifth issue: Al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿iqtadih﴾ with a kasra on the dal and with a damma on the ha due to the kasra, without a following yā'; and the others recited ﴿iqtadih﴾ with a sukun on the ha. However, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i delete it in connected speech (wasl) and affirm it in pausal speech (waqf), while the others affirm it in both connected speech and pausal speech.
In summary: consensus has been reached on affirming it in pausal speech. Al-Wahidi said: The correct form is affirmation in pausal speech and deletion in connected speech, because this ha' is a ha' that occurs in the sakta (the brief pause) in the position of the hamzat al-wasl at the beginning, since the ha' is for pausing just as the hamzat al-wasl is for beginning with a consonant cluster. Just as the hamzah does not appear in connected speech, so too the ha' should not appear except that those who affirmed it intended to conform to the Mushaf, for the ha' is written in the script, so they disliked departing from the script in both pausal and connected speech, and so they affirmed it. As for the recitation of Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Mujahid said: this is an error, because this ha' is the ha' of pausal speech, so it is not inflected in any situation; it is mentioned only to show the vowel of what precedes it. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: It is not an error; its basis is that the ha' is taken as a pronoun referring to the verbal noun (masdar), and the sense is: "So follow their guidance, follow the following (al-iqtida')," so the verbal noun is implied by the indication of the verb. Its analogy, when pausing, is that the ha' be made quiescent, because the ha' of the pronoun is made quiescent in pausal speech, as you say: ishtarih (buy it). And God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it﴾, its meaning is that when God commanded him to follow the guidance of the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, and among their guidance was abandoning the seeking of wages in conveying the religion and delivering the law, he therefore followed them in that, saying: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it﴾, nor do I seek from you wealth or payment. And His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ indicates that he, peace be upon him, was sent to all the people of the world, not to one people to the exclusion of others. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 91 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said, "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being." Say, "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people, which you make into scrolls, displaying them while concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say, "Allah." Then leave them in their discourse, playing.﴾

Know that we have mentioned in this book that the core of the Qur'an's concern rests upon establishing tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), prophethood (nubuwwah), and the return (ma'ad). He, exalted is He, when He related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he presented the proof of tawhid and the refutation of shirk, and Allah confirmed that proof with clear demonstrations, then proceeded after it to establish the matter of prophethood, saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾, since they denied prophethood and messengership. This is the explanation of the coherence of these verses, and that it is at the utmost of beauty. In the verse there are issues:

Issue one: Concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾, there are several views:

Ibn 'Abbas said: they did not magnify Allah with His true magnification. It is also narrated from him that he said its meaning is: they did not believe that Allah is capable of all things.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: they did not describe Him with His true description. Al-Akhfash said: they did not know Him with His true knowledge. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, verified this, saying: it is said "qaddara al-shay'" when one tests and examines a thing, desiring to know its measure; one says "qadara yaqduru qadran." From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "If it is cloudy over you, then estimate for it (faqdurū lahu)," meaning: seek to know it. This is its origin in the language. Then he said: it is said of one who knows a thing that he measures its measure, and if he does not know it with its attributes, then he does not measure its measure. So His saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ is correct in all the meanings mentioned.

Issue two: When He related of them that they did not measure Allah with His true measure, He explained the cause of it, which is their saying: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being."

Know that everyone who denies prophethood and messengership in reality has not known Allah with His true knowledge, and its demonstration is through several aspects:

The first: the one who denies resurrection and messengership either says that He, exalted is He, has not imposed any obligation upon any of creation at all, or says that He imposed obligations upon them. The first is false, because that would entail that He permitted for them all abominations and vices, such as reviling Allah, describing Him with what is not befitting to Him, belittling the prophets, messengers and the people of religion, turning away from thanking blessings, and repaying favour with harm. It is known that all of that is false. Or he concedes that He imposed commands and prohibitions upon creation, and in this case there must be a conveyor, a legislator and an explainer, and that is none but the Messenger.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that reason suffices for the obligation of duties and avoidance of what is repugnant?

We reply: Grant that the matter is as you say, yet it is not impossible to confirm the rational knowledge by the instructions legislated upon the tongues of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them. Thus it is established that everyone who prevents sending of prophets and messengers has impugned the wisdom of Allah, the exalted, and that is ignorance of the attribute of Divinity, and at that point His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ is true of him.

The second aspect in establishing this meaning: some people say that the sending of prophets and messengers is impossible, because it is impossible for a miracle to be manifested in accordance with his claim as confirmation of him. Those who hold this view have two positions:

The first position: that they say it is not within possibility to break customs or to bring about anything contrary to what custom has established.

The second position: those who concede the possibility of that, but they say that even granting the occurrence of these extraordinary acts that break customs, they have no indication of the truthfulness of the one claiming messengership. Both aspects entail a defect in the perfection of the power of Allah, the exalted.

As for the first position: it is established that bodies are alike, and it is established that what one thing can bear, its like must be able to bear. If that is so, then the body of the sun and the moon is capable of being torn and split.

If we say that the God is not capable of it, that would be a description of Him with incapacity and deficiency of power, and at that point it is true of this speaker: that he did not measure Allah with His true measure.

And if we say that He, exalted is He, is capable of it, then rationally there is no impossibility in the splitting of the moon or the occurrence of all other miracles.

As for the second position, namely that the occurrence of these extraordinary acts at the claim of one claiming prophethood indicates their truthfulness, this too is evident as is established in the books of the principles of jurisprudence. Thus it is established that everyone who denies the possibility of prophethood and messengership has described Allah with incapacity and deficiency of power, and everyone who says that has not measured Allah with His true measure.

The third aspect: since the createdness of the world has been established, we say: its having been created indicates that the God of the world is powerful, knowing and wise, and that all creation are His servants, and He is their owner absolutely and their king absolutely. The king who is obeyed must have command, prohibition and obligation over his servants, and must have promise for obedience and threat for disobedience. That is not complete nor perfected except by sending messengers and sending down books. So everyone who denies that has impugned His being a king who is obeyed, and whoever believes that has not measured Allah with His true measure. Thus it is established that everyone who says: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being" has not measured Allah with His true measure.

* * *

Issue three: In this verse there is a difficult discussion, which is to say: those whom Allah related as having said: ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾ — either it is said that they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, or it is said that they are the People of the Book among the Jews and Christians. If it is the first, then how is it possible to refute their statement with His saying: ﴿Who sent down the Book which Moses brought﴾? Because the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Brahmins, just as they deny the messengership of Muhammad (ﷺ), likewise they deny the messengership of all other prophets, so how is it fitting to direct this argument against them? As for if it is the second, namely that the speaker of this saying is a group of Jews and Christians, this too is difficult and problematic, because they do not say this statement, and how would they say it when their doctrine is that the Torah is a Book that Allah sent down upon Moses, and the Gospel is a Book that Allah sent down upon Jesus? Furthermore, this surah is Meccan, and the debates that occurred between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Jews and Christians were all Medinan, so how is it possible to apply this verse to them? This is the statement of the problem standing in this verse. Know that people differed concerning it in two views:

The first view: this verse was revealed concerning the Jews, and this is the well-known view among the majority. "Ibn 'Abbas said: Malik ibn al-Sayf was one of the rabbis and leaders of the Jews, and he was a fat man. He entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: I adjure you by Allah, who sent down the Torah upon Moses, do you find in it that Allah hates the fat rabbi, and you are the fat rabbi, and you have grown fat from the things the Jews feed you?" The people laughed, and Malik ibn al-Sayf became angry. Then he turned to 'Umar and said: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being." His people said to him: "Woe to you, what is this that has reached us from you?" He said: "It angered me." Then the Jews, because of this statement, removed him from their leadership and put Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf in his place. This is the well-known narration concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, and there are questions regarding it:

The first question: the wording, though it is general according to the basic language, may be restricted by custom. Do you not see that when a woman wants to leave the house and the husband becomes angry and says: "If you leave the house, you are divorced," many jurists have said: the wording, though general, is restricted by custom to that one occasion. So likewise here, the saying: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being" — though general according to the basic language, it is restricted by custom to that incident, so his saying: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being" means: Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being regarding His hating the fat rabbi,

and when this general statement is taken as restricted by this restriction, His saying: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought" does not nullify his statement. This is one of the questions.

The second question: Malik ibn al-Sayf was proud of being a Jew, openly displaying that, and with this doctrine it is utterly unlikely that he would say: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being," except in a manner of anger that bewilders the mind, or in a manner where the tongue cannot restrain itself. And it does not befit Allah, glorified and exalted is He, to send down the Qur'an, which remains for all time, in refutation of this kind of speech.

The third question: most have agreed that this surah is Meccan and was revealed all at once, while the debates of the Jews with the Messenger, peace be upon him, were Medinan. How then is it possible to apply this verse to that debate? Also, since the surah was revealed all at once, how can it be said that this particular verse was revealed concerning that specific incident? These are the questions that arise against this view. The closer view in my opinion is that perhaps Malik ibn al-Sayf, when he was hurt by this speech, criticized the prophethood of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and said: "Allah has not sent down anything upon you at all, and you are not a messenger from Allah at all." At this statement this verse was revealed, and its purpose is that since you have conceded that Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Torah upon Moses, peace be upon him, then at this point you cannot insist that He has sent down nothing upon me, because I am a human being and Moses is also a human being. Since you have conceded that Allah, exalted is He, sent down revelation and scripture upon a human being, it is impossible for you to assert with certainty that Allah has sent down nothing upon me. So the purpose of this verse is to show that what Muhammad, peace be upon him, claimed is not among the impossibilities, and that it is not for the Jewish opponent to insist on denying it; rather, at most he may demand from him a miracle, and if he brings it, that is the aim, and otherwise not. Either the Jew insists that Allah has sent down nothing at all upon Muhammad, despite acknowledging that Allah sent down the Book upon Moses, and that is sheer ignorance and blind imitation. With this interpretation the answer to the first two questions becomes clear.

As for the third question, namely his saying: this surah is Meccan and was revealed all at once, each of these two points prevents saying that the cause of the revelation of this verse is the debate with a Jew.

We reply: those who hold this view say: the whole surah is Meccan and was revealed all at once, except this verse, which was revealed in Medina concerning this incident. This is the end of the discussion in establishing this view.

The second view: the speaker of this saying, namely "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being," is a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh. This view has been mentioned by some of them.

[p. 63]

It remains to be said: the disbelievers of Quraysh deny the prophethood of all the prophets, peace be upon them, so how can the prophethood of Musa (Moses) be used as an argument against them? Moreover, what follows this verse does not befit the disbelievers of Quraysh but befits the Jews, namely His words: ﴿You make it into scrolls, displaying some and concealing much; and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers.﴾ It is known by necessity that these conditions befit none but the Jews. The view of those who say that the beginning of the verse addresses the disbelievers and the end addresses the Jews is corrupt, because it requires dismantling the verse's structure (nazm) and corrupting its composition, and that is unbecoming of the finest speech, let alone the speech of the Lord of the worlds. This is the statement of the difficulty according to this view.

[p. 63 continued]

As for the first question: it can be answered by saying that the disbelievers of Quraysh were intermingled with the Jews and Christians, and they had heard from both groups, by way of tawatur (mass transmission, i.e., reports so widespread that their truth is assured), of the overwhelming miracles at the hands of Musa, peace be upon him, such as the staff turning into a serpent, the splitting of the sea, the shading of the mountain, and others. The disbelievers used to attack the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the ground that they demanded from him the like of these miracles, and they would say: "If you bring us the like of these miracles, we will believe in you." Thus the totality of these statements amounted to something that obligates them to acknowledge the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him. Since this is so, it is not far-fetched to cite the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, as an argument against them in their saying: ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being.﴾

As for the second question: its answer is that since the disbelievers of Quraysh, the Jews and the Christians were all agreed in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), it is not far-fetched that a single speech should be addressed partly to the disbelievers of Makkah and partly to the Jews and Christians. This is what comes to mind in this difficult inquiry, and success is from Allah.

The fourth issue: the view of many of the researchers (muhaqqiqun) is that the minds of created beings never reach the true reality (kunh) of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, at all. Then, many adherents of this view argue for its soundness by His words: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾, meaning, they did not know Allah with His true knowledge. But this argument is far-fetched, because He, exalted is He, mentions this expression in the Qur'an in three places, and in all of them it is directed at the disbelievers. So here it is directed at the Jews or the disbelievers of Makkah, and likewise the matter is in the other two places. In that case, this argument has no benefit left. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fifth issue: there are rulings in this verse.

The first ruling:
An indefinite noun (nakirah) in a context of negation conveys generality. The evidence for this is this verse, for His words ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾ contain an indefinite noun in a context of negation. Had it not conveyed generality, then His words ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Musa brought?﴾ would not have been a refutation of it and a counter to it. And had it not been so, the argument would have been invalid. Since that is false, it is established that an indefinite noun in a context of negation is general. And Allah knows best.

The second ruling:
Counter-argument (naqd) undermines the soundness of a statement, because He, exalted is He, countered their saying ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾ with His words ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Musa brought?﴾. Had the counter-argument not indicated the corruption of the statement, the proof of Allah would not have been effective for this aim.

Know that the saying of one who says: pointing out a difference between the two cases prevents the counter-argument from being invalidating, is weak. For if this were so, the proof of Allah in this verse would collapse, because the Jew would say: "The miracles of Musa are more manifest and more dazzling than your miracles," and thus establishing prophethood there would not necessitate establishing it here. If the difference were acceptable, this proof would collapse, and since it is impermissible to say that it collapses, we know that the counter-argument in absolute terms is invalidating. And Allah knows best.

[p. 64]

The third ruling:
Al-Ghazali (ʿAlā-l-Ghazālī) philosophized and claimed that this verse is built upon the second figure (al-shakl al-thani) of the logical figures (al-ashkal al-mantiqiyya) of syllogism. This is because its gist returns to: Musa is one upon whom Allah, exalted is He, sent down something, and none of the humans is one upon whom Allah sent down anything. From the second figure it follows that Musa was not a human, and this is an absurd impossibility (khulf muhal). This impossibility is not due to the form of the syllogism, nor to the soundness of the first premise. So nothing remains except that it follows from assuming the soundness of the second premise, namely their saying: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being," so it is necessary to hold that it is false. Thus it is established that the indication of this verse for the intended conclusion is valid only upon acknowledging the soundness of the second figure of the logical figures, and upon acknowledging the soundness of reductio ad absurdum (qiyas al-khulf). And Allah knows best.

Know that when He, exalted is He, said ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Musa brought?﴾, He afterwards described the Book of Musa with attributes.

The first attribute: that it is a light (nur) and guidance (huda) for the people.

Know that He, exalted is He, called it a light by way of likening it to the light by which the path is made clear.

If they say: according to this interpretation, there is no difference between its being a light and its being guidance for the people, and conjoining one to the other necessitates difference.

We say: light has two attributes:
One of them: that it is in itself manifest and clear.
The second: that it is such that it is a cause for the manifestation of other things.

So what is meant by its being light and guidance are these two matters.

Know that He, exalted is He, also described the Qur'an with these two attributes in another verse, when He said: ﴿But We have made it a light, by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

The second attribute: His words ﴿You make it into scrolls, displaying some and concealing much﴾. On it are several issues:

The first issue: Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yajʿalūnahu﴾ (they make it) in the third person (ghayba). Likewise ﴿yubdūnahā﴾ (they display it) and ﴿yukhfūna﴾ (they conceal) are in the third person because they are absent. This is supported by His words: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said: Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being.﴾ Since these expressions came in the third-person form, the rest is likewise. As for the one who reads with the taʾ (second person, khitab), the implied sense is: Say to them, "You make it into scrolls, displaying some and concealing much." The evidence for this is His words ﴿and you were taught what you did not know﴾, which came in the second person, so what precedes it is likewise.

The second issue: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: His words ﴿yajʿalūnahu qarāṭīsa﴾ mean: they make it into possessors of scrolls, i.e., they deposit it in them.

If it is said: every book must be deposited in scrolls, so if this is the case for all books, what is the reason that Allah, exalted is He, relates this meaning in the context of blaming them?

We say: the blame does not fall on this meaning alone. Rather, what is meant is that when they made it into scrolls, and divided it and fragmented it, they were thereby able to display some and conceal some, and that which contained the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) was among what they concealed.

[p. 65]

If it is said: how could they be able to do that, when the Torah is a book that reached the people of the East and the West, and most of the people of knowledge recognized it and memorized it, and it is impossible to introduce addition and subtraction into such a book? The evidence for this is that a man in this age, if he wished to introduce addition and subtraction into the Qur'an, would not be able to do so; so the same holds for the Torah.

We say: we have mentioned in Surat al-Baqara that what is meant by distortion (tahrif) is interpreting the verses of the Torah with false and corrupt meanings, as the people of falsehood do in our time with the verses of the Qur'an.

If it is said: suppose that there were verses in the Torah indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), yet they were few, and the people did not conceal from the Torah anything but those verses. Why then did He say "and conceal much"?

We say: just as they concealed the verses indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), so also they concealed the verses containing rulings. Do you not see that they tried to conceal the verse containing the stoning of the married adulterer?

The third attribute: His words ﴿and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. The meaning is that the Torah contained good tidings of the coming of Muhammad, and the Jews, before the coming of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), used to recite those verses without understanding their meanings. Then when Allah sent Muhammad, it became clear that the intended meaning of those verses was his mission (ﷺ). This is the meaning of His words ﴿and you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the Torah with these three attributes, He said: "Say: Allah." The meaning is that He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book﴾, which has such and such attributes, and then said after it: "Say: Allah." The meaning is that sound reason and upright nature bear witness that a Book described with the aforementioned attributes, confirming the claim of its bearer with overwhelming and dazzling miracles like the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, can only be from Allah, exalted is He. Since this meaning became manifest through the manifestness of the decisive proof, He, exalted is He, therefore said to Muhammad: "Say: The One who sent down this Book is Allah, exalted is He." A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah﴾ [al-Anʿam: 19]. Also, the man who attempts to establish proof of the existence of the Creator says: "Who brought life into being after its absence? Who brought intellect into being after ignorance? Who placed in the eyeball the power of sight, and in the ear canal the power of hearing?" Then that same speaker himself says: "Allah." The point is that this proof and clear evidence have reached such a degree that every intelligent person must acknowledge them. So whether the opponent concedes it or not, the aim is achieved. Likewise here.

Then He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿Then leave them in their plunging, playing﴾. On it are two issues:

The first issue: the meaning is that when you have established the proof against them and reached this great degree in warnings and admonitions, then nothing of their affair remains upon you at all. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Upon you is only the conveying (of the message)﴾.

The second issue: some have said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This is far-fetched, because His words ﴿Then leave them in their plunging, playing﴾ are mentioned for the sake of threat, and that does not contradict the occurrence of fighting. Therefore the revelation of the verse that indicates the obligation of fighting does not remove anything of the implications of this verse, so no abrogation (naskh) occurs in it. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 92:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming that which is before it, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayers ever-attentive.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had refuted by proof the saying of the one who said, "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being," He mentioned after it that the Qur'an is the Book of Allah, which He sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him.

Know also that His saying "this" (*wa-hadha*) refers to the Qur'an, and He described it as a Book. The explanation of "Book" has already been given at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. Then He described it with many attributes:

**The first attribute:** His saying "We have sent it down." The purpose is to make known that it is from Allah, may He be exalted, and not from the Messenger. For it is not improbable that Allah would have singled out Muhammad (ﷺ) with many sciences by means of which he could compose the words of the Qur'an in this eloquent manner. So He, may He be exalted, made clear that the matter is not as they claim, and that He Himself undertook its sending down by revelation through the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him.

**The second attribute:** His saying, may He be exalted, "blessed" (*mubarak*). The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: a blessed Book means one whose good is abundant and whose blessing and benefit are lasting; it gives good tidings of reward and forgiveness, and it restrains from what is ugly and from disobedience. I say: knowledge is either theoretical (*nazariyyah*) or practical (*amaliyyah*). As for theoretical knowledge, the most noble and most complete of it is knowing the essence of Allah, His attributes, His acts, His rulings, and His names. You will not find this knowledge more complete or more noble than what you find in this Book. As for practical knowledge, what is sought is either the works of the limbs or the works of the hearts, and this is what is called the purification of character and the cleansing of the soul. You will not find these two kinds of knowledge like what you find in this Book. Moreover, the custom of Allah, may He be exalted, has been that whoever seeks it and holds fast to it attains the honour of this world and the felicity of the Hereafter.

The author of this book, Muhammad ibn Umar al-Razi, says: I have studied kinds of transmitted (*naqliyyah*) and rational (*aqliyyah*) sciences, yet no kind of happiness in religion and in worldly life has been attained for me through any of the sciences as much as has been attained through serving this science.

**The third attribute:** His saying ﴿confirming that which is before it﴾. The meaning is that it confirms the Books that came before it. In reality the matter is so, because what exists in the other divine Books is either the knowledge of fundamentals (*usul*) or the knowledge of branches (*furu'*).

As for the knowledge of fundamentals, variation in it cannot occur due to differences of times and places. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that what is mentioned in the Qur'an agrees and corresponds with what is in the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the rest of the divine Books.

As for the knowledge of branches, the divine Books that preceded the Qur'an contained good tidings of the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him. Since this is the case, it follows that in those Books the obligations found in them remain only until the time of the appearance of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him. After the appearance of his law, they become abrogated (*mansukhah*, subject to *naskh*). Thus it is established that those Books indicated the establishment of those rulings in this manner, and the Qur'an corresponds and agrees with this meaning. Therefore it is established that the Qur'an confirms all the divine Books in the totality of knowledge of fundamentals and branches.

**The fourth attribute:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾. Here there are several discussions:

**The first discussion:** They agreed that there is an omitted element here, and the implied meaning is: "that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities." They agreed that the Mother of Cities is Makkah, but they differed about the reason it was named by this name. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named so because the lands were spread out (*duhiyat*) from beneath it and around it. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: it was named so because it is the qiblah of the people of the world, so it is like the origin, and the rest of the lands and villages follow it. Also, among the foundations of the worship of the people of the world is the Hajj, which takes place in that town. For this reason, people gather to it as children gather to their mother. Also, since the people of the world gather there because of the Hajj, there necessarily occur there kinds of trade and benefits that do not occur in the rest of the lands. There is no doubt that earning and trade are among the foundations of livelihood. For this reason Makkah was named the Mother of Cities. It has also been said that Makkah was named the Mother of Cities because the Ka'bah is the first house that was set up for people. It has also been said that Makkah is the first town that was inhabited on earth.

Having known this, we say: His saying ﴿and those around it﴾ includes all the other towns and villages.

**The second discussion:** A group of the Jews claimed that Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, was a messenger only to the Arabs. They argued for the soundness of their claim with this verse, saying: He, may He be exalted, explained that He sent down this Qur'an upon him only so that he would convey it to the people of Makkah and to the villages surrounding it, and what is meant by them is the Arabian Peninsula. Had he been sent to all the worlds, the restriction in His saying ﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾ would have been meaningless.

The answer: the singling out of these places by mention does not indicate the negation of the ruling regarding what is other than them, except by the indication of the concept (*mafhum*), and that is weak. Especially since it has been established by clear, widespread transmission (*tawatur*), which is certain in the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, that he used to claim that he was a messenger to all the worlds. Also, His saying ﴿and those around it﴾ comprehends all the lands and villages surrounding it, and by this reckoning all the lands of the world are included. And Allah knows best.

**The third discussion:** Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read *liyundhira* with the *ya'* (the third-person form), making the Book the one who warns, because there is warning in it. Do you not see that He said: *liyundharu bihi* ("that they may be warned by it"), meaning by the Book, and He said: *wa-andhir bihi* ("and warn by it"), and He said: ﴿Indeed I only warn you by revelation﴾? So there is no impediment to attributing the warning to it by way of figurative extension (*ittisa'*). As for the others, they read *wa-litundhira* with the *ta'* (second-person form), addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), because the one commanded to warn and described as a warner is he. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], and He said: ﴿And warn by it those who fear﴾ [al-An'am: 51].

\* \* \*

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it﴾. The apparent meaning of this requires that belief in the Hereafter operates as a cause of belief in the Messenger (ﷺ). The scholars have mentioned several aspects in explaining this causal connection:

**First:** the one who believes in the Hereafter is the one who believes in the promise and threat, in reward and punishment. Whoever is like this greatly magnifies his desire to obtain reward and his fear of incurring punishment, and he exerts himself in reflection and contemplation on the proofs of monotheism (*tawhid*) and prophethood, and so he reaches knowledge and faith.

**Second:** the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, is founded upon belief in resurrection and the Last Day, and none of the prophets has placed greater emphasis on establishing this principle than is found in the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him. For this reason, belief in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, and in the truth of the Hereafter, are two mutually entailing matters.

**Third:** it is possible that the intent of this statement is to draw attention to the exclusion of the people of Makkah from accepting this religion. For what motivates one to bear the hardship of reflection and inference, and to give up worldly leadership, and to give up rancour and envy, is nothing but the desire for reward and the fear of punishment. And since the unbelievers of Makkah did not hold belief in resurrection and the Last Day, it was impossible for them to give up envy and give up leadership. Therefore it is far-fetched that they would accept this religion and acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿and they are over their prayers ever-attentive﴾. The meaning is that just as belief in the Hereafter moves a man to believe in prophethood, so it moves him to be ever-attentive to the prayers. No one may say: belief in the Hereafter moves one to all acts of obedience, so what is the benefit of singling out the prayer by mention? We say: the purpose of it is to draw attention to the fact that prayer is the most noble of acts of worship after belief in Allah, and the greatest of them in importance. Do you not see that the term "belief" (*iman*) has been applied to none of the outward acts of worship except to the prayer, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah would never make your faith (*iman*) vain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning your prayer? And the term "disbelief" (*kufr*) has been applied to none of the sins except to abandoning the prayer. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved." When the prayer was singled out for this kind of honour, it was necessary that Allah single it out by mention in this context. And Allah knows best.

[p. 69]

The Exalted said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"? If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels stretch out their hands, saying, "Yield up your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say against God other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that the Qur'an is a Book sent down from God, and made clear what it contains of the attributes of majesty, nobility and exaltedness, He mentioned after this what indicates the threat against the one who claims prophethood and messengerhood falsely and by way of lying and fabrication. He said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, magnified the threat against whoever mentions one of three things.

The first of them is to invent a lie against God. The exegetes said: this was revealed concerning Musaylima al-Kadhdhab (the great liar), lord of al-Yamama, and al-Aswad al-Ansi, lord of San'a, for both of them claimed prophethood and messengerhood from God by way of lying and fabrication. Musaylima used to say: "Muhammad is the messenger of Quraysh, and I am the messenger of Banu Hanifa."

The judge (al-Qadi) said: The one who invents a lie against God enters into it whoever claims messengerhood falsely, but it is not restricted to him, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion of revelation. So whoever attributes to God what is free of Him, whether in His essence, or in His attributes, or in His acts, falls under this threat.

He said: Fabrication against God concerning His attributes is like that of the Mujassima (anthropomorphists), and concerning His justice is like that of the Mujbira (determinists); for these have committed the gravest kind of injustice by inventing lies against God.

I say: As for his saying that the Mujassima have invented lies against God, it is true. But as for his saying that this is fabrication against God concerning His attributes, it is not correct. For the being of the Essence being a body and occupying a space is not an attribute; rather it is the very specific Essence itself. So whoever holds that the God of the worlds is not a body means that He says: all bodies and spatially occupying things are originated, and for all of them together there is a Creator who exists and does not occupy space. The Mujassim (anthropomorphist) denies this Essence. So the disagreement between the Unitarian (muwahhid) and the Mujassim is not about an attribute but about the Essence itself, because the Unitarian affirms this Essence and the Mujassim denies it. Thus it is established that this disagreement does not concern an attribute but the Essence.

As for his saying that the Mujbira have fabricated against God, Exalted is He, concerning His attributes, it is not correct. For it is said to him: the Mujbira added nothing to their saying: "the possible must have a determinant (murajjih)." If they lied in this proposition, how could they know the existence of God? And if they spoke truly in this, it necessarily follows that they acknowledge that the occurrence of an act is contingent upon the occurrence of the motive, by God's creation, and that is precisely what we call compulsion (jabr). Thus it is established that what he described as fabrication against God is false. Rather, the one who fabricates against God is the one who says: "The possible does not depend, for the preponderance of one of its two sides over the other, on the occurrence of a determinant." For whoever says this statement necessarily entails the negation of the Maker altogether, and indeed the negation of effects and effecting causes altogether.

The second kind of thing that God, Exalted is He, described as fabrication is His saying: ﴿or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾. The difference between this saying and what preceded it is that in the first, he claimed that revelation had come to him, and he did not deny the descent of revelation upon Muhammad (ﷺ). But in this saying he affirmed revelation for himself and denied it of Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is a combination of two great kinds of lying: affirming what does not exist, and negating what exists.

The third kind is His saying: ﴿I will send down the like of what God has sent down﴾. The exegetes said: what is meant is what al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said, namely his saying: "If we wished, we would say the like of this," and his saying about the Qur'an that it is "tales of the ancients." And everyone is able to produce its like. The upshot is that this speaker claims to contest the Qur'an. It is also narrated that Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh used to write down the revelation for the Messenger (ﷺ). When the words ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] were revealed, the Messenger dictated them to him, and when he reached His saying ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾, Abd Allah was amazed by it and said: "So blessed is God, the best of creators." The Messenger said: "Thus was the verse revealed." Abd Allah fell silent and said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then it has been revealed to me; and if he is a liar, then I have contested him." This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿I will send down the like of what was sent down﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, know that the beginning of the verse, namely His saying ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾, conveys a great threat in summary form, and His saying after that ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ is like the detailed explanation of that summary. The wrongdoers meant are those He mentioned. The "agonies of death" (ghamarat al-mawt) is the plural of ghamra, which is the severity of death. The ghamra of anything is its abundance and greatest part, from which comes "ghamrat al-ma'" (the flood of water) and "ghamrat al-harb" (the press of war). It is said: "ghamarahu al-shay'" when a thing overcame him and covered him. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of anyone who is in a great deal of something that has overwhelmed him, and "ghamarahu al-dayn" when the debt has increased upon him. This is the original meaning; then the word "al-ghamarat" is used for hardships and afflictions. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, meaning: you would see a tremendous matter. ﴿And the angels stretch out their hands﴾. Ibn Abbas said: the angels of punishment stretch out their hands, striking them and tormenting them, just as one says "basata ilayhi yadahu bil-makruh" (he stretched his hand to him with harm). ﴿Yield up your souls﴾. Here something is omitted, and the sense is: they say, "Yield up your souls." On this there are two issues.

The first issue: There is an objection to the verse, namely that they have no power to remove their spirits from their bodies, so what is the benefit of this statement?

We say: In explaining this phrase there are several aspects.

The first aspect: "If only you could see the wrongdoers when they arrive at the agonies of death in the Hereafter and are made to enter Hell." So the agonies of death are an expression for the kinds of severity and torments that befall them there, and the angels stretch out their hands against them with punishment, rebuking them, and saying to them: "Yield up your souls from this severe punishment, if you are able."

The second aspect: The meaning is: "If only you could see the wrongdoers in the agonies of death at the descent of death upon them in this world, while the angels stretch out their hands to seize their spirits, saying to them: 'Yield up your souls from these hardships, and free them from these calamities and pains.'"

The third aspect: His saying ﴿Yield up your souls﴾ means: bring them out to us from your bodies. This is an expression of violence and severity in taking the spirit out without respite or delay, and that they treat them like a creditor who is persistent and insistent, who stretches his hand toward the one owing him, presses him in demanding it, and gives him no respite, saying to him: "Hand over to me what you owe me right now, and I will not leave my place until I pull it out from your eyeballs."

The fourth aspect: This expression is a metaphor for the intensity of their state, and that they have reached such a degree of trial and severity that He Himself takes charge of taking away their spirits.

The fifth aspect: His saying ﴿Yield up your souls﴾ is not a command but a threat and a rebuke, like the saying of someone: "Go now, so that you may see what will befall you." The exegetes said: the soul of the believer is eager to leave to meet its Lord, while the soul of the disbeliever dislikes that, so leaving is hard for it, because it is going to the greatest punishment. As the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him; and whoever dislikes to meet God, God dislikes to meet him." This refers to the extraction of the spirit. So these disbelievers are compelled by the angels to have their spirits removed.

The second issue: Those who said that the human soul is a thing other than this frame and other than this body argued by this verse, saying: there is no doubt that His saying ﴿Yield up your souls﴾ means: bring out your souls from your bodies, and this indicates that the soul is distinct from the bodies. However, if we interpret the verse according to the first two of the five stated interpretations, this argument would not be complete.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "the punishment of humiliation" means the punishment by which severe humiliation occurs. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Shall he keep it despite disgrace, or bury it in the dust?﴾ [al-Nahl: 59]. What is meant is that He, Exalted is He, combined there between pain and humiliation, for reward has as its condition that it be a benefit accompanied by honour, and likewise punishment has as its condition that it be a harm accompanied by humiliation. Some said: "al-Hun" is the same as "al-Hawan" (humiliation), and "al-Hawn" is gentleness and ease. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]. And His saying: ﴿because you used to say against God other than the truth, and because you were arrogant toward His signs﴾ indicates that this severe punishment came about through the combination of two matters: fabrication against God, and arrogance toward the signs of God. I say: These two kinds of afflictions and calamities—you see most of those who are marked by knowledge deeply immersed in them and persistent in them. We seek refuge with God from them and from their effects and consequences.

Al-Wahidi mentioned that what is meant by His saying ﴿and because you were arrogant toward His signs﴾ is that they did not pray to Him. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever prostrates to God with a sincere intention has been freed from arrogance."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 94:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners in regard to you. Certainly your ties have been severed among you, and what you used to claim has strayed from you.﴾

Know that His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone﴾ admits of two interpretations:

The first: that this is coordinated with the words of the angels: ﴿Bring out your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. So He, may He be exalted, explained that just as they say that in the manner of rebuke, so too they say, relating from Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone﴾. Thus the whole speech is a report about them, and that they address these disbelievers with it. According to this reading, the speaker of these words may be the angels appointed to seize their souls, and it may be that the speakers are the angels appointed to punish them.

The second statement: that the speaker of these words is Allah, may He be exalted. The source of this difference is whether Allah, may He be exalted, speaks with the disbelievers or not. His saying, concerning the attribute of the disbelievers: ﴿and He will not speak to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77] necessitates that He does not speak with them. But His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], and His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6], require that He, may He be exalted, speaks with them. For this reason this difference arose. The first statement is stronger, because this verse is coordinated with what precedes it, and coordination necessitates sharing.

The second issue: ﴿furadá﴾ (alone, individually) is a plural form, and regarding its singular there are two opinions:

Ibn Qutaybah said: furadá is the plural of fardan, like sukara of sakran, and kusala of kaslan.

Others said: furadá is the plural of fareed, like rudafá of radeef.

Al-Farra' said: furadá is a plural whose singular is fard, fardah, fareed and fardan.

Once you know this, His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone﴾ is intended as reproach and rebuke. This is because they devoted their effort and exertion in this world to two things:

One of them: acquiring wealth and status.

The second: that they worshipped idols, believing that they would be intercessors for them before Allah. Then, when they arrived at the assembly of the Resurrection, none of that wealth remained with them, and they found no intercession from those idols for them before Allah, may He be exalted. So they remained alone, stripped of everything they had gathered in this world and relied upon. In contrast, the people of faith devoted their lives to acquiring true knowledge and righteous deeds, and those knowledge and righteous deeds remained with them in their graves and were present with them at the scene of the Resurrection. Thus, in reality, they did not arrive alone, but arrived with provision for the Day of Return.

[page 72]

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Certainly your ties have been severed among you﴾, and concerning this there are two issues:

The first issue: Nafi' and Hafs, from 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i read (بينكم) with a fatha (naṣb), while the rest read it with a damma (raf'). Al-Zajjaj said: the raf' is better, and its meaning is: your connection has been severed. The naṣb is permissible, and the meaning is: what you had in partnership among yourselves has been severed.

Abu 'Ali said: this word is used in two ways:

One of them: that it is a declinable noun, like al-iftiraq (separation), and the better usage is that it is an adverb of place (ẓarf). The nominative in the reading of the one who read (بينكم) with raf' is the word that was originally an adverb and then came to be used as a noun. The evidence that it can be a noun is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Since it is used as a noun in these places, it is permissible for the verb "taqaṭṭaʿa" (has been severed) to be attributed to it in the reading of the one who used the nominative. He said: and what indicates that this nominative word is the one used as an adverb is that it is either an adverb that has been extended in its use, or a verbal noun (maṣdar). The second possibility is invalid, since otherwise the meaning of the verse would be: "Your separation has been severed," and this is the opposite of what is intended. The intended meaning of the verse is: "Your connection has been severed, and what you used to rely upon has gone."

If it is said: how can it mean connection when its original sense is separation and disunion?

We say: this word is used only for two things that share some connection and union in certain respects, like their saying: "Between me and him is a partnership," and "Between me and him is a kinship." For this reason, it is fitting to use this word with the meaning of a bond. So His saying: ﴿Certainly your ties have been severed among you﴾ means: "Certainly your connection has been severed." As for the one who read "laqad taqaṭṭaʿa baynakum" with naṣb, its basis is that he implied a subject, and the implied meaning is: "Certainly your connection has been severed between you."
