Sibawayh said: they say, "If it is tomorrow, then come to me," meaning, "If the hope or the trial is tomorrow, then come to me," so the verb is implied because the situation indicates it. Likewise here. Ibn al-Anbari said: the implied meaning is: "Certainly what was between you has been severed," and it was omitted because its meaning is clear.

The second issue: Know that this verse contains a noble principle for understanding the conditions of the Resurrection:

The first point: the human soul was attached to this body only as an instrument for it to acquire true knowledge and virtuous character. When the soul departs from the body without having obtained these two aims at all, its regret grows great and its afflictions become severe, since it found such a noble instrument through which eternal happiness could be acquired, and then it wasted and ruined it, and gained nothing from it at all. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾.

The second point: this soul, although it did not acquire through this bodily instrument any spiritual happiness or spiritual perfection, has nevertheless done another deed worse than the first. This is because, throughout its life, it was in desire for acquiring wealth and status, in strengthening attachment to them, in reinforcing love for them, and in seeking them. In reality, the human being is directed from the physical world to the spiritual world. But this wretch reversed the matter and inverted the principle, and began to turn from the spiritual goal to the physical world, forgetting his purpose and being deceived by bodily pleasures. When he died, the matter was reversed, whether he liked it or not: he turned from the physical world to the spiritual world. The wealth that he had acquired remained behind his back, and he had spent his life in acquiring it. What remains behind a person's back cannot be benefited from by him, and perhaps it remains of no benefit, bent of neck and bent of head, because he turned toward it while being unable to benefit from it. This necessitates the utmost loss, grief and regret, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs﴾. This indicates that every wealth a person acquires and does not spend in the channels of goodness has this condition which Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned in this verse. But if he spends it on what brings honour to the command of Allah and compassion toward the creation of Allah, then he has not left that wealth behind his back, but has sent it forward before his face, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110].

The third point: those wretched people exhausted themselves in supporting false religions and corrupt doctrines, and they thought that they would benefit from them upon arrival at the assembly of the Resurrection. But when they arrive and witness what those doctrines contain of severe punishment and everlasting retribution, many kinds of torment come together in them. Among them is the torment of regret and remorse: that is, how they spent their wealth and endured severe hardship and great trials to acquire what brought them nothing but torment and suffering. Among them is the torment of shame: that is, it becomes clear to them that everything they believed in the abode of the world was utter ignorance and manifest error. Among them is the arising of intense despair together with great longing. There is no doubt that the sum of these conditions necessitates severe punishment and great spiritual pains. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners in regard to you﴾.

The fourth point: when it becomes clear to him that he has lost the matter by which he could have been able to acquire good things, and there has arisen in him the matter which necessitates the occurrence of harms, then if some hope of remedy remains for him in some respect, the pain is eased there and the grief is lessened. But when certainty and conviction arise that remedy is impossible and compensation for that loss is unattainable, then grief greatly intensifies and affliction becomes extremely strong there. To this is the allusion in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly your ties have been severed among you﴾, and the meaning is that the bond existing between the soul and the body has been severed, and there is no way to restore it again. When one comprehends the realities of these stages, it becomes clear that there is no explanation beyond this explanation in describing the conditions of these misguided people.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 95 (part 1 of 2):**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah, so how are you deluded?﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah the Exalted spoke about tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), then followed it with establishing the matter of prophethood (nubuwwah), and then spoke about some branches of this principle, He returns here to mentioning the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and the perfection of His knowledge, wisdom and power. This is to draw attention to the fact that the primary aim of all rational and transmitted discussions, and of every philosophical inquiry, is the knowledge of Allah through His essence, His attributes and His acts.

Concerning His saying ﴿splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ there are two views:

**The first view:** This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of al-Dahhak and Muqatil: ﴿splitter﴾ means "creator of the grain and the date-stone." Al-Wahidi said: "They treated *faliq* in the sense of *fatir* (originator)." I say: *al-fitr* means splitting, and likewise *al-falq*. Before a thing enters existence, it was a pure nonexistence and absolute negation. The intellect conceives from non-existence a continuous darkness with no opening, no cleaving and no splitting. When the originator and bringer-into-being brings it from non-existence into existence, it is as though, in imagination and supposition, He has split and cleft that non-existence, and brought the newly originated thing out through that split. By this interpretation, it is not far-fetched to take *al-faliq* as the one who brings into being, creates and originates.

**The second view,** which is the view of most scholars: *al-falq* is splitting, *al-habb* is that which is intended for its own sake, such as the seed of wheat, barley and other kinds, and *al-nawa* is the thing found inside a fruit, such as the stones of peaches, dates and others.

Having understood this, we say: when a grain or a stone is placed in moist earth and a period of time passes, Allah the Exalted brings forth in that grain or stone a split at its top and another split at its bottom. The split that appears at the top of the grain or stone brings forth from it the tree rising into the air, and the split that appears at the bottom of that grain brings forth from it the tree descending into the earth, which is called the roots of the tree. That grain or stone becomes the means of connecting the tree rising in the air with the tree descending in the earth.

Then there are wonders here:

**The first:** If the nature of that tree demands descent into the depths of the earth, how then does the tree rising into the air come forth from it? And if its nature demands rising into the air, how then does the tree descending into the earth come forth from it? Since these two trees are produced from it, while sense and reason witness that the nature of one of the two trees is opposed to the nature of the other, we know that this is not by the requirement of nature and inherent property, but by the requirement of bringing into being, origination, formation and invention.

**The second:** The interior of the earth is a dense, hard body, into which a strong needle cannot penetrate and a sharp, strong knife cannot sink. Yet we observe the tips of those roots to be extremely fine and delicate, such that if a person rubs them with his finger with the slightest force they turn into water. Then, despite their extreme delicacy, they are able to penetrate that hard earth and sink into the inner parts of those dense bodies. The acquisition of these strong powers by these weak bodies, which are extremely delicate, must come about by the decree of the Mighty, the Wise.

**The third:** From that stone a tree is produced, and in that tree there arise various natures. The bark of the wood has a particular nature, and inside that bark is the body of the wood, and in the middle of that wood is a soft, weak substance resembling carded wool. Then from the trunk of the tree its branches grow, and upon the branches first the leaves appear, then secondly the blossoms and flowers, then thirdly the fruit. Furthermore, the fruit may have four kinds of covering, as with the walnut: its outermost covering is that green husk, beneath it is the layer that resembles wood, beneath that is the layer which is like a thin membrane surrounding the kernel, and beneath that is the kernel itself. That kernel contains a dense body which is also like a husk, and a subtle body which is the oil, and this is the primary aim. Thus the production of these bodies, differing in their natures, attributes, colours, shapes and tastes, despite the equal influence of the natures, the stars, the four seasons and the four elements, indicates that they came into being by the arrangement of the Wise, the Merciful, the Chooser, the Powerful, and not by the arrangement of natures and elements.

**The fourth:** You find the four natures present in a single fruit. The citron (utrunj) has a peel that is hot and dry, its flesh is cold and moist, its juice is cold and dry, and its seed is hot and dry. Likewise the grape: its skin and its seeds are cold and dry, while its water and flesh are hot and moist. Thus these opposed natures and mutually repellent properties arise from one single grain, which necessarily requires the bringing into being by the Chooser, the Agent.

**The fifth:** You find the conditions of fruits to be different. Some have the kernel inside and the husk outside, as in the walnut and the almond. Some have the desired fruit on the outside and the wood on the inside, as with the peach and the apricot. Some have a stone which contains a kernel, as with the apricot and peach stones, and some have no kernel, as with the date stone. Some fruits have no husk either inside or outside, but are entirely edible, as with the fig. These are different conditions in these fruits. Moreover, these grains differ in shapes and forms: the shape of wheat is as if it were half a circle, the shape of barley is as if it were two cones joined at their bases, the shape of lentils is as if it were a circle, and the shape of chickpeas is of yet another form. These differing shapes must be for secrets and wisdoms, which the Creator knew would not be perfected in their composition except in that particular shape. Furthermore, the Creator, exalted is He, has placed in each kind of grain a different property and a different benefit. Also, one and the same fruit may be food for one animal and poison for another. Thus the difference of these qualities, shapes and conditions, along with the unity of the natures and the influences of the stars, indicates that all of these came about by the creation of the Chooser, the Wise Agent.

**The sixth:** When you take a single leaf from the leaves of a tree, you find one straight line in its middle, which, in relation to that leaf, is like the spinal cord in relation to the human body. Just as numerous nerves branch out from the spinal cord to the right and left of the human body, and from each branch further branches emerge, becoming ever finer until they leave the scope of sense and sight because of their smallness, so too in that leaf, from that great central line, separate lines branch out, and from each of them other different lines emerge, finer than the first, and this continues in this pattern until those lines leave the scope of sense and sight. The Exalted Creator did this so that the attractive powers embedded in the substance of that leaf can draw the subtle earthly parts through those narrow channels. When you have contemplated the Creator's care in producing that single leaf, you know that His care in creating the whole tree is more perfect, and you know that His care in forming all of vegetation is more perfect still.

Then, when you know that He, the Exalted, created the whole of vegetation for the benefit of animals, you know that His care in creating animals is more perfect. And when you know that the purpose of creating all animals is man, you know that His care in creating man is more perfect. Furthermore, Allah the Exalted created plants and animals in this world so that they would be food and medicine for man according to his body, while the purpose of creating man is knowledge, love and service, as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat: 56).

So look, O wretched one, with the eye of your head at that single leaf of that tree, and recognise the manner in which those veins and fibres are created within it. Then move from one level to what is above it, until you know that the ultimate purpose of all this is the attainment of knowledge and love in human spirits. At that point a door of unveilings without end will open for you, and it will become clear to you that the kinds of Allah's blessings upon you are unlimited, as He said: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ (Ibrahim: 34). All of this has arisen only from the manner of the creation of that leaf from the grain and the stone.

This, then, is a brief statement concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ Whenever a person comprehends it, he is able to divide and branch it out into endless detail. We ask Allah for success and guidance.

---

**The second issue:** As for His saying, ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living,﴾ there are several discussions:

**The first:** *Al-hayy* (the living) is the name for that which is characterised by life, and *al-mayyit* (the dead) is the name for that which is devoid of the attribute of life. On this basis, vegetation is not "living."

Having understood this, people differ over the interpretation of this "living" and "dead" in two views:

**The first view:** These two words are taken in their literal sense. Ibn 'Abbas said: He brings a living human out of a drop of semen, then He brings a dead drop of semen out of a living human. Likewise He brings a living chick out of an egg, then He brings a dead egg out of a hen. The intended meaning is that the living and the dead are opposites that are mutually exclusive, so that the coming of a like from a like could suggest that it occurs through nature and inherent property. But the coming of an opposite from an opposite is impossible to attribute to nature and inherent property; it must necessarily come about by the decree of the Wise Decreer and the All-Knowing Governor.

**The second view:** *Al-hayy* and *al-mayyit* are taken according to what we have mentioned, and also according to figurative meanings. There are several interpretations here:

**The first:** Al-Zajjaj said: He brings out fresh, tender, green vegetation from dry grain, and brings out dry matter from living, growing vegetation.

**The second:** Ibn 'Abbas said: He brings out a believer from an unbeliever, as in the case of Ibrahim, and an unbeliever from a believer, as in the case of the son of Nuh, and a disobedient person from an obedient one, and vice versa.

**The third:** Sometimes something that is definitely believed to cause harm becomes the cause of a great benefit, and vice versa. The physicians mention that a man was given a large quantity of opium in a drink so that he would die. When he consumed it, and the people thought he would die immediately, they lifted him from his place and placed him in a dark room. A huge snake came out and bit him, and that bite became the cause of removing the harm of the opium from him, because opium is killed by its intense coldness, while the venom of the viper kills by its intense heat. Thus that bite became the cause of the removal of the opium's harm. Here, something believed to be the greatest cause of evil gave rise to the greatest good, and sometimes it is the reverse. All these different conditions and opposing actions indicate that this world has a Wise Governor who does not neglect the interests of creation, and who has not left them without purpose. Beneath these discussions lie lofty and noble investigations.

**The second issue concerning this verse:** Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *al-mayyit* with a doubled *ya'* (*al-mayyit*) in both occurrences, while the rest read it with a single, unstressed *ya'* (*al-mayyit* pronounced with lightness) in both occurrences, and this is the case for this entire category throughout the Qur'an.

Third issue: someone might say that He first said, ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, and then said, ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾. Coordinating a noun (ism) with a verb (fi'l) is poor usage. What is the reason for choosing this form?

We say: His words, ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, are coordinated with His words, ﴿splits the grain and the date-stone﴾. His words, ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, serve as an explanation and elaboration of His words, ﴿splits the grain and the date-stone﴾, because splitting the grain and the date-stone to produce plants and growing trees is of the same kind as bringing the living from the dead, since what grows is treated as living, as you see in His words, ﴿and revives the earth after its death﴾ (al-Rum 30:19). There is another explanation too: the verbal form (lafz al-fi'l) indicates that the agent is concerned with that act at every moment and time.

The nominal form (lafz al-ism), however, does not indicate renewal or ongoing concern moment by moment. The Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 471 AH) gave an example of this in his book *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (*Proofs of Inimitability*). He said: His words, ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heaven?﴾ (Fatir 35:3), mention the provision with a verbal form, namely His words, "provides for you" (yarzuqukum), because the verbal form indicates that He, exalted is He, provides for them moment by moment and instant by instant.

[Page 77]

As for the nominal form, its example is His words, exalted is He: ﴿and their dog stretched out his forelegs at the threshold﴾ (al-Kahf 18:18). His words, ﴿stretching out﴾ (basit), indicate that it remains in that single state.

Having established this, we say: the living is more noble than the dead. Therefore the concern with bringing the living out of the dead must be greater than the concern with bringing the dead out of the living. For this reason the first category is expressed in the verbal form and the second in the nominal form, to alert the reader that the concern with producing the living from the dead is greater and more complete than the concern with producing the dead from the living. And Allah knows best what He intends.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿That is Allah; so how are you turned away?﴾ On this there are two questions.

First question: some have said its meaning is: ﴿That is Allah﴾, the one who arranges affairs, creates, benefits and harms, gives life and causes death, ﴿so how are you turned away﴾ in affirming the claim that idols should be worshipped?

The second: the intended meaning is that when you witnessed that He, exalted is He, brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and then you witnessed that He brought a living body out of a dead drop of semen (nutfah) once, how then do you deem it unlikely that He would bring a living body out of dead, crumbling dust once more? The aim is to reject their denial of resurrection (al-hashr) and gathering and raising up (al-nashr). Also, opposites are equal in relation to one another: just as transformation from one of two opposites into the other is not impossible, so transformation from the second into the first should not be impossible. Just as the occurrence of death after life is not impossible, the occurrence of life after death should not be impossible either. Under both interpretations, this yields the permissibility of affirming resurrection, gathering and raising up.

Second question: al-Sahib ibn 'Abbad relied on His words, ﴿so how are you turned away﴾, to argue that the act of the servant is not created by Allah, exalted is He. He said: if He had created the aversion (ifk) in them, how would it be fitting for Him to say, along with that, ﴿so how are you turned away﴾?

The answer to this: capacity (qudrah) is equally related to both opposites. If one of the two sides is preponderant over the other without a preponderant cause (murajjih), then this preponderance is not from the servant; it is pure coincidence. So how is it proper to say to him, ﴿so how are you turned away﴾? And if that preponderance depends on the occurrence of a preponderant cause, namely the motive (da'iyah) that draws one to the act, then the occurrence of that motive comes from Allah, exalted is He, and once it occurs the act becomes necessary. In that case, everything you have imposed on us applies to you. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 96 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He is the Cleaver of the dawn; He has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

Know that this is another kind of proof for the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power and His wisdom. The previous kind was derived from the states of plants and animals, while the kind mentioned in this verse is derived from celestial states. This is because the splitting of the darkness of night by the light of dawn is greater in the perfection of power than the splitting of the seed and the date-stone to produce plants and trees. Also, it is known necessarily that celestial states are greater in hearts and have a stronger impact than terrestrial states. The argument may be established in several ways:

The first: We say that dawn is of two kinds.

[Page 78]

The first dawn is the elongated dawn, like the tail of a wolf (sirhan). It is followed by pure darkness. Then after it rises the spreading dawn over the whole horizon. So we say: As for the first dawn, which is the elongated one followed by pure darkness, it is among the strongest proofs of the power and wisdom of Allah. This is because we say: That light either arises from the influence of the disc of the sun, or it does not. The first is false. The centre of the sun, when it reaches the circle of midnight, then for the people of the place for whom that circle is the horizon, the sun has risen from their east. In that place also is half of the globe of the earth. This implies that light has occurred in the eastern quarter of our town. That light would be spreading and diffused throughout all parts of the atmosphere, and that light must increase, at every hour, in strength, growth and perfection. If the first dawn were the effect of the disc of the sun, it would be impossible for it to be a stretched line; rather, it must be spread over the whole horizon, diffused in it entirely, and increasing and completing at every moment and instant. Since the matter is not like this, but rather we know that the first dawn appears like a rising white thread, so that the Arabs compare it to the tail of a wolf, and then after it there is pure darkness, and then the spreading dawn comes after that, we know that this elongated dawn is not from the influence of the disc of the sun, nor of the kind of its light. Therefore it must be that this is brought about by the creation of Allah the Exalted directly, as an indication that lights have no existence except by His creation, and that darknesses have no permanence except by His decree, as He said at the beginning of this surah: ﴿And made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

The second aspect in establishing this proof: When we investigated and reflected, we knew that the sun, the moon and the rest of the stars cast their light only upon the body facing them. As for that which is not facing them, it is impossible for their light to fall upon it. This is a premise agreed upon among the philosophers and the mathematicians who study the states of luminous light, and they have excellent formulations of it.

Having known this, we say: At the rising of dawn the sun is not raised above the horizon, so the body of the sun does not face any part of the surface of the earth, and so it is impossible for sunlight to fall upon the surface of the earth. If that is so, it is impossible for the light of dawn to be the effect of the disc of the sun, and therefore it must be by the creation of the free chooser (al-Fa'il al-Mukhtar).

If they say: Why should it not be possible to say that the sun, while it is beneath the earth, causes the air facing it to be illuminated, then that air faces the air standing above the earth, so the light of the air standing beneath the earth makes the air standing above the earth a cause of its light, and then that light continues to travel from one air to another air adjacent to it until it reaches the air surrounding us? This is the view upon which Abu 'Ali ibn al-Haytham relied in establishing this meaning in his book which he named "al-Manazir al-Kathhah" (The Dense Perspectives).

The answer: This excuse is false in two respects.

The first: Air is a transparent body devoid of colour, and whatever is so does not receive light, and colour is in its essence and substance. This is agreed upon among the philosophers. They argued for it by saying that if light settled on its surface, sight would stop at its surface. If that were so, sight would not pass through to what lies beyond it, and its seeing would prevent seeing what is beyond it. Since that is not the case, we know that it does not receive colour and light in its essence and substance. Whatever is like this is impossible for light to be reflected from it to another. Thus it is impossible for its light to become a cause of the light of another air facing it.

[Page 79]

If they say: Why should it not be possible to say that there occurred on the horizon dense parts of vapours and fumes, which, by their density, receive light from the disc of the sun, and then the occurrence of light in them becomes a cause of the occurrence of light in the air facing them? We say: If the cause were what you mention, then whenever the vapours and fumes on the horizon were more numerous, the light of the morning would have to be stronger. But the matter is not so; rather, it is the opposite. Therefore this excuse is refuted.

The second aspect in refuting this speech mentioned by Ibn al-Haytham: The circle that is the horizon for us is itself the circle of midday for another people. If that is so, then the circle which is midday in our town must be the horizon for those peoples.

Once this is established, we say: When the centre of the sun reaches the circle of midnight and passes beyond it, the sun has risen upon those peoples, and half the world is illuminated there. The quarter of the heavenly sphere that is the eastern quarter for the people of our town is exactly the western quarter in relation to that town. If that is so, then when the centre of the sun passes beyond the circle of midnight, its body has come to face the air of the eastern quarter of the people of our town. So if the air received the quality of light from the sun, the light and illumination would have to occur in the air of the eastern quarter of our town after midnight, and the air of the eastern quarter would have to become in the utmost state of brightness and luminosity after midnight. Since the matter is not like this, we know that air does not receive the quality of light in its essence. When this is refuted, the excuse mentioned by Ibn al-Haytham is refuted. We have thus mentioned two subtle, purely rational proofs that the creator of light and darkness is Allah the Exalted, not the disc of the sun. And Allah knows best.

The third aspect: Suppose that the light occurring in the world was indeed through the influence of the sun. Nevertheless, we say: Bodies are alike in the complete quiddity (al-Mahiyyah). When that is so, the occurrence of this property in the disc of the sun must be by the creation of the free chooser.

As for the explanation of the first stage: Bodies are alike in being bodies and occupying space. If difference occurred among them, that difference would have to be in a concept distinct from the concept of corporeality, because that by which they share must be distinct from that by which they differ. So we say: That matter is either a substrate (mahall) for corporeality, or inhering in it, or neither a substrate for it nor inhering in it. The first is false, because it implies that the body is an attribute subsisting in another essence, and that is impossible, because if that substrate is spatial and occupies a place, then the substrate of the body would be other than the body, which is impossible; and if it is not like that, then what is in the space would be inhering in a substrate that has no relation to any of the spaces or directions, and that is rejected by the immediate intellect.

The second is also false, because in this case the essences are the bodies, and that by which difference occurs is the attributes. Whatever is valid for a thing is valid for its like. Since the essences are alike in complete quiddity, it must be valid for each of them what is valid for the other, and that is what was sought.

The third is the claim that that by which difference occurs is neither a substrate for the body nor inhering in it, and the corruption of this division is evident. Thus it is established by this proof that bodies are alike.

Having established this, we say: Whatever is valid for one of two like things is also valid for the second like thing. When all bodies are equal in receiving all attributes in turn, the specification of the body of the sun with this brightness and this illumination must necessarily be by the specification of the free chooser. When this is established, the Cleaver of the dawn in reality is Allah the Exalted, and that is what was sought. And Allah knows best.

[Page 80]

The fourth aspect in establishing this objective: Darkness resembles non-existence. Indeed, decisive proof has shown that it is a negative concept, while light is pure existence. When night darkens, fear and dread arise in the hearts of all, sleep overcomes them and they become like the dead; movements cease, effects are suspended, and activities are withdrawn. When the light of dawn reaches this world, it is as if it breathed into the Trumpet the substance of life and the power of perception. Sleep weakens, and wakefulness begins to appear. And whenever the light of dawn is stronger and more complete, the manifestation of the power of sensation and movement in animals is more complete. It is known that among the greatest blessings of Allah upon creation is the power of life, sensation and movement. Since light is the primary cause of the occurrence of these states, the influence of Allah's power in creating light is among the greatest kinds of blessings and the most majestic kinds of bounty and generosity.

Having known this, His being the Cleaver of the dawn is, as a proof, a proof of the perfection of Allah's power, the most majestic kind of proofs; and as a bounty, mercy and benevolence from Allah upon creation, it is the most majestic kind and the most noble type. This is what came to our mind in establishing the indication of His words ﴿the Cleaver of the dawn﴾ upon the existence of the Creator, the Powerful, the Free Chooser, the Wise. And Allah knows best.

Let us conclude these proofs with a noble conclusion. We say: He, the Exalted, is the Cleaver of the darkness of non-existence by the dawn of origination and bringing into being; the Cleaver of the darkness of inanimateness by the dawn of life, intellect and right guidance; the Cleaver of the darkness of ignorance by the dawn of reason and perception; the Cleaver of the darkness of the corporeal world by freeing the holy soul to the dawn of the world of the spheres; and the Cleaver of the darkness of preoccupation with the world of contingent things by the dawn of the light of total absorption in knowing the Manager of the originated and the innovated.

* * *

Issue Three: On the interpretation of "al-Isbah" (the dawn). There are several views:

The first: Al-Layth said: Al-Subh and al-Sabah are the beginning of the day, and al-Isbah is also (the same). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿the Cleaver of the dawn﴾, meaning the dawn (al-Subh). The poet said:

*He has destroyed Riyah and the sons of Riyah; the alternation of evening and morning.*

The second view: That "al-Isbah" is a verbal noun (masdar) by which the dawn is named.

If it is said: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He, the Exalted, split the dawn, and the truth is not so, for the truth is that He, the Exalted, split the darkness by the dawn. So what is the meaning here? We say: There are several views:

The first: That the intended meaning is the Cleaver of the darkness of dawn. This is because the horizon on the northern, western and southern sides is filled with darkness and light, and light has appeared only on the eastern side, so it is as if the horizon were a sea filled with darkness. Then Allah the Exalted cleaved that dark sea by sending a rivulet of light into it. The summary is that the intended meaning is the Cleaver of the darkness of dawn by the light of dawn, and since the intended meaning is known, the omission is fine.

The second: Just as He cleaves the sea of darkness to reveal the light of dawn, so He cleaves the light of dawn from the whiteness of the day. So His words ﴿the Cleaver of the dawn﴾ mean the Cleaver of the dawn by the whiteness of the day.

The third view: the appearance of light at dawn is due to God splitting that darkness. So His saying ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ means "the one who makes dawn appear." But since the cause of that appearing is the splitting, the cause is named while the effect is meant.

The fourth view: some scholars said that *al-fāliq* (the splitter) means *al-khāliq* (the creator), so the meaning is "Creator of the dawn." On this reading the question disappears. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and made the night a resting place﴾: know that in this verse He mentions three kinds of cosmic evidence [p. 81] for the Oneness (of God).

The first is the appearance of the dawn, which we have explained as far as understanding allows.

The second is His saying ﴿and made the night a resting place﴾, and on it there are several discussions.

First discussion: The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *al-sakan* is that in which a man finds rest and calm, feeling at ease and comforted by it, such as a spouse or a beloved. From this, fire is called *sakan*, because one feels at ease with it. Do you not see that they call it "the one that brings companionship" (*al-mu'nisah*)? Then, a person finds calm in the night, because he has exhausted himself during the day and needs a time in which to rest, and that is the night.

If it is said: Do not the creatures remain in Paradise in the most pleasant life and the sweetest time, although there is no night there? So we know that the existence of night and day is not essential to pleasure and good in life. We answer: Our discussion concerns the fact that night and day are essential to the interests of this world. As for the Hereafter, these customs do not persist there, so the difference is clear.

Second discussion: ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿wa-jaʿala al-layl﴾ in the verbal form (*fiʿl*), while the rest read *jāʿil* in the form of the active participle. The argument of those who read the active participle is that what precedes it is the active participle, namely ﴿fāliq al-ḥabb﴾ and ﴿fāliq al-iṣbāḥ﴾, and *jāʿil* is also an active participle. The conjoined word must share the same form as the word it is conjoined to. The argument of those who read the verbal form is that ﴿wa-l-shamsa wa-l-qamar﴾ are in the accusative case, and this accusative needs a governing word. Nothing else can serve except to supply *jaʿala* (made) with the meaning of *wa-jāʿil* (and making) for "the sun and the moon as a reckoning," and this conveys the intended meaning.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

First discussion: Its meaning is that He determined the movement of the sun and the moon by a specific calculation, as He mentioned in Surat Yunus in His saying: ﴿It is He who made the sun a shining light and the moon a light, and determined for it stations that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. And He said in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿The sun and the moon run by reckoning﴾. The full explanation is that He determined the movement of the sun with a particular measure of speed and slowness such that its cycle completes in a year, and He determined the movement of the moon such that it completes its cycle in a month. By these measures the interests of the world are arranged across the four seasons, and by them what is needed is obtained: the ripening of fruits and the harvesting of crops. Had we supposed them to be faster or slower than what actually occurs, these interests would be disrupted. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿and the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾.

Second discussion: Regarding *al-ḥusbān* there are two views:
The first, which is the view of Abu al-Haytham, is that it is the plural of *ḥisāb*, like *rikāb* and *rukbān*, and *shihāb* and *shuhbān*.
The second is that *al-ḥusbān* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like *al-rujḥān* and *al-nuqṣān*. The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *al-ḥusbān* with a *ḍamma* is the verbal noun of *ḥasiba*, just as *al-ḥisbān* with a *kasra* is the verbal noun of *ḥasiba* (with a different vowel pattern), and its parallel is *al-kufrān*, *al-ghufrān*, and *al-shukrān*.

Having understood this, we say: The meaning of "made the sun and the moon a reckoning" is that He made them according to a calculation, because the reckoning of times is known only through their revolving and their course.

Third discussion: The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: ﴿wa-l-shamsa wa-l-qamar﴾ are read with all three vowel cases. The accusative is by supplying a verb indicated by His saying ﴿made the night﴾, that is, "and He made the sun and the moon a reckoning." The genitive is a conjunction with the wording of *al-layl* (the night). The nominative is by inception (*ibtidāʾ*), with the predicate omitted, its estimate being: "and the sun and the moon are made a reckoning," that is, "reckoned."

Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾. "The Almighty" points to the perfection of His power, and "the All-Knowing" points [p. 82] to the perfection of His knowledge. The meaning is that the determination of the bodies of the celestial spheres with their specific attributes, their limited configurations, and their movements measured by specific amounts of slowness and speed, cannot be achieved except by a perfect power that relates to all possibilities and a knowledge that penetrates all objects of knowledge, universal and particular. This is an explicit statement that the occurrence of these conditions and attributes is not by nature or inherent property, but by the specification of a free and choosing agent. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darkness of the land and the sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾

This is the third type of the proofs indicating the perfection of power, mercy and wisdom, namely that He, exalted is He, created these stars for the benefit of His servants, and these benefits are of several aspects:

The first aspect: He, exalted is He, created them so that creation may be guided by them to the paths and routes in the darkness of the land and the sea, where they see neither sun nor moon, because at that time they are guided by them to the roads and paths they wish to travel.

The second aspect: People derive from the movements of the sun the knowledge of the times of prayer, and they derive from the sun's movement by day the direction of the qiblah, and they derive from the states of the stars by night the knowledge of the qiblah.

The third aspect: He, exalted is He, mentioned in other than this surah that these stars are an adornment of the heaven. He said: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the heaven constellations﴾ [al-Furqan: 61], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars﴾ [al-Saffat: 6], and He said: ﴿By the heaven of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1].

The fourth aspect: He, exalted is He, mentioned among their benefits that they are missiles against the devils.

The fifth aspect: It may be said: ﴿that you may be guided by them in the darkness of the land and the sea﴾, meaning in the darknesses of ta'til (denial of divine attributes) and tashbih (anthropomorphism). For the one who practises ta'til denies that He is an agent who chooses, and the one who practises tashbih affirms that He, exalted is He, is a body specified by place. So He, exalted is He, created these stars so that one may be guided by them in these two kinds of darkness. As for being guided by them in the darkness of the land of ta'til, that is because we observe these stars differing in many attributes: some of them are wandering (planets) and some are fixed; the fixed ones are partly in the zodiac and partly at the poles; also the fixed ones are bright while the wandering ones are not bright; also some are large, pearl-like, of great light, and some are small, obscure, of little light; and also they have assigned their magnitudes to seven degrees.

Having known this, we say: We have shown that bodies are alike, and we have explained that when this is so, the specification of each one of them with a particular attribute is a proof that this is nothing but by the determination of a choosing Agent. This is the aspect of being guided by them in the darkness of the land of ta'til. As for the aspect of being guided by them in the darkness of the sea of tashbih, we say: there is no defect that detracts from the divinity of these stars except that they are bodies, and so they are composed of parts and components; also that they are finite and bounded; also that they are changing, moving, and passing from state to state. If these things are not defects in divinity, then it is impossible to impugn their divinity; but if they are defects in divinity, it is obligatory to declare God exalted above them all. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the God of the world, the heaven and the earth is exalted above corporeality, members, components, limit, end, place and direction. This is the explanation of being guided by these stars in the land of ta'til and the sea of tashbih. Although this is a departure from the literal meaning to its metaphorical sense, it is nevertheless close and fitting to the greatness of the Book of God, exalted is He.

The sixth aspect: Among the benefits of these stars is what God, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. Thus He alerted, in summary, that in the existence of each one of them there is lofty wisdom and noble benefit, and that whatever our intellect does not encompass in detail is not necessarily to be negated. Whoever wishes to measure the wisdom of God, exalted is He, in His dominion and kingdom by the measure of his imagination and the scale of his reasoning has indeed strayed into clear misguidance.

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned the derivation of proof from the states of these stars, He said: ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾, and in it there are several aspects:

The first: The meaning is that just as these stars can be used as guidance for paths in the darkness of the land and the sea, so likewise they can be used to recognise the Wise Creator and the perfection of His power and knowledge.

The second: The intended meaning of "knowledge" here is intellect ('aql). Thus His saying: ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ is similar to His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] up to His saying: ﴿are signs for a people who reason ('aqilun)﴾, and in Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190].

The third: The intended meaning of His saying ﴿for a people who know﴾ is for a people who reflect, contemplate, and derive the intelligible from the perceptible, and pass from the witnessed to the unseen.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 98:**

Allah's words: ﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul, then there is a place of lodging and a place of storing. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾

This is the fourth type of evidence for the existence of God, His perfect power and His knowledge, namely reasoning from the conditions of the human being. We say: there is no doubt that the single soul is Adam, peace be upon him, and he is a single soul. Hawwa' (Eve) was created from one of his ribs. Thus all people came from a single soul, which is Adam.

If it is said: What is the position regarding Jesus?

We reply: He too was created from Mary, who was herself created from her two parents.

If they say: Does not the Qur'an indicate that he was created from the Word (kalimah), or from the Spirit breathed into her? How then is this valid?

We reply: The word *min* ("from") indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah, the initial point of origin), and there is no dispute that the beginning of Jesus' formation, peace be upon him, was from Mary. This much is sufficient for the validity of this expression.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: There is a difference between His words *anshaa'akum* ("He produced you") and His words *khalaqakum* ("He created you"), because *anshaa'akum* indicates that He created you not from nothing as a beginning, but by way of growth and development, not from a source in the two parents, just as it is said of plants that God produced them, meaning growth and increase until the time of completion.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿fa-mustaqarrun wa-mustawda'un﴾ ("a place of lodging and a place of storing"), there are several points of discussion.

**The first point:** Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *fa-mustaqirrun* (with a kasrah on the qaf), while the rest read it with a fathah on the qaf. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Sibawayh said: it is said *qarra fi makanihi* and *istaqarra*. Whoever reads it with a kasrah on the qaf, *al-mustaqirr* carries the meaning of *al-qarr* (one who settles), and if this is so, its implied predicate must be *minkum* ("from among you"), meaning: from among you is one who settles. Whoever reads it with a fathah on the qaf, it is not an object, because *istaqarra* is intransitive and thus cannot take a direct object; it is therefore a noun of place (*ism makan*), so *al-mustaqarr* has the status of *al-maqarr* (the place of settling). If so, its implied predicate cannot be *minkum*; rather its predicate is *lakum* ("for you"), so the sense is: *lakum maqarr* ("for you is a place of settling"). As for *al-mustawda'*: *istawda'a* is a verb that takes two objects. You say: *istawda'tu Zaydan alfan* ("I deposited a thousand with Zayd") and *awda'tu mithlahu* ("I deposited the like of it"). So *al-mustawda'* may be a name for the person who deposited at that place, and it may also be the place itself.

Having understood this, we say: whoever reads *mustaqarran* with a fathah on the qaf makes *al-mustawda'* a place, so that it is like the word it is coordinated with, and the sense is: *fa-lakum makanu istiqrarin wa-makanu istida'in* ("for you is a place of settling and a place of depositing"). Whoever reads *fa-mustaqirrun* with a kasrah, the meaning is: from among you is one who settles, and from among you is one who is deposited, and the sense is: from among you is he who has settled, and from among you is he who has been deposited. And God knows best.

**The second point:** The difference between *al-mustaqarr* and *al-mustawda'* is that *al-mustaqarr* is closer to permanence than *al-mustawda'*. Thus a thing that has come to be in a place and is not on the verge of leaving is called *mustaqarr fihi* ("settled in it"). But if it has come to be in it while being on the verge of leaving, it is called *mustawda'* ("deposited"), because the deposited thing is in a situation where it may be reclaimed at any time and moment.

Having understood this, we say: the commentators differed greatly over the interpretation of these two expressions, giving several views:

The first, which is related from Ibn 'Abbas in most narrations, is that *al-mustaqarr* is the wombs and *al-mustawda'* is the loins. Kurayb said: Jarir wrote to Ibn 'Abbas asking him about this verse, and he replied: *al-mustawda'* is the loin (*sulb*) and *al-mustaqarr* is the womb (*rahim*). Then he recited: ﴿and We cause to remain in the wombs what We will﴾. Among the things that also support the strength of this view: a single drop of semen does not remain in the father's loins for a long time, whereas the fetus remains in the mother's womb for a long time. Since staying in the womb is longer than staying in the father's loins, it is more fitting to take *istiqrar* as referring to staying in the womb.

The second view: *al-mustaqarr* is the father's loins, and *al-mustawda'* is the mother's womb. This is because the drop of semen came to be in the father's loins without any external cause, whereas it came to be in the mother's womb through the action of another. So the deposit of that drop in the womb by the man is likened to a trust (*wadi'ah*). Since His words *fa-mustaqarrun wa-mustawda'un* require that the *mustaqarr* precede the *mustawda'*, and the coming to be of the drop in the father's loins precedes its coming to be in the mother's womb, it follows that *al-mustaqarr* is what is in the loins of fathers and *al-mustawda'* is what is in the wombs of mothers.

The third view, which is the view of al-Hasan: *al-mustaqarr* is a person's state after death, because if he was blessed then that blessedness has become fixed, and if he was wretched then that wretchedness has become fixed, and there is no change in human conditions after death. As for before death, conditions are changeable. The disbeliever may become a believer, and the heretic (zindiq) may become a sincere truth-teller (siddiq). These conditions, since they are on the verge of ceasing and perishing, are not far from being likened to a deposit, which is on the verge of being withdrawn.

The fourth view, which is the view of al-Asamm: *al-mustaqarr* is the one who was created from the first soul, entered this world and settled in it, and *al-mustawda'* is the one who has not yet been created but will be created.

The fifth view, also of al-Asamm: *al-mustaqarr* is the one who has settled in the abode of this world, and *al-mustawda'* is the one who is in the graves until he is resurrected. It is related from Qatadah the opposite of this, for he said: *mustaqarr* is in the grave and *mustawda'* is in this world.

The sixth view, the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani: the sense is: He is the One who produced you from a single soul, then among you is one who settles (a male), and among you is one who is deposited (a female). Except that He expressed the male by *mustaqarr* because the drop is only generated in his loins and only settles there, and He expressed the female by *mustawda'* because her womb is like a deposit for that drop. And God knows best.

**The third point:** The purport of the speech is that people were generated only from one person, who is Adam, peace be upon him. Then they differed in *al-mustaqarr* and *al-mustawda'* according to the aspects mentioned. We say: human persons are equal in corporeality (*jismiyyah*) and differ in the attributes by which the difference in *mustaqarr* and *mustawda'* arises. Difference in those attributes must have a cause and an agent. The cause is not corporeality and its necessary properties, for otherwise difference in attributes would be impossible. Therefore the cause must be the choosing, wise Agent. The parallel of this verse in indicating this is His words: ﴿and the difference of your tongues and your colours﴾ [al-Rum: 22].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾. The meaning of this detailing is that He clarified these proofs in a way that distinguishes some from others. Do you not see that He first held up the growth of plants and trees from grain and date-stones as evidence, then after it He cited the celestial proofs from three aspects, then after it He cited the conditions of human creation? So He distinguished some of these proofs from others and detailed some of them from others for a people who understand. And here there are discussions:

**The first:** His words *li-qawmin yafqahun* ("for a people who understand") apparently suggest that He sometimes does an act for a purpose and a wisdom.

The reply of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah and Community, the orthodox Sunni scholars): the *lam* here is the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*), or that statement is understood as a figurative comparison with one who does an act for a purpose.

**The second:** This verse indicates that He intended from the whole of creation understanding, comprehension and faith, and did not intend disbelief for any of them. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah.

The reply of Ahl al-Sunnah: the intended meaning is as if He said: I have only clarified this explanation for whoever knows, understands and comprehends, and they are the believers only and no others.

**The third:** He ended the preceding verse, which is the verse in which He reasoned from the conditions of the stars, with His words *ya'lamun* ("they know"), and He ended this verse with His words *yafqahun* ("they understand"). The difference is that the production of mankind from a single soul, and the disposing of them among different conditions, is more subtle and precise in workmanship and management. So mention of understanding (*fiqh*) here is because understanding indicates greater insight, strength, intelligence and comprehension. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 99 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing; then We brought forth from it green [growth], We bring forth from it grain layered [in ears], and from the palm trees, from their spathes, clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapes, and the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar. Look at their fruit when it bears fruit and at its ripening. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Know that this is the fifth type of the proofs indicating the perfection of Allah's power, His knowledge, His wisdom, His mercy, and the aspects of His beneficence toward His creation.

And know that these proofs, just as they are proofs, are also abundant blessings and complete favours. When speech is a proof from some aspects and a favour and beneficence from all aspects, its effect on the heart is great. At this point it becomes clear that one who is occupied with calling people to the path of truth should not turn away from this method. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky﴾, requires that rain descends from the sky. At this point people differed. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) said in his tafsir: He, exalted is He, sends the water from the sky to the clouds, and from the clouds to the earth. He said: Because the apparent text requires that rain descends from the sky, and turning away from the apparent meaning to interpretation is only needed when there is evidence that keeping the wording on its apparent sense is impossible, and in this place no evidence has been established for the impossibility of rain descending from the sky, so it is necessary to keep the wording on its apparent sense.

As for the view of one who says that many vapours gather within the earth, then rise and ascend into the air, where the cloud forms from them and drips, and that is the rain, al-Jubba'i argued against its corruption on several grounds:

The first: cold is found in the time of heat, indeed in the heart of summer, and we find rain falling at the coldest time without freezing, and this refutes their claim.

One may say: the proponents answer this, saying: there is no doubt that vapour consists of watery particles whose nature is cold. In the time of summer, heat dominates the outer surface of the cloud, so the cold flees to its interior, and there the cold strengthens because of gathering, so hail forms. As for the time of cold air, the cold dominates the outer surface of the cloud, so the cold does not strengthen within it, and therefore it does not congeal into ice but falls as water. This is what they have said.

It may be answered that the upper layer of the air is very cold according to you; when the day is cold, extremely cold, in the heart of winter, that layer is very cold, and the air surrounding the earth is also very cold, so the cold should intensify and rain should never occur in winter at all. Since we observe that it does occur, your claim is refuted, and God knows best.

The second argument, of what al-Jubba'i mentioned: he said: when vapours rise and ascend, they disperse, and when they disperse, drops of water are not generated from them. Rather, vapour only gathers when it meets a continuous smooth ceiling, like the ceilings of glazed bathhouses; otherwise, not much water flows from it. So when vapours ascend into the air, with no smooth continuous surface above them to which those vapours attach, it must be that no water arises from them.

One may say: the proponents answer this: when these vapours ascend and disperse, upon reaching the cold layer of the air during their ascent and dispersion, they become cold, and cold causes heaviness and descent. By the strength of that cold they return from ascent to descent. And since the world is spherical in shape, when they return from ascent to descent, they come from the vast surrounding space to the narrow centre. Those particles, for this reason, cling together and join, and from the joining of some of those particles come some drops of rain.

The third argument, of what al-Jubba'i mentioned: he said: if the generation of rain were from the ascent of vapours, then the vapours that rise from the seas are constant, so the descent of rain there should be constant. Since this is not the case, we know the corruption of their claim. He said: thus it is established by these aspects that the generation of rain is not from the vapour of the earth. Then he said: The proponents only needed this view because they believed that bodies are eternal, and if they are eternal, the entrance of increase and decrease into them is impossible, and then there is no meaning to the occurrence of events except the attribution of a new attribute to those particles after they had been characterized by other attributes. For this reason they resorted to explaining the coming-to-be of everything from a specific material. As for the Muslims, since they believe that bodies are originated, and that the Creator of the world is a free, chooser agent, able to create bodies however He wills and intends, at this point there is no need to devise these contrivances. Thus it is established that the apparent sense of the Qur'an in this verse indicates that water descends from the sky, and there is no proof against keeping this apparent sense, so it is necessary to hold it to its apparent sense. And among the things that confirm what we have said is that all the verses speak of rain descending from the sky. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [al-Furqan: 48], and He said: ﴿And He sends down upon you from the sky water to purify you thereby﴾ [al-Anfal: 11], and He said: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains containing hail﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. Thus it is established that the truth is that He, exalted is He, sends down rain from the sky, in the sense that He creates these bodies in the sky, then sends them down to the clouds, then from the clouds to the earth.

The second view: the intended meaning is the sending down of rain from the direction of the sky as water.

The third view: He sent down water from the cloud, and Allah, exalted is He, named the cloud "sky", because the Arabs call everything above you "sky", like the roof of the house. This is what has been said on this matter.

The second issue: al-Wahidi reported in al-Basit from Ibn 'Abbas: "By water here is meant rain, and not a single drop of rain descends except that an angel is with it." The philosophers interpret that angel as the nature inherent in that bodily substance which necessitates that descent. As for there being with it an angel from the angels of the heavens, the claim is problematic; and God knows best.

The third issue, His saying: ﴿So We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing﴾, in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, brought forth the vegetation through the medium of water, and this necessitates the doctrine of natural causation, which the theologians (mutakallimun) deny. We have elaborated on this question in surat al-Baqarah in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22], so there is no benefit in repeating it.

The second discussion: al-Farra' said: His saying: ﴿So We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing﴾ apparently requires that every thing have vegetation. This is not the case, so the intended meaning is: "So We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing that has vegetation." When this is so, whatever has no vegetation does not enter into it.

The third discussion: His saying: ﴿So We brought forth thereby﴾ after His saying "He sent down" is called iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and this is counted among eloquence.

Know that the scholars of Arabic grammar claimed that this is counted among eloquence, but they did not explain from which aspects it falls under this category. As for us, we have expounded on it at length in the explanation of His saying: ﴿until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus: 22], so there is no benefit in repeating it.

The fourth discussion: His saying: ﴿So We brought forth﴾ is in the plural form. God is one, single, without partner; but when a great king refers to himself, he refers to himself with the plural form, and so here. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed We sent it down﴾, ﴿Indeed We sent Noah﴾, ﴿Indeed We, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So We brought forth from it green [growth]﴾, al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of khadir is like the meaning of akhdar; it is said: "ikhdarra, so he is akhdar and khadir," as "a'warra, so he is a'war and 'awir." Al-Layth said: "al-khadir" in the Book of Allah is the crop, and in common speech every plant of greenness. I say: He, exalted is He, confined vegetation in the preceding verse to two categories, when He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾. That which sprouts from the grain is the crop, and that which sprouts from the date-stone is the tree. So He took this division into account in this verse as well, beginning with mention of the crop, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So We brought forth from it green [growth]﴾, namely the crop, as we have related from al-Layth. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means wheat, barley, sult, maize and rice. What is meant by this green is the green stalk that comes forth first, with the ear at its top. His saying: ﴿We bring forth from it grain layered [in ears]﴾ means: from that green [growth] He brings forth grain layered, some of it upon others, in a single ear. That is because the origin is that green stalk, and the ear is set upon it from above, and the grains are layered one above another; and above the ear there arise fine, sharp bodies like needles, and the purpose of their creation is to prevent birds from picking up those layered grains.

When He mentioned what sprouts from the grain, He followed it with mention of what sprouts from the date-stone, which is the second category, and said: ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, clusters hanging low﴾. Here there are discussions:

The first discussion: He, exalted is He, mentioned the crop before the palm tree, and this indicates that the crop is more excellent than the palm tree. Al-Jahiz composed a lengthy work on this topic.

The second discussion: al-Wahidi related from Abu 'Ubaydah that he said: "The palm tree 'atla'at' when it brings forth its spathe (tal'), and its spathe is its clusters before it splits open at the ighriid; and the ighriid is also called tal'. He said: The tal' is the first thing seen of the palm's bunch; the singular is tal'ah." As for ﴿qinwan﴾, al-Zajjaj said: qinwan is the plural of qinw, like sinwan and sinw. When you make the dual of qinw you say qinwan with a kasra on the nun, so this plural came in the form of the dual, and the i'rab (grammatical inflection) on the nun is for the plural.

Once you know the explanation of the word, we say: His saying ﴿qinwan dani-yah﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the stalks that have hung down from the spathe, low, within reach of one who picks them. It is also reported from him that he said: short palm trees whose clusters cling to the ground. Al-Zajjaj said: He did not say "and from them qinwan far-off," because the mention of one of the two categories indicates the second, as He said: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and He did not say "garments that protect you from the cold," because mention of one of two opposites indicates the other. So too here. It has also been said: He mentioned the near (dani-yah) and left out the far, because the blessing in the near is more complete and more abundant.

The third discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf said: qinwan is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), "and from the palm trees" is its predicate, "from its spathe" is a substitute for it, as if it were said: "and there is produced from the spathe of the palm trees qinwan." It is also permissible that the predicate be omitted, being indicated by "We brought forth" (akhrajna) upon it, its estimated form being: "and brought forth from the spathe of the palm trees are qinwan." And whoever reads "yukhraju minhu habbun mutarakib" (grain layered comes forth from it), qinwan according to him is conjoined to His saying "habb." And qinwan has been read with a damma and with a fatha on the qaf, as the plural of kawkab (star), because fi'lan is not of the pattern of broken plurals.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and gardens of grapes, and the olive and the pomegranate﴾, and in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: 'Asim read "jannatun" with a damma on the ta', and it is the reading of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him; and the rest read "jannatin" with a kasra on the ta'. As for the first reading, it has two aspects:

The first: that it is intended to mean, "and [there are] gardens of grapes," i.e., along with the palm trees.

Second, it may be conjoined to "qinwān" with the meaning: "and there come forth from the palm trees clusters (qinwān) and gardens of grapes." As for the reading in the accusative, its justification is that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿the growth of every thing﴾, and the implied meaning is: "And We brought forth by it gardens of grapes." Likewise His saying: ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾. The author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The better view is that both be in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), like His saying: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ [an-Nisa: 162], due to the excellence of these two kinds."

The second discussion: al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾ intends "the tree of the olive" and "the tree of the pomegranate," as He said: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning "its people."

The third discussion: Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned here four kinds of trees: the palm, the grape, the olive and the pomegranate. He placed the crops before the trees because crops are food, while the fruits of trees are fruit, and food takes precedence over fruit. He placed the palm before the other fruits because dates function as food with regard to the Arabs. Also, the philosophers (hukama') have explained that between it and animals there is a resemblance in many properties, such that that resemblance is not found in other kinds of plants. For this reason the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "Honour your aunt, the palm tree, for it was created from the leftover clay of Adam." He mentioned the grape right after the palm because the grape is the noblest of fruits, since from the moment it first appears it is beneficial until the end of its state. When it first appears on the tree, thin green threads appear, sour in taste yet pleasant to eat, and it is possible to make cooked dishes from them. Then after that the unripe grape (hisrim) appears, which is a noble food for the healthy and the sick, and unripe grape is made into light-tasting drinks beneficial to those with bile conditions, and cooked dishes are made from it, so it is as if it were the most delicious of sour dishes. Then when the grape is fully ripe, it is the most delicious and sweetest of fruits. Hanging grapes can be preserved for a year or less or more, and this is in truth the most delicious of stored fruits. Then four kinds of consumables remain from it: raisins, date-syrup (debs), wine and vinegar, and the benefits of these four cannot be mentioned except in volumes. As for wine, although the Shari'ah has forbidden it, He, exalted is He, said of it: ﴿and benefits for people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], then He said: ﴿but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. The best thing in the grape is its seed, and physicians make from it great-benefit digestive confections (jawarishanat) for the weak, moist stomach. Thus it is established that the grape is, as it were, the sultan of fruits. As for the olive, it too is
page 90
very beneficial, because it can be eaten as it is, and from it there is separated a large oil of great benefit for eating and for all other uses. As for the pomegranate, its state is extremely remarkable, because it is a body composed of four parts: its peel, its pith, its seeds and its juice.

As for the first three parts, which are the peel, the pith and the seeds, all of them are cold and dry, earthly, dense, astringent, and strongly astringent (ʿafṣa) in these qualities. As for the juice of the pomegranate, it is the opposite of these qualities: it is the most delicious and most refined of drinks, closest to balance, and most suited to balanced natures, and in it there is strengthening for a weak temperament; it is food in one respect and medicine in another. So when you reflect on the pomegranate you find the three parts described with complete earthly density, and you find the fourth part, the juice, described with subtlety and balance, so it is as if He, glorified is He, united in it two opposites that differ, and thus the indication of power and mercy in it is more complete and perfect.

Know that the kinds of plants are too many for volumes to explain them fully, so for this reason Allah, exalted is He, mentioned these four kinds, which are the noblest kinds of plants, and sufficed with mentioning them as a reminder of the rest. When He mentioned them He said: ﴿resembling one another and not resembling﴾, and concerning this there are discussions:

The first: concerning the interpretation of ﴿resembling﴾, there are several views:

The first: these fruits may resemble one another in colour and shape while differing in taste and sweetness, and they may differ in colour and shape while resembling one another in taste and sweetness. For grapes and pomegranates may resemble one another in appearance, colour and shape, yet differ in sweetness and sourness, and vice versa.

The second: in most fruits, what is in them of peel and seeds resembles one another in taste and property, but what is in them of flesh and moisture differs in taste.

The third: Qatadah said: the leaves of the trees are close to resembling one another, but their fruits differ. Others say: the trees resemble one another and the fruits differ.

The fourth: I say: you may take a cluster of grapes and see all its berries ripened, sweet and good, except for certain berries that remained in their first state of greenness, sourness and astringency. On this reckoning, some berries of that cluster resemble one another and some do not resemble.

The second discussion: It is said: "ishtabaha al-shay'ani and tashabaha" (the two things became alike), as in your saying "istawaya" and "tasawaya" (they became equal), and the ifti'al and tafa'ul forms often share meaning. And it was read: "mutashabihan wa-ghayra mutashabih."

The third discussion: He said "mushtabihan" and did not say "mushtabihin" either by sufficing with describing one of them, or on the reckoning: "and the olive, resembling and not resembling, and the pomegranate," similarly, as in the verse:
"He shot me with a matter from which I was and my father innocent, and because of hunger he shot me."

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit and at its ripening﴾, and concerning this there are discussions:

The first discussion: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "thumurihi" with a damma on the tha' and the mim; Abu 'Amr read "thumrihi" with a damma on the tha' and sukun on the mim; and the rest read with a fatha on the tha' and the mim. As for the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, it has two aspects:

The first, which is the clearer, is that the plural of "thumurihi" is "thumur," as they say "khashabah" and "khushub" (a piece of wood / pieces of wood). Allah said: ﴿as if they were propped-up planks (khushubun musannadah)﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. Likewise "akamah" and "ukum" (a hillock / hillocks). Then they lighten it, saying "ukm." The poet said:
page 91
"You see the hillocks prostrating before the hooves."

The second aspect: it is the plural of "thumurah" taken as "thimar," then "thimar" is pluralized as "thumur," so "thumur" is a plural of a plural. As for the reading of Abu 'Amr, its justification is that the lightening of "thumur" is "thumr," as they say "rusul" and "rusl" (messengers). As for the reading of the rest, its justification is that "thamar" is the plural of "thamarah," like "baqarah" and "baqar," "shajarah" and "shajar," and "kharazah" and "kharaz."

The second discussion: al-Wahidi said: "al-yan'" is ripeness. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is said "yana'a yayna'u," with fatha in the past and kasra in the future. Al-Layth said: "yani'at al-thamarah" with kasra, and "ayna'at" so it is "tayna'u" and "tuni'u" "iynaan" and "yan'an" with fatha on the ya', and "yun'an" with damma on the ya'; and the adjective is "yani'" and "muni'." The author of the Kashshaf said: it was also read "wa-yun'ihi" with damma on the ya', and Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-yani'ihi."

The third discussion: His saying ﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾ is a command to consider the state of the fruit at the beginning of its coming into being; and His saying ﴿and its ripening﴾ is a command to consider its state when it is complete and perfect. This is the locus of the argument and the proof, which is the purpose of this verse. For these fruits and blossoms come into being at first with particular attributes, and when they are complete and perfect they do not remain in their first states, but pass into states opposite to the earlier ones: for instance, what was described with the greenness of colour becomes coloured with blackness or redness, and what was described with sourness becomes described with sweetness, and perhaps what was at first cold by nature becomes hot by nature at the end. The occurrence of these changes and transformations must have a cause, and that cause is not the influence of the natures, the seasons, the stars and the spheres, because the relation of all these states to all these differing bodies is equal and alike, and equal relations cannot be causes of differing events. Since ascribing the occurrence of these events to natures, stars and spheres is invalid, it becomes necessary to ascribe them to the Capable, the Choosing, the Wise, the Merciful, who governs this world in accordance with mercy, benefit and wisdom. When Allah, glorified is He, drew attention to the indication contained in this subtle aspect, He said: ﴿Verily in that are signs for a people who believe﴾. The Qadi said: the intended meaning is for one who seeks faith in Allah, exalted is He, because it is a sign for those who believe and for those who do not believe. It may be that the reason for specifying the believers in mention is that they are the ones who benefited from it and not others, as was established earlier in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

One may say: rather, what is intended is that the indication of this proof for establishing the Capable, Choosing God is manifest, strong and clear, as though a questioner asked: why did people differ on this matter despite the existence of such a clear, manifest and strong indication? It is answered that the strength of the proof benefits and profits only when God decrees for the servant the attainment of faith.
