So it is as if it were said: this indication, in its strength and manifestness, is an indication for the one whose decree from God concerning him was faith in advance; but as for the one whose decree from God was disbelief in advance, he does not benefit from this indication at all. So the purpose of this specification is to draw attention to what we have mentioned. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 100 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God, though He created them; and they attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they describe.﴾

In this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned these five proofs from the signs of the lower world and the higher world, establishing divinity and the perfection of power and mercy, He then mentioned that among people there are those who ascribed partners to God. Know that this matter has already been mentioned, but what is mentioned here is other than what was mentioned before, because those who ascribed a partner to God are groups and sects.

The first group: the idol-worshippers. They say the idols are partners of God in worship, but they acknowledge that these idols have no power to create, originate or bring into being.

The second group: among the polytheists, those who say that the planets are the governors of this world. These are of two kinds. Some say they are necessary of existence in themselves; others say they are contingent of existence in themselves, originated, and their creator is God, exalted is He, except that He, glory be to Him, entrusted the management of this lower world to them. These are the ones about whom God related that Abraham, peace be upon him, debated with them by his saying: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ The explanation of this argument has already passed.

The third group: among the polytheists, those who said that for the whole of this world, with what is in it of heavens and earths, there are two gods: one of them the doer of good, and the second the doer of evil. The purpose of this verse is to relate the doctrine of these people. This is the exposition of the arrangement of the verse and the drawing of attention to what it contains of benefits.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾ was revealed concerning the zindiqs (heretics) who said: God and Iblis are two brothers; God, exalted is He, is the creator of men, animals, cattle and goods, and Iblis is the creator of beasts of prey, serpents, scorpions and evils.

Know that this statement which Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned is the best of the interpretations mentioned for this verse, because by this interpretation the verse gains an additional benefit different from what was mentioned in the preceding verses. Ibn ʿAbbas said: What strengthens this interpretation is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. He was described as being of the jinn because the word jinn is derived from concealment (istitar), and the angels and spiritual beings are not seen by the eyes, so they are as though hidden from the eyes; by this interpretation the word jinn was applied to them. I say: this is the doctrine of the Magians. Ibn ʿAbbas said "this is the saying of the zindiqs" because the Magians are called zindiqs, for the scripture which Zoroaster claimed had been sent down to him from God was named the Zand, and its adherent is called Zandi; then it was Arabized and it was said zindiq; then it was pluralized and it was said zanadiqa.

Page 93

Know that the Magians said: everything in this world of good comes from Yazdan, and all that is in it of evils comes from Ahriman, who is called Iblis in our law. Then they differed: most of them hold that Ahriman is originated, and they have strange statements about the manner of his origination; a few of them said that he is eternal and without beginning. On both views they agreed that he is a partner of God in the management of this world: the goods of this world are from God, exalted is He, and its evils are from Iblis. This is the explanation of what Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said.

If it is said: On this assumption, these people affirmed one partner for God, namely Iblis; so how does God relate about them that they affirmed partners for God?

The answer: they say that God's army is the angels and Iblis's army is the devils; the angels are in great multitude, and they are pure, sanctified spirits, and they inspire those human spirits with good deeds and acts of obedience. The devils also are in great multitude, and they cast evil whisperings into human spirits; and God with His army of angels fights against Iblis with his army of devils. For this reason God, exalted is He, related about them that they affirmed partners for God from among the jinn. This is the detail of this view.

Having known this, we say: His saying ﴿and He created them﴾ is an indication of the decisive proof that demonstrates the invalidity of Iblis being a partner of God, exalted is He, in His dominion, and its argument is in two ways:

The first: we have related from the Magians that most of them acknowledge that Iblis is not eternal but originated.

Having established this, we say: every originated thing has a creator and originator, and that is none other than God, glory be to Him, exalted is He. These Magians are therefore bound to hold with certainty that the creator of Iblis is God, exalted is He. Since Iblis is the root of all evils, calamities, corruptions and vices, and the Magians have conceded that his creator is God, exalted is He, they have then conceded that the God of the world is the creator of what is the root of evils, vices and corruptions. If that is so, it is impossible for them to say that there must be two gods, one of whom is the doer of goods and the second the doer of evils; because by this route it is established that the god of good is himself the creator of this which is the greatest evil. So His saying ﴿and He created them﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, is the creator of these devils according to the doctrine of the Magians; and if He is their creator, then they have acknowledged that the god of good is the doer of the greatest evils, and when they acknowledge that, the claim that there must be a god for goods and another god for evils falls.

The second way, in deducing the argument from His saying ﴿and He created them﴾: what we have demonstrated in this book and in the book "al-Arbaʿin fi Usul al-Din" is that whatever is other than the One is possible in its essence, and every possible-in-essence is originated; it follows that whatever is other than the One, the Real, the Unique, is originated. It is therefore necessary to hold with certainty that Iblis and all his hosts are characterized by origination and the coming into existence after non-existence; and then the aforementioned compulsion returns as we have established it. This is the statement of the principal purpose of this verse, and success is from God.

* * *

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾ means: "and they made the jinn partners with God."

If it is said: what is the benefit of the fronting (of the word "God")?

We say: Sibawayh said that they put first what is most important to them, namely the one they are concerned with. The benefit of this fronting is to magnify the idea that a partner should be taken for God, whether that partner is an angel, a jinn, a human, or something else. This is the reason for placing the name of God before the partners.

Having known this, we say: "al-Jinn" has been read in the accusative, nominative and genitive. As for the accusative, the well-known view is that it is a substitute (badal) for "partners" (shuraka'). Some verifiers said: this is weak, because a substitute is that which stands in the place of what it replaces; if it were said "they made the jinn partners with God," it would not be a meaningful sentence; rather, it is better to take it as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan). As for the reading in the nominative, when it is said "they made partners with God," this sentence, if it were left at that, would be valid to mean the jinn, the humans, the stone or the idol; so it is as if it were asked: "And who are those partners?" and it was answered: "The jinn." As for the reading in the genitive, it is by the idafa (construct) which is of specification (lil-tabyin).

The third issue: they differed in interpreting this association in three ways:

The first: what we have mentioned, that what is meant is relating the saying of one who affirms two gods for the world, one the doer of good and the second the doer of evil.

The second view: the unbelievers used to say: the angels are the daughters of God. These say: what is meant by the jinn is the angels; and the name was applied to them because the word jinn is derived from concealment, and the angels are hidden from the eyes. The one who holds this should have explained how, from their saying that the angels are the daughters of God, it follows that they made the angels partners with God, so that the wording of the verse would fit this meaning. Perhaps it may be said: these people used to say that the angels, although they are daughters of God, manage the affairs of this world, and in that case association arises.

The third view, which is the view of al-Hasan and a group of exegetes: the meaning is that the jinn called the unbelievers to worship idols and to the doctrine of association, and they accepted this from the jinn and obeyed them, so that by this means they became those who say the jinn are partners of God, exalted is He. I say: the truth is the first view, and the last two are very weak. As for interpreting this association by the saying of the Arabs, "the angels are the daughters of God," this is false for several reasons:

The first reason: God, exalted is He, related this doctrine in His saying: ﴿and they attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾. The assertion of daughters for God is nothing but the saying of one who says the angels are God's daughters; so if we interpret His saying ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾ in this sense, it would entail repetition in one place without benefit, and that is not permissible.

The second reason against this interpretation: the Arabs said "the angels are the daughters of God," and affirming a child for God is one thing, and affirming a partner for Him is another. The evidence for the difference between the two matters is that He distinguished between them in His saying: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3-4]; and if one of them were the very other, this detail in that surah would be pointless.

The third reason: those who affirm Yazdan and Ahriman expressly assert a partner for the god of the world in the management of this world; so turning the wording away from that and carrying it to the assertion of daughters is turning the word from its literal sense to its figurative sense without necessity, and that is not permissible.

As for the second view, namely the view of one who says the intended meaning of this association is that the unbelievers accepted the jinn's word about worshipping idols: this is extremely remote, because the one who calls to association cannot be named a partner of God, neither according to the literal sense of the word nor according to its figurative sense. Moreover, if we carried this verse to this meaning, repetition without benefit would occur, because

Page 95

the refutation of the idol-worshippers and the star-worshippers has already preceded in full detail. Thus the invalidity of these two views is established, and it becomes clear that the truth is the view we have supported and strengthened.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He created them﴾, there are two investigations:

The first investigation: they differed about what the pronoun in His saying "(He created them)" refers to, on two views:

The first view: it refers to "the jinn," and the meaning is that they said the jinn are partners of God; then these people acknowledged that Ahriman is originated; and among the Magians there are those who say that He exalted is He reflected upon the kingdom of His own self and magnified it, so a kind of wonder arose, and from that wonder the devil was generated; and among them is one who says He doubted the power of His own self, and from His doubt the devil was generated. These people therefore acknowledge that Ahriman is originated, and that his originator is God, exalted is He. So His saying "and He created them" is an indication of this meaning; and once it is established that this devil is created by God, exalted is He, it is impossible to make him a partner of God in the management of the world, because the Creator is stronger and more perfect than the created; and to make the weak and deficient a partner of the strong and perfect is impossible to the intellects.

The second view: the pronoun refers to those who associate, namely those who affirmed a partnership between God, exalted is He, and the jinn. This view, in my opinion, is weak for two reasons:

One of them: if we carry it to what we have mentioned, this single word becomes a conclusive, complete and perfect proof in refuting that doctrine; but if we carry it to this second meaning, no benefit appears from it.

Second, the principle that a pronoun returns to the nearest previously mentioned noun is obligatory, and the nearest mentioned item in this verse is the jinn. Therefore the pronoun must refer back to them.

Second discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it is read "wa-khalqahum" (and their creation), meaning their fabricating (ikhtilaq) of falsehood. That is, they made the jinn their creation in that they attributed their sacrifices to God, when they said: ﴿And God has commanded us to do them﴾ [al-A'raf 7:28].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And they invented for Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾. On this there are several discussions.

First discussion: I say: God, may He be exalted, related that some people affirmed Iblis as a partner to God. Then, after that, He related that other peoples affirmed sons and daughters for God. Those who affirmed sons are the Christians and a group of the Jews. Those who affirmed daughters are the Arabs, who say: "The angels are the daughters of God." His saying ﴿without knowledge﴾ serves as an indication of the decisive proof against the corruption of this claim. On this there are several points:

The first argument: God must be necessarily existent in His essence. Then His offspring is either necessarily existent in its essence or it is not. If it is necessarily existent in its essence, it would be self-sufficient, self-subsisting, with no dependence of its existence on another. Whoever is like this cannot be anyone's father at all, because a child implies derivation and need. If that child is possibly existent in its essence, then its existence is by the bringing-into-being of the necessarily existent being, and whoever is like this is a servant of Him and not His child. Thus it is established that whoever knows what God is will refrain from attributing sons and daughters to Him.

The second argument: a child is needed to take the parent's place after the parent's passing away. This can only be conceived in the case of one who passes away. As for one who is sanctified above that, a child cannot be conceived in his case.

The third argument: a child implies that it was produced from a part of the parent's parts, and this can only be conceived in the case of one who is composite, from whom some of his parts can separate. In the case of the single, unique, necessarily existent One, this is impossible. The essence of the matter is that whoever knows the reality of God knows it is impossible for Him to have a child. So His saying ﴿and they invented for Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾ is an allusion to this subtle point.

Second discussion: Nafi' read "wa-kharraqu" with a doubled ra'. The rest read "kharaqu" with a single ra'. Al-Wahidi said: the preferred reading is the single ra', because it is more common, while the doubled form indicates intensification and multiplicity.

Third discussion: Al-Farra' said: the meaning of "kharaqu" is "iftaʿalu" (they fabricated) and "iftaraw" (they forged). He said: kharaqu, ikhtaraqu, khalaqu, and ikhtalaqu, and iftaraw, all have one meaning. Al-Layth said: it is said "takharraqa al-kadhib" and "takhallaqahu" (he invented the lie). Al-Kashshaf related that al-Hasan was asked about this word, and he said: it is an Arabic word that they used to say; when a man told a lie in the assembly of people, some of them would say to him: "qad kharaqahā" (he has fabricated it). And God knows best. Then he said: it may also be from "kharaqa al-thawb" when he tore the garment, meaning they tore for Him sons and daughters.

Then God concluded the verse by saying: ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they describe﴾. His saying "subhanahu" (glory be to Him) is a declaration of God's transcendence above everything unfitting to Him. As for His saying "wa-taʿala" (and exalted), there is no doubt that it does not indicate elevation in place, because the purpose here is to declare God free from these corrupt sayings, and elevation in place does not convey this meaning. Thus it is established that the intended meaning here is exaltedness above every false belief and corrupt statement.

If they say: according to this interpretation, there is no difference between His saying "subhanahu" and His saying "wa-taʿala."

We say: a clear difference remains between them. The meaning of "subhanahu" is that this speaker glorifies Him and declares Him free of what is unfitting for Him. The meaning of "wa-taʿala" is that He is in His essence exalted and sanctified above these attributes, whether or not any glorifier glorifies Him. So glorification refers to the statements of those who glorify, while exaltedness refers to His essential attribute, which belongs to Him by His own essence and not by anything else.

[Page 96]

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 101:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a child when He has no consort? He created all things, and He is Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that when the Exalted had explained the corruption of the view of the various groups of the worldly polytheists, He began to establish the proofs against the corruption of the view of those who affirm a child for Him, so He said: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Know that the explanation of His words ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah. However, we shall point here to what is the principal purpose of this verse. We say: *ibda'* (origination) is an expression for bringing a thing into existence without a prior model. Accordingly, whoever produces a method in some art that no one before him had produced, it is said that he has *abda'* (originated) in it.

[Page 97]

Having understood this, we say: God the Exalted has granted to the Christians that 'Isa came into being without a father or a drop of semen; rather he came into being and entered existence, because God the Exalted brought him into existence without a prior father.

Having understood this, we say: the purpose of the verse is to say: You either mean by his being a child of God the Exalted that He originated him by way of *ibda'*, without a preceding drop of semen or a parent; or you mean by his being a child of God the Exalted what is customary and familiar from a human being being a child of his father; or you mean by his being a child of God a third concept, distinct from these two concepts.

As for the first possibility, it is false. This is because He, although He brings about events in this lower world on the basis of known causes and particular intermediaries, the Christians nonetheless affirm that the lower world is originated. If this is the case, it necessarily follows that they must acknowledge that He created the heavens and the earth without a preceding matter or duration. If this is the case, His bringing the heavens and the earth into being must be *ibda'*. Now, if it followed merely from His being an originator of 'Isa, peace be upon him, that He is his father, then it would follow from His being an originator of the heavens and the earth that He is their father. It is known that this is false by consensus. Thus it is established that merely His being an originator of 'Isa, peace be upon him, does not entail His being his father. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. He mentioned only the heavens and the earth and did not mention what is in them, because the coming into being of what is in the heavens and the earth is not by way of *ibda'*, whereas the coming into being of the very essence of the heavens and the earth was by way of *ibda'*. So the intended argument was accomplished by mentioning the heavens and the earth, not by mentioning what is in the heavens and the earth. This is the refutation of the first aspect.

As for the second possibility, namely that the people's meaning of begetting is the customary, familiar begetting among animals, this too is false, and the following aspects show it:

The first aspect: that begetting of that kind is valid only from one who has a consort and desire, and from whom a part separates and that part is retained within the body of that consort. These conditions hold only for a body that can be joined and separated, moved and at rest, bounded and finite, and that experiences desire and pleasure. All of this is impossible for the Creator of the world. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿How could He have a child when He has no consort?﴾

The second aspect: that obtaining a child by this means is valid only for one who is not able to create, originate and bring into being all at once. So when someone wills a child and cannot bring it into being all at once, he turns to obtaining it by the customary means. But as for one who is the creator of all possibilities and capable of all originations, when He wills to bring something into being He says to it: "Be," and it is. Whoever has the attributes and description we have mentioned is precluded from bringing a person into being by way of begetting. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿He created all things﴾.

The third aspect: this child is either eternal or originated. It is not permissible that he be eternal, because the eternal must necessarily be necessarily existent in its own essence, and whatever is necessarily existent in its essence is independent of anything else; therefore it is impossible for it to be the child of another. What remains is that if he were a child, he would necessarily be originated. We say: He, the Exalted, knows all knowables. Either He knows that in obtaining a child there is for Him perfection and benefit, or He knows that the matter is not so. If it is the first, then at no time can it be posited that God the Exalted created this child except that the motive to bring this child into being was already present before that. And whenever the motive to bring it into being was present before it, it necessarily follows that the child existed before that. This necessitates that this child be eternal, which is impossible. If it is the second, then it is established that He, the Exalted, knows that for Him there is in obtaining a child no perfection of state and no increase in rank in divinity. If this is the case, it necessarily follows that He must never bring him into being at any time. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿and He is Knowing of all things﴾.

There is another aspect in this matter: it is said that customary begetting arises only through the satisfaction of desire, and the satisfaction of desire necessitates pleasure, and pleasure is desired for its own sake. So if pleasure were valid for God the Exalted, even though it is desired for its own sake, it would necessarily follow that there is no time except that God's knowledge of obtaining that pleasure would move Him to obtain it before that time. This is because, since He, the Exalted, knows all knowables, this meaning must necessarily be known to Him. If this is the case, He must have obtained that pleasure in eternity, and so it follows that the child is eternal, and we have already shown that this is impossible. Thus it is established that His being Knowing of all knowables, together with His being eternal, prevents the validity of a child for Him. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿and He is Knowing of all things﴾.

Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that it is not possible to affirm a child for God the Exalted on the basis of these two known possibilities. As for affirming a child for God the Exalted on the basis of a third possibility, that is false, because it is inconceivable and not intelligible to the intellect. Therefore, to affirm begetting on the basis of that third possibility, which is inconceivable, is to plunge into sheer ignorance, and it is false. This is the purpose of this verse. Even if the earlier and later generations were to gather to mention in this matter a discourse equal to it in strength and perfection, they would be unable to do so. Praise belongs to God, who guided us to this, and we would not have been guided had God not guided us.

This is the first part of al-Razi's commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verse 102.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 102 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him. And He is Guardian over all things.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had established the proof for the existence of the God who is Capable, Choosing, Wise and Merciful, and had shown the corruption of the view of those who went to associating partners with Allah, and had detailed their doctrines in the best manner, and had shown the corruption of each one of them by the proofs appropriate to it, then He related the doctrine of those who affirmed sons and daughters for Allah, and showed by decisive proofs the corruption of saying so. At this point it became established that the God of the worlds is one single, Eternal (al-Samad), exalted above partner, equal, counterpart and rival, and exalted above offspring, sons and daughters. Thereupon He stated the conclusion, saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of everything other than Him, so worship Him and do not worship anyone besides Him.﴾ For He is the one who sets right the affairs of all His servants, who hears their supplication, sees their humility and submission, knows their need, and is the Guardian for everyone in the attainment of their affairs. Whoever reflects on this arrangement and order in establishing the call to Tawhid and declaring Him free of imperfection, and in showing the corruption of shirk, will know that there is no path clearer or more right than it. And in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "That" (dhalikum) is a reference to the One described by the attributes mentioned before, and it is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows are synonymous predicates (akhbar), namely: ﴿Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things﴾, meaning: that One who combines these attributes,
Page 99
so worship Him, in the sense that whoever has these attributes is the one deserving of worship, so worship Him and do not worship anyone other than Him.

The second issue: Know that He, may He be exalted, has shown in this surah, by many proofs, the dependence of creation upon a Creator, Originator, Innovator, Bringer-into-being and Manager, but He did not mention a separate proof that indicates the negation of partners, counterparts and rivals. Then He followed the proofs indicating the existence of the Maker by reporting the saying of those who affirmed a partner for Allah. This alone would necessitate the certainty of association from the jinn, and then He refuted it. Then after that He came with pure Tawhid, saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him.﴾ At this point the question arises: the sum of what preceded is the establishment of proof for the existence of the Creator and the refutation of the proof of those who affirmed a partner for Allah. How then does this alone necessitate the certainty of pure Tawhid? We say: the scholars have many ways of establishing Tawhid, and among them is this method.

Its establishment is from several aspects:

The first: The earlier scholars said: one Maker is sufficient, and whatever exceeds one, the discussion regarding it is equal (mutakafi'), so Tawhid becomes necessary. As for our saying "one Maker is sufficient": the God who is capable of all possible things and knows all knowable things is sufficient for being God of the world and its Manager. As for the claim that what exceeds one, the discussion regarding it is equal: the proof has not indicated the establishment of anything beyond one, so affirming one number is not preferable to affirming another number, and it would necessarily follow either the affirmation of infinitely many gods, which is impossible, or the affirmation of a specific number although that number is no more deserving than all other numbers, which is also impossible. When both parts are false, only Tawhid remains.

The second aspect of establishing this method: that the God who is capable of all possible things and knows all knowables is sufficient for managing the world. So if we assumed a second god, that second would either be an agent and originator of some of the events of this world, or not. The first is false, because each of the two, being capable of all possible things, makes each act of one of them, by its being the agent of that act, prevent the other from achieving what it can do, and that necessitates each one being a cause of the other's incapacity, which is impossible. If the second does not act, does not bring anything into being, then it is deficient and idle, and that is not suitable for divinity.

The third aspect of establishing this method: we say that this one God must necessarily be perfect in the attributes of divinity. So if we assumed a second god, that second would either share with the first all attributes of perfection, or not. If it shares with the first all attributes of perfection, then it must be distinguished from the first by something, for if no distinction occurred by any means, plurality and duality would not occur. And if distinction occurred by something, that distinguishing thing is either one of the attributes of perfection or not. If it is one of the attributes of perfection, while the distinction occurred by it, then not all attributes of perfection are shared between them. If that distinguishing thing is not one of the attributes of perfection, then the one described by it is described by an attribute that is not one of the attributes of perfection, and that is a deficiency. Thus it is established by these three aspects that the one God is sufficient for managing and originating the world, and that the additional one must be negated. This is the method that Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned here in establishing Tawhid. As for relying on the argument of mutual prevention (dalil al-tamana'), we have mentioned it in Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

The third issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited His saying: ﴿Creator of all things﴾ as evidence that He, may He be exalted, is the Creator of the deeds of the servants. They said: the deeds of the servants are things, and Allah, may He be exalted, is the Creator of all things by the ruling of this verse, so it necessarily follows that He is the Creator of them. Know that we have elaborated on this argument in the book "al-Jabr wal-Qadar," and we will here suffice with a few points from those words. The Mu'tazilah said: although this expression is general, there have come with this verse aspects which indicate that the deeds of the servants are excluded from this generality:

The first of them: He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Creator of all things, so worship Him.﴾ If the deeds of the servants entered under His saying "Creator of all things," the meaning of the verse would become: "I created your deeds, so you do them yourselves a second time," and it is known that this is corrupt.

The second: He, may He be exalted, only mentioned His saying "Creator of all things" in the context of praise and commendation of Himself, so if the deeds of the servants entered under it, it would cease to be praise and commendation, because it is not fitting for Him, glorified be He, to praise Himself for creating fornication, sodomy, theft and disbelief.

The third: He, may He be exalted, said after this verse: ﴿There have come to you clear evidences from your Lord; so whoever sees, it is for his own soul, and whoever is blind, it is against it.﴾ [al-An'am: 104] This is an explicit statement that the servant is independent in the act and the abandonment, and that there is absolutely no impediment for him from doing or abandoning. This indicates that the act of the servant is not created by Allah, may He be exalted, for if it were created by Allah, the servant would not be independent in it; for when Allah brings it into being, he cannot repel it, and when Allah does not bring it into being, he cannot attain it. Since this verse indicates that the servant is independent in the act and the abandonment, and it is established that this state prevents saying the act of the servant is created by Allah, it is established that the mention of His saying: ﴿so whoever sees, it is for his own soul, and whoever is blind, it is against it﴾ [al-An'am: 104] necessitates the specification of that generality.

The fourth: This verse is mentioned after His saying: ﴿and they made for Allah partners, the jinn﴾, and we have shown that what is meant by it is the narration of the doctrine of the Magians in affirming two gods for the world, one of which does pleasures and goods, and the other does pains and calamities. So His saying after that: ﴿there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things﴾ must be understood as an refutation of that doctrine, and that is only the case if we say that He, may He be exalted, is the Creator of everything in this world, of predators, insects, diseases and pains. So when we take His saying "Creator of all things" in this sense, the deeds of the servants do not enter under it. They said: thus it is established that these four proofs necessitate the exclusion of the deeds of the servants from the generality of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Creator of all things﴾.

The answer: We say that the decisive rational proof has supported the soundness of the apparent meaning of this verse, and its establishment is that the act depends upon the motive, the creator of the motive is Allah, may He be exalted, and the totality of power together with the motive necessitates the act, and that requires that He, may He be exalted, is the Creator of the acts of the servants. When this apparent meaning is confirmed by this decisive rational demonstration, doubts and objections disappear.

The fourth issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Creator of all things, so worship Him﴾ indicates that the ordering of the command to worship upon His being the Creator of all things is by the letter fa' (so), which denotes immediate consequence, and the ordering of a ruling upon a description by the letter fa' indicates causation. This requires that His being the Creator of things is what necessitates His being worshipped absolutely, and the deity is the one deserving of worship. This indicates the soundness of what some of our companions mention, that the deity (ilah) is an expression for the one capable of creating, originating, bringing into being and innovating.

The fifth issue: Many of the Mu'tazilah cited His saying: ﴿Creator of all things﴾ as evidence for the negation of attributes and that the Qur'an is created. As for the negation of attributes: they said: if He, may He be exalted, is knowing by knowledge and capable by power, then that knowledge and power are either said to be eternal or originated. The first is false, because the generality of His saying "Creator of all things" requires that He is the creator of all things; we have introduced specification into this generality with respect to His own essence, since it is impossible that He be the creator of Himself, so it must remain in its generality regarding everything else. And the affirmation of eternal attributes requires further specification within this generality, and that is not permissible.
Page 101
The second: the claim that the knowledge and power of Allah are originated is false by consensus, and because it would necessitate that the bringing into being of that knowledge and power depends upon a prior knowledge and another power, and that is impossible. As for their use of this verse to show that the Qur'an is created, they said: the Qur'an is a thing, and every thing is created by Allah, may He be exalted, by the ruling of this generality, so it follows that the Qur'an is created by Allah, may He be exalted. The most that can be said in this matter is that this generality has been entered by specification concerning the essence of Allah, may He be exalted; yet a specified general statement is an argument in what lies outside the place of specification. For this reason, the entry of this specification into this generality did not prevent the People of the Sunnah from citing it in establishing that the acts of the servants are created by Allah, may He be exalted.

Our companions' answer to this: we specify this generality by the proofs indicating that He, may He be exalted, is knowing by knowledge and capable by power, and by the proofs indicating that the speech of Allah, may He be exalted, is eternal.

* * *

The sixth issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾. What is meant by it is that the servant attains the perfection of Tawhid and its establishment, namely that although the servant believes that there is no deity except Him, and that there is no manager except Allah, may He be exalted, yet this world is the world of means (asbab).

I heard our shaykh, the imam, the ascetic, my father, may Allah have mercy on him, say: "Were it not for the means, no doubter would have doubted." Since this is the case, a person may attach his heart to apparent means: at times he relies on the ruler, and at times he turns for the attainment of his affairs to the vizier. Then he gains nothing but deprivation and finds nothing but multiplied sorrows. But the Truth, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾, and the purpose is that a person should know that there is no protector except Allah, and no setter-right of affairs except Allah; then his hope is cut off from everything other than Him, and he returns in none of his affairs except to Him.

The seventh issue: He said shortly before this verse: ﴿and He created all things﴾, and here He said: ﴿Creator of all things﴾, and this is like repetition.

The answer is in several aspects:

[Page 102]

The first point: His saying ﴿And He created everything﴾ refers to the past, whereas His saying ﴿Creator of everything﴾ is the active participle (ism al-fa'il), which encompasses all times.

The second point, and this is the verified position: He mentioned there His saying ﴿And He created everything﴾ to make it a premise in demonstrating the negation of offspring, and here He mentioned His saying ﴿Creator of everything﴾ to make it a premise in demonstrating that there is no one worthy of worship except Him. The summary is that this premise entails many rulings and various conclusions, so He mentions it time and again, so that in each place He may derive from it the conclusion that befits it.

The eighth issue: One may say that the ilah is the one who deserves to be worshipped, so His saying ﴿there is no ilah except Him﴾ means that none deserves worship except Him. What, then, is the benefit of His saying after that, (fa'buduhu) [so worship Him], for this gives the impression of repetition?

The answer: His saying ﴿there is no ilah except Him﴾ means that none deserves worship except Him, and His saying (fa'buduhu) means: do not worship anything other than Him.

The ninth issue: The people were acknowledging the existence of God, as He said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [Luqman: 25]. They did not apply the name Allah to anyone other than Allah, Glorified is He, as He said: ﴿Do you know of anyone with His name?﴾ [Maryam: 65]. Then He said: ﴿That is God, your Lord﴾, i.e., the One described by the attributes mentioned earlier is God, Exalted is He. Then He said after it: (your Lord), meaning the One who nurtures you and bestows upon you kindnesses through various kinds of nurture and forms of beneficence. These categories have reached such a multitude that the intellect is unable to count them, as He said: ﴿And if you tried to count God's blessings, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

Then He said: ﴿there is no ilah except Him﴾, meaning: since you have recognized the existence of the God who is beneficent, bountiful and generous, know that there is no god besides Him and no one worthy of worship besides Him.

Then He said: ﴿Creator of everything﴾, meaning: our saying "there is no god besides Him" is valid only because there is no creator of creation besides Him, and no manager of the world except Him. So this order is an appropriate and beneficial sequence.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 103 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No vision perceives Him, yet He perceives vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾.

In this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse that God, exalted is He, can be seen, and that the believers will see Him on the Day of Resurrection, from several angles.

The first angle in establishing this claim is to say: this verse indicates that God, exalted is He, can be seen.

Once this is established, it is necessary to be certain that the believers will see Him on the Day of Resurrection.

As for the first point, its establishment is this: God, exalted is He, praised Himself by saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾, and this is something that supports the opponent. On it they built their argument for establishing their position of denying vision.

Once this is established, we say: if God were not capable of being seen, the praise in His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ would not be achieved. Do you not see that the non-existent cannot be seen, and that knowledge, power, will and smells and tastes cannot be seen, and there is no praise for any of them in being in a state where they cannot be seen? Thus it is established that His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ conveys praise, and that this conveys praise only if He is capable of being seen. This indicates that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ conveys that He is capable of being seen. The complete verification of this is that when a thing is in itself such that its being seen is impossible, then the non-seeing of it does not entail praise or glorification of the thing. But if it is in itself capable of being seen, and then He is able to veil vision from seeing Him and perceiving Him, this complete power indicates praise and greatness. Thus it is established that this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable of being seen by virtue of His essence.

Once this is established, it is necessary to be certain that the believers will see Him on the Day of Resurrection. The proof for this is that there are two kinds of speakers: one who says He can be seen while the believers see Him, and one who says He is not seen and cannot be seen. As for the claim that He, exalted is He, can be seen while none of the believers sees Him, this is a claim that no one of the community has held, so it is false. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable of being seen in His essence. And it is established that whenever the matter is like this, it is necessary to be certain that the believers see Him. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that this verse indicates the occurrence of vision. This is a subtle inference from this verse.

[Page 103]

The second angle: we say that the intended meaning of "vision" (al-absar) in His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ is not the act of seeing itself, for sight never perceives anything at all in any place. Rather, the perceiver is the one who sees. Therefore it is necessary to be certain that what is meant by His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ is that those who see do not perceive Him. If this is so, then His saying ﴿and He perceives vision﴾ means that He perceives those who see. The Mu'tazilah of Basra agree with us that He, exalted is He, sees things, so He is among those who see. Thus His saying ﴿and He perceives vision﴾ requires that He, exalted is He, sees Himself. If the matter is like this, then He is capable of being seen in His essence, and He sees His own self. Whoever says that He, exalted is He, is capable of being seen in His own self, says that the believers will see Him on the Day of Resurrection. So this verse indicates both that He is capable of being seen and that the believers will see Him on the Day of Resurrection. If we want to make this inference more concise, we say: the intended meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He perceives vision﴾ is either the act of seeing itself or the one who sees. On either assumption, it follows that He, exalted is He, sees the sight of His own self, and that He sees the essence of His own self. Once this is established, it is necessary that the believers will see Him on the Day of Resurrection, because there is no one who makes a distinction.

The third angle concerning the inference from the verse: the word "al-absar" (vision) is a plural form to which the definite article "al-" has been attached, so it conveys comprehensiveness (istighraq). Thus His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ conveys that not all vision perceives Him. This conveys negation of universality, not universal negation.

Once you know this, we say: restricting this negation to the collective indicates that the judgment holds for some individuals of the collective. Do you not see that when a man says, "Not all people struck Zayd," this conveys that some of them struck him?

So when it is said, "Not all people believed in Muhammad (ﷺ)," this conveys that some people believed in him. Likewise His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ means: not all vision perceives Him. Therefore it must convey that some vision perceives Him. At most it may be said: this is a reliance on the argument from implication (dalil al-khitab). We say: grant that it is so, yet it is a sound argument, because if, on the assumption that no one at all perceives Him, the restriction of this negation to the collective as a collective were pointless, and preserving the speech of God, exalted is He, from pointlessness is obligatory.

The fourth angle in relying on this verse: it is reported that Dirar ibn 'Amr al-Kufi used to say that God, exalted is He, is not seen with the eye, but is seen with a sixth sense which God, exalted is He, will create on the Day of Resurrection. He was argued against with this verse, and he said: this verse indicates the restriction of the negation of God's being perceived to sight, and the restriction of a judgment to one thing indicates that the situation in other things is different. Therefore it must be that perceiving God by other than sight is permissible in general. And since it has been established that the other senses that exist now are not suitable for that, it is established that one may say that on the Day of Resurrection He will create a sixth sense by which the seeing and perceiving of God, exalted is He, will occur. So these are four angles derived from this verse which may be relied upon in establishing that the believers will see God on the Day of Resurrection.

* * *

The second issue: in relating the Mu'tazilah's inference from this verse for negating vision.

Know that they argue from this verse in two ways:

The first: they said, "Perceiving by sight is an expression for seeing, as evidence that if someone said, 'I perceived him with my sight but I did not see him,' or said, 'I saw him but did not perceive him with my sight,' his speech would be self-contradictory. Thus it is established that perceiving by sight is an expression for seeing."

[Page 104]

Once this is established, we say: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ requires that no vision sees Him in any state. The evidence for the soundness of this generality has two aspects:

The first: it is valid to make an exception of all individuals and all states from it, so one says, "No vision perceives Him except the sight of so-and-so," or "except in such-and-such a state." An exception removes from the speech what would otherwise have to be included. Thus it is established that the generality of this verse conveys the generality of negation over all individuals in all states, and this indicates that no one sees God, exalted is He, in any state.

The second aspect for showing that this verse conveys generality: "When 'Aishah (may God be pleased with her) rejected the statement of Ibn 'Abbas that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord on the night of the Mi'raj, she relied on this verse in support of her own position." If this verse were not conveying generality with respect to all individuals and all states, that argument would not have been complete. And there is no doubt that she was among the people most knowledgeable of the Arabic language. Thus it is established that this verse indicates negation with respect to all individuals, and that conveys the required claim.

The second: in establishing the Mu'tazilah's inference from this verse, they said: what precedes this verse up to this point contains praise and commendation, and His saying after that, ﴿and He perceives vision﴾, is also praise and commendation. Therefore His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ must be praise and commendation. Otherwise it would follow that something which is not praise and commendation occurred within what is praise and commendation, and that requires incoherence, which is not appropriate to the speech of God.

Once this is established, we say: whatever its non-existence would be praise, and that is not of the category of act, its existence would be a deficiency with respect to God, exalted is He, and deficiency upon God, exalted is He, is impossible, by His saying ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], and His saying ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3], and so on. Therefore it must be said that His being seen is impossible.

Know that these people restricted this to what is not of the category of act only because He, exalted is He, praised Himself by negating injustice from Himself in His saying ﴿And God does not desire injustice for the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 108], and His saying ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], even though, according to them, He is able to do injustice. So they mentioned this restriction to avert this objection against their speech. This is the furthest extent of the presentation of their position on this matter.

The answer to the first angle has several aspects:

The first: we do not accept that perceiving by sight is an expression for seeing. The evidence for this is that the word "perception" (idrak) in its original linguistic usage is an expression for reaching and arriving. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed we are overtaken (mudrakun)"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 61], meaning "we will be overtaken." And He said: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him (adrakahu)﴾ [Yunus: 90], meaning it reached him. It is said, "So-and-so overtook so-and-so (adraka fulanun fulanan)," and "the boy reached (adraka al-ghulam)," meaning he reached puberty, and "the fruit ripened (adraqat al-thamarah)," meaning it matured. Thus it is established that perception is reaching a thing.

Once you know this, we say: when the seen object has a limit and an end, and sight perceives it in all its limits, sides and ends, it is as if that sight encompassed it, and this seeing is called perception. But when sight does not encompass the sides of the seen object, that seeing is not called perception. The conclusion is that seeing is a genus under which are two species: seeing with encompassment, and seeing without encompassment. Seeing with encompassment is what is called perception. Therefore negating perception conveys negating one species of the two species of seeing, and negating a species does not entail negating the genus. So negating perception from God, exalted is He, does not entail negating seeing from God, exalted is He. This is a sound and acceptable point against the opponent's argument.

[Page 105]

We say: this is far-fetched, because perception is more specific than seeing, and affirming the more specific entails affirming the more general, while negating the more specific does not entail negating the more general. Thus it is established that the explanation we have mentioned refutes your claim and does not refute ours.

The second aspect of the objection: grant that perceiving by sight is an expression for seeing. But why do you say that His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ conveys generality of negation over all individuals, all states, and all times? As for the argument from the soundness of exception to establish generality of negation, it is countered by the soundness of exception from the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah), although that does not convey generality of negation. Rather, we grant that it conveys generality, but the negation of generality is different from the generality of negation. We have shown that this expression conveys only the negation of generality, and we have shown that the negation of generality entails the establishment of the particular. This is what we established in the explanation of the argument. As for his saying that 'Aishah (may God be pleased with her) relied on this verse in negating seeing, we say: knowledge of the vocabulary of the language is acquired from the scholars of language, but the manner of inferring from evidence is not to be taken on the basis of imitation. In sum, rational evidence shows that His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ conveys negation of generality, and clear reason establishes that the negation of generality is distinct from the generality of negation. Their aim is only achieved if the verse indicated the generality of negation, so their argument falls.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 103 (part 2 of 3):**

The third aspect: We say that the plural form (*sigha al-jam'*) may be understood as covering everything (*al-istighraq*), but it may also be understood as referring to a previously known group (*al-ma'hud al-sabiq*). If that is the case, then His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ indicates that the visions known in this world do not perceive Him. We agree with this meaning, for these eyes and these pupils, as long as they remain with these attributes that characterize them in this world, do not perceive God, Exalted is He. They would perceive God, Exalted is He, only if their attributes changed and their states were altered. So why do you say that when these changes occur they will not perceive God?

The fourth aspect: Let us grant that eyes absolutely do not perceive God, Exalted is He. Why, then, is it not possible for the perception of God, Exalted is He, to occur through a sixth sense different from these senses, as Dirar ibn 'Amr (a early Mu'tazili theologian) used to hold? On this assumption, there is no benefit in relying on this verse.

The fifth aspect: Suppose this verse is general. Still, the verses that indicate the affirmation of the vision of God, Exalted is He, are specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. At this point the discussion moves from this position to explaining whether those verses indicate that the vision of God, Exalted is He, will occur or not.

The sixth aspect: We say in accordance with the verse's wording, so we say: Let us grant that eyes do not perceive God, Exalted is He. Why do you say that those who see do not perceive God, Exalted is He? This is the total of the objections to the first aspect. As for the second aspect, we have already explained that it is impossible for praise to be achieved by negating vision if God, in His essence, were such that His vision was impossible. Rather, praise is achieved only if He were such that His vision is valid. Then, He, Exalted is He, veils the eyes from seeing Him, and by this method their entire argument collapses. Then we say: Negation cannot be a cause for the occurrence of praise and commendation, because pure negation and mere non-existence do not necessitate praise and commendation, and knowledge of this is necessary. Rather, when negation is a proof of the occurrence of an established attribute among the attributes of praise and commendation, it is said that this negation necessitates praise. An example of this is His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. This does not convey praise by considering this negation alone, for an inanimate object is also not overtaken by drowsiness or sleep. However, this negation, with respect to the Creator, Exalted is He, indicates that He is
[Page 106]
Exalted, knowing all knowable things forever, without change or cessation. Likewise, His saying: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14] indicates that He subsists by Himself and is self-sufficient in His essence, because an inanimate object also neither eats nor is fed.

Given this, we say: His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ cannot convey praise and commendation unless it indicates a positive existing meaning that conveys praise and commendation. That is what we have said, for it indicates that He, Exalted is He, is able to veil the eyes and prevent them from perceiving and seeing Him. With this explanation, the argument turns against them as proof. Thus the Mu'tazilah's (a rationalist theological school) use of this verse collapses entirely.

* * *

The third issue: Know that al-Qadi (the judge), in his tafsir, mentioned other aspects that indicate the negation of vision. In reality, these are outside the use of this verse, separate from the science of tafsir, and a plunge into the science of usul (foundations of jurisprudence and theology). Since al-Qadi did this, we will transmit them and answer them. Then we will mention for our companions aspects that indicate the validity of vision. As for al-Qadi, he relied on rational arguments:

The first: If the sense organ is sound, the object seen is present, and the required conditions are met, namely that there is no excessive nearness, no excessive distance, no veil, and the object is facing or in the position of facing, then seeing must occur. For if it were permissible, under these conditions, for seeing not to occur, it would be permissible for there to be trumpets and drums in our presence that we neither hear nor see, and that would entail sophistry.

They said: Once this is established, we say: The absence of excessive nearness, excessive distance, veil, and facing is impossible with respect to God, Exalted is He. So if His vision were valid, the cause of that vision would necessarily be the soundness of the sense organ and the object's being such that it can be seen. These two meanings exist at this time. So if He were such that He could be seen, His vision would have to occur at this time. Since this vision does not occur, we know that He cannot be seen.

The second argument: Everything that is seen is facing or in the position of facing, and God, Exalted is He, is not such. Therefore His vision must be impossible.

The third argument: Al-Qadi said: It is said to them: How will the people of Paradise see Him and not the people of Hell? Either He will be near them or facing them, so their situation with Him will differ from that of the people of Hell. This necessitates that He is a body that is subject to nearness, distance, and veiling.

The fourth argument: Al-Qadi said: If you say that the people of Paradise see Him in every state, even during intercourse and other times, that is false. Or if you say they see Him in one state and not another, that is also false, because this entails that He is sometimes near and sometimes far. Also, vision of Him is the greatest of pleasures, and if that is so, they must always be desiring that vision. Then if they do not see Him at some times, they fall into grief and sorrow, and that is not fitting for the attributes of the people of Paradise. This is the total of what he mentioned in *Kitab al-Tafsir*. Know that these arguments are extremely weak.

As for the first argument, it is said to him: Grant that the vision of bodies and accidents is necessary when the sense organ is sound, the object is present, and all other conditions are met. Why do you say that it necessarily follows that the vision of God, Exalted is He, is necessary when the sense organ is sound and the object is such that it can be seen? Do you not know that the essence of God, Exalted is He, differs from all other essences, and that a judgment established for one thing does not necessarily entail the same judgment for what differs from it? It is strange that these Mu'tazilah, both their first and last, relied on this argument, although they claim complete perspicacity and extreme shrewdness, and none of them noticed this objection or realized the weakness of this statement.
[Page 107]
As for the second argument, it is said to him: The dispute between us and you concerns whether an existing thing that is not specifically located in a place or direction can be seen or not. Then either you claim that knowledge that the vision of this existing thing, described with this attribute, is impossible is a self-evident knowledge, or you say it is an inferential knowledge. The first is false, for if knowledge of it were self-evident, disagreement about it would not have occurred among rational people. Also, assuming this knowledge were self-evident, it would be pointless to occupy oneself with mentioning proof. So abandon inference and be content with claiming self-evidence. If it is the second, then we say: Your statement that the object seen must be facing or in the position of facing is a repetition of the very claim itself, because the gist of your speech is that you said: The proof that what is neither facing nor in the position of facing cannot be seen is that everything seen must be facing or in the position of facing. It is known that there is no benefit in this statement except repeating the claim.

As for the third argument, it is said to him: Why is it not permissible to say that the people of Paradise see Him and the people of Hell do not see Him? Not because of nearness and distance as you mentioned, but because God creates the vision in the eyes of the people of Paradise and does not create it in the eyes of the people of Hell. If you return, in refuting this statement, to the claim that permitting it leads to permitting that there be trumpets and drums in our presence that we neither see nor hear, that would be a return to the first method, and its answer has already passed.

As for the fourth argument, it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that the believers see God, Exalted is He, in one state and not another? As for your saying that this requires saying He is sometimes near and sometimes far, it is said: This returns to the claim that sight occurs only under the mentioned conditions, and that is a return to the first method, whose answer has already passed.

As for his second statement, that vision is the greatest of pleasures, it is said to him: Although it is so, it is not far-fetched to say that they desire it in one state and not another, as evidenced by the fact that all other pleasures and benefits of Paradise are good and delightful, yet they occur in one state and not another. So it is the same here. This completes the discussion of the answers to the arguments he mentioned on this topic.

* * *

The fourth issue: On stating the arguments that indicate that the believers see God, Exalted is He. We will enumerate them here and refer their detailed explanation to the appropriate places:

The first: Moses, peace be upon him, requested vision from God, Exalted is He, and this indicates the permissibility of the vision of God, Exalted is He.

The second: He made vision conditional upon the mountain remaining in its place, when He said: ﴿But if it remains in its place, then you will see Me﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The mountain's remaining in place is possible, and what is conditional upon something possible is possible. These two proofs will be explained, God willing, in surah al-A'raf.

The third argument: Relying on His saying: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ in the ways already mentioned.

The fourth argument: Relying on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. Its explanation has already been mentioned in surah Yunus.

The fifth argument: Relying on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110]. The same applies to all verses containing "meeting." Its explanation has already passed in this tafsir many times and in various ways.
[Page 108]
The sixth argument: Relying on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾ [al-Insan: 20]. One reading of this verse is "malikan" (a king) with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, and the Muslims agreed that this king is none other than God, Exalted is He. In my view, relying on this verse is stronger than relying on other verses.

The seventh argument: Relying on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No indeed! Surely they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15]. The specification of the disbelievers for being veiled indicates that the believers will not be veiled from seeing God, Mighty and Majestic.

The eighth argument: Relying on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent, at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13-14]. The explanation of this argument will come in the tafsir of surah al-Najm.

The ninth argument: The pure hearts are naturally disposed to love knowing God, Exalted is He, in the most perfect way, and the most perfect way of knowing is vision. Therefore the vision of God, Exalted is He, must be desired by everyone. Once this is established, it is necessary to be certain that it will occur, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And therein you will have whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31].

The tenth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 107]. This verse indicates that God has made all the Gardens of Paradise a lodging for the believers, and it is not permissible to limit it to lodging. Rather, after the lodging there must be an honor greater in status than that lodging, and that is nothing but vision.

The eleventh proof: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]. The explanation of each of these aspects will come in its proper place in this book. As for the reports, there are many of them, among them the well-known hadith, his saying ﷺ: "You will see your Lord just as you see the moon on the night of the full moon; you will not be hindered in seeing Him." Know that the comparison lies in comparing the seeing with the seeing in clarity and manifestness, not in comparing the seen object with the seen object. Among them is what the majority agreed upon: that he ﷺ recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who do good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26], and said: "The best reward is Paradise, and the more is looking at the Face of Allah." Among them is that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, disagreed about whether the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah on the night of the Mi'raj (ascension), yet some of them did not declare others to be disbelievers on account of this, nor did they attribute innovation and misguidance to one another. This indicates that they were agreed that there is no rational impossibility in the seeing of Allah, exalted is He. This is the summary of the discussion on the transmitted (sam'iyyat) aspects of the question of seeing.

* * *

The fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He perceives the vision﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, sees things, perceives them, and apprehends them. That is because either the intended meaning of "the visions" is the very act of seeing, or the intended meaning is those who see. If it is the first, then it necessarily follows that He is a seer of the seeing of those who see and of the sight of those who perceive; and whoever says this says that He, exalted is He, sees all seen and perceived things. If it is the second, then it necessarily follows that He, exalted is He, sees those who perceive. On both interpretations, this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, perceives the perceptible and sees the visible.

The sixth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He perceives the vision﴾ conveys restriction (hasr). Its meaning is that He, exalted is He, is the One who perceives the visions, and none other than Allah, exalted is He, perceives them. The meaning is that the matter by which a living being becomes one who sees visible things, perceives perceptible things, and apprehends apprehensible things is a marvelous matter and a noble reality, which the intellect cannot comprehend in its essence. Yet, despite this, Allah, exalted is He, perceives its reality and has knowledge of its essence. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ is that none of the perceiving faculties encompasses His reality, and that no intellect stands upon the essence of His self-sufficiency (samadiyyah). Thus the visions fall short in perceiving Him, and the intellects recoil from reaching the arenas of His might. Just as nothing encompasses Him, His knowledge encompasses everything, and His perception reaches everything. This is the manner of the composition of this verse.

The seventh issue: His saying: ﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾. Subtlety (al-lutf) is the opposite of density (al-kathafah), and what is intended by it is fineness (al-riqqah). That is impossible with respect to Allah, so one must resort to interpretation (ta'wil) of it, and this is in several ways:

The first way: what is intended is the subtlety of His craftsmanship in composing the bodies of animals from fine parts, delicate membranes, and narrow passages that no one knows except Allah, exalted is He.

The second way: He, glorified is He, is subtle in bestowing favors, kindness, and mercy.

The third way: He is subtle toward His servants, in that He praises them when they obey, commands them to repent when they disobey, and does not cut off from them the shade of His mercy, whether they are obedient or sinners.

The fourth way: He is subtle toward them, in that He does not command them beyond their capacity and bestows upon them blessings beyond what they deserve. As for "the All-Aware" (al-Khabir): it is from khabar, which means knowledge. The meaning is that He is subtle toward His servants while being aware of what they are upon of committing sins and engaging in ugly deeds. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Al-Latif" means that He is too subtle to be perceived by visions, and "al-Khabir" means aware of every subtle thing; so He perceives the visions, and nothing is too subtle to escape His perception. This is a fine interpretation.

﴿Indeed there has come to you clear evidence (basa'ir) from your Lord. So whoever sees, it is for his own soul, and whoever is blind, it is against it. And I am not a guardian over you.﴾

**First issue:** Almighty God, when He had established these clear proofs and compelling arguments concerning these lofty and noble divine matters, returned to establishing the matter of the call, the conveying of the message, and the prophethood, and so He said: ﴿Indeed there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾. *Basa'ir* is the plural of *basira*. Just as *basar* (sight) is the name for the complete and perfect perception that is attained by the eye in the head, *basira* is the name for the complete perception that occurs in the heart. God says: ﴿Nay, man is evidence against himself﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:14], meaning he has complete knowledge of himself. By His saying ﴿Indeed there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ He intends the preceding verses, which in themselves are not *basa'ir*, but because of their strength and sublimity they produce *basa'ir* for whoever knows them and comprehends their realities. Since these verses are causes for the attainment of *basa'ir*, these verses themselves were called *basa'ir*. The purpose of this verse is to explain what relates to the Messenger and what does not relate to him.

As for the first category, which relates to the Messenger, it is the call to the true religion and the conveying of the proofs and clear signs therein. He, peace be upon him, did not fall short in conveying them, clarifying them, and removing doubts about them. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾.

As for the second category, which does not relate to the Messenger, it is their taking the initiative to believe and abandon disbelief. This does not relate to the Messenger; rather it relates to their own choice, and its benefit and harm return to them. The meaning is: whoever perceives the truth and believes, it is for his own soul that he has perceived, and it is to his soul that he has brought benefit; and whoever is blinded to it, it is against his own soul that he has become blind, and it is to his soul that he has brought harm by blindness. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: I do not preserve your deeds and recompense you for them; I am only a warner, and God is the Guardian over you.

**Second issue (on the rulings of this verse):** There are four, which al-Qadi mentioned.

The first: the purpose of these *basa'ir* is that they be benefited from by choice, by which one deserves reward, not that one be compelled toward them or forced into them, for that would nullify this purpose.

The second: God only guided us and made clear to us benefits, and the purposes of benefits return to us, not to benefits returning to God Most High.

The third: a person, by turning away from reflection and contemplation, harms himself, and he was not brought to this except from himself, not from his Lord.

The fourth: he is able to do both, which is why He said: ﴿So whoever sees, it is for his own soul, and whoever is blind, it is against it﴾. He said: In this is the refutation of the saying of the *Mujbira* (determinists) regarding the created being, and of the view that God imposes obligations without capacity.

Know that whenever the *Mu'tazila* (rationalist school) embark upon wisdom, philosophy, and command and prohibition, there is no way to deal with them except by countering them with the question of the one who makes the call (i.e., the question of the one who calls them), for it demolishes everything they mention.

**Third issue:** The intended meaning of seeing here is knowledge, and of blindness is ignorance. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46].

**Fourth issue:** The exegetes said: His saying ﴿So whoever sees, it is for his own soul, and whoever is blind, it is against it﴾ means: I will not take you to account for faith in the manner of a guardian over you and a trustee. They said: This was before the command to fight; when He commanded fighting, he became a guardian over them. Among them are those who say: the verse of fighting abrogates (*naskh*) this verse. But this is far-fetched. It seems that these exegetes are fond of multiplying abrogation without any need for it. The truth is what the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) establish: the default is the absence of abrogation, so it is obligatory to strive to minimize it as far as possible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 105:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We vary the verses, so that they may say, "You have studied [them]," and that We may make it clear to a people who know.﴾

Know that when Exalted God had completed His discourse on divine matters up to this point, He began from this point on to establish prophethood. So Exalted God began by relating the doubts of those who denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The first doubt: their saying, "O Muhammad, this Qur'an you have brought us is speech that you acquire from studying with scholars and debating with men of learning, and you arrange it on your own, then you recite it to us, and you claim that it is a revelation that came down to you from God Exalted. Then God Exalted answered it with many arguments. This is the statement of the arrangement, and in the verse there are issues:

Issue one: Know that what is meant by His saying, ﴿And thus We vary the verses﴾, is that He brings them successively, one state after another. Then He said, ﴿so that they may say, "You have studied [them]"﴾, and in this there are discussions.

First discussion: al-Wahidi related two views concerning the phrase darasa al-kitab (he studied the book):

The first: al-Asma'i said its origin is from their saying darasa al-ta'am (he threshed the food) when he trod it, yadrusuhu durasan, and al-diras means al-diyas in the dialect of the people of al-Sham. He said: and darasa al-kalam from this, meaning he makes it easy, so it lightens on his tongue.

The second: Abu al-Haytham said, "darastu al-kitab" means I made it familiar through much reading until its memorization became easy, from their saying darastu al-thawb adrusuhu darsan, so it is madrus and daris, meaning I wore it out, and from this the worn garment is called daris, because it has become soft. And al-dirasa is practice, and from it comes darastu al-surah until I memorized it. Then al-Wahidi said: this view is close to what al-Asma'i said, indeed it is the same, because the meaning in it returns to making easy and softening.
