Second discussion: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿dārasta﴾ with an alif and a fatha on the ta', and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Its interpretation is "you studied with the Jews and they studied with you," and there was between you and them a mutual study and discussion. This reading is strengthened by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but a falsehood he has invented, and other people have helped him with it."﴾ [al-Furqan: 4]. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿darasat﴾, meaning these narratives you recite to us are ancient, they have been effaced and wiped out, and passed away from the dars, which is the obliteration of traces and effacing of the outline. Al-Azhari said: whoever reads "darasat" its meaning is "they have become old," i.e., what you recite to us has become old and long-standing, and it is from their saying darasa al-athar yadrusu durusan.

Know that the author of al-Kashshaf related other readings here:

The first: ﴿darusat﴾ with a damma on the ra', as an intensification of ﴿darasat﴾, meaning its effacement became intense.

The second: ﴿durisat﴾ in the passive form, meaning it has become old and effaced.

The third: ﴿dārasat﴾, and they interpreted it as "the Jews studied with Muhammad."

The fourth: ﴿darasa﴾, meaning Muhammad studied.

The fifth: ﴿dārisāt﴾, in the sense "they are dārisāt," i.e., ancient, or possessing study, like ʿīshatun rāḍiyah.

Third discussion: The waw in His saying ﴿wa-liyaqūlū﴾ is a conjunction upon an implied element; the estimate is: "And thus We vary the verses, in order to establish the proof against them, and so that they may say." The conjoined element has been omitted because its meaning is clear.

Fourth discussion: Know that He, exalted is He, said ﴿And thus We vary the verses﴾, then mentioned the reason for which He varied these verses, which is two matters:

One of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that they may say, "You have studied [them]"﴾.

The second is His saying: ﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾. As for this second reason, there is no difficulty in it, because God Exalted made clear that the wisdom in this variation is that clarity, understanding and knowledge may appear from it. The discussion concerns only the first reason, which is His saying ﴿so that they may say, "You have studied [them]"﴾, because their saying to the Messenger, "You have studied," is disbelief on their part in the Qur'an and the Messenger. At this point the discussion of the question of compulsion and predestination returned. As for our companions (the Ash'aris), they took the statement according to its apparent sense, and said: its meaning is that We mentioned these proofs one state after another so that some of them would say, "You have studied," and so increase in disbelief upon disbelief, and as a confirmation for others so that they increase in faith upon faith. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He misguides many thereby and guides many thereby﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and His saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds filth to their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. As for the Mu'tazilah, they were perplexed. Al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi said: there is in it only one of two aspects:

The first: that this affirmation be taken to mean negation, the estimate being: "And thus We vary the verses so that they do not say, 'You have studied'"; a parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], meaning: lest you go astray.

The second: that this lam be taken as the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), the estimate being: the outcome of their affair, upon Our variation of these verses, is that they say this saying, relying on their own choice, turning away from what the reflection on these proofs would require. This is the full extent of the people's statement on this subject.

One may say: as for the first answer, it is weak for two reasons:

The first: that taking an affirmation to mean a negation is a distortion of the speech of God and an alteration of it, and opening this door requires that no trust remain either in its negation or in its affirmation, and that removes it from being a proof, and that is false.

The second: that even granting that this kind of alteration is permissible in general, it is absolutely unsuitable in this place. That is because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to reveal the verses of the Qur'an bit by bit, and the disbelievers used to say: Muhammad combines these verses with one another, reflects on them and arranges them verse by verse, then reveals them. If this were by revelation descending to him from heaven, why does he not bring this Qur'an all at once, just as Moses, peace be upon him, brought the Torah all at once?

Knowing this, we say: the variation of these verses state by state is what caused the doubt for the people, that Muhammad (ﷺ) brings this Qur'an by way of study, with reflection and discussion with other peoples. And according to what al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi say, it requires that the variation of these verses state after state necessitates that they refrain from saying that Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, brought this Qur'an by way of study and discussion. Thus it is established that the answer he gave is valid only if we take the variation of the verses as the cause for their refraining from that saying; yet we have shown that the variation of the verses is what necessitates that saying. So this objection falls.

As for the second answer, namely taking the lam as the lam of consequence, it is also far-fetched, because taking this lam as the lam of consequence is a metaphor, while taking it as the lam of purpose is literal, and the literal is stronger than the metaphorical. So if we say that the lam in His saying ﴿so that they may say, "You have studied"﴾ is the lam of consequence, and the lam in His saying ﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾ is literal, then the metaphor has come before the literal in mention, and that is not permitted. Thus through what we have mentioned, the weakness of these two answers is established, and that the truth is what we have mentioned: that what is meant by it is the very thing mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He misguides many thereby and guides many thereby﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. What confirms this interpretation is His saying: ﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾, meaning: We have only made it clear to these people; as for those who do not know, We have not made these verses clear to them. And since this shows that He has made it a clarification only for the believers, it is established that He has made it a misguidance for the disbelievers, and that is what we have said. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 106–107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord. There is no god but Him. And turn away from the polytheists.﴾

Know that when He, exalted be He, related that the disbelievers attributed this Qur'an's appearance to fabrication, or claimed that he (ﷺ) studies with certain people, acquires these sciences from them, then arranges them into a Qur'an and claims that it was sent down to him from God, He followed this with His saying: ﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord.﴾

[Page 113]

This was lest that statement become a cause of his slackening in conveying the call and the message. The purpose is to strengthen his heart and to remove the grief that arose from hearing that doubt. By His saying ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ He draws attention to the fact that, since God is One in divinity, obeying Him is obligatory, and it is not permissible to turn away from His obligations because of the ignorance of the ignorant or the deviation of the deviators.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾, it has been said that what is meant is abandoning confrontation, and for this reason some said that it is abrogated (mansukh). This is weak, because the command to abandon confrontation in the present circumstance does not indicate a command to abandon it permanently, and when the matter is so, there is no need to affirm abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one). It has also been said that what is meant is abandoning confrontation with them over the folly they commit, and that he, may the blessings of God be upon him, should turn to the way that is closer to acceptance and further from aversion and harshness.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated others with Him, nor have We made you a guardian over them, nor are you their keeper.﴾

Know that this statement also relates to their saying to the Messenger, peace be upon him, "You have only gathered this Qur'an from people's studying and discussing with them." It is as if He, exalted be He, were saying to him: Do not pay attention to the foolish talk of these disbelievers, and let their disbelief not weigh heavily upon you, for if I had willed to remove disbelief from them I would have been able to do so, but I left them with their disbelief. So you should not occupy your heart with their words.

Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) held fast to His saying ﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated others with Him﴾, the meaning being: had God willed that they not associate, they would not have associated. Since the consequent did not occur, we know that the antecedent did not occur, and so we know that God's will for their non-association did not take place. The Mu'tazilites (a theological school that affirmed human free will and divine justice) said: It has been established by proof that He willed from all of them faith, and that He did not will disbelief and polytheism from anyone. This verse, however, indicates that He did not will faith from all of them, so it is necessary to reconcile the two proofs. God's will for their faith is therefore understood as the will of voluntary faith that entails reward and praise, while His not willing their faith is understood as the faith that arises through compulsion, force and coercion. That is, He did not will for them that He should bring them to faith by way of compulsion and coercion, because that would nullify moral responsibility (taklif) and remove the human being from deserving reward.

This is what the people relied upon in this matter, and it is extremely weak, and several points show this:

The first: Without doubt, it is He who empowered the disbeliever to disbelieve. If the power of disbelief is not suitable for faith, then the one who created that power undoubtedly willed disbelief. If it is suitable for faith, the side of disbelief does not outweigh the side of faith except upon the occurrence of a motive calling to disbelief, otherwise one of the two equal possibilities would be preponderant over the other without a preponderant cause, and this is impossible. The combination of the power together with the motive to disbelief necessitates disbelief. And since the Creator of the power and of the motive is God, exalted be He, and it has been established that their combination necessitates disbelief, it has been established that He willed disbelief from the disbeliever.

The second: In stating this argument we say: He, exalted be He, knew that the disbeliever would not have faith, and the existence of faith together with the knowledge that there is no faith are opposites. When one of the two opposites exists, the occurrence of the other is impossible, and what is impossible, together with the knowledge that it is impossible, is not willed. So it is inconceivable to say that He wills faith from the disbeliever.

The third: Suppose that voluntary faith is better and more beneficial than faith obtained by compulsion and force. Nevertheless, since He knew that this more beneficial faith will never occur, it would have been required, by His wisdom and mercy, that He create faith in him by way of compulsion, for even if this faith does not entail great reward, at least it saves him from great punishment. Thus, leaving this faith uncreated in him by way of compulsion entails his falling into the severest torment, and this is not befitting of mercy and benevolence. An example of this: a man has a dear son, and this father is extremely compassionate, and this son is standing at the edge of the sea. The father says to him: "Dive into the depths of this sea so that you may extract from it the great, lofty and elevated pearls," and the father knows with certainty that if he dives into the sea he will perish and drown. If this father, looking after his son's interest and being compassionate toward him, is obliged to prevent him from diving into the depths of the sea, saying to him: "Give up seeking those pearls, for you will not find them and you will perish; rather, it is better for you to be content with little provision with safety." But to command him to dive into the depths of the sea while being fully certain that he will gain nothing from it but destruction, this indicates a lack of mercy and a pursuit of his destruction. So it is the same here. And God knows best.

Know that when He, exalted be He, made clear that no one has the power to remove disbelief from them, He concluded the discussion with what completes the enlightenment of the Messenger, peace be upon him. He, exalted be He, explained to him the extent of what was entrusted to him, mentioning that He did not make him a guardian over them nor a keeper, by way of preventing them. He only entrusted to him the conveying of the commands and prohibitions, in action and knowledge, and in clarifying through the mention of proofs and drawing attention to them. If they accept, its benefit returns to them; if not, its harm returns to them. In either case, he (ﷺ) does not depart from the mission, the prophethood and the conveying.
