The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 108:

God's words: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in hostility without knowledge. Thus We have made attractive to every community its deeds; then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do.﴾

Know that this statement is also connected to their saying to the Messenger, peace be upon him: "You have only gathered this Qur'an from people's study and discussion." It is not far-fetched that some Muslims, when they heard such speech from the disbelievers, became angry and reviled their gods in retaliation. So God forbade this act, because whenever you revile their gods, they become angry, and they may then speak of God in unseemly terms. To avoid this danger, one must avoid that speech. In sum, this is an admonition that when your opponent confronts you with ignorance and folly, you must not match his abuse with words of the same kind, for that opens the door to mutual reviling and foolishness, which is not becoming of people of reason. There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue:** The scholars have mentioned several views on the occasion of revelation of the verse.

The first: Ibn Abbas said: "When the verse ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98] was revealed, the polytheists said: 'Either you stop reviling and insulting our gods, or we will certainly revile your God.' So this verse was revealed." I say: I have two objections here.

The first: People agree that this surah was revealed all at once, so how can it be said that the occasion of revelation of this verse was such-and-such?

The second: The disbelievers acknowledged God, the Exalted, and they used to say: "We worship the idols only so that they may be intercessors for us with God, the Exalted." If that is so, how is it conceivable that they would dare to revile God?

[Page 115]

The second view on the occasion of revelation: al-Suddi said: "When the death of Abu Talib approached, the Quraysh said: 'Let us go to him and ask him to forbid his nephew from us, for we are ashamed to kill him after his death, and then the Arabs will say: he used to protect him, and when he died they killed him.' So Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith went to him along with a group, and they said to him: 'You are our elder,' and they spoke to him as they wished. Then he (Abu Talib) called Muhammad, peace be upon him, and said: 'These are your people and your paternal cousins. They ask you to leave them to their religion, and that they will leave you to your religion.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'Say: There is no god but God.' They refused. Abu Talib said: 'Say something other than this word, for your people dislike it.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'I will not say anything other than it, even if you bring me the sun and place it in my hand.' They said to him: 'Stop reviling our gods, or we will revile you, and who commands you to do this?' So this is the meaning of His words: ﴿so that they revile God in hostility without knowledge﴾."

Know that we have shown that these people acknowledged the existence of God, the Exalted, and therefore their daring to revile God is impossible. Rather, there are the following possibilities:

The first: Some of them may have held the doctrine of time (dahr, the view that the world is eternal and governed by time) and denied the Creator, and such a person would not have cared about this kind of folly.

The second: Whenever the Companions reviled the idols, they were in fact reviling the Messenger, peace be upon him. God therefore treats reviling the Messenger as reviling God, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to God﴾ [al-Fath: 10], and as in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who abuse God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57].

The third: Some of their ignorant ones may have believed that a devil inspires him to claim prophethood and messengership. Then, out of ignorance, they called that devil "the god of Muhammad, peace be upon him." So they would revile the god of Muhammad on the basis of this interpretation.

**The second issue:** Someone may say: reviling idols is among the foundations of acts of obedience, so how could God forbid it?

The answer: Although this reviling is an act of obedience, when it occurs in a manner that entails the existence of a great evil, it must be avoided. This is the case here, because this reviling would entail their reviling God and His Messenger, opening the door to folly, turning them away from accepting the religion, and placing anger and rage in their hearts. Because it entails these evils, the prohibition against it was issued.

**The third issue:** Al-Hasan recited ﴿fa-yasubbū Allāh ʿudūwan﴾ with a damma on the ʿayn and a shadda on the waw. It is said: "ʿadā fulān ʿadwan, ʿudwan, ʿudwānan and ʿidan," meaning he committed injustice, exceeding the proper measure. Al-Zajjaj said: "ʿadwan is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning is fa-yaʿdū ʿadwan (so they transgress in transgression)." He said: "It is also possible that it is with the implied preposition lām, and the meaning is: so that they attribute injustice to God."

**The fourth issue:** Al-Jubba'i said: This verse indicates that it is not permissible to act towards the disbelievers in a way that increases their distance from the truth and their aversion to it. For if it were permissible for God to do so, it would be permissible for Him to command it, and He would not have forbidden what we have mentioned. And He would not have commanded gentleness towards them when calling them, as in His words to Moses and Aaron: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. This demonstrates the falsity of the doctrine of the Mujbira (the determinists, who deny human agency).

**The fifth issue:** They said: This verse indicates that commanding the good may be deemed reprehensible if it leads to committing an evil, and forbidding an evil may be deemed reprehensible if it leads to an increase in evil. Probable opinion (ghalabat al-zann) takes the place of knowledge in this matter. It also contains a lesson for whoever calls to the religion, so that he does not occupy himself with what has no benefit for the objective. For describing idols as lifeless objects that neither benefit nor harm is sufficient to discredit their divinity, so there is no need, in addition to that, to revile them.

* * *

As for God's words: ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community its deeds﴾, our companions (the Ash'aris) took this as evidence that God is the One who makes disbelief attractive to the disbeliever, faith attractive to the believer, disobedience attractive to the disobedient, and obedience attractive to the obedient. Al-Ka'bi said: "Interpreting the verse in this sense is impossible, for God Himself says: ﴿Satan has adorned for them﴾ [Muhammad: 25], and He says: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghut (false objects of worship), who bring them out of the light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]."

Then the scholars gave several answers:

The first: Al-Jubba'i said: The meaning is: We made attractive to every past community what We commanded them to do, namely accepting the truth. Al-Ka'bi also gave this same answer, saying: The meaning is that God made attractive to them what they ought to do, but they did not refrain.

The second: Others said: The meaning is: We made attractive to every community of the disbelieving nations their evil deeds, that is, We left them to themselves and gave them respite until their evil deeds appeared good to them.

The third: We gave Satan respite until he made it attractive to them.

The fourth: We made it attractive in their own assumption and speech, when they say: "God commanded us to do this and made it attractive to us."

This is the entire collection of interpretations mentioned regarding this verse, and all of them are weak. The reason is that a decisive rational proof has established the validity of what the apparent wording of this text indicates. We have explained more than once that the occurrence of an act from a servant depends on the arising of a motive. We have also shown that this motive must be created by God, the Exalted. And the meaning of that motive is nothing but his knowledge, belief, or assumption that the act includes an additional benefit and a preponderant good. When that motive is produced by the act of God, the Exalted, and the motive means nothing other than his believing that the act includes additional benefit and preponderant good, it follows that it is impossible for a servant to perform any act, saying, movement, or stillness, unless God, the Exalted, makes that act attractive in his heart, conscience, and belief. Moreover, a person does not choose disbelief or ignorance initially while knowing that it is disbelief and ignorance; rather, he chooses it because he believes it to be faith, knowledge, truthfulness, and truth. So, were it not for a prior first ignorance, he would not have chosen this ignorance.

The second: We then transfer the discussion to why he chose that prior ignorance. If it was due to another prior ignorance, then it would follow that this continues without end, which is impossible. Since that is false, these ignorances must terminate in a first ignorance which God creates in him from the outset. Because of that ignorance, he assumed that disbelief was faith, truth, knowledge, and truthfulness. Thus it is established that it is impossible for the disbeliever to choose ignorance and disbelief unless God, the Exalted, makes that ignorance attractive in his heart. By these two decisive proofs, it is established that what the apparent meaning of this verse indicates is the truth from which there is no escape. And if this is the case, then all the interpretations mentioned have been invalidated, for recourse to interpretation occurs only when it is impossible to take the speech in its apparent sense. But since proof has been established that it is not possible to deviate from the apparent meaning, all these contrived interpretations have fallen away. And God knows best.

Moreover, God's words ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community its deeds﴾ following ﴿so that they revile God in hostility without knowledge﴾ indicate that their daring to commit that evil occurred through God's making it attractive. As for taking this to mean that God made good deeds attractive in the hearts of the nations, that is a statement disconnected from what precedes it. Furthermore, His words ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community its deeds﴾ encompass both the disbelieving and the believing nations, so restricting this statement to the believing community abandons the apparent generality. As for the remaining interpretations, al-Zamakhshari, the author of al-Kashshaf, mentioned them, and their weakness is not hidden. And God knows best.

As for God's words: ﴿Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do﴾, the purpose of it is that their affair is entrusted to God, the Exalted, and that God is aware of their conditions and informed of their inner thoughts. Their return on the Day of Resurrection is to God, and He will recompense each person according to the requirement of his deeds: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil.

[Page 118]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 109:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they swore by God their most solemn oaths that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it. Say: The signs are only with God. And what will make you aware that when they come, they will not believe?﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, relates of the disbelievers a doubt that calls his prophethood into question. It is their saying: "This Qur'an you have brought to us only because you study with the scholars and debate with the peoples who knew the Torah and the Gospel, and then you gather these surahs and these verses in this manner." Then He, may He be exalted, answered this doubt with what preceded. This verse contains another doubt, which is their saying to him: "This Qur'an, whatever its state, is not at all of the kind of miracles. Even if you, O Muhammad, had brought us an overpowering miracle and a manifest proof, we would have believed in you." They swore to this and emphasized the strength of that oath. So the purpose of this verse is to establish this doubt. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: They named the oath "qasam" (oath) only because the oath (yamin) is established to affirm the report that a person gives, whether affirming a thing or negating it. Since a report admits of truth and falsehood, the one reporting needs a means by which he seeks to give preference to the side of truth over the side of falsehood, and that means is the swearing of an oath. Since the need to mention the oath arises only when people, on hearing that report, divide into one who believes it and one who denies it, they called the oath a "qasam," and they formed that expression on the pattern of af'ala, saying: "Aqsama fulan yuqsimu iqsaman" (So-and-so swore an oath). They meant that he affirmed the oath he had chosen and attributed the truth to the oath he had chosen by means of the swearing and the oath.

The second issue: They mentioned several explanations for the occasion of revelation:

The first: They said: When the saying of He, may He be exalted, ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven, so that their necks would remain bowed before it﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:4] was revealed, the polytheists swore by God that if a sign came to them they would surely believe in it, so this verse was revealed.

The second: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "The polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'You tell us that Musa struck the rock with his staff and water gushed forth, that Isa revived the dead, and that Salih brought forth the she-camel from the mountain. So bring us also a sign, that we may believe you.' He ﷺ said: 'What is it that you wish?' They said: 'That you turn al-Safa into gold for us.' And they swore that if he did so, they would all follow him. The Prophet ﷺ stood up, supplicating, and Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: 'If you wish, that will happen, but if it happens and they do not believe with it, He will surely punish them; and if they are left, He will relent toward some of them.' He ﷺ said: 'Rather, He will relent toward some of them.' So God, may He be exalted, revealed this verse."

The third issue: They mentioned several explanations for His saying: ﴿jahd aymanihim﴾ (their most solemn oaths):

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: When a man swears by God, that is his "jahd yamin" (his most solemn oath).

Al-Zajjaj said: They exaggerated in the oaths. As for His saying: ﴿if a sign came to them﴾, they differed concerning what is meant by this sign. It was said: it is what we have related about turning al-Safa into gold. It was also said: it is the things mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they said: We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra' 17:90]. It was also said: the Prophet ﷺ used to inform them that the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal) used to descend upon the earlier nations who denied their prophets, so the polytheists asked for the like of it.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: The signs are only with God﴾, they mentioned several explanations for the word "'inda" (with). It is possible that the meaning is that He, may He be exalted, is the one exclusively empowered to bring about such signs and no other; for the miracles that testify to prophethood have the condition that none can bring them about except God, glorified and exalted. It is also possible that the intended sense of "with" (indiyya) is that the knowledge of whether bringing about these miracles would lead these disbelievers to faith or not is with God alone. The word "with" in this sense is as in His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am 6:59]. It is also possible that the intended meaning is that although they are presently non-existent, whenever He wills to bring them about, He brings them about; so they are like things kept with God, which He manifests whenever He wills, and it is not for you to dictate their demand. The word "with" in this sense here is as in His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but its treasuries are with Us﴾ [al-Hijr 15:21].

\* \* \*

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: "ma" is interrogative, and the subject of "yush'iru-kum" is the pronoun referring to "ma." The meaning is: "And what will make you know their faith?" The object has been omitted, and the omission of the object is common. The implied sense is: "And what will make you know their faith, that is, on the assumption that these signs come to them, they will not believe." As for His saying: ﴿that when they come, they will not believe﴾, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "anna-ha" with a kasra on the hamza, as a new sentence (isti'naf), and this is the good reading. The sense is: the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾, that is, "and what will make you aware of what will happen from them?" Then He began: ﴿that when they come, they will not believe﴾.

Sibawayh said: I asked al-Khalil about the reading with a fatha on the hamza in "anna," and I said: "Why is it not permissible that the sense be: 'What will make you know that He does not do it?'" Al-Khalil said: "That is not fitting here, for if He had said ﴿And what will make you aware that〉 with a fatha, that would become an excuse for them." This is the speech of al-Khalil, and its explanation appears through an example. If you prepare a banquet and ask the ruler of the town to attend, and he does not attend, and someone says to you: "If you yourself went to him, he would attend," then if you say: "And what will make you aware that if I went to him, he would attend?" the meaning would be: "Even if I went to him myself, he would not attend." Likewise here, His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe﴾ means: "that when they come, they believe." That would necessitate the coming of these signs, and this speech would become an excuse for the disbelievers in demanding the signs. The purpose of the verse is to refute their argument in demanding the signs. This is the exposition of al-Khalil's statement.

The other reciters read "anna-ha" with a fatha. In its interpretation there are several views:

The first: Al-Khalil said: "anna" here has the sense of "la'alla" (perhaps). The Arabs say: "Go to the market, perhaps (anna-ka) you will buy something for us," meaning "la'allaka." So it is as if He, may He be exalted, said: "Perhaps when they come they will not believe." Al-Wahidi said: "anna" in the sense of "la'alla" is common in their speech. The poet said:

"Show me a steed that died of fright, for I may see what you show me, or a stingy one who lives forever."

Another said:

"Are you about to hasten with us, for we see the open lands or the traces of the tents?"

And 'Adi ibn Hatim said:

"O reprover, what will make you know that my death is at an hour in the day or in the morning of tomorrow?"

Al-Wahidi said: 'Ali explained "la'alla maniyyati" (perhaps my death). The author of al-Kashshaf also related in this sense the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Halt upon the decayed encampment, for we weep over the dwellings as Ibn Khidam wept."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: The reading of Ubayy supports this view: "la'alla-ha idha ja'at-hum la yu'minun" (Perhaps when they come to them, they will not believe).

The second view concerning this reading: that you make "la" (not) an extraneous particle (silah). Its like is His saying: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:12], meaning "from prostrating." Likewise His saying: ﴿And forbidden for a town which We destroyed is that they should not return﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:95], meaning "that they should return." So here the sense is: "And what will make you aware that when they come they will believe?" and the meaning is that even if they came, they would not believe. Al-Zajjaj said: This view is weak, for what is extraneous is extraneous under all interpretations, whereas the one who reads "inna-ha" with a kasra has the word "la" in that reading not extraneous. Thus it is established that it is not permissible to make this word extraneous. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Why is it not permissible that it be extraneous under one of the two interpretations and meaningful under the second?

The readers also differed concerning His saying: ﴿they will not believe﴾. Some read it with the ya' (third person, "they"), and this is the preferable reading, for His saying: ﴿And they swore by God﴾ refers only to a specific group of people, and the evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted, after this verse: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [al-An'am 6:111], and not all people are described by this attribute. The meaning is: "And what will make you aware, O believers, that perhaps when the sign they demanded comes to them, they will not believe?" Therefore the ya' is the preferred reading.

Hamza and Ibn 'Amir read with the ta' (second person, "you"). This is by way of turning from the third person to address. The ones addressed in "tu'minun" are the absent swearers whom God informed that they would not believe. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd held that the address in His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾ is to the disbelievers who swore.

Mujahid said: "And what will make you aware that you will believe when they come?" This strengthens the reading of the one who reads "tu'minun" with the ta', according to what we mentioned first: the address in "And what will make you aware" is to the disbelievers who swore.

And according to what we mentioned second: the address in "And what will make you aware" is to the believers, because they wished for the revelation of the sign so that the polytheists would believe, and this is the preferred view. It is as if it was said to the believers: "You wish for that, but what will make you aware that they will believe?"

\* \* \*

The fourth issue: The summary of the discussion is that the people asked the Messenger for powerful miracles and swore that if they appeared they would believe. Then God, may He be exalted, made clear that although they swore to this, He knows that if these signs appeared they would not believe, and when the matter is so, it is not required by wisdom that their demand be granted. Al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi said: This verse indicates many rulings connected with supporting the Mu'tazila (i'tizal).

The first ruling: It indicates that if there were in what is known to God a grace (lutf) by which they would believe, He would surely have done it, for if it were permissible that He not do it, this reply would have no benefit; because if He does not grant their demand whether they believe or not, then making the refusal to grant it contingent on their not believing would not be orderly or coherent. Thus this verse indicates that He, may He be exalted, must do everything within His power of graces and wisdom.

The second ruling: This speech is only sound if the manifestation of these miracles has an effect in leading them to faith. According to the view of the Mujbira (Determinists), this is false, for in their view faith comes about only by God's creation: when He creates it, it occurs, and when He does not create it, it does not occur. But this is, in reality, still in place.

Someone might say: Suppose they do not believe at the manifestation of those miracles; why then was it not obligatory upon God to manifest them? Unless it was first established, before this discussion, that grace is obligatory upon God, the required point would follow from this verse. But al-Qadi made this verse a proof for the obligation of grace, and so it is established that his speech is weak.

As for the second point, namely his saying: "If all things come by God's creation, these graces have no effect upon it," we say: What we hold is that the influence on the act is the totality of power together with motive (da'i), and knowledge that this grace will be realized is one of the components of the motive. On this assumption, this grace has an effect in the occurrence of the act.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 110:**

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, just as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ This is also among the verses that support our position that disbelief and faith are by the decree and predestination (qadar) of God. Turning (taqallub) and reversing (qalb) are one and the same, and mean diverting a thing from its direction. The meaning of turning the hearts and sights is this: when the overwhelming signs they had demanded come to them, and they recognise how they indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger, yet God turns their hearts and their sight away from that correct direction, they remain in disbelief and do not benefit from those signs. The purpose of this verse is to confirm what we mentioned in the first verse, that even if those overwhelming signs came to them, they would never believe in them and would never benefit from their clear manifestation at all.

Al-Jubba'i (d. 303 AH), one of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that human beings create their own actions), answered regarding it, saying: the meaning of "And We turn their hearts and their sight" is that in Hell, over the flame of the fire and its embers, We turn their hearts and sight so that We may punish them, just as they did not believe in it the first time, in the abode of this world.

Al-Ka'bi answered regarding it: the meaning of His words "And We turn their hearts and their sight" is that We do not do for them what We do for believers of benefits and kindnesses, because they removed themselves from this limit by means of their disbelief.

Al-Qadi ('Abd al-Jabbar) answered: the meaning is that We turn their hearts and their sight within the signs that have already appeared, so you will not find them believing in them at the end, just as they did not believe in them at the beginning.

Know that all these interpretations are extremely weak. Nobody has the right to criticise us by saying: "You keep repeating these interpretations in every passage." For we say: these Mu'tazilah have a number of interpretations for the verses of recompense, and they repeat them in every verse. So we too repeat our answer to them in every verse, and we say: We have already shown that the original power (al-qudrah al-asliyyah) is equally suited to both opposites and both sides. When no inclining motive (da'iyah murajjihah) joins that power, the preponderance cannot occur. When the inclining motive joins, whether towards the act or towards the abandonment, the preponderance becomes manifest. That motive is nothing but from God, Exalted is He, to prevent an infinite regress (tasalsul, the endless chain of causes). The truth of these premises has been made clear by decisive, certain proofs that no rational person doubts.

This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful; He turns it however He wills." So the heart is as if suspended between the motive to act and the motive to abandon. If the motive to act arises in the heart, the side of action prevails; if the motive to abandon arises in it, the side of abandonment prevails. Since these two motives come into being only through God's bringing them into existence, creating them and originating them, He expressed them by the "two fingers of the Merciful." The reason for the appropriateness of this metaphor (isti'arah) is that a thing held between a person's two fingers is wholly within his power: if he wills, he holds it, and if he wills, he drops it. Here too the heart stands between these two motives, and these two motives arise by the creation of God Exalted, and the heart is subjected to these two motives. For this reason the metaphor is apt. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Turner of hearts and sights, make my heart firm upon Your religion." The meaning of his words "Turner of hearts" is that God Exalted turns it at one time from the motive of good to the motive of evil, and vice versa.

Once you know this principle, His words Exalted, "And We turn their hearts and their sight," are to be understood in this apparent and clear sense, which every sound nature and upright intellect attests to. There is absolutely no need for the far-fetched interpretations they have mentioned. God Exalted mentioned the turning of the hearts before the turning of the sights because the seat of motives and diversions is the heart. When the motive arises in the heart, the sight turns to it whether it wills or not; and when the diversions arise in the heart, the sight turns away from it. So although it sees in outward appearance, that seeing does not become a means of reaching the desired benefits. This is what is meant by His words, Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed veils over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. Since the heart is the source, and hearing and sight are its instruments, they must necessarily follow the states of the heart. For this reason, the verse begins with the mention of the turning of the hearts and then follows it with the mention of the turning of the sight. In the other verse, it begins with the mention of placing veils upon the heart and then follows it with the mention of hearing. This is the strong, rational, demonstrative discourse to which the wording of the Qur'an conforms. How, then, could it be appropriate to interpret this wording in those contrived ways they mentioned?

Let us return to what befits those weak expressions. As for the interpretation mentioned by al-Jubba'i, it is refuted, because God Exalted said: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight﴾, then He joined to it: ﴿and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. There is no doubt that His words "and We leave them" occur in this world. So if we say that the meaning of "And We turn their hearts and their sight" is that it occurs in the Hereafter, this would be a defect in the arrangement of God's speech, since it would place the later before the earlier and the earlier after the later without any benefit.

As for the interpretation mentioned by al-Ka'bi, it is also weak, because they deserved to be deprived of those kindnesses and benefits only because of their own choice of disbelief. It was they who brought themselves into that deprivation and forsaking. So how could it be appropriate to attribute it to God Exalted in His words: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight﴾?

As for the second interpretation mentioned by al-Qadi, it is also far-fetched, because the meaning of His words "And We turn their hearts and their sight" is the turning of the heart from one state to another, and its transfer from one attribute to another. But according to what al-Qadi says, the matter is not like that; rather, the heart remains in one state, except that God Exalted introduced the turning and alteration into the proofs. Thus it is established that the interpretations they mentioned are corrupt and utterly false.

[Page 122]

As for His words, Exalted: ﴿just as they did not believe in it the first time﴾, al-Wahidi said regarding it that there are two views:

The first view: the particle "ka" (like/as) is attached to an omitted element, and the sense is: "So they do not believe in these signs, just as they did not believe in the appearance of the signs the first time those signs came to them, such as the splitting of the moon and other signs." The meaning is: they do not believe the second time signs appear, just as they did not believe the first time. As for the pronoun in "bihi" (in it), it may refer to the Qur'an, or to Muhammad (ﷺ), or to what they demanded of signs.

The second view: some of them said: the "ka" in His words "just as they did not believe in it" carries the sense of recompense. The meaning of the verse is: "And We turn their hearts and their sight as a punishment for them for their abandonment of faith the first time," that is, just as they did not believe in it the first time, so likewise We turn their hearts and their sight the second time. According to this view, there is nothing omitted in the verse, and no need for any implied element in it.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted: ﴿and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾, al-Jubba'i said: "We leave them" means: We do not stand between them and their choice, nor do We prevent them from it by hastening their destruction or otherwise. Rather, We give them respite; if they persist in their transgression, that is from them, and this necessitates the confirmation of the proof against them. Our companions (the Ash'ariyyah) said: its meaning is that We turn their hearts from the truth to falsehood and leave them in that transgression, and in that error and blindness.

Someone may say to al-Jubba'i: You say that the God of the worlds wills for His servants only good and mercy. Why, then, did He leave this wretched person until he wandered blindly in his transgression? Why does He not rescue him from it by way of compulsion and force? At most, if He did that to him, he would not be deserving of reward, so he would merely miss the desert of reward, but he would be safe from punishment. But if He leaves him in that blindness, knowing that he will die upon it, then he does not gain the desert of reward, and he incurs great and everlasting punishment. So the corruption resulting from creating faith in him by way of compulsion is a single corruption, namely the loss of the desert of reward. But the corruption resulting from leaving him in that blindness and transgression until he dies upon it is the loss of the desert of reward together with the deserving of severe punishment. The Merciful, the Benevolent, who looks upon His servants, must necessarily prefer the side that is more beneficial and less corrupt. So we know that leaving that disbeliever in that blindness and transgression undermines the claim that He wills for him only good and kindness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered against them all things face to face, they would not have believed unless God willed. But most of them are ignorant.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, in this verse explained in detail what He had mentioned in summary in His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware that when it comes they will not believe?﴾ So He made clear that if He gave them what they asked for, namely the sending down of the angels and the bringing of the dead to life so that they would speak to them, and even if He increased upon that what their demands could not reach, by gathering against them all things face to face, they would not have believed unless God willed. There are several issues in the verse.

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: "The mockers of the Qur'an were five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth al-Zuhri, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and al-Harith ibn Handhala. Then they came to the Messenger (ﷺ) with a group of the people of Makkah and said to him: 'Show us the angels so that they may testify that you are the Messenger of God, or bring us some of our dead so that we may ask them whether what you say is true or false, or bring us God and the angels as a qabil,' that is, a guarantor for what you claim. So this verse was revealed." We have mentioned many times that they agreed that this surah was revealed all at once, so saying that this verse was revealed concerning that particular incident would be a difficult problem. But according to the way we have established, namely that its purpose is to answer what some of them said, that they swore by God with their most solemn oaths that if a sign came to them they would believe in Muhammad (peace be upon him), God mentioned this statement to show their lying, and that there is no benefit in sending down signs after signs and manifesting miracles after miracles. Rather, one miracle is necessary so that the truthful may be distinguished from the liar. As for adding to it, that is pure arbitrariness and there is no need for it. Otherwise they could ask, after the second miracle appears, for a third, and after the third for a fourth, and it would follow that the proof is never established and the matter never reaches a final limit and conclusion, and that would require closing the door of prophethood.

**The second issue:** Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *qiblan* (قِبَلًا) here and in al-Kahf with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba'. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on both in the two surahs. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it here and in al-Kahf with a kasra. Al-Wahidi said: Abu Zayd said: it is said, "I met so-and-so *qiblan*, *muqabalatan*, *qubulan*, *qibilan* and *qabilan*," all of which are one and the same, meaning face to face.

Al-Wahidi said: According to Abu Zayd's view, the meaning in the two readings is one, although the wordings differ. Some people have established a difference in meaning between the two words. As for one who reads *qiblan* with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', Abu 'Ubayda, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "by direct sight" (*'iyanan*). It is said: "I met him *qiblan*," that is, in direct observation. It was also narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Was Adam a prophet? He said: 'Yes, he was a prophet whom God addressed *qiblan*.'" As for one who reads *qubulan* (قُبُلًا), it has three possible meanings:

First: that it is the plural of *qabil*, which means a guarantor (*kafil*). It is said: "I took responsibility for the man" (*qabiltu bi-l-rajul uqbilu qubalatan*), that is, I was charged with him. The meaning would then be: if He gathered against them all things and they were made guarantors for the truth of what he says, they would still not believe. The point of the miracle in this is that among the gathered things some speak and some do not; so when God makes all of them speak and they all agree to accept this guarantee, that is among the greatest of miracles.

Second: that *qubulan* is the plural of *qubayl*, meaning a kind or group. The meaning is: "and We gathered against them all things, group by group." The point of the miracle in this is their gathering after their death, and that although they differ in their natures, they are assembled in one place.

Third: that *qubulan* has the meaning of *qiblan*, that is, face to face and by direct sight, as Abu Zayd explained it.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they would not have believed unless God willed﴾, there are two issues in it.

**The first issue:** The meaning of the verse is that if He manifested all those wondrous and strange things to these disbelievers, they would not believe unless God willed their faith. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: since they did not believe, this proof indicates that He did not will faith from them, and this is explicit on the question. The Mu'tazilah said: the proof indicates that He willed faith from all disbelievers. Al-Jubba'i mentioned the well-known arguments they have on this question:

First: if He did not will faith from them, faith would not be obligatory upon them, just as if He had not commanded them, it would not be obligatory upon them.

Second: if He willed disbelief from the disbeliever, the disbeliever would be obeying God by committing disbelief, because obedience has no meaning except by doing what is willed.

Third: if it were permissible for God to will disbelief, it would be permissible for Him to command it.

Fourth: if it were permissible for Him to will disbelief from them, it would be permissible for Him to command us to will disbelief from them.

They said: by these proofs it is established that He, exalted is He, willed from them only faith, and the apparent meaning of this verse requires that He willed faith from them. Contradiction between proofs is impossible, so reconciliation is required. Its method is for us to say: He willed from all of them the faith that they perform by way of choice (*ikhtiyar*), and He did not will from them the faith that results by way of compulsion (*ilja'*) and coercion (*qahr*). By this way the problem is removed.

Know that this statement is also weak in several respects:

The first: As for the faith that they call volitional faith (*al-iman al-ikhtiyari*), if by it they mean that his power is equally suitable for faith and disbelief, and then faith proceeds from it rather than disbelief, without any motivating cause and without any distinguishing will, then this is a claim that one of the two possibilities is preferred over the other without a preponderating cause, and that is impossible. Also, even granting that this is conceivable in general, the attainment of that faith would not come from him; rather it would be occurring without any cause and without any effective agent at all, because what is present there is only the power, which is equal in relation to the two opposites, and this bare power did not produce any specification of one of the two sides over the other in occurrence and preponderance. Then one of the two sides has come about by itself, so this would not proceed from him but would proceed without any cause whatsoever, and that nullifies the doctrine of act and agent, influence and influencer altogether, and no rational person would say it. Or else, what they call volitional faith means that his power, although suitable for both opposites, does not become a source of faith except when the motive for faith is added to that power. Then this would be a claim that the source of faith is the combination of the power with the motive, and that combination necessitates faith. That is exactly what they call compulsion (*jabr*), which you deny. Thus it is established that what they called volitional faith produces no intelligible, comprehensible meaning. You have known that this argument is extremely strong.

The second: Granting that volitional faith is distinguished from faith that comes about by God's creative act, we still say: His saying, ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ and so on, ﴿they would not have believed﴾, means: they would not have believed by volitional faith. The proof is that at the appearance of these things it is not unlikely that they would believe by way of compulsion and coercion. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿they would not have believed﴾ means: they would not have believed by way of choice. Then He made an exception from it, saying ﴿unless God wills﴾, and the excepted item must be of the same genus as that from which it is excepted. Faith that comes by compulsion and coercion is not of the same genus as volitional faith. Thus it is established that it is not permissible to say that what is meant by our words "unless God wills" is compelled faith; rather, what must be meant by it is volitional faith. Then our companions' proof is directed correctly and the Mu'tazilah's objection falls away entirely.

**The second issue:** Al-Jubba'i said: His saying, ﴿unless God wills﴾, indicates that the will of God, exalted is He, is originated (*hadith*), because if it were eternal (*qadim*) it would not be permissible to say that, just as one does not say: "Zayd does not go to Basra unless he professes the oneness of God." Its formulation is that when we say: "It will not be so unless God wills," this requires making the occurrence of this consequent contingent upon the occurrence of the will. So if the will were eternal, the condition would be eternal, and the occurrence of the condition entails the occurrence of the conditioned, so the consequent would be eternal. But the senses indicate that it is originated, so the condition must be originated, and if the condition is the will, it follows that the will is originated. This is the formulation of this argument.

The answer: Although the will is eternal, its relation to bringing about that originated thing in the present moment is an originated relation, and this measure suffices for the correctness of this statement.

Then God concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿But most of them are ignorant.﴾ Our companions said: the meaning is that they are ignorant that the whole matter is from God and by His decree and His predestination. The Mu'tazilah said: the meaning is that they were ignorant that they would remain disbelievers even when the signs they asked for appeared and the miracles they proposed came, and most of them were thinking that.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah al-An'am (6), verse 112:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with embellished speech as deception.﴾ ﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they fabricate.﴾

On this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, "Thus" (*wa-kadhalika*), is connected to something preceding it, and there are two views on what that something is.

The first view: it is connected to His saying, ﴿Thus We made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ (6:108), meaning: just as We did that, ﴿and thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾.

The second view: its meaning is "We have appointed for you an enemy just as We appointed for the prophets before you." So His saying "thus" is a conjunction with the sense of what came before, because what came before indicates that He, Exalted is He, appointed enemies for him.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾, is that He Himself is the One who made those enemies enemies of the Prophet (ﷺ). There is no doubt that that enmity is disobedience and disbelief. This implies that the Creator of good and evil, obedience and disobedience, faith and disbelief, is Allah, Exalted is He.

Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, a Mu'tazilite) answered this: the intended meaning of this "appointing" is judgment and declaration. When a man judges a person to be a disbeliever, it is said that he "declared him a disbeliever" (*kaffarahu*); and when he reports about someone's uprightness, it is said that he "declared him upright" (*addalahu*). Likewise here: when Exalted Allah clarified to the Messenger, peace be upon him, that they were his enemies, He therefore said that He had made them his enemies.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm answered: when Exalted Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to all the worlds and singled him out with that miracle, they envied him, and that envy became the cause of intense enmity. For this reason, with this interpretation, He said that He made them enemies of him. Its parallel is the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

*"You are the one who made them envious of me."*

Al-Ka'bi answered: Exalted Allah commanded the prophets to be hostile towards them and informed them that they were enemies to them. That requires that they become enemies of the prophets, because enmity arises only from both sides. For this reason, it is permissible to say that Exalted Allah made them enemies of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Know that these answers are extremely weak, because we have shown that actions are dependent upon motives, and these motives arise from Exalted Allah. When the matter is as such, our doctrine is confirmed.

**Another discussion:** Enmity and friendship cannot be acquired by a person's choice. A man may reach such a degree of enmity towards another that he is absolutely unable to remove that state from his heart; he may not even be able to conceal the traces of that enmity, and even if he used every effort and trick, he would be unable to do so. If the arising of enmity and friendship in the heart were by a person's choice, it would be necessary that a person be able to turn enmity into friendship and vice versa. And how could we not say this, when the poets recognised that this is beyond one's capacity? Al-Mutanabbi said:

*"What is wanted from the heart is your forgetting,*
*but natures refuse the one who transmits it."*

The lover whose passion is intense may use every trick to remove his love and yet cannot do so. Had that love and hatred been by his choice, he would not have been unable to remove it.

**The third issue:** The accusative in His saying ﴿devils﴾ (*shayatin*) has two possibilities.

The first: it is in apposition (*badal*) to His saying "enemy" (*'aduwwan*).

The second: "enemy" is in the accusative as a second object, and the implied meaning is: "and thus We have made the devils of mankind and jinn enemies of the prophets."

**The fourth issue:** Scholars differ on the meaning of "devils of mankind and jinn," in two views.

The first: the meaning is the rebellious ones among mankind and jinn; "shaytan" refers to every defiant, rebellious one among mankind and jinn. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas as transmitted by 'Ata', and of Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah. They said: among the jinn there are devils, and among mankind there are devils. The devil from the jinn, when he fails against a believer, goes to a rebellious one among mankind, who is a devil of mankind, and incites him against the believer in order to tempt him. The evidence for this is what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said to Abu Dharr: "Have you sought refuge in Allah from the evil of the devils of the jinn and of mankind?" He said: "I said: Are there devils among mankind?" He said: "Yes; they are worse than the devils of the jinn."

The second view: all of them are offspring of Iblis, except that he divided his offspring into two categories. He sent one category to whisper to mankind and the other category to whisper to the jinn. Thus both groups are devils of mankind and of jinn.

Some people said: the first view is better, because the aim of the verse is to complain about the foolishness of the disbelievers, who are the enemies, and they are the devils. Others said: the second view is better, because the wording of the verse requires the attribution of "devils" to "mankind and jinn," and attribution requires difference; on this reckoning, "devils" is a kind distinct from "jinn," and they are the offspring of Iblis.

**The fifth issue:** Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: "enemy" ('*aduwwan*) here means "enemies" (*a'da'*). Ibn al-Anbari recited:

*"If I do not benefit my friend with my affection,*
*then my enemy will not harm them by my hatred."*

He meant "my enemies," so he used the singular for the plural. There are parallels to this in the Qur'an, among them:

His saying: ﴿the honoured guests of Abraham﴾ (51:24): He made "honoured" (*al-mukramin*), which is plural, an adjective of "guest" (*dayf*), which is singular.

The second: His saying: ﴿and the tall palm trees with their spathes of fruit﴾ (50:10).

The third: His saying: ﴿or the children who have not known the private parts of women﴾ (24:31).

The fourth: His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who have believed﴾ (103:2–3).

The fifth: His saying: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel﴾ (3:93): He emphasised the singular with what is used to emphasise the plural.

It may be said: there is no need for this strained reading, since the sense is: "Thus We have appointed for each of the prophets one enemy," because it is not necessary for each prophet to have more than one enemy.

\* \* \*

[p. 127]

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿inspiring one another with embellished speech as deception﴾, the meaning is that those devils whisper to one another.

Know that it is not necessary that every act of disobedience that proceeds from a person be caused by the whispering of a devil; otherwise an infinite regress (*tasalsul*) or a circular dependence (*dawr*) would arise among these devils. It is therefore necessary to acknowledge that these vices and disobediences end in a first vice and a prior act of disobedience that came about not through the whispering of another devil.

Once this principle is established, we say: just as those devils cast whispers to mankind and jinn, so too some of them whisper to one another. People have various views on this. Some of them said: spirits are either celestial or terrestrial. Among the terrestrial spirits, some are good, pure, virtuous, commanding obedience and good deeds, and these are the terrestrial angels. Others are evil, filthy, wicked, commanding vices and acts of disobedience, and these are the devils. Just as those good spirits command people to acts of obedience and goodness, so too some of them command one another to acts of obedience. And just as the evil spirits command people to vices and reprehensible things, so too some of them command one another to those vices and to increasing them. As long as no kind of affinity exists between human souls and those spirits, that union does not occur. Human souls, if they are pure and free from blameworthy qualities, are of the kind of the pure spirits and join with them; and if they are evil and characterised by blameworthy qualities, they are of the kind of the evil spirits and join with them. Qualities of purity are many, and qualities of corruption and deficiency are many; and for each kind of these there are groups of humans and groups of terrestrial spirits, and according to that congeniality, resemblance and similarity, each kind joins its own kind. If this occurs in acts of good, the one who moves a person to them is an angel, and the strengthening of that thought is inspiration (*ilham*). If it occurs in the domain of evil, the one who moves a person to them is a devil, and the strengthening of that thought is whispering (*waswasa*).

Once you know this principle, we say: Exalted is He expressed this state mentioned above by His saying: ﴿inspiring one another with embellished speech as deception﴾, and it is incumbent upon us to explain three terms:

The first: *al-wahy* (inspiration), which is an expression for signalling and quick speech.

The second: *al-zukhruf* (embellishment), which is that whose inner part is false while its outer part is adorned and appears attractive. It is said: "So-and-so embellishes his speech" when he adorns it with falsehood and lies. Every fine thing that is camouflaged is called *muzakhraf* (embellished).

Know that the true account of this matter is that a person, as long as he does not believe that a matter contains a predominant good and an added benefit, will not desire it. For this reason the free agent is called "one who chooses" (*mukhtar*), since he seeks good and benefit. Then, if this belief corresponds to the reality, it is truth, sincerity and inspiration, even if it comes from an angel. If it does not correspond to the reality, then its outer part is adorned, because in his belief it is a cause of added benefit and predominant welfare, while its inner part is corrupt and false, because this belief does not correspond to the reality; so it is embellished. This is the true account of this statement.

The third: His saying "as deception" (*ghurura*). Al-Wahidi said: "*ghurura*" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and this verbal noun is taken as carried by the sense, because the meaning of inspiring embellished speech is the meaning of deception; it is as if He said: "they deceive with deception." The true account of it is that the deceived person is one who believes that a thing corresponds to benefit and welfare while in itself it is not so. Deception is either the very essence of this ignorance or a state arising from this ignorance. It has become clear from what we have mentioned that the influence of these evil spirits upon one another cannot be expressed in a more complete expression, nor one more powerful in indicating the full intent of His saying: ﴿inspiring one another with embellished speech as deception﴾.

\* \* \*

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾. Our companions (the Ash'aris) use this as evidence that disbelief and faith occur by the will of Exalted Allah, while the Mu'tazilites interpret it as the will of compulsion (*mashi'at al-ilja'*). This question has already been established in full detail, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

\* \* \*

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿so leave them and what they fabricate.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: "He wills what Iblis made attractive to them and deceived them with." The Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: this statement includes a strong warning against disbelief and a complete encouragement towards faith, and it requires the removal of grief from the heart of the Messenger, by imagining what Allah has prepared for those people because of their disbelief of various punishments, and what He has prepared for him of stations of reward, because of his patience with their foolishness and his gentleness towards them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may earn what they are earning.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that al-sagh (ṣaghw) in the language means inclination. It is said of a listener who inclines his sense toward the direction of a sound that he yuṣghī (listens attentively). It is also said: aṣgha al-ināʾ (he tilted the vessel) until some of it poured into the rest; and it is said of the moon when it inclines toward setting that it ṣagha and aṣgha. So His saying, "wa-li-taṣghā" (and that it may incline), means wa-li-tamīla (and that it may incline).

The second issue: The lām (the "li-") in His saying "wa-li-taṣghā" must have something it depends on. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: the implied meaning is: "And thus We made for every prophet an enemy from the devils of jinn and mankind, of whose attributes is that some of them inspire to others ornate speech as deception. And We did that so that the hearts of those who do not believe may incline to it," meaning: and We only caused the enmity to exist in the hearts of the devils who have the attributes we have mentioned, so that their ornate speech would be accepted by these disbelievers. They said: when we interpret the verse in this way, it appears that He, exalted is He, wills disbelief from the disbeliever. As for the Mu'tazilah, they answered this in three ways.

The first way, which is the one mentioned by al-Jubba'i, he said: this statement came in the form of a command, and its meaning is a rebuke, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice and urge on [them]﴾ [al-Isra' 17:64]. Likewise His saying: ﴿and that they may be pleased with it and that they may earn﴾. The sense of the statement is as if He said to the Messenger: ﴿So leave them and what they invent﴾ [al-An'am 6:137], then He said to them, by way of threat: "and that their hearts may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may earn what they are earning."

The second way, which is the one chosen by al-Ka'bi, is that this lām is the lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), meaning: the outcome of their affair will come to these states.

Al-Qadi said: It is far-fetched to say that this outcome occurs in the Hereafter, because compulsion (al-ilja') occurs in the Hereafter; so it is not permissible that the hearts of the disbelievers incline to accepting the false doctrine, nor that they be pleased with it, nor that they commit the sin. Rather, it must be understood that the outcome of their affair is that they accept falsehoods, are pleased with them, and act upon them.

Page 129
The third way, which is the one chosen by Abu Muslim, he said: The lām in His saying, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ is connected to His saying, ﴿some of them inspire to others ornate speech as deception﴾. The meaning is that some of them inspire to others ornate speech in order that they be deceived by it, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may earn﴾ the sins. The intended meaning is that the aim of the devils from that inspiration is the totality of these meanings. This is the sum of what they have mentioned on this subject.

As for the first way, which al-Jubba'i relied upon, it is weak for several reasons mentioned by al-Qadi:

The first of them: the waw in His saying "wa-li-taṣghā" requires that it be connected to what precedes it, so taking it as a new beginning is far-fetched.

The second of them: the lām in His saying "wa-li-taṣghā" is the lām of purpose (kay), so it is far-fetched to say that it is the lām of command, and that is close to being an alteration (taḥrīf) of the words of God, which is not permissible.

As for the second way, namely that this lām is the lām of consequence, it is weak, because they all agreed that this is a metaphorical usage, while taking it as "kay" (in order that) is literal; so our statement is more preferable.

As for the third way, which Abu Muslim mentioned, it is the best of the ways mentioned on this subject. For we say: His saying, ﴿some of them inspire to others ornate speech as deception﴾ requires that the purpose of that inspiration be deception. If we connect to it His saying, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe may incline to it﴾, this is also the very essence of deception, not merely its meaning, except that it inclines him toward something whose inner reality is ugly and whose outer appearance is fair. And His saying, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe may incline to it﴾ is the very same inclining; so if we connected it, it would follow that the conjoined is the very same as the conjoined-to, which is not permissible. But if we say: the sense of the statement is "And thus We made for every prophet an enemy who by nature inspires ornate speech for the sake of deception, and We made such a person an enemy of the Prophet only so that the hearts of the disbelievers may incline to him, and thereby they may keep away, by that cause, from accepting the call of that prophet," then on this reading there is no requirement of conjoining a thing to itself. Thus it is established that what we have mentioned is more preferable.

The third issue: Our companions claimed that structure (al-bunyah) is not a condition for life; so the living one is the part in which life subsists, and the knowing one is the part in which knowledge subsists. The Mu'tazilah said: the living and the knowing is the whole, not that part.

Having known this, we say: Our companions argued from this verse for the soundness of their view, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe may incline to it﴾, so the one described as inclining and desiring is the heart, not the whole living being, and this indicates our view.

The fourth issue: Those who said that the human being is something distinct from the body differed. Some of them said: the first thing connected is the heart, and through it the soul is connected to the rest of the organs such as the brain and the liver. Others said: the heart is the connection of the animal soul, and the brain is the connection of the natural soul. The first group relied on this verse, for He, exalted is He, made the locus of inclination, which is an expression for leaning and will, the heart; and this indicates that what is connected to the soul is the heart.

The fifth issue: The pronoun in His saying "wa-li-taṣghā ilayhi afʾidatu" refers to "zukhruf al-qawl" (ornate speech), and likewise in His saying "wa-li-yarḍawhu" (and that they may be pleased with it).

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿and that they may earn what they are earning﴾, know that al-iqtirāf is al-iktisāb (acquiring, earning). It is said in a proverb: "Confession removes the earning (of sin)," just as it is said: "Repentance erases the sin." Al-Zajjaj said: "li-yaqtarifū" means li-yakhtalifū (that they may disagree) and li-yakdhibū (that they may lie), but the first is more correct.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 114:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book, fully detailed? And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth. So do not be among the doubters.﴾

Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, related about the disbelievers that they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them they would believe in it, He answered them by saying that there is no benefit in manifesting those signs, because if He had manifested them they would have persisted in their disbelief. Then, in this verse, He made clear that the proof indicating His prophethood has already been established and completed, so what they ask for is a request for more, and that is not something that deserves attention. We say that the proof indicating his prophethood has been established for two reasons:

The first reason: Allah has decided his prophethood in that He sent down to him the Book, clear and detailed, comprising many sciences and complete eloquence, and creation has been unable to produce its like. The manifestation of such an inimitable miracle upon him indicates that Allah, exalted is He, has decided his prophethood. So His saying, ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ means: Say, O Muhammad, "You are dictating what miracles to seek, so is it rational to seek a judge other than Allah?" For everyone says that this is not permissible. Then say: He, exalted is He, has judged the validity of my prophethood by granting me this detailed Book, complete and reaching the limit of inimitability.

The second reason: Among the matters indicating his prophethood is that the Torah and the Gospel contain verses indicating that Muhammad, peace be upon him, is a true messenger, and that the Qur'an is a true book from Allah, exalted is He. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth.﴾ In sum, both reasons are mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

As for His saying, exalted is He, at the end of the verse: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, there are several interpretations:

First: This is of the type of incitement and stirring up, like His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾ [al-An'am: 41].

Second: The implied meaning is: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning the fact that the People of the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth.

Third: It is possible that His saying "So do not be" is addressed to each individual, and the meaning is that since the proofs have become manifest, no one should have doubt about them.

Fourth: It has been said that although this address is outwardly to the Messenger, what is intended by it is his community.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ — Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read (munazzalun) with the shadda (intensive form), and the rest read it without the shadda. The difference between tanzil and inzal has been mentioned by us many times.

The third issue: al-Wahidi said: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ The hakam (judge) and the hakim (ruler/judge) are one and the same according to the linguists, except that some of the interpreters said: the hakam is more complete than the hakim, because the hakim is everyone who judges, whereas the hakam is the one who judges only with truth. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, is a true hakam who judges only with truth. So when He manifested the single miracle, which is the Qur'an, He decided the validity of this prophethood, and there is no rank above His judgment, so it is necessary to affirm with certainty the validity of this prophethood. As for whether He manifests all the other miracles or not, it has no bearing on this matter, once it has been established that He, exalted is He, has judged the validity of this prophethood through the manifestation of the single miracle.

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿kalimatu rabbika﴾ (the word of your Lord) without the alif, in the singular. The rest read ﴿kalimātu﴾ (the words) in the plural. The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Maʿānī) said: the words "kalimah" and "kalimāt" both mean what has come of promise, threat, reward and punishment. There is no alteration or change in it, as He said: ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾ [Qaf: 29]. Whoever reads "kalimāt" in the plural says: because its meaning is plural, it must be pluralized in the wording. Whoever reads in the singular says: they have said that "the word" (kalimah) may be used to mean many words when they are governed by one governing principle, as when they say: "Zuhayr said in his kalimah," meaning his qaṣīdah (ode), and "Qass said in his kalimah," meaning his sermon. Likewise, the whole Qur'an is one word in being true, truthful and miraculous.

**The second issue:** The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that in the previous verse He explained that the Qur'an is inimitable. In this verse He mentions that ﴿the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. The intended meaning of "the word" is the Qur'an, that is, the Qur'an has been completed in being a miracle indicating the truthfulness of Muḥammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿in truth and justice﴾ means: it has been completed in perfect truth and justice. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: ﴿ṣidqan wa ʿadlan﴾ are two verbal nouns (maṣdar) put in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) of "the word", and the implied sense is: truthful and just. This is the way this verse connects with what comes before it.

**The third issue:** Know that this verse indicates that the word of Allah, exalted is He, is described by many attributes.

The first attribute: that it is complete. To this points His saying ﴿the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. Concerning the meaning of this completeness there are several views:

The first: what we have mentioned, that it is sufficient and comprehensive in being a miracle indicating the truthfulness of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The second: that it is sufficient in explaining what the responsible persons need, until the Resurrection, both in action and in knowledge.

The third: that the ruling of Allah, exalted is He, is what came to be in eternity (al-azal), and nothing new occurs after that. What came to be in eternity is the completeness, and addition to it is impossible. This view is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The pen has dried with what is to be until the Day of Resurrection."

The second attribute of the words of Allah: that they are truthful. The proof for this is that falsehood is a deficiency, and deficiency is impossible for Allah. It is not permissible to establish that lying about Allah is impossible by means of the textual proofs (al-dalāʾil al-samʿiyyah), because the soundness of the textual proofs depends on the impossibility of lying about Allah. So if we were to establish the impossibility of lying about Allah by textual proofs, it would entail circularity (al-dawr), which is invalid.

Know that just as this statement indicates that breaking a promise from Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, it also indicates that breaking His threat is impossible. This contrasts with what al-Wāḥidī said in his exegesis of His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 93], that the breaking of Allah's threat is permissible. This is because the promise and threat of Allah are both the word of Allah. Since this verse indicates that the word of Allah must be described as truthful, then just as breaking a promise is impossible, so too breaking a threat is impossible.

The third attribute of the words of Allah: that they are just. Concerning it there are two views:

The first: all that is in the Qur'an is of two kinds: information (khabar) and obligation (taklīf). As for information, it means everything Allah reports about the existence or non-existence of something. It includes information about the existence of the essence of Allah, exalted is He, and about the occurrence of His attributes, that is, that He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful, All-Hearing, All-Seeing. It includes information about the attributes of transcendence and exaltation, such as His saying: ﴿He neither begets nor is born﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ: 3], and His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. It includes information about the categories of Allah's actions, and the manner of His governance of the dominion of the heavens and the earth and the two worlds of spirits and bodies. It includes every matter concerning the rulings of Allah, exalted is He, regarding promise, threat, reward and punishment. It includes information about the states of earlier peoples and information about unseen future events. All these categories fall under information. As for obligation, it includes every command and prohibition directed from Him, glory be to Him, to His servant, whether that servant is an angel, a human, a jinn or a devil, and whether that is in our law or in the laws of the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, or in the laws of the nearest angels who are the inhabitants of the heavens, Paradise, Hell, the Throne and what lies beyond it, of whose conditions none knows except Allah, exalted is He.

Once you know that the subjects of the Qur'an are confined to these two divisions, we say: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth﴾, if it belongs to the category of information, and ﴿and justice﴾, if it belongs to the category of obligations. This is a division of the utmost elegance.

The second view, concerning the explanation of His saying "and justice": whatever Allah, exalted is He, reports of promise, threat, reward and punishment is truthful, because it must necessarily come to pass. And after it comes to pass, it is just, because His actions are exalted above being described by the attribute of injustice.

The fourth attribute of the word of Allah is His saying: ﴿None can alter His words﴾. Concerning it there are several views:

The first: we have shown that what is meant by His saying ﴿the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾ is that it is complete in being a miracle indicating the truthfulness of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿None can alter His words﴾. The meaning is that these disbelievers cast doubts about its being a sign of the truthfulness of Muḥammad (ﷺ), but those doubts have no effect on these proofs, which are not at all susceptible to alteration. This is because that indication is manifest, lasting, clear and strong, and does not disappear because of the nonsense of the disbelievers or the doubts of those ignorant ones.

The second view: that what is meant is that it remains protected from distortion and alteration, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9].

The third view: that what is meant is that it is protected from contradiction, as He said: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 82].

The fourth view: that what is meant is that the rulings of Allah, exalted is He, do not accept change or cessation, because they are eternal, and what is eternal does not cease.

Know that this view is one of the strong foundations used to establish compulsion (jabr, the doctrine that human actions are predetermined). This is because, when He, exalted is He, decreed for Zayd happiness and for ʿAmr wretchedness, and then said: ﴿None can alter His words﴾, it follows that the blessed cannot become wretched and the wretched cannot become blessed. So the blessed is one who was blessed in his mother's womb, and the wretched is one who was wretched in his mother's womb.
