Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 116–117:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of God. They follow only conjecture, and they are only guessing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows best who strays from His way, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had answered the doubts of the disbelievers, and then demonstrated by proof the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, He explained that after the removal of doubt and the appearance of proof, the rational person should not turn his attention to the words of the ignorant, nor should he be disturbed by their corrupt words. So He said: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of God.﴾ This indicates that most of the people of the earth were misguided, because misguiding others must necessarily be preceded by being astray. Know that the occurrence of this error and misguidance does not fall outside one of three matters:

The first: the investigations related to divinity (al-ilahiyyat). The truth in them is one, whereas falsehood is manifold. Among them is the affirmation of association (shirk), either as the zanadiqa (heretics) say, which is what God informed of in His saying: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾ [al-An'am: 100], or as the worshippers of the stars say, or as the worshippers of idols say.

The second: the investigations related to prophethood (al-nubuwwat). Either as one who denies prophethood absolutely says, or as one who denies resurrection (al-nashr) says, or as one who denies the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ says. Within this category enter the investigations related to the return (al-ma'ad).

The third: the investigations related to the rulings (al-ahkam), and they are many. The disbelievers used to forbid the baha'ir, the sawa'ib and the wasa'il, and made lawful the carrion. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾ in what they believe about the ruling, judging falsehood to be truth and truth to be falsehood, ﴿they will mislead you from the way of God﴾, that is, from the path and the methodology of truthfulness.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and they are only guessing.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: the meaning is that these disbelievers who dispute with you about your religion and your doctrine are not certain of the soundness of their doctrines; rather, they follow only conjecture, and they are liars in their claim of certainty. Many of the exegetes say: the meaning of that conjecture is their returning, in establishing their doctrines, to the imitation (taqlid) of their forefathers, not to any reasoning at all.

The second issue: those who deny analogy (qiyas) have held fast to this verse. They said: We have seen that God, exalted is He, has intensified the censure of the disbelievers in many verses of the Qur'an because they follow conjecture, and that which God, exalted is He, makes a cause of censuring the disbelievers must be at the furthest degree of blame. And acting on analogy necessitates following conjecture, so it must be blameworthy and forbidden. It cannot be said: since a conclusive proof has come establishing that it is a valid proof, acting on it is acting on a certain proof, not on a probable one. For we say: this is refuted in several respects:

The first: that conclusive proof is either rational or revealed (sam'i). The first is void, because reason has no scope in determining whether acting on analogy is permissible or impermissible, especially according to those who deny that reason makes things good or bad.

The second is also void, because a revealed proof is only conclusive if it is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) and its wording does not admit of any meaning other than this single one. Had such a proof existed, people would know by necessity that analogy is a valid proof, and disagreement about it among the community would have been removed. Since that is not found, we know that a conclusive proof for the validity of analogy is absent.

The second: suppose a conclusive proof were found that analogy is a valid proof. Still, acting on analogy is not complete except with the following of conjecture. Its explanation: reliance on analogy rests on two stages:

The first: that the ruling in the place of agreement (mahall al-wifaq) is grounded in such-and-such a cause (illah).

The second: that this meaning is present in the place of disagreement (mahall al-khilaf). If these two stages are known with certainty and conviction, then there is no dispute among rational people about its validity. But if their combination, or one of them, is probable, then acting on this analogy is not complete except by following conjecture, and in that case it falls under the text indicating that following conjecture is blameworthy.

The answer: why could it not be said that conjecture is a term for a prevailing belief when it is not founded on an indicator (amarah), and that this is like the belief of the disbelievers; but when a prevailing belief is founded on an indicator, this belief is not called conjecture. By this route this argument falls away.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows best who strays from His way, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: in its interpretation there are two opinions:

The first: that the meaning is that after you have come to know what the truth is and what falsehood is, do not be grieved over them, but entrust their affair to their Creator, for He, exalted is He, knows who is guided and who is astray, and He will recompense each one according to what befits his deed.

The second: that the meaning is that these disbelievers, although they display from themselves a claim of certainty and conviction, are liars, and God, exalted is He, knows the condition of their hearts and their inner selves, and is aware that they are bewildered in the path of error, wandering in the valleys of ignorance.

The second issue: regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows best who strays from His way, and He knows best those who are guided﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: some have said that "a'lam" (knows best) here means "ya'lam" (knows), and the sense is: Indeed your Lord knows who strays from His way, and He knows those who are guided.

We say: there is no doubt that any variation in the knowledge of God, exalted is He, is impossible. Rather, the intent of this expression is that the concern for displaying the guidance of the guided is greater than the concern for displaying the error of the erring. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own selves, and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ [al-Isra': 7], where He mentioned good twice and evil once.

The second: that the position of "man" (who) is nominative as the subject of a predicate (mubtada'), and its wording is that of an interrogative, and the meaning is: Indeed your Lord is the One who knows best which of the people strays from His way. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may know which of the two parties best computes﴾ [al-Kahf: 12]. This is the view of al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs.﴾

There are discussions regarding this verse, which we will mention in the form of question and answer.

Page 135
The first question: The "fa" (so) in His saying ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ requires a connection with what came before. So what is that thing?
The answer: His saying "So eat" is a consequence of the denunciation of following the misguiders who make lawful what is unlawful and make unlawful what is lawful. That is because they used to say to the Muslims: "You claim that you worship Allah, so what Allah has killed is more worthy that you eat it than what you have killed yourselves." So Allah said to the Muslims: "If you are truly established in faith, then eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned," and that is what has been slaughtered with the basmala (the invocation "In the name of Allah").

The second question: The people (the polytheists) used to permit eating what was slaughtered in the name of Allah and did not dispute about it. The dispute was only that they also permitted eating carrion (al-maytah), while the Muslims prohibited it. If that is so, then the revelation of a command permitting what has the name of Allah mentioned over it would be pointless, because it establishes a ruling in what is agreed upon and leaves the ruling in what is disputed unaddressed.

The answer: There are two aspects to this:

The first: Perhaps the people used to prohibit eating what was slaughtered (al-muzakkah) and permit eating carrion, so Allah, exalted is He, refuted them on both matters: He ruled the lawfulness of the slaughtered animal by His saying ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾, and the prohibition of carrion by His saying ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾.

The second: We may take His saying ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ to mean that the intended sense is: make your eating restricted to that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned. On this view, the meaning is the prohibition of eating carrion only.

The third question: His saying ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ is in the imperative form, and it is for permission. This permission is established for both the believer and the non-believer, and the word "in" (if) in His saying ﴿if you are believers in His signs﴾ indicates a condition.

The answer: The estimated meaning is: let your eating be restricted to that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs. The intended sense is that if He had ruled the permissibility of eating carrion, that would have cast doubt on his being a believer.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And why should you not eat of that over which the Name of God has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to? Indeed, many lead others astray by their desires without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' and Hafs, on the authority of Asim, recited ﴿wa-qad faṣṣala lakum mā ḥarrama ʿalaykum﴾ with a fatḥah on both verbs (faṣṣala and ḥarrama). Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr recited with a ḍammah on both. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, recited faṣṣala with a fatḥah and ḥurrima with a ḍammah. Whoever recited with a fatḥah on both has argued with two considerations:

The first: he held to the fatḥah of faṣṣala by His saying: ﴿We have indeed detailed the signs (qad faṣṣalnā al-āyāt)﴾, and to the fatḥah of ḥarrama by His saying: ﴿Recite what your Lord has forbidden you (ma ḥarrama rabbukum ʿalaykum)﴾ [al-An'am: 151].

The second consideration: holding to His saying: ﴿over which the Name of God has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾, so the verb must have God as its agent, since the Name of God was mentioned earlier. As for those who recited with a ḍammah on both, their proof is His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾ and His saying (ḥurrimat): it is a detailing of what was stated in summary in this verse. Since in the detail it must be said ﴿ḥurrimat ʿalaykum al-maytah﴾ with the passive form, the summary must likewise be so, namely His saying ﴿mā ḥarrama ʿalaykum﴾. And since ḥurrima with a ḍammah on the ḥā' is established as necessary, likewise faṣṣala must be with a ḍammah on the fā', because this detailed matter is precisely that same forbidden matter stated in summary. Also, He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It is He who sent down to you the Book, detailed (mufaṣṣalan)﴾, and His saying "mufaṣṣalan" indicates faṣṣala. As for whoever recited faṣṣala with a fatḥah and ḥurrima with a ḍammah, his proof for faṣṣala is His saying ﴿We have indeed detailed the signs﴾, and for ḥurrima His saying ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion﴾.

The second issue: His saying ﴿and He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾. Most exegetes said that what is meant is His saying, at the beginning of Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine﴾. There is a difficulty in this: Surat al-An'am is Meccan, while Surat al-Ma'idah is Medinan, and it is the last thing God sent down at Medina. His saying "and He has already detailed" requires that this detailed matter precede this summary, whereas the Medinan comes later than the Meccan, and what comes later cannot be earlier. Rather, it is better to say that what is meant is His saying after this verse: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. Although this verse is mentioned only a little after this verse, such a small degree of delay does not prevent it from being what is meant, and God knows best. His saying ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾ means: necessity has called you to eat it because of the severity of hunger.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, many lead others astray by their desires﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr recited "liyaḍillūna" with a fatḥah on the yā'; likewise in Yunus "rabbanā liyaḍillū", in Ibrahim "liyaḍillū", in al-Hajj "thāniya ʿiṭfihi liyaḍilla", in Luqman "lahw al-ḥadīth liyaḍilla", and in al-Zumar "andādan liyaḍilla". ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited all of these with a ḍammah on the yā'. Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir recited here and in Yunus with a fatḥah on the yā', and in the other places with a ḍammah. Whoever recited with a fatḥah pointed to his being astray (ḍāll), and whoever recited with a ḍammah pointed to his being one who leads astray (muḍill). He said: this is stronger in censure, because every one who leads astray must be astray, while one may be astray without leading others astray; so the one who leads astray deserves censure more than the one who is astray.

The second issue: What is meant by "liyuḍillūna" is said to be ʿAmr ibn Luhayy and those among the polytheists after him, because he was the first to alter the religion of Isma'il, and he adopted the baḥā'ir and sawā'ib and ate carrion. His saying "without knowledge" means that ʿAmr ibn Luhayy embarked on these doctrines out of pure ignorance and utter error. Al-Zajjaj said: what is meant are those who make carrion lawful and argue with you about its permissibility, and they argue for it by saying: since what you slaughter is lawful, then what God slaughters is more deserving of being lawful. Likewise, in everything in which they go astray, such as the worship of idols and the disparagement of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, they follow only desire and appetite, and they have neither insight nor knowledge.

The third issue: This verse indicates that speaking about religion merely by imitation (taqlid) is forbidden, because speaking by imitation is speaking purely from caprice and appetite, and the verse indicates that this is forbidden.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾ means that He is the One who knows what is in their hearts and inner consciousness of transgression, the seeking to support falsehood, and the striving to conceal the truth. And since He knows their states and is able to requite them, He, may He be exalted, will requite them for it. The purpose of this statement is threat and warning. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 120:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that He had detailed the prohibited things, He followed it with what requires abandoning them entirely, by His saying: ﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin.﴾ By "sin" is meant that which necessitates sin. The scholars have mentioned two views regarding "the outward of sin and its inward":

The first: "the outward of sin" is the public declaration of fornication, and "its inward" is the concealment of it. Al-Dahhak said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to regard fornication as permissible so long as it was secret, so God, exalted is He, prohibited by this verse both its secret and its public forms.

The second: this prohibition is general over all prohibited things, and this is the more correct view, because restricting a general expression to a particular case without evidence is not permissible. Then it has been said: what is meant is what you publicize and what you conceal. It has also been said: what you do and what you intend. Ibn al-Anbari said: He means, "Abandon sin in all its aspects," just as you say, "I did not take from this property a little or a lot," meaning, "I did not take from it in any way whatsoever." Others said: the meaning of the verse is a prohibition against sin, together with a clarification that it does not cease to be sin by reason of being hidden and concealed. It may also be said: what is meant by His saying, "And leave the outward of sin," is a prohibition against undertaking sin; then He said, "and its inward," so that it becomes clear that the motive for abandoning that sin should be the fear of God, not the fear of people. Others said: "the outward of sin" refers to the deeds of the limbs, and "its inward" refers to the deeds of the hearts, such as arrogance, envy, self-admiration, and wishing harm to the Muslims; and it includes belief, resolve, looking, suspicion, wishful longing, and grieving over good things. By this, the corruption of the view of one who says that what occurs in the heart is not held against a person when it is not accompanied by action becomes evident, for He, exalted is He, has forbidden all these categories in this verse.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾ The meaning of "iqtiraf" (committing, perpetrating) has already been mentioned. The apparent sense of the text indicates that the sinner must be punished, except that the Muslims are unanimous that if he repents he will not be punished. Our companions (the Ash'aris) added a second condition, namely that God, exalted is He, may pardon the sinner and forgo his punishment, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills.﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 121:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a transgression. And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, indeed you would be associators [of others with God].﴾

Page 138

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained that it is permissible to eat what is slaughtered in the name of God, He mentioned after it the prohibition of what the name of God has not been mentioned over, which includes carrion (al-maytah), and includes what is slaughtered in the mention of idols. The purpose of this is to nullify what the polytheists had claimed. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: It is related from ʿAṭāʾ that he said: Everything over which the name of God has not been mentioned, of food or drink, is forbidden, holding to the generality of this verse. As for the rest of the jurists, they agreed to restrict this generality to slaughter, and then they differed. Mālik said: Every slaughter over which the name of God has not been mentioned is forbidden, whether that mention was omitted deliberately or through forgetfulness. This is also the view of Ibn Sīrīn and a group of the theologians (mutakallimūn). Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: If the mention is omitted deliberately, it is forbidden; if it is omitted through forgetfulness, it is permissible.

Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, said: What is left without the invocation of the name is permissible, whether it was omitted deliberately or in error, provided the slaughterer is qualified to slaughter. We have discussed this issue at length in the commentary on His saying: ﴿except what you have slaughtered properly﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3], so there is no benefit in repeating it. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, said: This prohibition is restricted to what is slaughtered in the name of the idols (nuṣub). Several points indicate this:

The first of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for indeed it is a transgression﴾. And the Muslims have agreed that eating the slaughter of a Muslim who omitted the invocation of the name is not considered transgression (fisq).

The second of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾. And this dispute was only about the matter of carrion. It is related that some of the polytheists said to the Muslims: What the falcon and the dog kill, you eat, but what God kills, you do not eat. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās that they said: You eat what you kill yourselves, and you do not eat what God kills. So this dispute is restricted to the eating of carrion.

The third of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you would be associators﴾. This is restricted to what is slaughtered in the name of the idols, meaning: if you are content with this slaughter which was slaughtered in the name of the divinity of the idols, then you have accepted their divinity, and that necessitates shirk. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, said: Although the beginning of the verse is general according to its wording, when its end contains these three restrictions, we know that the intended meaning of that generality is this particular sense. What confirms this meaning is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a transgression﴾. So this prohibition has become restricted to the case where this act is a transgression. Then we sought in the Book of God, exalted is He, when it becomes a transgression, and we found this transgression explained in another verse, which is His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, except that it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination, or a transgression, that over which other than God has been invoked﴾ [al-Anʿām: 145]. So transgression in this verse is explained as that over which other than God has been invoked. And if this is so, then His saying: ﴿Do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a transgression﴾ is restricted to what has been invoked over other than God.

The second position: We set aside holding to these restricting arguments, but we say: Why do you claim that the mention of God was not present here? The evidence for this is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The remembrance of God is with the Muslim, whether he speaks or does not speak." This remembrance is to be understood as remembrance of the heart.

The third position: We say: Suppose this evidence requires prohibition, yet all the other proofs mentioned in this issue require permissibility, and when they conflict, the preponderant one must be permissibility, because the original rule regarding edibles is permissibility. Also, all the general statements that imply the permissibility of eating and benefiting from things indicate this, such as His saying: ﴿He created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], and His saying: ﴿Eat and drink﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60], because it is pleasant to the senses, so it must be permissible, by His saying: ﴿Lawful for you are the good things﴾. And because it is property, since the natural disposition inclines toward it, so it must not be forbidden, based on what is related from

Page 139

the Prophet (ﷺ) that he "forbade the squandering of property." This is the presentation of the argument in this issue. Nevertheless, we say: It is better for the Muslim to avoid it, because the apparent sense of this text is strong.

The second issue: To what does the pronoun in His saying: ﴿for indeed it is a transgression﴾ refer? There are two opinions. The first: His saying "do not eat" (lā taʾkulū) indicates eating, because the verb indicates the verbal noun (maṣdar), so this pronoun refers to that verbal noun. The second: It is as if He made that over which the name of God has not been mentioned to be itself a transgression, by way of exaggeration.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾, there are two opinions. The first: The intended meaning of "the devils" here is Iblīs and his hosts, who whispered to their allies among the polytheists to dispute with Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his companions about eating carrion. The second: ʿIkrimah said: "And indeed the devils," meaning the rebellious ones of the Magians (Majūs), inspire their allies among the polytheists of Quraysh. This is because when the prohibition of carrion was revealed, the Magians of Persia heard it and wrote to Quraysh, and there was correspondence between them, saying: Muḥammad and his companions claim that they follow the command of God, yet they claim that what they slaughter is lawful and what God kills is unlawful. So something of this came into the minds of some Muslims, and God, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if you obey them﴾, meaning in permitting carrion, ﴿indeed you would be associators﴾. Al-Zajjāj said: In this there is evidence that whoever invokes anything of what God, exalted is He, has forbidden, or forbids anything of what God, exalted is He, has permitted, is an associator, and he was named an associator only because he established a judge other than God, exalted is He, and this is shirk.

The third issue: Al-Kaʿbī said: The verse is evidence that faith (īmān) is a name for all acts of obedience, although its meaning in language is affirmation (taṣdīq), just as God, exalted is He, made shirk a name for everything that opposes God, exalted is He, although in language it is specific to one who believes that God has a partner. The proof is that He, exalted is He, named the obedience of the believers to the polytheists in permitting carrion "shirk."

A objector may say: Why is it not possible that the intended meaning of shirk here is the belief that God, exalted is He, has a partner in judgment and obligation? By this interpretation, the meaning of this shirk returns only to belief.

**Page 140**

**Issue 1:** Know that when the Most High mentioned in the previous verse that the polytheists dispute with the believers concerning the religion of Allah, He mentioned a parable that illustrates the state of the guided believer and the state of the misguided disbeliever. He clarified that the guided believer is like one who was dead, then was made alive and given a light by which he is guided in his affairs, while the disbeliever is like one who is immersed in darkness with no escape from it, and so he remains perplexed forever.

Then He said: ﴿Thus the deeds they used to do have been made appealing to the disbelievers.﴾ At this point the question of compulsion and predestination (al-jabr wal-qadar) arises. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: The one who makes it appealing is Allah the Most High. Their proof is what has already been mentioned: that an act depends on the occurrence of a motive (da'i), and the occurrence of that motive must be by the creation of Allah the Most High. A motive is an expression for knowledge, belief, or opinion that the act includes a greater benefit and a preponderant good. This motive has no meaning except this making-appealing. So when the one who brings this motive into existence is Allah the Most High, the one who makes it appealing is necessarily Allah the Most High.

The Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazila) said: The one who makes it appealing is Satan. They relate from al-Hasan that he said: "By Allah, Satan made it appealing to them." Know that this view is extremely weak, for several reasons:

The first: the decisive proof we have mentioned.

The second: this parable is mentioned so that Allah may distinguish the state of the Muslim from that of the disbeliever, and Satan would be included in that. If Satan's commitment to that disbelief was due to another satan, then it would necessitate going on to another maker-of-appeal without end. Otherwise, there must be another maker-of-appeal besides Satan.

The third: He has explicitly stated that the one who makes it appealing is none other than Him, both before this verse and after it. As for before it, His words: ﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge. Thus We have made appealing to every community their deeds.﴾ As for after this verse, His words: ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals.﴾

**Issue 2:** His words ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life﴾. Nafi' recited "mayyitan" with a doubled letter (shaddah), while the others recited it without doubling. The lexicographers (ahl al-lugha) said: "mayt" with lightening is the same as "mayyit," and their meaning is one, whether doubled or lightened.

**Issue 3:** The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He has described the disbelievers as dead in His words: ﴿They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ [al-Nahl: 21] Also in His words: ﴿that he may warn whoever is alive﴾ [Ya-Sin: 70], and in His words: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80], and in His words: ﴿Nor are the blind and the seeing alike﴾ [Fatir: 19], ﴿nor are the living and the dead alike﴾ [Fatir: 22]. Since disbelief has been made death and the disbeliever dead, guidance has been made life and the guided person living. Disbelief was made death because it is ignorance, and ignorance necessitates bewilderment and standing still, like death which necessitates stillness. Also, the dead person does not find guidance to anything, and neither does the ignorant person. Guidance is knowledge and sight, and knowledge and sight are the cause of attaining right direction and success in salvation.

His words ﴿and made for him a light by which he walks among the people﴾ are a conjunction with His words "so We brought him to life." Therefore this light must be different from that life. What comes to mind, and Allah knows best, is that human souls have four levels of knowledge.

The first: their being prepared to receive these forms of knowledge. This original preparedness differs among souls. Sometimes a soul is characterized by a complete, strong, noble preparedness, and sometimes that preparedness is little and weak, and its possessor is dull and deficient.

The second level: that it acquires the universal primary sciences, which are called reason ('aql).

The third level: that the person attempts to compose those self-evident truths and, through their combinations, reaches the knowledge of acquired unknowns. However, those cognitions may not be present in actuality, but they are such that whenever their possessor wishes to recall and summon them, he is able to do so.

The fourth level: that those cognitions, sacred forms of knowledge and spiritual manifestations, are present in actuality, and the essence of that soul is illuminated by those cognitions, lit by them, and perfected by their manifestation within it.

Having known this, we say:

**Page 141**

The first level, which is merely the existence of preparedness, is what is called death.

The second level, in which the self-evident universal sciences are present within it, is what is referred to by His words "so We brought him to life."

The third level is the composition of self-evident truths until one reaches, through their combinations, the knowledge of theoretical unknowns. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿and made for him a light.﴾

The fourth level is His words: ﴿by which he walks among the people,﴾ which indicates that he is summoning those sacred manifestations and looking at them. At this point the degrees of the happiness of the human soul are complete.

It may also be said: life is an expression for the preparedness residing in the essence of the soul, and light is an expression for bringing the light of revelation and the Revelation (tanzil) through it. For sight requires two things: soundness of the sense organ and the rising of the sun. Likewise, insight requires two things: soundness of the faculty of reason and the rising of the light of revelation and the Revelation. For this reason, the exegetes said: the intended meaning of this light is the Qur'an. Others said: it is the light of religion. Others said: it is the light of wisdom. These views are all close in meaning, and the verified position is what we have mentioned.

As for the parable of the disbeliever, it is like one ﴿in darkness, never to emerge from it.﴾ In His words ﴿never to emerge from it﴾ there is a subtle rational point: when a thing's occurrence with another thing continues, it becomes like an essential matter and a necessary attribute of it. So when the disbeliever's remaining in the darkness of ignorance and blameworthy character continues, those darknesses become like an essential attribute necessarily attached to him, making it difficult to remove them from him. We seek refuge in Allah from this state. Also, the one standing in darkness remains bewildered, unable to find the way to his good, so fear, dread, helplessness, and standing still overcome him.

* * *

**Issue 4:** The scholars differed as to whether these two parables are specific to two particular individuals or general to every believer and disbeliever. There are two views:

The first: that it is specific to two particular individuals. Within this view there are several reports:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: Abu Jahl threw filth at the Prophet (ﷺ), while Hamza had not yet accepted Islam. When Hamza was informed of this upon returning from a hunt with his bow in his hand, he went straight to Abu Jahl, targeted him with the bow, and began striking his head. Abu Jahl said to him: "Do you not see what he has brought? He has made our minds foolish and reviled our gods!" Hamza said: "You are the most foolish of people, worshipping stones besides Allah. I testify that there is no god but Allah, alone without partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger." So this verse was revealed.

The second report: Muqatil said: This verse was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl. The reason was that he said: "The sons of 'Abd Manaf have competed with us in nobility, until we became like two racehorses. They said: 'Among us is a prophet to whom revelation comes.' By Allah, we will not believe in him unless revelation comes to us as it comes to him." So this verse was revealed.

The third report: 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl.

The fourth report: al-Dahhak said: It was revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abu Jahl.

The second view: that this verse is general concerning all believers and disbelievers. This is the correct view, because if the meaning applies to all, then restricting it would be sheer arbitrariness. Also, we have mentioned that this surah was revealed all at once, so the claim that the cause of revelation of this particular verse was such-and-such is problematic, unless it is said that the Prophet (ﷺ) stated that the intended meaning of Allah the Most High in this general verse is a specific person.

**Page 142**

**Issue 5:** This verse is also among the strongest proofs that disbelief and faith are from Allah the Most High. For His words "so We brought him to life" and His words "and made for him a light by which he walks among the people" have been shown to be an allusion to knowledge and guidance. This indicates that all these matters occur only from Allah the Most High and by His permission. Rational proofs support its soundness, and this is the proof of the motive as we have summarized. Also, no rational person chooses ignorance and disbelief for himself. It is impossible that a person would choose to make himself ignorant and disbelieving. So when he intended to acquire faith and knowledge, and that did not occur, but its opposite, disbelief and ignorance, occurred instead, we know that this came about through the creation of another.

If they say: He chose it only because he believed that ignorance was knowledge.

We reply: The outcome of this statement is that he chose this ignorance because of a prior ignorance. If the discussion regarding that prior ignorance is the same as regarding this one, then it necessitates going on without end. Otherwise, it is necessary to end at an ignorance that occurs in him by His bringing it into existence and creating it, and that is what was to be proven.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 123:

﴿And thus We have placed in every town its greatest criminals so that they may plot therein; but they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The *kaf* (**al-kaf**, the particle of comparison) in His words "**And thus** (wa-kadhalika)" requires a comparison, and there are two views. The first: just as We placed its chiefs in Makkah so that they would plot therein, so too We placed in every town its greatest criminals. The second: it is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: just as We made their deeds appear attractive to the disbelievers, so too We have placed (these criminals).

**The second issue:** *Akabir* is the plural of *al-akbar* (**al-akbar**, "greatest"), which functions as a noun. The verse is according to inversion (*taqdim wa-ta'khir*), and its underlying sense is: We placed their criminals as greatest ones (*ja'alna mujrimiha akabira*). It is not permissible for *akabir* to be in a construct phrase (*idafah*), for the meaning would not be complete and one would need to supply a second object for *ja'ala* (**ja'ala**, "to make/place"). For when you say "I made Zayd," and stop, the sentence does not convey a complete meaning until you say "a leader" or "a humiliated one" or the like, because *ja'ala* requires two objects. Also, if you put *akabir* in a construct phrase, you have made the attribute (*sifah*) into a construct with its qualified noun (*mawsuf*), and this is not permissible according to the Basrans (**al-Basriyyun**, the grammarians of Basra).

**The third issue:** The sense of the verse becomes: We placed in every town its criminals as greatest ones so that they would plot therein. This implies that God, exalted is He, only placed them in this attribute because He willed from them that they should plot against people. This also indicates that good and evil are by the will of God, exalted is He.

Al-Jubba'i (**al-Jubba'i**, a Mu'tazilah theologian) answered this: the *lam* here is to be understood as **lam al-'aqibah** (the *lam* of consequence, indicating an outcome rather than an intention). Others said: since God did not prevent them from plotting, He became like one who wills it, so the speech came in the manner of a figure of resemblance. This question together with its answer has been repeated many times, beyond limit and enumeration.

[Page 143]

**The fourth issue:** Al-Zajjaj (**al-Zajjaj**, the grammarian and Qur'an exegete) said: God only made the criminals greatest because, by virtue of their leadership, they are more capable of treachery, deceit, and promoting falsehoods among people than others are. Moreover, abundance of wealth and strength of position move a person to exaggerate in preserving them, and that preservation is not complete except through all the blameworthy qualities: treachery, deceit, lying, backbiting, slander, and false oaths. Even if wealth and position had no fault other than that God, exalted is He, has decreed that only those who possess wealth and position are described with these blameworthy attributes, that would suffice as proof of the baseness of wealth and position.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿but they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive﴾. What is meant by this is what God, exalted is He, mentioned in another verse: ﴿And the evil plot does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. We have explained the reality of this at the beginning of surah al-Baqarah in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15].

The Mu'tazilah (**al-Mu'tazilah**, the rationalist school of theology) said: There is no doubt that His words ﴿but they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive﴾ are mentioned in the context of threat and reproach. So if what precedes this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, willed from them that they plot against people, then how is it fitting for the Merciful, the Generous, the Wise, the Forbearing to will from them plotting, and create plotting in them, then threaten them for it and punish them with the most severe punishment for it? Know that the objection to this speech with the well-known arguments has been mentioned by us many times.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 124:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When a sign comes to them, they say: "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God. God knows best where to place His message. Those who committed crime will be struck with humiliation before God and a severe punishment for their scheming."﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related the deceit and envy of these disbelievers: that whenever an overpowering miracle came to them that points to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), they said: "We will not believe until we are given the same rank from God." This indicates the extreme of their envy, and that they remained persistent in disbelief not out of seeking proof and evidence, but out of extreme envy. The commentators said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "By God, if prophethood were true, I would be more deserving of it than Muhammad, for I have more wealth and children than he does." So this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak said: each one of them wanted to be singled out for revelation and messengership, as God, exalted is He, informed about them in His saying: ﴿Rather, each man among them desires to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52]. The apparent meaning of the verse we are interpreting also indicates this, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When a sign comes to them, they say: "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God."﴾ This indicates that a group of them were saying this statement. Also, what precedes this verse indicates this as well, namely His saying: ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals to scheme therein﴾. Then, immediately after that verse, He mentioned that they said: ﴿We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God.﴾ Its apparent meaning indicates that the scheming mentioned in the first verse is this wicked statement.

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the well-known one: the people meant that prophethood and messengership should be granted to them, as it was granted to Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, and that they should be leaders, not followers, and masters, not servants.

The second opinion, which is the view of al-Hasan, and is reported from Ibn Abbas: the meaning is that when a verse from the Qur'an came to them commanding them to follow the Prophet, they said: "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God." This is the statement of the polytheists of the Arabs: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 90], up to His saying: ﴿until you send down to us a book that we can read﴾ [al-Isra: 93], from God to Abu Jahl and to so-and-so and so-and-so, a separate book. On this interpretation, the people did not ask for prophethood; rather, they asked that overpowering signs and manifest miracles come to them, like the miracles of the earlier prophets, so that they would prove the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace. The verifiers said: the first opinion is stronger and more fitting, because His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ fits only the first opinion. And for one who supports the second opinion, he may say: when they proposed those overpowering signs, if God had answered them and manifested those miracles according to their request, they would have come close to the rank of messengership, and then His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ could serve as a response to this statement.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾, the meaning is that messengership has a specific place, and it is not suitable to be placed except in it. Whoever is specifically described with those qualities for which messengership is suitable to be placed in him is a messenger, and otherwise not. And the one who knows those qualities is none other than God, exalted is He.

Know that people have differed on this question. Some of them said: souls and spirits are equal in their complete essence, so the granting of prophethood and messengership to some of them and not others is an honor, a benevolence and a favor from God. Others said: rather, human souls differ in their substances and essences. Some of them are good, pure, free from the attachments of corporeal things, radiant with divine lights, elevated and illumined. And some are base, turbid, loving of corporeal things. So a soul that is not of the first category is not fit to receive revelation and messengership. Then the first category itself differs in increase and decrease, strength and weakness, down to levels without end. Therefore the ranks of the messengers are necessarily different: among them is one to whom strong miracles were given with few followers, and among them is one to whom a single miracle or two were given and who had a great following; among them is one for whom gentleness prevailed, and among them is one for whom severity prevailed. This kind of discussion is extensive, and it is not fitting to mention it in this place. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ contains an alert to another subtlety, namely: the least that is necessary for the attainment of prophethood and messengership is freedom from deceit, treachery, rancor and envy.

His saying: ﴿We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God﴾ is itself deceit, treachery and envy, so how can the attainment of prophethood and messengership be conceived together with these qualities? Then God, exalted is He, made clear that because they are described by these blameworthy qualities, humiliation before God and a severe punishment will befall them. Its explanation: reward is not complete except through two things, honoring and benefit, and punishment is also complete only through two things: disgrace and harm. God, exalted is He, threatened them with the combination of these two matters in this verse. As for disgrace, it is His saying "will befall them": ﴿humiliation before God and a severe punishment﴾. He placed mention of humiliation before mention of harm because these people only rebelled against obedience to Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, seeking honor and dignity. So God, exalted is He, made clear that He will confront them with the opposite of what they sought; the first thing that reaches them is humiliation, abasement and degradation. And in His saying "(humiliation)"

(before God) there are several aspects:

The first: the intended meaning is that this humiliation will occur in the Hereafter, where there is no judge whose judgment is executed other than Him.

The second: they will be struck with humiliation by God's decree and command in the world. Since that humiliation is of this kind, it is permissible to attribute it to "before God."

The third: the intended meaning is ﴿will befall those who committed crime: humiliation﴾, and then he resumed and said "(before God)," meaning: this has been prepared for them, and the purpose of it is emphasis.

The fourth: the intended meaning is: humiliation from God. On this reading, the word "from" must be supplied. As for the explanation of harm and punishment, it is His saying: ﴿and a severe punishment﴾. Thus this statement establishes that He has prepared for them great disgrace and severe punishment, then He made clear that this befalls them because of their scheming, their lying and their envy.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 125 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing up into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe﴾.

In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited this verse to demonstrate that misguidance and guidance are from Allah, Exalted is He.

Know that this verse, just as its wording indicates our position, its wording also indicates the decisive rational proof on this issue. Its explanation: the servant is able to believe and able to think, so his capacity with respect to these two matters is equal. Therefore it is impossible for belief to proceed from him instead of disbelief, or disbelief instead of belief, unless a motive (dā'iyah) arises in the heart toward it. We have explained this many times in this book. That motive has no meaning except his knowledge, belief, or assumption that the act contains an additional benefit and a preponderant advantage. When this meaning arises in the heart, it moves him to do that thing. And if knowledge, belief, or assumption arises in the heart that the act contains additional harm and a preponderant corruption, it moves him to abandon it. We have shown by proof that the arising of these motives must necessarily be from Allah, Exalted is He, and that the totality of capacity together with the motive necessitates the act.

Having established this, we say: it is impossible for belief to proceed from the servant unless Allah creates in his heart the belief that belief has preponderant benefit and additional advantage. When this belief arises in the heart, the heart inclines, and an intense desire to attain it arises in the soul. This is the expansion of the breast to belief. As for when there arises in the heart the belief that belief in Muhammad, for example, is the cause of great corruption in religion and worldly life, and necessitates many harms, then upon the arising of this belief there follows an intense aversion from belief in Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is what is meant by His saying that He makes his breast tight and constricted. Thus the meaning of the verse becomes: whoever Allah intends to believe, He strengthens his motives toward belief; and whoever Allah intends to disbelieve, He strengthens his obstacles against belief and strengthens his motives toward disbelief.

[p. 146]

Since it has been established by rational proof that the matter is so, it is established that the wording of the Qur'an includes these rational proofs. When decisive demonstration corresponds with the explicit wording of the Qur'an, there is nothing beyond it of clarification or proof.

The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) said: For us, regarding this verse, there are two positions.

The first position: demonstrating that there is no indication in this verse for your view.

The second position: the interpretation that conforms to our school and our view.

As for the first position, its establishment is through several aspects:

The first aspect: this verse does not state that Allah misguides a people or causes them to be misguided. It states nothing more than that whenever He wills to guide a person, He does such-and-such to him, and whenever He wills to mislead him, He does such-and-such to him. The verse does not say that He wills that or does not will it. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿If We had intended to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence, if We were doers﴾ [al-Anbiya' 17]. Here Allah explained that He would do amusement if He willed it, and there is no dispute that He does not will that nor does He do it.

The second aspect: He did not say, "Whoever He wills to mislead from Islam," but rather said, ﴿and whoever He wills to mislead﴾. So why do you say that the intended meaning is "whoever He wills to mislead from belief"?

The third aspect: at the end of the verse He clarified that He does this act to this disbeliever only as recompense for his disbelief, and that it is not by way of initiation. He said: ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾.

The fourth aspect: His saying, ﴿and whoever He wills to mislead, He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾, indicates that making the breast tight and constricted precedes the occurrence of misguidance, and that this preceding condition has an effect on the occurrence of misguidance. This is invalid by consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars). As for us, we do not hold this. As for you, the cause of ignorance and misguidance is that Allah creates it in him by His power. Thus it has been established by these four aspects that this verse does not indicate your view.

As for the second position, namely that the interpretation of this verse in a manner suitable to our view: its establishment is through several aspects.

The first, which al-Jubba'i chose and al-Qadi (Abd al-Jabbar) supported, is that we say: the meaning of the verse is: whoever Allah wills to guide to the Garden on the Day of Resurrection, He expands his breast to Islam until he remains firm upon it and does not depart from it. The explanation of this expansion is that He does for him lutf (divine favours, grace) that move him to persist in belief and to be steadfast upon it. This type of lutf is one that cannot be done for the believer except after he has become a believer; and after he becomes a believer, it moves him to persist in belief and to be steadfast upon it. To this refers His saying: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart﴾ [al-Taghabun 11], and His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾ [al-'Ankabut 69]. So when a servant believes and Allah wills his steadfastness, then He expands his breast, that is, He does for him the lutf that necessitates his steadfastness upon belief and its continuance. As for when he disbelieves and is obstinate, and Allah, Exalted is He, wills to mislead him from the path to the Garden, then at that time He casts into his breast constriction and tightness.

Then al-Jubba'i asked himself and said: How is this valid when we find disbelievers with contented souls, having no grief at all and no sorrow?

He answered: He, Exalted is He, did not inform that He does this to them at every time, so it is not impossible that they be, at some times, content in heart.

Al-Qadi asked himself another question upon this answer, saying: Then you must affirm concerning every disbeliever that he finds in himself that constriction and tightness at some times.

He answered him by saying: Thus we say. Repelling this is not possible, especially when the proofs of Allah appear, and when the victory of Allah for the believers becomes manifest, and when humiliation and abasement appear among them. This is the utmost statement of this answer.

The second interpretation: They said, why is it not permissible to say that the meaning is: "Whoever Allah wills to guide to the Garden, He expands his breast to Islam"? That is, He expands his breast to Islam at that time when He guides him to the Garden. For when he sees that because of belief he attains this high rank and noble station, he increases in desire for belief, and greater expansion and inclination toward it arise in his heart. And whoever Allah wills to mislead on the Day of Resurrection from the path to the Garden, at that time He constricts his breast, and his breast is made tight by the intense grief that befalls him upon being deprived of the Garden and entering the Fire. They said: this is a near interpretation, and the wording admits of it, so it is obligatory to take the wording in this sense.

The third interpretation: it is said that there has occurred in the speech a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir), so the meaning is: whoever expands his own breast to belief, Allah has willed to guide him, that is, to single him out with the lutf that calls to steadfastness upon belief, or to guide him in the sense that He guides him to the path of the Garden. And whoever has his breast made tight and constricted from belief, Allah has willed to mislead him from the path of the Garden, or to mislead him in the sense that He withholds from him the lutf that calls to steadfastness upon belief. This is the totality of their speech on this subject.

As for the answer to what they stated first, namely that Allah, Exalted is He, did not say in this verse that He misleads him, but rather what is mentioned in it is that if He willed to mislead him, He would do such-and-such:

We say: His saying at the end of the verse, ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾, is an explicit statement that He does that misguidance to them, because the particle "kāf" (like, thus) in His saying "kadhālika" (thus) indicates comparison, and the meaning is: just as We placed that constriction and tightness in his breast, so likewise We place defilement upon the hearts of those who do not believe.

As for the answer to what they stated second, namely His saying, "and whoever He wills to mislead from religion":

We say: His saying at the end of the verse, ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾, is an explicit statement that the meaning of His saying, ﴿and whoever He wills to mislead﴾ is that He misleads him from religion.

As for the answer to what they stated third, namely that His saying, ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾, indicates that He casts that constriction and tightness into their breasts only as recompense for their disbelief:

We say: We do not concede that this is the meaning. Rather the meaning is: thus Allah places defilement upon the hearts of those for whom it has been decreed that they will not believe. If we take this verse in this sense, what they mentioned falls away.

As for the answer to what they stated fourth, namely that the apparent meaning of the verse requires that the constriction and tightness of the breast be something prior to misguidance and causing it:

We say: The matter is so, for when Allah creates in his heart a belief that belief in Muhammad ﷺ necessitates blame in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, this belief necessitates the soul's turning away and the heart's aversion from accepting that belief. There arises in that heart an aversion and recoil from accepting that belief. This state resembles intense constriction, for when a path is narrow, the one who enters cannot enter it. Likewise, when this belief arises in the heart, belief is prevented from entering it. Because of this resemblance from this aspect, the words "constriction" and "tightness" are applied to it. Thus this objection falls away.

As for the first of the three interpretations they mentioned:

The answer to it is that the sum of that statement returns to explaining the constriction and tightness as the overpowering of grief and sorrow over the heart of the disbeliever. This is far-fetched, because Allah distinguished the disbeliever from the believer by this constriction and tightness. If the meaning were the arising of grief and sorrow in the heart of the disbeliever, then what arises in the heart of the disbeliever of griefs, cares, and sorrows would have to be greater than what arises in the heart of the believer, by an increase that everyone recognizes. It is known that the matter is not so; rather, the grief of the disbeliever and the believer is equal, and indeed grief and trial with respect to the believer are greater. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver ceilings for their houses﴾ [al-Zukhruf 33]. And he, peace be upon him, said: "Trials are imposed upon the prophets, then upon the friends of Allah, then upon the most excellent, and then the next most excellent."

As for the second of the three interpretations, it is also rejected, because its essence returns to clarifying what is already clear. For everyone knows by necessity that whoever Allah guides to the Garden through belief, he rejoices because of that guidance, and his breast expands to belief with greater expansion at that time. Likewise the statement concerning His saying, ﴿and whoever He wills to mislead﴾ [al-Zukhruf 33]: the meaning is whoever He misleads from the path of the Garden, his heart constricts at that time, for the occurrence of this meaning is known by necessity. Therefore, interpreting the verse in this way removes this verse from its benefit.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 125 (part 2 of 3):

As for the third of the three aspects, it requires disentangling the structure of the verse. The verse requires that the expansion of the breast ("sharh al-sadr") come first from God, and that guidance and faith follow from it. You have reversed the matter, saying: the servant first makes his own breast expanded, and then God, after that, guides him, in the sense that He singles him out with additional favours that encourage him to remain steadfast in faith. Verbal proofs can only be relied upon if we retain the compositions and orderings within them. But if we nullify and remove them, it is impossible to rely upon any of them at all. Opening this door requires that none of the verses can be relied upon, and this is an attack on the Qur'an and removes it from being a proof. This is the decisive word on these questions. Then we conclude the discussion of this issue with this compelling conclusion: we have shown that the act of faith depends on there arising in the heart a resolute motive toward the act of faith, and the agent of that motive is God, Exalted. The same holds for the side of disbelief. The wording of the verse conforms to this meaning, because the sense of the verse is: whoever God wills to guide, He strengthens in his heart what calls him to faith; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He casts into his heart what turns him away from faith and calls him to disbelief. Rational proof has established that the matter must be so. On this reckoning, all the questions you have raised fall away. And God knows best what is correct.

* * *

The third issue: on the explanation of the words of the verse. As for "sharh al-sadr" (expansion of the breast), there are two interpretations of it.

The first interpretation: al-Layth said: it is said, "God expanded his breast, so it expanded," meaning He widened his breast to accept that matter, so it became wide. I say: al-Layth explained the expansion of the breast as the widening of the breast. There is no doubt that what is meant is not that He widens his breast in the literal sense, for that is clearly impossible. Rather, we must explain the widening of the breast. So we say: its verification is what we mentioned earlier, and there is no harm in repeating it. We say: when a person believes that in some action its benefit is greater and its good outweighs its harm, his nature inclines toward it, his desire to attain it grows strong, and in the heart arises an intense readiness to achieve it. This state is called the breadth of the soul. And when he believes that in some action its evil is greater and its harm outweighs its benefit, aversion from it grows strong, and in his nature arises repulsion and recoil from accepting it. It is known that when a path is narrow, the one entering cannot enter it, and when it is wide, the one entering can enter it. So when there arises the belief that a certain matter has greater benefit and good, and inclination toward it arises, that inclination has arisen in that heart, and it is said: the breast has expanded for it. And when there arises the belief that it has greater harm and corruption, no inclination toward it arises in the heart, and it is said: it is narrow. Thus the breast has become like a narrow path that cannot be entered. This is the verification of the discussion of the breadth and narrowness of the breast.

The second interpretation: concerning the meaning of "sharh" (expansion). It is said: "So-and-so expanded his matter" when he made it manifest and clarified it, and "he explained the issue" when it was problematic and he made it clear.

Know that the term "sharh" is not specific to the side of truth, because it occurs in reference to Islam in His saying: ﴿Is one whose breast God has expanded for Islam...﴾ [al-Zumar 39:22], and in reference to disbelief in His saying: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief...﴾ [al-Nahl 16:106]. The exegetes said: when this verse was revealed, "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked and it was said to him: How does God expand his breast? He, peace be upon him, said: 'He casts light into it until it widens and expands.' It was said to him: Is there a sign by which one may recognise this? He, peace be upon him, said: 'Turning toward the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death descends.'" I say: this hadith is among the strongest proofs for the soundness of what we have mentioned concerning the explanation of God's expansion of the breast. Its explanation: when a person conceives that occupation with the works of the Hereafter is greater in benefit and good, and that occupation with worldly works is greater in harm and evil, and when certainty about this arises, whether through proof, experience, or imitation, then the desire for the Hereafter must necessarily follow from the arising of this belief. This is what is meant by turning toward the abode of eternity and recoil from the abode of the worldly life, and this is what is meant by withdrawing from the abode of delusion. As for preparing for death before death descends, it comprises both matters, namely, recoil from the worldly life and desire for the Hereafter.

Having understood this, we say: the motive for an act must arise before the act occurs, and the expansion of the breast for faith is an expression for the arising of the motive toward faith. For this reason, the apparent sense of this verse indicates that the expansion of the breast precedes the attainment of Islam, and the same applies to the side of disbelief.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast narrow and constricted (ḥaraj)﴾, there are several points.

The first point: Ibn Kathir read "ḍayqan" (ضَيْقًا) with the yā' sukūn (ضَيْقًا with a quiescent yā') and so throughout the Qur'an, while the rest read it with a shaddah on the yā' and a kasrah. It is possible that the doubled and the single form carry one meaning, like sayyid and sayd, hayyin and hayn, layyin and layn, mayyit and mayt. Nafi' and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "ḥarijan" (حَرِجًا) with a kasrah on the rā', while the rest read it with a fatḥah. Al-Farra' said: in its kasrah and its fatḥah it is in the position of wajal and wajil, qarad and qarid, and danaf and danif. Al-Zajjaj said: ḥaraj in the language means the narrowest of the narrow, and its meaning is that it is extremely narrow. Whoever says "a man with ḥaraj of the breast" with a fatḥah on the rā', its meaning is "one who has ḥaraj in his breast." And whoever says "ḥarij" makes him an active participle (fā'il). Likewise, "rajul danaf" means "one possessed of danaf," while "danif" is an adjective.

The second point: Some said: ḥarij, with a kasrah on the rā', means narrow, while ḥaraj with a fatḥah is the plural of ḥarajah, which is a place with dense trees that a grazing animal cannot reach. Al-Wahidi related two reports on this matter. The first: it is related from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited this verse and said: "Is there anyone here from the Banu Bakr?" A man said: "Yes." He said: "What is the ḥarajah among you?" He said: "A valley thick with trees, interlaced, with no path in it." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Thus is the heart of the disbeliever."

The second: al-Wahidi related from Abu al-Salt al-Thaqafi who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, recited this verse, then said: "Bring me a man from Kinanah whom they have made a shepherd." They brought him, and 'Umar said to him: "O youth, what is the ḥarajah among you?" He said: "The ḥarajah among us is a tree surrounded by trees, so that no grazing animal or wild beast can reach it." 'Umar said: "Thus is the heart of the disbeliever; nothing of goodness reaches it."

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As though he were climbing up into the sky﴾, there are two points.

The first point: Ibn Kathir read "yaṣ'adu" (يَصْعَدُ) with a quiescent ṣād. Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "yaṣṣā'adu" (يَصّاعَدُ) with an alif and a shaddah on the ṣād, meaning "yatasā'adu" (he ascends). The rest read "yaṣṣa''adu" (يَصَّعَّدُ) with a shaddah on the ṣād and the ʿayn, without an alif. As for the reading of Ibn Kathir, "yaṣ'adu," it is from ṣu'ud (ascent), and the meaning is that in his aversion to Islam and his burden with it, he is like one who laboriously attempts to climb into the sky. Just as that laborious effort is burdensome upon the heart, so faith is burdensome upon the heart of the disbeliever. As for the reading of Abu Bakr, "yaṣṣā'adu," it is like "yatasā'adu." As for the reading of the rest, "yaṣṣa''adu," it means "yatasa''adu," so the tā' was assimilated into the ṣād. The meaning of yatasa''adu is that he undertakes what is burdensome to him.

The second point: concerning the manner of this comparison, there are two interpretations.

The first: just as when a person is charged with climbing into the sky, that charge is burdensome upon him, grave and difficult for him, and his aversion from it grows strong, so the disbeliever finds faith burdensome, and his aversion from it is great.

The second: the meaning is that his heart recoils from Islam and turns away from accepting faith, so that distancing is compared to the distance of one who ascends from the earth to the sky.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Thus God places defilement (rijs) upon those who do not believe﴾, there are two points.

The first point: the particle "kaf" in His saying "thus" (kadhalika) indicates comparison with something, and there are two views on it.

The first: the meaning is that God places defilement upon them as He placed narrowness of breast in their hearts.

The second: al-Zajjaj said the meaning is: like what We have related to you, God places defilement.

The second point: the scholars differed on the interpretation of "rijs" (defilement). Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Satan, whom God empowers over them. Mujahid said: "rijs" is that which has no good in it. 'Ata' said: "rijs" is punishment. Al-Zajjaj said: "rijs" is curse in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

Let us conclude the exegesis of this verse with what is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: we discussed the matter of the Qadariyya (those who deny predestination) in the presence of Ibn 'Umar. He said: "The Qadariyya have been cursed on the tongue of seventy prophets, among them our Prophet (ﷺ). When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out, when people have been gathered such that all can hear: where are the adversaries of God? Then the Qadariyya will stand up." The judge (al-Qadi) included this hadith in his exegesis and said: this hadith is among the strongest indications that the Qadariyya are those who attribute the actions of servants to God, in decree, predestination and creation. For those who say this, they are the adversaries of God, because they say to God: "What sin do we have that You should punish us, when You are the One who created it in us, willed it from us, decreed it upon us, and created us only for it, and You did not facilitate for us anything other than it?" Such people must be adversaries of God on account of this argument. As for those who say that God empowered and removed the excuse, and that the servant came from his own self, their speech conforms to what is applied to them of inflicting punishment, so they are not adversaries of God, but rather are submissive to God. This is the judge's statement, and it is very strange. This is because it may be said to him: it is far from you that you did not know, from the doctrines of your opponents, that the servant has no proof against God and no entitlement in any respect, and that everything the Lord does to the servant is wisdom and rightness, and the servant has no objection or dispute against the Lord. How then does a person whose religion and belief is this become an adversary of God, Exalted is He?

Those who are adversaries of God are the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school), and this may be established on several grounds:

The first: they claim against God that reward and compensation are obligatory, and they say: "If You did not give me that, You would have ceased to be God and would have been deposed from lordship and become one of the foolish." So the one whose doctrine and belief is that is the adversary of God, Exalted is He.

The second: whoever persisted in disbelief for seventy years, then at the end of his life said from the heart, "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God," and then died, and the Lord of the worlds gave him exceeding blessings and additional ranks for a thousand thousand years, then wished to withdraw those blessings from him for a single moment, that servant would say: "O God, I beseech You, and then I beseech You not to abandon that even for a single moment, for if You abandon it for a single moment You will have been deposed from divinity." The summary: the servant's taking that faith for a single moment obliged God to continue those blessings for an endless duration, and there is no way for Him at all to escape this obligation. This is the adversarial position. As for the one who says that no one among the angels and prophets has any right upon God, Exalted is He, and that everything that reaches them of reward is a bounty and kindness from God, Exalted is He, such a person is not an adversary.

**The third aspect:** Regarding the formulation of this dispute, it is related that when Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari (may Allah have mercy on him) left the circle of his teacher Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i and abandoned his school, and his objections to the latter's statements increased, the estrangement between them grew severe. One day it so happened that al-Jubba'i held a session of admonition (majlis al-tadhkir), and a large number of people attended. Abu al-Hasan went to that session and sat in one of its corners, concealed from al-Jubba'i. He said to one of the old women present there: "I will teach you a question. Put it to this shaykh. Say to him: 'I had three sons. One was extremely devout and ascetic, the second was extremely unbelieving and wicked, and the third was a child who had not reached maturity. They all died in these conditions. So inform me, O shaykh, about their states.'"

Al-Jubba'i said: "As for the ascetic, he is in the ranks of Paradise. As for the unbeliever, he is in the depths of the Fire. As for the child, he is among those who are safe."

She said: "Say to him: 'If the child wished to go to those lofty ranks in which his devout brother is, would that be possible for him?'"

Al-Jubba'i said: "No, because Allah will say to him: 'You only reached those lofty ranks because you exhausted yourself in knowledge and action, and you do not have that.'"

Abu al-Hasan said: "Say to him: 'If the child then said: O Lord of the worlds, the fault is not mine, for You caused me to die before maturity; had You granted me respite, I might have surpassed my ascetic brother in asceticism and religion.'"

Al-Jubba'i said: "Allah will say to him: 'I knew that if you had lived, you would have transgressed and disbelieved, and you would have deserved the Fire. So before you reached that state, I took your welfare into account and caused you to die, so that you might be saved from punishment.'"

Abu al-Hasan said: "Say to him: 'If the unbelieving, wicked brother raised his head from the lowest depth of the Fire and said: O Lord of the worlds, O most wise of judges, O most merciful of the merciful, as You knew of that young brother that if he reached maturity he would disbelieve, You knew this of me. Why, then, did You take his welfare into account and not take my welfare into account?'"

[p. 152]

The narrator said: When the discourse reached this point, al-Jubba'i fell silent. When he looked, he saw Abu al-Hasan, and he knew that this question was from him and not from the old woman.

Then Abu al-Husayn al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) came after four or more generations following al-Jubba'i, and he wished to answer this question. He said: "We are not satisfied, concerning these three brothers, with this answer you have mentioned. Rather, we have two other answers beyond what you have mentioned." Then he said: "It is based on a question on which our shaykhs differed, namely: is it obligatory upon Allah to impose obligation (taklif) upon the servant or not? The Basrans said: imposing obligation is pure grace and kindness (tafdul wa ihsan), and it is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He. The Baghdadis said: it is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He."

He said: "If we branch from the view of the Basrans, then Allah, exalted is He, may say to that child: 'I prolonged the life of your ascetic brother and imposed obligation upon him by way of grace. It does not follow that because I have shown this grace to your brother the ascetic, I must show the same grace to you.'

"But if we branch from the view of the Baghdadis, then the answer is that it may be said: the prolongation of your brother's life and the imposition of obligation upon him was a kindness toward him, and no corruption returned from it to others; therefore I did it.
