As for prolonging your life and imposing obligation upon you, it would have entailed a corruption returning to others; for this reason I did not do that with you. Thus the difference is made clear."

This is a summary of the words of Abu al-Husayn al-Basri, striving to free his earlier shaykh from al-Ash'ari's question, or rather striving to free his God from the servant's question.

I say, before entering into the answer to the words of Abu al-Husayn: the validity of this subtle debate between the servant and Allah is only necessary according to the view of the Mu'tazila. As for according to the view of our companions (may Allah have mercy on them), there is absolutely no debate between the servant and the Lord, and it is not for the servant to say to his Lord: "Why did You do such-and-such?" or "Why did You not do such-and-such?" Thus it is established that the adversaries of Allah are the Mu'tazila, not the People of the Sunna, and this strengthens our aim and achieves our purpose.

Then we say:

As for the first answer, namely that prolonging life and imposing obligation is grace, and so it is permissible to single out some with it over others: we say this statement is refuted. For when He, exalted is He, has bestowed grace upon one of them, then withholding it from the second is ugly on the part of Allah, exalted is He, because bestowing it upon this second does not constitute a burdensome act for Allah, exalted is He, nor does it necessitate any entry of deficiency into His dominion in any way, and this second one has need of that grace. Such withholding is ugly among created beings. Do you not see that whoever prevents another from looking into his mirror set upon the wall for the general public, that prevention is ugly on his part, because it is a prevention of benefit without any harm being averted from him and without any benefit reaching him? If the rational judgment of goodness and ugliness is acceptable, then let it be acceptable here; and if it is not acceptable, it is not acceptable in any case at all, and the universal principle of your school collapses. Thus it is established that this answer is corrupt.

As for the second answer: it too is corrupt. This is because our saying "imposing obligation on him includes a corruption" does not mean that this imposition in itself necessitates the occurrence of that corruption, for otherwise that corruption would necessarily occur forever in the case of everyone, and that is false. Rather, it means: Allah, exalted is He, knew that if He imposed obligation upon this person, another person would freely choose an ugly act. If this circumstance required that Allah abandon his obligation, then likewise He knew of that unbeliever that if He imposed obligation upon him, he would choose disbelief at that obligation; so it was necessary that He abandon imposing obligation upon him. And that entails the ugliness of imposing obligation upon one whom Allah knows will disbelieve. If this is not necessary here, it is not necessary there either. As for the claim that it is obligatory upon Him, exalted is He, to abandon imposing obligation when He knows that another will choose an ugly act at that obligation, yet it is not obligatory upon Him to abandon it when He, exalted is He, knows that the very person will choose the ugly act at that obligation, this is sheer arbitrariness.

Thus it is established that the answer which Abu al-Husayn derived by the subtlety of his thought and the precision of his inquiry, after four generations, is weak. And it is clear that the adversaries of Allah are the Mu'tazila, not our companions. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is the path of your Lord, straight. We have detailed the signs for a people who remember﴾.

There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: His saying, "This" (wa-hadha), is a demonstrative referring to something previously mentioned. Regarding it there are two opinions. The first, which is the stronger in my view, is that it refers to what He mentioned and established in the preceding verse, namely that an act depends on a motive, and that the arrival of that motive comes from God, Exalted is He. Therefore the act must come from God, Exalted is He, and this necessitates pure monotheism (tawhid al-mahd), which is that He, Exalted is He, is the originator of all existing beings and possible things. He called it a "path" (sirat) because knowledge of it leads to knowledge of the true tawhid. He described it as "straight" (mustaqim) because the saying of the Mu'tazilah is not straight. This is because the preponderance of one of the two sides of a possible thing over the other either depends on a determining factor (murajjih) or does not depend on one. If it depends on a determining factor, it follows that the act does not proceed from the capable agent except when the motive is joined to it, and then our position is established: everything occurs by the decree and destiny of God, and the Mu'tazilah's view is refuted. If the preponderance of one side of a possible thing over the other does not depend on a determining factor, then this independence must obtain in all possible and originated things, and then it would necessitate the negation of creation and the Creator, and the nullification of the doctrine of act and agent, and of influence and influencer. As for the claim that this preponderance requires an influencer in some cases but not in others, as these Mu'tazilah maintain, it is crooked and not straight. What is straight is the judgment that need is established absolutely, and that necessitates precisely our doctrine. This is the view I prefer in interpreting this verse.

The second opinion: His saying, "This is the path of your Lord, straight," refers to everything previously mentioned in the entire Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means this which you are upon, O Muhammad, is the religion of your Lord, straight. Ibn Mas'ud said: it means the Qur'an. The first opinion is preferable, because returning the demonstrative to the nearest thing mentioned is more appropriate.

Having established this, we say: when God, Exalted is He, commanded following what is in the preceding verse, it must be among the muhkamat (clear, definitive verses) and not among the mutashabihat (ambiguous verses). For when God mentions something and emphasizes the command to hold fast to it, return to it, and rely upon it, it must be among the muhkamat. Thus it is established that the preceding verse is among the muhkamat, that it must be applied to its apparent meaning, and that it is forbidden to alter it by ta'wil (figurative interpretation).

The second issue: al-Wahidi said: "mustaqiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and the element governing it is the meaning of "hadha" (this). This is because "dha" implies the sense of pointing, as in your saying: "This is Zayd standing," meaning: I point to him in his state of standing. And when the element governing the circumstantial qualifier is the meaning of a verb and not the verb itself, it is not permissible to place the circumstantial qualifier before it: one cannot say "standing this is Zayd," but one may say "laughing came Zayd."

As for His saying: ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾.

We say: As for the detailing of the signs, its meaning is mentioning them distinctly, one by one, such that none of them is mixed with another. God, Exalted is He, has clarified the soundness of the doctrine of qada' and qadar in many consecutive and successive verses of this surah, by many methods and various aspects.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿for a people who remember﴾, what I think, and God knows best, is that He, Exalted is He, only made the closing of this verse this word because it is established in the mind of everyone that one of the two sides of a possible thing is not preferred over the other except by a determining factor. It is as though He, Exalted is He, were saying to the Mu'tazili: O Mu'tazili, remember what is established in your intellect, that a possible thing does not have one of its two sides preferred over the other except by a determining factor, until the doubt is entirely removed from your heart regarding the issue of qada' and qadar.

**The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 6, Verse 127**

"﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector because of what they used to do.﴾"

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the greatness of His blessings in the Straight Path, and explained that He has prepared a provision made ready for those who are among those mentioned, He then explained the noble benefit that results from holding fast to that Straight Path. So He said: ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord.﴾ In this verse there are several honours.

The first type: His saying ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace﴾. This implies *al-ḥaṣr* (restriction, meaning exclusivity). Its meaning is: the Abode of Peace is for them and not for others. Regarding His saying ﴿the Abode of Peace﴾, there are two views.

The first view: *al-Salam* (Peace) is one of the names of God, exalted is He, so "the Abode of Peace" is the abode attributed to God, exalted is He, just as the Ka'bah is called "the House of God" and a caliph is called "the servant of God."

The second view: *al-Salam* is an attribute of the Abode. Within this there are two aspects:

The first: the meaning is "the abode of safety" (*dar al-salamah*). The Arabs add this *ha'* (*tā' marbūṭah*) to many verbal nouns and omit it, saying *ḍalāl* and *ḍalālah* (error), *safāh* and *safāhah* (folly), *ladhādh* and *ladhādhah* (pleasure), and *ridā'* and *ridā'ah* (suckling).

The second: *al-Salam* is the plural of *al-salamah* (safety), and Paradise is named by this name because all kinds of safety are present in it in their entirety.

Having understood these two views: those who held the first view said so because it is more excellent, since attributing the Abode to God, exalted is He, is the utmost in ennobling and magnifying its status and elevating its rank, so mention of this attribution is an exaggeration in glorifying the matter. Those who held the second view preferred their opinion for two reasons:

The first: describing the Abode as "the abode of safety" is more effective in encouraging desire than attributing the Abode to God, exalted is He.

The second: describing God, exalted is He, as *al-Salam* is originally a metaphor, and He was described by it because He is the possessor of peace (*dhu al-salam*). So when it is possible to take the speech in its literal sense, that is more appropriate.

The second type: among the benefits mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾. There are several interpretations of it:

The first interpretation: the meaning is that it is prepared in His presence, just as rights are prepared, made ready and present. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their reward with their Lord﴾. This is the utmost in explaining their arrival at it and their being confident of that.

The second interpretation, which is closer to verification: His saying ﴿with their Lord﴾ indicates that this stored-up matter is described as being near to God, exalted is He. This nearness is not by place or direction; therefore it must be by nobility, loftiness and rank. This indicates that the thing has reached such a degree of perfection and exaltedness that no one knows its true reality except God, exalted is He. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the comfort of the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17].

The third interpretation: He said about the angels: ﴿and those with Him are not too proud﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]. He said about the believers in this world, "I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake." He also said, "I am as My servant thinks of Me." He said about their description on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. He said about their abode: ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord.﴾ And He said about their reward: ﴿Their reward with their Lord﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8]. This indicates that the attainment of the perfection of the attribute of servanthood is by means of the attribute of being "with Him."

The third type of honours mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and He is their Protector (*walī*)﴾. *Al-Walī* means "the near one." So His saying "with their Lord" indicates their nearness to God, exalted is He, and His saying ﴿and He is their Protector﴾ indicates God's nearness to them. We do not see in reason any rank for the servant higher than this rank. Moreover, His saying ﴿and He is their Protector﴾ conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*), meaning: they have no protector except Him. And how could this honour not be, since it was obtained through the monotheism mentioned in His saying: ﴿So whomever God wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam, and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾. Those people have known from this verse that the one who manages and decrees is none other than Him, that the one who benefits and harms is none other than Him, that the one who makes happy and makes wretched is none other than Him, and that there is no originator of existent and possible things except Him. When they recognised this, they cut themselves off from everything other than Him. So their return was only to Him, their reliance was only upon Him, their intimacy was only with Him, and their submission was only to Him. When they became wholly this way, inevitably God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and He is their Protector.﴾ This is an informing that He, exalted is He, undertakes all their interests in religion and in this world, and this includes protection, guarding, help, support, bringing good things, and warding off calamities and afflictions.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿because of what they used to do﴾. He mentioned this only so that a person would not cut himself off from action, for action is indispensable. The verification of this matter is that there is a strong connection between the soul and the body. Just as psychological states descend from the soul to the body, as when one imagines something that angers him and the effect appears on the body, so that the body becomes heated and warm, likewise bodily states ascend from the body to the soul. So when a person persists in acts of righteousness and goodness, the effects appropriate to them appear in the very essence of the soul. This indicates that the seeker must necessarily undertake action, and that there is absolutely no way for him to abandon it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 6, verse 128:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day He gathers them all together, He will say: "O assembly of jinn, you have taken much from mankind." And their allies from mankind will say: "Our Lord, some of us have profited from others, and we have reached the term You appointed for us." He will say: "The Fire is your abode, wherein you will abide eternally, except as Allah wills. Indeed your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the condition of those who hold fast to the Straight Path, He then explained the condition of those who are the opposite of that, so that the account of the people of Paradise would be followed by the account of the people of the Fire, and so that the threat would be mentioned after the promise. In this passage there are several issues:

**The first issue:** ﴿On the Day He gathers them﴾ is in the accusative case governed by an omitted verb. The meaning is: "Remember the Day We gather them," or "On the Day We gather them, We will say, 'O assembly of jinn,'" or "On the Day We gather them and say, 'O assembly of jinn,'" (this is the case of what cannot be described because of its severity).

**The second issue:** To what does the pronoun in His saying ﴿On the Day He gathers them﴾ refer? There are two views. The first is that it refers to what is known, not to what has been mentioned, namely the two weighty creatures (humans and jinn) and all the accountable beings whom Allah is known to raise. The second is that it refers to the devils mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils among mankind and jinn, who inspire one another with decorated speech as deception﴾.

**The third issue:** In the verse there is an omitted element, and the implied meaning is: "On the Day We gather them all, We will say, 'O assembly of jinn.'" Thus the one who speaks is Allah, exalted is He, just as He is the one who gathers them all. This utterance from Him, exalted is He, after the gathering can only be a rebuke and a clarification of the fact that, although they rebelled in this world, their state in the Hereafter ends in submission, compliance and admission of guilt. Al-Zajjaj said: The implied meaning is "then it will be said to them, 'O assembly of jinn,'" because it is unlikely that Allah, exalted is He, would speak Himself with the disbelievers, as is evidenced by His saying, describing the disbelievers: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174].

As for His saying ﴿you have taken much from mankind﴾, we say: this necessarily requires interpretation. This is because the jinn are not able to "take much" from the very substance of humans, since the one who has power over the body, over giving life and over action is none other than Allah, exalted is He. Therefore the intended meaning must be: "you have taken much by calling to misguidance, and it has found acceptance."

As for His saying: ﴿And their allies from mankind said﴾, the closer view is that there is an omission in it. Just as He addressed the jinn with rebuke, so He addressed mankind with reproach, because the calling came from the jinn and the acceptance came from mankind, and the partnership exists between the two groups. So when He rebuked both groups, He here relates the answer of mankind, which is their saying: ﴿Our Lord, some of us have profited from others﴾. Thus they described themselves as being absorbed in the benefits of this world and in enjoying its pleasures, until they reached the point at which they became certain of the evil of their outcome.

Then there are two views here:

The first is that their saying "some of us have profited from others" means that the jinn profited from mankind and mankind profited from the jinn. On this view, there are two views on what this profit consisted of:

The first view: The meaning of this profit is that when a man travelled and nightfall came upon him in a barren land and he feared for himself, he would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the foolish ones of his people," and so he would spend the night secure in himself. This is the profit of mankind from the jinn. As for the profit of the jinn from mankind, it is that when a human sought refuge with a jinn, that was a form of exalting the jinn on their part, and the jinn would say: "I have become the master of jinn and mankind," because the human had acknowledged that the jinn could ward off harm from him. This is the view of al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Kalbi and Ibn Jurayj, and they argued for its soundness with His saying: ﴿And there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6].

The second view regarding the explanation of this profit: Mankind used to obey the jinn and submit to their rule, so the jinn became like chiefs, and mankind like followers, servants, obedient and submissive, who do not oppose their chief and master in anything small or great. There is no doubt that this chief benefited from this servant; this is the profit of the jinn from mankind. As for the profit of mankind from the jinn, the jinn used to guide them to kinds of desires, pleasures and good things, and make those matters easy for them. This view is the choice of al-Zajjaj, who said: This is better than the previous view, and the evidence for it is His saying: ﴿you have taken much from mankind﴾, and those among mankind who would say, "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley," are few.

The second view: His saying ﴿Our Lord, some of us have profited from others﴾ is the speech of mankind alone, because the profit of the jinn from mankind and the reverse is a rare matter that hardly appears. As for the profit of some humans from others, it is an evident matter. Therefore the speech must be taken to refer to this. Also, His saying ﴿And their allies from mankind said: "Our Lord, some of us have profited from others"﴾ is the speech of the humans who are the allies of the jinn, so the meaning of the profit of some of them from others must be the profit of some of those people from others.

Then He, exalted is He, said, relating about them: ﴿and we have reached the term You appointed for us﴾. The meaning is that this profiting was present until a specific term and a limited time, then disappointment, regret and remorse came from a place where they would not benefit. They differed as to what that term was: Some said it is the time of death. Others said it is the time of being left free and empowered. And some people said it is the time of reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. Those who held the first view said that it indicates that everyone who dies, whether killed or otherwise, dies at his appointed term, because they acknowledged: "We have reached the term You appointed for us," and among them were those who were killed and those who were not killed.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾. The word al-mathwā (abode) means the station, the dwelling place and the destination. Then it is not far-fetched that a person may have a station and a dwelling place, and then he dies and is released by death from that abode. So Allah, exalted is He, clarified that this station and abode is everlasting and perpetual, and this is His saying: ﴿wherein you will abide eternally﴾.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except as Allah wills﴾, and there are several views on this:

The first: What is meant by it is the exception of the times of reckoning, because during those states they are not abiding eternally in the Fire.

The second: What is meant is the times in which they are moved from the torment of the Fire to the torment of al-Zamharir (the extreme cold). It is related that they enter a valley in which there is intense cold, so they seek to be returned from that cold to the heat of the Blazing Fire.

The third:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah, exalted is He, made an exception for a group whom He knew in advance would become Muslims and would affirm the Prophet (ﷺ). According to this view, the word *mā* must have the meaning of *man* (whoever). Al-Zajjaj said: The first view is better, because the meaning of the exception is only from the Day of Resurrection, since His saying ﴿On the Day He gathers them all together﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿wherein you will abide eternally﴾ from the time they are raised ﴿except as Allah wills﴾ regarding the length of their being gathered from their graves and the length of their time under reckoning.

The fourth: Abu Muslim said: This exception does not refer back to the eternity, but refers back to the appointed term set for them. So it is as if they said: "And we have reached the term You appointed for us," meaning the term You designated for us, except for the one whom You destroyed before the designated term. This is like His saying: ﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-Anʿam: 6], and as He did with the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud, whom Allah destroyed before the term which, had they believed, they would have remained until they reached it. So the summary of the speech is that they say: "Some of us have profited from others, and we have reached what You designated for us as the term, except for whom You wished to cut off and You cut him off before that because of his disbelief and error."

Know that although this view is possible, it abandons the apparent arrangement of the words of this verse. Since it is possible to keep the verse on its apparent meaning, there is no need for this strained interpretation.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾, meaning: in what He does of reward and punishment and all other forms of recompense. As if He, exalted is He, is saying: "I only decreed for these disbelievers the punishment of eternity because I know that they deserve it." And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: His saying ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾: *al-mathwā* is a noun of the verbal noun (masdar), not of place, because His saying ﴿wherein you will abide eternally﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and a noun of place does not function as a verb. So His saying ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾ means: "The Fire is deserving that you remain in it eternally."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 129:

The First Issue: There are several benefits in the verse.

The First Benefit: Know that when Exalted God related about the jinn and mankind that some of them take others as allies (tawalla), He made clear that this only occurs by His decree and judgment, so He said: ﴿And thus do We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾. The proof that the matter is so is that power (qudrah) is capable of both sides, namely enmity and friendship. So if there were no occurrence of a motive (da'iyah) toward friendship, friendship would not have come about, and that motive does not arise except by the creation of God Exalted, to cut off an infinite regress (tasalsul). Thus it is established by this proof that He, Exalted, is the one who makes some of the wrongdoers allies of others. And by this explanation this verse becomes a proof for us in the question of compulsion (jabr) and divine decree (qadar).

The Second Benefit: When Exalted God explained regarding the people of Paradise that they have the Abode of Peace (dar al-salam), He made clear that He Himself is their Protecting Friend (wali) in the sense of safeguarding, guarding, aiding and supporting. Likewise, when He explained the condition of the people of the Fire, He mentioned that their dwelling and abode is the Fire, then He made clear that their allies are those who resemble them in wrongdoing, disgrace and punishment. This is a fine and beautiful connection.

Page 159

The Third Benefit: The particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) in His saying ﴿And thus do We make﴾ requires something previously mentioned, and the implied meaning is: as if He had said, just as We sent down upon the jinn and mankind who were mentioned before the painful, lasting punishment from which there is no escape, ﴿so do We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾.

The Fourth Benefit: ﴿And thus do We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾ because kinship of nature (jinsiyyah) is the cause of joining. Evil souls join with what resembles them in evil, and likewise regarding pure souls. So everyone takes interest in the affair of one who resembles him in support, aid and strengthening. And God knows best.

The Second Issue: The verse indicates that whenever the subjects are wrongdoers, God Exalted empowers over them a wrongdoer like them. If they wish to be freed from that unjust ruler, then let them abandon wrongdoing. Also, the verse indicates that people must have a ruler and governor, because if Exalted God does not leave the people of wrongdoing without an unjust ruler, then it is more fitting that He not leave the people of righteousness without a ruler who leads them to increase in righteousness. Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "People are only fit to have a ruler who is just or unjust." They denied his saying "or unjust," so he said: "Yes, he secures the path, and enables the establishment of the prayers and the pilgrimage to the House."

It is narrated that Abu Dharr asked the Messenger (ﷺ) for a position of authority, and he said to him: "You are weak, and it is a trust, and on the Day of Resurrection it is a disgrace and a regret, except for the one who takes it with its right and fulfills what is incumbent upon him in it."

And from Malik ibn Dinar: It came in some of God's books: "I am God, the Master of kings. The hearts of kings and their forelocks are in My hand. Whoever obeys Me, I will make them a mercy upon him, and whoever disobeys Me, I will make them a punishment upon him. Do not occupy yourselves with cursing the kings, but turn to Me, and I will incline them toward you."

As for His saying ﴿because of what they used to earn﴾, the meaning is: We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others because that part acquires wrongdoing, and what is meant by it is what we have explained, that kinship of nature is a cause of joining.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 130:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind! Did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your day? They said: We bear witness against ourselves. The life of this world deceived them, and they bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾

Know that this verse is part of what Allah, exalted is He, mentions in rebuking the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, exalted is He, makes clear that they will have no way to deny, so they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers, and that they were punished only after the proof had been established against them. There are several issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** The scholars of language said: *al-Ma'shar* (the assembly) is every group whose affair is one, among whom there is companionship and association, and its plural is *al-ma'ashir*. As for His statement, ﴿messengers from among you﴾, the scholars differed over whether there was a messenger from among the jinn or not. Al-Dahhak said:

[p. 160]
Messengers were sent from among the jinn just as they were sent from among humankind, and he recited this verse, and he recited His statement: ﴿And there was no community but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. Al-Dahhak could argue on another basis, which is His statement: ﴿And if We had made it an angel, We would have made it a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. The exegetes said: the reason for this is that a human's companionship with a human is more complete than his companionship with an angel, so in the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, it was necessary that the messenger to humankind be from humankind, so that this companionship would be complete.
If this principle is established, then this reason exists among the jinn, so it is necessary that the messenger of the jinn be from among the jinn.

The second view, which is the view of the majority, is that there was never a messenger from among the jinn at all, and that the messengers were only from among humankind. I have not found any proof for this view except the claim of *ijma'* (scholarly consensus), and this is far-fetched, because how can a consensus be established when there is disagreement? It may be argued for this view with His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of 'Imran over the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33]. They agreed that the intended meaning of this choosing is prophethood, so it is necessary that prophethood be restricted to these people only. As for Al-Dahhak's reliance on the apparent meaning of this verse, the response to it is from several aspects:

**The first:** He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind! Did there not come to you messengers from among you﴾. This requires that the messengers of the jinn and humankind be a part of this collective whole. If the messengers were from humankind, then the messengers would be a part of that collective whole, and this alone suffices to keep the wording on its apparent meaning. So the apparent meaning of this verse does not necessitate affirming a messenger from among the jinn.

**The second:** It is not far-fetched to say that the messengers were from humankind, but Allah, exalted is He, would cast the call into the hearts of a group of the jinn so that they would hear the words of the messengers, go to their people among the jinn, inform them of what they had heard from the messengers, and warn them about it, just as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a group of the jinn﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. Those jinn were messengers of the messengers, and so they were messengers of Allah, exalted is He. The evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, called the messengers of 'Isa his own messengers, when He said: ﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14]. The explanation of this is that He, exalted is He, rebuked the disbelievers with this verse only because He removed their excuse and eliminated their argument, by sending the messengers to all of them as bearers of good tidings and warners. When the good tidings and the warning reached all of them by this means, what is intended from removing the excuse and eliminating the argument was achieved, so the purpose was accomplished.

**The third answer:** Al-Wahidi said: His statement, exalted is He, ﴿messengers from among you﴾ means from one of you, and that is humankind. It is like His statement: ﴿From both of them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], meaning from one of the two, which is the salt water that is not sweet.

Know that the first two answers do not require abandoning the apparent meaning. As for this third answer, it does require abandoning the apparent meaning, and it is not permissible to resort to it except with a separate (explicit) proof.

As for His statement, ﴿who relate to you My signs﴾, what is meant is drawing attention to the proofs by recitation and by interpretation. ﴿And warn you of the meeting of this your day﴾, meaning they warn you of the punishment of this day. They then found nothing but confession, which is why they said: ﴿We bear witness against ourselves.﴾

If they ask: What is the reason that they confessed to disbelief in this verse, while they denied it in His statement: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]?

We say: The Day of Resurrection is a long day, and the states within it vary. Sometimes they confess and sometimes they deny, and that indicates the intensity of

[p. 161]
their fear and the turmoil of their states, for whoever's fear is great, the disturbance in his speech is great.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the life of this world deceived them.﴾ The meaning is that when they confessed to disbelief against themselves, it is as if He, exalted is He, were saying: They only fell into that disbelief because the life of this world deceived them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾ What is meant is that although they went to great lengths in hostility toward the prophets and in attacking their laws and miracles, the final outcome of their affair is that they confessed against themselves to disbelief. Some people have interpreted His statement, ﴿and they bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers﴾, to mean that their limbs will bear witness against them of polytheism and disbelief, and their purpose is to avoid repetition in the verse. Whichever way it is, the purpose of describing their states on the Day of Resurrection is to deter them in this world from disbelief and disobedience.

Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) rely on His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your day?﴾ as evidence that obligation does not arise at all before the revelation of the Law. For if obligation and deserving punishment had arisen before the revelation of the Law, this justification and this mention would have had no benefit.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 6, verse 131:**

God's words: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were unaware.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, explained that He punishes the disbelievers only after He has sent them prophets and messengers, He then showed through this verse that this is the justice, the truth, and the obligation. The verse raises several issues.

**First issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) said: "His words *dhalika* ('that') refer to what preceded: the sending of the messengers to them and their warning of the evil end. It is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is: 'The matter is that.'"

* * *

As for His words ﴿*an lam yakun rabbuka muhlika al-qura bi-zulm*﴾ ('that your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly'), there are several interpretations:

The first: *an* is causal (*ta'lil*), and the meaning is: "The matter is what We have related to you, because your Lord is not one who destroys the towns unjustly." Here the word *an* is the one that puts the verb in the subjunctive.

The second: it may be the lightened form (*mukhaffafa*) of the heavy *an*, and the meaning is: "Because your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly." The pronoun in the phrase *li-annahu* is the pronoun of the matter and the situation, and the implied meaning is: "Because the matter and the situation is that your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly."

The third: that the phrase ﴿*an lam yakun rabbuka*﴾ be taken as a substitute (*badal*) for the word *dhalika* ('that'), as in His words: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter: that the root of these people would be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66].

As for His words *bi-zulm* ('unjustly'), there are two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is "Your Lord would not destroy the towns on account of an injustice that they committed."

The second: the meaning intended is "Your Lord would not destroy the towns as an injustice against them." This is like His words: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud: 117] in Surah Hud.

According to the first interpretation, the injustice is an act of the disbelievers. According to the second, it refers to an act of God, exalted is He. The first interpretation is more fitting to our doctrine, because the second one gives the impression that if God had destroyed them before the sending of the messengers, He would have been unjust. This is not our position, because He judges as He wills and does as He desires, and no one may object to Him regarding any of His acts. As for the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), this second interpretation agrees with their doctrine and accords with their belief. As for our companions (the Ash'aris), whoever interprets the verse according to this second interpretation says: "If God did that, He would not be unjust, but it would have the appearance of injustice as we have explained, so He is described as unjust figuratively." The full discussion of these two views is mentioned in Surah Hud at His words: ﴿unjustly while their people are reformers﴾.

* * *

As for His words ﴿*wa-ahluha ghafilun*﴾ ('while their people were unaware'), the meaning of this heedlessness is not that a person neglects what he is admonished with. Rather, its meaning is that God has not made clear to them the nature of their situation, nor removed their excuse and their pretext.

Know that our companions use this verse to establish that obligation does not arise before the revealed law (*shar'*), and that pure reason alone does not indicate obligation at all. They said: "It indicates that God does not punish anyone for any matter except after the sending of a messenger." The Mu'tazila said: "It indicates from another aspect that obligation may be established before the coming of the law, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people were unaware﴾. This injustice is either attributed to the servant or to God, exalted is He. If it is the first, then this indicates the possibility that injustice may proceed from him before the sending of a messenger, and an act is only an injustice before the sending of messengers if it was ugly and a sin before the sending of the messengers, and that is what is sought. If it is the second, then that implies that this act would be ugly from God, exalted is He, and that is not complete except with the acknowledgment that reason makes things good and bad."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 132:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they have done, and your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Ibn ʿĀmir alone recited "taʿmalūna" with the letter tāʾ, in the mode of direct address (khiṭāb), while the rest recited it with the letter yāʾ, in the third-person mode (ghaybah).

The second issue: Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained the conditions of the people of reward and degrees, and the conditions of the people of punishment and deeper levels, He stated a general principle, saying: ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they have done﴾. Concerning the verse there are two opinions:

The first opinion: His saying ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they have done﴾ is general, covering both the obedient and the disobedient. The meaning is: for every doer who acts, there are degrees in his action; at times he is in a deficient degree, and at times he advances from it to a complete degree. And He, may He be exalted, knows them with complete detail, so He assigns to each degree of those degrees the recompense that befits it: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they have done﴾ is specific to the people of obedience, because the word "degree" (darajah) is fitting only for them. And His saying ﴿and your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾ is specific to the people of disbelief and disobedience. The correct view is the first.

The third issue: Know that this verse also indicates the soundness of our view in the question of compulsion (jabr) and divine decree (qadar). That is because He, may He be exalted, judged for each one, at a specific time and according to a specific act, a specific degree, and He knew that very degree precisely, and recorded that specific degree in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and called the ranks of the nearest angels to witness it. So if that degree did not come about for that person, that judgment would be void, that knowledge would become ignorance, and that witnessing would become falsehood; and all of that is impossible. Thus it is established that for all there are degrees according to what they have done, and your Lord is not unaware of what you do. And since the matter is so, the pen has dried over what is to be until the Day of Resurrection, and the happy one is he who was made happy in his mother's womb, and the wretched one is he who was made wretched in his mother's womb.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 133–134 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and make succeed you whom He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.﴾ ﴿What you are promised will surely come, and you cannot escape.﴾

In the verse there are issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the reward of those who obey and the punishment of those who disobey and commit what is forbidden, and mentioned that each group has a specific rank and a determined station, He clarified that the singling out of the obedient for reward and of the sinners for punishment is not because He needs the obedience of the obedient or is diminished by the disobedience of the sinners. He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient in His essence above all the worlds. Yet, despite being Self-Sufficient, His mercy is general and complete. There is no way to arrange these human spirits and human souls and bring them to the ranks of the blessed righteous except by arranging encouragement toward obedience and warning against what is prohibited. So He said: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy.﴾ From His mercy towards creation is the arrangement of reward and punishment for obedience and disobedience. Here we need to explain two matters.

The first: explaining that He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient. We say: He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient in His essence, attributes, actions and judgments, free of everything other than Himself. For if He were in need, He would be perfected by that act, and whoever is perfected by another is deficient in his essence, and that is impossible for Allah. Also, every affirmation or negation that is posited: if His essence is sufficient for its realization, then that affirmation or negation must persist as long as His essence persists. If His essence is not sufficient, then the occurrence of that state and its non-occurrence depend on the existence or non-existence of a separate cause. Then His essence would not be free of that affirmation and negation, and both depend on the existence or non-existence of that separate cause. What depends on something that depends on another thing depends on that thing itself. So it follows that His essence would be dependent on another, and what is dependent on another is contingent in its essence. Thus the Necessary Existent in its essence would be contingent in its essence, and that is impossible. It is established, then, that He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient absolutely.

Know that His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ conveys restriction (*hasr*), meaning: there is no self-sufficient one except Him, and the matter is so, because the Necessary Existent in its essence is one, and everything other than Him is contingent in its essence, and the contingent in its essence is in need. Thus it is established that there is no self-sufficient one except Him. By this decisive proof, the correctness of His, glorified is He, saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ is established.

As for establishing that He is ﴿the Possessor of Mercy﴾, the evidence for it is that there is no doubt about the existence of goods, happiness, pleasures and comforts, whether in terms of bodily conditions or spiritual conditions. It is established by the proof we mentioned that everything other than Him is contingent in its essence, and it enters existence only by His bringing it into being, His creating and fashioning it. Thus it is established that everything that has entered existence of goods, comforts, honours and felicities is from the Truth, glorified is He, and by His bringing it into being and creating it. Then induction shows that good predominates over evil. For the sick, though many, are fewer than the healthy; the hungry, though many, are fewer than the satisfied; the blind, though many, are fewer than the seeing. Thus it is established that there is no escaping acknowledgment of the occurrence of mercy and comfort, and it is established that good is more prevalent than evil, pain and calamity, and it is established that the source of all those comforts and goods is Allah, exalted is He. So by this proof it is established that He, exalted is He, is ﴿the Possessor of Mercy﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy﴾ conveys restriction, for its meaning is: there is no mercy except from Him. The matter is so because what exists is either necessary in its essence or contingent in its essence. The necessary in its essence is one, so everything other than Him is from Him, and mercy falls within what is other than Him. Thus it is established that there is no mercy except from the Truth. By this proof the correctness of this restriction is established. It is established that there is no self-sufficient one except Him, and it is established that there is no merciful one except Him.

If someone says: how can we deny the mercy of parents towards a child, or of a master towards his slave, and likewise all other kinds of mercy?

The answer: all of it, on close examination, is from Allah. The following points show this:

**First:** Had He, exalted is He, not placed in the heart of this merciful one the impulse of mercy, he would not have acted with mercy. Since the one who creates that impulse is Allah, the Merciful is Allah. Do you not see that a person may be extremely angry at someone with a hard heart towards him, then turn gentle, merciful and compassionate? His transformation from the first state to the second is only by the transformation of those impulses. Thus it is established that the Turner of hearts is Allah, exalted is He, by proof, cutting off infinite regress, and by the Qur'an, which is His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes﴾ [Al-An'am: 110]. So it is established that there is no mercy except from Allah.

**Second:** Suppose that merciful one gave food, clothing and gold, yet there is no soundness of temperament and no ability to benefit from those things. Otherwise, how would benefit occur? The one who gave soundness of temperament, power and capacity is, in reality, the Merciful.

**Third:** Everyone who gives something to another gives it for the sake of some return, which is either praise in this world, or reward in the Hereafter, or removing natural tenderness from the heart. But He, exalted is He, gives without any purpose at all. So He is the Merciful, the Generous. Thus, by these certain, definitive, conclusive proofs, the correctness of His, glorified and exalted is He, saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy﴾ is established, in the sense that there is no self-sufficient one and no merciful one except Him. When it is established that He is self-sufficient over all, it follows that He is not perfected by the obedience of the obedient, nor diminished by the sins of the sinners. And when it is established that He is the Possessor of Mercy, it follows that He did not ordain punishment for sins or reward for obedience except for the sake of mercy, bounty, generosity, munificence and kindness, as He said in another verse: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls, and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ [Al-Isra': 7]. This general explanation is sufficient on this topic. As for the detailed explanation of that state and its full clarification, it does not befit this place.

**The second issue:** As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), they said: this verse is an indication of the proof that He is just, free of committing ugliness, and that He is merciful, doing good to His servants. As for the first claim, they said its formulation is: He, exalted is He, knows the ugliness of ugly acts and knows that He is independent of them, and whoever is like this is exalted above committing ugliness.

As for the first premise, its formulation is completed only through a combination of three premises:

The first: among events there are things that are ugly, such as injustice, foolishness, lying and backbiting. This premise is not mentioned in the verse because of its obvious clarity.

The second: that He, exalted is He, is knowing of all knowable things, and the indication of this is His saying before this verse: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾.

The third: that He, exalted is He, is independent of needs, and the indication of this is His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾.

When the combination of these three premises is established, it is established that He, exalted is He, knows the ugliness of ugly acts and knows that He is independent of them. When this is established, it is impossible for Him to be a doer of them, because whoever commits an ugly act does so either out of ignorance of its being ugly or out of need. So if He knows everything, it is impossible for Him to be ignorant of the ugliness of ugly acts. And if He is independent of everything, it is impossible for Him to be in need of committing ugly acts. This indicates that He, exalted is He, is far above committing ugly acts and exalted above them. Then it is certain that He does not wrong anyone. When He assigned His servants arduous acts, it became necessary that He reward them for them. And when He ordained punishment and torment for committing sins, it became necessary that He be just in them. By this path it is established that He, exalted is He, is just in everything.

If someone says: suppose that by this path injustice is negated from Him, exalted is He, what is the benefit of obligation (*taklif*)?

The answer: obligation is a kindness and mercy, as is established in the *Books of Kalam* (*Kutub al-Kalam*). So His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ is an indication of the first station, and His saying ﴿the Possessor of Mercy﴾ is an indication of the second station. This is the explanation of the proofs which groups of intelligent people derived from this verse in support of their position.

Know, my brother, that all of them only seek to sanctify and magnify (Allah). I heard Shaykh the Imam, my father Diya' al-Din Umar ibn al-Husayn, may Allah have mercy on him, say: I heard Shaykh Abu al-Qasim Sulayman ibn Nasir al-Ansari say: Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni school) looked at magnifying Allah in terms of power and the sweeping execution of His will, while the Mu'tazilah looked at magnifying Allah in terms of justice and His freedom from doing what is not fitting. When you reflect, you will know that no one describes Allah except with magnification, honour, sanctification and transcendence. But some of them erred and some of them were correct, and the hope of all of them is attached to this word: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you and make succeed you whom He wills﴾. The meaning is that when He described Himself as the Possessor of Mercy, it might have been possible for someone to suppose that although He is the Possessor of Mercy, His mercy has a specific source and a particular place. So Allah, exalted is He, clarified that He is able to place mercy in other creatures, and able to create another people and place His mercy in them. In this way, His self-sufficiency over the worlds is more complete and perfect. The purpose is to alert that restricting mercy to these people is not because He cannot manifest His mercy except by creating them.

As for His saying ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾, the closest meaning is that it refers to destruction, and it may also refer to causing death, and it may also mean that He does not bring them to the level of obligation. As for His saying ﴿and make succeed you﴾, it means: after your removal, because succession can only occur as a replacement for something that has passed away. As for His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾, it refers to a third and a fourth creation. The scholars differed. Some said: another creation like jinn and humans, who would be more obedient. Abu Muslim said: rather, it means that He is able to create a third creation different from jinn and humans. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this view is closer, because people know by habit that Allah is able to bring into existence the likes of this creation. So when it is understood as a third and a fourth creation, it is stronger in indicating power. It is as if He, exalted is He, alerted that His power is not confined to one kind over another among the creatures who are fit for His great mercy, which is reward. Thus He made clear by this path that, out of His mercy towards these present people, He kept them and granted them respite, and if He willed, He would have caused them to die, destroyed them, and replaced them with others. Then He, exalted is He, clarified the reason for His power over that by saying: ﴿just as He produced you from the descendants of another people﴾. For when a rational person reflects, he knows that Allah, exalted is He, created the human from a drop of semen in which there is no trace of his form, little or much. So it must be that this is by sheer power and wisdom. And if the matter is so, then just as Allah, exalted is He, was able to shape these bodies in this specific form, likewise He is able to shape them in a form different from it.

All the reciters read *dhurriyyati* (ذُرِّيَّةِ) with a *damma* on the *dhal* (ذُرِّيَّةِ), while Zayd ibn Thabit read it with a *kasra* on the *dhal* (ذِرِّيَّةِ). Al-Kisa'i said: both are dialectal variants (*lughatan*).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape it.﴾ Al-Hasan said: that is, the coming of the Hour, because they used to deny the Resurrection. I say there is another possibility in this: that the promise (al-wa'd) is specific to the announcement of reward, whereas the threat (al-wa'id) is specific to the announcement of punishment. So His saying ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming﴾ means that everything connected with the promise of reward is certainly coming without doubt. The specification of the promise with this certainty indicates that the side of the threat is not like that. This interpretation is reinforced by the end of the verse, where He says: ﴿and you cannot escape Us﴾, meaning you will not get out of Our power and Our judgment. The conclusion is that when He mentioned the promise, He affirmed with certainty that it is coming, and when He mentioned the threat, He added nothing beyond His saying ﴿and you cannot escape Us﴾. This indicates that the side of mercy and kindness is dominant.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 133–134 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and make succeed you whom He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.﴾ ﴿What you are promised will surely come, and you cannot escape.﴾

In the verse there are issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the reward of those who obey and the punishment of those who disobey and commit what is forbidden, and mentioned that each group has a specific rank and a determined station, He clarified that the singling out of the obedient for reward and of the sinners for punishment is not because He needs the obedience of the obedient or is diminished by the disobedience of the sinners. He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient in His essence above all the worlds. Yet, despite being Self-Sufficient, His mercy is general and complete. There is no way to arrange these human spirits and human souls and bring them to the ranks of the blessed righteous except by arranging encouragement toward obedience and warning against what is prohibited. So He said: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy.﴾ From His mercy towards creation is the arrangement of reward and punishment for obedience and disobedience. Here we need to explain two matters.

The first: explaining that He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient. We say: He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient in His essence, attributes, actions and judgments, free of everything other than Himself. For if He were in need, He would be perfected by that act, and whoever is perfected by another is deficient in his essence, and that is impossible for Allah. Also, every affirmation or negation that is posited: if His essence is sufficient for its realization, then that affirmation or negation must persist as long as His essence persists. If His essence is not sufficient, then the occurrence of that state and its non-occurrence depend on the existence or non-existence of a separate cause. Then His essence would not be free of that affirmation and negation, and both depend on the existence or non-existence of that separate cause. What depends on something that depends on another thing depends on that thing itself. So it follows that His essence would be dependent on another, and what is dependent on another is contingent in its essence. Thus the Necessary Existent in its essence would be contingent in its essence, and that is impossible. It is established, then, that He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient absolutely.

Know that His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ conveys restriction (*hasr*), meaning: there is no self-sufficient one except Him, and the matter is so, because the Necessary Existent in its essence is one, and everything other than Him is contingent in its essence, and the contingent in its essence is in need. Thus it is established that there is no self-sufficient one except Him. By this decisive proof, the correctness of His, glorified is He, saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ is established.

As for establishing that He is ﴿the Possessor of Mercy﴾, the evidence for it is that there is no doubt about the existence of goods, happiness, pleasures and comforts, whether in terms of bodily conditions or spiritual conditions. It is established by the proof we mentioned that everything other than Him is contingent in its essence, and it enters existence only by His bringing it into being, His creating and fashioning it. Thus it is established that everything that has entered existence of goods, comforts, honours and felicities is from the Truth, glorified is He, and by His bringing it into being and creating it. Then induction shows that good predominates over evil. For the sick, though many, are fewer than the healthy; the hungry, though many, are fewer than the satisfied; the blind, though many, are fewer than the seeing. Thus it is established that there is no escaping acknowledgment of the occurrence of mercy and comfort, and it is established that good is more prevalent than evil, pain and calamity, and it is established that the source of all those comforts and goods is Allah, exalted is He. So by this proof it is established that He, exalted is He, is ﴿the Possessor of Mercy﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy﴾ conveys restriction, for its meaning is: there is no mercy except from Him. The matter is so because what exists is either necessary in its essence or contingent in its essence. The necessary in its essence is one, so everything other than Him is from Him, and mercy falls within what is other than Him. Thus it is established that there is no mercy except from the Truth. By this proof the correctness of this restriction is established. It is established that there is no self-sufficient one except Him, and it is established that there is no merciful one except Him.

If someone says: how can we deny the mercy of parents towards a child, or of a master towards his slave, and likewise all other kinds of mercy?

The answer: all of it, on close examination, is from Allah. The following points show this:

**First:** Had He, exalted is He, not placed in the heart of this merciful one the impulse of mercy, he would not have acted with mercy. Since the one who creates that impulse is Allah, the Merciful is Allah. Do you not see that a person may be extremely angry at someone with a hard heart towards him, then turn gentle, merciful and compassionate? His transformation from the first state to the second is only by the transformation of those impulses. Thus it is established that the Turner of hearts is Allah, exalted is He, by proof, cutting off infinite regress, and by the Qur'an, which is His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes﴾ [Al-An'am: 110]. So it is established that there is no mercy except from Allah.

**Second:** Suppose that merciful one gave food, clothing and gold, yet there is no soundness of temperament and no ability to benefit from those things. Otherwise, how would benefit occur? The one who gave soundness of temperament, power and capacity is, in reality, the Merciful.

**Third:** Everyone who gives something to another gives it for the sake of some return, which is either praise in this world, or reward in the Hereafter, or removing natural tenderness from the heart. But He, exalted is He, gives without any purpose at all. So He is the Merciful, the Generous. Thus, by these certain, definitive, conclusive proofs, the correctness of His, glorified and exalted is He, saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy﴾ is established, in the sense that there is no self-sufficient one and no merciful one except Him. When it is established that He is self-sufficient over all, it follows that He is not perfected by the obedience of the obedient, nor diminished by the sins of the sinners. And when it is established that He is the Possessor of Mercy, it follows that He did not ordain punishment for sins or reward for obedience except for the sake of mercy, bounty, generosity, munificence and kindness, as He said in another verse: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls, and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ [Al-Isra': 7]. This general explanation is sufficient on this topic. As for the detailed explanation of that state and its full clarification, it does not befit this place.

**The second issue:** As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), they said: this verse is an indication of the proof that He is just, free of committing ugliness, and that He is merciful, doing good to His servants. As for the first claim, they said its formulation is: He, exalted is He, knows the ugliness of ugly acts and knows that He is independent of them, and whoever is like this is exalted above committing ugliness.

As for the first premise, its formulation is completed only through a combination of three premises:

The first: among events there are things that are ugly, such as injustice, foolishness, lying and backbiting. This premise is not mentioned in the verse because of its obvious clarity.

The second: that He, exalted is He, is knowing of all knowable things, and the indication of this is His saying before this verse: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾.

The third: that He, exalted is He, is independent of needs, and the indication of this is His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾.

When the combination of these three premises is established, it is established that He, exalted is He, knows the ugliness of ugly acts and knows that He is independent of them. When this is established, it is impossible for Him to be a doer of them, because whoever commits an ugly act does so either out of ignorance of its being ugly or out of need. So if He knows everything, it is impossible for Him to be ignorant of the ugliness of ugly acts. And if He is independent of everything, it is impossible for Him to be in need of committing ugly acts. This indicates that He, exalted is He, is far above committing ugly acts and exalted above them. Then it is certain that He does not wrong anyone. When He assigned His servants arduous acts, it became necessary that He reward them for them. And when He ordained punishment and torment for committing sins, it became necessary that He be just in them. By this path it is established that He, exalted is He, is just in everything.

If someone says: suppose that by this path injustice is negated from Him, exalted is He, what is the benefit of obligation (*taklif*)?

The answer: obligation is a kindness and mercy, as is established in the *Books of Kalam* (*Kutub al-Kalam*). So His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ is an indication of the first station, and His saying ﴿the Possessor of Mercy﴾ is an indication of the second station. This is the explanation of the proofs which groups of intelligent people derived from this verse in support of their position.

Know, my brother, that all of them only seek to sanctify and magnify (Allah). I heard Shaykh the Imam, my father Diya' al-Din Umar ibn al-Husayn, may Allah have mercy on him, say: I heard Shaykh Abu al-Qasim Sulayman ibn Nasir al-Ansari say: Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni school) looked at magnifying Allah in terms of power and the sweeping execution of His will, while the Mu'tazilah looked at magnifying Allah in terms of justice and His freedom from doing what is not fitting. When you reflect, you will know that no one describes Allah except with magnification, honour, sanctification and transcendence. But some of them erred and some of them were correct, and the hope of all of them is attached to this word: ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you and make succeed you whom He wills﴾. The meaning is that when He described Himself as the Possessor of Mercy, it might have been possible for someone to suppose that although He is the Possessor of Mercy, His mercy has a specific source and a particular place. So Allah, exalted is He, clarified that He is able to place mercy in other creatures, and able to create another people and place His mercy in them. In this way, His self-sufficiency over the worlds is more complete and perfect. The purpose is to alert that restricting mercy to these people is not because He cannot manifest His mercy except by creating them.

As for His saying ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾, the closest meaning is that it refers to destruction, and it may also refer to causing death, and it may also mean that He does not bring them to the level of obligation. As for His saying ﴿and make succeed you﴾, it means: after your removal, because succession can only occur as a replacement for something that has passed away. As for His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾, it refers to a third and a fourth creation. The scholars differed. Some said: another creation like jinn and humans, who would be more obedient. Abu Muslim said: rather, it means that He is able to create a third creation different from jinn and humans. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this view is closer, because people know by habit that Allah is able to bring into existence the likes of this creation. So when it is understood as a third and a fourth creation, it is stronger in indicating power. It is as if He, exalted is He, alerted that His power is not confined to one kind over another among the creatures who are fit for His great mercy, which is reward. Thus He made clear by this path that, out of His mercy towards these present people, He kept them and granted them respite, and if He willed, He would have caused them to die, destroyed them, and replaced them with others. Then He, exalted is He, clarified the reason for His power over that by saying: ﴿just as He produced you from the descendants of another people﴾. For when a rational person reflects, he knows that Allah, exalted is He, created the human from a drop of semen in which there is no trace of his form, little or much. So it must be that this is by sheer power and wisdom. And if the matter is so, then just as Allah, exalted is He, was able to shape these bodies in this specific form, likewise He is able to shape them in a form different from it.
