Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape it.﴾ Al-Hasan said: that is, the coming of the Hour, because they used to deny the Resurrection. I say there is another possibility in this: that the promise (al-wa'd) is specific to the announcement of reward, whereas the threat (al-wa'id) is specific to the announcement of punishment. So His saying ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming﴾ means that everything connected with the promise of reward is certainly coming without doubt. The specification of the promise with this certainty indicates that the side of the threat is not like that. This interpretation is reinforced by the end of the verse, where He says: ﴿and you cannot escape Us﴾, meaning you will not get out of Our power and Our judgment. The conclusion is that when He mentioned the promise, He affirmed with certainty that it is coming, and when He mentioned the threat, He added nothing beyond His saying ﴿and you cannot escape Us﴾. This indicates that the side of mercy and kindness is dominant.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 135:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your station; indeed I am acting. So you will come to know to whom the ultimate abode belongs. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾

Know that when He mentioned, by His saying ﴿What you are promised is surely coming﴾, He commanded His Messenger, after that, to threaten those disbelievers who deny the Resurrection. So He said: ﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your station"﴾. In this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "makanatikum" (مَكاناتِكم) with an alif, in the plural form throughout the Qur'an, while the others read "ʿala makanatikum" (عَلى مَكانَتِكم). al-Wahidi said: the preferred form is the singular, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and verbal nouns are mostly singular, though they may sometimes also be pluralized; but the more common is the first.

The second discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf said: makanah may be a verbal noun, as in one says "makana makanah" when one becomes firmly established to the utmost degree; and it may mean "place," as in one says makan and makanah, and muqam and muqamah. So His saying ﴿act according to your station﴾ may mean: act according to your firm establishment in your affair and your utmost ability and capacity. It may also mean: act according to your state in which you are; one says to a man who is commanded to remain in a certain state: "Stay on your station, O so-and-so," meaning, remain upon what you are upon and do not deviate from it. ﴿Indeed I am acting﴾, that is, I am acting according to my station upon which I am. The meaning is: remain steadfast in your disbelief and enmity, for I am steadfast upon Islam and upon harming you. ﴿So you will come to know﴾ which of us will have the praiseworthy outcome. The manner of this command is like His saying: ﴿Do what you wish﴾, and it is the delegation of the matter to them by way of threat.

The third discussion: Concerning "man" in His saying ﴿So you will come to know to whom the ultimate abode belongs﴾, al-Farra' mentioned two possibilities regarding its grammatical position (iʿrab):

First: it is in the accusative, since knowledge falls upon it.

Second: it is in the nominative, meaning: you will know which of us the ultimate abode will belong to, like His saying: ﴿that We may know which of the two parties﴾ [al-Kahf: 12].

The fourth discussion: His saying ﴿So you will come to know to whom the ultimate abode belongs﴾ may give the impression that the disbeliever does not have the ultimate abode, and this is problematic.

We say: the outcome may be "upon" the disbeliever rather than "to" him, just as one says "lahum al-kathrah wa lahum al-zafar" (for them is the majority and for them is victory), and in the opposite case one says "ʿalaykum al-kathrah wa al-zafar" (upon you is the majority and victory).

The fifth discussion: Hamzah and al-Kisai read "man yakun" (مَن يَكُونُ) with the yaʾ, and also in Surah al-Qasas, while the others read it with the taʾ in both surahs. al-Wahidi said: ʿaqibah is a verbal noun like ʿafiyah, and its feminine marking is not real (ghayr haqiqi). So whoever uses the feminine form, it is like His saying: ﴿so the Cry seized them﴾ [al-Hijr: 73], and whoever uses the masculine form, it is like His saying: ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾ [Hud: 67]; and He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ [Yunus: 57], and in another verse: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾, and the purpose of it is to clarify that His saying ﴿act according to your station﴾ is a threat and an intimidation, not a command and a request. Its meaning is: these disbelievers will not succeed, nor will they attain their aims at all.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 136:

"And they assign to Allah a share of what He has created of crops and livestock, and they say, 'This is for Allah, by their claim, and this is for our partners.' So what is for their partners does not reach Allah, but what is for Allah reaches their partners. Evil is what they judge." ﴿Wa-ja'alū li-Llāhi mimmā dhara'a mina al-ḥarthi wa-al-an'āmi naṣīban fa-qālū hādhā li-Llāhi bi-zaʿmihim wa-hādhā li-shurakā'inā fa-mā kāna li-shurakā'ihim fa-lā yaṣilu ilā Llāhi wa-mā kāna li-Llāhi fa-huwa yaṣilu ilā shurakā'ihim sā'a mā yaḥkumūn﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the ugliness of their way in denying the resurrection and the Last Day, He then mentioned, following it, various kinds of their ignorance and the feebleness of their statements, as a warning about the weakness of their minds and the scantiness of their understanding, and as a deterrent to intelligent people from paying attention to their words. Among these is that they assign to Allah a portion of their crops, such as dates and wheat, and of their livestock, such as sheep, goats, camels and cattle. They said: ﴿This is for Allah, by their claim﴾, meaning by their lie.

If it is said: Is it not the case that all things belong to Allah? How, then, are they accused of lying in their saying "This is for Allah"?

We say: Their setting apart the two portions, one portion for Allah and one portion for Satan, is the lie. Al-Zajjaj said: The sense of the sentence is "They assigned to Allah a portion and to their partners a portion," and this omitted part is indicated by the detailed statement of the two divisions that follows, namely His saying: ﴿This is for Allah, by their claim, and this is for our partners.﴾ He called the idols their partners because they assigned them a portion of their wealth, which they spent upon them.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So what is for their partners does not reach Allah, but what is for Allah reaches their partners.﴾ There are several interpretations of this:

First: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The polytheists would assign to Allah a portion of their crops and livestock, and to the idols a portion. What was for the idol they spent upon it, and what was for Allah they gave to the children and the needy, and they never ate from it at all. Then, if something fell from what they had assigned to Allah into the portion of the idols, they left it and said: "Allah is free of need of this." But if something fell from what they had assigned to the idols into the portion of Allah, they took it back and returned it to the portion of the idol, and said: "It (the idol) is poor."

Second: Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: Whenever the property of their idols was lost, they would take in its place from what belonged to Allah, and they would not do the like with what belonged to Allah, mighty and majestic.

Third: Mujahid said: The meaning is that when what they had assigned to Satan in the portion of Allah was flooded by irrigation, they would block it up, and if it was the opposite, they would leave it.

Fourth: Qatada said: When drought struck them, they would make use of what belonged to Allah and spare what they had assigned to their partners.

Fifth: Muqatil said: If the portion of the gods grew and increased while the portion of Allah did not grow, they would leave the portion of the gods to them, and say: "If He had willed, He would have made His own portion grow." And if the portion of Allah grew while the portion of the gods did not, they would say: "Our gods must have provision," and they would take the portion of Allah and give it to the keepers (al-sadana, the attendants of the shrines). This is His saying: ﴿So what is for their partners﴾, meaning from the increase of the crops and livestock, ﴿does not reach Allah﴾, meaning the needy. He said "reach Allah" only because they used to set it apart for Allah and call it "the portion of Allah." And what was for Allah reaches them. Then Allah condemned this act, saying: ﴿Evil is what they judge.﴾ The scholars mentioned many aspects of this evil:

First: They preferred the side of the idols in care and protection over the side of Allah, the Exalted, and this is folly.

Second: They assigned part of the portion to Allah and part to other than Him, although He is the Creator of all, and this too is folly.

Third: That ruling is one they invented on their own, for which neither reason nor revelation bore witness to its soundness, and so it too was folly.

Fourth: If setting apart a portion for the idols were good, then setting apart a portion for every stone and clod would be good.

Fifth: The idols have no influence in producing crops and livestock, and they have no power to benefit from that portion either, so setting apart a portion for them was pointless. Thus it is established by these aspects that it is ﴿evil is what they judge﴾. The purpose in relating such corrupt doctrines is that people should know the scantiness of the intellects of those who hold these doctrines, that this should become a cause of their being despised in the eyes of intelligent people, and that no one should pay attention to their speech at all.

The Words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus have their partner-gods made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children, to bring about their destruction and to confuse them regarding their religion. And had Allah willed, they would not have done so; so leave them and what they invent.﴾

Page 169

Concerning the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is the second category of their corrupt rulings and their false doctrines. His words "And thus" (wa-kadhalika) are conjoined to His words: ﴿And they assign to Allah a share of what He has created of crops and livestock﴾. That is, just as they did that, so likewise their partner-gods made the killing of children attractive to many of them. The meaning is that their assigning a share to Allah and a share to the partners is the utmost in ignorance of the knowing Creator and Benefactor, and their undertaking to kill their own children is the utmost in folly and misguidance. This indicates an admonition that their rulings and conditions resemble one another in their baseness and vileness.

The second issue: The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) used to bury their daughters alive, out of fear of poverty or out of fear of marrying them off, and this is what is meant by this verse. They differed over the meaning of "the partners." Mujahid said: "Their partners are their devils, who commanded them to bury their children out of fear of destitution. The devils were called partners because they obeyed them in disobedience to Allah the Exalted, and the partners were attributed to them because they had taken them, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾" Al-Kalbi said: "Their gods had custodians and attendants, and they were the ones who used to make the killing of their children attractive to the disbelievers. A man would stand up in the Jahiliyyah and swear by Allah: 'If a son of such-and-such number is born to me, I will surely slaughter one of them,' just as Abd al-Muttalib swore concerning his son Abdullah." According to this view, the "partners" are the custodians, and they were named partners just as the devils were named partners in the saying of Mujahid.

The third issue: Ibn Amir alone recited "zuyyina" with a damma on the zay and a kasra on the ya, and with a damma on the lam of "qatlu" and with "awlādahum" in the accusative, and "shurakā'ihim" in the genitive. The others recited "zayyana" with a fatha on the zay and the ya, "qatla" with a fatha on the lam, "awlādihim" in the genitive, and "shurakā'uhum" in the nominative. As for the reasoning behind Ibn Amir's recitation, the intended sense is: "The killing of their partners' children was made attractive to many of the polytheists," except that he separated the genitive construct and its genitive complement by the direct object, which is "the children." This is disliked even in poetry, as in the verse of the poet:

"So I thrust her with a thrust, like the thrust of the she-camel, the father of Mazadah."

If it is disliked in poetry, how much more so in the Qur'an, which is inimitable in eloquence. They said: "What led Ibn Amir to this recitation is that he saw in some of the codices 'shurakā'ihim' written with a ya. Had he recited with the genitive for both 'the children' and 'the partners,' on the grounds that the children are their partners in their wealth, he would have found an alternative to this irregularity." As for the well-known recitation, it contains only the fronting of the object before the subject, and its parallel is His words: ﴿The faith of a soul will not benefit it﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and His words: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. The reason for fronting the object is that they put first what is more important, and what they are concerned with is more significant; the point of astonishment here is their undertaking to kill their own children, and for this reason this construction arose.

Then He, the Exalted, said: "to bring about their destruction" (liyurduhum). Al-irda' in the lexicon means destruction, and in the Qur'an: ﴿You nearly brought me to ruin﴾ [al-Saffat: 56]. Ibn Abbas said: "To bring them to destruction in the Fire." The lam here is understood as the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), as in His words: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. And ﴿and to confuse them regarding their religion﴾ [al-An'am: 137], meaning, to mix it up; for they were upon the religion of Isma'il, so this one who brought them these corrupt conditions intended to turn them away from that true religion.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done so.﴾ Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: this indicates that everything the polytheists did occurs by the will of Allah, the Exalted. The Mu'tazilah said: it is to be understood as the will of compulsion (mashi'at al-ilja'), and its mention has preceded many times. ﴿So leave them and what they invent⦆

Page 170

(they invent). This is according to the principle of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Do whatever you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. And His words: ﴿and what they invent﴾ indicate that they used to say that Allah had commanded them to kill their children, and so they were liars in that claim.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 138:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "These are livestock and tilth, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we will," by their assertion; and there are livestock whose backs are forbidden, and livestock over which they do not mention the name of Allah, fabricating against Him. He will recompense them for what they used to invent.﴾

Know that this is a third category of their corrupt rulings. They divided their livestock into categories. The first of them is that they said: ﴿These are livestock and tilth, forbidden (ḥijr)﴾. The word ḥijr here is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), like dhibḥ (slaughter) and ṭaḥn (grinding). In describing with it, the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural are alike, because its ruling is that of nouns rather than adjectives. The root meaning of ḥijr is prohibition, and the intellect is called ḥijr because it prevents one from vile deeds. And one says "Fulān is in the ḥijr of the judge," meaning in his protection. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah read ḥujr with a ḍammah on the ḥā'. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbās: ḥaraj, which derives from constriction. When they designated something of their tilth and livestock for their idols, they said: ﴿none may eat of them except whom we will﴾, meaning the servants of the idols, and men to the exclusion of women.

The second category of their livestock, of which they said: ﴿and there are livestock whose backs are forbidden﴾, are the baḥīrah, the sawā'ib and the ḥawāmī, and its explanation has passed in Surat al-Mā'idah.

The third category: ﴿and livestock over which they do not mention the name of Allah﴾ at slaughter; rather they mention over them the names of the idols. It has also been said that they do not perform Ḥajj upon them, nor do they recite the talbiyah upon their backs.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿fabricating against Him﴾. Its accusative case is either as an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), or as an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad), because their saying that is in the sense of fabrication.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will recompense them for what they used to invent﴾, and the purpose of it is a warning (waʿīd).

**Verse 139:** "And they say: 'What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our females; but if it is stillborn, then they all share in it.' He will surely recompense them for their attribution. Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing."

(Page 171)

There are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** This is a fourth category of their corrupt customs. They used to say that regarding the fetuses of the *bahair* (she-camels whose ears were slit, a practice of the pre-Islamic Arabs) and the *sawa'ib* (camels set free for their gods), whatever was born alive was exclusively for the males, and females could not eat from it. Whatever was born dead, males and females shared in it. ﴿He will surely recompense them for their attribution﴾: what is meant is a threat. ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾, so that the rebuke falls in accordance with wisdom and in proportion to what they deserve.

**The second issue:** Ibn al-Anbari mentioned three opinions regarding the feminine form of *khalisah* (exclusively): two from al-Farra' and one from al-Kisa'i.

First: the *ha'* (tā' marbūṭah) is not a marker of feminine gender but serves to intensify the description, as they say *rawiyah* (great transmitter), *allamah* (very learned), *nassabah* (expert in genealogies), *al-dahiyah* (the calamity), and *al-taghiyah* (the tyrant). Similarly one says: "He is *khalisah* to me" and "He is *khalis* to me." This is the opinion of al-Kisa'i.

The second opinion: the word *ma* (what) in His saying ﴿what is in the wombs of these cattle﴾ refers to fetuses. When it refers to something feminine, it is permissible to make its predicate feminine according to meaning and masculine according to the wording, as in this verse: its predicate, which is *khalisah*, is feminine in accordance with its meaning, while in His saying *muharram* (forbidden) it is masculine in accordance with the wording.

The third: that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the implied construction is *dhu khalisah* (possessing exclusivity), as they say: "Your gift is well-being (*afiyah*), rain is mercy (*rahmah*), and cheap prices are blessing (*ni'mah*)."

**The third issue:** Ibn Amir recited ﴿wa-in takun﴾ with a *ta'* (feminine verb), and *maytatan* (dead) in the accusative. Ibn Kathir recited *yakun* with a *ya'* (masculine verb) and *maytatun* in the nominative. Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, recited *takun* with a *ta'* and *maytatan* in the accusative. The rest recited *yakun* with a *ya'* and *maytatan* in the accusative.

As for the recitation of Ibn Amir, its justification is that he attached the feminine marker to the verb because the subject was feminine in wording.

As for the recitation of Ibn Kathir, its justification is that His saying *maytatun* is the subject of *yakun*, and its predicate is implied: the meaning is "if there is for them a dead one (*maytatun*)," or "if there is there a dead one." It is masculine because *maytatah* carries the meaning of *mayyit* (dead male).

Abu Ali said: the verb was not given the feminine marker because the subject it is attributed to has a non-real feminine gender, and *kawn* (being) does not need a predicate, since it has the meaning of *hadatha* (happened) and *waqa'a* (occurred).

As for the recitation of Asim, *takun* with a *ta'* and *maytatan* in the accusative, the implied meaning is: "if the thing mentioned be *maytatan* (a dead one)." He made the verb feminine for this reason.

As for the recitation of the rest, *wa-in yakun* with a *ya'* and *maytatan* in the accusative, its interpretation is: "if the thing mentioned be *maytatan*." They made the verb masculine because it is attributed to a pronoun referring to what precedes in His saying ﴿what is in the wombs of these cattle﴾, which is masculine. The word *maytatan* is in the accusative because the verb is attributed to the pronoun.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 140:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those have lost who killed their children in foolishness without knowledge, and made unlawful what Allah had provided them, inventing a lie against Allah. They have certainly gone astray, and they were not guided.﴾

There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: He, exalted is He, mentioned earlier their killing of their children and their making unlawful what Allah had provided them. Then He combined these two matters in this verse and explained what follows from this ruling, namely loss (khusran), foolishness (safahah), lack of knowledge, the making unlawful of what Allah had provided, fabricating against Allah, going astray, and not being guided. These are seven matters, and each one of them is by itself a complete cause for blame.

As for the first, which is loss: this is because a child is a great blessing from Allah upon the servant. So when he strives to eliminate it, he has lost a great loss, especially since he deserves, for that elimination, great blame in this world and great punishment in the Hereafter. As for the blame in this world, it is because people say, "He killed his child out of fear that the child would eat his food," and there is no blame in this world more severe than this. As for the punishment in the Hereafter, it is because the bond of parenthood is among the greatest causes of love. So when love is present and he proceeds to inflict the greatest harm upon him, that is among the greatest kinds of sins, and so it necessitates the greatest kinds of punishment.

The second kind: safahah, which is an expression for blameworthy levity. This is because killing a child only occurs out of fear of poverty, and although poverty is a harm, killing is greater harm than it. Also, this killing is immediate, whereas that poverty is imagined. So committing the greatest harms with certainty out of caution against a small, imagined harm is without doubt foolishness.

The third kind: His saying, ﴿without knowledge﴾. The meaning is that this foolishness only arose from lack of knowledge, and there is no doubt that ignorance is among the greatest abominations and ugly deeds.

The fourth kind: the making unlawful of what Allah has made lawful for them. This is also among the greatest kinds of folly, because it deprives oneself of those benefits and good things, and by that deprivation it merits the greatest kinds of torment and punishment.

The fifth kind: fabricating against Allah. It is well known that audacity against Allah and fabrication against Him are among the greatest sins and the gravest major sins.

The sixth kind: going astray from right guidance regarding the interests of religion and the benefits of this world.

The seventh kind: that they were not guided. The benefit in this is that a person may go astray from the truth, unless he returns to guidance. So He, exalted is He, explained that they had gone astray and guidance had never been attained by them at all. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, blamed those described as killing children and making unlawful what Allah, exalted is He, had made lawful for them, with these seven attributes which necessitate the greatest kinds of blame, and that is the utmost degree of emphasis.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised, and the palm trees and crops of diverse fruit, and the olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not love the excessive.﴾

Page 173

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, made the foundation of this noble Book rest upon establishing tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, the resurrection (al-ma'ad), and affirming qada' and qadar (divine decree and predestination). He, exalted is He, dwelt at length on establishing these principles, and the discourse reached the description of the states of the blessed and the wretched. Then it moved from that to disparaging the way of those who denied resurrection and the Last Day. Then it followed this with relating their weak sayings and corrupt statements on four issues. The purpose was to alert to the feebleness of their intellects and the scantiness of their attainments, and to deter people from giving heed to their words and from being deceived by their dubious claims. When He had completed these matters, He returned after them to what was the original purpose, namely, establishing the proofs for affirming tawhid, and so He said: ﴿It is He who produces gardens, trellised…﴾.

Know that this proof has already been mentioned in this surah, namely His saying: ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth by it the growth of every thing, and We bring forth from it green [foliage], from which We bring forth grain piled up; and from the palm trees, from their pollen, are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapevines, and the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar. Look at their fruit when they bear fruit and [at] its ripening. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

In the earlier verse, He mentioned five kinds: the crops, the palm trees, the gardens of grapes, the olive, and the pomegranate. In this verse that we are explaining, He mentioned these same five, but in a different order, for He mentioned the grapes, then the palm trees, then the crops, then the olive, then the pomegranate. In the earlier verse He said ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾ (mushtabihan wa-ghayra mutashabih), and in this verse ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾ (mutashabihan wa-ghayra mutashabih). Then in the earlier verse He said ﴿Look at their fruit when they bear fruit and [at] its ripening﴾, so He there commanded contemplation of their conditions and inference from them to the existence of the Wise Creator. In this verse He said ﴿Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾, so He permitted benefiting from them and commanded that a portion of them be given to the poor. The distinction between the two verses is that there He commanded inference from them to the Wise Creator, and here He permitted benefit from them. This is an alert that commanding inference from them to the Wise Creator takes precedence over permission to benefit from them, because what results from inference from them is an everlasting spiritual happiness, whereas what results from benefiting from these is a bodily happiness that quickly passes away. The former is more deserving of precedence, and therefore God, exalted is He, placed the command to infer from them before the permission to benefit from them.

The second issue: His saying ﴿It is He who produces﴾ (anshaa) means "created." It is said: "the thing grew" (nasha'a al-shay'u yansha'u nash'atan wa-nash'a'a) when it appeared and rose up, and God "produces it" (yunshi'uhu inshaa'an), that is, makes it appear and raises it. His saying ﴿gardens, trellised﴾ (jannatin ma'rushat): it is said "I trellised the vine" ('arrashtu al-karma u'arrishuhu 'arshan, wa-'arrashtuhu ta'rishan) when you bend the sticks upon which the vine shoots are let to run. The singular is 'arsh, the plural 'urush; it is also said 'arish, whose plural is 'urush (sic: 'uruṣh). And "the grapevine climbed the trellis" (i'tara'a al-'inabu al-'arisha i'tirashan) when it rose over it.

Having understood this, we say: concerning His saying ﴿trellised and untrellised﴾ there are several opinions. First: the trellised and the untrellised are both the vine, for some grapes are trellised and some are not, but remain spread out over the surface of the earth. Second: the trellised are the grapes for which trellises are made, and the untrellised are everything that grows spread out over the surface of the earth, such as pumpkins and watermelons. Third: the trellised are those that need a trellis to be made for them on which they are carried and which holds them up, namely the vine and what is similar to it; the untrellised is the upright tree which, through the evenness of its growth and its rising high owing to the strength of its trunk, is independent of trellising. Fourth: the trellised are those found in orchards and inhabited areas, of what people plant and attend to, so they trellis it; and "untrellised" are those which God, exalted is He, caused to grow wild in the deserts and mountains, so it is untrellised. His saying:

Page 174

﴿and the palm trees and crops﴾: Ibn 'Abbas explained "crops" here as all the grains that are used for food. ﴿diverse fruit (mukhtalifan ukuluhu)﴾: that is, each of them has a taste different from the taste of the other. "Ukul" (produce, what is eaten) is everything that is eaten, and here what is meant is the fruit of the palm and the crops. The discussion of "ukul" has passed at His saying ﴿it yielded its produce doubled﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265]. His saying "mukhtalifan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal): that is, He produced it in a state of diversity of its produce, and He had produced it before the appearance of its produce and the produce of its fruit.

The answer: He produced them in the state of diversity of their fruit, and the truth of this does not conflict with the truth that He produced them before that as well. Also, it is in the accusative as a state, although it is eaten after a period of time, because the diversity of its produce is anticipated, just as you say: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow," meaning, intended for hunting with it tomorrow. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read "ukluhu" with the kaf lightened, and the rest read "ukuluhu" throughout the Qur'an. As for the singular pronoun in His saying ﴿diverse its produce﴾, the reason is that He was content with mentioning one of the two rather than repeating it for both together, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they scatter toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], meaning "toward them both," and His saying ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

* * *

As for His saying ﴿similar and dissimilar﴾ (mutashabihan wa-ghayra mutashabih), its explanation has already passed in the earlier verse.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit﴾, and concerning this there are discussions.

The first discussion: when He mentioned how He created these things, He mentioned the essential purpose of creating them, which is the benefit of the responsible persons from them, so He said ﴿Eat of their fruit﴾. They differed about what the benefit of it is. Some said: permission. Others said: rather, the purpose of it is the permission to eat before the right (haqq) is given out, because when He made the right obligatory in it, it would have been permissible for Him to forbid the owner from consuming it on account of the poor having a share in it; rather, this is the apparent meaning. So God, exalted is He, permitted this eating, and the obligation of the right in it was removed from being a hindrance to this disposal. Some said: rather, God permitted that to show that the aim in creating these blessings is either eating or giving in charity, and He mentioned eating before charity because the preservation of the self takes precedence over the preservation of others. God said: ﴿And do not forget your portion of the world, and do good as God has done good to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 77].

The second discussion: some have held, citing His saying ﴿Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit﴾, that the basic principle regarding benefits is permissibility and freedom (al-ibahah wa-al-ițlaq), because His saying "eat" (kulu) is a general address that embraces everyone, so this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth﴾. Also, it is possible to cite it for the principle that the basic position is the non-obligation of charity, and whoever claims its obligation is the one needing proof. Therefore it is cited regarding a madman who regains his sanity in the middle of the month, that he is not obliged to make up what has passed, and regarding one who begins a voluntary fast, that he is not obliged to complete it.

The third discussion: His saying ﴿Eat of their fruit﴾ indicates that the form of command may occur in a context other than obligation and other than recommendation. At this point some said: the basic principle in usage is the literal meaning, so this form must be taken to convey the lifting of prohibition; for this reason they said: the command implies permissibility. However, we say: we know necessarily from the language of the Arabs that this form conveys preferring the doing of the act, and that taking it to mean permissibility is not resorted to except with a separate indication.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "hasadihi" (harvest) with a fathah on the ha', and the rest with a kasrah on the ha'.

Page 175

al-Wahidi said: all the lexicographers say: hasad and hisad, jadad and jidad, qitaf and qitaf, judhadh and jidhadh. Sibawayh said: they used the verbal nouns when they wanted to denote the time of the action, on the pattern fa'al, and sometimes they said fi'al for it.

The second discussion: concerning the interpretation of His saying ﴿and give its due﴾ there are three opinions:

The first opinion: Ibn 'Abbas, in the transmission of 'Ata', said that it means the tenth of what the sky waters, and half the tenth of what is irrigated by water-wheels. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, Tawus and al-Dahhak.

If they say: how can one pay zakat on the day of harvest when the grain is still in the ear? And also, this surah is Meccan, and the imposition of zakat is Medinan.

We say: since applying His saying ﴿and give its due﴾ according to its apparent meaning is impossible on account of the proof you have mentioned, we therefore take it to mean that the right of zakat becomes attached to it at that time; the meaning is: resolve to give the right on the day of harvest, and do not delay it beyond the first time at which giving is possible.

As for the answer to the second question: we do not concede that zakat was not obligatory in Mecca; rather, there is no dispute that the Medinan verse came with its imposition, but that does not preclude that it was obligatory in Mecca as well. It has also been said: this verse is Medinan.

The second opinion: that this is a right in property other than zakat. Mujahid said: when you harvest and the poor are present, cast some of it for them; when you thresh it and winnow it, cast some of it for them; when you sift it, cast some of it for them; and when you know its measure, set aside its zakat.

The third opinion: that this was before the obligation of zakat, and when zakat was prescribed, this was abrogated (nusikha). This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The most correct is the first opinion. The proof for it is that His saying ﴿and give its due﴾ is fittingly mentioned only if that right was known before the revelation of this verse, lest this verse remain unspecified (mujmalah). The Prayer and Peace be upon him said: "There is no right in property other than zakat," so it is necessary that the intended right here be the right of zakat.

The third discussion: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾, after mentioning the five kinds, which are the grapes, the palm, the olive and the pomegranate, indicates the obligation of zakat on all of them, and this requires the obligation of zakat on fruits, as Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, used to say.

If they say: the word "harvest" (hasad) is specific to crops. We say: the word "harvest" (hasd) in the basic language is not specific to crops; the proof of this is that hasd in the language means cutting, and that covers all. Also, the pronoun in His saying "hasadihi" must return to the nearest of the things mentioned, and that is the olive and the pomegranate, so the pronoun must refer to them.

The fourth discussion: Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: the tenth is obligatory on both the little and the much. The majority said that it is not obligatory except when it reaches five wasq. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, argued with this verse, saying: His saying ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ requires the establishment of a right in the little and the much, so if that right is zakat, it is necessary to hold that zakat is obligatory on the little and the much.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not be excessive (wa-la tusrifu)﴾, know that the lexicographers have two opinions on the interpretation of israf (excess): First: Ibn al-A'rabi said: sarf is exceeding what has been set as a limit for you. Second: Shimr said: sarf of property is what goes from it without any benefit.

Page 176

Having understood this, we say: the exegetes have several opinions:

First: that if a person gives away all his wealth and does not provide anything for his dependants, he has committed excess, because it has come in a report: "Begin with yourself, then with those whom you support."

Narrated that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas set out to (a stand of) five hundred palm trees, cut them down, and distributed them all in a single day, without bringing anything of them into his own house. So Allah the Exalted revealed His saying: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be extravagant﴾, meaning: do not give all of it away.

The second view: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "do not be extravagant" means do not withhold the charity. These two views share the point that the meaning of extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit, except that the first is exceeding in giving, and the second is exceeding in withholding.

The third: Muqatil said: its meaning is: do not associate the idols with the tilled crops and the livestock. This too falls under the category of exceeding limits, because whoever associates idols with the tilled crops and the livestock has gone beyond what was prescribed for him.

The fourth: al-Zuhri said its meaning is: do not spend in disobedience to Allah the Exalted. Mujahid said: if Abu Qubays were gold and a man spent it in obedience to Allah the Exalted, he would not be extravagant; but if he spent a single dirham in disobedience to Allah, he would be extravagant. This is the meaning that Hatim al-Ta'i intended when it was said to him: "There is no good in extravagance," and he replied: "There is no extravagance in good." This is in line with the second view of the meaning of extravagance, for whoever spends in disobedience to Allah has spent on something that holds no benefit.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾. The purpose of this is deterrence, because every accountable person whom Allah the Exalted does not love is among the people of the Fire. The evidence for this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said: "We are the children of Allah and His beloved." Say: "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]. This indicates that everyone whom Allah loves is not among the people of the Fire. And this implies, in some respects, that whoever Allah does not love is among the people of the Fire.

[p. 177]

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the manner of His bounty to His servants through the vegetal benefits, He followed it with mention of His bounty to them through the animal benefits. So He said: ﴿And of the cattle, some for carrying and some for flesh﴾. There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: the "wa" (and) in His words ﴿And of the cattle, some for carrying and some for flesh﴾ requires coordination with what came before, His words ﴿It is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾. The sense is: He is the One who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised, and produced from the cattle some for carrying and some for flesh. The opinions regarding the meanings of "hamulah" (carrying animals) and "farsh" (flesh animals) are many. The two closest to clarity are:

First: "hamulah" refers to what carries loads, and "farsh" refers to what is spread out for slaughter, or whose wool, fleece, and hair are woven into bedding.

Second: "hamulah" refers to the large animals suitable for carrying, and "farsh" refers to the young animals, such as weaned camels, calves, and sheep, because they lie close to the ground due to the smallness of their bodies, like a spread carpet.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, meaning what He has made lawful for you. The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: He, may He be exalted, commanded eating of the provision and forbade eating what is unlawful; it follows that the provision is not unlawful.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾, that is, in declaring things lawful and unlawful from your own selves, as the people of ignorance (ahl al-jahiliyyah, the pre-Islamic Arabs) did. "Khutuwat" is the plural of "khutwah", which is the space between the two feet. Al-Zajjaj said: In ﴿footsteps of Satan﴾ there are three readings: with a damma on the ta', with a fatha, and with a sukun, and its meaning is: the paths of Satan. That is, do not travel the path that Satan embellishes for you.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, that is, of clear enmity. He expelled Adam from the Garden, and he is the one who said: ﴿I will surely seize his descendants, except for a few﴾ [al-Isra: 62].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿eight pairs﴾. Regarding this there are two investigations.

The first investigation: concerning the grammatical status of His words "thamaniyata" (eight), there are two views:

First: al-Farra' said: "thamaniyata" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿carrying and flesh animals﴾.

Second: the sense is: ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you, eight pairs﴾.

The second investigation: a single one, when it is alone, is called "fard" (single). When there is with it another of its kind, it is called "zawj" (pair), and they are "zawjan" (two pairs). The evidence is His words: ﴿He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ [al-Najm: 45], and His words: ﴿eight pairs﴾, which He then explained by His words: ﴿two of the sheep and two of the goats﴾, ﴿two of the camels and two of the cattle﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿two of the sheep﴾, meaning the male and the female. "Dan" (the sheep) refers to the woolly ones among the small livestock. This is what I hold regarding this verse, and Allah knows best His intent.

* * *

Likewise here.

* * *

The discussion of preferring one of the two views over the other is well known.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 145–147 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination, or a transgression dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor exceeding the limit, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws; and of the cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs carry, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone. That was Our recompense for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful.﴾ ﴿So if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is of vast mercy, but His punishment will not be averted from the criminal people."﴾

Allah the Exalted, when He had explained the corruption of the method of the people of ignorance regarding what is lawful and unlawful among foods, followed it with the correct explanation on this subject, so He said: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me"﴾. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Hamzah recited "إلّا أنْ تَكُونَ" with the ta', "مَيْتَةً" with the accusative (naṣb), on the estimate: unless the thing, or the soul, or the body (juththah) be carrion. Ibn ʿAmir recited "إلّا أنْ تَكُونَ" with the ta', "مَيْتَةٌ" with the nominative (raf'), in the sense: unless carrion occurs or comes to be. The rest recited "إلّا أنْ يَكُونَ مَيْتَةً", meaning: unless the food eaten be carrion, or unless what is found be carrion.

The second issue: When Allah the Exalted explained that prohibition and permission are established only by revelation, He said: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it"﴾, meaning, to one who consumes it. He mentioned this to make clear that the purpose of it is to explain what is lawful and unlawful among foods. Then He mentioned four things:
First: carrion.
Second: flowing blood.
Third: the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination.
Fourth: transgression, which is that which is dedicated to other than Allah.

So His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾, except these four, is an exaggeration in explaining that nothing is forbidden except these four. This is because it has been established that there is no way to know the forbidden and the permitted except by revelation; and it has been established that no revelation from Allah the Exalted came except to Muhammad, peace be upon him; and it has been established that He commands him to say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me any forbidden thing among the forbidden things except these four." This is an exaggeration in explaining that nothing is forbidden except these four.

Know that this surah is Meccan. In this Meccan surah Allah the Exalted explained that nothing is forbidden except these four, then He confirmed this by saying in Surat an-Nahl: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled﴾

﴿neither desiring nor exceeding the limit, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The word "innama" (only) conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). So we have two Meccan verses that indicate the restriction of the forbidden things to these four. Then in Surat al-Baqarah, which is also Medinan, He explained that nothing is forbidden except these four, saying: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. The word "innama" conveys restriction, so this Medinan verse corresponds to that Meccan verse, because the word "innama" conveys restriction. So "innama" in the Medinan verse corresponds to His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾ except such and such in the Meccan verse. Then in Surat al-Ma'idah He mentioned His saying: ﴿Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. The exegetes agreed that what is meant by His saying "except what is recited to you" is what He mentioned shortly after this verse, namely: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that over which other than Allah has been invoked, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered﴾. All these things are kinds of carrion, and He only repeated them in mention because they used to judge them as lawful. Thus it is established that the Sharia from its beginning to its end was settled upon this ruling and this restriction.

* * *

If someone says: Upholding this restriction obliges you to permit impurities and loathsome things, and it also obliges permitting wine. Moreover, it obliges you to permit the strangled, the beaten, the fallen and the gored, although Allah has judged their prohibition.

We say: This does not oblige us, for several reasons:

The first: He the Exalted said in this verse: ﴿or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination﴾, and its meaning is that Allah only forbade the flesh of swine because it is impure. This indicates that impurity is the cause (ʿillah) for forbidding eating, so it is necessary that every impure thing be forbidden to eat. Since this is mentioned in the verse, the question falls away.

The second: He the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿and He forbids them the foul things﴾ [al-Araf: 157], and this requires the prohibition of all foul things, and impurities are foul things, so it is necessary to affirm their prohibition.

The third: The community is unanimous on the impermissibility of consuming impurities. Suppose we accept that this surah is specified by the transmitted, mass-reported evidence from the religion of Muhammad concerning impurities; then what is other than them remains in accordance with the original ruling, adhering to the generality of the Book of Allah in the Meccan verse and the Medinan verse. This is a complete established principle in the matter of what is lawful and unlawful among foods.

As for wine, the answer regarding it is: it is impure, so it falls under "abomination" and falls under His saying: ﴿and He forbids them the foul things﴾. Also, its specification has been established by the mass-transmitted report from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ in its prohibition, and by His saying (so avoid it) and by His saying: ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. A general text that has been specified remains a proof in what lies outside the place of specification, so this verse remains a proof in what is other than it.

As for his saying that it obliges permitting the beaten, the fallen and the gored:

The answer to it is from several aspects:
First: that they are carrion, so they fall under this verse.
Second: that we specify the generality of this verse by that verse.
Third: that we say, if they are carrion they fall under this verse, and if they are not carrion we specify them by that verse.

If someone says: The forbidden things among foods are more than what is mentioned in this verse, so what is its purpose?

They answered it from several aspects:
One: that the meaning is: I do not find any forbidden thing of what the people of ignorance used to forbid, such as the baḥāʾir and the sawāʾib and others, except what is mentioned in this verse.
Second: that the intended meaning is that at the time of the revelation of this verse there was no prohibition beyond what is stated in this verse, and then other forbidden things were found after that.
Third: suppose the wording is general; still, specifying the generality of the Qur'an by a single report (khabar al-wahid) is permissible, so we specify this generality by single reports.
Fourth: the requirement of this verse is that we say He does not find [it] in the Qur'an, and it is possible that Allah the Exalted forbids what is other than these four upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace be upon him.

It may be said: These answers are weak.

As for the first answer: it is weak for several reasons:
One: it is not permissible that what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾ be what the people of ignorance forbade of the sawa'ib, the baha'ir and others, for if that were meant, carrion, blood, the flesh of swine and what was slaughtered on the altars would not be included under it. And if these things were not included under His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾, its exception of them would not be fitting. Since we see that these things are excepted from that phrase, we know that what is meant by that phrase is not what they claimed.
Second: He the Exalted judged the falsity of their claim regarding the prohibition of those things; then in this verse He specified the forbidden things to these four, and the permitting of those things which the people of ignorance forbade does not prevent the permitting of others. So it is necessary to keep this verse upon its generality, because specifying it entails abandoning its generality without evidence.
Third: He the Exalted said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you﴾ and mentioned these four things, and "innama" conveys restriction. This verse in Surat al-Baqarah is not preceded by a narration of the statements of the people of ignorance regarding the prohibition of the baha'ir and sawa'ib, so this excuse falls away.

As for their second answer, namely that the intended meaning is that at the time of the revelation of this verse nothing was forbidden except these four:

The answer to it is from several aspects:
First: His saying the Exalted in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ is a Medinan verse, revealed after the Sharia had become settled; and "innama" conveys restriction. So these two verses indicate that the ruling established in the Sharia of Muhammad, peace be upon him, from its beginning to its end, is nothing but the restriction of the forbidden things to these things.
Second: since it has been established by the implication of these two verses that the forbidden things are restricted to these four, this is an acknowledgment of the permissibility of everything else. So the claim that a fifth thing is forbidden would be abrogation (naskh). There is no doubt that the basis of the Sharia is that the original state is the absence of abrogation; for if the possibility of a later abrogating text were equal to the possibility that the ruling remains as it was, then it would be impossible to rely on any of the texts to establish any of the rulings, given the possibility that one would say: though it was established, it has ceased. Since all agree that the original state is non-abrogation, and that whoever claims abrogation is the one who needs evidence, we know the falsity of this objection.

As for their third answer, namely that we specify the generality of the Qur'an by a single report: we say that this is not a matter of specification, but is clear abrogation; because His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it"﴾ is an exaggeration that nothing is forbidden except these four, and His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion﴾ and so on, is an explicit restriction of the forbidden things to these four, since "innama" conveys restriction. So saying that the matter is not so would be a rejection of what was established by the implication of these two verses, that it was established at the beginning of the Sharia in Mecca and at its end in Medina; and abrogating the Qur'an by a single report is not permissible.

As for their fourth answer, it is also weak, because His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me"﴾ encompasses everything that was revelation, whether that revelation was the Qur'an or other than it. Moreover, His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion﴾ removes this possibility. Thus it is established by the argument we have mentioned the strength of this statement and the soundness of this position, which was the position held by Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him. Among the weak objections is that many jurists specified the generality of this verse by what is reported that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whatever the Arabs find repugnant is forbidden." It is known that what the Arabs find repugnant is not fixed; the chief of the Arabs, indeed the chief of all worlds, Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, when he saw them eating the lizard (ḍabb) said: "My nature loathes it," yet this aversion did not become a cause for forbidding the lizard. As for the rest of the Arabs, some of them find nothing repugnant, and they may differ regarding some things, so some people find them repugnant and others find them good. So we know that the matter of repugnance is not fixed, but varies with individuals and circumstances. How, then, is it permissible to abrogate this definitive text by that matter which has no fixed measure nor known standard?

* * *

**Third issue:** Know that we have already discussed the matters related to these four things in Surah al-Baqarah comprehensively, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

The first is the carrion (*maytah*). The exception to it is in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Two kinds of carrion have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts."

The second is flowing blood (*al-damm al-masfuh*). *Al-saff* means pouring. One says *safaha al-dam safhan* (he poured the blood) and *safaha huwa sufuhan* (it flowed) when it ran. Abu 'Ubaydah recited a verse of Kuthayyir:

*"I say, while my tears are pouring at her abode, / May God's peace be upon you, and the tears are flowing."*

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means what flows from livestock while they are alive, and what flows from the veins at the time of slaughter. According to this interpretation, the liver and spleen are not included, because they are solid, nor is the blood mixed into the meat, since it is not flowing. Abu Mijlaz was asked about the meat stained with blood, and about the Qadari (a Qadari who asked) who said: "Redness of blood is seen in it." He said: "There is no harm in it; only flowing blood was forbidden."

The third is the flesh of swine, for it is *rijs* (filth).

The fourth is His saying: ﴿or a sinful thing over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾. It is joined to His saying: ﴿unless it be carrion or flowing blood﴾. What was dedicated to other than God is called "sinful" because it has fully entered the realm of sin, just as one says: "So-and-so is generosity and munificence" when he is complete in both. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a sin﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, the meaning is that when He had explained that these four things are forbidden, He explained that in cases of necessity that prohibition is lifted. We have already fully explained the interpretation of this verse in Surah al-Baqarah. His saying after it, ﴿indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, indicates that a concession is granted.

Then God, exalted is He, explained that He forbade the Jews other things besides these four, and they are of two types.

The first: God, exalted is He, forbade them every animal with claws (*dhu zufur*), and in this there are several discussions.

**The first discussion:** Al-Wahidi said: regarding *al-zufur* there are dialects: *zufur* with a *damma* on the *fa'*, which is the highest of them; *zufr* with a sukun on the *fa'*; *zifr* with a kasra on the *za'* and sukun on the *fa'*, which is the recitation of al-Hasan; and *zifir* with a kasra on both, which is the recitation of Abu al-Sammal.

**The second discussion:** Al-Wahidi said: they differed about what "every animal with claws" that God forbade to the Jews refers to. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is camels only. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, it is camels and the ostrich, and this is the view of Mujahid. 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim said: it is every bird of prey with talons and every solid-hoofed animal. Then he said: "Thus say the commentators." He also said: the hoof was called a *zufr* by way of metaphor. I say: the interpretation of *zufr* as a hoof is far-fetched for two reasons:

The first: a hoof is hardly ever called a *zufr*.

The second: if the matter were so, it would have to be said that God forbade them every animal that has a hoof, and that is false, because the verse indicates that sheep and cattle are permitted to them, though they have hooves.

Given this, we must interpret *zufr* as claws and talons, because claws are the tools of predatory birds in hunting, and talons are the tools of beasts of prey in hunting. On this interpretation, it includes all kinds of predators, dogs and cats, and it includes the birds that hunt, because this attribute encompasses these kinds.

* * *

Given this, we say: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ indicates that this prohibition is restricted to them, for two reasons:

The first: His saying "And upon those who were Jews We forbade" such-and-such indicates exclusivity in the language.

The second: if this prohibition were established for everyone, His saying "And upon those who were Jews We forbade" would have no purpose. Thus it is established that the prohibition of beasts of prey and birds with claws is specific to the Jews, and therefore it must not be forbidden to Muslims. So this verse indicates the non-prohibition of these animals for Muslims. At this point we say: what is narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade every animal with fangs among beasts of prey and every bird with talons," is weak, because it is a *khabar al-wahid* (a single-transmission report) contrary to the Book of God, exalted is He, and therefore it must not be accepted. On this interpretation, the view of Malik on this issue is strengthened.

The second type of things that God, exalted is He, forbade specifically to the Jews is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fats﴾. So God explained that He forbade the Jews the fats of cattle and sheep. Then in the verse there are two opinions.

The first: God, exalted is He, made three exceptions from this prohibition:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿except what their backs carry﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: except the fat that adheres to the back, for I did not forbid it. Qatadah said: except what adheres to the back and side from the inner parts of their bellies. I say: there is no fat on the back and side except the white, thick flesh that adheres to the red flesh. On this interpretation, that thick adhering flesh is called "fat," and on this interpretation, if one swears not to eat fat, he must break his oath by eating that thick flesh.

The second exception is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or the entrails﴾. Al-Wahidi said: they are the intestines and the viscera; their singular is *hawiyah* and *hawiyyah*. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is *al-hawiyyah* or *al-hawiyah*, which is the coil found in the belly of a sheep. Ibn al-Sikkit said: one says *hawiyah* and *hawaya*, like *rawiyah* and *rawaya*.

Knowing this, the meaning is that the fats adhering to the intestines and viscera are not forbidden.

The third exception is His saying: ﴿or what is mixed with bone﴾. They said: it is the fat of the rump according to the consensus of all the commentators. Ibn Jurayj said: every fat on the standing part (the back), the side, the head, and in the two eyes and two ears. He says: whatever is mixed with bone is lawful for them. On this interpretation, the fat that God forbade them is the *thurb* (the fat covering the intestines) and the fat of the kidneys.

The second opinion regarding the verse: His saying ﴿or the entrails﴾ is not conjoined to the exception, but to what is excepted from; the meaning is: "Their fats were forbidden to them, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone, except what their backs carry, for it is not forbidden." They said:

And the particle "or" entered in the same way as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24]. The meaning: all of these are deserving of disobedience, so disobey this one and disobey that one. Likewise here, the meaning is: We forbade them this and that.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾. The meaning: We only specified them with this prohibition as a recompense for their rebellion, which was their killing of the prophets, their taking of usury, and their consuming of people's wealth falsely. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [an-Nisa': 160].

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, We are truthful﴾, that is, in reporting their rebellion, and in reporting that We specified them with this prohibition because of their rebellion. Al-Qadi said: the prohibition itself cannot be a punishment for a crime committed by them, because obligation (*taklif*) is an exposure to reward, and exposure to reward is a favor, so it is not permissible that the obligation be a recompense for a prior crime.

The answer: the prohibition of benefiting [from these things] may be for an increase in the deserving of reward, and it may also be for a prior crime; and neither of these is far-fetched.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they deny you﴾, meaning: if they deny you in your claim of prophethood and messengership, and deny you in conveying these rulings, ﴿then say: Your Lord is possessor of vast mercy﴾, so for that reason He does not hasten punishment upon you, ﴿and His punishment will not be turned back﴾, that is, His torment when its time comes, ﴿from the guilty people﴾, meaning those who deny you in what you say. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 145–147 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination, or a transgression dedicated to other than Allah. Ibn ʿAmir recited "إلّا أنْ تَكُونَ" with the ta', "مَيْتَةٌ" with the nominative (raf'), in the sense: unless carrion occurs or comes to be. The rest recited "إلّا أنْ يَكُونَ مَيْتَةً", meaning: unless the food eaten be carrion, or unless what is found be carrion.

He mentioned this to make clear that the purpose of it is to explain what is lawful and unlawful among foods. Then He mentioned four things:

Second: flowing blood.

This is an exaggeration in explaining that nothing is forbidden except these four.
