It is known that what the Arabs find repugnant is not fixed; the chief of the Arabs, indeed the chief of all worlds, Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, when he saw them eating the lizard (ḍabb) said: "My nature loathes it," yet this aversion did not become a cause for forbidding the lizard. As for the rest of the Arabs, some of them find nothing repugnant, and they may differ regarding some things, so some people find them repugnant and others find them good. So we know that the matter of repugnance is not fixed, but varies with individuals and circumstances. How, then, is it permissible to abrogate this definitive text by that matter which has no fixed measure nor known standard?

* * *

**Third issue:** Know that we have already discussed the matters related to these four things in Surah al-Baqarah comprehensively, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

The first is the carrion (*maytah*). The exception to it is in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Two kinds of carrion have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts."

The second is flowing blood (*al-damm al-masfuh*). *Al-saff* means pouring. One says *safaha al-dam safhan* (he poured the blood) and *safaha huwa sufuhan* (it flowed) when it ran. Abu 'Ubaydah recited a verse of Kuthayyir:

*"I say, while my tears are pouring at her abode, / May God's peace be upon you, and the tears are flowing."*

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means what flows from livestock while they are alive, and what flows from the veins at the time of slaughter. According to this interpretation, the liver and spleen are not included, because they are solid, nor is the blood mixed into the meat, since it is not flowing. Abu Mijlaz was asked about the meat stained with blood, and about the Qadari (a Qadari who asked) who said: "Redness of blood is seen in it." He said: "There is no harm in it; only flowing blood was forbidden."

The third is the flesh of swine, for it is *rijs* (filth).

The fourth is His saying: ﴿or a sinful thing over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾. It is joined to His saying: ﴿unless it be carrion or flowing blood﴾. What was dedicated to other than God is called "sinful" because it has fully entered the realm of sin, just as one says: "So-and-so is generosity and munificence" when he is complete in both. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a sin﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, the meaning is that when He had explained that these four things are forbidden, He explained that in cases of necessity that prohibition is lifted. We have already fully explained the interpretation of this verse in Surah al-Baqarah. His saying after it, ﴿indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, indicates that a concession is granted.

Then God, exalted is He, explained that He forbade the Jews other things besides these four, and they are of two types.

The first: God, exalted is He, forbade them every animal with claws (*dhu zufur*), and in this there are several discussions.

**The first discussion:** Al-Wahidi said: regarding *al-zufur* there are dialects: *zufur* with a *damma* on the *fa'*, which is the highest of them; *zufr* with a sukun on the *fa'*; *zifr* with a kasra on the *za'* and sukun on the *fa'*, which is the recitation of al-Hasan; and *zifir* with a kasra on both, which is the recitation of Abu al-Sammal.

**The second discussion:** Al-Wahidi said: they differed about what "every animal with claws" that God forbade to the Jews refers to. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is camels only. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, it is camels and the ostrich, and this is the view of Mujahid. 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim said: it is every bird of prey with talons and every solid-hoofed animal. Then he said: "Thus say the commentators." He also said: the hoof was called a *zufr* by way of metaphor. I say: the interpretation of *zufr* as a hoof is far-fetched for two reasons:

The first: a hoof is hardly ever called a *zufr*.

The second: if the matter were so, it would have to be said that God forbade them every animal that has a hoof, and that is false, because the verse indicates that sheep and cattle are permitted to them, though they have hooves.

Given this, we must interpret *zufr* as claws and talons, because claws are the tools of predatory birds in hunting, and talons are the tools of beasts of prey in hunting. On this interpretation, it includes all kinds of predators, dogs and cats, and it includes the birds that hunt, because this attribute encompasses these kinds.

* * *

Given this, we say: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ indicates that this prohibition is restricted to them, for two reasons:

The first: His saying "And upon those who were Jews We forbade" such-and-such indicates exclusivity in the language.

The second: if this prohibition were established for everyone, His saying "And upon those who were Jews We forbade" would have no purpose. Thus it is established that the prohibition of beasts of prey and birds with claws is specific to the Jews, and therefore it must not be forbidden to Muslims. So this verse indicates the non-prohibition of these animals for Muslims. At this point we say: what is narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade every animal with fangs among beasts of prey and every bird with talons," is weak, because it is a *khabar al-wahid* (a single-transmission report) contrary to the Book of God, exalted is He, and therefore it must not be accepted. On this interpretation, the view of Malik on this issue is strengthened.

The second type of things that God, exalted is He, forbade specifically to the Jews is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fats﴾. So God explained that He forbade the Jews the fats of cattle and sheep. Then in the verse there are two opinions.

The first: God, exalted is He, made three exceptions from this prohibition:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿except what their backs carry﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: except the fat that adheres to the back, for I did not forbid it. Qatadah said: except what adheres to the back and side from the inner parts of their bellies. I say: there is no fat on the back and side except the white, thick flesh that adheres to the red flesh. On this interpretation, that thick adhering flesh is called "fat," and on this interpretation, if one swears not to eat fat, he must break his oath by eating that thick flesh.

The second exception is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or the entrails﴾. Al-Wahidi said: they are the intestines and the viscera; their singular is *hawiyah* and *hawiyyah*. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is *al-hawiyyah* or *al-hawiyah*, which is the coil found in the belly of a sheep. Ibn al-Sikkit said: one says *hawiyah* and *hawaya*, like *rawiyah* and *rawaya*.

Knowing this, the meaning is that the fats adhering to the intestines and viscera are not forbidden.

The third exception is His saying: ﴿or what is mixed with bone﴾. They said: it is the fat of the rump according to the consensus of all the commentators. Ibn Jurayj said: every fat on the standing part (the back), the side, the head, and in the two eyes and two ears. He says: whatever is mixed with bone is lawful for them. On this interpretation, the fat that God forbade them is the *thurb* (the fat covering the intestines) and the fat of the kidneys.

The second opinion regarding the verse: His saying ﴿or the entrails﴾ is not conjoined to the exception, but to what is excepted from; the meaning is: "Their fats were forbidden to them, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone, except what their backs carry, for it is not forbidden." They said:

And the particle "or" entered in the same way as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24]. The meaning: all of these are deserving of disobedience, so disobey this one and disobey that one. Likewise here, the meaning is: We forbade them this and that.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾. The meaning: We only specified them with this prohibition as a recompense for their rebellion, which was their killing of the prophets, their taking of usury, and their consuming of people's wealth falsely. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [an-Nisa': 160].

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, We are truthful﴾, that is, in reporting their rebellion, and in reporting that We specified them with this prohibition because of their rebellion. Al-Qadi said: the prohibition itself cannot be a punishment for a crime committed by them, because obligation (*taklif*) is an exposure to reward, and exposure to reward is a favor, so it is not permissible that the obligation be a recompense for a prior crime.

The answer: the prohibition of benefiting [from these things] may be for an increase in the deserving of reward, and it may also be for a prior crime; and neither of these is far-fetched.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they deny you﴾, meaning: if they deny you in your claim of prophethood and messengership, and deny you in conveying these rulings, ﴿then say: Your Lord is possessor of vast mercy﴾, so for that reason He does not hasten punishment upon you, ﴿and His punishment will not be turned back﴾, that is, His torment when its time comes, ﴿from the guilty people﴾, meaning those who deny you in what you say. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verses 145–147 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination, or a transgression dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor exceeding the limit, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws; and of the cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs carry, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone. That was Our recompense for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful.﴾ ﴿So if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is of vast mercy, but His punishment will not be averted from the criminal people."﴾

Allah the Exalted, when He had explained the corruption of the method of the people of ignorance regarding what is lawful and unlawful among foods, followed it with the correct explanation on this subject, so He said: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me"﴾. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Hamzah recited "إلّا أنْ تَكُونَ" with the ta', "مَيْتَةً" with the accusative (naṣb), on the estimate: unless the thing, or the soul, or the body (juththah) be carrion. Ibn ʿAmir recited "إلّا أنْ تَكُونَ" with the ta', "مَيْتَةٌ" with the nominative (raf'), in the sense: unless carrion occurs or comes to be. The rest recited "إلّا أنْ يَكُونَ مَيْتَةً", meaning: unless the food eaten be carrion, or unless what is found be carrion.

The second issue: When Allah the Exalted explained that prohibition and permission are established only by revelation, He said: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it"﴾, meaning, to one who consumes it. He mentioned this to make clear that the purpose of it is to explain what is lawful and unlawful among foods. Then He mentioned four things:
First: carrion.
Second: flowing blood.
Third: the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination.
Fourth: transgression, which is that which is dedicated to other than Allah.

So His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾, except these four, is an exaggeration in explaining that nothing is forbidden except these four. This is because it has been established that there is no way to know the forbidden and the permitted except by revelation; and it has been established that no revelation from Allah the Exalted came except to Muhammad, peace be upon him; and it has been established that He commands him to say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me any forbidden thing among the forbidden things except these four." This is an exaggeration in explaining that nothing is forbidden except these four.

Know that this surah is Meccan. In this Meccan surah Allah the Exalted explained that nothing is forbidden except these four, then He confirmed this by saying in Surat an-Nahl: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled﴾

﴿neither desiring nor exceeding the limit, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The word "innama" (only) conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). So we have two Meccan verses that indicate the restriction of the forbidden things to these four. Then in Surat al-Baqarah, which is also Medinan, He explained that nothing is forbidden except these four, saying: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. The word "innama" conveys restriction, so this Medinan verse corresponds to that Meccan verse, because the word "innama" conveys restriction. So "innama" in the Medinan verse corresponds to His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾ except such and such in the Meccan verse. Then in Surat al-Ma'idah He mentioned His saying: ﴿Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. The exegetes agreed that what is meant by His saying "except what is recited to you" is what He mentioned shortly after this verse, namely: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that over which other than Allah has been invoked, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered﴾. All these things are kinds of carrion, and He only repeated them in mention because they used to judge them as lawful. Thus it is established that the Sharia from its beginning to its end was settled upon this ruling and this restriction.

* * *

If someone says: Upholding this restriction obliges you to permit impurities and loathsome things, and it also obliges permitting wine. Moreover, it obliges you to permit the strangled, the beaten, the fallen and the gored, although Allah has judged their prohibition.

We say: This does not oblige us, for several reasons:

The first: He the Exalted said in this verse: ﴿or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination﴾, and its meaning is that Allah only forbade the flesh of swine because it is impure. This indicates that impurity is the cause (ʿillah) for forbidding eating, so it is necessary that every impure thing be forbidden to eat. Since this is mentioned in the verse, the question falls away.

The second: He the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿and He forbids them the foul things﴾ [al-Araf: 157], and this requires the prohibition of all foul things, and impurities are foul things, so it is necessary to affirm their prohibition.

The third: The community is unanimous on the impermissibility of consuming impurities. Suppose we accept that this surah is specified by the transmitted, mass-reported evidence from the religion of Muhammad concerning impurities; then what is other than them remains in accordance with the original ruling, adhering to the generality of the Book of Allah in the Meccan verse and the Medinan verse. This is a complete established principle in the matter of what is lawful and unlawful among foods.

As for wine, the answer regarding it is: it is impure, so it falls under "abomination" and falls under His saying: ﴿and He forbids them the foul things﴾. Also, its specification has been established by the mass-transmitted report from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ in its prohibition, and by His saying (so avoid it) and by His saying: ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. A general text that has been specified remains a proof in what lies outside the place of specification, so this verse remains a proof in what is other than it.

As for his saying that it obliges permitting the beaten, the fallen and the gored:

The answer to it is from several aspects:
First: that they are carrion, so they fall under this verse.
Second: that we specify the generality of this verse by that verse.
Third: that we say, if they are carrion they fall under this verse, and if they are not carrion we specify them by that verse.

If someone says: The forbidden things among foods are more than what is mentioned in this verse, so what is its purpose?

They answered it from several aspects:
One: that the meaning is: I do not find any forbidden thing of what the people of ignorance used to forbid, such as the baḥāʾir and the sawāʾib and others, except what is mentioned in this verse.
Second: that the intended meaning is that at the time of the revelation of this verse there was no prohibition beyond what is stated in this verse, and then other forbidden things were found after that.
Third: suppose the wording is general; still, specifying the generality of the Qur'an by a single report (khabar al-wahid) is permissible, so we specify this generality by single reports.
Fourth: the requirement of this verse is that we say He does not find [it] in the Qur'an, and it is possible that Allah the Exalted forbids what is other than these four upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace be upon him.

It may be said: These answers are weak.

As for the first answer: it is weak for several reasons:
One: it is not permissible that what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾ be what the people of ignorance forbade of the sawa'ib, the baha'ir and others, for if that were meant, carrion, blood, the flesh of swine and what was slaughtered on the altars would not be included under it. And if these things were not included under His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"﴾, its exception of them would not be fitting. Since we see that these things are excepted from that phrase, we know that what is meant by that phrase is not what they claimed.
Second: He the Exalted judged the falsity of their claim regarding the prohibition of those things; then in this verse He specified the forbidden things to these four, and the permitting of those things which the people of ignorance forbade does not prevent the permitting of others. So it is necessary to keep this verse upon its generality, because specifying it entails abandoning its generality without evidence.
Third: He the Exalted said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you﴾ and mentioned these four things, and "innama" conveys restriction. This verse in Surat al-Baqarah is not preceded by a narration of the statements of the people of ignorance regarding the prohibition of the baha'ir and sawa'ib, so this excuse falls away.

As for their second answer, namely that the intended meaning is that at the time of the revelation of this verse nothing was forbidden except these four:

The answer to it is from several aspects:
First: His saying the Exalted in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ is a Medinan verse, revealed after the Sharia had become settled; and "innama" conveys restriction. So these two verses indicate that the ruling established in the Sharia of Muhammad, peace be upon him, from its beginning to its end, is nothing but the restriction of the forbidden things to these things.
Second: since it has been established by the implication of these two verses that the forbidden things are restricted to these four, this is an acknowledgment of the permissibility of everything else. So the claim that a fifth thing is forbidden would be abrogation (naskh). There is no doubt that the basis of the Sharia is that the original state is the absence of abrogation; for if the possibility of a later abrogating text were equal to the possibility that the ruling remains as it was, then it would be impossible to rely on any of the texts to establish any of the rulings, given the possibility that one would say: though it was established, it has ceased. Since all agree that the original state is non-abrogation, and that whoever claims abrogation is the one who needs evidence, we know the falsity of this objection.

As for their third answer, namely that we specify the generality of the Qur'an by a single report: we say that this is not a matter of specification, but is clear abrogation; because His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it"﴾ is an exaggeration that nothing is forbidden except these four, and His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion﴾ and so on, is an explicit restriction of the forbidden things to these four, since "innama" conveys restriction. So saying that the matter is not so would be a rejection of what was established by the implication of these two verses, that it was established at the beginning of the Sharia in Mecca and at its end in Medina; and abrogating the Qur'an by a single report is not permissible.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, We are truthful﴾, that is, in reporting their rebellion, and in reporting that We specified them with this prohibition because of their rebellion. Know that when He, exalted is He, related of the people of ignorance (jahiliyya) their presumption to rule in the religion of God without proof or evidence, He related their excuse for everything they undertook of disbelief. They say: "Had God willed that we not disbelieve, He would have prevented us from this disbelief. Since He did not prevent us from it, it is established that He wills it. So when God wills it from us, its abandonment becomes impossible for us, and we are excused in it." In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that the Mu'tazila claimed that this verse indicates their view on the question of the will of created beings, in seven aspects.

Page 185

The first aspect: He, exalted is He, related from the disbelievers the explicit statement of the Mujbira (Determinists), which is their saying: "Had God willed that we not ascribe partners, we would not have ascribed partners." He related this statement from them only in the context of blame and reproach, so it is necessary that this doctrine be blameworthy and false.

The second aspect: He, exalted is He, said: "denied" (kadhdhaba), and in it there are two readings, with light (takhfif) and with emphasis (tashdid). As for the reading with light, it is an explicit statement that they lied in that saying, and that indicates that what the Mujbira say on this question is a lie. As for the reading with emphasis, it cannot be taken to mean that the people deserved blame because they denied the prophets, for if we took the verse this way, this meaning would be the opposite of the meaning indicated by the reading "kadhaba" with light, and then one of the two readings would be the opposite of the other, and that would entail contradiction in the speech of God, exalted is He. When this is invalid, it is necessary to interpret it as meaning that whoever denied a prophet of earlier times, he denied him by this path, because he says that everything happens by the will of God, exalted is He: "What I am upon of disbelief came about by the will of God, exalted is He, so He did not prevent me from it." This is a path specific to all the disbelievers, earlier and later, in denying the prophets and in repelling their call from themselves. So when we take the verse in this sense, the reading with emphasis becomes a confirmation of the reading with light, and the combination of the two readings indicates the refutation of the saying of the Mujbira.

The third aspect: the proof of the verse for our view is His saying, exalted is He: "until they tasted Our might," and this indicates that they deserved the threat from God, exalted is He, in their going to this doctrine.

The fourth doctrine: His saying, exalted is He: "Say: Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us?" There is no doubt that this is a question in the manner of denunciation, and that indicates that those who hold this saying have no knowledge or proof for it, and this indicates the corruption of this doctrine, because everything that is true has knowledge behind its saying.

The fifth aspect: His saying, exalted is He: "You follow nothing but conjecture (zann)," while He said in other verses: "Surely conjecture avails nothing against the truth" [al-Najm: 28].

The sixth aspect: His saying, exalted is He: "and you only guess (yakhrusun)," and guessing (kharş) is the most vile type of lying. Also He, exalted is He, said: "Killed are the conjecturers" [al-Dhariyat: 10].

The seventh aspect: His saying, exalted is He: "Say: To God belongs the conclusive proof." Its explanation: they argued, in repelling the call of the prophets and messengers against themselves, by saying: "Everything that occurs is by the will of God, exalted is He. And if God willed that of us, how can we abandon it? And if we are unable to abandon it, how does He command us to abandon it? Is it within our capacity and power to bring about an act contrary to the will of God, exalted is He?" This is the argument of the disbelievers against the prophets, and He, exalted is He, said: "Say: To God belongs the conclusive proof," and that is from two aspects:

The first aspect: He, exalted is He, gave you complete intellects, sufficient understandings, hearing ears, and seeing eyes, and empowered you over good and evil, and removed excuses and impediments from you entirely. So if you will, you go to doing good deeds, and if you will, to doing sins and wrongs. This capacity and ability is known to be established by necessity, and the removal of impediments and obstacles is likewise known to be established by necessity. Since the matter is so, your claim that you are unable to have faith and obedience is a false claim. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that you have no conclusive proof against God; rather, the conclusive proof belongs to God against you.

Page 186

The second aspect: you say: "If our acts were occurring contrary to the will of God, exalted is He, we would have overcome God and subdued Him, and brought about the act in opposition to Him and contrary to Him, and that would entail that He is incapable and weak, and that would impugn His being a god." He, exalted is He, answered this: the incapacity and weakness would only follow if I were not able to compel them to faith and obedience by way of coercion and compulsion, and I am able to do that, and this is what is meant by His saying: "Had He willed, He would have guided you all." But I do not compel you to faith and obedience by way of coercion and compulsion, because that would nullify the wisdom sought from the obligation. Thus it is established by this explanation that what they say, that if we brought about an act contrary to the will of God, it would follow from it that He, exalted is He, is incapable and weak, is a false statement.

This is the utmost that can be mentioned in the Mu'tazila's reliance on this verse.

The well-founded answer in this matter is that we say: we have shown that this surah, from its beginning to its end, indicates the soundness of our view and our doctrine, and we have related in every verse what they mention of interpretations, and answered them with clear, strong answers, reinforced by decisive rational proofs.

Since this is established, if the meaning of this verse were what you have stated, a clear contradiction would occur in the Book of God, exalted is He, for that would entail the greatest kind of attack upon it.

Since this is established, we say: He, exalted is He, related of the people that they said: "Had God willed, we would not have ascribed partners." Then He mentioned after it: "Thus did those before them deny." This indicates that the people said that since everything is by the will and decree of God, exalted is He, the obligation would be vain, and so the claims of the prophets would be false, and their prophethood and messengership false. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that using this path to nullify prophethood is false, because He is a God who does what He wills and decrees what He desires, and no one has objection to His act. He wills disbelief from the disbeliever, and yet He sends prophets to him and commands him to have faith; the coming of a command contrary to the will is not impossible.

The summary: He, exalted is He, related that the disbelievers hold fast to the will of God, exalted is He, in nullifying the prophethood of the prophets. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that this inference is corrupt and false, for the will of God in all matters does not entail the repelling of the prophets' call. On this path alone this inference falls entirely, and all the aspects you have mentioned in denunciation and reproach return to your holding fast to the establishment of God's will as a means of repelling the prophets' call. So the outcome is that this inference is false, and there is absolutely nothing in it indicating that the saying of will is false.

If they say: this excuse only holds if we read His saying, exalted is He: "Thus did he deny" with emphasis. As for when we read it with light, this excuse falls away entirely. We say concerning it two aspects:

The first: we deny the soundness of this reading. The proof for this is that we have shown that this surah, from its beginning to its end, indicates our view. So if this verse indicated their view, contradiction would occur, and the Qur'an would cease to be the speech of God, exalted is He. This contradiction is removed by not accepting this reading, so it is necessary to resort to it.

The second: granting the soundness of this reading, we still interpret it as meaning that they lied in claiming that it follows from the establishment of God's will in all the acts of the servants that the prophethood of the prophets falls and their call is nullified. When we interpret it in this way, the Mu'tazila have no reliance at all on this verse. Praise belongs to God who helped us to emerge from this strong obligation, and among what strengthens what we have mentioned

Page 187

is what is related: that when Ibn 'Abbas, after the loss of his sight, was asked what he says about one who says there is no qadar (divine decree), he said: "If there is anyone in the house of them, I would attack him. Woe to him! Does he not read: ﴿Indeed We have created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49] ﴿Indeed We bring the dead to life and record what they have sent forth and their traces﴾ [Ya Sin: 12]?" Ibn 'Abbas also said: "The first thing God created was the pen; He said to it: 'Write the decree,' so it ran with what will be until the Hour." And he, may the blessings of God be upon him, said: "The deniers of qadar are the Magians of this community."

* * *

The second issue: Sibawayh held that conjoining an apparent noun to a pronoun that is a subject within the verb is ugly (qabih), so it is not permitted to say: "qumtu wa Zayd" (I stood and Zayd). That is because the conjoined-to is the root, the conjoined is a branch, the pronoun is weak, and the noun is strong, and making the strong a branch of the weak is not permitted.

Having understood this principle, we say: if the speech is in the affirmative, it is required to emphasize the pronoun, so we say: "qumtu ana wa Zayd" (I stood, I, and Zayd), and if it is in the negative, you say: "ma qumtu wa la Zayd" (I did not stand, nor Zayd).

Having established this, we say that His saying: "Had God willed, we would not have ascribed partners, nor would our fathers" — "wa la ababuna" is conjoined to the pronoun in His saying "ma ashrakna," except that the word "la" intervened between them, so the conjunction was therefore fine.

In the Jami' of al-Isfahani it is said: the conjunctive particle must come after the word that emphasizes the pronoun, so that the conjunction is fine and the mentioned difficulty of conjoining the strong to the weak is removed. This aim is only achieved if we say: "ma ashrakna nahnu wa la ababuna," so that the word "la" precedes the conjunctive particle. Here, however, the conjunctive particle precedes "la," and then the mentioned difficulty returns.

The answer: when "la" was introduced before "ababuna," this necessitated supposing a verb there, because directing the negation to the essences of the fathers is impossible; rather, this negation must be directed to an act proceeding from them, and that is associating partners, so the supposition is: "ma ashrakna wa la ashraka ababuna" (we did not associate partners, nor did our fathers associate partners). On this supposition the difficulty disappears.

* * *

The third issue: our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued for their saying that everything is by the will of God, exalted is He, with His saying: "Then had He willed, He would have guided you all." For the word "law" (lau) in the language indicates the non-occurrence of one thing due to the non-occurrence of another, so this indicates that He, exalted is He, did not will to guide them, and also did not guide them.

Its explanation according to rational proof: if the disbeliever's capacity for disbelief is not a capacity for faith, then God, exalted is He, on this supposition, did not empower him for faith; so if He willed faith from him, He would have willed an act without capacity for the act, and that is impossible, and the will of the impossible is impossible. And if the capacity for disbelief is a capacity for faith, then the preponderance of one of the two sides depends on the occurrence of the determining motive.

If we say that He, exalted is He, created that motive, then the determining motive has come into being together with the capacity, and the two together necessitate the act. Therefore, when the act does not occur, we know that the motive did not come into being. If the motive did not come into being, the act of faith was impossible for him. And if that was impossible for him, it was impossible for God to will it from him, because willing what is impossible is itself impossible. It is thus established that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that He, exalted is He, did not will faith from the disbelievers. The rational proof we have set forth also indicates this. Their view is therefore refuted in every respect.

As for their statement that this verse is to be understood as referring to the will of compulsion (*mashi'at al-ilja'*), we say: this interpretation would only be acceptable if rational proof had established the impossibility of taking this statement in its apparent sense. But if rational proof has established that the truth is nothing other than what this apparent sense indicates, then how can one turn away from it?

Furthermore, we say that this argument is invalid in several respects:

The first: this statement necessarily requires an implied element. We say the implied meaning is: "If He had willed guidance, He would have guided you." You say the implied meaning is: "If He had willed guidance by way of compulsion (*'ala sabil al-ilja'*), He would have guided you." Your implication is therefore greater, and so your view is less preferable (*marjuh*).

The second: He, exalted is He, wills from the disbeliever voluntary faith (*al-iman al-ikhtiyari*). Faith obtained through compulsion is not the same as faith obtained through choice. On this assumption, it follows that He, exalted is He, is unable to bring about what He wills, since what He wills is voluntary faith, and He is absolutely unable to bring it about. Therefore, the affirmation of incapacity is entailed.

The third: this statement depends on distinguishing between faith obtained through choice and faith obtained through compulsion. As for faith obtained through choice, its occurrence is impossible except when there is a decisive motive (*da'iya jazima*) and a binding will (*irada lazima*). For the motive upon which the occurrence of the act depends is either such that the act necessarily follows from it, or it is not. If the act necessarily follows, then it is the necessary motive (*al-da'iya al-daruriyya*), and in that case there is no difference between it and the motive obtained through compulsion. If the act does not necessarily follow from it, then the act may fail to occur after it. Let us suppose that the act sometimes fails to occur after it and sometimes does not fail to occur. The distinction between one of these two times and the other must then be due to an additional determining factor. What existed before that was the complete motive, and we have supposed it to be so; this is a contradiction (*khulf*). Then, when this additional qualification is added, if the act now necessarily follows, there is no difference between it and the necessary motive; and if it still does not necessarily follow, it requires a further additional qualification, and this leads to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), which is impossible. It is thus established that the distinction they mention between the voluntary motive and the necessary motive, although it appears valid at first sight, yields nothing upon critical examination and inquiry.

Furthermore, we say that this argument is invalid in several respects:

The first: this statement necessarily requires an implied element. We say the implied meaning is: "If He had willed guidance, He would have guided you." You say the implied meaning is: "If He had willed guidance by way of compulsion (*'ala sabil al-ilja'*), He would have guided you." Your implication is therefore greater, and so your view is less preferable (*marjuh*).

The second: He, exalted is He, wills from the disbeliever voluntary faith (*al-iman al-ikhtiyari*). Faith obtained through compulsion is not the same as faith obtained through choice. On this assumption, it follows that He, exalted is He, is unable to bring about what He wills, since what He wills is voluntary faith, and He is absolutely unable to bring it about. Therefore, the affirmation of incapacity is entailed.

The third: this statement depends on distinguishing between faith obtained through choice and faith obtained through compulsion. As for faith obtained through choice, its occurrence is impossible except when there is a decisive motive (*da'iya jazima*) and a binding will (*irada lazima*). For the motive upon which the occurrence of the act depends is either such that the act necessarily follows from it, or it is not. If the act necessarily follows, then it is the necessary motive (*al-da'iya al-daruriyya*), and in that case there is no difference between it and the motive obtained through compulsion. If the act does not necessarily follow from it, then the act may fail to occur after it. Let us suppose that the act sometimes fails to occur after it and sometimes does not fail to occur. The distinction between one of these two times and the other must then be due to an additional determining factor. What existed before that was the complete motive, and we have supposed it to be so; this is a contradiction (*khulf*). Then, when this additional qualification is added, if the act now necessarily follows, there is no difference between it and the necessary motive; and if it still does not necessarily follow, it requires a further additional qualification, and this leads to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), which is impossible. It is thus established that the distinction they mention between the voluntary motive and the necessary motive, although it appears valid at first sight, yields nothing upon critical examination and inquiry.

[p. 188]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 150:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this. And if they testify, do not testify along with them, and do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and who ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, had refuted all kinds of the disbelievers' arguments, He made clear that they have no witnesses at all for their claim. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: "halumma" (hallumma, "come, bring") is a word of calling someone to a thing, and the meaning is: bring your witnesses. On it there are two views. The first: it is used uniformly for the singular, the dual, and the plural, and for the masculine and the feminine. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses who testify﴾, and He said: ﴿And those who say to their brothers, "Come to us"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18]. The second dialect: for two it is said halumma (halumma-a), for the plural halummu, for a woman halummi, for two women halumma, and for the plural of women hallumma-na. The first is more eloquent.

The second issue: concerning the origin of this word there are two views. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said that it is "ha" to which "lumma" was joined, meaning "gather," and it may carry the sense of "come near." It is said: "li-fulan lamma," meaning nearness. Then the two were made like a single word. The benefit of our saying "ha" is to win over the one commanded and to call for his turning toward the matter. But since its use became frequent, the alif was dropped from it for lightness, as in your saying: lam ubal, lam ara, lam taku. Al-Farra' said: its origin is "hal, umma," they meant by "hal" the interrogative particle.

Page 189
And by our saying "umma," meaning: intend. The implied sense is: has he intended? The purpose of this interrogation is the command to intend, as if you were saying: intend. There is another view on it, which is to say: the original form was that they said: "hal laka fi al-ta'am, amm," meaning: is there an intention? Then it spread to all uses, just as the word "ta'ala" was restricted to a specific form and then became general.

The third issue: by calling for the production of witnesses from the disbelievers, He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that they have no witness for the prohibition they imposed, and the meaning of "halumma" is: bring forward your witnesses.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And if they testify, do not testify along with them﴾, as a warning that they are liars. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that if such testimony came from them, it would be from following desire. So He commanded His Prophet not to follow their desires. Then He increased the condemnation of that by saying that they do not believe in the Hereafter, and they were among those who deny resurrection and rising again. He further condemned them by saying that they ascribe equals to their Lord, making partners for Him. And Allah knows best.

[p. 190]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, that you show kindness to your parents, that you do not kill your children out of poverty—We provide for you and for them—that you do not draw near to indecencies, whether apparent or hidden, and that you do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right. This He has enjoined upon you, that perhaps you will understand."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the corruption of what the disbelievers said, that God had forbidden us such-and-such and such-and-such, He followed it with an explanation of the things He had forbidden them, which are the things mentioned in this verse. In it there are several issues.

The first issue: The author of the *Kashshaf* said: "*Ta'āla* (come) is one of those specific words that became general. Its original usage was for someone who is in a higher place to say it to someone lower than him, and then it became common and general. The *mā* in His saying ﴿what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ is in the accusative case, and there are two views on what governs it:

The first: it is in the accusative governed by "*utlu*" (recite), and the meaning is: recite that which He has forbidden you.

The second: it is in the accusative governed by *ḥarrama* (forbade), and the meaning is: recite the things which He has forbidden you."

If it is asked: His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him, and show kindness to your parents﴾ is like an elaboration of what was summarized in His saying ﴿what your Lord has forbidden you﴾, and this is false, because abandoning association and showing kindness to parents are obligatory, not forbidden.

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the intended meaning of prohibition (*taḥrīm*) is that He makes for it a specific protected boundary (*ḥarīm*), by explaining it in a precise, determined way. So His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ means: recite to you what He has explained with a complete explanation such that it makes for it a specific boundary.
[p. 191 precedes this text; continuing] On this interpretation, the question disappears. The second: the speech was complete and ended at His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾, then He began anew saying ﴿upon you: that you do not associate﴾, as one says "upon you is peace." Or the speech was complete and ended at His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you upon you﴾, then He began anew saying ﴿that you do not associate anything with Him﴾, in the sense of "lest you associate", and the implied meaning is: recite what your Lord has forbidden you upon you, lest you associate anything with Him. The third: the *an* in His saying ﴿that you do not associate﴾ is explanatory, in the sense of "that is", and the meaning of the verse is: recite what your Lord has forbidden you, that is, do not associate; that prohibition is His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾.

If it is asked: His saying ﴿and show kindness to your parents﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾, so His saying ﴿and show kindness to your parents﴾ must explain His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾, and it would follow that kindness to parents is forbidden, and this is false.

We say: When He made kindness to them obligatory, He thereby forbade harming them.

* * *

The second issue: In this verse He, exalted is He, made obligatory five matters. The first is His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, has explained the categories of polytheists in this sūrah in the best manner. This is because a group of polytheists make idols partners of God, exalted is He, and to them refers His saying, as a narration about Abraham: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed I see you and your people in manifest error."﴾ [al-An'ām 6:74].

The second group among the polytheists are the worshippers of the stars, those about whom God related that Abraham, peace be upon him, refuted their claim with his saying: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾

The third group are those about whom God, exalted is He, related: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾ [al-An'ām 6:100], and they are those who hold to Yazdan and Ahriman.

The fourth group are those who attributed to God sons and daughters. He established proofs against the corruption of the views of these groups and sects. When He had shown by argument the corruption of the view of these groups, He said here: ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾.

The second type of matters He made obligatory here is His saying ﴿and show kindness to your parents﴾. He mentioned this obligation after the first, because the greatest of blessings upon a human being is the blessing of God, exalted is He, and after it comes the blessing of parents, because the true cause of a human's existence is God, glorified is He, while apparently it is the two parents. Then their blessings upon a human are great, namely the blessing of upbringing, compassion, and protection from loss and destruction during childhood.

The third type is His saying ﴿and do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾. So after observing the rights of the two parents, He made obligatory the observance of the rights of children. His saying ﴿do not kill your children out of poverty﴾ means: out of fear of poverty. He explicitly mentioned fear in His saying ﴿do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:31]. What is meant is the prohibition of infanticide (*wa'd*), since they used to bury daughters alive, some out of jealousy, and some out of fear of poverty, which was the predominant cause. God explained the corruption of this reason by His saying ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, because since God is responsible for the provision of parent and child, just as it is obligatory on parents to preserve their own lives and to rely on God for their sustenance, the same applies to the case of the child. Shimr said: *amlaqa* is both intransitive and transitive. It is said: *amlaqa al-rajul* (the man became destitute), so he is *mumliq*, when he became poor; this is intransitive. And *amlaqa al-dahr mā 'indahu* (time ruined what he had), when it corrupts it; and *al-imlāq* is corruption.

[p. 192 precedes this text; continuing] — (*The following is on p. 191 in the source; order preserved.*)

The fourth type is His saying ﴿and do not draw near to indecencies, whether apparent or hidden﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They used to dislike fornication openly, and would commit it secretly, so God forbade them fornication both openly and secretly." It is better not to restrict this prohibition to a specific kind, but to let it apply in its generality to all indecencies, apparent and hidden, because the wording is general. The meaning which makes this prohibition obligatory, namely that it is an indecency, is also general, and with the generality of both wording and meaning, specification would be contrary to the evidence. In His saying ﴿whether apparent or hidden﴾ there is a subtle point: when a person refrains from sin outwardly but does not refrain from it inwardly, this indicates that his refraining is not for the sake of servitude to God and obedience to Him, but for fear of people's blame. That is false, because whoever finds people's blame weightier in his heart than the punishment of God and the like, is at risk of disbelief. Whoever abandons sin both outwardly and inwardly indicates that he abandoned it out of exalting God's command, fear of His punishment, and desire for His servitude.

The fifth type is His saying ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾.

Know that this is included in the category of indecencies, but He singled it out for mention for two reasons. The first: singling out indicates glorification and magnification, as in His saying ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel and Michael﴾. The second: He, exalted is He, intended to make an exception from it, and this exception cannot be made within the general category of indecencies.

Having understood this, we say: His saying ﴿except by right﴾ means that killing a forbidden soul may be a right on account of a crime it commits. The hadith also agrees with it, namely his saying, peace be upon him (ﷺ): "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, adultery after marriage, and killing a soul without right." The Qur'an indicated a fourth cause, namely His saying: ﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:33].

The conclusion: the original ruling regarding taking a soul is prohibition, and its permissibility is not established except by a separate proof. Then, when He, exalted is He, had explained the states of these five categories, He followed it with a word that brings the heart closer to acceptance, saying ﴿This He has enjoined upon you﴾, because of the gentleness and tenderness in this expression, and all of that is so that the responsible person may be closer to acceptance. Then He followed it with His saying ﴿that perhaps you will understand﴾, meaning: so that you may understand the benefits of these obligations and their advantages in religion and in worldly life.

* His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not draw near to the property of the orphan except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity. And give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfill the covenant of God. This He has enjoined upon you, that perhaps you will remember.﴾

[p. 192] Know that in the first verse He mentioned five kinds of obligations, which are matters that are apparent and clear, requiring no reflection or effort. Then in this verse He mentioned four kinds of obligations, which are hidden matters, for which the rational person needs reflection, contemplation, and effort to know their extent.

The first kind of obligation mentioned in this verse is His saying ﴿And do not draw near to the property of the orphan except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, said in Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿In this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:220]. The meaning here: do not draw near to the property of the orphan except by striving to increase it, gaining profit from it, and attending to what is beneficial for him. Then if the guardian is poor and in need, he may take in a reasonable manner; and if he is wealthy and abstains from it, that is better. So His saying ﴿except in the way that is best﴾ has the same meaning as His saying ﴿Whoever is rich, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:6].

* * *

As for His saying ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, the meaning is: guard his property until he reaches his maturity, and when he reaches his maturity, hand over his property to him. As for the meaning and explanation of *ashudd* (maturity): al-Layth said: "*al-Ashudd* is the stage at which a man reaches wisdom and understanding." Al-Farra' said: "*al-Ashudd*: its singular is *shadd* by analogy, but I have not heard a singular for it." Abu al-Haytham said: "The singular of *al-Ashudd* is *shiddah*, just as the singular of *al-an'um* (blessings) is *ni'mah*, and *shiddah* is strength and vigor, and *al-shadid* is a strong man." They interpreted the attainment of *al-ashudd* in this verse as puberty, on condition that right judgment is perceived in him. We have thoroughly examined this matter at the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisā'.

The second kind: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice.﴾

Know that everything which reaches complete perfection has been fulfilled and completed. It is said: *dirham wāfin* (a full dirham) and *kayl wāfin* (a full measure). *Awfaytuhu ḥaqqahu* (I gave him his full right), and *waffaytuhu* when you completed it. *Awfā al-kayl* means he completed it and did not reduce anything from it. His saying ﴿and the weight﴾ means weighing with a balance. His saying ﴿with justice﴾ means with equity, without fraud or shortfall.

If it is asked: The fulfilling of measure and weight is itself justice, so what is the benefit of this repetition?

We answer: God commanded the giver to fulfill the right of the one entitled to it without diminishing it, and commanded the one who has the right to take his right without seeking more.

Know that since it is possible that a person might imagine that it is obligatory to achieve exact precision, and that is very difficult in justice, God followed it with what removes this hardship, saying ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾. That is, what is obligatory in giving full measure and weight is this degree which is possible in preserving measure and weight. As for absolute precision, it is not obligatory. The Qadi said: "If God has lightened this burden for the responsible person, while the extreme strictness is within his capacity, how could it be supposed that God obligates the disbeliever to believe while he has no power over it? Rather, they said: He creates disbelief in him, wills it from him, judges it upon him, creates in him the power that necessitates that disbelief and the motive that necessitates it, and then forbids him from it. So since He, exalted is He, does not permit that degree of severity and constriction upon the servant, namely fulfilling measure and weight in an exact way, how could He permit imposing such constriction and severity upon the servant?"

Know that we counter the Qadi and his shaykhs in this matter with the question of divine knowledge and the question of the divine motive (*dā'ī*), and at that point the argument collapses and this discourse loses its splendor and brilliance.

[p. 193]

The third category of obligations mentioned in this verse is His saying, ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near kinsman﴾. Know that this too is among the hidden matters in which God has made the fulfilment of trust obligatory. The exegetes restricted it to giving testimony alone and to commanding and forbidding alone. Al-Qadi said: The matter is not so; rather, it includes everything connected with speech. It includes what a person says in calling to the religion and in establishing its proofs, by presenting the proof in summary, free of padding and excess, in familiar and commonly used words close to people's understanding. It includes that commanding good and forbidding evil be carried out in a just manner, without excess in causing harm or alienation and without falling short of the required measure. It includes the reports a man relates, that he add nothing to them and omit nothing from them. Among these is conveying messages on behalf of people, for it is obligatory to convey them without addition or omission. It includes the judgment of the judge expressed in speech.

Then God made clear that this must be applied equally to the near and the distant, because its purpose is to seek the good pleasure of God, and that purpose does not differ between the near and the distant.

The fourth category of these obligations is His saying, ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. This is among the hidden matters, because a man may make an oath to himself, so that the oath is hidden, and his keeping of it or breaking it is also hidden. When God had mentioned these categories, He said: ﴿This He has enjoined upon you, that you may remember﴾.

If it is asked: what is the reason that He ended the first verse with His saying, ﴿that you may understand﴾, and ended this verse with His saying, ﴿that you may remember﴾?

We say: because the five obligations mentioned in the first are manifest and clear matters, so it was necessary that they be understood and comprehended. As for the four obligations mentioned in this verse, they are hidden and obscure matters, in which striving (ijtihad) and reflection are necessary until one arrives at the point of moderation. For this reason He said, ﴿that you may remember﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, read (تَذَكَّرُونَ) with a light pronunciation, while the rest read (تَذَّكَّرُونَ) with the dhal doubled, throughout the Qur'an. Both have one meaning.

[Page 3]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it; and do not follow the other paths, lest they scatter you away from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing﴾.

His saying, ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it; and do not follow the other paths, lest they scatter you away from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing﴾.

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn 'Amir read (وأنْ هَذا), with a fathah on the alif and a sukun on the nun. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وإنَّ) with a kasrah on the alif and a doubled nun. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, its original form is (وإنَّهُ هَذا صِراطِي), where the ha' is the pronoun of the matter and the subject, and when this condition holds, the particle is lightened. Al-A'sha said:

In a band of youths like Indian swords, they know that every one who goes barefoot and every one who wears shoes is doomed.

That is: they know that he is doomed. As for the kasrah on (إنَّ), the implied sense is (أتْلُ ما حَرَّمَ) ("recite what He forbade"), and (أتْلُ أنَّ هَذا صِراطِي) means "I say". It was also said that it is resumptive. As for the fathah on (أنَّ), al-Farra' said: the fathah of (أنَّ) comes from the verb (أتْلُ) being applied to it, meaning, "And I recite to you that this is My straight path." He said: If you wish, you may make it in the genitive, with the sense: "This He has enjoined upon you, and [also] that this is My straight path."

Abu 'Ali said: As for the one who reads (أنَّ) with a fathah, the analogy of Sibawayh's view is that he took it as governed by His saying (فاتَّبِعُوهُ), with the implied sense: "Because this is My straight path, so follow it," like His saying, ﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52]. Sibawayh said: because this community of yours is one community. And concerning His saying, ﴿And indeed the mosques are for God, so do not call upon anyone along with God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18], the meaning is: "and because the mosques are for God."

Second issue: The readers agreed on the sukun of the ya' in (صِراطِي), except Ibn 'Amir, who read it with a fathah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (سِراطِي) with a sin, Hamzah read it between the sad and the zay, and the rest read it with a pure sad. All of these are dialectal forms. The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-A'mash read (وهَذا صِراطِي), and in the codex of 'Abd Allah it is (وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكم), and in the codex of Ubayy it is (وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكَ).

[Page 4]

Third issue: When He made clear in the two preceding verses what He had enjoined, He summed it up at the end in a summary that requires the inclusion of what came before and the inclusion of the rest of the Sharia within it. So He said, ﴿And this is My straight path﴾. Thus there is included in it everything the Messenger (ﷺ) explained of the religion of Islam, which is the upright method and the straight path. So follow its whole and its details, and do not deviate from it, lest you fall into misguidance.

From Ibn Mas'ud: the Prophet (ﷺ) drew a line, then said: "This is the path of guidance." Then he drew lines to its right and to its left, then said: "These are paths, on each of which there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it﴾.

From Ibn 'Abbas: these verses are decisive (muhkamat), no part of them has been abrogated by anything in all the Books. Whoever acts upon them enters Paradise, and whoever abandons them enters the Fire.

Fourth issue: This verse shows that everything that is true is one. It does not follow from this that everything that is one is true. So if the truth is one, everything other than it is false, and what is other than the truth is many things. Therefore it must be judged that every multiplicity is false. But it does not follow that every falsehood is multiple, in accordance with what we established in the first case.

The third group are those about whom God, exalted is He, related: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾ [al-An'ām 6:100], and they are those who hold to Yazdan and Ahriman.

The fourth group are those who attributed to God sons and daughters. He established proofs against the corruption of the views of these groups and sects. When He had shown by argument the corruption of the view of these groups, He said here: ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾.

The second type of matters He made obligatory here is His saying ﴿and show kindness to your parents﴾. He mentioned this obligation after the first, because the greatest of blessings upon a human being is the blessing of God, exalted is He, and after it comes the blessing of parents, because the true cause of a human's existence is God, glorified is He, while apparently it is the two parents. Then their blessings upon a human are great, namely the blessing of upbringing, compassion, and protection from loss and destruction during childhood.

The third type is His saying ﴿and do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾. So after observing the rights of the two parents, He made obligatory the observance of the rights of children. His saying ﴿do not kill your children out of poverty﴾ means: out of fear of poverty. He explicitly mentioned fear in His saying ﴿do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:31]. What is meant is the prohibition of infanticide (*wa'd*), since they used to bury daughters alive, some out of jealousy, and some out of fear of poverty, which was the predominant cause. God explained the corruption of this reason by His saying ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, because since God is responsible for the provision of parent and child, just as it is obligatory on parents to preserve their own lives and to rely on God for their sustenance, the same applies to the case of the child. Shimr said: *amlaqa* is both intransitive and transitive. It is said: *amlaqa al-rajul* (the man became destitute), so he is *mumliq*, when he became poor; this is intransitive. And *amlaqa al-dahr mā 'indahu* (time ruined what he had), when it corrupts it; and *al-imlāq* is corruption.
