The fourth type is His saying ﴿and do not draw near to indecencies, whether apparent or hidden﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They used to dislike fornication openly, and would commit it secretly, so God forbade them fornication both openly and secretly." It is better not to restrict this prohibition to a specific kind, but to let it apply in its generality to all indecencies, apparent and hidden, because the wording is general. The meaning which makes this prohibition obligatory, namely that it is an indecency, is also general, and with the generality of both wording and meaning, specification would be contrary to the evidence. In His saying ﴿whether apparent or hidden﴾ there is a subtle point: when a person refrains from sin outwardly but does not refrain from it inwardly, this indicates that his refraining is not for the sake of servitude to God and obedience to Him, but for fear of people's blame. That is false, because whoever finds people's blame weightier in his heart than the punishment of God and the like, is at risk of disbelief. Whoever abandons sin both outwardly and inwardly indicates that he abandoned it out of exalting God's command, fear of His punishment, and desire for His servitude.

The fifth type is His saying ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾.

Know that this is included in the category of indecencies, but He singled it out for mention for two reasons. The first: singling out indicates glorification and magnification, as in His saying ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel and Michael﴾. The second: He, exalted is He, intended to make an exception from it, and this exception cannot be made within the general category of indecencies.

Having understood this, we say: His saying ﴿except by right﴾ means that killing a forbidden soul may be a right on account of a crime it commits. The hadith also agrees with it, namely his saying, peace be upon him (ﷺ): "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, adultery after marriage, and killing a soul without right." The Qur'an indicated a fourth cause, namely His saying: ﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:33].

The conclusion: the original ruling regarding taking a soul is prohibition, and its permissibility is not established except by a separate proof. Then, when He, exalted is He, had explained the states of these five categories, He followed it with a word that brings the heart closer to acceptance, saying ﴿This He has enjoined upon you﴾, because of the gentleness and tenderness in this expression, and all of that is so that the responsible person may be closer to acceptance. Then He followed it with His saying ﴿that perhaps you will understand﴾, meaning: so that you may understand the benefits of these obligations and their advantages in religion and in worldly life.

* His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not draw near to the property of the orphan except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity. And give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfill the covenant of God. This He has enjoined upon you, that perhaps you will remember.﴾

[p. 192] Know that in the first verse He mentioned five kinds of obligations, which are matters that are apparent and clear, requiring no reflection or effort. Then in this verse He mentioned four kinds of obligations, which are hidden matters, for which the rational person needs reflection, contemplation, and effort to know their extent.

The first kind of obligation mentioned in this verse is His saying ﴿And do not draw near to the property of the orphan except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, said in Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿In this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is best﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:220]. The meaning here: do not draw near to the property of the orphan except by striving to increase it, gaining profit from it, and attending to what is beneficial for him. Then if the guardian is poor and in need, he may take in a reasonable manner; and if he is wealthy and abstains from it, that is better. So His saying ﴿except in the way that is best﴾ has the same meaning as His saying ﴿Whoever is rich, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:6].

* * *

As for His saying ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾, the meaning is: guard his property until he reaches his maturity, and when he reaches his maturity, hand over his property to him. As for the meaning and explanation of *ashudd* (maturity): al-Layth said: "*al-Ashudd* is the stage at which a man reaches wisdom and understanding." Al-Farra' said: "*al-Ashudd*: its singular is *shadd* by analogy, but I have not heard a singular for it." Abu al-Haytham said: "The singular of *al-Ashudd* is *shiddah*, just as the singular of *al-an'um* (blessings) is *ni'mah*, and *shiddah* is strength and vigor, and *al-shadid* is a strong man." They interpreted the attainment of *al-ashudd* in this verse as puberty, on condition that right judgment is perceived in him. We have thoroughly examined this matter at the beginning of Sūrat al-Nisā'.

The second kind: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice.﴾

Know that everything which reaches complete perfection has been fulfilled and completed. It is said: *dirham wāfin* (a full dirham) and *kayl wāfin* (a full measure). *Awfaytuhu ḥaqqahu* (I gave him his full right), and *waffaytuhu* when you completed it. *Awfā al-kayl* means he completed it and did not reduce anything from it. His saying ﴿and the weight﴾ means weighing with a balance. His saying ﴿with justice﴾ means with equity, without fraud or shortfall.

If it is asked: The fulfilling of measure and weight is itself justice, so what is the benefit of this repetition?

We answer: God commanded the giver to fulfill the right of the one entitled to it without diminishing it, and commanded the one who has the right to take his right without seeking more.

Know that since it is possible that a person might imagine that it is obligatory to achieve exact precision, and that is very difficult in justice, God followed it with what removes this hardship, saying ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾. That is, what is obligatory in giving full measure and weight is this degree which is possible in preserving measure and weight. As for absolute precision, it is not obligatory. The Qadi said: "If God has lightened this burden for the responsible person, while the extreme strictness is within his capacity, how could it be supposed that God obligates the disbeliever to believe while he has no power over it? Rather, they said: He creates disbelief in him, wills it from him, judges it upon him, creates in him the power that necessitates that disbelief and the motive that necessitates it, and then forbids him from it. So since He, exalted is He, does not permit that degree of severity and constriction upon the servant, namely fulfilling measure and weight in an exact way, how could He permit imposing such constriction and severity upon the servant?"

Know that we counter the Qadi and his shaykhs in this matter with the question of divine knowledge and the question of the divine motive (*dā'ī*), and at that point the argument collapses and this discourse loses its splendor and brilliance.

[p. 193]

The third category of obligations mentioned in this verse is His saying, ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near kinsman﴾. Know that this too is among the hidden matters in which God has made the fulfilment of trust obligatory. The exegetes restricted it to giving testimony alone and to commanding and forbidding alone. Al-Qadi said: The matter is not so; rather, it includes everything connected with speech. It includes what a person says in calling to the religion and in establishing its proofs, by presenting the proof in summary, free of padding and excess, in familiar and commonly used words close to people's understanding. It includes that commanding good and forbidding evil be carried out in a just manner, without excess in causing harm or alienation and without falling short of the required measure. It includes the reports a man relates, that he add nothing to them and omit nothing from them. Among these is conveying messages on behalf of people, for it is obligatory to convey them without addition or omission. It includes the judgment of the judge expressed in speech.

Then God made clear that this must be applied equally to the near and the distant, because its purpose is to seek the good pleasure of God, and that purpose does not differ between the near and the distant.

The fourth category of these obligations is His saying, ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. This is among the hidden matters, because a man may make an oath to himself, so that the oath is hidden, and his keeping of it or breaking it is also hidden. When God had mentioned these categories, He said: ﴿This He has enjoined upon you, that you may remember﴾.

If it is asked: what is the reason that He ended the first verse with His saying, ﴿that you may understand﴾, and ended this verse with His saying, ﴿that you may remember﴾?

We say: because the five obligations mentioned in the first are manifest and clear matters, so it was necessary that they be understood and comprehended. As for the four obligations mentioned in this verse, they are hidden and obscure matters, in which striving (ijtihad) and reflection are necessary until one arrives at the point of moderation. For this reason He said, ﴿that you may remember﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, read (تَذَكَّرُونَ) with a light pronunciation, while the rest read (تَذَّكَّرُونَ) with the dhal doubled, throughout the Qur'an. Both have one meaning.

* * *

[Page 3]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it; and do not follow the other paths, lest they scatter you away from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing﴾.

His saying, ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it; and do not follow the other paths, lest they scatter you away from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing﴾.

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn 'Amir read (وأنْ هَذا), with a fathah on the alif and a sukun on the nun. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وإنَّ) with a kasrah on the alif and a doubled nun. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, its original form is (وإنَّهُ هَذا صِراطِي), where the ha' is the pronoun of the matter and the subject, and when this condition holds, the particle is lightened. Al-A'sha said:

In a band of youths like Indian swords, they know that every one who goes barefoot and every one who wears shoes is doomed.

That is: they know that he is doomed. As for the kasrah on (إنَّ), the implied sense is (أتْلُ ما حَرَّمَ) ("recite what He forbade"), and (أتْلُ أنَّ هَذا صِراطِي) means "I say". It was also said that it is resumptive. As for the fathah on (أنَّ), al-Farra' said: the fathah of (أنَّ) comes from the verb (أتْلُ) being applied to it, meaning, "And I recite to you that this is My straight path." He said: If you wish, you may make it in the genitive, with the sense: "This He has enjoined upon you, and [also] that this is My straight path."

Abu 'Ali said: As for the one who reads (أنَّ) with a fathah, the analogy of Sibawayh's view is that he took it as governed by His saying (فاتَّبِعُوهُ), with the implied sense: "Because this is My straight path, so follow it," like His saying, ﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52]. Sibawayh said: because this community of yours is one community. And concerning His saying, ﴿And indeed the mosques are for God, so do not call upon anyone along with God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18], the meaning is: "and because the mosques are for God."

Second issue: The readers agreed on the sukun of the ya' in (صِراطِي), except Ibn 'Amir, who read it with a fathah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (سِراطِي) with a sin, Hamzah read it between the sad and the zay, and the rest read it with a pure sad. All of these are dialectal forms. The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-A'mash read (وهَذا صِراطِي), and in the codex of 'Abd Allah it is (وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكم), and in the codex of Ubayy it is (وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكَ).

[Page 4]

Third issue: When He made clear in the two preceding verses what He had enjoined, He summed it up at the end in a summary that requires the inclusion of what came before and the inclusion of the rest of the Sharia within it. So He said, ﴿And this is My straight path﴾. Thus there is included in it everything the Messenger (ﷺ) explained of the religion of Islam, which is the upright method and the straight path. So follow its whole and its details, and do not deviate from it, lest you fall into misguidance.

From Ibn Mas'ud: the Prophet (ﷺ) drew a line, then said: "This is the path of guidance." Then he drew lines to its right and to its left, then said: "These are paths, on each of which there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it﴾.

From Ibn 'Abbas: these verses are decisive (muhkamat), no part of them has been abrogated by anything in all the Books. Whoever acts upon them enters Paradise, and whoever abandons them enters the Fire.

Fourth issue: This verse shows that everything that is true is one. It does not follow from this that everything that is one is true. So if the truth is one, everything other than it is false, and what is other than the truth is many things. Therefore it must be judged that every multiplicity is false. But it does not follow that every falsehood is multiple, in accordance with what we established in the first case.

[p. 190]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, that you show kindness to your parents, that you do not kill your children out of poverty—We provide for you and for them—that you do not draw near to indecencies, whether apparent or hidden, and that you do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right. This He has enjoined upon you, that perhaps you will understand."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the corruption of what the disbelievers said, that God had forbidden us such-and-such and such-and-such, He followed it with an explanation of the things He had forbidden them, which are the things mentioned in this verse. In it there are several issues.

The first issue: The author of the *Kashshaf* said: "*Ta'āla* (come) is one of those specific words that became general. Its original usage was for someone who is in a higher place to say it to someone lower than him, and then it became common and general. The *mā* in His saying ﴿what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ is in the accusative case, and there are two views on what governs it:

The first: it is in the accusative governed by "*utlu*" (recite), and the meaning is: recite that which He has forbidden you.

The second: it is in the accusative governed by *ḥarrama* (forbade), and the meaning is: recite the things which He has forbidden you."

If it is asked: His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him, and show kindness to your parents﴾ is like an elaboration of what was summarized in His saying ﴿what your Lord has forbidden you﴾, and this is false, because abandoning association and showing kindness to parents are obligatory, not forbidden.

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the intended meaning of prohibition (*taḥrīm*) is that He makes for it a specific protected boundary (*ḥarīm*), by explaining it in a precise, determined way. So His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ means: recite to you what He has explained with a complete explanation such that it makes for it a specific boundary.
[p. 191 precedes this text; continuing] On this interpretation, the question disappears. The second: the speech was complete and ended at His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾, then He began anew saying ﴿upon you: that you do not associate﴾, as one says "upon you is peace." Or the speech was complete and ended at His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you upon you﴾, then He began anew saying ﴿that you do not associate anything with Him﴾, in the sense of "lest you associate", and the implied meaning is: recite what your Lord has forbidden you upon you, lest you associate anything with Him. The third: the *an* in His saying ﴿that you do not associate﴾ is explanatory, in the sense of "that is", and the meaning of the verse is: recite what your Lord has forbidden you, that is, do not associate; that prohibition is His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾.

If it is asked: His saying ﴿and show kindness to your parents﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾, so His saying ﴿and show kindness to your parents﴾ must explain His saying ﴿recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾, and it would follow that kindness to parents is forbidden, and this is false.

We say: When He made kindness to them obligatory, He thereby forbade harming them.

[p. 193]

The third category of obligations mentioned in this verse is His saying, ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near kinsman﴾. Know that this too is among the hidden matters in which God has made the fulfilment of trust obligatory. The exegetes restricted it to giving testimony alone and to commanding and forbidding alone. Al-Qadi said: The matter is not so; rather, it includes everything connected with speech. It includes what a person says in calling to the religion and in establishing its proofs, by presenting the proof in summary, free of padding and excess, in familiar and commonly used words close to people's understanding. It includes that commanding good and forbidding evil be carried out in a just manner, without excess in causing harm or alienation and without falling short of the required measure. It includes the reports a man relates, that he add nothing to them and omit nothing from them. Among these is conveying messages on behalf of people, for it is obligatory to convey them without addition or omission. It includes the judgment of the judge expressed in speech.

Then God made clear that this must be applied equally to the near and the distant, because its purpose is to seek the good pleasure of God, and that purpose does not differ between the near and the distant.

The fourth category of these obligations is His saying, ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. This is among the hidden matters, because a man may make an oath to himself, so that the oath is hidden, and his keeping of it or breaking it is also hidden. When God had mentioned these categories, He said: ﴿This He has enjoined upon you, that you may remember﴾.

If it is asked: what is the reason that He ended the first verse with His saying, ﴿that you may understand﴾, and ended this verse with His saying, ﴿that you may remember﴾?

We say: because the five obligations mentioned in the first are manifest and clear matters, so it was necessary that they be understood and comprehended. As for the four obligations mentioned in this verse, they are hidden and obscure matters, in which striving (ijtihad) and reflection are necessary until one arrives at the point of moderation. For this reason He said, ﴿that you may remember﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, read (تَذَكَّرُونَ) with a light pronunciation, while the rest read (تَذَّكَّرُونَ) with the dhal doubled, throughout the Qur'an. Both have one meaning.

[Page 3]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it; and do not follow the other paths, lest they scatter you away from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing﴾.

His saying, ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it; and do not follow the other paths, lest they scatter you away from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may be God-fearing﴾.

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn 'Amir read (وأنْ هَذا), with a fathah on the alif and a sukun on the nun. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وإنَّ) with a kasrah on the alif and a doubled nun. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, its original form is (وإنَّهُ هَذا صِراطِي), where the ha' is the pronoun of the matter and the subject, and when this condition holds, the particle is lightened. Al-A'sha said:

In a band of youths like Indian swords, they know that every one who goes barefoot and every one who wears shoes is doomed.

That is: they know that he is doomed. As for the kasrah on (إنَّ), the implied sense is (أتْلُ ما حَرَّمَ) ("recite what He forbade"), and (أتْلُ أنَّ هَذا صِراطِي) means "I say". It was also said that it is resumptive. As for the fathah on (أنَّ), al-Farra' said: the fathah of (أنَّ) comes from the verb (أتْلُ) being applied to it, meaning, "And I recite to you that this is My straight path." He said: If you wish, you may make it in the genitive, with the sense: "This He has enjoined upon you, and [also] that this is My straight path."

Abu 'Ali said: As for the one who reads (أنَّ) with a fathah, the analogy of Sibawayh's view is that he took it as governed by His saying (فاتَّبِعُوهُ), with the implied sense: "Because this is My straight path, so follow it," like His saying, ﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52]. Sibawayh said: because this community of yours is one community. And concerning His saying, ﴿And indeed the mosques are for God, so do not call upon anyone along with God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18], the meaning is: "and because the mosques are for God."

Second issue: The readers agreed on the sukun of the ya' in (صِراطِي), except Ibn 'Amir, who read it with a fathah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (سِراطِي) with a sin, Hamzah read it between the sad and the zay, and the rest read it with a pure sad. All of these are dialectal forms. The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-A'mash read (وهَذا صِراطِي), and in the codex of 'Abd Allah it is (وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكم), and in the codex of Ubayy it is (وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكَ).

[Page 4]

Third issue: When He made clear in the two preceding verses what He had enjoined, He summed it up at the end in a summary that requires the inclusion of what came before and the inclusion of the rest of the Sharia within it. So He said, ﴿And this is My straight path﴾. Thus there is included in it everything the Messenger (ﷺ) explained of the religion of Islam, which is the upright method and the straight path. So follow its whole and its details, and do not deviate from it, lest you fall into misguidance.

From Ibn Mas'ud: the Prophet (ﷺ) drew a line, then said: "This is the path of guidance." Then he drew lines to its right and to its left, then said: "These are paths, on each of which there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it﴾.

From Ibn 'Abbas: these verses are decisive (muhkamat), no part of them has been abrogated by anything in all the Books. Whoever acts upon them enters Paradise, and whoever abandons them enters the Fire.

Fourth issue: This verse shows that everything that is true is one. It does not follow from this that everything that is one is true. So if the truth is one, everything other than it is false, and what is other than the truth is many things. Therefore it must be judged that every multiplicity is false. But it does not follow that every falsehood is multiple, in accordance with what we established in the first case.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 154:

His saying, ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book, complete [in blessing] for the one who did good, and as a detailed explanation of all things, and as guidance and mercy, that they might believe in the meeting with their Lord﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿Then We gave﴾, has several interpretations.

The first: the implied meaning is: "Then I inform you, after enumerating the prohibitions and the other rulings, that We gave Moses the Book." The word "then" (thumma) is mentioned to indicate the delay of one report after another, not the delay of the event itself. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ [al-A'raf: 11].

The second: the nine obligations mentioned in the previous verse cannot differ according to the difference of the revealed laws (shara'i'). Rather, they are rulings that are firmly established from the beginning of the period of obligation until the Resurrection. As for the laws in which repentance was specific to them, they came into being only after those nine obligations. So the meaning of the verse is: when He mentioned them, He said, "That is what He has enjoined upon you, O children of Adam, both in the past and in the present. Then, after that, We gave Moses the Book."

The third: there is an ellipsis in it. Its implied meaning is: "Then say, O Muhammad, that We gave Moses..." So the meaning is: "Recite what has been revealed to you, then recite to them the report of what We gave Moses."

As for His saying, ﴿complete for the one who did good﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: its meaning is "complete in honor and blessing for the one who did good," that is, for everyone who was a doer of good and righteous. This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): (عَلى الَّذِينَ أحْسَنُوا) ("for those who did good").

The second: the intended meaning is "complete in blessing and honor for the servant who did good in conveying [the message] and in everything he was commanded to do."

The third: "complete upon the one whom Moses perfected in knowledge and laws," from "aḥsana al-shay'" when one has mastered knowing it, that is, an increase upon his knowledge in the manner of completion. Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (عَلى الَّذِي أحْسَنُ) ("upon the one who is best"), that is, upon the one who is best, with the subject omitted, like the reading of the one who read (مَثَلًا ما بَعُوضَةٌ) with the nominative [ending on the word for gnat]. [p. 5] The meaning of the verse is: "upon the one who is best in religion and most pleasing to Him." Or it may be said: the intended meaning is "We gave Moses the Book complete," that is, perfect and whole, in the best form in which books can be. That is, in the best manner. This is the meaning of al-Kalbi's words: "He completed the Book for him in its best form." Then He, exalted is He, explained what the Torah contains of blessings in religion, which is the detailing of all things. What is intended by this is what pertains to religion. Included in this is the explanation of the prophethood of Our Messenger (ﷺ), his religion, his law, and the rest of the proofs and rulings, except those that were abrogated (naskh) from them. For this reason He said: ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾. Guidance is well known, and it is indication (al-dalala). Mercy is blessing. ﴿that they might believe in the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is, so that they might believe in the meeting with their Lord. What is intended by "the meeting" is the meeting with what Allah has promised them of reward and punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 155–157:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and fear God, that you may receive mercy﴾ ﴿Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than them." Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and guidance and mercy. Who, then, is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them? We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with an evil punishment.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿And this is a Book﴾, undoubtedly refers to the Qur'an. The benefit of describing it as blessed (mubarak) is that it is firm and that abrogation (naskh) does not reach it, as is the case with the two Books (the Torah and the Gospel). Alternatively, it means that it is abundant in good and benefit.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿so follow it﴾, and its meaning is clear.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and fear God, that you may receive mercy﴾, meaning, so that you may be shown mercy. Regarding this there are three opinions. It has been said: fear opposing it in hope of mercy. It has been said: fear so that you may be shown mercy, that is, so that the aim of piety is God's mercy. It has been said: fear so that you may be shown mercy as a reward for piety.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾, and regarding this there are several aspects:

The first aspect: al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said that the implied meaning is: We sent it down so that you would not say, then the preposition and the negative particle were omitted, as in His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176] and His saying: ﴿mountains lest they sway with you﴾ [al-Nahl: 15], meaning: lest.

The second aspect, which is the view of the Basrans, is that its meaning is: We sent it down out of dislike that you should say. They do not permit the implicit insertion of "la" (not), since it is not permissible to say: "I came to honour you" meaning "not to honour you." We have already explained the verification of this issue at the end of Surah al-Nisa'.

Page 6
The third aspect: al-Farra' said: it is permissible for "an" (that) to be connected to "ittaqu" (fear), and the interpretation is: "And fear that you say: The Book was only sent down..."

Second discussion: His saying, ﴿that you say﴾, is addressed to the people of Mecca, and the meaning is: out of dislike that the people of Mecca should say that the Book, which is the Torah and the Gospel, was sent down to two groups before us, namely the Jews and the Christians. ﴿And we were indeed unaware﴾: "in" here is the light (mukhaffafa) form of the heavy (thaqila) one, and the lam is the one that distinguishes it from the negating particle. The original is: "and indeed we were unaware of their study." The purpose of these verses is to establish the proof against them by sending down the Qur'an upon Muhammad, so that they would not say on the Day of Resurrection: "The Torah and the Gospel were sent down to two groups before us, and we were unaware of what is in them." So God cut off their excuse by sending down the Qur'an to them. His saying, ﴿and we were indeed unaware of their study﴾, means: we did not know what they were, because their Book was not in our language. The meaning of ﴿or lest you should say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than them"﴾ explains the first in that its meaning is: lest they say and argue by it. Then He, exalted is He, explained the cutting off of their argument by this, and said: ﴿Now there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾, which is the Qur'an and what the Messenger brought, ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾.

If it is said: the clear proof (bayyina) and guidance (huda) are one thing, so what is the benefit of the repetition?

We say: the Qur'an is a clear proof regarding what is known through revelation (sam'), and it is guidance regarding what is known through revelation and reason ('aql). Since the benefit differs, this conjunction is valid. We have already explained that the meaning of "mercy" is that it is a blessing in religion.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who, then, is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God﴾. The aim is to magnify the disbelief of one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them, that is, prevents others from them, because the first is misguidance, and the second is hindering from the truth and leading astray.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with an evil punishment﴾, and it is like His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of God, We will increase their punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 158:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come, or that some of the signs of your Lord should come? On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or had not earned good through its faith. Say: "Wait, we too are waiting."﴾

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (ya'tiyahum) with the yā' (ya), and likewise in Surat al-Nahl; the rest read (ta'tiyahum) with the tā' (ta).

Know that when He, exalted is He, had made clear that He sent down the Book only to remove excuses and to remove the cause of pretext, and made clear that they will never believe, and described circumstances that necessitate despair of their entering into faith, He said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them﴾. A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Do they await anything but that God should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. The meaning of (yanzurun) is (yantazirun, they await). (Hal) is an interrogative whose meaning is negation. The sense of the verse is: they will not believe in you unless one of these three matters comes to them:

Page 7
namely, the coming of the angels, or the coming of the Lord, or the coming of the overpowering signs from the Lord.

If it is said: does His saying ﴿or that your Lord should come﴾ indicate the permissibility of coming and going upon God?

We say: the answer to this is in several respects:

First: this is a report of their words, and they were disbelievers, and the belief of a disbeliever is not a proof.

Second: this is figurative. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So God came upon their building﴾ [al-Nahl: 26], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who harm God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57].

Third: there exist decisive proofs that coming and going upon God, exalted is He, is impossible, and the closest of them is the saying of the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), may the blessings of God be upon him, in refuting the worshippers of the stars: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾.

If it is said: His saying ﴿or that your Lord should come﴾ cannot be taken to mean the establishing of a sign of His power, because on this reading it would become the very same as His saying ﴿Do they await anything but that they should come to them﴾, so it is necessary to take it to mean the coming of the Lord.

We say: the relied-upon answer is that this is a report of the doctrine of the disbelievers, so it is not a proof. It has also been said: "your Lord comes" means with punishment, or "some of the signs of your Lord come," which means the overpowering miracles.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before﴾. They are agreed that the intended meaning of these signs is the portents of the Hour. From al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "We were discussing the matter of the Hour when the Messenger of God ﷺ looked down upon us and said: 'What are you discussing?' We said: 'We are discussing the Hour.' He said: 'It will not come until you see before it ten signs: the smoke, the beast of the earth, a sinking in the East, a sinking in the West, a sinking in the Arabian Peninsula, the Dajjal, the rising of the sun from its west, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the descent of 'Isa, and a fire that will emerge from Aden.'" His saying ﴿if it had not believed before﴾ is a qualifier of (nafsan, a soul). His saying ﴿or had not earned good through its faith﴾ is a second qualifier, conjoined to the first qualifier. The meaning is: when the portents of the Hour appear, the time of obligation has passed, so faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before that, nor one that did not earn good through its faith before that.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Wait, we too are waiting"﴾, which is a warning and a threat.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 159:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you have no part in them at all. Their affair is only with Allah; then He will inform them of what they used to do.﴾

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (faraqu) with an alif, while the rest read (farraqu). The meaning of the two readings, upon careful examination, is one and the same: for whoever divides his religion, in the sense that he affirms some parts of it and denies others, has in reality separated himself from it. There are several views on the verse:

The first view: the intended meaning is all the religious communities. Ibn Abbas said: he means the polytheists. Some of them worship the angels and claim that they are the daughters of Allah, and some of them worship idols and say: "These are our intercessors with Allah." This is the meaning of ﴿they divided their religion and became sects﴾, that is, factions and parties in misguidance.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: they are the Jews and the Christians, because the Christians split into sects and declared one another to be unbelievers, and likewise the Jews, although they are people of one Book, and the Jews declare the Christians to be unbelievers.

The second view: the intended meaning of the verse is that they took up some parts and abandoned others, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], and He also said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and wish to make distinctions between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"...﴾

The third view: Mujahid said: those who divided their religion from this Ummah are the people of innovations (bida') and doubts (shubuhat). Know that the intended meaning of the verse is to urge that the word of the Muslims be one, that they not split apart in religion, and that they not innovate innovations.

As for His saying, ﴿you have no part in them at all﴾, there are two views:

The first: you are free of them and they are free of you. Its interpretation is: you are far from their sayings and their doctrines, and the punishment that necessarily follows from those falsehoods is confined to them and does not extend beyond them.

The second: you have no part in their fighting at all. Al-Suddi said: they say that he was not commanded to fight them, and when he was commanded to fight them, it was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation). This is far-fetched, because the meaning is that you have no part in fighting them at this time; the coming of a command to fight at another time does not necessitate abrogation.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Their affair is only with Allah﴾, that is, concerning respite and delay, and uprooting and destruction. ﴿Then He will inform them of what they used to do﴾, and the intended meaning is a warning.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 160:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, he will have ten times the like of it; and whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with the like of it, and they will not be wronged.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Some said: The good deed is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and the evil deed is shirk (polytheism). This is far-fetched. Rather, it must be understood in its general sense, either by adhering to the wording or because it is a ruling attached to a suitable description (wasf munasib), which requires that the ruling be causally linked (mu'allal) to that description. Therefore it must be general, because of the generality of the cause ('illah).

The second issue: al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The ha' (taa marbuta) has been omitted from ʿashr (ten), and al-amthal is the plural of mithl, and mithl is masculine; because what is intended is "ten good deeds like it" (ʿashru ḥasanātin amthāluhā). Then the good deeds were omitted and al-amthal, which are its description, were put in their place. The omission of the modified noun is common in speech. This is strengthened by the reading of those who read ʿashrun amthāluhā with raf' (nominative) and tanwin.

The third issue: Our position is that reward is, in reality, a bounty (tafaddul) from Allah, the Exalted, and on this basis there is no difficulty in the verse. As for the Mu'tazilah, they distinguished between reward (thawab) and bounty (tafaddul), saying that reward is a benefit that is deserved, and bounty is a benefit that is not deserved. Then, in deriving their doctrines, they differed. Some of them said: These ten are a bounty, and the reward is other than them; this is the view of al-Jubba'i. He said: Because if the one were a reward and the nine were a bounty, it would follow that the reward is less than the bounty, and that is not permissible. For if it were permissible for the bounty to be equal to the reward in quantity and nobility, nothing of any benefit would remain in obligation (taklif), and it would become futile and ugly. And since this has been shown to be false, we know that the reward must be greater in measure and in magnitude than the bounty.
Others said: It is not far-fetched that one of these nine is a reward, and the remaining nine are a bounty, except that this one would be more abundant, greater, and higher in rank than the remaining nine.

The fourth issue: Some said: The specification of ten is not intended as a limit; rather, it intends multiplication in general, like the saying of one who says: "If you bestow a favour upon me, I will repay you with ten times its like," and in threat one says: "If you speak to me once, I will speak to you ten times," and he does not intend a limit. So too here. The proof that it cannot be taken as a limit is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with the like of it﴾, meaning the recompense equals it and matches it. Abu Dharr narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Exalted, said: The good deed is ten, or I increase it, and the evil deed is one, or I pardon it. So woe to him whose single units overcome his tens." And he (ﷺ) said: "Allah says: When My servant intends a good deed, write it for him as a good deed even if he does not do it; and if he does it, then ten like it. And if he intends an evil deed, do not write it; and if he does it, then one evil deed." His words ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ mean: nothing is diminished from the reward of their obedience, and nothing is added to the punishment of their evil deeds.

There are two questions concerning the verse:

The first question: How does the disbelief of an hour necessitate eternal punishment at the utmost degree of severity?

Its answer: The disbeliever was resolved that, if he lived forever, he would remain upon that belief forever. Since that resolve was perpetual, he is punished with eternal punishment, unlike the sinning Muslim, who has the resolve to abandon that sin; therefore his punishment is cut off.

The second question: Freeing one slave was at one time made a substitute for fasting sixty days, in the expiation of zihar, and at another time was made a substitute for fasting a few days. That indicates that equality is not taken into account.

Its answer: Equality is achieved only through the stipulation and ruling of the Law (shar').

The third question: If someone inflicts two wounds (muwadihatan) on a person's head, two compensations (arsh) become obligatory. If he removes the barrier between them, the obligation becomes the compensation for a single wound. Here the offence has increased while the penalty has decreased, so equality is not taken into account.

Its answer: That is among the acts of worship (ta'abbudat) and stipulations (tahakkumat) of the Law.

The fourth question: In return for the destruction of more than one of each of the limbs, a full diya (blood-money) is obligatory; then if he kills him and destroys all the limbs, only one diya is obligatory. That prevents the saying that equality is observed.

Its answer: That is from the category of the stipulations (tahakkumat) of the Shari'ah. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 161–163:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a right religion, the creed of Abraham, a man of pure faith (hanif), and he was not of the polytheists﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, taught His Messenger the kinds of proofs of tawhid (divine unity), and refuted those who claim partners, rivals and opposites to God, and went to great lengths in establishing the affirmation of tawhid against those who deny qadar (divine decree and predestination), and refuted the people of ignorance (jahiliyyah) in their falsehoods, He commanded him to close the speech with His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord has guided me to a straight path﴾. This indicates that guidance is not attained except through God. The word "dinan" (religion) is in the accusative for two reasons:

The first: it is in apposition (badal) to the place of "sirat" (path); because its meaning is "my Lord has guided me to a straight path," as He said: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ [al-Fath: 2].

The second: that the implied meaning is: "Adhere to a religion." As for His saying "qiyaman" (upright), the author of al-Kashshaf said: "qayyim" is on the pattern fay'il from qama, like sayyid from sada, and it is more emphatic than qa'im (standing). The people of Kufa read "qiyaman" with a kasra on the qaf and a light ya. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning standing (qiyam), like "sighar" and "kibar," "hiwal" and "shiba'," and the interpretation is: a religion possessing uprightness; and describing the religion with this attribute is by way of emphasis.

As for His saying: ﴿the creed of Abraham, a man of pure faith (hanif)﴾: "millata" (creed) is in apposition to His saying "dinan qiyaman," and "hanifan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of Abraham. The meaning is: my Lord has guided me and made me know the creed of Abraham, in the state of it being described as hanifiyyah. Then He said, describing Abraham: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, and the purpose of this is to refute the polytheists.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice (nusuk), my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿He has no partner. And of this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾.

Know that just as He, exalted is He, made known to him the upright religion, He made known to him how to uphold it and perform it. So His saying: ﴿Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds﴾ indicates that he performs it with sincerity (ikhlas), and He emphasized this with His saying: ﴿He has no partner﴾. This indicates that in acts of worship it is not sufficient that they be performed in any manner whatsoever; rather they must be performed with complete sincerity. This is among the strongest proofs that a condition for the validity of prayer is that it be performed joined with sincerity.

As for His saying: ﴿nusuki﴾ (my sacrifice): it was said that the intended meaning of nusk is the sacrificial animal itself; one says: "whoever does such-and-such, upon him is a nusk," i.e., a blood that he sheds; and He combined prayer and slaughter, as in His saying: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾ [al-Kawthar: 2]. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that he said: "nusk" means ingots of silver; every ingot of it is a nasika. It was also said of the one who worships devotedly that he is a nasik, because he has purified his soul from the filth of sins and cleansed it like an ingot freed from impurity. According to this interpretation, nusk is everything by which you draw near to God, exalted is He, though in common usage it is predominantly used for slaughter. As for His saying: ﴿my living and my dying﴾, i.e., my life and my death are for God.

Page 11
Know that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds﴾, thus affirming that all of them belong to God. Living and dying are not "for God" in the sense that they are performed for obedience to God, for that is impossible; rather the meaning of their belonging to God is that they occur by the creation of God, exalted is He. Likewise, the meaning of prayer and nusk being for God is explained as their occurring by the creation of God, and this is among the clearest proofs that the worshipper's acts of obedience are created by God, exalted is He.

Nafi' read "mahyaya" with a sukun on the ya and a fatha on it in "mamati." Sukun on the ya in "mahyaya" is anomalous and not in use, because it joins two sukuns which do not meet in this way in prose or verse. Some said it is a dialect of some of them. The summary of the matter: He, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to declare that his prayer, all his acts of worship, his living and his dying are all occurring by the creation of God, exalted is He, and His measuring, decree and judgment. Then He explicitly stated that there is no partner to Him in creation. The sense is: then he says, "And of this I have been commanded," i.e., with this tawhid I have been commanded.

Then he says: ﴿and I am the first of the Muslims﴾, i.e., those who submit to the decree and predestination of God. It is known that he is not the first of every Muslim, so it must be that the intended meaning is that he was the first of the Muslims of his time.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 6, verse 164:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, when He is the Lord of everything? Every soul earns only against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears another's burden. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.﴾

Know that when the Exalted commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to pure tawhid (the oneness of God), which is that he should say: ﴿Indeed, my prayer and my sacrifice, my living and my dying, are for Allah, Lord of the worlds, who has no partner﴾ up to His words ﴿He has no partner﴾, He commanded him to mention what serves as a proof for the soundness of this tawhid. Its explanation is in two respects.

The first: The categories of polytheists are four. The worshippers of idols associated partners with Allah; the worshippers of the stars associated partners with Allah; those who speak of Yazdan and Ahriman (the two principles of good and evil), and they are the ones concerning whom Allah said: ﴿and they have made the jinn partners with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 100], associated partners with Allah; and those who say that the Messiah is the son of Allah and the angels are His daughters, they too associated partners with Allah. These are the groups of polytheists, and all of them acknowledge that Allah is the Creator of everything. This is because the worshippers of idols acknowledge that Allah, glory be to Him, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and of everything in the world of existing things, and that He is the Creator of the idols and the images entirely.

As for the worshippers of the stars, they acknowledge that Allah is their Creator and Originator. As for those who speak of Yazdan and Ahriman, they too acknowledge that the Satan is originated, and that its Originator is Allah, glory be to Him. As for those who speak of the Messiah and the angels, they acknowledge that Allah is the Creator of everything. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the groups of polytheists unanimously agreed that Allah is the Creator of these partners.

Having known this, Allah, glory be to Him, said to him: O Muhammad: ﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?﴾ Although those who took a lord other than Allah acknowledged that Allah is the Creator of those things, does it enter the intellect to make the one who is lorded over a partner to the Lord, to make the slave a partner to the master, and to make the created a partner to the Creator?

Since the matter is as such, it is established by this proof that taking a lord other than Allah, the Exalted, is a corrupt saying and a false religion.

[Page 12]

The second respect in establishing this statement: the existent is either necessary in itself (wajib li-dhatihi) or possible in itself (mumkin li-dhatihi). It is established that the necessary in itself is one. Thus it is established that whatever is other than Him is possible in itself, and it is established that the possible in itself does not come into existence except by the bringing into existence of the necessary in itself. Since the matter is as such, He, the Exalted, is the Lord of everything.

Once this is established, we say: clear reason testifies that it is not permissible to make the one who is lorded over a partner to the Lord, or to make the created a partner to the Creator. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, when He is the Lord of everything?﴾ Then, when He, the Exalted, clarified this tawhid by this compelling and decisive proof, He clarified that no blame or punishment returns to them from their disbelief and their polytheism. So He said: ﴿Every soul earns only against itself﴾, meaning that the sin of the wrongdoer falls upon him alone and not upon another. ﴿And no bearer of burdens bears another's burden﴾, that is, no sinful soul is seized for the sin of another. Then the Exalted clarified that the return of these polytheists is to a place where there is no judge and no commander except Allah, the Exalted. This is His words: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.﴾

The Almighty says: ﴿It is He who made you successors on the earth and raised some of you above others in rank, that He may test you in what He has given you. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that in His saying ﴿He made you successors on the earth﴾ there are several aspects:

The first: He made them successors on the earth, because Muhammad, upon him be peace and blessings, is the Seal of the Prophets, so his community succeeded all the other nations.

The second: He made them succeed one another.

The third: they are the vicegerents (khulafa') of God on His earth, who possess it and dispose of it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and raised some of you above others in rank﴾, in nobility, intellect, wealth, status, and provision. The manifestation of this disparity is not due to incapacity, ignorance, or miserliness, for He, exalted is He, is high above these attributes. It is rather for the sake of trial (ibtila') and testing (imtihan), and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿that He may test you in what He has given you﴾. We have already mentioned that the true reality of trial and testing is impossible with respect to God, but what is intended is obligation (taklif), which is an act that, if it proceeded from one of us, would resemble trial and testing, so it was named by this name because of this resemblance.

Then this person who is obligated either falls short in what he was charged with, or fulfils it fully. If he is the first, his share is intimidation and warning, which is His saying ﴿indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾. He described the punishment as swift because what is coming is near. If he is the second, namely one who is complete in those acts of obedience, his share is honour and encouragement (targhib), which is His saying ﴿and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning He forgives sins and conceals faults in this world by the veil of His grace, generosity, and mercy, and in the Hereafter by pouring out upon him the various kinds of His blessings.

This discourse has reached, in explaining admonition, warning, encouragement, and intimidation, a point beyond which nothing more can be added. This is the end of the discussion on the tafsir of Surat al-An'am, and praise belongs to God, the King, the All-Knowing.
